en: The *Tripurārahasya*,
*Jñānakhaṇḍa*,
accompanied by the commentary *Tātparyadīpikā* composed by Śrīnivāsabhaṭṭa.
Oṃ, salutations to her whose form is the bliss of the ultimate cause, who consists of supreme consciousness,
and who shines as the mirror for the variegated painting of the universe.
Victorious is this supreme and glorious Tripurā, the witness of all,
who, in the form of the Guru, delivers her devotees from the cycle of worldly existence.
Having bowed to the god Vighneśvara, this *Tātparyadīpikā* [Commentary on the Essential Meaning] of the *Jñānakhaṇḍa* within the secret cycle of Tripurā is now being composed.
Having boarded the boat of the Guru’s speech, I desire to cross the great ocean of the section on knowledge, through the company of the venerable Goddess who acts as my navigator.
In this world, indeed, the venerable Hāritāyana, desiring to lift up those people submerged in the mire of suffering,
has composed the *Tripurārahasya*, the supreme among histories, in verse form. And therein, the primary subject intended is precisely the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Regarding consciousness: having first composed the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa— which is the primary cause for devotion that accomplishes that [consciousness]—

I shall now, without obstacle, complete the Jñānakhaṇḍa which I intend to undertake for the sake of those seekers who possess the requisite qualification through hearing the Māhātmya and other means, so that they may realize the reality of their own Self.

To bring the work to completion, the author composes at the outset a benediction consisting of a salutation to the deity who is one's own Self—the subject matter of the treatise—in order to perpetuate the tradition: "Oṃ namaḥ. That bliss which is of the nature of the Cause—that is, the bliss of Brahman as the cause of all, since there is no distinction—is her very form. Such is she.

That supreme, undivided consciousness is identical with that [reality] and has that as its sole form. Thus, the world itself—this wondrous painting—is her form, serving as the locus for reflections like those in a mirror.
She who shines forth in such a manner, indicated by the syllable *Oṃ*, manifests specifically both in particular forms and in a universal form.

It shines forth. Homage to it! The meaning of the entire scripture is encapsulated in this verse: the undivided reality of consciousness (*cittattva*) is the object of knowledge according to the scriptures; that very same reality, consisting of bliss, is the cause of the universe. It is not [the cause] through *prakṛti* or other such principles, as if the world were a reflection in a mirror; rather, the variegated manifestation of the universe occurs within that very [consciousness]. Herein—

The three sections (the three sections consisting of Māhātmya, Jñāna, and Caryā) are encapsulated by Śiva, Śakti, and the Praṇava, beginning with "Oṃ Namaḥ" and concluding with "Hrīṃ Tripurāyai. Its essential meaning is this: the entire universe is of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
This treatise is for the purpose of awakening [the student] to the fact that there is only the reality of one's own mind. || 1 ||
O Nārada, have you heard with an attentive mind this majesty of the one called Tripura, which is the means for attaining the Supreme? (2)
In the first chapter, by means of measured verses [composed of] the consonants *ka* through *ṭa*,
*pa*, and the *ya*-group, the numbers are indicated by the letters at the end of the *piṇḍas*; two eyes (*2*) should be understood as zero (*0*), and likewise when a vowel alone is mentioned—
thus it is stated in the verse cited by Bhāskararāya in his own *Nāthanavaratnamālāmañjūṣā*.

By the two syllables *sa ta* according to their numerical value (*prāmāṇyena*), the numbers 6 and 7 are grasped, following the principle that "the movement of digits is from right to left" (*aṅkānāṃ vāmato gatiḥ*).
Thus, it is indicated that the first chapter consists of 67 verses by means of these two conventional letters (*saṃketākṣara*).
This same method should be understood for the opening verses of the commentaries on other chapters as well. [This is achieved] through worship and other forms of devotional practice.
The arising of reflection in Rāma, whose mind was pure, is now described.
In order to engage the listener, [the author says] "that which has been heard," and so forth. 2.
Now, today I shall relate to you the most wonderful section on knowledge,
hearing which a person never again encounters sorrow anywhere.
He states the very nature of its great wonderfulness with the words: "Having heard which... (verse 3).
Having thoroughly examined the Vedic, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, and likewise the Pāśupata systems of knowledge, this which has been definitively determined [is as follows].

In order to state that the knowledge under discussion is the most excellent of all, he says: "Vedic," etc. "Vedic" means pertaining to the Upaniṣads. "Vaiṣṇava" refers to that taught in the *Pāñcarātra*. "Śaiva" refers to that contained in the *Ṣaḍardha-śāstra*.
"Śākta" refers to that taught in the *Mahocchuṣma* and other [texts]. "Pāśupata" refers to that taught in the *Kāma-śāstra*. [And] "vijñāna" (higher knowledge).
The web of logical arguments that determine the reality of the self. (k: determining the reality) || 4 ||
Nothing else resembling this knowledge should ascend to the mind;
it has been set forth by me, the teacher Śrīdatta, for Bhārgava.

Precisely because it is the most excellent of all, he says: "This is not [like that]. The meaning is that no other [method] ascends to the mental plane in the manner prescribed by the bestowed Guru. || 5 ||

Though it is endowed with both logical proof and empirical perception and is manifoldly illustrated, if anyone of deluded intellect does not understand even what has been stated here, [then what can be done]? (6)
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of logical proof" (*upapatti*). Logical proof (*upapatti*) means reasoning (*yukti*); it is the experience of the perceiver.

It is variegated by many discourses. Here, the statement that "knowledge must indeed ascend to the mind" is confirmed by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), as expressed in the word "here" (*atra*) in verse 6.
Struck down solely by fate, he is indeed like a lifeless pillar; there is no doubt that even the knowledge directly imparted by Śiva would not enter him.
Listen to that which I shall relate to you, existing as the essence of the Jñānakhaṇḍa;
oh, how wonderful is the conduct of the virtuous, surpassing all qualities!

That scripture, existing in the form of the section on knowledge (*jñānakhaṇḍa*), praises Nārada—who is almost omniscient and who desires to hear the narrative from him—saying: "Aho! [He is] superior and most excellent in all qualities. (8)
Since even this divine sage listens to something from me,
it is characteristic of the virtuous that they possess an innate disposition toward showing favor.
This is service. 9.
Just as the power of intoxication is inherent in musk by its very nature,
so too [is this power] in me, having heard from the mouth of Dattātreya the majesty and glory of his greatness.
Thus, as stated in the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa [of the Tripurārahasya]— which was printed in the year 1932 by the Kāśī Saṃskṛta Granthamālā in Vārāṇasī and may be seen here— [verse 10].
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who delights all people and possesses auspicious intentions, had his virtuous heart captivated by devotion; he became silent for a moment.
He whose mind is pure, having been captivated by devotion and has become absorbed [in the Divine]. || 11 ||
Then, having attained an outward state of being, his eyes filled with the bliss of fullness, his body thick with horripilation, and his inner self overflowing with joy; || 12 ||
Ānanda means one whose tears are of joy. He is filled—that is, complete—with that bliss born of devotion which is his own and internal. || 12 ||
Joy, as if unable to contain itself, seemed to issue forth through the pores of his skin;
he prostrated himself like a staff at the feet of the Guru who had bestowed [the teaching] upon him. (13)
The connection is as follows: the joy arising within his own heart, as if emerging through the bursting open of the pores of his skin, took on a form thick with horripilation. || 13 ||
Rising up, filled with joy, he spoke with a voice faltering from emotion: "O Śrī Guru, by your grace, I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose. (14)
What he said is precisely what he expresses here with the words "blessed" (dhanya). || 14 ||
For me, Śiva himself—the ocean of compassion—is my manifest Guru;
when he is pleased, even the state of Brahmā is regarded as equal to a blade of grass. || 15 ||
Since even death attains the nature of the self through a satisfied Guru, that Guru Maheśvara has today become pleased with me all of a sudden. (16)
Death caused by pleasing the guru becomes one's own self; [this occurs] unexpectedly and without apparent cause. He is to be propitiated with great effort. || 16 ||
"O Guru, it was through your compassion that I thought, 'I have attained everything';
now, O Lord, the entirety of your majesty has been heard by me through your grace. (17)
He spoke to the Guru, beginning with "O Lord," and so forth. || 17 ||
I desire to worship that supreme goddess Tripurā;
O Guru, please tell me the method for her worship out of your great compassion. (18)
Thus entreated, Dattaguru, perceiving in the descendant of Bhṛgu a fitness for the worship of Tripura, augmented by pure faith and devotion, [consented].
He initiated him in due order for the purpose of worshipping Tripura;
and Jāmadagnya, having received the auspicious initiation into the Traipura [tradition],...
This entire sequence is superior to all initiations, brings about the awakening to the reality of the Fullness (pūrṇatattva),
and is endowed with the latent impressions of mantras and yantras.
The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of mantra and yantra are the various types of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); the sequence (*krama*) is the manual (*paddhati*). || 21 ||
Then Bhārgava, having obtained the nectar from the lotus-face of his illustrious guru like a bee, was inwardly satisfied and filled with joy from the very beginning.
Satisfaction is the cessation of the desire to know the sequence of worship; from me, who am intoxicated by being filled with the bliss produced thereby, [I am] the supremely intoxicated. || 22 ||
Permitted by Śrīnātha and intent upon the accomplishment of Tripurā,
he circumambulated his guru, bowed to him, and departed for Mount Mahendra.
There, having constructed an auspicious dwelling that brought great happiness,
he then remained devoted to worship for twelve years.
Devoted to the regular and occasional rites, intent upon worship and japa, he was always single-mindedly focused on the meditation on the form of the venerable Tripureśānī. || 25 ||
Thus, because he did not abandon her, twelve years passed for him like a single moment.
Then, on one occasion, while sitting comfortably, the son of Narmadā reflected: || 26 ||
Indeed, that which Saṃvarta spoke to me in the past when he was earnestly entreated by me on the road— I did not understand even a fraction of it at that time.
This occurred prior to the defeat by Rāma; this should be understood from the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa. That is the knowledge spoken by Saṃvarta. || 27 ||
And because I forgot it, I did not previously ask my guru about the majesty of the power of Tripurā, though it had been heard from the mouth of my venerable teacher. || 28 ||
I forgot to ask. || 28 ||
However, it was known there that Saṃvarta had previously spoken thus:
"In the course of discussing creation, I asked my teacher about a certain matter. (29)
The passage beginning with "mayā sṛṣṭiḥ" and so forth should also be understood from the first section (the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa), specifically from verses 49 to 62 of the tenth chapter. || 29 ||
At that time, after my teacher had related the story of the mat-maker, he did not speak of anything irrelevant; thus, that matter remained for me exactly as it was.
Why did he not say that? He replied: "Because it was irrelevant" (*aprakṛtatvāt*). Such [a thing] is unknown. || 30 ||
I do not know even in the slightest degree this destiny of the world; why has this great, tumultuous display of the universe arisen? (31)
Where does it go again, and where does it find its abode?
I perceive everything to be unstable; there is nothing whatsoever anywhere that is firm.
It is unstable, undergoing transformation at every moment. || 32 ||
Why is worldly transaction generally stable, and why is this [universe] also like this?
I behold the wondrous activity of the world as something devoid of reflection.

Wondering how this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) regarding an object that is inherently unstable—such as "this village has been acquired for the sake of my son"—can appear to be stable, he says: "The transaction...
[referring to the verse]. [She is] "unreflective," meaning devoid of inquiry. || 33 ||
"Oh, how the worldly conduct of everyone is observed to be exactly like that of a blind man following another blind man as he moves about! (34)
He says that the conventional usage proceeds solely through a succession of the blind: "Alas! (verse 34).
For in this matter, my own conduct must serve as the illustration for me in every respect;
surely, what occurred during my childhood has not been clearly reflected upon by me. (35)

Regarding this, he states that the illustration is his own conduct itself, saying "the example" (*nidarśanam*). Conduct (*kṛti*) is one's own behavior. He expresses that very point with the word "surely" (*nūnam*); "by me" (*me*) means by myself. || 35 ||
In childhood my conduct was one way, and in youth it was quite another; now my activities are entirely different in every respect. (36)
I do not know in any way what the fruit of these has been—whatever was done, at whatever time, in whatever manner, and by whomsoever. (37)
Having understood that to be exactly so, yet preceded by a reliance on the fruit, [he asks:
"What fruit has been attained there, or by whom has the happiness of the self been achieved? (38)
Reliance on the fruit is the certainty of attaining the fruit. || 38 ||
Moreover, whatever in the world appears fruitful when not investigated is indeed not fruit at all;
for I consider that not to be true fruit, since one must act toward it again. (39)
And regarding the result, such as wealth and so forth, he says "yacceti" (line 39), meaning that its status as a result exists precisely through non-investigation.
Tell me, how could one who desires fruit ever obtain it again once the fruit has been attained, since every person always acts solely out of a longing for fruit? (40)
He explains how it is that immediately after the attainment of what is considered the fruit, there arises precisely the desire which is the cause of engagement:
"That very thing is declared to be the fruit—either the cessation of suffering or happiness.
As long as there remains something yet to be done, there is neither the destruction of suffering nor happiness. (41)
One might object: "Even when some fruit has been attained, it is indeed reasonable to perform further practice for the sake of attaining another fruit.
Anticipating this doubt, he states "the fruit" (*phalam*) in order to say that this is not so, and thereby defines the nature of the fruit.
He says "and happiness" (*sukhaṃ ca vā*) because it is not logical for non-existence (*abhāva*), which is unreal, to possess the status of a fruit. || 41 ||
The very sense of "having to act" is said to be the supreme suffering among all sufferings;
if that exists, how can there be for you the absence of suffering or happiness? (42)
Among all forms of suffering, the sense of "having to do" (kartavyatā) is the greatest; these two—namely, the absence of suffering and happiness—are [the primary concerns]. 42.

Just as applying sandalwood paste to the foot of one whose entire body has been burnt, so too is the attainment of pleasure for one who still has duties remaining said to be [merely] a minor benefit in this world. (43)
He establishes this very point through examples, beginning with "Just as" (yathā), etc. (43).
Just as one whose heart is pierced by an arrow finds relief in the embrace of the throngs of apsarases,
so too is the attainment of happiness in this world said to belong to one who has remaining duties to perform.
Just as a man afflicted by a wasting disease hears the sound of singing,
so too is the attainment of pleasure described here for one who still has duties remaining to be performed.
For those great-souled ones who abide in the world as having nothing further to do, their intentions are fulfilled and they are perfectly cool throughout all their bodies. (46)

Then, in response to the inquiry "Who is happy?", he says: "of those who are happy" (*sukhinām*). "That which is not to be done"—the state of being such is "non-action" (*akartavyatā*). This alone is the characteristic of the happy ones; such is the sense. To distinguish the happy one from others, he says: "complete," and so forth.

The intention—the mind—of others is incomplete because there remains something yet to be attained, and it is empty because their desires have not been fulfilled. Likewise, other great souls consider themselves deficient; and this is evident, for even a universal monarch considers himself inferior to Indra, despite the presence of a crown upon his head.
Because of the absence of a necklace upon your neck, suffering persists; thus, you are not cool in all your limbs. || 46 ||
If happiness could exist for anyone anywhere even while there is still work remaining to be done, then a man impaled on a stake would experience the pleasure born of perfumes and garlands. (47)
With something such as a garment, a garland, or the like. || 47 ||
Oh, how great and wonderful this is! Amidst the turmoil of hundreds of duties, there is happiness here for the sake of which people always act.
Oh, how great is the majesty of reflection! What can I say of men? Even those overwhelmed by the mountain of endless duties attain supreme bliss. (49)
Just as a universal monarch always strives for happiness, even so does one who delights in wandering for alms strive constantly. (50)
Individually, they both attain happiness and consider their task accomplished;
therefore, I shall follow them one by one, wherever they go.
I follow after them along that path which they traverse in succession, without deliberation. || 51 ||
Without even considering the consequences, he is like a blind man following another blind man;
therefore, enough with this intellect of yours—go once more to the Ocean of Compassion.

The reason for this is stated as "without considering the result. By "medhayā" is meant a certainty produced without inquiry. The meaning is: having proceeded with this inquiry, [one should act] so long as the inquiry has not ceased. || 52 ||
Having desired to know that which is to be known, I shall reach the most auspicious further shore beyond the ocean of doubt, by relying on the raft of the Guru’s words. (53)
Vicikitsā is doubt; one who has taken refuge in that very boat, which is the word of the Guru.
Having thus resolved, the son of Jamadagni, whose intention was auspicious,
set out suddenly from that great mountain, longing for a vision of his guru.
Having quickly reached Gandhamādana, the king of mountains, he beheld his preceptor seated in the lotus posture, appearing like the sun stationed upon the earth. || 55 ||
He prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before the footstool,
and with his head he pressed against the lotus-foot resting upon his own hand.
Then, with a gracious mind, Dattātreya joined Rāma— who was thus prostrate—
with blessings and raised him up with affection.
"My child, arise! After a long time, I see you returned today.
Tell me of the events concerning your own self, as it has remained free from affliction. (Or: "Tell me of the events concerning your own self, as it has remained in a state of health.")
Self-existence (ātmabhava) refers to that which has arisen, produced within the body and so forth. || 58 ||
Then, rising at the command of his guru and seated upon the sacrificial fire-grass as directed by his guru, he, with a serene soul and palms joined in reverence, spoke: (59)
O Śrī Guru, ocean of compassion, how could one who is bathed in the nectar of your grace be overcome by the diseases created by fate? (60)
The word "atha" (now/then) has the sense of "even" (api). Its meaning is: "even by those created by the Creator. || 60 ||
But how could a most terrifying disease, like a fierce-rayed sun, cause me distress when I am situated within the orb of the nectar-rayed moon that is your compassionate self? (61)
Both my inner and outer self have been gladdened by your compassion; yet it remains forever devoid of joy without the separation from the lotus-feet of your honor. 62.
The internal is the mind; the external is the body. Separation from the lotus feet of Your Honor is disjunction. || 62 ||
Previously, there was not even a slight trace of anything else that brought me pain anywhere;
yet today, by the sight of the lotus feet of Your Honor, that has indeed returned.
O Śrī Guru, indeed, the state of perfection and absorption has been attained by you in every respect;
yet something that occurred some time ago still revolves within my heart. (64)
The fullness of bliss; that which had long been present in the heart has now arisen as something to be asked about.
With my inner mind long filled with doubt, I desire to ask you about that;
having been commanded by you today, I shall inquire into what I am uncertain of. (65)
One whose inner mind has long harbored doubt regarding the matter to be inquired about.
Having heard these words of Bhārgava, Dattātreya, the ocean of compassion,
with a heart full of joy, then spoke affectionately to Rāma Bhārgava.
Ask, O Bhārgava, whatever you have long desired to ask today; I am pleased by your devotion and shall speak that which you wish to know.
[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Inquiry of Bhārgava," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Tripurārahasya, the most excellent of glorious histories.]
[Thus ends the first chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrītripurārahasya (in the *gh* manuscript: of the Śrītripurārahasya).]
[Then the second chapter:
Thus commanded, the son of Jamadagni, having bowed to the sage, the son of Atri— (Note: In some manuscripts, the order of the first and second halves of this verse is reversed.)
Bowing down with humility, he began to inquire.
In this chapter, the refutation of what ought to be done is carried out through verses measured by the Vedas;
furthermore, the praise of thorough reflection is also proclaimed.
"Ask," he was thus commanded. *Praśraya* means humility or modesty. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, O venerable Guru, O Noble One, Omniscient One, Treasure of Compassion!
Formerly, I indeed harbored anger toward the royal lineages for a specific reason. (2)
He describes the manner in which he himself attained world-weariness with the verse beginning "In the city... (verse 2).
I have indeed thrice seven times cast that entire Kṣatriya race— along with the embryos in the womb and the infants at the breast— into a lake filled with the blood of the Kṣatriyas.
That is because of anger. || 3 ||
The hosts of ancestors, being fully gratified and satisfied by the weight of my devotion, quelled my anger; and by the command of my father, I too became pacified.
I, blinded by anger and arrogant in my strength, have once again encountered that very Śrī Rāma, who is Hari himself, now dwelling in Ayodhyā.
Because of his arrogance, he was cast down and defeated by the Blessed One;
yet, somehow, he escaped alive through the compassion of that one who honors the Brahmins.
Then, having become thoroughly disillusioned with that which is cultivated [by worldly existence], I arrived before me;
thereafter, I lamented in many ways along the path.
Lamentation is mere prattle. || 7 ||
I unexpectedly encountered Saṃvarta, the lord of the Avadhūtas, on the road;
hidden like a fire covered by ashes, I recognized him only with great difficulty.
He approached and reached [it]. || 8 ||
Like one scorched by heat [seeking] the frost, having approached him who was cool to all my limbs,
I then attained an extreme state of coldness.
"What kind of dissolution did Rāma encounter, and of what nature was it? To this he says: "Scorched," etc. He states the fruit of that union: "Having united," etc. (9).
When I asked him about his own well-being, he spoke words as sweet as nectar; having extracted the very essence from everything like a solid core, he imparted it to me.
"Peśalam" means beautiful. All [this] is for the purpose of the question. || 10 ||
Just as a pauper cannot touch a queen, so was I unable to touch her then;
yet, being entreated by me once more, he then pointed you out to me.
That was stated by Saṃvarta. "Raṅka" means a poor person. || 11 ||

Then I obtained that pair of feet, which was like a blind man finding a gathering of people—bringing him extreme happiness. (Note: In manuscript *gh*, the sequence of the line is "tanme andho tadbhava"). 12.
I do not know anything at all that the sage Saṃvarta has spoken;
I have heard the entire majesty [of this] which brings about devotion to Tripura. (13)
He states within himself that section concerning hearing which was spoken by Saṃvarta: "It has been heard," [verse 13].
That goddess, who possesses your form, is eternally established within my heart;
for me, abiding in this manner, what fruit is attained? (14)

She is in the form of the Bhava [Śiva] and in the form of the Guru. Since the result—namely, the mental state in the form of the deity—has already been attained, further worship would be like grinding what has already been ground; thus he says "in this way" (evam). || 14 ||
O Blessed One, please tell out of compassion that which Saṃvarta spoke in the past:
for without knowing it, there is nowhere any fulfillment of one's purpose.
If it is argued, "What is the use of what was said regarding cosmic dissolution? One should simply perform worship," he says: "Without having known... (verse 15).
Thus it has been said: "Whatever is done by me without knowing [the truth], that appears on all sides like the play of a child. (16)
He says that without knowing that [Brahman], all other worship or ritual action is in vain, as it has been stated: "That has been said. (16)
Indeed, in the past, I have repeatedly worshipped the gods, headed by Śakra, with sacrifices featuring abundant offerings and high priestly fees, as well as vast quantities of food. (17)
If it is argued that ritual action and the like are not useless because their fruits exist, [the author] says "no," beginning with the word "purā" (in the past):
[those sacrifices] in which there was an *ucchraya*, meaning an abundance or excellence, of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). || 17 ||
"I have heard from the mouth of Saṃvarta that it yields but little fruit;
I consider that [fruit] to be truly insignificant, for it is in every respect nothing but suffering. (18)
Regarding the phrase "that [is] small": the sense is that if such supreme deeds as these result in only a small fruit, what need is there to mention others?
Anticipating the objection that even if the fruit is small, it is not non-existent, he says "I consider" (manye), meaning that even a small fruit is essentially of the nature of suffering. || 18 ||
That which is not pleasant cannot be suffering; rather, suffering is considered to be slight pleasure, since it is said that when pleasure ceases, suffering becomes even more intense. (19)
He explains this very point: "It is not happiness. The reason for that is: "Because... (verse 19).
Not only this much, but there is even greater majesty than this:
that death would never again have any application there.

If it is objected, "Since a stream of minor happiness has already been obtained through the performance of ritual acts (*karmadhāraya*), what is the use of knowledge?", he says: "It is not merely this much. He states that very fear: "By death," etc.
The sense is that the devouring by death is difficult to ward off by means of ritual acts. || 20 ||
In this very way, whatever is performed by me in the ritual of Tripurā appears to me like the play of a child, because all of that is merely my own mental construction.

Now, one might object: "Action (karma) is indeed of such a nature, but worship (upāsana), because of its connection with the Supreme Deity, is not so. Anticipating this doubt, he states that even worship is equal to dry ritual action in terms of its result, saying: "Thus" (evam). That which is being performed by me (me) in the procedure for the worship of Tripura—
The meaning is: "just like karma. For this very reason, it is said to be "like a child's play. The reason for this is: "because it is mental" (verse 21).
Regarding what was stated by you: "To do that [which you propose] would be otherwise than this;
and it would certainly be otherwise because of its reliance on a different mode of expression" (verse 22).

He states the similarity of meditation (*upāsana*) to ritual action (*karman*) with the words "this" (*etad*). That which is meditation—there is a diversity of expressions, meaning a diversity of scriptures. The meaning is that, due to the variety of scriptures, it can be performed according to the manner you have described, or otherwise, either regularly or irregularly. || 22 ||
Moreover, it is understood to be diverse according to the difference in its objects;
how can this be equal to a sacrifice, when it is commensurate with an unreal fruit? (23)

Furthermore, it can be made otherwise by means of different objects of focus, such as the *śāligrāma* stone or the *Narmadā* river. Since it is practiced in these various ways, this form of meditation is determined to be equal to ritual acts such as sacrifices (*kratu*) in that its fruit is unreal. The implication is: "How could it not be equal to a sacrifice? || 23 ||
Since it is essentially unreal, how could it be equal to the real?
Moreover, this must be performed eternally; there is no end to it anywhere.
Since it is mental in nature, it is unreal even in its own form; therefore, how could it produce a real result?
The underlying sense is that this follows from the scriptural statement: "There is nothing uncreated by what is created" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
If it is argued that it is not proper to speak thus because the scripture, being of the nature of the Lord’s volition, is inconceivable, [the author] says:
I have perceived that Blessed One, Saṃvarta, who is entirely cooling, having emerged from the flames of the poison of the slightest trace of what must be done. || 25 ||

If it is argued that the attainment of supreme bliss occurs only for one who practices throughout their entire life, he says: "He was characterized [by me]. If it is argued that supreme bliss was not attained by him, he says: "He is entirely cool. The intention is that there can be no contradiction regarding what is directly perceived. If it is asked, "How did you know that he was entirely cool? he says: [The verse continues: "By whom was he seen? By whom was he heard? By whom was he touched? By whom was he smelled? By whom was his taste known? By whom was he conceived? By whom was he born? By whom was he grown? By whom was he seen as old? By whom was he seen as dead? By whom was he cremated? By whom was he buried? By whom was he scattered? By whom was he devoured? By whom was he reduced to dust? By whom was he carried away? By whom was he consumed? By whom was he remembered? By whom was he forgotten? By whom was he praised? By whom was he reviled? By whom was he honored? By whom was he despised? By whom was he loved? By whom was he hated? By whom was he abandoned? By whom was he embraced? By whom was he seen as beautiful? By whom was he seen as ugly? By whom was he seen as dear? By whom was he seen as hateful? By whom was he seen as beneficial? By whom was he seen as harmful? By whom was he seen as pure? By whom was he seen as impure? By whom was he seen as virtuous? By whom was he seen as wicked? By whom was he seen as wise? By whom was he seen as foolish? By whom was he seen as learned? By whom was he seen as ignorant? By whom was he seen as noble? By whom was he seen as base? By whom was he seen as high-born? By whom was he seen as low-born? By whom was he seen as wealthy? By whom was he seen as poor? By whom was he seen as powerful? By whom was he seen as weak? By whom was he seen as healthy? By whom was he seen as sick? By whom was he seen as happy? By whom was he seen as miserable? By whom was he seen as liberated? By whom was he seen as bound? By whom was he seen as free? By whom was he seen as enslaved? By whom was he seen as a master? By whom was he seen as a friend? By whom was he seen as an enemy? By whom was he seen as neutral? By whom was he seen as a relative? By whom was he seen as a stranger? By whom was he seen as a teacher? By whom was he seen as a disciple? By whom was he seen as a father? By whom was he seen as a mother? By whom was he seen as a son? By whom was he seen as a daughter? By whom was he seen as a brother? By whom was he seen as a sister? By whom was he seen as a husband? By whom was he seen as a wife? By whom was he seen as a lover? By whom was he seen as a beloved? By whom was he seen as a kinsman? By whom was he seen as a non-kinsman? By whom was he seen as a benefactor? By whom was he seen as a malefactor? By whom was he seen as a protector? By whom was he seen as a destroyer? By whom was he seen as a savior? By whom was he seen as a betrayer? By whom was he seen as a refuge? By whom was he seen as a source of fear? By whom was he seen as a source of security? By whom was he seen as a cause of joy? By whom was he seen as a cause of sorrow? By whom was he seen as a cause of peace? By whom was he seen as a cause of turmoil? By whom was he seen as a cause of life? By whom was he seen as a cause of death? By whom was he seen as a cause of birth? By whom was he seen as a cause of cessation? By whom was he seen as a cause of existence? By whom was he seen as a cause of nirvana? By whom was he seen as a cause of bondage? By whom was he seen as a cause of liberation?"
"It must be done. Because it has emerged from that [source], it is cool. || 25 ||
As if smiling, he took recourse to the path of fearlessness for the governance of the world, like an elephant covered in cool water in a forest engulfed by a forest fire. || 26 ||

And he is not merely a fool who partakes in the fruit of evil, because he has taken recourse to the path of fearlessness and remains as if laughing at worldly conventions. There is an illustration for his total coolness: "in the forest" (vana). || 26 ||
Delighted by the savoring of the nectar of being freed from all duties, how has he reached this state, and what was it that he said to me previously? (27)
How can he be one of great bliss merely by the absence of duty? To this he says: "All," etc.

The very state of having duties is the cause of great suffering; for we observe exhaustion in worldly activity, and it is precisely from the absence of that [activity] that there is happiness, as happiness is observed in deep sleep—this is the intended meaning. This state...
Through the renunciation of karma, Saṃvarta attained the state of fearlessness. || 27 ||
O Guru, you ought to tell all of this to me out of your great compassion;
deliver me, who am swallowed by the serpent of the time for action.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of this for you?", he says: "It is to be performed. (28)
Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself like a staff, grasping the feet with his head;
then [the Lord] beheld Bhārgava, who was thus situated as a vessel for liberation (or devotion).
One who is thus afflicted and desirous of liberation. || 29 ||
Then Datta, whose very nature was compassion, began to speak:
"O child Bhārgava, you are blessed, for such is your intellect. (30)
The cognition that what ought to be done is a cause of suffering. || 30 ||
Like the attainment of a boat for one sinking in the ocean, such is the meeting of a virtuous person with ritual actions. (31)

He praises *buddhi* (intellect) [with the verse beginning] "In the ocean... The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Those two have met. To the objection raised by Rāma that meditation is as futile as a child's play, he replies by demonstrating the fruit [of such practice]: "To this extent... This means the attainment of *buddhi*. || 31 ||
She causes her own self to ascend to the supremely purifying state;
she is the Goddess Tripurā, whose form is the space within the hearts of all. 32.
The connection is that she, having approached, causes [the disciple] to ascend. Into what? Into the supremely purifying, faultless state called liberation (mokṣa).

How does the ascent to that state occur through ritual actions by means of the attainment of the intellect? To this he says: "She" (sā)—[she who], by being manifested in the space of the heart, takes on that very form. || 32 ||
For a devotee who has no other refuge, such a form quickly manifests within the heart and shall liberate him from the snare of death.

The meaning is as follows: she who is of such a form—that is, whose nature is the aforementioned intellect—and who has transformed herself into the form of that aforementioned intellect and so forth, she alone shall grant liberation. || 33 ||
As long as a man does not remain firm and fearless toward the Vetālas that must be dealt with, he never attains happiness, being like one possessed by a Vetāla. (34)
He states that this cognition establishes the status of the word by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*) with the words "as long as" (verse 34).
How can there be any auspiciousness for men who have been bitten by the snake of the time for performing their duties, as if their limbs were overwhelmed by the flames of a terrifying venom? (35)
He says that for those burdened with duties, there is no happiness, just as for those bitten by a snake: "Of men," and so forth. (35)
Behold indeed this world, swooned by its contact with the poison of duty;
blinded, it does not recognize the action that is for its own welfare.
He does not know; behold the world as being of such a nature. 36.
Otherwise, he acts again and again falls into delusion;
for such is this world, swooning from the poison of its duties. (37)
"Otherwise" means that, instead of acting for the sake of achieving what is beneficial, one acts otherwise by abandoning that very means; the reason for this is "being stupefied by poison. || 37 ||
Since beginningless time, he has been cooked in a terrifying ocean of poison;
for it is just as when certain travelers reached the great mountain Vindhya. (38)

If it is asked from what time this delusion has been present in the living being (*jīva*), he says: "beginningless" (*anādi*). Here, he introduces a narrative as an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*):
"Overcome by the weight of hunger, they saw fruits in the forest. (38)
Desiring the fruits of the *tinduka* tree, they quickly ate handfuls of its poisonous fruit. (39)
Driven by extreme hunger, their senses and sense-objects were destroyed as they devoured it;
then, their limbs blazed with the flames of that poison, they were deeply tormented.
Now, one might object that although the poison-clump (*viṣamuṣṭi*) and the *tinduka* fruit are similar in shape, they are not similar in taste; therefore, he says:
"Those whose sense of taste is destroyed" (verse 40).
Blinded and searching for a means to pacify the heat of that poison, they failed to recognize the fruit in their grasp because of their attachment to the *tinduka* fruit. (41)
Not knowing that the fruit had been eaten by the fist.
Thinking the flame to be in his own body, he ate the fruit of the *dhattūra* plant; through delusion, perceiving it as a *jambīra* fruit, he consumed it with ghee, thinking it well-eaten. (42)
Thinking that the flame produced from the *tindū* fruit was [something else], they approached it and were consumed; that was the *dhattūra* fruit. 42.
Then they became insane and lost their way;
blinded, they fell into deep ravines and low-lying ground. (43)
With all their limbs mangled by thorns, their arms, thighs, and feet broken,
they reviled one another and raised a great clamor in their quarrel.
They struck one another with fists, stones, and wooden clubs;
then, with all their limbs shattered, they reached a certain city.
At midnight, by the power of destiny, they arrived at the city gate;
they were stopped by the gatekeepers from entering.
Because they were unaware of the place and the time, they raised a great clamor;
then, when they were struck excessively by the gatekeepers, (47)
They engaged in a quarrel with the guardians of the gates. || 47 ||
Then they all became intent on flight;
some fell into the moat and were devoured by crocodiles and other creatures. || 48 ||
By the makaras and other creatures dwelling in the water of the moat. || 48 ||
Some who fell into the pits and wells gave up their lives;
others were struck down by them, while some were captured alive. || 49 ||
Thus, people who desire their own welfare, yet are stupefied by the objects of action, truly go to utter destruction, blinded indeed by delusion. (50)
He applies this to the case under discussion with the words "in the same way" (evam). || 50 ||
"You are indeed fortunate, O Bhārgava, since you have attained such exaltation;
for reflection is the root of everything and should be the first step. (51)
Because you have crossed over the ocean of delusion, you are fortunate. What is that prosperity? He says: "Investigation" would be the root. || 51 ||
Know this for certain: in attaining the great palace of supreme bliss, for whom and how could the attainment of security ever occur without thorough investigation? (52)
Since this is so, therefore know that the first step is the attainment of the palace. For this very reason it is said: "Thorough deliberation is supreme;
lack of deliberation is death. People who are struck down by a lack of deliberation perish, while one who acts with reflection triumphs everywhere through the attainment of their desired goals. (53)
The Daityas and Yātudhānas are entirely devoid of discernment;
the gods, who are supreme in discernment, partake of happiness in every respect. (54)
Who are killed by non-investigation, or who are made happy by investigation? To this he says: "By non-investigation," etc. (54).
By relying on Viṣṇu through discernment, they always conquer their adversaries;
discernment is the seed of the tree of happiness, possessing the power of sprouting. 55.
The gods conquer their adversaries, such as the Daityas and others. "Possessing the power of a sprout" means that the seed is not fruitless; this is the intended sense. || 55 ||
Through discernment, a person shines forth as superior to all;
through discernment, the sacred law (vidhi) is exalted, and through discernment, Hari is worshipped. (56)
Through inquiry, the omniscient Maheśvara became Śiva;
through lack of inquiry, Rāma, the best among the wise, became attached to the deer. (57)
Having reached the highest state of distress, he then crossed the ocean by means of his deliberation and,
having bound the city of Laṅkā, which was crowded with hosts of Rākṣasas, he attacked it.
It has indeed been heard by you that even Vidhi, having become deluded through a lack of discernment,
met his own decapitation due to his arrogance.
Having granted the boon to the asura without due deliberation, Mahādeva, fearing his own reduction to ashes, became intent on flight. || 60 ||
Due to a lack of discernment, Hari previously slew the wife of Bhṛgu and consequently experienced supreme, utterly unbearable suffering caused by her curse. (61)
In this way, other gods, celestial beings, demons, humans, and animals indeed fall into calamity solely through the power of non-discrimination. (62)
O Bhārgava, those wise ones are indeed highly fortunate whom discrimination never abandons anywhere; let there be constant salutation to them.
He praises those intent on investigation: "Great... (verse 63).
Having obtained [an opportunity], those who act without reflection are deluded on all sides;
but by acting after reflection, one is liberated from all boundless perils. (64)
Indeed, that which ought not to be done, yet causes suffering, people perceive as something to be done through a lack of discernment;
thus they become utterly deluded regarding all sufferings, including those arising from boundless calamities that bring about unavoidable misery.
Thus, for a long time, this world remained devoid of inquiry;
as long as there is no inquiry, how can there be any investigation? (65)
He states the contradiction between *vicāra* and *avicāra* with an illustration: "Of whom... (verse 65).

Where is cool water in a desert scorched by the fierce rays of the summer sun? Likewise, how can there be peace for one surrounded by the garlands of flames from the fire of long-standing lack of discernment? (66)
If it is argued that, "Just as a sudden rain may fall even in summer, so too will inquiry arise of its own accord," he says "no" with the words "evam" (thus). || 66 ||
How could the cool touch of discernment come to be without practice?
Yet, in this matter, there is but one supreme practice that excels all others. (67)

If it is argued that the means (*sādhana*) must be an established ritual action (*karma*), he says "no"—namely, "only one. It is superior to all other means that accomplish different fruits; the sense is that its result is necessarily consummated. The supreme [form] of the deity residing in the lotus-heart of all has been described.
Without her, how could there be a great means for anyone to achieve supreme welfare? (68)
What then? He says: "Supreme compassion. (68)
The sun of discernment destroys the great darkness of non-discernment;
in that regard, the root cause is the propitiation of the deity through devotion. (69)

When the supreme Goddess, being thoroughly pleased, takes pity upon the blinding darkness of one born blind— a darkness that cannot be dispelled by the sun or other luminaries— she then assumes the form of discernment within the space of the mind, like the sun. (70)

He describes the manner in which inquiry (*vicāra*) arises from the propitiation of the deity: "Propitiated... The meaning is that through her grace, she herself becomes the very form of inquiry. The intended sense is that prior to the arising of grace, she was indeed of the nature of non-inquiry. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Caṇḍīstava*: "And she alone is the cause of bondage to saṃsāra..."
"The Sovereign of all sovereigns" (1.58). || 70 ||
Therefore, [one should worship] that Supreme Goddess Tripurā, who is one's own essential nature,
the glorious Great Mistress, the auspicious Śivā, who consists of consciousness and whose abode is within all.
That worship, moreover, is not directed toward forms such as Indra or the Moon, but rather toward her who is beautiful within; thus he says: "one's own self," etc. (71).
One should propitiate [the deity] through the gateway of a true guru in due order, without guile;
even in that propitiation, the root cause should be pure devotion and faith.
He explains the manner of propitiation: "without deceit" (akāpaṭyāt). Deceit is the intention for a reward. || 72 ||
Even there, it is proclaimed that hearing of the greatness [of the deity] is the root;
therefore, O Rāma, the greatness has been set forth first for you. (73)
In that regard as well, it was set forth—that is, proclaimed—at the beginning of the *Bhakti* [chapter]. || 73 ||
By hearing that [teaching], you have now attained auspiciousness;
for reflection is the root of the highest good, and because of it, no fear has arisen in you. (74)
Until the arising of discernment, there is a very great fear for one who is seized day after day by the defect of a non-discerning self. (75)
For just as in one seized by a combination of humors, fear may persist even while taking medicine, as long as the constituent elements remain impure. (76)

Here is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): "Just as" (*yathā*). Even for one afflicted by a great disorder of the humors (*sannipāta-mahādoṣa*), as long as the purification of the elements (*dhātu-śuddhi*) does not occur through the consumption of a potent medicine, there is indeed fear, because a contrary result is sometimes observed.
Likewise, even for one devoted to the propitiation of the deity, there is fear due to non-investigation until the arising of investigation; such is the meaning. || 76 ||
Human life bears fruit only when the supreme inquiry is attained;
for as many births as it may take, until such supreme inquiry occurs for men. (77)
The other is the means for achieving liberation. || 77 ||
To that extent, the trees of birth are barren, fruitless due to their cause;
only that tree of birth is fruitful wherein there is discernment.
Those men who lack discernment are like frogs in a well;
just as a frog born within a well knows nothing at all. (79)
They are like frogs in a well. || 79 ||
Whether auspicious or inauspicious, it perishes right there in the well;
likewise, people too are born in vain within the well of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). 80.
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, they never understand it regarding their own selves;
arising again and again, they perish and do not know what is for their own benefit.
Having attained the notion of happiness amidst sufferings and the conviction of suffering within pleasures through the power of non-investigation, they are cooked in the fire of worldly existence.

The notion that sons and others—who are actually means of suffering—are means of happiness; the certain conviction that detachment and so forth—which are actually means of happiness—are means of suffering;
and *sṛti*, which is the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of birth and so on. || 82 ||
And though being afflicted by suffering, they do not abandon that in any way, just as a great donkey does not abandon it even when struck by a hundred kicks to its feet. (83)
That [wealth] and so forth are means for suffering; here is an illustration: "Just as... (verse 83).
Just as a person follows after a female donkey, so does one wander in saṃsāra;
but you, O Rāma, being composed of discernment, have reached the further shore of suffering.
"So be it. The meaning is that even while being afflicted again and again, he does not abandon the wandering—that is, the engagement in the terrible cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). || 84 ||
[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Inquiry," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the second chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the third chapter:
Having heard the words spoken by Dattātreya, the son of Jamadagni, filled with great curiosity and endowed with humility, questioned him once again. (1)
In the preceding chapter, it was stated that devotion arises from hearing of the majesty [of the Lord], from that [devotion] comes worship, and from that the dawn of inquiry.
Regarding that, Hāritāyana (K: *tāya namaḥ*) asks Dattātreya what the cause for hearing of the majesty itself is; thus he says: "O Dattātreya... (1).
O Blessed One, that which was spoken by the venerable Guru is exactly so;
yet, due to a lack of inquiry, people have in every way met with destruction beyond it. (2)
Through reflection, there may arise what is beneficial, and its cause is also heard as the "hearing of the majesty"; such being the case, I have a great doubt regarding this. (3)
In that regard, upon hearing of his greatness. || 3 ||
Or how could even that means be attainable? What would it be in that case? If it were innate, why has it not been heard by everyone? (4)
If it is argued that even this hearing of the majesty [of the Lord] is merely natural, like hunger, thirst, and so forth, for every living being, he says: "By all," etc. (Verse 4).
Until now, I have not obtained any news here;
they have encountered suffering even greater than mine and have been frustrated at every step.

If it is argued that this is the very nature of those like you, just as [it is the nature of others] to possess heroism, valor, and so forth, he says: "Or I... In this context, regarding the hearing of his majesty, if it is argued that the root cause here is simply the attainment of suffering, he says: "Suffering... (5)
"From where did they obtain this means of accomplishment? Tell me this out of compassion.
Thus questioned, Datta, the ocean of mercy, spoke again with joy.
The meaning is: "Just as I have been struck down and defeated by Rāma, why have others—who too have been struck down at every step—not heard of his greatness? Speak thus. || 6 ||
Listen, O Rāma, I shall declare the supreme cause of ultimate well-being:
association with the virtuous is the highest root that destroys all suffering. (7)
The *nidāna* is the primary cause; it is the ultimate root, the primary cause. || 7 ||
Association with the virtuous is said to be the seed for attaining the fruit of the ultimate truth; and you, indeed, have been associated with that great-souled Satyavarta.
Having come together and reached this state which results in the fruit of spiritual welfare, for it is the virtuous alone who, when united, bestow supreme happiness. (9)
And Rāma himself illustrates this with the words "And you" (tvaṃ ca). He praises the company of the virtuous with the words "The virtuous" (santaḥ). || 9 ||
Without the company of the virtuous, by whom and when has the supreme good ever been attained?
For in this world, whatever kind of association a person encounters, such is what he receives. (10)
He attains that fruit in every respect; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding this, O Rāma, listen as I shall relate this story to you. (11)

That fruit is either good or bad, corresponding to the nature of one's association. In the previous chapter, it was stated that Saṃvarta taught Vijñāna [the knowledge] and described Saṃvarta’s own state of being; now, in order to explain all of that as the fruit of virtuous association, he begins the narrative with the words "In this regard" (atra). 11.
Formerly, there was a lord of Daśārṇa known as Muktācūḍa;
he had two sons, Hemacūḍa and Maṇicūḍa.
Both were handsome and virtuous, and proficient in all branches of knowledge;
once, out of enthusiasm for hunting, they were surrounded by their armies.
Indeed, those two of great strength, bearing bows and arrows, entered the formidable forest of the Sahya mountain, which was teeming with lions, tigers, and other beasts.
Then, with swift ease, they struck deer, lions, boars, buffaloes, and wolves there with sharpened arrows discharged from their bows.
The sky was covered with dust, resembling the night of universal dissolution;
neither rock, nor tree, nor even a person could be seen there. || 17 ||
"How could this mountain, shrouded in darkness, perceive the distinction between high and low?
The army has been struck down by showers of pebbles and has utterly fled. (18)
Some took refuge among the trees, some among the rocks, and others in caves;
even the two princes, mounted on their horses, fled far away.
They approached him and took refuge in him. || 19 ||
Somewhere there, Hemacūḍa reached an ascetic hermitage that was exceedingly beautiful, filled with groves of plantain and date trees. (20)
There he saw a certain beautiful maiden, like a flame of fire,
radiant in her form with the luster of refined gold.
Seeing her, who was as beautiful as a lotus, the prince, as if smiling, asked: "Who are you, O lotus-faced one, in this forest? (22)
"Though situated fearlessly as if in a place devoid of fear, in this desolate and terrifying wilderness—who are you, by whom are you here, and how do you dwell all alone? (23)
The connection [of the verse] is: "For what reason do you dwell? How is it that you dwell alone? (23)
Thus questioned, that blameless maiden said to the prince:
"Welcome to you, O prince; please accept this seat. (24)
The *viṣṭara* is the seat. || 24 ||
This is indeed the duty of ascetics: namely, the honoring of a guest.
I see that you are exhausted and distressed by the fierce wind. (25)
If it is asked why worship is performed at the very beginning without first answering my question, he says:
"Of the ascetics" (*tapasvinām*). He states another reason for that very point: "You who are weary" (*śrāntam tvām*).
Thus, while the two princes were slaying wild deer, [the following occurred].
A fierce wind arose, raining down gravel and stones. (The sixteenth verse, which was placed here, should be inserted between lines 2 and 3.
Having tied his horse to a date tree, he sat there, free from fatigue.
Having been told, "You ought to hear my life-story," he did accordingly.
The blameless woman fed him fruits and gave him excellent flavors to drink; thus she provided rest for that prince. (27)
It possesses the six tastes and has sweet water. || 27 ||
She spoke with a voice tender from the flow of honey:
"O Prince, there is a sage named Vyāghrapāda who takes refuge in the state of Śiva. (28)
With a graceful and beautiful manner. || 28 ||
By him, through the power of his own austerity, the most meritorious worlds were conquered;
for he, the knower of the high and the low, was constantly honored by the leaders of sages.
He knows the higher and the lower; he knows Brahman. || 29 ||
I am her daughter by right of dharma, renowned as Hemalekhā;
she is a Vidyādharī named Vidyunmālā, enchanting in all her limbs. (30)
In order to establish that she is indeed his daughter of Dharma, he says: "By way of Dharma. The meaning is: "not born of the body. "Like lightning" [is the simile]. || 30 ||
Once, he went to bathe at that river Veṇā;
at that same time, Suṣeṇa, the king of Vaṅga, arrived there for the same purpose.
He beheld that woman, the beauty of the world, plunging into the river,
her fine garments wet and clinging so closely that her two full breasts were clearly revealed.
Struck there by the arrows of desire, he then entreated her;
yet she, infatuated by his beauty, accepted his words.
The construction is "atha sāpi" (then she too). She accepted it, that is, she consented. || 33 ||
Then, having united with her, the king departed toward his own city;
that Vidyādharī also conceived a fetus from the seed of the royal sage.
Fearing an offense against her husband, she abandoned the fetus here and departed;
I was then born as a maiden from that royal sage of unfailing potency. (35)

Here, on the bank of the Veṇā river—[the word] "Amoghā" [is used] because, due to the infallible potency (*amoghavīrya*) of the royal seer (*rājarṣi*), I was born as a girl from his seed without even reaching full development in the womb; such is the meaning. || 35 ||
Vyāghrapāda, having arrived for the purpose of performing the twilight devotions, saw me; out of compassion, he took me up and protected me as a mother would. (36)
For he who protects according to dharma is indeed called a father;
I am his daughter by dharma, devoted solely to the service of my father. (37)
By virtue of its greatness, I have no fear whatsoever here;
nor can this [place] ever be overcome by gods, asuras, or even those of wicked intent.
He provides the answer to the question, "How do you dwell alone? with the words, "Of that... (verse 38).
"The hermitage ought to be entered [only at the proper time]; entering at the wrong time brings about misfortune.
This is the conduct I have described; stay here for a while, O prince. (39)
"My father, the Blessed One, will come; listen to that.
Having approached him and paid homage, you shall then depart tomorrow morning with your desire fulfilled. (40)

Perceiving the prince’s intention toward herself, she spoke to manifest her own acceptance: "And having obtained what is desired... The underlying meaning is: "Because we are well-suited to one another, he will surely give me to you. "Kalye" means at dawn. (40)
Having heard Hemalekhā’s words, he was infatuated by her beauty;
afraid to say anything further, he became as if despondent.
Fearing the greatness of the Sage, he [expressed] a certain intention of his own. || 41 ||
Then, perceiving that the prince had fallen under the sway of passion, that wise woman spoke again: "O prince, maintain your fortitude. (42)
"Your father is arriving this very moment; therefore, enjoy what you desire.
While she was speaking thus, that great sage Vyāghrapāda—
Having gathered a collection of leaves, flowers, and other offerings from the forest, he returned;
seeing that the sage had arrived, the prince rose up to meet him. (44)
Having prostrated and announced his name, he sat down and was instructed by him;
then, seeing the prince whose appearance had been transformed by passion, [he spoke]. (45)
It has been taught and commanded. || 45 ||
Having understood everything through his yogic vision and considering it appropriate at that time,
the sage gave Hemalekhā to him for the purpose of marriage.
He understood their entire intention; that was the giving of the maiden to him. 46.
The prince, also being pleased, took her and went to the city;
Muktācūḍa was exceedingly delighted by the performance of the great festival.
The lord of the earth performed his marriage according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, the prince was constantly devoted to sporting with her.
In the palaces, in the rows of forest groves, and on the sandy banks,
the prince shone like a streak of gold that does not excessively crave worldly enjoyments.
Seeing her constantly indifferent, he once asked her in private:
"Why, my dear, are you not devoted to me, even though I am devoted to you? (50)
O lady of pure smiles, why are you not utterly attached to enjoyments?
Are there no enjoyments here suitable for your mind? From where has this [indifference] come? (51)
From where? From what cause? "Bhogāḥ" means objects of enjoyment and the means of enjoyment. Whence comes this indifference? || 51 ||
To me, you do not appear to be attached even to the most excellent enjoyments;
how can there be for me any pleasure-giving delight when you are devoid of attachment? (52)

With the intention that "enjoyments are indeed unsurpassed," he says: "in the most excellent. Even toward enjoyments that are most excellent and unattainable, you do not appear to be detached. If it is asked, "What is the use of your attachment to these? he replies: "In you.
The intention is that pleasure arises from the excellence of mutual attachment alone. || 52 ||
Even though I am attached to you, you appear to have your mind fixed elsewhere;
even when addressed by me repeatedly, you do not hear anything at all.

"How was it determined by you that I am unattached? To this he says: "Though attached," and so forth. The ellipsis is: even though I am attached to you and my being is solely directed toward you, you appear as if your mind were fixed elsewhere.
If it is asked, "How did you perceive that your mind was fixed elsewhere? he says: "By your speech," and so forth. || 53 ||
Even though he has arrived and been clinging to your neck for a long time, you perceive it only after a while, asking "When did my lord arrive? as if you were unaware.
Though it has been clinging to your throat for a long time, you ask when it arrived. || 54 ||
Why does your mind not become attached to exquisite enjoyments that are difficult to find anywhere? Why do you not take pleasure in anything at all? (55)
If it is asked how it is known that the mind does not become attached even to things that are charming and beautiful, he says:
"Nothing whatsoever. For you do not rejoice in anything—even in that which is unobtainable—as something to be enjoyed, thinking, "Ah, how exceedingly beautiful! || 55 ||
Whenever I approach you while you stand with your eyes closed, separated from me,
I see you then and there.
Tell me how there might be happiness for me in you, who are liberated from enjoyments and sense-objects, just as there would be for one joined with a wooden woman. (57)
Nothing that I desire is apart from what you favor;
in every way, I have followed after you, just as the night-lotus follows the moonlight. 58.
And he says, "It is not yours," meaning that he has not followed after you. || 58 ||
Therefore, tell me from where that thought arose, O beloved dearer than life;
by this means my mind may be purified, for I adjure you, my love. (59)
Thus, it is turned away from sense objects. || 59 ||
[Thus ends the third chapter in the section on the Greatness of Association with the Virtuous, within the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the third chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the fourth chapter:
Having heard these words from her beloved as he pressed her to his neck,
that blameless princess, with a slight smile upon her face, spoke to the prince.
In this chapter, titled "The Measurement," the distaste for the snares of worldly enjoyment is clearly demonstrated through a narrative for the sake of dispassion.
"Blameless" means that for her, who has known all that is to be known, there is no turning away from sense objects due to ignorance or the like; this is the intended meaning. || 1 ||
Desiring to awaken the prince, she spoke these words with skillful reasoning:
"O Prince, listen to my words; I am not indifferent toward you."

"Desiring to awaken him," meaning possessed by the wish "I shall awaken him," [she acts] "by means of reasoning"; the sense is that trust in her own words alone is impossible for him. This is what will be stated hereafter. || 2 ||
"What might be most dear in this world, and what indeed might be most unpleasant?"—my mind, though constantly devoted to such inquiry, finds no end to these questions. (3)

If you ask, "If you are not dispassionate, then why is this so? she replies: "What would it matter?"—meaning that for her, inquiry alone is the supreme and primary object of meditation; [she seeks] the end, which is certainty. || 3 ||
"I have been constantly meditating on this for a long time, yet due to the power of my feminine nature, I do not understand its true essence; you ought to explain it to me according to the truth. (4)

If it is asked, "What is the fruit of this meditation for you?", he says: "The nature of woman," etc. "Reality" (tattvam) means the true state (yāthārthyam), the essential nature of what is pleasant and unpleasant. || 4 ||
Thus addressed, Hemacūḍa laughed and said to his beloved:
"It is certainly true, without a doubt, that women are of dull intellect."
For even beasts, birds, and reptiles distinguish between the pleasant and the unpleasant,
since it is observed that they behave toward both the agreeable and the disagreeable.

If it is asked, "From where [does this arise] for those of deluded intellect? he says: "By 'dear one' (priyā). The sense is: when even animals know [this], what need is there for deliberation in that regard? || 6 ||
What need is there for much reflection here regarding engagement and withdrawal?
That from which happiness arises is dear; that from which suffering arises is not dear.

If it is asked, "How was this cognition of cattle and other animals understood by you? he says: "By activity" (*pravṛtti*). The meaning is that [the existence of pleasure and pain] is inferred from the engagement with and withdrawal from what is pleasant and unpleasant. Here, the point is well known even among animals. If it is then asked, "In that case, state the definition of the pleasant and the unpleasant," he says: "Pleasure" (*sukha*). (7)
"Why do you constantly dwell in such a state of bewilderment here, my dear?
Having heard these affectionate words, Hemalekhā spoke again to her beloved:
In this case, it refers to a well-known meaning. || 8 ||
It is true that women are of a simple nature and lack sound discernment;
nevertheless, I must be enlightened by you, who possess perfect discernment. (9)
Thorough investigation is right reflection. || 9 ||
Having been enlightened by you, I shall cast off this anxiety;
therefore, from now on, I shall be constantly devoted to enjoyments with you day after day.
I become attached to enjoyments; therefore, [this occurs] immediately after awakening. || 10 ||
O King, you who possess subtle discernment have indeed pointed out that pleasure and pain arise from those two things which you designated as the agreeable and the disagreeable. (11)
He restates the definition of "tallakṣaṇa" in order to refute it, beginning with the words "O King," and so forth. || 11 ||
Pleasure and pain are indeed one and the same; their distinction arises from differences in time, place, and form.
Why, then, should a firm conviction be established regarding them in this world? (12)

"Bhidā" means by way of distinction. A single entity may produce both pleasure and pain through distinctions such as time and so forth. "In this case," that is, regarding such an entity; "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) refers to the state of having a nature established as invariably being a means to pleasure alone.
"Resolute" (*adhyavasāyinī*) means possessing certainty. || 12 ||
Just as fire, due to differences in time, yields distinct results, so too does it do so through differences in place and differences in form. (13)
He explains that very point with the words "yataḥ" (since): [it is] precisely the bestower of separate fruits such as pleasure and so forth. || 13 ||
Fire is indeed pleasant in the cold season, but unpleasant in the heat;
likewise, due to the differences between cold and hot regions, it is both pleasant and unpleasant.
Having analyzed this very point, he says: "Cold," etc. (14).
Cold is pleasant to those whose nature is cold, while the opposite is pleasant to others;
furthermore, it is described as such according to whether its intensity is greater or lesser.
He says "cold" etc., meaning that it is likewise even when there is a difference in the form and appearance of the nature [of fire].

He says "then" etc., meaning that it is likewise even when there is a difference in the small or great form and appearance of fire. Thus, pleasure and pain are [respectively] the pleasant and the unpleasant by virtue of being the means of accomplishing them. 15.
In this way, wealth, wives, sons, a kingdom, and likewise other things are transitory;
yet even so, the great king was surrounded by wives, sons, and riches. (16)

He extends the stated point to other cases with the word "evam" (thus). "The other" refers to cattle and so forth. Having stated that in this way nothing is a means to pleasure alone, he says "athāpi" (even though), meaning that there is no such thing as being a means to pleasure at all. The meaning is: even though there exists every possible means to pleasure. "Mahārāja Muktācūḍa" [is the example]. || 16 ||
Why does he grieve day after day, and why do others not grieve?
Surely this enjoyment intended for happiness should be endless; yet, even though he possesses all the means of pleasure such as a wife and the like, why does he grieve daily? As for the others...
Those who are free from passion are devoid of the means for pleasure. [An objection: "But surely my father experienced grief because he did not obtain all objects of the senses;
therefore, all objects of the senses together constitute the means for pleasure. To this, he says: "This which... (verse 17).
No one has ever obtained that entirety from which happiness might arise;
listen also regarding whatever happiness might come from any gain whatsoever.
[The author] says "no one" because it is impossible to obtain that [entirety] due to its infinity.
If it is argued that even if there is no gain of everything, one might still experience some happiness upon obtaining something at some time, he says:
"Even there" (tatrāpi). This means: even with regard to that happiness. || 18 ||
O Protector, that cannot be happiness because it is intermingled with suffering;
for suffering is said to be of two kinds: external and internal. (19)

"Intermingled with suffering": because pleasure and pain are of contradictory natures—like light and darkness—they cannot coexist at the same time. Therefore, since suffering is being experienced at that moment, it is not the pleasure you intend [to describe]. This is the sense. Now, [one might object]: "No..."
Anticipating the objection that there is no experience of suffering at that time, he analyzes [the situation] in order to establish that suffering, saying: "But suffering... (verse 19).
The external [fever] is produced from the body, arising from the imbalance of the elements (dhātus) and so forth; the internal is said to be mental, and that arises from desire.
The *dhātus* are wind, bile, and so forth; by "and so forth," boils, injuries, and the like are included. (20)
The mind must be the greater [enemy], by which this entire world is swallowed;
for desire alone is the seed of the tree of suffering, possessing very firm power. (21)
The mental [body] is greater than the physical body. Why is it greater? To this he says: "By which...

He states its greater magnitude even in comparison to the nature of a seed: "Desire alone... The sense is that it possesses very firm power, meaning it inevitably results in its fruit; the humors of the elements and so forth are not like this, because they are easily remedied.
By means of which even the gods, Indra and the others, though ever-risen and dwelling in heaven, have attained the state of servants and perform [its bidding] day and night.
For this very reason, he says "by which" (yayā) to show that she is seen even by those who feed on nectar (amṛtāśinaḥ). The meaning is "by desire.

The intention is that the gods are indeed incapable of countering her [power] either by resorting to regions superior in qualities consisting of heaven, or by drinking the nectar that is the cause of perpetual rising. || 22 ||
O King, know that whatever happiness exists even when only a trace of desire remains is indeed suffering, for it is the same as that which occurs even among worms. (23)
If it is argued that, just as light and darkness are not mutually exclusive in dim twilight, the coexistence of pleasure and pain is accepted at the time of desire, [the author] says: "Pleasure.
Since pleasure mixed with pain is possible even among worms whose very nature is suffering, that is not primary pleasure; rather—

Tell me, what happiness could there be for humans, which is joined with such meager desires, when even the happiness of animals, insects, and worms— which is like a mere glimmer of light in thick darkness— is far superior? (24)

If it is argued that even that appearance of happiness is indeed superior for a mortal compared to other beings, he says "no," [introducing the verse with] "Better..."—where "tiryak" means a beast; "kīṭāḥ" refers to winged insects; "kṛmayaḥ" refers to wingless worms; and by the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), birds are included.
(Note: *vayāṃsi* is absent in manuscript *kh*).

For animals and the like, because their desires are few and not accumulated, there is a semblance of happiness, like the appearance of light mixed with darkness at dawn. For humans, however, because they are beset by infinite desires, it is like the light of a firefly situated in thick darkness.
The meaning is that because it is incapable of performing a function, it is not even a semblance of pleasure. || 24 ||
If one who is beset by hundreds of desires could become happy here in this world by obtaining even a single thing, then tell me, who indeed would not be happy? (25)
If one were happy even by such pleasure as this, no one would ever be miserable; thus he says: "He desires," etc. Something such as a garland, sandalwood, and so forth. (25)
If one whose entire body has been scorched by fire were to have their body become cool through even a tiny drop of sandalwood paste, then that person too would become happy. (26)
In that case, one might argue that even in the midst of great suffering, one would be happy; to this he says: "entirely," etc.
A drop of *pāṭīra* is a drop of sandalwood. || 26 ||
A man indeed attains happiness from the embrace of his beloved; yet, in that very same state, suffering surely arises from the shifting of the body's limbs. (27)

If it is argued that in the embrace of a beloved, there is indeed only pleasure because all external things are forgotten, he replies with the words "of the beloved" (*priyāyāḥ*). At that very time of embracing, the binding—meaning the mutual interlocking of limbs—is uneven and painful. The sense is that because it is accompanied by such suffering, even that [embrace] is not purely pleasurable.
Indeed, exhaustion arises for all from the intensity of sexual passion;
thereafter, there is fatigue like that of a beast carrying a heavy burden. (28)
He demonstrates the universal experience that there is suffering in acts such as embracing by stating "pleasure" (ratīti).
This means immediately following the immersion in pleasure. Regarding the point that this exhaustion is rooted in suffering, he provides an illustration:
"exertion" (bhāreti). This exhaustion is produced by suffering because it is of the nature of exhaustion.
Like an animal exhausted from carrying a burden. || 28 ||
O Lord, how do you perceive that happiness? Please explain this to me:
what happiness arises from the union with a beloved, which is produced by the friction of the channels (nāḍīs)? || 29 ||
Thus, since this is joined with suffering, how can you regard that as happiness? (29)
Tell me, is there nothing here belonging to us dogs that you possess? For what you have exceeds that, arising from the beauty you have seen.

The friction of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃghaṭṭa*) is the rubbing of the organs of bliss; the pleasure produced by that even exists for dogs, and thus it is not a pleasure to be desired by the wise—this is the sense. Therefore, [the pleasure] arising from the friction of the channels is *atirikta*, meaning excessive.
It is born from the sight of beauty (*dṛṣṭa-saundarya-sambhava*), that is, produced by the perception of beauty. || 30 ||
That arises solely from self-conceit, just like [the joy] in union with a woman in a dream;
for instance, in the past, there was a certain prince who was more beautiful than the god of love. (31)
Regarding the fact that pleasures such as the sight of beauty arise from conceit, he tells a narrative: "In a city," etc. (31).
Having obtained a certain beautiful woman who was enchanting to all,
that prince became exceedingly attached to her.
Her mind, however, was attached to another royal servant;
that servant then deceived the prince through a clever stratagem. (33)
Having given him an excessive amount of wine for the purpose of intoxication,
she then sent a certain ill-formed maidservant to him who was blinded by liquor.
He states the reasoning itself: "madirām" (wine), etc.; "atimātram" means in great abundance. || 34 ||
Thus, blinded by intoxication, the king’s son enjoyed that wife of his, the most beautiful woman in all the world, for a long time there. (35)
The prince enjoyed a maidservant—a slave girl—who had been sent to him by one blinded by intoxication;
the intended meaning is that he enjoyed the wife of that very prince. || 35 ||
Going to his maidservant every day, he considered himself equal [to her], thinking:
