"I am blessed to have obtained such a woman, the beauty of the world and the beloved of my life. (36)
The prince conceives of himself, thinking, "I am fortunate," and so forth. || 36 ||
"I always approach [him], for there is no one equal to me anywhere.
While time passed in this manner, once, by the turn of fate, [this occurred]. (37)
Having set down his drink, the servant departed on urgent business;
then the prince drank that drink, but not to excess. (38)
He is a servant. When there is an absolute or necessary task, "ātyantika" means abundant. || 38 ||
With his mind eager for pleasure, he went quickly from that place to his beloved bedchamber, which was endowed with the abundance of every luxury.
On account of some sign or omen, he did not drink. || 39 ||
Like the Lord of the Gods in the Nandana grove approaching Śacī’s chamber,
he approached that maidservant who was seated upon a most excellent couch.
The residence of Śacī, situated in the Nandana grove—supreme and most excellent—was sent by her servant. || 40 ||
Overpowered by the force of passion, he enjoyed her with extreme delight;
then, at the conclusion of the pleasure, he recognized that maidservant of deformed appearance.
Driven by the force of passion, he did not even examine her first. || 41 ||
Apprehensive and indignant, wondering "What is this?", he asked after her, thinking only, "Where is that beloved of mine? (42)

Thinking, "Who is this? he was filled with doubt; "I have been deceived by her," he reflected with resignation; "She is not capable of deceiving me, so what is this?"—pondering thus, he asked, "Where is she? and so forth. || 42 ||
Having been questioned thus by him, that maidservant, perceiving him to be free from intoxication, was terrified; trembling, she then said nothing at all to him. (43)
Regarding that prince: the connection is with "having observed" from the conduct of the maidservant. || 43 ||
Perceiving both the injustice and his own deception, the prince,
his eyes red with rage, seized the maidservant by the hair with his left hand.
An improper statement is one that is inconsistent. 44.
The prince took up his sword with his right hand and, threatening her, replied: "Speak the truth exactly as it happened. (45)
A sword is a kṛpāṇī. || 45 ||
"If not, your life shall swiftly cease even for a moment.
Hearing those words, she became terrified, desiring to save her life. (46)
Therefore, the construction [of the sentence] is: "Speak quickly. (46)
He related all that had occurred long ago exactly as it happened,
and he also showed him that woman who was well-accompanied by her servant.
That was her beloved conduct; it was past conduct, which she maintained and practiced. || 47 ||
In one place, on the ground upon a mat, he saw a servant who was dark-complexioned with tawny eyes,
tall in stature, with all his limbs soiled, a harsh face, and loathsome to behold.
Tall and lofty. || 48 ||
Having embraced her, who was exhausted from lovemaking, with all his limbs out of affection, he placed his own face upon the face of her whose neck was encircled by his soft, vine-like arms. (49)
Having embraced with all his limbs, he is one whose neck is covered or entwined by a creeper. || 49 ||
Having pressed her lotus-face against his feet and embraced him firmly with her two legs, she held her heavy,
beautiful breasts close to his hands.
The prince beheld her like a spring creeper covered with flower buds, or like Rohiṇī overtaken by Rāhu.
Having observed her in such a state, her mindfulness lost through sleep,
he became utterly bewildered for a moment, and then regained his composure.
For a moment, he fell into a state of utter delusion. || 52 ||
"Listen indeed to what the prince has said regarding me:
'Fie upon me, who am utterly ignoble, foolish, and deluded by intoxication! (53)
Fie on those who are deeply attached to women, and fie on those lowest of men!
Lustful women do not belong to anyone, just as the śārikā birds belong to no tree. (54)
"Fie upon the lowest of men! [and] "O śārikā bird!"—the meaning is that they go wherever their desired fruit is found. || 54 ||
"What shall I say to myself, like a bewildered young buffalo, when I know her who has been dearer to me than life for so very long? (55)
A young buffalo is a buffalo that has just been born; the intended meaning is that it is as charmingly and excessively dull-witted as such. || 55 ||
Women should not belong to anyone at all, for they are like courtesans to a libertine; he who places his mind in trust upon women is indeed a wild donkey.

"In the same way, [the opponent] says that all women [are like this]," [to which the author replies,] "No. Regarding the term "wild donkey": the intention is that a domestic donkey might, through association with people, occasionally come to know something of other states of being. || 56 ||
The existence of an autumnal cloud is indeed momentary and unstable; yet the existence of women is even more fragile and exceedingly fickle than that. (57)
"Pelavā" means very light. || 57 ||
Indeed, until this very day, I did not realize such a feminine nature—that you, devoted to me with your whole soul, have abandoned me and followed after a servant! 58.
Attached to another, her feelings for me concealed, she feigns affection for me like an actress in a circle of libertines, displaying her devotion as a mere pretense. (59)
An illustration regarding attachment that is merely a pretense is as follows: "like an actress," thus [verse 59].
With my mind intoxicated by wine, I did not perceive her even in the slightest degree;
thinking that she was attached to me like a shadow, my mind was full of confidence. (60)

Having been deceived by that maid who was not to be looked upon, and having long been united with her, who indeed on the surface of the earth could be more intoxicated or more utterly deluded than I? (61)
"Deceived by her, I have united with a maidservant. || 61 ||
"Alas! This wretched servant, whose form is deformed in every limb, has for a long time deceived me with such confidence. (62)
The reason for this is: "one who acts thus. "Wretched" means extremely censurable. || 62 ||
What supreme beauty has she seen here that surpasses all else, such that she has drawn away from me the gaze of the world, which is captivated by her own loveliness? (63)
By whom the gaze—the looking—of the people was captivated by his beauty. || 63 ||
"Having abandoned him who was devoted to you in every way, you have come here"—
having lamented thus in many ways, he then became exceedingly despondent.
In every way, one who is enamored is *anurakta*; one who is despondent is *virakta*. || 64 ||
The prince went to the forest, having abandoned all attachments;
therefore, O Prince, this beauty has arisen from the mind. 65.

The meaning is: because that deluded prince, by consorting for a long time with a maidservant of extremely loathsome appearance, attained that pleasure for a long duration merely through the conceit that "this is indeed Lokasundarī herself"; [therefore, it was] arisen from the mind, [that is,] imagined by the mind. || 65 ||
Just as you find exceeding delight in me, preceded by the gaze of one who perceives me as supremely fortunate, so too— or even more so— do you find it in her.
He confirms this very point by means of an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as); "tadviśeṣataḥ" means in a form even more superior than that.
They find ultimate delight even in women who are deformed;
regarding this, I shall state the proof to you—listen with a concentrated mind, my dear. (67)
In this context, regarding the mental nature of beauty, [the author] provides the process (*prakriyā*) conducive to conviction (*pratyaya*), that is, to certainty. 67.
For that woman who is perceived is well-established externally, while she whose nature consists of the reflection thereof is dependent upon the mind. (68)
Outside of the mind, elsewhere. || 68 ||
Taking the form of a mental resolve, he repeatedly scratched at her excellence with his mind; thereupon, desire arrived once again.
Repeatedly sketching her elegance and beauty; "thereafter" (tadanu) means immediately following that thorough sketch; [he sketches] his longing for her as the object. || 69 ||
A man whose senses are agitated finds delight in her in every respect;
but when the senses are not agitated, there would be no delight even in a beautiful woman.
"Whose generative organ is agitated"—the ellipsis is "having turned away from all other desires.

When, for a man overwhelmed by a thousand desires, the arousal of the desire for sexual union with a woman becomes even more intense through the description of her beauty and so forth, then all other desires become subordinate. (k, kh)
[The state] becomes [so]. Thus, he says "unagitated" (akṣubdhā), because in the absence of agitation there is no pleasure anywhere.
(70) In that regard, the root is constant observation; furthermore, it is excellence.
Therefore, agitation is never seen even among young women or among yogis. (71)
In that regard, concerning agitation (*kṣobha*), he confirms this by way of its exclusion (*vyatireka*): "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 71 ||
And so, whatever delight a man finds in anyone—whether in a beautiful woman or another—he should describe the excellence of that very thing. (72)

He states that it is the description of beauty itself that is the cause of agitation, not beauty per se, with the words "And so" (*tathā ca*). Whether the excellence (*sauṣṭava*) is established or unestablished [is irrelevant]. || 72 ||
Women are seen with bodies of an extremely loathsome appearance;
yet they are seen in union with young men for the sake of offspring. (73)

Regarding this, he states an illustration: "They are seen," and so forth. Those whose bodies—that is, the configuration of their limbs—possess a loathsome appearance; such as these are seen in the world, and they are also seen in the company of young men. Now, one might object: since union occurs in secret, how can they be seen by others in their company?
If it is said: "Because of the cause of offspring" (verse 73).
If there were either a description of their deformity or a failure to describe their excellence, how indeed could human beings find delight in them? (74)
If it is argued that there might still be consistency even without the mention of excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) in those cases, he says: "Virūpa" [and so on].
Non-mention of excellence means non-mention regarding excellence. In those [cases] which are discordant (*virūpa*). 74.
What more need be said? Alas! For men whose minds are distracted by desire, even in the lowest limb, beauty shines forth as preeminent in every respect. (75)

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a description of beauty in one who is deformed? he says, "Is this not strange to lovers?"— explaining that for those whose minds are cast away or distracted,
even that which is base, inferior, fanned by the smoke of exhaled breaths, drenched with urine and the like, and equal to a cavity in a wound of a moist vein— is not surprising.
Even in the case of the womb and other limbs, it is superior to those with faces on all sides and so forth. || 75 ||
If one were to look for beauty in a limb that is drenched with impurities and urine, where would one find it? That beauty belongs to me alone. (76)
Therefore, O prince, observe this very beauty;
without self-conceit, it can never be a cause of happiness anywhere. (77)
Therefore, because beauty consists merely of mental construction. || 77 ||
If beauty were innate in the body, like the sweetness of honey, then tell me, why does it not shine forth in infants and young children? (78)
Beauty is not natural like the sweetness of honey; thus, by this alternative means, he establishes that beauty is mental. (Verse 78) "Like honey," etc.
In various regions, men are seen with diverse forms:
some with one foot, some with one eye, some with long ears, and some with the faces of horses. (79)
Lovers have no pleasure in those who are unattractive; even when seen occasionally, such a person does not bring complete happiness.
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by means of the description of residing in another land, [beginning with] the word "deśa" (land).
Some had ears serving as coverings, some had mouths like ploughshares, and some had protruding fangs; some were noseless, some had long noses, some were covered in hair, and others were hairless.

Some had tawny hair, some white hair, some were hairless, and others had thick hair; some were the color of leprosy, some the color of crows, some were tawny, and others had limbs that were blood-red. || 81 ||
In this way, O Prince, observe how mortals of many kinds find pleasure with women of their own kind, just as you do. (82)
Listen; behold! || 82 ||
Among all things that serve as means to happiness, the female form stands preeminent;
it is beloved by all, and even the gods are infatuated with it.
In order to describe the nature of the body, he says: "Happiness," etc. (83).
O prince, examine with your keen intellect the bodies of men as well as those of women—how they appear to be dear and exceedingly beautiful, yet what they truly are in reality. (84)
It is smeared with flesh, moist with blood, bound by veins, and stretched over by skin; it is a cage of bones covered with hair, afflicted by bile and phlegm. (85)
It is produced by, or associated with, bile and phlegm. || 85 ||
This bag of excrement and urine, produced from semen and blood, emerging from the opening of the urinary tract—alas, it is held dear here in this world! (86)
Tell me, how could there be any difference between those men who take delight in such extreme loathsomeness and the worms that feed on excrement? (87)
O Prince, this body is indeed exceedingly dear to you; therefore, discern through analytical wisdom the distinct nature of its constituent elements. (88)

Contemplate the separate existence of the elements—such as skin, blood, and so forth—through discernment, that is, by means of analytical vision. The implication is that when one contemplates in this way, where is there any such thing as beauty and the like? || 88 ||
In this same way, one should apply this principle elsewhere regarding the six tastes, such as sweet and sour;
however, one should discern their nature of transformation through subtle vision. (89)

Having thus removed the dearness of the body in the form of its being a means to pleasure, he rejects it with respect to food by saying "thus" (*evam*). [This refers to] elsewhere than the body; that is, regarding food (*bhojye*) which is to be consumed. (89)
Even for everything that has been eaten, its transformation into excrement occurs;
there is no doubt about this in any way, as it has been observed by everyone. (90)
He states the very nature of the transformation: "Having been consumed," etc. (90).
"Tell me, since the world is established in this way, what could be pleasant and what could be unpleasant?
Thus addressed, Hemacūḍa then understood the distaste for sense objects.
Having heard that unprecedented web of words, he was immediately struck with wonder;
he reflected further upon everything that had been spoken by Hemalekhā.
Unprecedented, never heard before.
Having become disillusioned with worldly enjoyments, he attained supreme detachment;
then, having gradually questioned his beloved and come to know that state, [he departed].
He for whom weariness has arisen and the sense of "enough" [with worldly existence] exists; that supreme state is the state of the Self. 93.
Having realized that the solitary consciousness, which resides within the self, is Tripura herself in the form of the Self,
he became one whose soul was liberated, perceiving all things as being his own self.
Abiding in the self, existing within all; having the form of the self, whose nature is immediate presence;
he for whom the vision of everything has become his own self. 94.
Thereupon, his younger brother Maṇicūḍa also became liberated while yet alive; even though he was Muktācūḍa's son, he attained liberation through his elder brother.
Muktācūḍa’s beloved wife also attained knowledge through her daughter-in-law;
likewise, the ministers and the citizens became possessed of wisdom. (96)
The beloved of Muktācūḍa, the mother of Hemacūḍa—[the word] "was instructed" is to be supplied—with her daughter-in-law Hemalekhā;
[thus they were] possessed of knowledge through their mutual instruction. || 96 ||
In that city, no one was born who was unlearned;
it resembled the city of Brahmā, where the latent impressions of worldly existence had been stilled.
It resembles the city of Brahmā and is equal to Satyaloka. The latent impressions of worldly existence consist of desire, anger, and so forth. 97.
And that vast city shone as the most excellent on earth,
where parrots and mainas indeed recited while staying in their cages.
The reason for its being the supreme is stated in the verse beginning with "wherein" (yatra). || 98 ||
Worship your own self, which is consciousness and free from the object of thought; there is no object of thought other than consciousness, just as a reflection exists only within a mirror. (99)

Regarding what they recite, it says: "The form of consciousness. O people! Abandoning the pursuit of sense objects, worship your own Self. The intended meaning is that the pursuit of sense objects is the root of suffering.
Of what nature is this Self? To that it says: "the form of consciousness" (*citirūpam*). Consciousness (*citi*) is pure awareness (*prajñāna*); that alone is its form.

For him, there is no external worship such as ritual offerings and the like; rather, his worship consists in abiding in the sense of "I-ness" (or, according to the reading *matiḥ* found in the printed *Cidvilāsa-stava*, in the state of consciousness). [Note:
Even in this verse cited in the *Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā*, the reading is indeed *matiḥ*.]

According to the principle stated [in the *Citsukhī*, page 250, section 5], "That I am" is precisely the state of possessing an unshakable certainty (*niṣprakampa-niścaya*). If it is argued that this does not exist for us because [the self] is included within the aggregate of the body and so forth, he says:

"Free from objects of consciousness" (*cetyavarjitam*) means free from objects of consciousness such as the body and so forth, which are manifested by consciousness. If one asks why this is so, he says: "It does not exist. The sense is that objects of consciousness, such as the body and so forth, simply do not exist at all, like the horn of a hare.
If it is asked, "If it does not exist like the horn of a hare, how is it manifested? [the answer is: consciousness itself is what is manifested.

He says it is nothing other than this: "other than consciousness. If it is asked, "If it is consciousness alone, how is there an appearance as the body and so forth?", he replies: "Like a reflection in a mirror.
Herein lies the essential truth of the scriptures: consciousness alone is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), because it is not an object of the notion of "this" (*idampratyaya*).

Everything else is of the nature of the non-self (*anātmarūpa*), because it is an object of the notion "this. That reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), however, by virtue of its conformity with the continuity of memory, is one and persists through manifold states;
for, since its nature is pure consciousness (*citimātra*), no distinguishing attribute (*bhedaka-dharma*) is established.

Even within the bodies of gods, demons, humans, and so forth, there is indeed only oneness. Since time, space, and other such factors are entirely submerged within that [oneness], it is not even reasonable to suspect that they could differentiate it, as they would otherwise be like the horns of a man.
Such a reality of the Self, which is the undivided essence of consciousness alone, is precisely what is well-known from the scriptures.

Paramaśiva, through His power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*)— known as *māyā*, which is adept at effecting the impossible and intent on concealing His own true nature— first manifests the impurity consisting of ignorance (*avidyā-mala*), and subsequently brings about this manifestation of duality. This manifested duality, being an object of perception (*dṛśya*), does not arise from a seed like a sprout.

It has been originated from Śiva as its cause; nor is it of the nature of a transformation of the cause, like a jar produced from the modification of a lump of clay, because it follows the unmodified nature of the cause. Nor is it an illusory appearance (*vivarta*), like a snake in a rope, because of the perception of duality between consciousness (*cit*) and the object of consciousness (*cetya*). Therefore, by the power of the mirror’s purity, while [the cause] remains unmodified...

Just as there is the manifestation of a reflection within oneself, so too is there the manifestation of the object of consciousness (*cetya*) within consciousness (*cit*) by its own power. Nor is it the case that, because a mirror requires a reflection that possesses a form identical to the original object (*bimba*), here too [in the case of consciousness], there must be a dependence on a visible object of reflection.

It should not be suspected that the establishment of an external visible object occurs with an identical or similar form, because in the case of a reflection in a mirror, the external original (bimba) is not the material cause (upādāna), since it does not persist in the effect; rather, it is merely the efficient cause (nimitta).

And in the case of a jar and so forth, the efficient cause is the staff and so on; furthermore, that [efficient cause] is variable, as seen in the case of a wheel turned by the hand and other such means.

This follows from the arising of the jar. Thus, it is precisely the power of absolute freedom called *māyā* that is accepted as the instrumental cause for the reflection of the object of perception (*dṛśya*) within consciousness; therefore, there is no logical inconsistency.
For otherwise, if the object of perception were external to consciousness, its manifestation would not be possible except by way of reflection.

Because manifestation is untenable, and because connection with consciousness is untenable— for even that connection, being itself an object of perception, is unestablished due to the fallacy of infinite regress; and if there were no dependence on a connection with consciousness, [the object] would exist at all times.

There must be either the manifestation or the non-manifestation of the object of perception; in this very way, all positions such as "manifestness" (*prakaṭatā*)—which is synonymous with "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*)—are rejected. (The nature of manifestness, which is another term for cognizedness, is set forth by Kumārila Bhaṭṭa in the treatises expounding his system.)

This should be examined; the detailed exposition of this is to be found in the *Pratyabhijñā* and other works (by "and other works," one should include the *Tantrāloka* composed by Abhinavagupta and so forth).
Therefore, the manifestation of the visible world occurs solely through the modality of reflection. || 99 ||
Consciousness is the object of consciousness; I am consciousness; consciousness is all that moves and is immobile.
Since everything shines following consciousness, it is indeed due to its own sovereignty.
Since even the manifold reflection is nothing but the mirror itself, he says: "Consciousness" (*citih*). "The object of cognition" (*cetyam*) is that which is visible.

"The moving and the unmoving" refers to subjects other than myself. The reason why "everything is consciousness" is stated by the word "since" (*yataḥ*): just as all reflections shine forth only by being apprehended as inherent in the mirror.

If it is argued that reflections consist of the nature of the mirror, and thus all this—the objects of cognition and so forth—appears only by having entered into consciousness (*cit*), [the author] replies with the words "But she... (*sā tu*). The sense is that because her very essence is consciousness (*cidātmatva*), she has no need for entry into anything else; for the state of being consciousness is simply the quality of being independent luminosity (*svatantra-prakāśatva*). || 100 ||
Therefore, casting aside delusion and possessing the right vision that perceives only consciousness, all people should resort to consciousness—the luminous one which is the support of all. (101)

Since the world, which consists of reflected images, is not other than consciousness, he states that consciousness possesses a capacity superior to that of a mirror by saying "illuminating everything. The point is that a mirror is merely the locus of reflections; it is not itself an illuminator. The "discarding of error" refers to the apprehension of invalidity. For this very reason, [the text says] "those who possess the excellent vision of pure consciousness alone."
Right view is the vision of the truth; for according to the principle that all knowledge is non-erroneous with respect to its substratum (*dharmī*). || 101 ||
On one occasion, having heard such highly auspicious words from the parrots,
the Brahmins, Vāmadeva and others, announced the name of the city.
Because from it arises great liberation. || 102 ||
Since even animals here call this place "Vidyā" (Knowledge),
let it therefore become renowned by the name "The City of Renowned Knowledge."
Even today that city remains by that very name;
therefore, O Rāma, association with the virtuous is the root of the arising of all auspiciousness. (104)
Therefore, for that reason of naming. || 104 ||
Through association with Hemalekhā, all became knowers of wisdom;
therefore, O Rāma, know that association is the supreme root of well-being. 105.
He concludes: "Therefore," [as stated in verse] 105.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Fruit of Association with the Virtuous," in the Hemacūḍopākhyāna of the Jñānakhaṇḍa within the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tātparyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Jñānakhaṇḍa* of the *Tripurārahasya*.
[Now begins the fifth chapter:
Having thus heard the greatness of association with the virtuous as spoken by the son of Atri,
With a greatly delighted mind, he proceeded once more to ask.
In this regard, with verses beginning with "rāvāya," Hemalekhā,
desiring the welfare of her beloved, spoke of bondage and liberation as residing within the self through cryptic statements.
Rāma, having heard this, [said]: || 1 ||
"O Lord, this which has been spoken by you is true and is a cause of auspiciousness; and this very form of association with the virtuous has been realized through direct perception. (2)
It is experienced as cultivated due to the connection with the [previous] dissolution. || 2 ||
Whatever kind of association one obtains, such shall be the fruit thereof;
even all women, through their association with Hemalekhā, became possessed of great merit.
All were inhabitants of the great city. || 3 ||
O ocean of compassion, I wish to hear further: how was Hemacūḍa enlightened by her? Tell me that in detail.
Thus questioned by Rāma, Dattātreya said to him:
"Listen, O Bhārgava, I shall relate a most purifying story. (5)
Being questioned, he [spoke] that which is supremely purifying because it pacifies the defects of cyclic existence. || 5 ||
Having heard her words in this way, perceiving sense-objects as tasteless and having become disillusioned with them, he appeared as if dejected in spirit.

Thus, he was one who had developed world-weariness through the realization of the distaste for sense objects, and who possessed the thought that enough was enough regarding the enjoyment of those objects;
being thus, he was as if dejected, as if distressed. (6)
Falling under the sway of the latent impressions (vāsanā) born from long-standing attachment to sense objects,
he was indeed unable to suddenly either abandon or grasp them.
He states the reason for the dejection: "For a long time," etc. [It concerns] the objects of the senses, whether to abandon them, to acquire them, or to enjoy them. (7)
Overcome with great shame, the prince said nothing at all to his beloved;
thus, for several days, he passed his time agitated by anxious thoughts.

Having heard these affectionate words, he said nothing; for he was deeply ashamed, having been rendered speechless by the woman. Thus, being incapable of both renunciation and enjoyment, [he remained as he was]. (8)
While his senses were attached to their objects, he remembered what his beloved had said;
though reproaching himself, he nevertheless enjoyed them under the sway of latent impressions.

If it is asked, "How is there incapacity in both cases, since one side or the other must necessarily be chosen? he replies: "Regarding objects" (*viṣayeṣu*). When they have become manifest, that is, when they are present; having remembered that which was spoken by his beloved as the cause of distaste, he ate while censuring himself, thinking, "Shame on me! I am accepting such an object. Now, [one might object]:...
Why does it not avoid [the fault]? To this he says: "By the power of latent impressions" (vāsanāvaśāt). || 9 ||
Under the influence of the force of latent impressions (vāsanā), one pursues sense objects;
yet, upon seeing those very objects, one reflects on the defects previously pointed out by one's beloved.
Having described the manner of enjoying objects that are present, he speaks regarding objects not present: "Vāsanā" (habitual tendency).
It "follows," meaning it reaches the vicinity of the object. [It follows] the defects of objects as spoken by one's beloved. 10.
With a heart agitated by grief, he desponds again and again;
thus his mind became like one situated upon a swaying swing.

He whose heart and mind are agitated and deeply disturbed by grief desponds—that is, he encounters suffering. Like one situated on a swaying swing, he falls toward sense objects due to latent impressions (vāsanā), yet upon attaining those objects, he rises away from them through the recollection of their defects. || 11 ||
Whether it be food, clothing, ornaments, a woman, a vehicle,
or even friends and well-wishers— these truly do not bring happiness to one who is ill-fated.

Thus, he says "bhojyam" (food), etc., stating that even the slightest amount of food and such does not bring happiness to Hemacūḍa, who is possessed of both the defect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and false views (*dṛṣṭi*). (Note: *naiṣat* is the universal reading for *neṣat*. 12.
As if he had lost all his wealth, he grieved incessantly;
overcome by latent desires, he was unable to renounce everything immediately. (13)
Therefore, being possessed by a vision of its faults, he was not able to enjoy it in that way;
thus, under the sway of grief, his face and eyes became pale.

The meaning is that one who is possessed of both latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the perception of defects (*doṣadṛṣṭi*) is unable either to renounce or to enjoy [objects], because of their mutual obstruction. || 14 ||
Once, having observed him in private, Hemalekhā said:
"O Lord, why do you not appear as joyful as before? (15)
"Rahaḥ" means in a secluded place. He asks him in order to test him: "What, O Lord? (verse 15).
I see you as if you were grieving; why is your condition thus? Is it that your physical body is constantly afflicted by ailments? (16)

Regarding the term "corporeal" (śārīra): it refers to the Self (ātman) that has attained identity with the body. The sense is that suffering does not exist in either the body or the Self alone. || 16 ||
The wise declare that there is indeed fear of disease regarding enjoyments;
for when the body arises from the three humors, diseases arise from the imbalance of those humors.

If it is asked, "How can there be any suspicion of disease for me, a great royal prince attended by the best of physicians? he replies: "In pleasures. This means: in auspicious pleasures (*śubhabhoga*). It refers to that state where the three humors—wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*)—exist in perfect balance and stability. (17)
Diseases generally persist by pervading the entire body;
for indeed, an imbalance born of the humors is entirely incurable. (18)

The sense is that since the imbalance of the *doṣas* caused by irregular eating and so forth is inevitable for those who enjoy the aforementioned pleasures, their bodies will necessarily be pervaded by disease. If it is asked, "How can there be an imbalance of the *doṣas* in people like me, who are intent on remedying such imbalances? he says: "In every way" (*sarvathā*). [This refers to] that which is produced by the imbalance of the *doṣas*.

The disease is to be treated, and not merely the imbalance of the humors (doṣa); the point is that the mere imbalance of the humors in the pre-morbid stage of a disease is generally difficult to perceive. || 18 ||
From food, clothing, speech, sight, and touch, as well as from time, place, and action, defects indeed attain an imbalance. (19)

He states the causes for the imbalance arising from the *doṣas* (in the verse beginning with): "From food," and so forth. The qualities of cold, heat, and so on, are well known in the case of food. Likewise [are they] in the case of clothing made of silk, wool, and the like. In the case of speech, there is the quality of heat (*uṣṇaguṇa*) when it is used excessively.

The experience of heat, cold, and so forth is well known through the sight and touch of fire, water, and the like; through seasons such as summer and winter; and through regions such as arid lands and marshy areas. It is also [experienced] through action—such as digging and the like—or, alternatively, through sinful deeds.
(From) karma arises the imbalance of the humors (doṣa). || 19 ||
Therefore, its manifestation in the world has become entirely imperceptible;
for this reason, when an imbalance occurs, medical treatment is prescribed. (20)

Therefore, because the causes of the imbalance of the *doṣas* are manifold, [the treatment] for that imbalance [is prescribed]. If it is argued that those with subtle vision can perceive the arising of that imbalance, he says "no," [explaining] "for this reason":
because the arising of the imbalance is initially imperceptible, for that reason, medical treatment (*cikitsā*) has been proclaimed in the treatise. (20)
No remedy has ever been taught by anyone anywhere for the non-arising of imbalance;
likewise, my dear, why indeed does this sorrow arise in you? (21)
Since there is no arising of objects that cause disharmony, medical treatment has not been mentioned. || 21 ||
Having heard this, the prince then said to Hemalekhā:
"O beloved, listen; I shall tell you the cause of my grief."
Then, immediately after the question. || 22 ||
Indeed, that which was previously a source of happiness for me has been destroyed by your words;
now I do not see anything at all that increases my joy.
That [objection] has now been refuted by your statement. If one asks why, he says: "No. (23)
Just as a territory granted by a king, though providing pleasure on all sides,
does not bring happiness to one who is condemned to death, so too there is no happiness for me from that.

If it is argued that another means of happiness should be procured because this one has perished, he says: "By the king. It is not that [the object] has perished in its own nature; rather, just as there was no happiness for him from the territory and so forth given by the king to his enemy, so too, although the means exists, there is no happiness for me from it. (24)
"While serving sense objects, I am always like one held in bondage.
Therefore, my dear, I ask you: tell me, by doing what shall I attain happiness? (25)

If it is argued, "If you find no happiness in sense objects, then abandon them," he replies, "I am unable to abandon them," with the words: "The sense objects... [as if] "seized by forced labor. Just as people seized by the king's soldiers for the sake of royal business are unable to abandon that task and must perform it, so too am I seized by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Constantly indulging in sense-objects, he has attained suffering (the past participle *kta* is used here in the active sense); this is the ellipsis. || 25 ||
Thus questioned by him, Hemalekhā then said:
"Surely he has reached a state of profound world-weariness upon hearing my words."
He said to himself: "From hearing—that is, from listening to the sacred revelation. || 26 ||
There exists within you the seed of excellence, since you have become such as this; for those in whom excellence is impossible to conceive, they [speak] thus through the weaving of words. (27)
Thus, having become one who has found distaste for sense objects, [he is so] by means of such compositions of speech and dense collections of words similar to what I have spoken. (27)
For the deity who is one's own self, when long propitiated and dwelling within the heart, is never distinguished by even the slightest distinction when she is pleased. 28.

The meaning is that they do not abandon their former state even in the slightest degree, not even by a fraction. If it is asked, "If the mere hearing of such words is the cause of this distaste, why does it not arise in everyone?", he replies with the word "ciram" (for a long time), indicating that it is due to the absence of the underlying cause. || 28 ||
"Only for him by whom Tripurā has been attained can such a state exist"—having reflected thus, the exceedingly wise woman desired to enlighten her beloved. (29)

Such is this state, which is devoid of the relish of sense objects; the implication is that this condition does not apply to everyone, as they lack the fundamental cause, which is the propitiation of the deity. || 29 ||
Concealing her own erudition, she spoke under another's name:
"Listen, O prince, to this ancient account of what happened to me."

"Concealing [her own learning]" means: she thinks, "If I were to manifest my own scholarship, there might arise in him the suspicion that I am conceited about my erudition; consequently, he would have no confidence in my words. Therefore, the sense is that she conceals her own learning.
Here, under the pretext of another, she describes the manner of her own liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra.

"Listen," he says. "Ancient" means that bondage has no beginning in time (a compound containing a *bahuvrīhi*: "that which has a beginningless time"; the meaning is "because bondage is beginningless in time"). || 30 ||
Long ago, my mother gave me a certain female companion for play;
she, though naturally virtuous, became associated with one who was unchaste.
"Pure" (*puru*) means that because bondage is beginningless for any particular creation, it is impossible for there to be a "first time" for all [creations].

"Mother" (*mātṛ*) refers to the self-luminous, pure consciousness (*śuddhaciti*). "Companion" (*sakhī*) refers to the intellect (*buddhi*). Regarding the word "certain" (*kāñcit*): by describing her as if her family and lineage were unknown, it is indicated that the intellect is beginningless, since she is not perceived as being composed of parts of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*).
The pure consciousness (śuddhacit) is the mother because the individual living consciousness (jīvacit) is a portion of it.

Since the play consisting of the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth depends upon the intellect (buddhi), it is said that [the Supreme Being] gave a female companion for the sake of play. At the time of dissolution (pralaya), the intellect is dissolved; therefore, at the beginning of creation—

Because it manifested through the cognition caused by the ripening of karma, it was said "he gave," as if it were something previously unobtained. That cognition is real by its very nature because it is dominated by the quality of *sattva* and is of the nature of luminosity;
it is real in itself because it does not depend on any other mental state for its own existence. This is according to the external [Vaiśeṣika] position.

"By its own nature" means being virtuous (*sādhvī*). "Non-existent" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). "Associated with" means that, having abandoned its pure form as the Self (*ātmākāratā*), it has attained the nature of the visible world, which is the effect of ignorance. The word "certain" (*kāñcit*) is an adjective indicating its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*). However, in the case of the scriptural position (*āgamapakṣa*), [it refers] to consciousness (*cit*).

Ignorance is precisely the cognition of being limited. And this ignorance is clearly defined as "bondage" (*bandha*) by the author of the commentary on the *Śivasūtra* in the aphorism: "And this ignorance is bondage" (1.2). According to this view, since there is no indeterminacy (*anirvacanīyatva*), [the world] is not illusory.

It should be understood that the power of this ignorance (*kāñcit-ajñāna*) is immeasurable. As it has been said: "The error [is] great; though there is no snake in the rope, it causes terror even unto death.
This is the first half of the verse. Its power indeed cannot be discerned. (Pañcadaśī)
(Thus, Sā. 28). In both cases, it should be understood as being "non-existent" because its nature is that of the unreal. || 31 ||
Endowed with the power to create wonders of various kinds,
she met my friend without being noticed by my mother.

That is ignorance (*avidyā*). While it remained unobserved by my mother, the pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*), it united with my friend, the intellect (*buddhi*), behind the back of my mother. The meaning is that because of the opposition between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), the intellect, which has ignorance as its object, is distinct from that which has pure consciousness alone as its object.
The intended meaning is as follows: in the system of the Āgamas, the state of the manifestation of pure consciousness alone is the *śakti-tattva*.

The state of the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—in the form "I am all this, consisting of both consciousness and the unconscious"—is the *śuddha-vidyā-tattva*. The state of the manifestation of limited consciousness alone is the *avidyā-tattva*. [This applies to] both limited consciousness and its object.

The process is that the state of manifestation is the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). Thus, it should be understood that because the intellect does not have pure consciousness as its object, it remains unperceived. || 32 ||
That friend of mine is utterly devoted to unchaste conduct;
she is dearer to me than my own life, for I am always under her control. (33)
He says that her intellect was always intent upon the visible world (*asad*): "Unreal" (*asad*) means that whose conduct (*cāritra*) is of a false nature;
she is ignorance (*avidyā*). She was dearer to me even than my own life-breaths.
Therefore, being under her sway, I became [identified with her] through the superimposition of mutual identity. 33.
Without her, my existence could not endure anywhere for even half a moment;
she, by her stainless nature, remains having brought me under her sway. (34)
"Not that" refers to that cognition (*buddhi*). "Configuration" (*saṃsthā*) means stability (*sthiti*).

Regarding the non-existence of cognition, it has been stated—relying on the *Bhāmatī* tradition of Vācaspati Miśra, according to which the individual soul (*jīva*) is delimited by cognition (*buddhyavacchinna*), and relying on the *Vivaraṇa* tradition of Svayaṃprakāśayati, according to which the individual soul is the reflection of cognition in the intellect (*buddhipratibimba*)—that [the soul] is not that [cognition].

The detailed exposition of this is to be found in the *Siddhāntaleśasaṃgraha* composed by Appayadīkṣita. It is quite clear that, under both views—that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection in the intellect (*buddhi*) or that it is the intellect itself—the existence of the *jīva* would be impossible. However, according to the scriptural (*āgama*) view, it is like the case of a prince brought up in the family of hunters.

The Great Lord (Maheśvara) himself—whose supreme sovereignty is veiled by His own freedom—is the individual soul (jīva). The intended meaning is that without his intellect (buddhi), there would be no "establishment," that is, no stable existence or the empirical functioning of duality. That intellect is endowed with a stainless nature, consisting primarily of the quality of purity (sattva). [It perceives] Me, who am called the individual soul and am limited...

Whether she is like a reflection or has attained identity [with him], in the external sense, she—being born of a pure lineage—remains having brought me under her control through her stainless nature and because of our equal character; such is the intended meaning, and it is indeed logical. || 34 ||
She immediately and directly became one whose self-nature was absorbed in that [state], joined with that wicked actress who possessed a manifold nature. (35)
[The intellect] has as its intrinsic nature that [object], having a form conjoined with the intellect; however, according to the externalist view, the meaning is "the mind directed toward that.

That refers to my friend, the intellect. By means of that ignorance—described as "corrupt" because it is the cause of its own destruction—a wondrous, marvelous, and inconceivable (or, according to manuscripts *k* and *kh*, unformed) nature [is produced].
Her own nature is such that she is called Naṭyā (the Actress), because she captivates [the hearts of beings] by displaying her own divine play (līlā). || 35 ||
She was brought there by her son acting in her absence and accused by him;
her son was extremely foolish, his eyes rolling from intoxication.

"Bringer of indirect activity"—meaning she has been brought to, or led toward, a state of exclusively desiring indirect objects such as heaven and the like. By that "unreal" [one], my friend—the intellect—[was affected]. The sense is that through ignorance (avidyā), the intellect became intent upon desiring heaven and so forth.
According to the external interpretation, the "unreal" one was brought to an indirect state—that is, a secluded condition—and was assailed by her own son.
"She has become my friend" means that she has been assailed by delusion (*moha*), which is the son of her own ignorance (*avidyā*).

The sense is that the intellect (*buddhi*) has, through ignorance, attained a particular state of mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of delusion, which obstructs right inquiry while it is intent upon desire. The cause of that ignorance's stupidity (*mauḍhya*) is as follows:
"Madirā," and so forth. This qualification is intended to illuminate that my intellect became deluded and turned toward sinful conduct.
He would always enjoy her by taking hold of her even in my very presence;
with all her limbs thus seized by him, she was enjoyed by him day after day.
He says that his friend's intellect has become abundant with delusion through the practice of evil:
"Having assailed," etc. "In my presence" means that the intellect's manifestation is dependent upon the light of consciousness (citprakāśa);
this is the intended meaning. That intellect [was assailed] by that delusion. || 37 ||
He never left me, and I was touched by him as well;
consequently, a son was born to that fool, possessing a form similar to his own.

That friend never left me, even at the time of union with my beloved; the intended meaning is that this is because the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) are manifested only by relying upon the light of consciousness (*cit-prakāśa*). For that reason—that she did not leave me—I was touched by that "dear friend," who is in fact the deluded self (*mūḍha-ātman*).

The sense is that it is of the nature of delusion (*moha*) and so forth belonging to consciousness (*cit*), which has attained identity with the intellect (*buddhi*)—whether that intellect is delimited by the mind or has attained identity with it—just as the space delimited by a jar or fire that has attained identity with an iron ball possesses a circular or other such shape.
*Tataḥ* means after long association. For the deluded one, there is a son in the form of the mind, which is of a shape similar to its own [delusion].

[The mind] is born. Although the mind exists even prior [to this], nevertheless, like a son already present in the father’s body by way of his own vigor (*vīrya*), the mind previously existed in a subtle form; however, immediately after its connection with delusion (*moha*) in the intellect (*buddhi*), because of the increase of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and so forth, the mind became fully developed, like a son born from the father—this is the intended meaning.
Because it is of the nature of non-existence, its form should be understood as being similar [to that]. || 38 ||
He quickly became a youth of extremely fickle disposition,
possessed of his father’s folly and his grandmother’s virtues.

Young and capable of worldly activity, he is shrouded by the quality of dullness arising from the delusion of his father, and by that capacity which, without depending on anything other than itself, serves as the material cause for the manifold creation of his grandmother, Ignorance (avidyā). || 39 ||
He was surrounded by his grandmother named Śūnyā and his father named Mūḍha, who possessed the power to manifest many diverse magical emanations.

Having first stated their names, he describes the qualities of the mind: "By the grandmother," etc. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the grandmother of the mind; because its own nature dissolves upon investigation, she is named "Void" (*śūnya*). Delusion (*moha*) is the father;
because it causes a state of bewilderment, it is called "Bewildered" (*mūḍha*). From these two, the one named "Unsteady" (*asthira*) was instructed.
The connection. || 40 ||
Named Asthira, he became trained and himself exceedingly skilled;
indeed, he attained a speed that was unimpeded and ever-increasingly swift.

Through his father’s instruction he attained delusion; through his grandmother’s instruction he attained the capacity for diverse creation. Being himself exceedingly clever, he attained an unobstructed course—meaning a course that is faster than fast, exceedingly swift. Thus, under the influence of the delusion of the intellect, the mind became firmly rooted.

The intended meaning of the distinguished work (*viśiṣṭagrantha*)— [whether by Śiṣṭa or Vaśiṣṭa]— is that [the mind] was at times unstable due to its constant flickering, intent upon endless and diverse imaginings, and averse to inquiry because of its delusion. || 41 ||
Thus my friend, though pure by nature from birth, has attained extreme defilement through association with the unchaste. (42)
She was accompanied by her friend, her beloved son, and one possessed of a wicked nature; she herself was endowed with a firm affection for them due to their long-standing association.

In the manner thus described, my friend— the intellect— has fallen into extreme impurity, which obscures the nature of *sattva* and is characterized by *tamas*, due to association with the unchaste, that is, through attachment to ignorance (*avidyā*). This has occurred because of a firm attachment to her friend,
ignorance, and to her beloved son, delusion (*moha*), as well as to the mind (*manas*), all of which possess an unreal nature.

Because it is always transformed into that very form, the meaning is as follows: the intellect (*buddhi*), having abandoned its own true nature (*satsvarūpa*), exists perpetually through the nature of delusion (*moha*) and through the nature of determining the beauty and other qualities of objects imagined by the mind. || 43 ||
My friend gradually abandoned her passion for me in every way; as for me, being naturally straightforward, I was able to easily relinquish that union. (44)
"Jahau" means: due to her firm attachment to those who were deluded by the passage of time, she abandoned her attachment and affection for me.

The intended meaning is that even the investigation into the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of a limited consciousness characterized as an agent and an enjoyer, did not exist in her intellect. Now, if this is so, has your own attachment to her also been abandoned? (k, kh: "then")

If it be argued that this might be so, he says "no"—namely, "I [am not]. She is straight by nature. The intended meaning is that for those who are naturally straightforward, affection arises solely without any external cause such as the pleasure derived from another. || 44 ||
Lacking self-control, I was entirely devoted to her and followed her in every way;
meanwhile, her foolish lover was constantly enjoying her company.
Because my pleasure is not dependent on any external cause, she is unable to abandon her affection; for this very reason, being devoted to that [pleasure], she follows it in every way.

The meaning is that she became one whose character was identical to His. The sense is that, because my nature consists of pure consciousness (cinmātra), she attained a conformity with the intellect (buddhi) through association with the attributes of the intellect, which are like reflections. Now...
Thus, immediately after attaining conformity with the intellect. || 45 ||
He became entirely intent on forcibly assailing me;
yet I, though pure by nature, did not in reality fall under his power.
Thinking, "She has followed my beloved," that fool became intent on forcibly seizing me as well for his enjoyment. Even though this occurred, I, being pure by nature, did not fall under his power.
For even when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the objects of the intellect are dense, the identity with the *jīva* does not depart. Thus...

Although there is the appearance of contact with delusion in the form of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) on the part of consciousness (*cit*) which has attained identity with the intellect (*buddhi*),
there is in reality no contact with delusion, just as in the case of a reflection in a mirror (in this reading, the previous word *darpaṇasya* is unnecessary).
The state of being. || 46 ||
Nevertheless, a great scandal arose against me everywhere in the world: "This [earth] is being enjoyed in every way by a fool. (47)

*Parīvādaḥ* means censure. He explains the very nature of censure with the words "by the deluded one" (*mūḍhena*). The intended meaning is that the undiscriminating person superimposes the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) upon the Self in every respect and in all places. || 47 ||
Having entrusted her son, named Asthira, to me, my friend was embraced by her beloved and became entirely devoted to him.

That intellect was her companion; "intent on that" means intent on delusion. The sense is that the intellect, being unable even to determine what was imagined by the mind, became of a single form with delusion alone. || 48 ||
Then, having been properly cherished and nourished by me while still unstable, he reached maturity and,
with the consent of his grandmother, entered into a union with a woman.

Then, after I had been entrusted as a son to my grandmother— that is, to Mūḍhamātā (the Mother of Delusion), which is to say, to Ignorance— she, having attained the state of being the extreme delusion of the intellect, caused the mind, which had entered into identity with the consciousness,
to become capable of conceptualization; the intention is that it then became solely intent upon such conceptualization.
Since conceptualization is conducive to ignorance, it should be understood that it is approved by Him. (49)
For that beloved of his, named Capalā, at every moment assumes a different and charming form that is pleasing to her lover. (50)
And imagination is called "fickle"; it belongs to the dear mind. 50.
Thus, by virtue of her own exceptional skill, that most proficient woman brought him—who was dear to her and capable of producing wonder—under her complete control. 51.
The intention is that, by the power of his own skill, he brought under control the mind which was intent on various conceptualizations at every moment. || 51 ||
Though unstable, it travels and returns constantly for hundreds of innumerable yojanas in a mere instant, yet it never experiences fatigue.
The mind is unstable. || 52 ||
Whenever he desires to go somewhere or whenever he becomes unsteady, she,
though fickle herself, indeed assumes his desired form.
"It strives" means that wherever the mind goes, there it indeed performs manifold and diverse conceptualizations; such is the sense. || 53 ||
Staying here and there, she indeed delights her own beloved;
thus that fickle woman is fully joined with the unsteady. 54.

"Delights indeed" means that she herself, having internally conceived a kingdom of the mind and so forth, attains the semblance of happiness produced by that; such is the sense. The construction is: "being united, she gave birth to sons."
She gave birth to five sons who were devoted to their mother and father;
they are capable and have been established by me as the fivefold friendship.

"Suṣuve" means "gave birth to. The "sons" are the organs of cognition (*jñānendriyas*). Since the functions of the sense organs do not arise when the mind is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), it is through the mind's conceptualization that the sense organs proceed outward.
Because the outward movement of the sense organs is dependent upon the mind’s conceptualization, they should be understood as being "devoted to mother and father."
"By my friend she has been placed [within me]"—thus is described the attainment of identity with the mind. || 55 ||
Out of affection for my friend, I made those sons exceedingly powerful;
then those five sons of the fickle woman became separate from one another.

They made those sons even more powerful—meaning, through the excellence of their identity with the mind (*cittādātmya*), they became equal to independent luminosity (*svatantra-prakāśa*). They established an excellent, wondrous, and exceedingly vast abode; being perfectly cultivated by their mother, they brought their father under their own control. (57)

"Variegated" (*vicitram*) means the locus for the perception of various scents and so forth; "vast" (*ativistṛtam*), because even when grasping countless objects, it is not filled by their contents; and they made it the "excellent abode" (*śreṣṭham āyatanam*) because all worldly activity depends upon it—the intended meaning is that [the sense-faculties] came to be presided over by their respective spheres (*golaka*). *Mātrā*.

The meaning is that [the senses] have been manifested and nourished by conceptualization; the mind, being intent on discursive thought, has always been directed outward through the gateway of the sense organs. || 57 ||
Moment by moment, they lead that father to his own abode;
however, being unstable there, he enters the abode of the eldest son.
He demonstrates the subjugation of the father by analyzing it as follows: "They bring [him]"—the eldest son is the sense organ of hearing. || 58 ||
He heard various sounds, both melodious and otherwise;
in some places there was sweet singing, and in others, very charming instrumental music. (59)
The others are various. He says this very thing [in the verse]: "In some cases," etc. (59).
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Atharvan mantras, the Śāstras, Āgamas, and Itihāsas, and even the tinkling of ornaments—[all these were heard]. (60)
And hearing the song of the swarms of bees and the sweet fifth-note warbling of the cuckoo—
thus listening to such enchanting sounds at the direction of his son.
The sense is that the mind enters the faculty of hearing and, through the door of the ear, transforms itself into the form of various sounds. || 61 ||
Delighted, he first fell under the influence of his son, but then the son commanded otherwise;
he heard terrifying sounds, harsh and piercing to the ears, which were contrary [to his wishes].

"Under the influence of her son, she directed her ears firmly [toward him]; otherwise, she would have commanded differently. This means that because the mind's apprehension of external objects is dependent upon the senses, she "listened" by way of directing the senses. || 62 ||
The roaring of lions and other beasts, the thundering of clouds, and likewise the crash of lightning—terrifying and capable of shattering the cosmic egg and causing miscarriages—[were heard]. (63)
The phrase beginning with "brahmāṇḍa" is a specific qualification for the sound of a thunderbolt. || 63 ||

Having heard this, he was greatly alarmed and likewise heard elsewhere the sounds of weeping, lamentation, and various expressions of grief and sorrow. (Note: In this verse, the order of the first and second halves [pādas] is inverted.)
Then, led by the second son, Asthira went to that palace;
there he saw auspicious seats of soft touch.
The second son is the sense of touch. || 65 ||
And beds and garments, even those with a rough touch, as well as objects with a cold touch and likewise those with a warm touch. (66)
Having observed various objects with touches that were neither hot nor cold, he was delighted upon seeing what was beneficial and despondent at seeing what was harmful. (67)
Then, having reached the abode of the third son, that unstable one beheld various objects of beautiful form and diverse colors.
The third is the eye. || 68 ||
Red, white, yellow, blue, green, and pale-red; as well as smoke-colored, tawny, brownish-grey, black, and variegated. (69)
[He saw beings] that were thick, thin, minute, long, extended, and likewise round;
half-circular, elongated circles, beautiful, and terrifying. (70)
Since the visual faculty has as its objects forms, their various dimensions, and so forth, he says: "gross, impermanent," and so on. (70)
He saw his father again, seeing at one place things loathsome, radiant, fierce, and sight-stealing, and elsewhere things beneficial and their opposites.
[They are] without light and without darkness; of what kind? Depriving the vision [of truth]. (71)
Following this method of restraint, he made his own meditation manifold;
there, he gradually obtained flowers, fruits, and various kinds of food.
The fourth is the *rāsana*, which is to be known as that which is inferred from taste, such as flowers and so forth. || 72 ||
There were indeed flavorful drinks, foods to be licked, sucked, and eaten—sweet as nectar, as well as others of sour taste. (73)
Some are pungent, some bitter, and some astringent;
others are alkaline, sweet, or sour, as well as pungent, sour, and salty. (74)
"Sweet, sour, and so forth" refers to a mixed flavor (miśrarasa). || 74 ||
Then the youngest son, accompanied by his own offspring, tasted various pungent and bitter juices of diverse natures. (75)
The last is the nose. || 75 ||
He led his father to his own station, which was exceedingly wonderful;
there, he offered him many flowers and fruits. (76)
Grasses, grains, and herbs, as well as all other things from every side— those with pleasant fragrances and those with foul odors, those with mild scents and those with pungent smells. || 77 ||
"Entities" means objects. He states those very things as "fragrant," and so forth. || 77 ||
Entering and even settling within the house of his sons, he encountered the scents of delusion, the scents of knowledge, and the variously variegated scents of fainting.
The scent of delusion produces delusion; the same applies to what follows. 78.
He delighted in what was beneficial at times and despaired at times over what was harmful;
always intent on coming and going, he shone within the dwellings of his sons. (79)
Out of affection for their father, those sons, being deprived of him,
never at any time experienced various sensual pleasures, even to a slight degree.
"They are the sons" means that the sense organs lack the capacity to grasp their objects independently, having abandoned the mind (manas). This is the intended meaning. || 80 ||
But the unstable one, having enjoyed those many sensory objects in the house of his son and having stolen other sensory objects as well, secretly leads them to his own abode. (81)

The mind, being attached to the sense organs, encounters external objects and experiences the pleasure and other sensations produced by them at that very moment. Furthermore, having grasped certain objects internally through the medium of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) in a hidden form, it remains in its own seat within the heart and conceptualizes that object through recollection and so forth.
He says that one experiences that pleasure: "unsteady" (asthira). || 81 ||
Together with his fickle wife, but without his sons, he himself constantly enjoys [pleasures] in secret; moreover, there is another fickle woman, his sister.
In secret, in dreams, and so forth; other [is] hope. 82.
Mahāśanā chose as her husband that man who was pleasing to her mind, even though he was unstable;
for when he became excessively attached to her, he indeed became unstable.
The meaning is that hope for the enjoyment of those unstable objects has increased as if it were permanent.
Then, intent on procuring enjoyments for her pleasure, he brought much [food], yet having consumed it in a mere moment, [she remained unsatisfied]. || 84 ||
Due to his extreme attachment to that great hunger, he was constantly intent on procuring objects of enjoyment for her pleasure. (84)
Furthermore, overcome by hunger, he always sends word for what is dear [to her] for the sake of procuring enjoyments; she, too, constantly looks on to procure it. (85)
The intended meaning is that his mind, possessed by insatiable desires, was always intent upon the means of attaining sense objects. || 85 ||
Having eaten in an instant that food brought by her five sons and well-prepared by her beloved husband as well, she was once again tormented by hunger. (86)
By the sons of a co-wife, that is, by the sense-faculties. || 86 ||
She always sent word regarding her enjoyments and her dear sons;
then, in a short time, she gave birth to a pair of sons.
Regarding the acquisition of enjoyments, that is, in the matter of procuring them. || 87 ||
Jvālāmukha was the elder of the two, while the other was of censurable conduct; nevertheless, those two sons were always most dear to their mother. (88)

Between those two sons, the elder was Jvālāmukha-Krodha (Anger with a Fiery Face), and the other was Lobha (Greed) of censurable conduct. The intention is that because of the mother Āśā’s (Hope) excessive longing, the predominance of Krodha and Lobha came about. || 88 ||
When he, being unstable and attached to great hunger, becomes closely joined [to it], then his entire body is licked by the flames from the mouth of the fire. (89)
The essential meaning is that whenever one is under the sway of desire, at those very times one encounters great suffering produced by anger and greed. || 89 ||
Unsteady and extremely afflicted, he indeed fell into a deep swoon;
at times, he was joined by his beloved son who followed a censurable conduct.
Indeed, he becomes censured by all, for he is born as one equal to the dead;
thus, when he has become unstable, he is solely intent upon the experience of suffering.
From greed comes contemptibility, and from that, a state equal to death is evident. || 91 ||
Then my friend, who was virtuous by nature, out of excessive affection for her son named Asthira, became united with him in his suffering.

Thus, when the mind (manas) encounters extreme suffering, because of the identity of the mind and the intellect (buddhi), the intellect also encounters suffering; so he says: "Then... Here, "friend" refers to the intellect, and "son" refers to the mind. || 92 ||
Overwhelmed by the burden of suffering, joined with one of censurable conduct,
and likewise embraced by her grandson Jvālāmukha, she remained steadfast in her virtue.
Severely scorched and censured by the world, she became as if dead;
and I, who had always followed her, O beloved, became almost extinguished myself. (94)

Regarding that friend: because her own adjunct, the intellect (buddhi), is pervaded by rajas and tamas, its essential nature does not manifest; thus, it should be understood as being almost extinguished. || 94 ||
Thus, for many years, she was afflicted by the suffering of her friend; he became unstable and lacked self-control due to his addiction to excessive eating. (95)
"I was suffering"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. || 95 ||
By some past action, he reached a city with ten gates at one time;
there, afflicted by great hunger, he was joined by his sons, mother, and others.
The city is the body, possessing ten gates along with the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). This occurs due to some *prārabdha* karma;
in the external sense, however, it refers to actions such as battle, or at the time of creation following a dissolution. (96)
Desiring happiness, he dwelt there while experiencing misery day and night;
with all his limbs scorched by his two sons, he was reviled every single day. (97)
"Seeking happiness": the sense is that by the mere desire for happiness, only suffering is obtained. || 97 ||
For he was always being pulled hither and thither by his two beloved wives,
even as he entered and settled down within the five abodes of his sons.
By means of the two beloved conceptualizations; [it refers] to the sons, that is, the sense faculties. || 98 ||
She falls into extreme exhaustion and finds no happiness anywhere;
likewise, my friend is utterly distressed by the suffering of her son. (99)
The mind is the son; the intellect is the friend. || 99 ||
She, who was possessed of a conduct as censurable as Jvālāmukha and who was a great eater, lived in that city for what seemed like a state of unconsciousness.
Due to the departure of the sattvic portion, she is as if unconscious in that city, which is her body; "mahāśanā" means great desire. 100.
She was nourished by her foolish father-in-law, who was known as Śūnya, and likewise greatly fostered by her co-wife, who was named Capalā. || 101 ||
By the ignorance called "emptiness," which is the grandmother of the Lord. || 101 ||
Standing before him, she brought her fickle husband under her own control;
and there, out of affection for my friend, I remained, devoted to her.

He says that the mind is "overcome" by a deeply rooted disposition arising from the conceptualizations of ignorance and delusion—this is what is meant by the word "unsteady. By the word "friend," the sense is that for consciousness (cit), which has attained identity with the intellect (buddhi), imitation of the intellect is necessarily constant. || 102 ||
O beloved, if I were not there for even a single moment, I would be as good as dead from grief for my friend, though I am intent on protecting everyone.
"If I..."—the sense is that, like a reflection without a mirror, nothing superimposed can exist without a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). || 103 ||

Not even a single one among them would have survived there, for everything was indeed protected by me; yet, being empty, I attained emptiness, and through my folly, I reached the state of a fool. (104)
Because it is the locus of all, he speaks of its imitation of everything (the meaning is:
its imitation, following, or manifestation in the form of everything). [This is expressed in] "by the void," and so forth; it is joined with the void. 104.
From the unstable, one attains instability; from the fickle, fickleness;
from the flame-mouthed, a state of burning; and from the censurable conduct, the nature of that very conduct.
And through union with my friend, I likewise assumed her various forms;
yet if I were to release my friend, she would perish in a mere instant. (106)
He states that my nature as consciousness possesses manifold forms solely due to its identity with the intellect (*buddhi*), saying: "through union with a female friend" (*sakhī-saṃyogataḥ*).
Regarding the word "female friend": the intention is that since I am the substratum even of the intellect, the intellect itself could not exist without me. (106)
"Because of my association with them, all foolish people indeed call me unfaithful; yet the wise know me to be pure and stainless. (107)

Due to the association—that is, the coexistence—of those [attributes] such as intellect and the rest, all people declare me, though pure, to be unfaithful; for this very reason, they are deluded. [They perceive] the Self, which is of the nature of pure, indivisible consciousness, merely through its imitation of the forms of momentary, visible objects.

The intended meaning is that the Buddhists and others assert [the self] to be momentary. However, the wise, possessing subtle intellects, disregard that view because it renders impossible all worldly transactions—the root of which is the continuity of memory and so forth—and instead know me to be stainless, free from the impurity of limitations such as time and space. || 107 ||
My mother is a great saintly being, pure and of stainless form;
she is vaster than space and subtler than an atom. (108)

If it is asked, "How can there be purity for one who has associated with the wicked?", [the author] first praises the Mother in order to state that it is due to the majesty of the great mantra obtained from her: "The Great Chaste One," and so forth.
According to the external perspective, she is the Great Chaste One, a woman of great devotion to her husband; therefore, she is pure, being free from mental defects.

She is of stainless form and free from bodily defects. She is more expansive than even space in terms of her fame. She is subtle because she is endowed with a subtle intellect and other qualities, being subtler than even an atom. In the internal sense, she is the Great Chaste One (*mahāsatī*), whose nature is an uninterrupted existence; she is utterly pure.

The meaning is that she is of one essence because her nature is pure consciousness alone; she is of stainless form, being unassailed by the impurities of ignorance and the like which veil the true nature [of reality]; she is more expansive even than space because she pervades through both causality and luminosity; and she is woven through even the interior of the most minute atom.
And because it is difficult to know, it is subtle in comparison to the atom.
Though omniscient, she knows nothing; though the agent of all, she is devoid of action;
though the support of all, she has no support; though the foundation of all, she is not dependent. || 109 ||

From the external perspective, although she is by nature omniscient, due to the absence of the conceit induced by that [knowledge], she remains as if knowing nothing at all; the same applies hereafter. She is the support (*āśraya*) because she nourishes all, and the substratum (*ādhāra*) of all arts (*kalā*).
From the internal perspective, however, omniscience and so forth are produced by the objects of perception; thus, she is inherently one who knows only a little, and so on.
Because it manifests everywhere, it is the support of all. 109.
Though she possesses all forms, she is formless; though joined with everything, she is unjoined.
Though appearing everywhere, she is not known by anyone anywhere. 110.

In the external sense, she is one who possesses every form, endowed with the beauty of all limbs, possessed of all wealth, grain, and so forth, and renowned for shining everywhere through feminine virtues such as compassion and good character; yet, although well-known, she is not known by anyone anywhere because she always remains within the inner apartments. But in the internal sense:
Just as a mirror, although it possesses all reflected forms, is to be understood as being devoid of the nature of those reflections, so it is here:

though the mirror appears in every part of the reflection, it is not known by anyone apart from the reflection; likewise, consciousness (cit), though appearing everywhere within all entities (bhāva), is not known apart from those entities.
Mahānandā is herself beyond joy; she is devoid of mother and father, and she has sons like me who are beyond counting.

On the external level, she possesses great joy caused by worldly prosperity; yet, even being such, she is "joyless" (*anānandā*) because her joy is not manifest to others due to the absence of arrogance arising from that joy. She has abandoned both mother and father, for, through her status as a great chaste woman devoted solely to her husband, she has renounced affection for her parents.

The intended meaning is as follows: In the internal sense, although she is of the nature of great bliss (*mahānanda*), she is "without bliss" (*anānandā*) because no bliss other than her own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is possible.
Because she is eternal, she is "devoid of mother and father. She is "beyond number" (*asaṃkhyā*), meaning she is free from numerical limitation. || 111 ||
Just as the countless waves of the ocean are all of the same nature, O Prince, so indeed do all those sisters become equal in their conduct to me.

Just as the waves are innumerable, so too is my host of sisters innumerable. By this illustration, it should be understood that in reality, the daughters are not distinct from the mother. Their conduct is devoted to their friends and family. (112)
And I, Mahāmantravatī, joined with all these groups of female friends, was devoted to her, who was like a mother to me in her very nature. (113)
"Thus, even though I am associated with and devoted to the wicked, I remain untouched by their defects. If one asks why this is so, he says: "I possess such power of mantra.
In the internal sense, however, the "great mantra" is the power of *māyā*. By means of that, I [remain] in my pure essential nature, even regarding that which is impossible to accomplish.
The intended meaning is: "I shall accomplish the illumination of saṃsāra. || 113 ||
In this city, whenever the friend’s son becomes utterly exhausted, he then lies down quite securely and without hesitation upon his mother’s lap. (114)
Having thus related his own history by way of digression, he again describes the history of the friend’s son and others:

"But in the internal state (*āntarapakṣe*), due to the exhaustion of matured karma through experience and because other [karmas] have not yet matured, the mind rests in the lap of the mother Intellect (*buddhi*) in the interim, attaining dissolution. (114)
But when that unstable one is asleep, then his sons and others attain sleep; no other whatsoever remains awake. (115)

The sons are the senses, as well as anger and greed; by the word "etcetera," the wife and mother are included. However, from the internal perspective, the intended meaning is that when the mind has dissolved, everything—the senses and so forth—has likewise dissolved. || 115 ||
Then his dear friend, named Pracāra, who was devoted to the unstable one, protected that city by constantly patrolling at the pair of eastern gates.
She who is the mother even of one who is unstable is my friend’s daughter;
she who is her friend is my mother-in-law, who is unchaste by nature. (117)

Then, at the time of total sleep—that is, during deep slumber—the "movement" is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Since it is possible for both [mind and breath] to be restrained when either one of the two, mind or breath, is restrained, the vital breath possesses the qualities of being dear and a friend.
