The "pair of former doors" refers to the two nostrils. When she, my friend and unstable mother, is together with her son, that is, with her offspring and so forth—then...
"She slept" is the ellipsis; her friend and mother-in-law, whose name is "Emptiness," is Ignorance (avidyā). || 117 ||
Having covered them all, she protected them along with her son;
thus, while everyone was asleep, she then approached her own mother.

She protects all the unstable ones and so forth while they are asleep, together with her son named Delusion (*moha*). The intended meaning is that, from the internal perspective, everything becomes shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*), whose nature is delusion. || 118 ||
Indeed, I am delighted when embraced by my mother for a long time;
yet, day after day, I quickly follow after them as soon as they have risen. (119)

Regarding the internal state, however, the intended meaning is that during deep sleep, due to the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that cause differentiation, one attains a state of fullness and becomes blissful—that is, one becomes of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*). "I am following along" means that I attain identity with each of those [states].
This friend of the unstable one is this very powerful force known as "activity" (*pracāra*).
Day after day, he nourishes all those with unstable faces.
The vital breath (prāṇa) is called "circulation" (pracāra). It nourishes the mind, the ears, and so forth, which have unstable openings.

The sense is that the mind and the other faculties possess the capacity rooted in the essence of the food-juice (annarasa), which is cooked by the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) stimulated by the prāṇa. || 120 ||
Having become manifold from his single state, he pervades and protects the city and its inhabitants every day, and he also unites them all together.
That is the vital breath (prāṇa). It unites—that is, it joins—[the senses] with their respective objects through its various functions, such as the activity of prāṇa and so forth. || 121 ||
For without that [thread], they would indeed be disjoined and utterly lost, like pearls separated from one another when the string of a necklace is missing. (122)
He states, by means of an illustration, that this very [Self] is woven through the mind and other faculties in the form of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), using the phrase "without him":

"separated" means disconnected from their objects; "destroyed" means rendered as good as lost due to their incapacity for action; they are like gems strung together in the form of a garland. Of these—
The sense is that just as the state of being a garland perishes for those things that have become separate. || 122 ||
Having thus united with me, he joined me with all [the others] in that supreme city;
for I have indeed been fully restored to life by him in that city as its architect.

"Having united," meaning having attained identity with Me; [the Lord] unites Me with all [the faculties]. The purport is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the rest attain identity with the mind (*citta*) precisely through the medium of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This will be explained further on in the passage beginning with:
"When the thread of the vital breath is within the senses, the internal organ, and so forth" (20.35).

"Regarding the term *sūtradhāra*: just as the stage manager (*sūtradhāra*) is the initiator of the drama, so too is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) the initiator of the activities of the mind and the other faculties. || 123 ||
When that city was worn out, he would swiftly lead her to another city;
by adopting such a course of action, he became the lord of the cities.

"In that city" means in the body. "He leads them"—that is, the intellect and the other faculties. The sense is that at the time of departure, because the intellect and the others dissolve into the vital breath (prāṇa), it is the vital breath that leads them. He became the lord, the mind known as "unsteady. || 124 ||
Surely, among many diverse things that are unstable,
even the son of Satī is unstable in succession, despite having taken refuge in the Great Power.
The phrase "of many Purāṇas" is to be connected with what precedes it. [He is] the vital breath (prāṇa) of great strength. || 125 ||
And by me, through the complete union with my two wives, Capalā and Mahāśanā, has the state of being a partaker of suffering been cultivated in every way to the utmost degree. (126)
If it is asked, "How can even the son of a virtuous woman—who has been nurtured by you, who possess great mantras, and who relies upon great power—be a partaker of suffering?
[the author] replies, "From association with an unvirtuous wife and so forth," beginning with the verse starting "capala... (verse 126).
And by a pair of sons named Jvālāmukha and Nindyavṛtta,
as well as by five other sons, he was dragged away in every direction.
"Drawn away" means that through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is the arising of desire; from that, activity toward sense objects;
and caused by that, the arising of anger and greed. The intention is that by this, one becomes a partaker of suffering. || 127 ||
His self overwhelmed by great afflictions and devoid of even a trace of happiness, he was dragged hither and thither in various places by his five sons. || 128 ||
He explains the manner in which the great afflictions are acquired, beginning with the words "from this," and so forth. (128)
In some places, being excessively agitated by the flickering [flame], he fell into exhaustion;
in other places, for the sake of great food, he rushed about to eat.
He became weary; that is, he experienced suffering. || 129 ||
In some places, seized by the flames of the fire-mouths, with his feet and head scorched,
he falls into a great swoon, remaining unconscious of any remedy for it.
The remedy for that—the remedy for anger—is tranquility. || 130 ||
Having encountered a censurable situation somewhere, being reviled and rebuked by others, he, overwhelmed with grief, considers himself as good as dead. (131)
Through reproach and threats, he considers himself as good as dead; therefore, he becomes consumed by grief. || 131 ||
Accompanied by a wicked wife and son, deluded and born of a low family,
he is constantly overwhelmed by his wife and son and led away by them.
Because he has foolish sons, he is born of a low family. || 132 ||
He dwelt with them indeed in various cities, both high and low;
in some places, in regions filled with wildernesses and inhabited by tribes of flesh-eaters.
He dwells together with them in various places, both high and low—that is, among those who are superior and inferior.
Regarding such a person’s attainment of hell, he says: "In some places" means in cities filled and pervaded by *kāntāras*, which are wildernesses;
and in those inhabited by a "troop of flesh-eaters," meaning a multitude of carnivorous creatures such as jackals and the like.
The intended meaning is that one perceives one's own body as being situated in a vast forest and pervaded by crows and other such creatures. || 133 ||
In some places they are in regions of extreme heat, in others in places frozen by cold;
in some they dwell amidst flowing putrid waters, and in others in dense, pitch-black darkness.
"Pūtī" means those situated in rivers characterized by foul odors; the grammatical connection is that he dwelt within the bodies of trees and other such things in the densest darkness. 134.
Thus, as my son— who was unstable— was further afflicted by extreme suffering,
my friend too became bewildered by grief due to that constant association with misery.
O beloved, although her true nature was ever present, I remained utterly deluded day after day, like a fool, being solely devoted to that family. (136)
I am virtuous by my very nature; in reality, because there is no attachment to that [nature], I am also pure by nature. "In vain" means pointlessly, without cause. || 136 ||

For who, having fallen into bad company, could ever obtain even a slight measure of happiness? Just as a man traveling through a desert in the summer heat might fail to find relief from his thirst. (137)
If it is asked, "Why have you fallen into such folly? he says, "For who indeed... [referring to] the result of bad association.
When a very long time had passed in this manner, that friend of mine, overcome with extreme exhaustion, met with me in private. (138)

Thus, through the experience of suffering, when the past has come to an end, "having met" means that somehow, by the grace of Īśvara, she— whose form is pure consciousness— became united with me in solitude, in a secluded state where sense objects do not appear; this is to be understood from the internal perspective.
Having obtained the counsel of Madekasaṅga and others, and having secured a virtuous husband, she conquered her own son, killed him, and bound his children and the rest. (139)

Because of the absence of attachment to *māyā*. There is the logical connection between purity (*śuddhi*) and the manifestation of the form of the Self (*ātman*), because detachment (*vairāgya*) and the vision of the Self (*ātma-darśana*) are mutual causes for one another. As it has been said: "Devotion, the experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.2.42), and so forth.
And as it is said: "Upon seeing the Supreme, one turns back" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.55). Through dispassion, [one attains] discernment, the true lord;
[one attains] the mind, the son. Having slain anger and greed, and having bound the senses. || 139 ||
Having united with me, she quickly reached my mother’s city;
there, being free from all taint, she embraced my mother again and again. (140)

"Having united with me," that is, having attained the state of perfect oneness through non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). The term "united" (*saṅgatā*) previously referred to the knowledge resulting from investigation through hearing (*śravaṇa*); now, the distinction is that it becomes direct (*aparokṣa*) through reflection (*manana*) and meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*). My mother’s city.
The state of being the unconditioned, pure consciousness-self; "swiftly" means in the moment immediately following [the arising of] knowledge.

By the phrase "embrace again and again my Mother," the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is to be understood. The repetition "again and again" indicates that within the intervals of the intellect (*buddhi*), there is the appearance of duality. For this very reason, he says "stainless."

The meaning is that for one whose form is like a burnt cloth—namely, for one in whom the appearance of duality has been consumed—it does not, as before, produce the defilement consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are the root of *saṃsāra*. This very point has been stated [in the Bhagavad Gītā]:
"Even having slain these worlds, he neither slays nor is he bound" (BhG 18.17). || 140 ||
Her very nature immediately became immersed in an ocean of bliss;
in the same way, you too, having restrained the misconduct arising from your friend, [should act]. (141)

[Objection: "But surely, even in the absence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are the root of *saṃsāra*, there would still be experienced suffering. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Bliss," etc. The intended meaning is that since it is precisely the conceit (*abhimāna*), which is the cause of the latent impressions, that constitutes the cause of suffering. By using the first person [in the verb] "it did not exist" (*abhavat*), he shows that bondage and liberation belong to the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, and not [to the Self]. Thus ends [the section on] such liberation.
The phrase "mine" (mama) has been explained; it refers to the mind arising from friendship. || 141 ||
"O Lord, having reached your own mother, may you always attain happiness.
O Lord, this abode of bliss, experienced by me myself, has been told to you. (142)
"Having attained" means having attained, together with the intellect (*buddhi*), the state of being of the nature of pure consciousness delimited [by the intellect]. || 142 ||
[Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Bandha," within the "Story of Hemacūḍa" in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the sixth chapter:
Having thus heard the beloved’s words, Hemacūḍa was greatly amazed;
laughing, he then questioned that wise beloved, though he himself was ignorant.
In this chapter, it is correctly demonstrated through verses that faith is the excellent means for attaining the highest good,
whereas fallacious reasoning leads only to misfortune.
"O beloved, that which you have spoken appears to me as if inscribed in the sky;
today your word is without support, yet I know this entirely."
Like something inscribed [in the sky]; the meaning is "as if impossible. It is without support and without object. || 2 ||
Surely you are born of an Apsaras, nurtured by a seer in the forest;
though your youth has begun, you have not yet fully attained the bloom of adolescence.
If one asks "Why?", he says: "Surely" (*nūnam*), meaning "completely" (*alam*) or "absolutely" (*atyantam*). || 3 ||
With words resembling the speech of one possessed by a spirit, you will describe the duration of many thousands of years in an excessive manner. (4)
With excessive, extreme, and abundant speech. || 4 ||
Without a detailed account, how can I understand the truth?
Tell me: where is that friend of yours, and where is the son of your friend who has been bound? (5)
If it is asked, "Whence [comes] the lack of coherence in my words?"—the word "lack of coherence" (*asandarbhatā*) being read as a separate term—the author says: "He speaks. || 5 ||
"Where are those cities situated? Tell me that.
But what is the use of that account? Tell me instead, where is that female friend? (6)
I have not obtained a female companion from my mother; consider that matter.
There is a noble lady in my father's own inner apartments, for no other is dear to him.
"I did not obtain the female companion given to me by my mother. My noble mother is in the inner apartments;
inquire about her and ask her. Furthermore, I have no other mother who might have given me such a companion," he said to his father. || 7 ||
"Tell me quickly, where is that friend of mine, or her son?
I consider your words to be like a reference to the son of a barren woman in this world. (8)
Your statement is like a word in common worldly usage that relies upon the son of a barren woman.
As a certain actor said in the composition of a buffoon’s speech:
"The son of a barren woman has mounted a great chariot that is a mere reflection. (9)
He says that very thing: "Just as," etc. A *naṭika* is an actor (*naṭa*). || 9 ||
His limbs adorned with golden ornaments superimposed upon mother-of-pearl,
he fought with weapons made from human horn in the forest of the sky.
Having slain the future king and conquered the city of the Gandharvas,
he indeed sports in the stream of Marīci with women from his dreams.
"I consider your words to be entirely inconsistent.
Having heard these affectionate words, that clever woman spoke to him again: (12)
Likewise, it is incoherent, like the words of the Vidūṣaka as previously described. || 12 ||
O Lord, how could that which has been spoken by me to you be without purpose?
The word of those like me can never be without foundation. (13)
For falsehood is the destroyer of ascetic merits; how could it exist among those of truthful character?
How could leprosy (meaning white leprosy or skin disease) appear in the family of ascetics, as if it were endowed with beauty? 14.

If it is asked, "Why is your word not false?", he says: "It is false. He speaks with an illustration, saying: "Among ascetics, and especially among us who are of truthful character, that [falsehood] is utterly impossible"—namely, verse 14:
"For he who, out of dishonesty, employs another meaning for one who desires to know..."
For him, there is no means of happiness in the world, neither above nor below.

Regarding the seeker (*jijñāsu*), he states that through untruthful speech there is the destruction of the worlds of merit (*puṇyaloka*) in the verse beginning with "yaḥ" (verse 15): "By means of another's purpose—that is, by meaningless speech arising from untruth—there is no [attainment of] the world."
Listen to my words, O Prince: in this world, a person afflicted by cataracts does not immediately regain normal vision merely through a multitude of words about eye-salves. (16)
With the intention that what was spoken by me cannot be understood by you, a fool, merely by hearing it once, he says: "Listen" (verse 16).
The dull-witted person knows only what is untrue, even when told for his own benefit;
why then should I, who am your beloved and desire your welfare, join you with falsehoods? 17.

Even when spoken with benefit and affection, a person of dull intellect perceives it as untrue; therefore, what you have understood in this manner is indeed improper, since I, though a poor ascetic devoted to truth and your beloved, am merely seeking to know [the truth] about you.
(One who desires to know: "Why do I join with unreal things?"—the meaning is: "I do not join them at all. || 17 ||
Reflect with a discerning mind upon that which I have said, even if it be untrue;
for is not a mortal man indeed skilled in all worldly transactions? (18)
If you say, "Is it not true that untruthfulness, recklessness, and cruelty are innate to women?"—
since you are skilled in discerning this, he says "even" (*api*) so that you may examine it with a "good mind," that is,
with an intellect endowed with subtle reasoning. Indeed, I...
If it is argued that even one who is skilled might wonder, "How shall I examine your words regarding a past object?", he says: "The world... (verse 18).
Having examined even a single part, one thoroughly understands the entire state of existence;
I shall provide you with an illustration here for your consideration. (19)

In the world, one knows the state of truthfulness and moral conduct only after examining it in some particular transaction from a single perspective. Therefore, I have previously stated that I shall provide an illustration of what you experienced as truth, reminding you of that experience; this is for the purpose of examining my own words here. || 19 ||
That entire realm which formerly was the means for accomplishing all my desires—why does it not today, after a long time, become a means for happiness at my word? (20)

"Yaḥ" (that which): that object which was previously apprehended as a means to happiness is now experienced quite otherwise through my words. The sense is: "Know that since what was previously stated is true, this too must certainly be true. || 20 ||
That very same person achieves happiness today; how indeed could it be otherwise for others?
By this very illustration, you ought to understand your own doctrine.
If it is argued that "because of the difference in time, that [wealth] is not the means for happiness [as it was when I was intoxicated];

therefore, this [state of yours] is not caused by my words," he says: "That very same [wealth]. By this illustration—namely, the experience of what I have stated—he intends to establish the certainty that his own view is false as stated by me.
To know whether it is a valid means of knowledge or not. || 21 ||
Listen, O King, to what I say with a straightforward and stainless intellect:
lack of confidence [in the world] and lack of confidence in the words of the trustworthy would become a steadfast enemy— such is the connection [of the meaning].
In this world, he shall be an enemy to his foes, yet remain steadfast in the words of the trustworthy. || 22 ||
In order to say "have faith in my words," he praises faith: lack of confidence is *aśraddhā*. || 22 ||
Faith is like a mother; she always protects the one who has taken refuge in her from great fears in every way, just as a loving mother protects her child—of this there is no doubt. (23)
Fortune, happiness, and fame abandon the fool who lacks faith in the trustworthy;
that man who is devoid of faith is inferior in every respect. (24)
For this very reason, he would be inferior in every respect. || 24 ||
Faith is indeed the nurse of the worlds; faith is the life of all.
Tell me, how could a child who lacks faith toward his mother continue to live? (25)

"Without faith" means that in the absence of the conviction that "my mother will surely act for my benefit," the food and other things she provides would be rejected, and the child would not survive; this is the sense. || 25 ||
How can a youth who lacks faith prosper happily with his wife?
Likewise, how can an old man attain the state of the virtuous through his offspring? (26)
If one lacks faith in one's wife, thinking "she might kill me while I am asleep," happiness will not arise due to the emergence of such contrary suspicion. It is the same for an old man as well:
why would a farmer, lacking faith in a certain path or a state of comfort, plow the earth? Indeed, he would not.
There would be no activity whatsoever, whether in renunciation or even in acquisition.

For one who lacks faith, there can be no engagement whatsoever, because it is impossible for them to ascertain that [an action] is a means to a desired end; thus he says: "One who lacks faith," etc. (27).
If it is argued that the stability of the worlds would perish through the loss of faith, and that the worldly course of action proceeds from the adherence to a single [view], then listen. (28)
If it is argued that there is no objection to the absence of activity (pravṛtti), he says "no" with the word *śraddhā*.

"Lack of faith" (*śraddhāvaidhurya*) means the absence of faith; the remainder of the sentence is: "when the absence of activity has been established by means of its connection—that is, by the existence of that [lack of faith] as the cause. The "subsistence" (*sthiti*) of the worlds—that is, of living beings—is worldly conduct consisting of the experience of pleasure and so forth.

"Perishing would perish; [perishing] would come into being"—by changing the case endings, this results in the meaning: "the perishing of the legal proceeding would come into being through the proximity of the subject matter of the proceeding.
The state of the world, established by direct perception, cannot be denied.

Therefore, the meaning is that the existence of faith, which is the root of that [activity], is established. Now, one might object: "Faith is not established by the fact that the activity which causes the maintenance of the world would otherwise be inexplicable," because such activity can be explained in another way. To this he says: "ekānta" (exclusive). By the inclusion of the term "ekānta," the meaning is "from the apprehension of pervasion" (vyāpti). [The example is] the farmer.

The meaning is that, having repeatedly observed the attainment or non-attainment of grain when plowing has been performed or not performed, and having determined the pervasion of plowing with respect to the attainment of grain, one engages in plowing; it is not out of faith that one engages. To this, he says: "Listen" (verse 28).
Or even if one grasps at a single extreme, why is faith established there?
For even in that case, one who takes refuge in a single extreme has faith as his only refuge. (29)
Faith (*śraddhā*) is a conviction consisting of esteem, [expressed as] "this must be exactly so. This being the case, how can your faith be established or firm when you grasp at one-sided views?
For you, who deny faith, in certain matters—

The intention is this: how can there be a possibility of the cause being accompanied by the effect, even when that future effect is imperceptible, based merely on the experience of the concomitance between cause and effect? Alternatively, since activity is established as something that cannot be denied because its fruit—the experience of pleasure and so forth—is undeniable, [the means must also be known]. Once that [activity] is established...

Whether one holds that the basis of activity is rooted in faith rather than being rooted solely in dogmatic adherence, from where does faith itself arise? To this, he says "even there. This means that even if one accepts that activity proceeds from dogmatic adherence, you have nonetheless admitted that faith is present. || 29 ||
Therefore, without the nectar of faith, the world would surely perish from lack of sustenance;
therefore, having attained firm faith, proceed toward ultimate happiness. 30.

Since activity is not possible without faith, the worldly transaction would perish due to the absence of activity in its absence. "Not having faith" means that there would be no engagement because of doubt regarding inhalation, exhalation, and their cessation; this is the intended meaning.
Since even worldly happiness cannot exist without faith, therefore, having gained faith in my words... || 30 ||
If you think that faith should not be practiced by those who are inferior, listen to this:
O son of a king, even this worldly activity exists solely through faith.

"Surely faith should be placed in the words of the wise, and not in those of the inferior, such as the low-born or the deluded"—having thus restated that objection, he refutes it with the verse beginning "śraddhā" (faith). The meaning of "iyam" (this) is as follows: even the activity consisting of the admission that "faith should not be placed in the inferior" would itself have to occur through faith alone. || 31 ||
Having heard those words of his beloved, "How then shall your activity proceed?",
Hemacūḍa spoke again to his sweet-speaking wife.
If there were no faith, how could there be the aforementioned engagement in the form of acceptance? To this he says:
O beloved, one must certainly place trust in everything when it occurs;
one should direct faith toward the virtuous by which one may attain the highest good. (33)

In every respect, without an investigation into what is superior or inferior, faith—like that of the common people who say "the virtuous exist" and so forth—would meet its destruction like that of fish; this is the connection with the distant [consequence]. || 33 ||
One who desires the highest good should place faith in the non-existent;
otherwise, it is like a very sharp and crooked hook within [the mouth]. 34.

Otherwise, if the hook were absent—not meaning non-existent, but rather not being present in the place of the wicked fisherman—the fish would meet with that same destruction they meet through faith; since there is destruction even when [the hook] is absent due to faith, therefore [this is so]. || 34 ||
By means of well-ground fish [meat] placed outside the sacrificial area, one meets with destruction;
therefore, faith should be placed only in those who are virtuous, never in those who are not. 35.
Those who, having placed their faith in the wicked, went to destruction, and others likewise who, through the power of faith, were joined with the good—these are the examples. (36)
Those who, like fish, have perished through faith in the wicked, and those who are endowed with excellence through faith in the virtuous— all these are illustrations and examples in my teaching.
Therefore, it is only through dependent origination that faith is appropriate, and not otherwise.
Thus, how could there be any activity for you? Such is the question posed to you. (37)

Faith is appropriate to exercise only after one has known through the cognition "it is so. This being the case, how is it that you have proceeded [to act]? Thus, the previously stated question is a censure. [How so? By no means am I intent on prohibiting faith; rather, for the virtuous, faith should be directed toward the virtuous and not elsewhere. For the virtuous...
The sense is: "I have proceeded in this manner solely on account of the words of the great multitude. || 37 ||
Having been addressed thus, Hemalekhā spoke again to her dear husband:
"Listen, O prince, to these words being spoken by me. (38)
As for what you asked regarding how the question is posed, I shall explain that to you:
from where does your certainty arise as to whether this [self] exists or does not exist? (39)
If you say that faith must be placed in those who exist, then how do you reach the certainty that this very person exists? (39)

If this conviction is true, there will indeed be auspiciousness here through genuine faith; moreover, if that [conviction] possesses the defining characteristics, then faith is conjoined with those characteristics. (40)

If it is argued that this is established by another statement, [the author] says "when this exists," intending that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). The intended meaning is that this very determination (*niścaya*) is not possible. "That too exists" refers even to the determination itself. "By way of its definition" means by the property of exclusion from the non-existent (*asad-vyāvṛtti-dharma*).
Regarding "faith": through another statement such as "this is the definition," this knowledge of the definition must come to be.
The meaning is that if there is an infinite regress, it remains in that very state. || 40 ||

If you say that the knowledge of the characteristics [of the self] comes from valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), then listen to this: for one who lacks faith, what could constitute a valid means of cognition? Let that be well-examined. (41)

"From valid cognition" (pramāṇāt) means by way of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). "What is the valid cognition for one who lacks faith?"—this is the underlying intention: for engagement with another's scripture is possible only through faith, not through dry reasoning (*śuṣkatarka*). This is because, even though the co-occurrence of being earthen and being scratchable by iron is repeatedly apprehended, [it does not hold] in the case of a diamond (*hīraka*).
Because deviation is observed, nothing can be known by means of mere reasoning alone. || 41 ||
For otherwise, the knower would not be non-contradicted in any respect;
therefore, the entire world proceeds by relying upon faith. (42)

Therefore, he says "otherwise" [to show that] there is no means of valid cognition other than scripture (*āgama*) that impels one toward the accomplishment of human goals and is non-contradictory; for even in the case of other means of valid cognition, there is the possibility— just as in the case of a true scripture— that they might be free from defects.

If a cognizer were to act on the basis of being entirely non-contradictory, he would never be contradicted; nor would he be defeated by the failure to obtain the result aimed at through that activity.
This is because there is the possibility of contradiction in other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, [one should rely] on the true scripture (*sadāgama*).

Relying on faith alone, even a farmer proceeds by depending on traditional instruction (*āgama*), preceded by the removal of obstacles through an auspicious moment and other such rites. And any discrepancy observed therein is not caused by a defect in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but is caused solely by a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For this very reason:
The sense is that the activity [of the agent] occurs again in that very same place, due to the conceit of having once more accomplished the completeness of the causal complex (sāmagrī). || 42 ||
I shall explain its nature; listen with a steady mind.
For it is either characterized by unsettled reasoning or entirely beyond reasoning. (43)
"Of that kind" means the manner of attaining the highest good through faith. "One with unsettled reasoning" refers to one possessed of dry logic. "One without reasoning" refers to a fool. || 43 ||
A person in this world, or even in the next, may not attain the highest good;
however, for one who does not rely on mere reasoning, that highest good may eventually arise in due course of time.

"Better not," [he says]. This is because one would not engage in the first [course] due to a lack of confidence, while for the second, there is the possibility of a deficiency in the causal conditions (*sāmagrī*).

He states "therein" (*tatra*)—meaning, between those two—to show that for the second course, the attainment of the fruit might possibly occur, like a stone thrown by a blind man accidentally striking down a fruit. || 44 ||
For one whose reasoning is unstable, there can be no well-being whatsoever.
Long ago, on Mount Sahya, on the banks of the Godāvarī, there was indeed a descendant of Kuśika. (45)
Regarding the point that for one whose reasoning is unstable, there is no way to attain the highest good, he tells a historical narrative (itihāsa), beginning with "In a city... (45).
He dwelt there with a tranquil mind, having understood the true nature of the world;
his disciples, numbering in the hundreds, remained there by virtue of their reliance upon their teacher.

He is both peaceful and wise; his nature is unassailed by desire and the like, and his mind is abundant with faith and devotion. For this very reason, he has realized the true essence of the world (*lokasatattvaka*). That which is perceived or seen is the "world" (*loka*), namely the visible realm. For the supreme reality of the visible is that which is the Supreme Light, the Supreme Śiva.
Thus, according to the tradition of the scriptures, he is one by whom the true nature—the essential reality which is the mere manifestation of the substratum—is known. || 46 ||
Once, having followed their teacher, they spoke to one another in order to determine the constitution of the world according to their respective intellects.

Those disciples followed after their teacher—that is, behind his back—having gone together in order to determine the state of the world. Then, for the sake of that determination, they spoke to one another according to the quality of their own respective intellects. || 47 ||
Then a certain very wise Brahmin named Śuṅga arrived there;
by his skill of intellect, he refuted the opinion expressed by everyone. (48)

In that assembly of Kauśika’s disciples, there was one named Śuṅga, who was a great scholar skilled in dry logic— or rather, the sense is that he was "great and ignorant," meaning one who did not know the true reality of the world. Because of his intellectual cleverness, he did not criticize [the teachings] by means of reasoning consistent with the Āgamas, but rather...
"Merely through cleverness of intellect"—the sense is: by means of dry logic. || 48 ||
Then, his wisdom destroyed by lack of faith and skilled in disputation, he spoke among the twice-born who had declared that truth is what is measured by the means of valid cognition. (49)

If it is asked, "Why is there no respect for his scriptures? he says: "By means of lack of faith. For this very reason, being skilled in disputation, he resorts to *vitaṇḍā* (cavil)—that is to say, at that time when the disciples of Kauśika were engaged in discourse suitable for determining the reality of the objects of perception. [He asserts that] truth is that which is cognized by a flawless means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
When those [questions] have been stated, the connection is "then he said" (athāha). || 49 ||
Indeed, Śuṅga, who relied solely on logic and whose reasoning was unstable,
spoke there during that debate, casting aspersions upon everyone.

One whose reasoning is unstable is called a *śuṅga*. He relies on dry logic (*śuṣkatarka*) during the course of a formal debate (*vādakathā*), that is, within a discussion distinct from mere wrangling (*jalpa*) or cavil (*vitaṇḍā*). || 50 ||
O Brahmins, listen to my words: nothing whatsoever is established as true except that which is measured by valid means of knowledge; that alone is declared to be the truth. (51)

"O Brahmins, the statement of Śuṅga," and so forth. The objection is that what you seek to establish as true is not established anywhere, even throughout the three periods of time. "That which is cognized," and so forth, is a restatement of the view of Kauśika’s disciple. For this is indeed what has been asserted by you. (51)
In that case, [the cognition] produced by that faulty [cause] would surely not be valid;
therefore, first of all, the non-defectiveness of the means of knowledge must be ascertained. (52)

Among those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that which appears through a means of cognition possessed of defects is indeed unapprehended and unreal. Therefore, one who examines the real and the unreal must first ascertain the non-defective nature of the means of cognition;
thus he says, "must be ascertained. For reality does not belong to anything merely by virtue of its appearing, as is the case with mother-of-pearl silver and the like.

Because it would follow that [everything] would be real. Therefore, since reality belongs only to that which is cognized by a non-defective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the point is that the determination of the reality of an entity is dependent solely upon the determination of the non-defectiveness of the means of valid cognition. || 52 ||
If that [validity] were produced by another means of knowledge, then one should reflect in the same way regarding that as well;
thus, due to this infinite regress, nothing would ever be established through valid cognition. (53)

He says (*sā pramāṇa*) [in verse 53]: "The ascertainment that a means of knowledge is free from defects is also dependent upon another means of knowledge; thus, due to infinite regress which destroys the very root, truth is never established anywhere."
Therefore, neither the knower, nor the known object, nor the means of knowledge is established.
Consequently, this manifold conceptual construction stands with the void as its basis. (54)

Therefore, because the absence of defects in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has not been ascertained, the visible object (*dṛśya*)—though cognized—is not established as real. Consequently, since reality is not established, various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), such as "I see this with my eye," have only emptiness as their objective support. Furthermore, the desired goal is not established by means of inference (*anumāna*) and other valid cognitions, because they are beset by the aforementioned defects.

And because they depend upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor should it be argued, "How is emptiness established for you by means of reasoning (*tarka*)? For in the establishment of emptiness, the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is of no use, since its nature consists merely in the non-establishment of anything else. || 54 ||
That [emptiness] too has attained the nature of emptiness because it is not an object of valid cognition;
therefore, the definitive conclusion is that nothing exists as emptiness. || 55 ||

For this very reason, he says: "That too. Even the object that is empty has attained emptiness, because it is not the object of a certain, non-defective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, "empty" would not be some kind of entity, since its nature consists merely in the non-establishment of anything else. Or rather: "But surely..."

If it is argued that even when the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) are established, the stream of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-dhārā*)—being self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*)—remains, and thus there is no residue of mere emptiness (*śūnyamātra-śeṣa*), [the author] says: "That too" (*so'pi*). The meaning is "conceptual construction as well.
Because that [stream of concepts] lacks finality (*anavasthā*) and is not an object for another means of knowledge, it must be self-luminous.

Because of the contradiction between agent, object, and the act itself, that [conceptualization] also attains the nature of emptiness. Therefore, even that which has the form of conceptual construction does not establish existence; thus, the final determination is that it is indeed emptiness alone. || 55 ||
Having heard these words of Śuṅga, some of those lowest of the twice-born took refuge in that fallacious conclusion and became proponents of the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavādins). || 56 ||
Among those disciples of Kauśika, the lowest of the twice-born, whose hearts were devoid of substance, [adopted] that Śuṅga doctrine. 56.
Those twice-born ones whose hearts were devoted to the essence perished, having reached that supreme state of emptiness which was the teaching of Śuṅga. (57)

Through the certainty that all things are empty, considering even their own selves to be empty, they have attained the state of emptiness as a state of stability; yet they have not entered into a state of non-existence, because in reality it is impossible for an existent thing to become non-existent. They possess a "heart of essence," meaning a heart devoted to essential inquiry.
Those whose minds [are such]. || 57 ||
Having scrutinized Kauśika, they became concentrated in heart;
therefore, having entirely abandoned that unstable reasoning, [they remained steadfast]. (58)
By that which was spoken by Kauśika, because doubt is destroyed, the heart becomes composed; for from unstable reasoning comes the attainment of misfortune. Therefore [this is so]. 58.
"Only one whose reasoning is always dependent upon the true scriptures shall attain the highest good"—
thus was Hemacūḍa addressed by his exceedingly steadfast beloved.
One for whom reasoning is subordinate to and in conformity with the true tradition (sadāgama); [this is said] by one who is steadfast and learned. || 59 ||
Filled with great wonder, he questioned that noble-minded woman once more:
"O beloved, I did not previously know such erudition as this of yours! (60)
Seeing such inconceivable learning in a woman, he was struck with wonder. || 60 ||
You are blessed, and I too am blessed, who have come to you;
for how is it that you speak with such faith regarding the attainment of all that is most auspicious?
He has arrived; he has come together. || 61 ||
Wherein should faith be placed, or wherein is it not praised?
For indeed, due to the infinity of scriptures and their reliance on contradictory meanings, [how could one decide]? (62)
When it is said that "faith in the scriptures (āgama) must be observed," one asks, "In what [scripture] should faith be placed?"—given that even the scriptures are not in agreement.
To this, he replies: "In what? If it is argued that although the scriptures disagree, one should place faith in whichever one where there is unity of meaning, he says: "Contradictory... (verse 62).

Due to the differences in the opinions of teachers, due to the differences in the opinions of commentators, and because one's own intellect lacks stability, what is to be accepted and what is not? || 63 ||
There is no contradiction in meaning even among the Buddhist, Ārhata, and Vedic scriptures themselves;
rather, he states that there is contradiction even within each individual scripture due to differences in the opinions of the teachers (*ācārya*), as expressed by the word "teachers. This is clear.
For instance, among the teachers of the Vedic and other scriptures, such as Jaimini, Patañjali, and others...

Regarding the phrase "mutual contradiction of opinions": likewise, there is a mutual contradiction in the commentaries of those who explain the treatise of Jaimini, such as Śabara, Kumārila, and others. If it is argued that even in the face of such mutual contradictions, one should investigate with one's own intellect and place faith in whatever is best, [the author] says: (##-)

The meaning is that because there is a difference in the state of cognition due to the difference in time, various types of reasoning can arise for the very same person at different times; thus, there is no finality [in the argument]. || 63 ||
Whatever is desired by someone, that very thing he speaks of with absolute certainty as "existent," O beloved— even if it is something else entirely, unascertained, and even detrimental.

He states the mutual contradiction between the teacher and others as follows: "That which... He asserts that as the means [of proof], while the other is not intended. "Undetermined" means not ascertained as being the means [of proof]. || 64 ||
This being the case, no one here can ever reach an end;
even he who asserts that emptiness is the reality would likewise refute the non-empty.
In that regard, regarding the scriptures (*āgama*): even when such a contradiction exists, and even when this investigation has been conducted, one must reach a final certainty (*anta*). || 65 ||
"How could that be untrustworthy, for it is indeed consistent with scripture?
Tell me this clearly, my dear; for nothing inconceivable exists for you."

Even by Śuṅga, a proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*) was taught, and the doctrine of non-emptiness was refuted. Furthermore, that view is entirely consistent with scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, he asks: "Why should this view not be accepted? Tell me this. [The opponent replies: "It is not to be accepted," even though this...
This objection is difficult to resolve; nevertheless, it is conceivable that this has been considered by you because you are almost omniscient—intending this, he says: "For this is not... (66).
[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Praise of Faith," in the Hemacūḍopākhyāna of the Jñānakhaṇḍa within the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories.]
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya. || 6 ||
[Now begins the seventh chapter.
Thus questioned by her most beloved husband,
the wise Hemalekhā, who thoroughly understood the nature of the world, spoke correctly.
In this chapter, it is stated that by knowing Śiva through the words of the Vedas, through faith, human effort, and reasoning, and by worshipping Him, one shall thereafter attain the highest good.
That by which the knower of the world [perceives] its stability, its substratum, or its essential nature. (k: "essential nature" is not present) || 1 ||
Listen, my dearest one; with a steady mind and with great respect, I shall speak.
For the mind is indeed like a monkey, always restless. (2)
"Steady-minded" means having a mind not directed elsewhere. "With devotion" means through the firm resolve: "This alone must be heard by me.

He states the respective fruits of these two [qualities] as follows: "The mind," etc. The sense is that steadiness does not belong to the mind by its own nature. Since this is so, therefore one should apply the phrase "steadyminded" accordingly. (2)
Since ordinary people have thus incurred such great misfortune, it is clearly seen that a flickering mind is indeed the source of all suffering. (3)
If it is asked, "What would happen to me through that instability?", he says: "Because" (yataḥ). This means: because of the movement of the mind. || 3 ||
Since one indeed finds happiness in deep sleep due to the absence of movement, therefore, having made the mind steady, listen to what I shall tell you. (4)
He demonstrates through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that suffering arises precisely from the movement of the mind, by the words "since" (*yataḥ*). "Everyone experiences [this].

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: since the movement of the mind obstructs the fruit of innate, ever-present happiness, it will all the more surely obstruct the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*). Thus ends the section.
That which is heard with disrespect is equivalent to what was not heard at all;
it will be utterly fruitless, just like a painting on a tree in a picture.

"Listened to with disrespect" means it was heard without faith and with an unconcentrated mind, merely at first hearing. "Fruitless" means that which has no fruit. For this [knowledge] which is about to be described does not bring fruit by mere hearing alone, like a song; rather, it does so through the medium of reflection (*manana*) and so forth. Likewise:
The sense is that in the absence of reverence, there is no engagement in reflection and so forth; thus, like a tree depicted in a painting, hearing would be useless. That [refers to] hearing. || 5 ||
Abandoning that unstable reasoning which leads to ruin,
a person who relies upon sound reasoning will swiftly attain excellent fruit.
Relying upon right reasoning, one should quickly become solely intent on the means of accomplishment; having attained the faith born of right reasoning, a person here becomes a partaker of the fruit.

If it is objected: "Surely, even for one who has abandoned dry logic (*śuṣkatarka*) and places his trust in what you have said, yet remains devoted to correct reasoning (*sattarka*), no attainment of the fruit is observed," he says: "One who is solely intent on the means" (*sādhanaikapara*). If it is further objected: "Enough with correct reasoning; even by means of fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*), the fruit shall come to me simply through being intent on the means," he says:

Regarding the term *sattarka* (sound reasoning): since the establishment of the Lord—which is rooted in the sound reasoning to be described later—is difficult to achieve for one who employs fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*), their faith in worshipping Him is cast far away. Thus, an act of worship performed solely [without such faith] is like an offering or gift given without faith; and according to the principle stated in the *Bhagavad Gītā* (17.28), "That neither reaches the hereafter nor this world," it would be fruitless. (k:)
(The phrase "it is fruitless" means: the intention is that only one who is intent upon the means through faith born of right reasoning becomes a partaker of the fruit. || 7 ||
O beloved, abandon that unstable reasoning and look instead with faith upon this worldly activity, which is fruitful.

That [truth], being well-established, resides within you. Behold the fruitful activity of those endowed with faith who are free from unstable reasoning; the meaning is that the fruit thereof is not beyond perception. || 8 ||
Just as a farmer plows the earth at the properly considered time,
so too does one obtain silver, gold, gems, medicinal herbs, and other such things through faith alone.
He explains that very process with the words "by well-reasoned [inference]" (*sutarkitena*). Well-reasoned inference (*sutarka*) is an inference not contradicted by scripture (*āgama*).

By means of that time which is suitable for the plowing of fields as taught in the scriptures and is characterized by the absence of obstacles to crops such as drought—[that time] being the cause, he plows. But he does not do so through a lack of faith everywhere due to the instability of reasoning.
The sense is that she remains silent just like you. || 9 ||
They determine [the truth] through sound reasoning, having abandoned the instability of mere logic;
therefore, having determined the welfare of the self through sound reasoning and faith, [one should act]. 10.

Likewise, experts determine through scripture and reasoning alone that even this gold and so forth, though characterized by extreme subtlety, is worth such a price, possesses such qualities, and cures such diseases; and for the most part, they do not err. Thus he says:

"They determine" means this: a person of sound reasoning may occasionally be contradicted, but unlike one whose reasoning is unstable, he does not undergo the loss of self through the doctrine of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*). Therefore, the connection [of the verse] is as follows: having determined and ascertained what is beneficial for the self, one should strive for its accomplishment. || 10 ||
One should strive for its accomplishment; for there is no end to [mere] reasoning.
One should desist from human effort, like men who follow a horn. 11.
He says "not so" (na hi) [in verse 11] to show that one should not become averse to human effort by imagining universal emptiness through improper reasoning, like those people who follow the Śuṅgas.
One who is devoted to human effort through faith will never be frustrated;
by relying on firm human exertion, how could one not attain the fruit? 12.

"Pauruṣa" means human effort (*puruṣayatna*). One should not be discouraged by the non-attainment of results; for the absence of results in some cases is due to a lack of firm effort, as he says with the word "firmly. || 12 ||
Through human effort, farmers obtain grain, merchants obtain wealth, kings obtain the fortune of sovereignty, and Brahmins obtain knowledge, which is the refuge of all happiness. (13)
Because it is joined with firm manly effort, it is not without fruit; thus he says with conviction, "from manly effort" (pauruṣāt). || 13 ||
Śūdras attained wages, the gods attained nectar, and ascetics attained the highest world; others too obtained their desired goals solely through the action of human effort.
Tell me, after due reflection: what result has ever been attained, by whom, when, and in what manner, by a person who is unstable in reasoning and devoid of faith? (15)
What fruit is there even in the slightest? At what time, and how could it be attained without the means of accomplishment? || 15 ||
When there is a failure of results in some instances, leading to a lack of confidence in all cases,
one should recognize that person as struck by fate, appearing in the form of an enemy to oneself.

If it is objected that even for farmers and others, a lack of fruit is sometimes observed, [the author] says "in some cases" (kvacit), implying that the failure to act would be rooted in mere folly for that reason alone; "confidence" (āśvāsa) means faith (śraddhā).

Therefore, relying upon human effort nourished by faith and sound reasoning, one should take recourse in that which is the most excellent means among all things conducive to the highest good. || 17 ||

It is nourished by faith and right reasoning (*sattarka*). The sense is that through right reasoning faith arises, and through faith there is the increase of human effort (*pauruṣa*). Now, although various means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), such as Karma-yoga and others, are well known in the scriptures, which among them is [the one] my [means]?
If it is asked, "How should one rely [on them]? he says: "Of those who possess excellence" (śreyasām). || 17 ||
In that regard, the variety of means of proof is seen to be manifold;
among them, that which establishes the probandum in every respect is indeed the primary one. (18)
Now, if it is asked: "Is there not a primacy for the means of attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), and what is that? he says:
Among various means perceived as distinct due to their diversity, that which accomplishes the goal—the fruit—in every respect;
according to the principle beginning with "In this [path], there is no loss of effort" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 2.40), there is no failure regarding the result.
"No," it was said; [that is,] "in every way. || 18 ||
One should quickly determine that through sound reasoning and direct experience, and then begin its practice;
I shall explain all of that to you—listen to it with focused attention.

If it is asked, "How is this also to be ascertained? he says: "That" (tat). Having determined—that is, having ascertained—therein, regarding the human body, which is the source of the highest good and is difficult to obtain, [he speaks] because it is seized by death: "Swiftly" (āśu).
If it is asked, "Or how might my ascertainment come about? he says: "That" (tat). [This refers to] the primary highest good and its means of accomplishment.
This is the meaning. || 19 ||
One should recognize that as truly superior from which one does not grieve further;
for sorrow arises from every side, as is seen by the subtle eye.

Therein, first, he states the primary meaning of the term *śreyas* (the highest good): "The highest good (*śreyaḥ*). Now, if it is argued that such [a thing] is simply wealth and the like, he says "no," and states: "Sorrow (*śoka*). If it is asked how wealth and the like result in sorrow, he says:
"It is seen" (verse 20).
That which is permeated by grief is not beneficial in any way whatsoever—neither wealth, nor sons, nor wives, nor kingdom, nor treasury, nor army, nor fame. (21)
He says that very thing: "That which... [and so on]. "Anusaṃbhinna" means joined or united. || 21 ||
Knowledge, intellect, vision, the body, and the wealth of beauty—all this, because of its instability, is as if placed within the mouth of a serpent of Time. 22.
He states the distinction with the words "knowledge," and so forth. "Vision" is the instrument. "Attainments of beauty" refers to the acquisitions of excellence.
He says that all this is "joined with suffering" because it brings about grief, on the grounds that everything is seized by destruction;
thus he says "all. || 22 ||
Since it exists as the very essence of the seed of the great power that sprouts sorrow, how could it be fit to be the means for attaining ultimate bliss? (23)

The meaning is that, like a seed endowed with great power for producing the sprout of sorrow, the power of that sprout cannot be destroyed by ordinary means. Therefore, such a state is not at all a means for attaining ultimate bliss; thus he asks: "Why? (verse 23).
Therefore, this alone should primarily be considered the supreme good;
for such is the delusion regarding wealth and other objects that they are to be grasped. (24)
Therefore, since wealth and the like are not the means [to the goal], "the good" (*śreyaḥ*) refers to the means of attaining the good.

This is the propitiation of the deity which is about to be described. How is it that the attainment of the good occurs through the propitiation of the deity alone? It is in order to establish this that [the author says] "thus" (*evam*) here; the meaning is "by way of being the means to the good. As for "that which" (*yat*): that which...
The meaning is "delusion. || 24 ||
For Maheśvara is indeed the deluder, arisen from delusion alone;
since he is the creator of the entire world, therefore all beings are deluded by him. || 25 ||

If it is asked, "Who is this deluder?", he says: "Maheśvara. If it is asked, "Of what nature is Maheśvara?", he says: "He who... (verse 25), meaning that he is established as the creator of the world and is not to be denied.
Even a small portion of knowledge, when relied upon here, deludes only some people and not all; for that knowledge is indeed limited. (26)

If it is asked how this [power] has such capacity, he says: "It deludes. A magician is limited by a small body and so forth; his knowledge is limited, and thus he does not possess the power to delude everyone. || 26 ||
Since people have not transcended one who is of little knowledge and deceitful, who would be able to transcend Mahādeva, the master of great illusion? || 27 ||
He says that it is impossible to cross the delusion of that [teacher] without first propitiating the deceiver: "one who has little knowledge" (verse 27).
For he who understands even the slightest illusion in the world through counter-knowledge has emerged from delusion; established in himself, he attains imperishable happiness.
"Of little illusion"—the word "to cease" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Self-abiding" means free from the fear of the snake and other things created by that illusion.
"Indestructible" means not subject to destruction by that illusion. || 28 ||
Even such a science as this cannot be obtained in any way by one who does not rely upon that Magician, nor until he has been propitiated in every respect. (29)

Even such a spell as this is one that obstructs those with little deceit (*alpamāyāpratirodhinī*). [The phrase] "that person of little deceit" refers to him. "Since" (*yāvat*) means because; it cannot be obtained without relying upon him—that is, without propitiating him in every way through gifts of wealth, service, and so forth.
The connection is with the subsequent clause: "without having propitiated him in every way. (29)
Therefore, how can there be a crossing over of great delusion without propitiating that Great Illusionist? For this reason, one should take refuge in him by all means. || 30 ||
Therefore, because there is no crossing over delusion when there is no clarity. || 30 ||
Whoever properly propitiates him, having obtained his grace, will certainly attain transcendence through that great knowledge, even from the delusion of that [world]. (31)

"Truly" means without deceit. Having attained the "great vidyā"—the knowledge of the non-dual, auspicious Self—one understands the true nature of Mahāmāyā; this is the implied meaning. "Due to that delusion" means due to the delusion produced by Mahāmāyā. || 31 ||
Other yogas have also been taught for the practice that accomplishes the highest good;
yet, without your grace, O Maheśvara, they would not lead to the attainment of their fruit.

Yogas are the methods consisting of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth; the phrase "as the cause" is to be understood as referring to their role in the performance of actions that lead to the highest good (*śreyas*).
Therefore, one should first worship Maheśa, the cause of the universe;
through devotion, he shall quickly accomplish those yogas that destroy delusion. (33)

"From that" means: because no spiritual practice whatsoever can reach its culmination in its fruit without the propitiation of God; therefore, [this is said]. "In the beginning" means: at the commencement of all spiritual practices. If one asks why this is so, he says: "The cause of the universe. Because He is the creator of all, without His grace... [nothing is achieved].
The sense is that something will eventually succeed. || 33 ||
This world, which is perceived as an effect, is seen directly to possess parts; thus, even though it is not seen to have been produced by an unseen agent, it is nonetheless [an effect]. (34)

Anticipating the objection, "How is this Lord established as the creator of the world?", he begins to prove the existence of the Lord with the words "etad" (this). The meaning is: "that which is perceived by direct perception. And that world is indeed an effect, just as it is directly perceived. Thus... (as follows).

[It] does not exist; [it] is perceived. If it is argued that while the effects such as jars and the like indeed do not exist [independently], this is not the case for the earth, oceans, mountains, and so forth—[the author] replies: "Because they too possess parts," thereby establishing their status as effects. This applies even to those whose commencement is unperceived (*adṛṣṭārambha*).
Earth and the other elements also arise from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
By means of the reasoning that "there must be an effect," and by means of many firm scriptural traditions,
one should determine therein a creator who is distinct from all other creators.
The meaning is that by the reasoning (*tarka*) that "whatever possesses parts is an effect," earth and the other elements possess origination.

Now, one might object: even so, since atoms, space, and so forth are partless and thus not effects, it cannot be said that the entire world is an effect. This is not so, because their status as effects is established by the reason of being knowable (*vedyatva*). Nor [is it contradicted] by their partlessness.

He states that the absence of being an effect can be established because the inference based on the reason of "being cognizable" (*vedyatva*) is more firmly grounded due to its concordance with many scriptures, saying: "with many scriptures.
And thus says the scripture: "The one God, generating heaven and earth... (*Ṛgveda* 10.81.3).

"From the Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), "He created all that is visible, beginning with space and air," and so forth. Thus, once it is established that the entire visible world is an effect, he states that one may then prove that this world, as an effect, must have been preceded by an agent.
"One should determine" means that one should take the agent [of the world] as the object of ascertainment regarding earth and so forth. Now, one might object:

"In the case of specific effects such as jars, this would be proving what is already established by well-known potters and the like. Anticipating this, he says: "[An agent] distinct from all [known] agents. "Then there was neither non-existence nor existence" (Ṛgveda 10.129.1).

The sense is that, in accordance with such scriptures as "Before creation, not even an atom of this visible world existed," since there is no material cause (upādāna) or other requirements in a beginningless creation, and because he does not depend upon them,
this agent has been established as distinct from all [ordinary] agents. || 35 ||
Even if some scripture here were to declare the world to be without a creator, that [claim] is thoroughly refuted by many other scriptures firmly established through reasoning. (36)
But surely, just as the reasoning that establishes the world as an effect is firm due to its agreement with scripture, why should the reasoning that proves it is not an effect not also be firm?
For this world is indeed without a creator, relying solely upon its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

Anticipating the objection that this is consistent with the *Bārhaspatya* scriptures through such passages as these, [the author] begins the refutation of the Cārvāka doctrine with the words "Even though," arguing that this is not a true scripture (*sadāgama*), but merely a semblance of a scripture (*āgamābhāsa*). A certain scripture is the *Cārvāka* scripture. Herein follows the Cārvāka system: [The text continues: "Even though there is some scripture, namely the *Cārvāka* scripture... and so forth. This is the Cārvāka methodology.
Earth, water, fire, and air—this is the fourfold set of principles established by the means of direct perception; a fifth does not exist.
This world, consisting of the aggregate [of elements], is differentiated at every moment;
each subsequent [moment] is like a net of worlds from each preceding one.
Thus, this world has such an intrinsic nature and is established within itself;
just as the power of intoxication arises from molasses, water, and so forth, due to their inherent nature.
Thus, when the drop of semen and blood is deposited within the womb of a woman,
consciousness indeed arises, which is the locus of both action and knowledge.
Just as water endowed with intoxicating power is called liquor,
so too the body joined with consciousness is called a person (puruṣa).
Happiness is the goal of man, which would be heaven; suffering, however, would be hell.
These two proceed from their own inherent nature alone, and not otherwise.
Samsara is described as being nothing but the appearance of pleasure and pain; yet, just as the power of intoxication from liquor is destroyed by its own nature, [so too is samsara].
"Thus, the destruction of consciousness is indeed called liberation by the wise;

for one who is dead, there is neither heaven nor any hell whatsoever. This is the Cārvāka scripture, [refuted] by many scriptures belonging to both theists and atheists that are established through reasoning.
The connection is that [the view] must indeed be abandoned because it is sublated by subsequent reasonings. || 36 ||
Where the very destruction of the self is the goal, based solely on direct perception, that is merely a semblance of scripture; for it does not have the Great One as its basis.

It has been stated that [the opponent's view] is a fallacy because it contradicts numerous scriptures; now, he states that it is likewise [invalid] because it contradicts universal experience, beginning with the words "wherein" (*yatra*).
Saṃsāra, which consists of a continuous flow of birth, death, and so forth, is to be abandoned because its nature is suffering. Of this very saṃsāra...

When non-existence (*abhāva*) is established through the elimination of signs (*nimitta*), the experience of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*); for this very reason, it is to be accepted by all.
Indeed, the view of those who maintain that liberation is a human goal—that it is established by means of reasoning, scripture, and so forth—is as follows. This being the case:

Any scripture in which it is stated that the destruction of the self (*ātman*) is the very goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), based solely on the reliance upon perception as the only means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is merely a semblance of scripture (*āgamābhāsa*). For this very reason, such a scripture is not to be accepted by the great ones who discern the essential from the non-essential as a source for achieving the goals of human life. [The destruction of the self...]
The Cārvāka, asserting that "human purpose" (*puruṣārtha*) [is the goal], should be questioned: Is this destruction of the self some kind of human purpose? Or is it the destruction of its collection?
Or rather, the destruction of the universal self (*ātmasāmānya*)? Not the first, because in your view, the self is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Because the destruction of one's own self would already have been attained, and because the other two [alternatives] are impossible;

nor is there the destruction of one's own mental continuum, because at the time of the destruction of one's own self, since the self does not exist, the destruction of one's own self cannot be attained, and thus it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). This is so even if it were something unattainable...

If [the destruction of the self] were for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), then the destruction of another’s self would also follow as being for the sake of the person. Furthermore, if it is argued that the destruction of one's own self is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it is either unestablished by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or simply non-existent—if you say it is "unestablished," then it would follow that even a man’s horn would likewise be a human goal; if it is "established," [then the same objection applies].

If this is so, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it established? For perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is caused by sensory contact, is not possible regarding the past and the future. Nor do you accept any other means of valid cognition, such as inference (*anumāna*) and the like.
Since you assert that perception alone is the means of valid cognition, [how can you establish] things such as molasses-water and the like?

It should be understood that by demonstrating that the emergence of intoxicating power and so forth cannot serve as an example, the proof for the emergence of consciousness and so forth is likewise non-existent; it is equivalent to saying, "My tongue refuses to speak [such nonsense]. || 37 ||
Indeed, that scripture which is devised solely through dry logic must certainly be abandoned;
for it is said by some others as well that this world is eternal. (38)

He states that this treatise was not composed by an omniscient being, using the word "dry" (*śuṣka*). "Dry" means a reasoning (*tarka*) devoid of logical justification (*upapatti*); "fashioned solely by that" means having that alone as its foundation.
Having thus refuted the Cārvāka doctrine, which stands as the counter-position to the present subject, [he refutes] one of a similar nature...
He proceeds to refute the Sāṃkhya doctrine with the words "by others" (anyaiḥ). The meaning is that it is eternal and of the nature of existence (*sat*).
For they, being proponents of transformation (*pariṇāmavādinaḥ*), assert that the world is indeed existent by virtue of its inclusion within the cause. || 38 ||
Furthermore, the claim that it has an unintelligent creator is also inconsistent;
for action is preceded by intelligence, and such action is not observed in the absence of intelligence. (39)
Regarding the term "non-intelligent" (*abuddhimat*): the principle of *prakṛti*, whose nature consists in the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*, is the root cause of the universe.

And that is non-intelligent—that is, devoid of conscious activity and insentient. For just as a lump of clay, undergoing transformation into the form of a jar, requires a maker such as a potter, it is not so [with *prakṛti*].

The principle of *prakṛti*, undergoing transformation into the form of the world, requires some agent external to itself; therefore, the meaning is that because it is independent in the activity of the world, it is the creator of the world—this is the non-theistic Sāṃkhya doctrine. For here, *prakṛti* [acts] through its *sattva* aspect, which is like a mirror.

The internal self, which is pure consciousness, perceives the Puruṣa and its own portion consisting of darkness as the object of perception by way of reflection. Thus, through this very relationship between the seer and the seen existing as reflections, the Puruṣa, having fallen into non-discrimination from Prakṛti, engages in the false conceit: "I know the pot."

This is logical. This indeed is the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the person (*puruṣa*). For when the person, through discernment, knows the Self as distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then—like one who has recognized a thief—because primordial nature no longer approaches that person, there is no grasping of the reflection of the person.

It is their view that one is liberated through the absence of false conceit (*mṛṣābhimāna*). For in this system, it is accepted that the manifestation of the seer (*dṛkprakāśa*) occurs due to the connection of consciousness (*cit*), which exists as a reflection, with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). In that regard, is the consciousness existing as a reflection insentient by nature because it possesses a substrate, or is it sentient by nature because its primary cause is consciousness itself?

In the first case, it is untenable for an insentient entity (*jaḍa*) to be the manifestation of the visible. If one were to accept that an insentient entity is the manifestation of the visible, then since everything would be accounted for simply through its connection with a portion of *sattva* belonging to *prakṛti*, the postulation of the reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*) would result in futility. In the second case as well, regarding the visible...

Furthermore, because the primary consciousness itself has entered into the relationship [with the object], the reflection of consciousness is indeed redundant. Nor can it be argued that— just as a mirror, though it does not illuminate objects like jars, nevertheless illuminates them through the secondary sunlight reflected within it— the reflection of consciousness alone is what illuminates the visible world.
Because the reflection of the sun's heat, like light, does not possess the quality of illumination itself, as it merely acts as an auxiliary for the illumination of jars and other objects;

nor is it appropriate to say that the consciousness which has become a reflection possesses a dual nature of both conscious and insentient, or that it is distinct from both, due to contradiction and because it would constitute an abandonment of established doctrine. And yet...

Because a change in intrinsic nature is impossible, and because it is impossible for *prakṛti*—which has the nature of activity toward the *puruṣa*—to have the nature of cessation immediately after the knowledge of discrimination, bondage must be something to be abandoned; with this intention, [the author] says: [The following verse: "Since the nature of the *guṇas* is such that they act for another, and since their nature is to cease once their purpose is fulfilled, the *puruṣa*, though pure, appears as if active through the reflection of consciousness. (SK 20) In this regard, the meaning is as follows: the *guṇas* possess a nature of acting for the sake of another, namely the *puruṣa*. Furthermore, once their purpose has been accomplished, they possess a nature of ceasing. Therefore, even though the *puruṣa* is essentially pure, it appears as if active due to the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*). This is the intended meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is as follows: the *guṇas* have the nature of acting for the sake of another, and they have the nature of ceasing once their purpose is fulfilled. Consequently, although the *puruṣa* is pure, it appears as if active through the reflection of consciousness. This is the intended meaning. The meaning is that because the production of jars and the like is preceded by an intelligent agent—since they are preceded by the thought of a potter and others, such as "I am making a jar of this kind"—the world cannot have an unintelligent primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as its creator. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of intelligence": it is because one observes the performance of actions such as making a jar even in the case of a potter depicted in a painting. (39)
Moreover, due to the support of many scriptures, the agent here must indeed be intelligent;
for it is observed everywhere that an effect has an intelligent creator. (40)

"Much indeed... [Thus it is said: "He thought, 'Let me now create the worlds'" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1), and "Let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2). For the Blessed Lord, the primordial creator, having first reflected upon the universe, fashioned it as something distinct and without material cause, like a yogi; such is the support provided by many scriptural passages.

The meaning is as follows: since the world has such a basis that is favorable [to its production], it must have an intelligent agent as its creator, because it is an effect, like a jar; thus, by virtue of this powerful reasoning (*balavat-tarka*), the creator of the world must be intelligent alone, and not the non-intelligent *prakṛti*. [Objection: There is a lack of available examples (*dṛṣṭānta-daurbhalya*) for an effect having an intelligent creator.

"He avoids [the objection] everywhere" means that, just as in the Sāṃkhya system it is difficult to find an example for proving agency in the insentient principle of *prakṛti*, such a difficulty does not exist here; this is the intended meaning. || 40 ||
Thus, by means of both sound reasoning and authoritative scripture, this world has a creator;
and that creator must be distinct from ordinary worldly agents. (41)

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "it is established as having an agent. Now, one might object: "Just as the potter and others are the agents of jars and such things, let some person be established as the agent of the beginning [of the universe]; however, his status as the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is not thereby established. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He is the agent" (verse 41).
Because the nature of the effect is inconceivable, [the cause] possesses inconceivable and infinite power;
its capacity is unlimited because it conforms to the requirements of the effect. || 42 ||

In this regard, the reason is: "because its nature is inconceivable. How the earth remains in water, or how water exists in the sky—in such ways, the inconceivability of the effect (*kārya*) is to be understood.
He states precisely the distinction from an ordinary worldly agent by saying "inconceivable": that power [of the Lord] is not such that it can be defined as being of this kind or of such magnitude.
