She is neither conceivable nor finite. Having extracted this very point, he says: "indeterminate. She is to be known in the world as conforming to [the nature of] effects (*kāryaguṇa*). He states her distinction from worldly agents precisely by saying: "inconceivable.
Her power is such that it cannot be conceived as being "of this kind" or "to such an extent," nor is it finite. Having extracted this very point, he says: [indeterminate].

"Unlimited" means that in the world, an agent is observed only to be commensurate with the task at hand; therefore, the sense is that for a universe that is unlimited, the agent must likewise possess unlimited power. || 42 ||
He is indeed capable of rescuing those who have sought refuge in every way; therefore, always take refuge in him with your whole being. 43.
Having established the Lord by this much of the text, he now declares His state as the one worthy of refuge:
"He [protects] those who have surrendered," and so forth. Since it is thus, therefore, to Him, the Creator of the world; "with one's whole being" means with freedom from desire.
For those who possess desire, their state is divided: half of their being—that is, half of their mind—resides in the object of desire, and half resides in the Lord.
The state of being. || 43 ||
I shall declare an illustration to you; listen to the cause of conviction.
Even Miteśvara was propitiated here in this world through his lack of deceit.

They have taken refuge with their whole being; this is the illustration and the example regarding the attainment of the fruit. "Pratyaya" means trust. It is "with their whole being" because of their lack of deceit. 44.
He who has properly propitiated this Lord of the World, the God, unites a man with his desired goals for his ultimate welfare by means of his entire being. (45)
The connection is that he was propitiated with his whole being—through body, speech, and mind—for the sake of the highest good and happiness. || 45 ||
Tell me, what would he not grant to him—he who is the sole beloved of the world of devotees?
For in this world, men may be lords, yet they are unstable and lack compassion. (46)

To that lay follower (*upāsaka*), one should not fail to grant what is desired; rather, the meaning is that one must certainly grant it. Or else, the meaning is: "What is there that one would not grant? Indeed, one should grant everything. Now, it may be argued that for limited lords (*miteśvara*), the granting of desired objects is appropriate because they attain satisfaction through the fulfillment of their own cherished state of being served. But how can this apply to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)?
It is appropriate for one who possesses limited sovereignty to experience satisfaction upon attaining their desires, as they have not yet attained all their wishes;
however, for the Supreme Lord, since his desires are already fulfilled, there can be no possibility of either satisfaction or dissatisfaction.
Furthermore, the experience of satisfaction itself is the causal factor in the bestowal of desired fruits by the one who is worshipped.

The intention of the passage beginning with "nanu" and ending with "cedāha" is as follows: [An objection is raised: "Since he has already attained all desires, how can there be a lack of satisfaction such that he would grant the desired objects to those who worship him? To this, he replies:
"He is the sole lover of his devotees. Because his very nature is one of affection (*vatsala*) toward his devotees, he bestows the fruits [of their practice].
The sense is that this is logical. Furthermore, he states (in verse 46) "puruṣāḥ" [to show] that while the attainment of results from limited lords is uncertain, it is certain from the Supreme Lord.
They are merciless and ungrateful; therefore, their fruit is unstable. The Supreme Lord, however, is an ocean of compassion, grateful, and perfectly established.
Therefore, because [the other] is possessed of the fourfold nature of qualities such as instability and lack of certainty, it is unstable and indefinite.
But the Lord (*īśvara*) is not of such a kind; thus he says "Supreme Lord" (*parameśa*). Since this is so, the attainment of the fruit will indeed occur—this is the remainder of the sense. || 47 ||
Otherwise, in this beginningless saṃsāra, how could it attain blamelessness?
Furthermore, tell me, how could the course of the world remain established?
If it is asked, "How is this determined?", he says: "Otherwise. The sense is that if there were a lack of affection (*avatsalatva*) and so forth, he would not be beyond reproach;
and if there were an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the established course of worldly affairs (*lokayātrā*) brought about by him would not be possible. || 48 ||
Since the kingdom of one who lacks stability is seen to be ruined, therefore he is proclaimed to be both an ocean of compassion and well-established. (49)
"Instability": the sense is that if God were unstable, the world-system created by Him would perish at any moment.
Seek refuge in him alone with devotion and with your whole being;
he will unite you with the highest good, so do not fail to be intent upon him.
"With your whole being" means with total detachment. "In regard to the highest good" means in the accomplishment of the supreme welfare. "Do not become intent upon that" means:
because the means for accomplishing the supreme welfare are difficult to discern, do not be devoted to that;
rather, worship the Lord now. Through your worship, the Lord, being pleased, will unite you with that [supreme goal].

This is the meaning. By this, it should be understood that the doubt as to which means of proof (*sādhana*) should be adopted—given the existence of different means of proof among the various conflicting views—is cast aside. || 50 ||
Worship is of many kinds, arising from the desire for worldly objects or for liberation;
however, that which is occasional and devoid of such motives is true worship. (51)

To state that the worship of the Lord alone, when performed without desire, is in every way the bestower of fruit, he says: "Worship. Worship performed out of distress—that is, the pain caused by disease and the like—or out of a desire for wealth—that is, the longing for riches and so forth—is well known everywhere. [In contrast,] it is without cause (*nirhetuka*).
Worship free from desire is worship of the Truth, because it is accompanied by true results. || 51 ||
This has been observed everywhere: when the Lord is served by one who is distressed, He may at times, overcome by compassion, liberate that person from their suffering.
He establishes this very point by means of a worldly example: "This is observed," [verse 52].
Or perhaps one might remain indifferent due to the varying degrees of devotion;
in this very way, even for one seeking wealth, the fruit is both limited and uncertain. (53)
"By way of gradation": the sense is that when there is excellence in worship, [the Lord] releases one from suffering; otherwise, He might neglect them. "In this manner":

through the gradation of worship, there is either the attainment or non-attainment of the goal. Thus, for those possessing desires, the fruit of worship is both indefinite and limited; because that for which the worship is performed is finite, and because the object of worship is ungrateful (kṛtaghna).
The meaning is: "and because the fruit has not been attained. || 53 ||
Having long ago understood the causelessness of the causeless lay follower, Miteśvara too became unstable and fell under his power. (54)
"Dependent on that" means dependent on the practitioner. || 54 ||
Due to his state of ignorance, it would take a long time for him to realize the causelessness [of this];
yet he is the Lord of All, the God who is the master of everyone’s heart. (55)
He says "this one" (*eṣa*) to show that while Miteśvara requires a delay of time in order for his own worshippers to attain knowledge of causelessness, such [delay] does not exist even for Īśvara.
He is the Lord of the Heart (*hṛdayeśa*) because, as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), he dwells within the hearts of all. || 55 ||
He knows everything at that time and shall swiftly grant the fruit;
the Lord is intent upon providing for the sake of the distressed person who seeks wealth.

Since He knows by His very nature everything that has entered the heart of the worshipper, therefore, at that very time—namely, at the moment the worship begins—He does not grant the fruit immediately even to those seeking wealth or truth; rather, He grants it after the ripening of karma. Thus he says: "The afflicted" (*ārtam*).
For that purpose, for the sake of the desired object. || 56 ||

The All-pervading Lord, having observed the ripening of karma through His own inherent necessity, ordains the fruit for the devotee who is without other cause and has no other refuge but Himself. (57)

One’s own destiny (*svaniyati*) is the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that "this shall be thus as created by oneself. [The subject] is joined with that; that is to say, without transgressing it. Regarding the phrase "the ripening of karma" (*karmapākam*): here this should be noted—that the ripening of karma is its capacity to yield a fruit. And that [capacity] is, in some cases, produced by a specific time of the karmas, and in other cases...
It is produced by the cooperation of another action; indeed, an action that has been conjoined with another action is called "intense" (*utkaṭa*).
As it is said in the Śivāgama: "The ripening of an action occurs through time, or even from another action.
And elsewhere: "One experiences the fruit right here in this world through extremely intense merits and sins."
The meaning is "awaiting such a ripening of karma"; "one's own" means belonging to oneself. || 57 ||
Having understood this with his whole being, one should become the provider of yoga and kṣema for him,
disregarding the ripening of karma and shaking off one's own destiny.

Having recognized him as one's own, [one should serve him] with one's whole being—through mind, speech, and so forth—as the provider of *yogakṣema*. *Yoga* is the attainment of what has not yet been attained;

*kṣema* is the preservation of what has already been attained. The sense is that he himself performs both of these for that person. The term *niyati* (destiny) is indicative of *prārabdha* (the karma of this life); the meaning is "having shaken off both destiny and *prārabdha*."
Having thoroughly accomplished that means, one should swiftly unite it with the fruit;
for this alone is the state of Great Lordship, which consists in the greatness of absolute freedom.

Having properly accomplished that means for one who is free from desire by removing obstacles—[an objector might say: "But surely destiny (niyati) is entirely impossible to transgress? [To this] he says: "This very thing" (etadeva). The meaning is that it is precisely the transgression of destiny and so forth. || 59 ||
Even *prārabdha* karma or destiny becomes powerless when one is turned away from Maheśa;
this is illustrated in the case of Mṛkaṇḍu’s son, who was utterly devoted to the Lord (*ekā kathā*, to be found in the thirty-third chapter of the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa). || 60 ||

If it is objected that there is a contradiction with scripture—given the statement, "Indeed, even in the case of transgressing *prārabdha* and *niyati*, the *prārabdha* would not go to destruction, nor would *niyati* be otherwise"—the author replies: "The *prārabdha*... The intended meaning is that the purport of scripture is that the majesty of *prārabdha* and *niyati* applies only to one who is turned away from the Great Lord (*maheśa*).
This is not established by scripture alone, but is also established by tradition; thus he says: "This... (verse 60).
It is known by all that Maheśa has transgressed the laws of destiny and what was previously begun;
I shall state the proof for this to you—listen, O you who are dear as life—to what is being uttered.
The transgression of destiny and of what has been commenced; here, regarding the transgression of destiny and of what has been commenced which are not to be transgressed;
[he states] the logical justification (*upapatti*). || 61 ||
Although the destiny of what has already begun is indeed impossible to transgress, nevertheless,
that destiny cannot be averted by those who lack human effort.
Of those things that are non-human, meaning devoid of human effort. || 62 ||
For this very reason, prārabdha karma is exhausted by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
It does not sufficiently bind one to the miseries encountered in the visible world.
If it is asked, "From where is this known?", he says: "Precisely for that reason. [This means] by yogins devoted to *prāṇāyāma* through the practice of breath control.
If it is asked, "How is this known?", he says: "By direct perception," namely, "not them" (verse 63).
Those who turn their backs on manly effort are swallowed by the serpent of destiny;
this is indeed ordained by necessity, and it is experienced exactly so—and not otherwise.
If it is asked, "How can there be such a defeat of what has been commenced by human effort? [the author] replies, "In that very same way, from destiny and inherent nature," stating "this" (etad).
The meaning is that the removal of what was commenced by human effort occurs in that same manner. The sense is that destiny must be postulated in accordance with experience. || 64 ||
Niyati is the power of Īśa, whose sole nature is volition;
for Īśa is indeed one whose will is true, and therefore she is truly unassailable.
For this very reason, that is, precisely because of the possession of the power of true resolve. || 65 ||
Even that [intellect] becomes dulled when directed toward one who is solely devoted to the Supreme Lord;
yet it remains undulled, for such is its very nature. (66)

That *niyati* (destiny) is also untransgressible. If it is objected that "untransgressibility" and "being blunted" are contradictory, he says: "unblunted. For that *niyati* is of such a nature that it is indeed blunted in one who is devoted to the Supreme Lord. The underlying sense is this: for *prārabdha* (the karma already commenced)...
That karma which is oriented toward fruition is likewise determined by *niyati* (the principle of necessity) as being conquered by the yogi; thus it is so ordained.
In the present context, even one who is a practitioner of *niṣkāma* (desireless) devotion becomes a yogi through the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), and by this means that [karma] is also conquered.
Furthermore, that which has already begun (*prārabdha*) is indeed unavoidable for one who is not a yogi. And such is *niyati*.

That [law] is of the nature of the Blessed One’s resolve and is by all means of an inviolable character. Nevertheless, it is its very nature that it becomes blunted when directed toward those who are solely devoted to the Blessed One;
thus, it remains unblunted everywhere else. || 66 ||
Therefore, abandoning fallacious reasoning, take refuge in Maheśa;
for he, being without motive, will establish you in the highest good. 67.

Since even *prārabdha* (commenced karma) and *niyati* (destiny) do not constitute an obstacle for one who is intent upon the Blessed One, therefore—by being causeless and free from desire—that Maheśa [is the goal]. 67.
This alone is the first step toward the palace of security;
apart from this, there is no possibility of even the slightest fruit elsewhere. (68)
This alone is the very practice of worship by way of causelessness; elsewhere, it is a means [to an end]. || 68 ||
Having heard these words spoken by his beloved, Rāma Hemacūḍa, with a heart exceedingly joyful, then questioned that wife of his once more. (69)
"O beloved, speak to Maheśvara—who might be my refuge, the creator of all, the independent self, by whose power the universe is governed. (70)

Having heard that the Supreme Lord is the creator of the world and such, and considering that being a creator necessarily entails possessing a body, he asks: "In whom among the embodied beings, such as Śiva and others, have you determined the status of being the Lord?"—to him they replied: "Some indeed call him Viṣṇu, others Śiva, and some Gaṇeśvara."
Likewise, [one should worship] Sūrya, Nṛsiṃha and others, as well as the Buddha, the Sugata himself. || 71 ||
If it is asked, "Whence does this doubt of yours arise here?", he replies that it is because of the lack of unanimity among the scriptures (*śāstra-anaikya*):
"Him" (referring to *buddha*)—namely, the Buddha and the Sugata, according to certain followers of the Buddhist school. (71)
They have proclaimed in many ways that Arhat, Vāsudeva, Prāṇa, Soma, Pāvaka, Karma, Pradhāna, and Aṇu are [the ultimate reality], and so forth. (72)
The Jains declare him to be an Arhat; the Pāñcarātras, Vāsudeva; and those who worship Prāṇa and the rest, [declare him] to be Prāṇa and so forth.
Although the agency of karma and the other factors was already refuted previously, they are enumerated again here by way of incidental discussion.
The nature of the cause of the world is indeed divided by various opinions; explain to me where, in that regard, the notion of an "Īśvara" (Lord) should be applied. (73)
Thus, the nature of the cause and creator of the world is differentiated by various diverse opinions; therefore, he says: "In that regard" (tatra). || 73 ||
For it is certain that there is nothing unknown to him, since that Blessed One Vyāghrapāda has perceived both the higher and the lower. (74)
Vyāghrapāda is your father. || 74 ||
Therefore, even for women, this knowledge shines forth in such a way. Tell it to me, who am full of faith and dear to you, O speaker of nectar (O beloved speaker of nectar)! || 75 ||
Therefore, because of that connection. || 75 ||
Thus questioned by her beloved, Hemalekhā spoke with joy:
"O Lord, I shall tell you; listen to the decision of the Lord."
For the Lord is the creator of the dissolution and origination of the web of the universe;
he is Viṣṇu, he is Śiva, he is the Creator (Brahmā), and he is both Sūrya and Soma.
He alone, in every way and in his entirety, is described by all [the scriptures];
he is neither Śiva, nor Viṣṇu, nor the Creator (Brahmā), nor anyone else at all.
Having declared that every being— whether Viṣṇu, Śiva, or anyone else designated by the Vaiṣṇavas and others— is indeed that very same Supreme Lord,

whose independent conscious nature (svatantra-cid-rūpa) is the underlying essence pervading all forms of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and so forth; he has thus described His state as the Self of all, and stated that the visible, gross body, which is mutually distinct, does not belong to Him.
He negates that it is a real form with the words "not Śiva," and so forth. (78)
I shall now declare this to you; listen with the utmost concentration.
They call Śiva the creator, the five-faced and three-eyed one. (79)
"This is Śiva" and "this is not Śiva"—those who hold such views are the Śaivas. || 79 ||
That agent is conscious and possesses a body, just like the maker of a pot;
for even in the world, a conscious agent is indeed observed to possess a body. (80)
It is accompanied by the gross body. If one asks why this is so, he explains by dividing [the categories], saying "in the world"; the agent is the potter and so forth. || 80 ||
Neither a bodiless nor an insentient entity is ever observed to be an agent anywhere;
for in that regard, primary agency can belong only to that which is sentient. (81)
Thus, agency is observed to belong only to the conscious being as qualified by a body; nevertheless, between that body and the consciousness therein— || 81 ||
For in dreams, this living being, having abandoned the gross body,
creates all desired things by means of a body consisting of consciousness.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? [the author] says that the elemental body cannot be the agent because of its variability: "In dreams...
He states that the dream-body is not of such a nature: "...consciousness... (82).
Therefore, the body is the instrument for the conscious self (cit-ātman) in its activity;
for living beings require instruments, since their autonomy is incomplete. (83)

Therefore, since an effect can occur even without a gross body, there is a deviation [from the rule]. If it is argued that, even as an instrument, the Lord requires either a gross or a mental body, he says "no"—namely, "of the individual souls" (jīvānām). || 83 ||
But the Blessed One, as the creator of the world, by virtue of his perfect sovereignty, creates the entire universe without depending on anything whatsoever. (84)

He says "the Lord" to show that although individual souls (jīvas), due to their incomplete sovereignty, depend upon instruments and the like, the Lord, who possesses complete sovereignty, has no dependence whatsoever on anything. [The term] "unimpaired" means complete. 84.
Therefore, the body does not exist at all; this is indeed the primary conclusion.
Otherwise, like [the bodies] in the world, it would be the locus for the agent's appropriation. (85)

Therefore, since there is no purpose in postulating a body for him, otherwise—if he were dependent on instruments and so forth like a potter—the creator Lord would also have to depend upon a substratum for his material cause. || 85 ||
And likewise, when joined with the accumulation of causes such as place, time, and so forth, the Great Lord, while creating the world, would become just like a living soul (jīva). (86)

The meaning is that [the Lord] would become merely a collection, an aggregate—that is to say, a totality—and thus His status as the Lord (Īśvaratva) would be destroyed. This is because He would be like a potter or similar craftsmen. || 86 ||
Furthermore, even prior to the creation of the world, his perfect sovereignty would be obstructed;
that universal agency would fail to be accomplished, and it would be thwarted—of this there is no doubt. (87)

To the objection that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "The world" (*jagat*). The world, consisting of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth, would be established even prior to the creation of the world. The point is that if God requires a material cause and so on for the act of creating the world, then the eternity of that material cause and the rest is established. To the suggestion, "Let it be so," he replies: "That [material cause and so forth]. If one asks, "Let it be," he says: [the following].

Regarding the phrase "omnipotence" (*sarvakartṛtva*): since the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth would have to be established prior to creation, [the Lord] would not be their agent; thus, his omnipotence would be contradicted.
Furthermore, if he were merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and lacked the status of being the material cause, his very nature as the Lord (*īśvara*) would be untenable.
The intention is as follows: as stated by Kṣemarājācārya—this verse, which is cited in the *Spandapradīpikā* (p.
23) as a verse from the *Āgamarahasya*—"Those who designate the Lord as a causal agent..."
"A handful of sesame seeds has been offered here by these [people] to the Mistress;
alas, they proclaim the state of a lord of love for one who has been brought under control by approaching the limbs of another. Thus it is said.

Moreover, if God were merely the efficient cause— given his eternity— the production of an effect would not be possible. For the proponents of the theory of origination (*ārambhavādins*) maintain that prior to creation, fragile atoms, having been conjoined by the will of God, become the initiators of the effect.

This is not tenable; for in the world, it is a conscious being that acts by conforming to the will of another, not an unconscious one. Thus, the conformity of atoms to the will of God is indeed untenable. [Objection: But surely such is the power of God that even atoms must conform to His will. [Reply: This is true.

The Lord is indeed possessed of unlimited power; by that very supernatural power, the Blessed One is capable of the act of creating the world without depending on material causes or other such factors. Even this being so, the admission of dependence upon atoms and the like for the Blessed One’s act of creation is merely a manifestation of devotion to dualistic doctrine.

Thus it should be understood. By this, the Sāṃkhya with a Lord (Seśvara-sāṃkhya) is also refuted; it should be understood that for us, who rely solely upon scripture and whose supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord is capable of sustaining all accepted worldly transactions, there is not even a scent of inconsistency. Now, [one might object]:

In order to distance [the Lord] from the faults of partiality and cruelty, it must be accepted by all that karma is the instrumental cause for the activity of the world. If it is argued that, in this way, the dependence of the Lord upon something else is established, we reply: True, this is indeed an insurmountable difficulty for the proponents of dualism; however, for us, the proponents of non-dualism—

By the analogy of a reflection in a mirror, since the entire universe consists of the single essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*), even action (*karman*) is non-different from the nature of the Supreme Lord; thus, because it requires nothing else, there is not even a trace of room for any defect.
If it is objected: "Even so, since agency regarding objects such as a pot resides in the potter and others, the Lord is not the agent of everything," we say: no.

There is no fault [in this], because the potter-soul is non-different from the Lord. Furthermore, just as an act performed by a king’s servant is considered an act of the king, so too that which is created by Brahmā and others is an act of the Lord. As it has been stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"For indeed, this potter [acts] through the very sovereignty of the Lord."
"By means of the sequence of processing that specific clay and so forth, one should produce a jar. (1.41) || 87 ||
Therefore, one should create the world without depending on the visible body and so forth;
consequently, O beloved of the vital breath, the gross body does not exist in reality.
Therefore, because sovereignty is obstructed when there is dependence on a body and so forth. || 88 ||
For those of gross intellect are deluded by this formless supreme nature;
yet, for those endowed with devotion, it is meditated upon by them in whatever manner and wherever they may be.
Now, if the body does not exist in reality, then from where does this body of Viṣṇu and others arise? To this he says: "Others," etc.

In this Lord, they are deluded—that is, they fall into confusion and do not know Him. Such are those who are likewise endowed with devotion. In whatever place—such as Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, and so forth—as follows:
Just as [he appears] in forms such as five-faced or one-faced. || 89 ||
In this way, the Lord himself, who is a wish-fulfilling gem for his devotees, assumes manifold forms;
therefore, the Lord is indeed consciousness, and his body is supreme consciousness itself.
"By oneself" means not in dependence upon mother, father, and so forth; this is the sense.
For this very reason, since such bodies are fashioned by mere will, [she is] supreme, undivided consciousness. || 90 ||
Consciousness alone is the Great Being, the Sovereign Empress,
the Supreme Goddess; within her, Tripurā shines, undivided yet appearing as if divided.
"It is consciousness alone. For consciousness, established in its own essential nature, is like a waveless ocean; it is the fourth state (*turīya*), free from the three qualities (*tripuṣā*).
When that very consciousness, through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), attains the state of sentience characterized by being the agent of the act of consciousing, it is called the Lord (*īśvara*).
This is what the Vedāntins call the "effect-Brahman" (*kārya-brahma*). That...
Consciousness is the Great Being, whose true nature is undivided. She is the Sovereign Empress, independent;
the Supreme Goddess, possessing unsurpassed sovereignty; Tripurā, who is the Fourth State. The meaning is that she shines everywhere and at all times without distinction. || 91 ||
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is like a city in a mirror;
because of its identity with that [divine] form, there is no perception of superior or inferior therein.

If it is argued that that consciousness does not shine anywhere at all, but rather only the world shines, he says: "Like a mirror," etc. For just as a city of reflections, though non-different from the mirror, appears as if distinct from the mirror, so too within this consciousness [the world consisting of] the moving and the unmoving [appears].

The world, though non-different from that [Consciousness], appears as if distinct. For just as children, seeing a reflection, do not recognize the mirror, so too fools, even while perceiving the world, do not recognize Consciousness.
And thus, this very one called "Lord" is singular even in Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others; therefore, in that regard, within Viṣṇu, Śiva, and so forth—
One should practice meditation on the superior and the inferior. || 92 ||
Others, however, maintain that primacy and so forth are indeed imagined within the essential nature [of Brahman].
Therefore, the wise person should meditate upon the supreme form, which is partless. 93.
If it is asked, "How is it that superiority and so forth are described in the scriptures?", he says: "Others [hold this view]. Regarding the gross [body]:
therefore, since that status of being primary is imagined and not real; [the reality is] partless and bodiless. (93)
One who is incapable [of perceiving the subtle] attains unsurpassed welfare by meditating upon that gross form which is firmly established in the intellect;
for otherwise, his progress toward liberation would not occur even in ten million births. || 94 ||
If it is asked, "Surely that form can be worshipped by the wise; what else is to be done by another? he says:

"Because of incapacity. The meaning is that whatever form is firmly established in the intellect—that is, to which the intellect is firmly attached—that form is to be worshipped. Otherwise, there is no way [to reach the goal] without propitiating the Lord.
The attainment of the means for the supreme good. This is a six-footed verse (ṣaṭcaraṇa-śloka). || 94 ||
[Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Lord," in the account of Hemacūḍa within the glorious Jñānakhaṇḍa.]
[Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the eighth chapter:
Having thus heard the words of his beloved and having realized the reality of the Great Lord (Maheśitṛ),
he became certain that the Triple City (Tripura) consists of pure consciousness (cinmaya), as determined by the speech of Hemalekhā.
In this chapter, having offered praise through verses of measured portions, the explanation of the hidden meaning of Hemalekhā’s words is thoroughly investigated for the sake of detachment.
Having known through indirect means that the Traipura is the fourth state—that form which is purely consciousness and is the very reality (tattva) of the Lord—|||

With a heart full of confidence, having learned from his gurus that Tripurā— the Great Goddess whose nature is composed of the three qualities— is supreme, he was illuminated by her great sovereignty.

Having learned from his gurus that [the Goddess] consists of qualities (*guṇarūpā*), possesses qualities (*saguṇarūpā*), and has a form endowed with qualities (*saguṇamūrti*), as well as her mantras and so forth—the ellipsis being "having understood this"—he was manifested with great sovereignty, pierced by the power of the Supreme Lord’s grace. This is what is meant:
"Hemacūḍa became firmly devoted to Her with single-minded intent."
In this manner, several months passed while they were engaged in the worship of others.
That [city] is Tripura. Single-mindedness is firm devotion; following after it is worship. || 3 ||
Tripurā, the Supreme Sovereign, bestowed her grace upon his heart;
his mind, turned away from sense-objects, shone forth, intent on spiritual inquiry.

He states what kind of serene confidence (*prasāda*) he then produced: "from the object" (*viṣayāt*), meaning intent upon the investigation of the true nature (*svarūpa*), being devoted to such inquiry. (4)
In this world, nothing is so difficult to find without the assistance of others as a mind inclined toward discernment, which is the primary cause of liberation. (5)
Such is the state of being inclined toward investigation preceded by turning away from sense objects. To explain why this is difficult to attain, he says:
"That which... (verse 5).
O Rāma, as long as the mind does not become supremely intent on inquiry,
there is no union with the highest good by any means whatsoever, even through hundreds of methods.
Then, on another day, he again met with his beloved in private, his mind intent upon profound reflection.
Now, immediately after the perfection of being intent upon investigation. || 7 ||
She saw her beloved approaching his own home from afar;
rising up, she brought him forward and seated him upon her own seat.
*Niketa* means a house. || 8 ||
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with the washing of his feet and other honors,
he spoke these supreme words, beautiful as the flowing of nectar.
"O beloved! Today at last I see you;
indeed, your body appears free from disease, for this body is truly the abode of illness. (10)
Preṣṭha means most beloved. || 10 ||
Tell me that account, for which reason I was not remembered by you;
surely it is never the case that you have looked upon me or spoken to me without [first addressing] me.
That is the account of the body (*śārīra*). If it is asked, "From where does this [great] esteem for you arise? he says: "Because... (verse 11).
Not even a fraction of the day has passed; how then can this state have been established?
I believe your conduct is not on the path that is agreeable to you.

Thus, since you have neither remembered nor seen me—or indeed, [as the variant suggests,] since there is no such thing as seeing me—how could you have remained [in that state]? I do not believe it even in a dream.
Whether it was in a dream or elsewhere, tell me how this came to be;
how was even a single night spent by you as if it were equal to an eon?
The sense is: "How could such a possibility exist elsewhere while you are awake? This being so, how did your state come to be thus?
"Without me— or rather, even a single moment without me— was as unbearable as an entire eon," she said,
and having embraced him, she then remained for a moment as if exhausted.
"Even a single moment without me is extremely difficult to endure. || 14 ||
He too, embraced by his beloved, did not undergo even the slightest change;
he said, "O beloved, you ought not to delude me in this way. (15)
Due to his firm dispassion, he did not undergo even the slightest transformation through the embrace of his beloved or similar acts.
Realizing that she had set out to delude him, he said: "O beloved," [verse 15].
I know you very well; there is no cause for your grief.
You are wise, knowing both the higher and the lower; how indeed could delusion touch you?
"How could there not be grief at separation from you? To this, he says: "In the high and the low" (parāvareti). || 16 ||
I have come to ask you about the truth; listen as I speak of that which I shall tell you.
Clearly explain to me that account of your own past which was previously related.

"I have not come here to play as I did before," he said; thus [he spoke of] "the reality" (*tattvam*). "My mother is a great virtuous woman" (5.108), and so forth, refers to his own past conduct previously described. || 17 ||
Who is said to be your mother, or your friend, and who is their husband? Who are their sons and the rest as well? Tell me, where are they, and what is your relationship to them? (18)
These are the mother and the others. || 18 ||
This is not well understood by me; I do not consider that to be a falsehood.
However, everything you have spoken was said entirely under some pretext. (19)
That which you have spoken is not falsely uttered; rather, it was spoken by means of a designation for something else. || 19 ||
Discriminate that for me and explain it clearly so that I may understand it;
I have taken refuge in you—sever the doubt in my heart. (20)
Thus addressed, Hemalekhā, her face and eyes radiant with joy,
perceived that he was of perfectly pure intellect and endowed with a supreme desire to favor others.
[This is] endowed with the grace of Parā Tripurā. || 21 ||
Surely this man is utterly turned away from sense-objects due to his extreme fortitude;
he has been pierced by the power of Maheśānī (or, according to variants, by Viṣṇu’s power or by great sovereignty), and thus the accumulation of his merit has borne fruit.
By the power of grace. || 22 ||
This is the time for awakening; therefore, I shall awaken him.
O Lord, what great fortune you have attained through the power of the Master's grace! (23)
The ellipsis is: "Thinking that this is the time for awakening, he spoke thus. "By you" (te) means by thee. || 23 ||
Otherwise, one never perceives the distaste for sense objects;
this should be known as the primary characteristic of the Lord’s grace from the very beginning. (24)
Otherwise, in the absence of fortune (*bhāgya*) at some time and so forth; "this" refers to what is about to be stated. "The characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) means the indicator.
Regarding the word "from the beginning" (*āditaḥ*): the sense is that when there is the grace of the Lord (*īśānugraha*), it arises right at the outset. || 24 ||
I shall now truly declare to you another [state]: the distaste for enjoyments and a mind inclined toward inquiry—the conduct prescribed for one who is ever established in the Self. (25)
Furthermore, there is a second [verse]: "The mode of subsistence (vṛtti), the state (sthiti) which is ever-abiding"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 25 ||
Supreme Consciousness is my mother; Intellect is considered my friend; and Ignorance is called my unchaste wife, with whom that Intellect is closely associated. (26)
The power of ignorance, however, is clearly manifested in the world, in that it presents a snake upon a rope and thereby instills great fear. (27)
Mahāmoha was his son, and Manas became his son;
his wife was Kalpanā, and they had five sons.
Those five are the organs of knowledge; their locus is the physical orb (golaka).
The fading away of objects, however, is the mental impression (saṃskāra) of the mind. || 29 ||
The enjoyment of that [body] would be like the enjoyment of a dream; and that which is its own sister is conceptualization (kalpanā).
Desire (āśā) would be the "great eater," and its two sons are the body and speech.
Its enjoyment is the enjoyment of objects that have been forgotten. || 30 ||
Anger and greed—those two have been described; that city, however, is the body.
That which is my great mantra is indeed the manifestation of its own essential nature.
Prāṇa is declared to be the movement, the dear friend of the mind;
the hells, beginning with Kāntāra, are likewise proclaimed—all this has been fully described. || 32 ||
Union with the Buddha is called samādhi by me;
reaching the world of my Mother is declared to be liberation, O dear one. (33)
Thus has my own life-story been told; surely you too are of such a kind.
Therefore, having understood this well through proper reasoning, attain the supreme good.
This is his own account. || 34 ||
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the illustrious Jñānakhaṇḍa, in the narrative of Hemacūḍa, within the exposition of the story of worldly existence.]
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrītripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the ninth chapter:
Having heard what was thus spoken by his beloved, Hemacūḍa was greatly amazed;
with a voice faltering with joy, he proceeded to speak again. (1)

In this regard, having discerned his own essential nature through verses whose syllable-counts are not deficient (*nonāṅka*), Hemacūḍa attained the state established within his own self; this is what is being stated.
Again, [he] spoke to Hemalekhā. || 1 ||
"O beloved, you are blessed and skillful; oh, what a magnificent expanse of your knowledge! For how could I describe all that has been told to me in the form of this narrative? (2)

The majesty of knowledge is its greatness. Since my entire own life’s experience has been told by means of another’s instruction through narration, what more can I describe? (2) Such a life story of mine was never known to me anywhere.
By your words, I now perceive that clearly, as plainly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of my hand. || 3 ||
At a certain time, that experience of one's own self takes the form of the feeling of suffering through anger, greed, and so forth. (3)
Aha! I remember and experience within me the wonderful activity of the world.
What is that supreme Consciousness, the Mother? And how can there be any birth for Her?
I clearly remember the past and experience the present within my own inner self; the activity of people is merely worldly transaction. || 4 ||
"Who indeed are we, and what is our true nature? Tell that to me.
Thus questioned by Rāma regarding his beloved, Hemalekhā spoke.

By the narrative beginning with "My mother was a great satī" (5.108), the supreme consciousness (*paraciti*) is declared to be the goal (*upeya*), and it is stated that one's own self is a portion thereof. In that context, having asked about the nature of the goal with "What is that supreme [consciousness]?
(9.4), he asks about the nature of his own self: "And who are we?"—referring to the body.

Because the body and so forth are determined to be non-self through the hearing of [the Self's] priority and the hearing of the vital breaths and so forth as its retinue, this question— "Who is this?"— should be understood as referring to the Self, since designations such as "person" (puruṣa) reside in the aggregate. || 5 ||
"O Lord, listen; I shall explain this hidden meaning with reverence.
Examine the nature of the self with an utterly pure intellect. (6)

Regarding the phrase "of hidden meaning": this question is so profound that it is truly impossible to answer; nevertheless, I shall provide some response. He states that very point: "Examine [this]. The sense is that since the supreme consciousness (*parā citiḥ*) is almost as good as known once the pure nature of the Self is known, the first question is set aside and an answer is given to the second.
Reflect upon this yourself. Regarding that, he states the means: "by means of extreme purification.
Impurity is the outward orientation of the intellect—the internal organ—through the doors of the senses and so forth;
purity, indeed, is its inward orientation through the abandonment of that [outwardness]. And thus, there is the non-selfhood of the external body and so on.
The meaning is that, having reached this certainty, by turning the intellect inward, the true nature of the Self can be known by oneself alone. || 6 ||
It is neither visible nor can it be expressed; therefore, how shall I speak of it?
Once you have realized the true nature of your own self, you will indeed know the Mother.

If it is asked, "Is the reality of the self not known by you? Why is it not spoken? he says, "It is not seen," and so forth. The meaning is that it is not an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). The sense is that an object of knowledge can be known through the instruction of another; however, because that [reality] is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), [it cannot be so known].

The intended meaning is that because the property which serves as the cause for the application of words is absent, it cannot be denoted by them either. Now, if it is asked, "In that case, tell me of that Supreme Consciousness who is the Mother," he says: "Known" (jñāta). || 7 ||
For there is no instruction regarding one's own nature; therefore, devoid of an instructor,
behold your own form by means of your own self, resting upon pure awareness.

Since its own nature is neither visible nor expressible, there can be no direct instruction regarding it; thus he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). "Instruction" (*ādeśa*) means teaching. If it is asked, "In that case, how is it to be known?", he replies: "By one's own self" (*svātmanā*).
The meaning is that it exists as the form of the pure Self. That is to say, it exists as the form of pure consciousness, free from all objects.

The meaning is as follows: or rather, the sense is that it exists by its own nature as the pure subject (draṣṭṛmātra), which is established through the exclusion of the non-self consisting of the visible object. If one asks, "Where do I perceive such a thing?", he says: "In the pure," etc.
That is, in the pure intellect (buddhi), which is devoid of the forms of objects, [it is perceived] independently of the operation of the instruments [of perception].
The intended meaning is that its own nature (svarūpa) is what is to be known. || 8 ||
Shining with its own radiance, it illuminates all beings from the gods down to the animals;
it shines everywhere, for everyone, at all times, yet remains devoid of the conceit of "I."
If it is asked, "Since that is invisible, how can I see it?", he says: "O Lord. The Lord is Sadāśiva, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the worm called the extremely subtle *stamba* (the stationary plant);
he manifests as the Self of all beings from the gods down to the animals. If so, one might ask, "Why then does he not manifest to me?"
If it is asked: "Not illuminated by cognitions"—by cognitions that are delimited and have the form of the visible;

that which has no illumination [from them]—because the intellect is covered by the forms of the visible, it does not shine forth absolutely, but rather shines only as if the sun were shrouded by thick clouds.
The meaning is that in a cognition devoid of the form of the visible object, [the object] shines forth intensely, like the sun in a cloudless sky.
If it is argued that because it appears in cognition alone, it follows that there is a delimitation [of the object], he says:
"everywhere. That which appears as a jar or the like—everywhere, at all times, and in relation to everyone—shines only through its own manifestation.

The sense is that just as the light of the sun, which shines everywhere, is fully manifested upon a wall, so too is [the Self] manifested in pure consciousness (*śuddhabuddhi*). Now, one might object: "When the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has ceased, that [Self] would not shine; how then [can it be said to be manifest]?"
If it is asked, "In all cases?", he says: "devoid of mental construction" (*mānavarjitam*). This means it is not an object for the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since the operation of an instrument does not apply to its agent, for this very reason it is also "unperceivable"—this is the intended meaning. || 9 ||
"How, where, when, and by whom could even a fraction of it be described?
'Show me my own eye'—thus has this been said by my beloved just now. (10)

Since no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates therein, how, in what form, in which place, at what time, and by what means of valid cognition could it be characterized even in the slightest degree?
Because it is not an object of any means of valid cognition, one cannot say, "This is such-and-such," at this time and in this place.
The intended meaning is that it is simply impossible to define. Here is an illustration: "My eye. [This means:
"Define this as the Self. || 10 ||
The teacher has no utility here, just as in the act of seeing with one's eyes; for even a great master, however skillful, how could he show another their own eye? (11)

Since the self is itself indefinable, the teacher has no direct utility in the vision of the self; thus he says: "Not here. "Nipuṇaḥ" means skillful or proficient. "Mahān" means endowed with greatness through asceticism, majesty, and so forth. || 11 ||
Therefore, the Guru is the means here, because he demonstrates that means.
I shall tell you that means; listen to it with a restrained mind. (12)

If this is so, what then should the teacher do for the disciple? To this he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). Because [the disciple] is incapable of discerning [the Self], the teacher—by means of that [instruction] through which one approaches (upa-ayati) [the truth] nearby—brings the Self, which has appeared as something far away (*parāg-dṛś*) to the disciple's vision, into proximity by generating the inward-turned vision (*pratyag-dṛṣṭi*). Thus does the teacher act.
The intended meaning is as follows: regarding the realization of the Self (*ātmāvagama*), he applies the term "means" (*upāya*) to the Guru, [expressing it as] "that means.
This is because he demonstrates that means—the instrument—for that vision of the Self. Therefore, because the Guru demonstrates the means, I shall declare that means. || 12 ||
As long as you perceive within yourself the notion "this is mine," that supreme, innate form of yours in which "mine" does not appear will not shine forth.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: having discerned that which you perceive as "self" up to "mine," and that which is beyond those—distinct from them and in which the notions of "thine" and "mine" do not appear—that is your own true nature. || 13 ||
Having gone to a solitary place and reflected upon this, whatever appears through the sense of "mine-ness," abandon each and every one of those and focus upon the Supreme Self.

Having gone to a solitary place, reflect upon that which I have said: "That which appears as 'mine' does not truly shine [as mine]. Discern it, discern it thoroughly. In this manner, at the time of discernment, having abandoned whatever appears through the sense of "mineness" and having determined it to be non-self (*anātman*), thereafter, recognize that which is unassailed by "mineness" as your own Self (*svātman*). || 14 ||
Just as I appear to you through the notion of "mine," yet I have no selfhood in you;
so too, because of mere relationship, [the world] is "mine" [to me], for I am not essentially constituted by it. (15)
He explains this very point by analyzing it with the words "Just as" (yathā): [the quality] does not belong to its own nature, nor is it included within its own nature. || 15 ||
Having renounced everything for my sake—that which is otherwise impossible to give up—perceive that Self and attain the supreme good. (16)

"Having thus abandoned through the certainty of 'I am not' every object that appears as 'mine,' that which remains as the nature of the renouncer— the form of pure conscious light, the ultimate limit of all abandonment, which cannot itself be abandoned"—
having been addressed thus by his beloved, Hemacūḍa rose up quickly.
Having mounted his horse, he went out from the city at that very moment. || 17 ||
Having entered the garden, which was like the Nandana grove, he entered in an instant a lofty crystal palace situated within the forest.
An *udyāna* is a pleasure grove; *unnamra* means high or elevated. || 18 ||
Having dismissed all his attendants, he commanded the gatekeepers:
"Let no one enter here while I am engaged in solitary reflection."
"Here," meaning in my presence; "the One," meaning the non-dual Self which is the ultimate limit of all negation;
"its investigation" means its discernment; [this occurs] while I am intent upon that—such is the sense. || 19 ||
The king’s ministers, the preceptors, or even the king himself must not enter here as long as I have not given you my command. (20)
Having spoken thus, he ascended to the top of the palace and entered the ninth story;
there, at a variegated window that overlooks all the worlds, he remained.
The ninth stage among the stages existing one above the other, wherein there is the observation of all worlds;
that is to say, it is exceedingly high. || 21 ||
Seated alone upon a seat rich with soft cotton,
he fixed his mind firmly and then engaged in reflection.
"Surely all these people are utterly deluded;
for not even a single one here understands their own self in the slightest degree. (23)
Everyone performs various activities for the sake of their own self; some constantly study the scriptures and the auxiliary branches of the Vedas.
For the sake of one's own happiness; "āmnāya" means the Veda. || 24 ||
Some acquire wealth, some rule the earth;
others fight with their enemies, while others are solely addicted to sensual enjoyments. (25)
"These [beings] perform this for their own sake; who among them could be the self?
No one here knows this [self]; whence, then, does this delusion arise? (26)
"Alas! Having acted without truly knowing myself, I now reflect upon that deed today as something as futile as an act performed in a dream. (27)
It was done by me; since it was done out of ignorance, it is therefore in vain. || 27 ||
House, grain, kingdom, wealth, wife, cattle, and so forth—
none of these constitute my true nature, because they rest upon the substrate of "non-I-ness" (anahaṃtā). || 28 ||
He states the manner of investigation with the words beginning "gṛhe" (in the house), etc. Regarding "non-I-ness" (*anahantā*):
because it does not manifest as "I," it lacks the status of being a substratum for I-ness (*ahantā*). || 28 ||
"For the sake of my purpose and for the sake of becoming a being, I shall indeed be a body in every way;
I am surely a descendant of the Kṣatriyas with a fair complexion—of this there is no doubt. (29)
"Madartheti": Because it is the object of the notion "I" (asmad-pratyaya), the body would be "I" for the reason that [it is] "me. He confirms this very point with the word "nūnam" (surely). || 29 ||
"Even these other people are likewise overcome by the sense of 'I'";
having thus resolved, the prince meditated upon that body. (30)

He considers that even for these people, the "I" (ahantā) is indeed the body itself; likewise, these [beings] are nothing but the body-self (dehātman). He meditated upon, that is, reflected on, the body as being the self. 30.
Then he proceeded to refute the notion that the body is the self:
"Alas! How can this body be the locus of the sense of 'mine'? (31)
Now, immediately following meditation: having perceived the true nature of the body and recollecting what Hemalekhā said—that the basis of "mine-ness" is non-self—she says: "Aho! (Verse 31).
"This aggregate of blood, bones, and so forth, which undergoes transformation at every moment—surely that must be my form; yet this [body] is seen to be severed. (32)
"How might my form come to be? He also states another reason: "severed," etc. (32).

By virtue of being equal to wood or a clod of earth, and because it exists otherwise in states such as dreaming, I am not the body; nor am I anything other than this vital breath (prāṇa), which is likewise of that same nature.

Since a limb such as the hand, which is a part of the body, when severed is perceived to be equal to a piece of wood or a clod of earth because it no longer serves as the locus for the sense of "I," how then can my form be the body? Furthermore,
in dreams and other states, this body is perceived as existing in a completely different manner through the process of mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*).
The sense is that because the body is determined to be of a single nature throughout waking and dreaming states, it lacks selfhood due to its distinct form;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), deep sleep or another birth is included. Such [a body] is the locus of notions such as "mine-ness" (*mamatva*). || 33 ||
Since I am not the mind nor the intellect, because these have been impelled by me, I am therefore certainly other than everything from the body up to the intellect; of this there is no doubt.
"Mameritam" means spoken with the sense of "mine-ness. Therefore, because the body and so forth are the substrata of mine-ness [it follows that they are not the self]. || 34 ||
Because there is no cause for the non-appearance of the thought "I do not exist at any time," I remain manifest at all times; of this there is no doubt. (35)

Since the body and so forth are non-self because they are the locus of the sense of "mine," and since nothing else is perceived, and because only emptiness is perceived in deep sleep, it might follow that the self is empty; to this, he says: "I. Because there is never an absence of the manifestation "I am not," the "I" which manifests at all times remains indeed as the very nature of existence.
The meaning is that [the self] is not of the nature of emptiness. Even in deep sleep, there is no authoritative cognition such as "I do not exist.

For if the experiencer were absent at that time, the recollection upon waking—"I was not aware of anything"—would be impossible, as it would entail the non-perception of all objects of perception. Thus, the self is not of the nature of emptiness.
The sense is that "I am" indeed shines forth at all times, because there is never an absence of the manifestation "I am not.
"But as for me who am manifesting, by what means is my manifestation?
I do not clearly know that; why is this not known by me? (36)

For what reason? By what specific cause does there arise the clear manifestation of the knowledge "I am this," when [the Self] is appearing only in a general way, like the sun obscured by clouds? I do not know; from what cause is this not known? || 36 ||
On this earth, objects such as a jar appear through the eyes and other [senses], and not otherwise;
this vital breath (prāṇa) appears through the skin, and the mind is impelled by cognition.
By means of knowledge—that is, by the cause which consists of the effect characterized as knowledge—it is inferred, that is, it is cognized through the relationship of cause and effect. || 37 ||
In this way, by what means would my intellect [perceive], since I do not know this manifestation?
For if the Self were not manifest to me simply through the manifestation of these [objects], [then how could it be so]? (38)

The meaning is that the intellect (*buddhi*) is thus inferred through its effect. "Me" refers to myself. Now, the word "atha" indicates the possibility of a cause. For just as a pure mirror does not appear at the time when a reflection manifests, so too he considers that the Self does not appear because these [objects] appear as non-Self.
"Of these," [it is said]. || 38 ||
"In that case, I shall examine these; from that, illumination will arise for me.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he abandoned the objects of the mental faculty.

Having thus determined that the appearance of the visible world is a common cause for the cognition of the self, he says: "Then [tarhi]". If the self does not appear because of the non-appearance of the non-self, then I do not discern these states of non-self; for these do not appear by themselves.

Because things that have not been reflected upon do not manifest. For just as at the time of reflecting on a jar, nothing other than it manifests, so too at the time of reflecting on the non-self, the Self does not manifest;
the sense is that the manifestation of the Self would occur through the reflection upon what is other [than itself].
"This reflection is of such a kind," and so forth—this is the mental delineation (*mānasollekha*).
By means of the mind—that internal organ consisting of the faculty of thought in the form of subtle cognition—it becomes the object of the mind; that is, it is the mental delineation. (39)
Then, in that very instant, he beheld a profound darkness;
his mind became certain that "this is my own form. (40)

Now, the construction [of the sentence] is as follows: that which arises immediately after the non-apprehension of any mere object whatsoever is "darkness" (tamaḥ), and this is the very nature of the self (ātmanaḥ rūpam).
"In a mere moment" means in the moment following the perception of darkness. "One whose mind is certain" means one by whom the mental modification consisting of darkness has been ascertained. 40.
Then he experienced incomparable joy and thought once more:
"Surely I shall see him again. Thus his mind was indeed restrained.
The joy [felt] because "the self has been seen" is born of delusion. || 41 ||
The flickering [mind], restrained by haṭhayoga, beheld for a mere moment a radiant mass of light, without beginning or end. || 42 ||

"I shall slightly scrape away the flickering mind by means of haṭhayoga"—this is merely through the persistent attachment of a firm resolve, and not through the practice of breath control, suppression, and so forth. It is luminous, being densely concentrated on light alone. || 42 ||
Having awakened, he reflected, filled with wonder: "What is this?
Oh, I see various things; how indeed is this? (43)

Having awakened in a mere moment by turning away from cessation, he was struck with wonder, thinking: "How is it that this darkness and this light—this contradictory nature of the self—are one and the same? (43)
"I shall see him again"—thus he restrained his mind at that time;
his consciousness, dissolved by sleep, shone forth for a very long time with great steadiness.

Then, immediately after that obstruction—by means of sleep, which consists in the absence of the commonality of matured karma—the mind becomes dissolved; the instrumental case is used here because sleep is the cause. || 44 ||
There he beheld a web of dreams consisting of various and manifold visions;
then, having awakened, he indeed fell into a state of profound reflection.
Am I covered by sleep that I am beholding these dreams? Ah, could it be that both darkness and light are of the nature of a dream? (46)
One considers that even what is seen, beginning with darkness, must be of the nature of a dream; thus [he says], "darkness. (46)
"But as for dreams, they are a delight of the mind; how can I avoid them?
Having firmly resolved, 'I shall see them again after restraining myself,' [he proceeds]. (47)
As I set out to restrain the mind, my mind continues to wander; how should I act in this matter?
Thus he reflects—[on] "the dream. This is the dream. 47.
He restrained the mind by force, and it became steady;
at that moment, he felt as if submerged within an ocean of bliss.

The construction is: "he firmly restrained the mind. Then, immediately after that restraint, the mind became steady for a short while. At that time—namely, in the state where the mind was restrained. || 48 ||
Again, due to the movement of his mind, he quickly became awakened [from that state], wondering:
"Was this a dream for me, or was it a delusion of the mind? (49)

Awakened and fallen from cessation, not knowing his own self—which at the time of cessation was of the nature of mere bliss—he conceptualizes it as "What is this? (as if he were [previously] ignorant). || 49 ||
Or could this indeed be true? It appears to me as something inconceivable:
how is it that I have not experienced even the slightest bit of happiness, despite having attained [everything]? (50)

Since the experience of happiness occurs everywhere through the experience of sense objects, one might raise the objection: "How can there be an experience of happiness at the time of cessation without experiencing anything at all?"—[expressed as] "I did not experience [anything]. (50)
"Aha! There is nothing here equal to even this slight fragment of happiness.
How is it that I, who was as ignorant as one in deep sleep, have remained in such bliss? (51)
There is some kind of happiness; like deep sleep, I remain seized by delusion through the non-perception of the external and internal. How, then, can there be this experience of happiness? (51)
I do not perceive any cause for this at all; how could it be so?
Although I set out today to understand the Self, I have not yet known it.
In this case, regarding the attainment of pleasure, how could that pleasure exist without a cause? (52)
I see myself and others as distinct from one another; what could this be? Is it light or darkness, or happiness, or perhaps something else? (53)
The grammatical connection is "I did not know myself. "This or that" refers to forms such as darkness, light, and so forth. The particle *api* has the sense of *eva* (indeed). Thus, the meaning is:
"or rather, it is indeed something other than light and the rest. || 53 ||
"May my self likewise become of this sequential nature; I do not reach its end here. Therefore, I ask again my wise beloved. (54)
Or else, the Self might be of the nature of a collection (saṅgha) characterized by a sequence of states such as darkness and so forth as they have been experienced;
regarding this, I do not reach a final certainty. || 54 ||
Having thus resolved, the prince summoned the gatekeeper and issued this command:
"Bring Hemalekhā into my presence."
Then, having arrived in a moment by the command of the Lord of Dvārakā,
she ascended the great palace as the light of the moon ascends Mount Meru.
Then he saw the prince, whose mind was peaceful,
motionless and free from agitation, with the entire circle of his senses withdrawn.

Hemalekhā saw him—tranquil and motionless. "Self" refers to the body and the mind. "Movement" (calaḥ) refers to the circulation of the vital breath (prāṇa). "Modification" refers to desire and the like. || 57 ||
Approaching quickly, she immediately ascended that seat;
once she was seated upon the same seat with him, in half a moment— || 58 ||
To her husband's side; upon that Hemalekhā, he [was] Hemacūḍa. || 58 ||
Opening her eyes, she looked toward her side where he was standing;
being gazed upon by him, she quickly embraced her beloved out of affection.
He gazed upon his beloved; she was gazed upon by him. 59.
Then his beloved spoke these beautiful words, flowing with nectar:
"O Lord, have you been summoned by someone? Is your body free from ailment? (60)
"Tell me the reason for which I have been summoned, and for what purpose I have come.
Thus questioned by his beloved, he spoke to her, his own dear one. (61)
"O beloved, instructed by you, I have settled here in this secluded place, intent on inquiry for the sake of discerning the characteristics of the nature of my own self. (62)

"Vicāra" (investigation) is that which is supremely to be adopted, meaning it is devoted to that; "vijñāna" (higher knowledge) is the characteristic of one's own nature, and since it is the cause of liberation, the connection is that one is "supremely devoted to investigation for the sake of that. || 62 ||
Moreover, how could that [object] be perceived as distinct by one who is intent upon it, given that the self is always attained and is also manifest? (63)

"By one intent upon that" means by one whose mind is not directed elsewhere. "Variegated" (*citram*) means manifold. "Separate" means utterly distinct, such as the forms of light, darkness, and so forth. He states what was reflected upon by himself [in this regard]: "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*).
Because it is the very nature of the self, there is the state of being attained; because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), there is the state of appearing. || 63 ||
Thinking that speaking incorrectly is caused by speaking otherwise, one who is well-established should cease speaking otherwise. (64)

Even for such [an object], there is an incorrect manifestation due to the cause of the manifestation of something else; the manifestation of others—the manifestation produced by the senses and so forth—is brought about by obstructing [the true nature]. 64.
I saw darkness and then a light quite different from it;
in one place I attained great happiness—tell me, my beloved, what is this? (65)
"Is this indeed the form of the Self, or might it be something else somewhere? Having investigated this thoroughly, tell me so that I may recognize it. (66)
This very [state] is one of light, darkness, and so forth; the other is distinct from light, darkness, and the like, occurring elsewhere than in meditative absorption (samādhi). 66.
Thus addressed, Hemalekhā, who knew both the higher and the lower, spoke:
"Listen, my dear, I shall tell you everything with a concentrated mind. (67)
This resolve you have cultivated regarding the restraint of external [objects] is considered auspicious by all, and is highly esteemed by those who know the Self. (68)
*Vyavasāya* means effort. It is *śubha* (auspicious) because it yields auspicious results; it is *sumukhya* (foremost) because it is the immediate means [to success]. || 68 ||
Without that [nature], it has never been attained by anyone, anywhere, at any time;
nor does it function as a cause for its attainment, because it is already in a state of being attained. (69)
By that cessation; that is, the realization of the non-dual Self. At some time and in some place.

Now, if it is argued that because the knowledge of the Self is produced by means (*sādhana*) and is thus like the knowledge of a jar or other objects, the Self would consequently be insentient (*jaḍa*) and non-Self (*anātman*), just like a jar—therefore he says: "Not that," and so on. That...

"Cessation" [refers to] the attainment of that; [that is,] the attainment of self-consciousness (*ātmavijñāna*). In the present context, what is intended to be expressed is consciousness whose very nature is the Self, and not consciousness *of* the Self. Therefore, the sense is that it is "attained. (69)
If there is no attainment, there can be no selfhood; if there is selfhood, how could there be non-attainment?
The self is entirely unattainable; its attainment does not exist.
He establishes this very point with the words: "In the case of non-attainment" (aprāptau). || 70 ||
Since that which has not been attained would have to be attained because of its being the self, there is no attainment [of it];
even its cessation does not have attainment as its purpose—see here the illustration.
Its cessation is the cessation of the mind; "nidarśana" means an illustration or example. || 71 ||
Just as in the world something shrouded by darkness is obtained through lamps and the like once that darkness has ceased—as if it had already been reached—so it is in this case. 72.
Something such as a jar; because that darkness is suppressed—that is, removed—by lamps, the sun, and so forth, the jar and other objects are reached.

Just as a jar or similar object, though already present there, appears as if it has been newly attained through the removal of darkness, so too the reality of the Self, which is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness alone, appears as if veiled by conceptual constructions arising from latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
By the cessation of conceptual construction, it remains as if it has been attained; thus, the sense is that cessation itself does not possess the nature of being an attainer. || 72 ||
Just as someone with a distracted mind, having forgotten a coin somewhere, [recovers it] again through meditative concentration by ceasing other thoughts; || 73 ||

With the intention that, in this case, there can be no obscuring agent distinct from its own nature as there is with darkness, he states another example, beginning with "yathā" (just as). "Niṣka" means gold. || 73 ||

Just as one might find a lost gold coin that has been recovered, so too does one attain that [Self]; in this matter, cessation is not the cause for the attainment of the gold coin, nor is it the cause for the attainment of the Self. || 74 ||

The second occurrence of the word "yathā" (as) should be construed as "just as it was obtained, so [is it] obtained. In this context, just as it is said that a lost gold coin (*niṣka*) is found unlost, so too the Self (*ātman*), though previously unobtained, becomes obtained. Here, just as the cessation of other thoughts is not the cause for obtaining the gold coin, so too in the present case, cessation is not the cause. || 74 ||
In the acquisition of its own nature, there would be no cause for the cessation of an external object;
you have not perceived its own self-nature because you lack proficiency regarding it. (75)

It is the cessation of external objects. If it is asked, "In that case, why was the self not perceived by me even through cessation? he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). "Vyutpatti" means familiarity with the object. || 75 ||
Just as one who is unaccustomed to light, having entered a royal assembly at night and seeing both the courtiers and the lamps, does not recognize the source of the illumination; || 76 ||
Regarding the point that one does not discern even what is being seen due to a lack of proficiency (*avyutpatti*), he provides an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*).

For a light that has issued from a lamp, though it possesses a brilliant form and illuminates objects, is not recognized by one who lacks familiarity with it. It should be understood that "in this same way, it was not discerned by you. (76)
Listen, my dear: at the end of cessation, indeed, darkness is perceived;
from the perception of darkness onwards, your remaining state persists.

Having thus stated that lack of proficiency (*avyutpatti*) is the cause for not perceiving its own nature, he says "Listen" (*śṛṇu*) for the sake of attaining proficiency in that regard. For cessation (*nirodha*) is the state free from conceptual construction (*avikalpadaśā*).
Since conceptual constructions such as "darkness," "beholding," or "form" are impossible therein, it is said to be "at the end of cessation."
At the beginning of the perception of such darkness—

in the prior state consisting of non-conceptual form— that residual nature of yours which remains, the remaining form that persists, is indeed the nature of the self as consciousness, distinct from the body and so forth.

And that [consciousness] manifests at the time of conceptualization precisely as conjoined with the object of perception (*dṛśya*). At the time of cessation, when the object of perception has fallen away, that which remains as pure consciousness alone is called the "residual form" (*śeṣabhāva*). Nor can such a residual state be denied.
It is possible [to know it] because it manifests through its own self-luminosity, and because one who has emerged from that state reflects: "For all this time, I was not aware of anything. || 77 ||
Always cultivate that state which bestows supreme bliss;
for in this matter, all others are possessed by the planet of great delusion and have their vision turned away.

Meditate constantly on that state—the remaining state—which is of the nature of pure vision devoid of the visible; remain intent on the continuous connection [of awareness], thinking "I am this. [This is] through the absence of the appearance of duality, which is the root of suffering.

Because there is an absence of anything that obscures bliss in the form of suffering and so forth, it manifests as the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); therefore, it is said to "bestow supreme bliss. In this very suchness of one's own nature (*svarūpa*), all the knowers of the scriptures and the yogis [are established].

Those whose vision is turned away (*parāgdṛśaḥ*)—meaning those whose internal organs are directed outward (*bahirmukhāntaḥkaraṇāḥ*), who are intent on the dogmatic attachment that "I see" as something delimited (*paricchinnābhiniveśaparāḥ*).
As it has been said: "That supreme state is unattainable by one whose vision is turned away, thinking 'I see'. (78)
Though they searched and searched, they did not attain that state of realization;
for in this world there are those who know the scriptures, who are skillful, and who are clever logicians. (79)

Since all there are seized by great delusion (*mahāmoha*), he says: "having sought" (*anviṣya*). They are frustrated and exhausted because they have not attained that state. That cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists of the continuous connection with the remaining states of being. Now, one might object: "Let this cultivation not exist; let us attain the goals of human life through the scriptures, fearlessness, sound reasoning, and so forth. To this he replies: "No."
(–) "There are" refers to those learned in the scriptures who are devoted to hearing; the skillful logicians who are devoted to reflection.

The sense is that even such persons, being "outward-looking" due to the absence of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), grieve indeed because they fail to attain the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). || 79 ||
Without knowing this reality, people grieve indeed day and night;
for that state is not attained by means of mere verbal artifice. (80)
In the case of the meaning of words and the meaning of what has been heard, reflection consists of that alone, namely, skillful contemplation. (80)
As long as a wise person continues to investigate or even analyze, that [object] is not attained; for it is simply not something that can be grasped.

[Objection: "Surely even an extremely subtle meaning of the scriptures ascends to the mind through repeated hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*); likewise, this state [of the Self] too would become established in the mind through repeated hearing and reflection alone—what need is there for *nididhyāsana*, which consists of restraint? [Reply: No; as for the word "until" (*yāvat*), it refers to investigation (*anveṣaṇa*).
[The stages are] hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*vicāra*), and contemplation (*manana*). If one asks why it is so, he says:

"Because" (*yataḥ*). The sense is that because this [reality] is beyond grasping and transcendent (*alaukika*), it cannot be established in the mind through mere hearing and reflection alone. || 81 ||
Having gone far, that is not attained; for it is always attained by remaining still.
That is not to be known through deliberation; it shines forth through non-deliberation.
He states its very transcendence: "having gone" (*gatvā*)—[variant *yataḥ*].
Here, "going" is the extension of the senses; "staying" is their non-extension. "Reflection" (*vicāra*) is thinking, the extension of the mind (*citta*);
"non-reflection" (*avicāra*) is the absence thereof. For the object is indeed external (*parāg*).

The meaning is this: while external objects can be known through the operation of the senses and internal objects through reflection, this [Self], by virtue of its nature as immediate presence (*pratyagrūpatva*), is difficult to discern without the restraint of the senses and the mind. || 82 ||

Just as one's own reflection on the surface of a mirror cannot be reached by running, so too nothing whatsoever can be attained through action; for it is like the thousands of reflections seen in a stainless mirror.
Regarding the point that [the goal] is not attained by means of active operation, he provides an illustration with the words "running" (*dhāvan*).

The intended meaning is that the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not extend to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Furthermore, since this is difficult to understand even for one who is disciplined and lacks proficiency regarding the reality (*vastu*), he provides yet another illustration for the sake of proficiency in that reality.
He explains [this] with the words "as follows" (yathā). || 83 ||
Just as even a child does not see a mirror while looking at it, so indeed does a person fail to see [the Self] while looking;
for one sees the reflection of the world in the great mirror of one's own Self. 84.

The connection is that even though a child who is untrained looks into a mirror, he does not see it; he does not recognize, "This is a mirror.
