He applies this to the point of the illustration with the words, "so too the person": the reflection belongs to the world (*jāgatam*), that is, it pertains to the world. (84)

One does not recognize one's own self because of the absence of proficiency in it, just as one who is accustomed to space does not perceive that which is situated within space while looking at it. 85.
He provides another illustration for the purpose of establishing the mind, beginning with "just as": proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is indeed familiarity with an object.

For just as a person who has somehow become familiar with space—knowing that space is characterized by providing room—when seeing the entire world everywhere, sees both the world and the space that is its support.

The meaning is this: just as one who is entirely unacquainted with space does not perceive space— even while seeing the entire world which rests upon space— so too, one whose own nature (ātman) is unacquainted does not perceive the Self— even while seeing the world reflected within one's own self.
The world does not perceive space, nor likewise its own essential nature;
O Lord, behold with subtle vision this world, which consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.

Because the Self was not perceived even through cessation due to a lack of understanding, it was stated [in verse 9.77], "Your remaining state persists there for the sake of that very understanding," and so forth. Nevertheless, observing the beloved's continued lack of understanding in that regard, he speaks again in another manner to bring about that understanding, beginning with the word "O Lord" (*nātha*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "the world exists."
In that regard, knowledge is established by itself; in its absence, nothing exists.
It is the authority for all means of valid cognition; otherwise, it would be invalid by itself. (87)

Although the world is manifold, it is briefly of two forms: knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Among these, the object of knowledge is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is of the nature of the non-self (*anātmarūpa*); thus, its detailed definition is unnecessary. Therefore, he defines only knowledge, beginning with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Between those two—

This is the meaning: [it exists] independently, without depending on its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If that were absent, nothing would appear; therefore, the intended sense is that it cannot be denied.
Now, an objection: it is untenable to say "nothing would exist" in its absence, because of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Anticipating the objection that "the object of cognition (*prameya*) is already established," [the author replies]: Only when the validity of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established will the object of cognition be established by those means; yet the validity of the means of cognition is not established without the act of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) with respect to the object of cognition, and in that [act of exclusion]...

In the act of cognition, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) possesses no independence, because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*), like an axe. Therefore, with the underlying intention that since the status of being a means of knowledge cannot be established for the means of knowledge themselves without a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*) cannot be established either, he says: "of the means of knowledge," [meaning] the means of knowledge of the means of knowledge.

The meaning is that it is the establisher of its own nature (*svarūpa*). Now, one might object: "Indeed, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself cognized; thus, if there is a dependence on a means of valid cognition for the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*) due to the dependence on yet another cognizer for that [cognizer] as well.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "not a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*). That which does not possess a means of valid cognition is [the subject]. (k, kh)
[Objection: "In that case, how does it exist? To this he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*).
The meaning is that it is independent of anything else with respect to its own existence. || 87 ||
Since it is established from the beginning and independent of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
its establishment can never occur through the relationship between that which is to be established and the means of establishing it.

If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says: "Because... [and] "independent of means of knowledge" (*pramāṇānapekṣam*). Since the knower, being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is always manifest, he does not depend on the light of a lamp—just as the solar light does not depend on the illumination of a lamp. The intended meaning is that there is no utility for a means of knowledge, which illuminates what was previously unilluminated, in that regard. Therefore...

Because there is no dependence on a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). "Accomplisher of attainment" (*siddhisādhaka*): "attainment" (*siddhi*) means either origination or cognition; "accomplisher" (*sādhaka*) means that which effects those two. The meaning is: the means of accomplishing them, whether it be a means of origination or a means of cognition. "The state of being an accomplisher of attainment" (*siddhisādhakasya bhāvaḥ*) refers to existence (*sattva*). [This is established] by virtue of the existence of that which accomplishes origination and so forth.
The sense is that its establishment never occurs; for neither the arising nor the manifestation of the conscious self (*cidātman*) is possible through any other means.
In the case of the arising or manifestation of the conscious self, there must be a requirement for an agent and an instrument.

Thus, since a distinction within consciousness is impossible due to its unity, it is logically untenable for the self to be both the agent and the instrument of its own establishment. [This applies to] the insentient self (*acidātmā*).
The intended meaning is this: how could one who is himself unestablished bring about the establishment of another without first establishing his own consciousness?
This has been elaborated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā* by means of the aphorism: "In the agent, who is the knower" (1.2). || 88 ||
For one who is deluded regarding that, there is neither question nor answer;
yet that surface of the great mirror remains undeniable. (89)

In that regard, concerning the nature of cognition itself, for one who is mistaken and intent on the objection that "there is no cognition," there is neither a question nor an answer; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. This is because an insentient object of knowledge, whose essential nature is restricted solely to its own form, lacks the capacity for conceptualization as to whether it exists or does not exist elsewhere.
The intended meaning is that since the accomplishment of everything depends upon knowledge, when that [knowledge] is denied, questions and so forth cannot be established.
Since, in the case of its denial, questions such as "does it exist" or "does it not exist" are untenable, he says: "it is not to be denied.
Now, one might object: there are two entities, namely knowledge and the object of knowledge; therefore, if knowledge is denied, how can there be the manifestation of the object?

Thus, it is [the subject] that would be impaired, but not the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeyasvarūpa*). Having raised the doubt as to how this could be so—given that "in its absence, nothing exists at all"—he says "that great mirror" (*tanmahādarśa*) in order to state that the object of knowledge is not separate from knowledge. (89)
Therein, indeed, everything shines like a reflection in a mirror;
there is no delimitation by either space or time. (90)

In that [reality], which is like the surface of a great mirror and whose essence is gnosis (*jñāna*), the sense is this: just as there is no reflection whatsoever without a mirror, so too there is no object of knowledge (*jñeya*) without gnosis. Now, one might object: "It is not the case that everything shines within it, such that everything would consist of reflections."
Anticipating the objection that space and time, which delimit [objects], are not included therein, he says "not so" by means of the words "by space" (deśena). || 90 ||
Since it appears within those [two], how could there be a determination by them?
For the appearance of a determination is like that of objects in the sky.
If it is asked, "How is there no determination of that which is known by place and time? he says:

"Within that" (*tadantare*). For just as a jar or the like, being illuminated by a lamp, is indeed submerged within the illumination of that lamp, so too is every part of the jar and so forth [submerged].

Just as an object that is not pervaded by the light of a lamp does not appear [as illuminated], so too all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), while being illumined by cognition, are indeed submerged within that cognition. Thus, even from the experience "the cognition has the form of a jar" and so forth, the appearing form of the jar and the like is internal to the cognition itself; for it is not [otherwise].
A pot or other object distinct from the form of the pot and so forth appearing within cognition is not accepted as existing externally to cognition,
because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and a lack of purpose;
for a pot or similar object whose nature is inferred from its reflection is, by definition, manifested by the inferential cognition itself.

Furthermore, because it is submerged within that [object], its inclusion within knowledge is established. Thus, since space and time are also objects of knowledge, they are established as being included within knowledge; the point is that there can be no determination of oneself by that which is included within oneself.
*Paricchidi* means determination (*paricchitti*). [Objection: But how is it that "this is ignorance" is not known at this moment?

If it is argued that there is an appearance of limitation, [the author] says "of limitation" (*paricchedasya*), meaning that for all-pervasive and undivided space (*ākāśa*), there is merely an appearance of limitation— just as by jars and other objects submerged within it— by means of "entities" (*vastubhiḥ*), such as jars and the like. || 91 ||
O Prince! Observe with subtle vision your own body, wherein this entire universe shines within the universal consciousness. (92)

Thus, having extracted this knowledge—which is unbroken, undivided, and self-luminous—that very thing is to be characterized in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as your own innate nature; so he says, "O Prince. By the term "one of subtle vision," the meaning is: by one who is inward-turned and devoid of the forms of sense-objects. For just as [the nature] of a jar or the like is gross—

Form (*rūpa*) is the specific appearance (*ākāra*), whereas the subtle is the universal earth (*pṛthivī-sāmānya*) which permeates all modifications of the earthly element. In this same way, the universal consciousness (*sāmānyaciti*) is the universal sentience (*sāmānyacaitanya*) that permeates all perceptions of their respective forms; recognize that as your own innate body. Regarding the word "world" (*jagat*): that which is of the nature of universal consciousness shines forth during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and [the same] during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
The sense is that in the state of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), that very [consciousness] is the substratum of the world, like a mirror for reflections.
(92) Through the perfect accomplishment of immersion (*samāveśa*) into that, one attains universal agency (*sarvakartṛtva*).
I shall explain the means of perceiving it, by which you attain that state. (93)
If it is objected that even when the essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been characterized through such great effort, no fruit whatsoever is seen, he says: "The immersion (*samāveśa*) into that.
This refers to the immersion into that universal consciousness (*sāmānyacaitanya*), which is the substratum of the manifestation of the universe and has been thus characterized.

"Contemplation" (*nididhyāsana*) refers to the uninterrupted continuous reflection that "I am He"; its "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) means its maturation, which is to say, its effortless persistence. "Universal agency" (*sarvakartṛtva*) is the state of being identical with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
As it has been said: [citation].
Destroy incomplete manifestation through the firmness of immersion in complete manifestation. Create worlds as you desire; worship Śambhu and become the teacher of the world. (Vijñānabhairavapañjikā)

52. Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "If universal consciousness (*sāmānyacaitanya*) is also a specific state like that of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), how can it be said to be continuous throughout all states? To this he replies: "Of that" (*tasya*). This means "of universal consciousness. "Apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) refers to the locus of apprehension. Because—
Because of my word; that state is the locus of universal consciousness. || 93 ||
Likewise, observe with subtle intelligence the distinctions within consciousness at the intermediate stage between sleep and waking, as well as in the interval between consciousness and its objects.

He says that very thing in the passage beginning with "sleep" (*nidrā*) and so forth. "Universal consciousness" (*sāmānyacaitanya*) refers to non-conceptual knowledge devoid of the forms of objects; the connection [of the sentence] is that one should recognize that which abides in the interval between sleep and waking. "Sleep" (*nidrā*) is deep slumber (*suṣupti*). "Waking" (*jāgrad*) is the stream of conceptual knowledge. From the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)...

In the waking state, there is the apprehension of objects by means of the gross sense organs, which are distinct [from the mind]. In the dream state, however, there is the apprehension of mental objects consisting of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) by means of the mind that has entered within and attained a state of identity with those [objects], resembling a piece of ice submerged in water. Furthermore, in deep sleep, the mind is devoid of the sense organs.

It dissolves into its own source, which is *prakṛti*. At that time, *prakṛti* remains with its portion of *tamas* emerging, thereby veiling the portions of *sattva* and *rajas*. Then, like the sun shrouded by thick clouds, the Self (*ātman*) too, covered by *tamas*, shines only dimly. And so it is said:
In the intermediate moment between waking and deep sleep, because the mind is on the verge of dissolution, there is no grasping of objects;

yet, because the primordial darkness (*prākṛta-tamas*) has not completely unfolded, there is no veiling of one's own nature. Thus, the conscious self (*cidātman*), having not assumed the form of an object, remains manifest.

It has the nature of universal consciousness. Thus, within the variety of cognitions, the distinction between cognitions consists in their having the form of a jar, the form of a cloth, and so forth. Likewise, in the interval—that is, in the midst—of these distinct cognitions, the cognition's very form as a jar is not itself the form as a cloth, because that distinction is well-established.
Once that distinction is established, the pure intermediate state, devoid of forms such as jars and the like, is indeed unavoidable.

Thus, between consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the object of knowledge (*vedya*), "consciousness" is the seer whose nature is the I-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*). Just as the water of a pond, when its gate is opened, becomes one with the water of a field by means of a canal, so too [does consciousness merge].
At the time of perceiving an object, the consciousness of the seer becomes unified with the consciousness of the seen through the medium of the instruments of perception.

In this process, within the body and so forth—which stand in the place of the seer—there is consciousness in the form of the seer; in the sky, which is the object of sight, there is that same consciousness in the form of the solar orb; but in the middle, it is pure and devoid of any form.
The true nature of the self is consciousness devoid of the forms of objects;
the meaning is that these [faculties] are the loci for its apprehension. || 94 ||
This state is one's own true nature, attaining which one is no longer deluded;
it is solely through ignorance of this that the world has come to be as it is. 95.

But surely this is the locus for the perception of the Self; and thus, having perceived it there—[as the text says] "there, the perceived Self is of what nature?"—he replies: "This. This very word is its own form; there is nothing whatsoever beyond it. It is pure consciousness alone, with the forms of the perceptible abandoned.
The meaning is that this is the true nature of the Seer. Having attained this and firmly realized "I am," [one is freed from suffering];
for it is by the mere ignorance of this—that is, by the failure to realize "I am"—that such great misery consisting of suffering arises.
When pure consciousness is known as the true nature of the Self, then all those various forms [appear] like reflections in a mirror.

The point is that just as a reflected tiger or the like does not cause suffering when its status as a mere mental construction is certain, so too it is with the appearance of the perceived object. || 95 ||
Here there is neither form nor taste, nor smell, touch, or sound;
neither suffering nor pleasure, nor indeed anything grasped, nor any grasper. (96)

Since pure consciousness alone is the true nature of the Self, perceivable even in such states [of objective manifestation], therefore, even during the state in which the forms of objects appear, nothing exists apart from its own essential nature—just as reflections in a mirror. Thus he says: "Not... (na). Here, "in this" refers to the Self.

Sound is that which is sounded. This is a negation in a general form of color-form and the other [sensory objects], which have already been negated in their specific forms as "not graspable. The grasper consists of the sense faculties and so forth. || 96 ||
He is the support of all, possessing all forms, yet devoid of everything;
he is the Lord of All, the Sustainer, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Sadāśiva. || 97 ||

Like a mirror for reflections, it is the locus of all that is visible and likewise possesses all forms; yet, in reality, it is devoid of everything. The sense is this: just as a mirror, despite being the locus for all reflections and so forth, is in reality devoid of everything, so too is this case. Who is that supreme consciousness, the subject? (9.4) Thus [it is asked].

And thus the question was asked: "Or are we [your mother]? (9.5). To that, the answer was previously given: "Then, through knowledge of the nature of your own self, you shall indeed know your mother" (9.7). Thereupon, Hemalekhā was questioned again and, having analyzed the nature of her own self with great detail, she spoke.

Now he teaches that such a pure form of one's own self is indeed the nature of the supreme consciousness (*paracid*), which is the form of the subject (*mātṛ*): "This" (*eṣā*). The meaning is that the Self is pure, consisting of universal consciousness. He is the Lord of all, beginning with Brahmā; He is the Fourth Lord (*turyeśa*), the Lord of the act of concealment (*tirodhāna*).

Rudra; Sadāśiva is the fifth, the bestower of grace. For just as in a mirror, although there is a distinction among the portions of the mirror delimited by various reflections according to their respective forms, that mirror remains pervading the entire mirror as the common form of the mirror—so it is with him.

The meaning is this: although there is a distinction [of the Self] in the form of consciousness delimited by various bodies and so forth—which are like reflections—this very [Self] is the Lord of All and so on, because it is the thread running through everything in the form of the universal consciousness perceived in states such as meditative absorption (samādhi). || 97 ||
Behold: having restrained his own self within by means of the true Self, and having abandoned its outward diffusion, he is intent upon inward expansion. (98)

He says, "Behold," meaning that such a reality of the Self is not difficult for you to perceive once you have become proficient through my instructions. By the word "slightly" (*īṣat*), he indicates that there is no need for prolonged restraint;
rather, having restrained the mind for a moment by not delineating the forms of objects, behold that very nature.
[The opponent asks: "Since that form is invisible, how can one say 'I see'? To this he replies: "By its own self as being" (*svātmanā satā*).

For it is not possible to see it as "this is such-and-such"; rather, it is [seen] immediately by way of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) which is a universal non-different from one's own self that serves as the limit of cessation.

The sense is that [the mind] should be restrained by means of the acceptance of the universal [self], expressed as "I am," which possesses a particularity non-different from its own nature shining forth within, having turned away from the insentience produced in the newborn [mind]. He explains how the mind is to be restrained: "being possessed of effort" (udyamavān) is the meaning. Herein, the internal expansion [of the mind] consists in the abandonment of external expansion.
Adherence (*abhiniveśa*) itself, consisting of firm grasping, is nothing other than this [activity], because no further activity is possible within its own nature (*svarūpa*). || 98 ||
Abandoning the thought "I see," like a blind man with a steady mind,
and having relinquished both seeing and not-seeing, quickly take refuge in that which you truly are.
Even so, for one who is attached to the notion "I see myself," the true nature [of the Self] is difficult to perceive; therefore, he says:
"See it as abiding with an immovable self"—the connection is that it abides in a form devoid of all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*).
As it has been said: "As long as even the thought 'I see' unfolds, the state of being a seer persists."
"Even with hundreds of efforts, you do not perceive your own sovereign majesty. Having analyzed this very point, he says again:
"That state of delusion which is the nature of deep sleep—having abandoned both of those distinct forms, you who remain having firmly resolved 'I am not,' and whatever your true nature may be."

By process of elimination, you are that which is of the nature of the fourth state (*turya*)—the universal consciousness (*sāmānyacaitanya*)—which is not [limited by] the three states; you are that very form, you are indeed of that nature.
Worship Him alone as the Self, as the Self that is the fourth state, the witness of the three states.
The meaning is: "Abandoning delay of time, resort to [him] quickly. || 99 ||
Thus addressed by his beloved, Hemacūḍa, perceiving that footprint, rested for a long time and then forgot everything outside of it. || 100 ||
Having acted thus and having perceived that state, rest is non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi). || 100 ||
[Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Resting of Hemacūḍa," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrītripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the tenth chapter:
Then Hemalekhā beheld her beloved who had attained the supreme state;
yet he did not stir from that highest station even for a moment.
In this chapter, having been awakened again by his beloved through verses on the elements (*dhātu*),
he attained external meditative absorption (*bāhyasamādhi*) and became firmly established as one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
He by whom stability has been attained in the supreme, universal form of consciousness, neither agitates nor awakens [it]. || 1 ||
Having awakened and opened his eyes, he beheld the world together with his beloved; desiring once more to find rest at her feet, he moved with great speed. (2)
"With the beloved" means accompanied by the beloved. "Resting in that state" is samādhi. || 2 ||
Even as he closed his eyes,
she, whose speech was as beautiful as nectar, took her beloved by the hand and spoke.
She is Hemalekhā. || 3 ||
"O Lord, what have you resolved? Speak! From the closing or the opening of your eyes, what will happen to you? Proclaim your gain or loss."
"Resolved" means determined. By means of closing [the eyes] and so forth, whatever gain or loss may occur—proclaim those two. (4)
"What is not obtained by opening [the eyes], and what is obtained by closing them?
Tell me that, O Beloved; I wish to hear your teaching. (5)
The analysis of this very point is as follows: "Having opened [the eyes]" refers to the acceptance of the established position. || 5 ||
Thus questioned by her, he spoke like one intoxicated with pride,
though sluggish and weary from the weight of his indolence, reluctant even to address her.
Manthara is slow in his dealings. || 6 ||
O beloved, after a long time I have indeed attained ultimate rest;
there is no rest for me anywhere in the external world, which abounds in suffering.
Rest, repose, and happiness unmixed with suffering—this [is what is meant] in external worldly activity. || 7 ||

Blinded by misfortune, I have until now failed to perceive the true bliss of my own self, remaining instead occupied with external affairs that are for the most part as trivial as chewing on dregs or rumination.
happiness) || 8 ||

*Ṛjīṣa* is a portion of sugarcane from which the juice has been extracted. *Romantha* is well known among animals as the chewing of what has already been chewed. And that very thing is both food and drink, a beloved limb, and a source of delusion.
"The tasting of this is surely always like the rumination of an animal," according to the manner stated [in the verse]; the sense is that there is nothing unprecedented about it.
Though not blind, he is as if blind due to misfortune. The true happiness pertaining to one's own self is real;
the sense is that it is not unreal and momentary like sensual pleasure. || 8 ||
Just as someone wandering for alms does not recognize his own treasure,
so too have I, again and again, failed to know the ocean of my own bliss.
The ocean of bliss connected with one's own self.

Considering sensual pleasure to be the highest, yet flooded with a multitude of sufferings and as fleeting as a flash of lightning, one should remain steadfast through the power of devotion to that [Supreme]. (10)

The construction is: "thinking it to be supreme and stable. "Dissolving like lightning" means that which perishes or dissolves in a mere instant, like lightning. "Devotion to that" means taking refuge in that [state]. || 10 ||
Struck by sufferings, he has surely found no rest;
alas, people are devoid of the knowledge that discriminates between suffering and happiness! (11)

"Rest" (*viśrānti*) means happiness unmixed with suffering. He says "Alas! (*aho*) because people, through their misconception of suffering as happiness, experience nothing but suffering amidst their sorrows. (11)
Those seeking happiness always vainly accumulate a mass of suffering;
therefore, enough with this experience of suffering, which is indeed brought about by one's own efforts.
The mass of suffering, the web of means for producing suffering—wealth, houses, and so forth. || 12 ||
O beloved, show mercy toward me; I entreat you with palms joined in reverence.
I long for rest within my own self, which is the nature of bliss.
Rest is the meditative absorption (samādhi) consisting in abiding in one's own true nature, which is characterized by the bliss previously described. || 13 ||
Alas, you appear to be struck by fate; for even though you know this state, you abandon rest therein and strive in vain for suffering. (14)
You act; you are intent upon worldly affairs. || 14 ||
Thus addressed, that wise woman smiled slightly and said to her beloved:
"O Lord, you do not know that most purifying state. (15)
Having smiled—that is, having manifested a smile—that [reality] is the undivided nature of universal consciousness. It was not known;
that is, it was not recognized as "I am. It is supremely purifying, being devoid even of a trace of the impurity of duality. || 15 ||
That state where the wise, whose intentions are purified, remain without delusion,
is far from you, just as the sky is for one standing on the earth.

In that full state which is the nature of non-dual consciousness, those who remain—having attained a firm conviction that "I am [That]"—are not deluded; the sense is that they perceive no difference in their own true nature whether their eyes are open or closed. With purified dispositions, their minds having transcended the latent impressions of duality, the wise have attained that state. 16
Something may be well known to you that is yet like the unknown;
whether with eyes closed or opened, that state is not perceived.

Even though something has been discerned by you who are dependent on cessation (*nirodha*), because that discernment is without objective reality (*avastu*), it is not known as pure; thus, it is merely like that which is unknown. If one asks why this is so, he says: "Having closed [the eyes]," etc. (17).
Whether one has not performed it or has performed it, that [state] can never be obtained;
whether one has not gone or has gone, one cannot reach that station.

"Without having done so," etc. The meaning is that because it is self-luminous, eternally existent, and all-pervading, there is no distinction [in its nature] due to closing the eyes, movement, or other such actions; for these do not affect its essential nature. || 18 ||
How could that which was attained be considered complete merely by closing the eyes, or by going there and returning?
Yet, it is fulfilled simply by opening the eyelashes, even though they are measured by only eight barley grains.

Otherwise, there would be a loss of fullness and so forth; thus he says "closing the eyes. "Full" is an elliptical expression for both "self-luminous" and "eternal. Since the concealment of the Full by the opening of the eyes is utterly contradictory, he says with derision: "the eight barley-corns. (19)
If that [state] were then hidden, would not the state indeed be full?
Oh, what a greatness of delusion! What wonder can I say of it? (20)

The phrase "nanu" (surely) in the sense of "it would indeed be complete when [the Lord] has become invisible" is a statement made with derision; he expresses this very point clearly with the word "aho" (oh!). || 20 ||
That within which millions upon millions of cosmic eggs are situated at its very corners becomes concealed by the mere opening of the eyelid of one whose measure is but a finger-breadth. 21.
The connection is that it is a marvel that [the world] is concealed within that Self, which is of the nature of universal consciousness. || 21 ||
Listen, O prince, to this essence of truth which I declare:
as long as the knot has not been severed, one does not attain happiness.

Thus, in order to state the cause of delusion (*moha*), he says: "Listen. Regarding the phrase "the essence of reality" (*tattvasāram*): it is the extracted form of reality, whose nature is universal consciousness (*sāmānyasaṃvidātman*). The connection [of the sentence] is: "Listen to that which I am about to say. He says [further]: because there is no piercing of the knots (*granthi*), even though it is known, it is as if unknown.
There are millions of knots manifested from the rope of delusion; therein, the non-perception of one's own true nature is declared to be the rope of delusion. (23)

A knot is said to be that which is tied by the twisting of a rope and so forth. The knots under discussion, however, consist of the twisting and tying of the rope of delusion (*moharajju*). If it is asked what that rope of delusion is, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*), [verse 23].
Where those knots exist, consisting of the nature of perverted grasping, there occurs the conviction of selfhood regarding the body and other primary objects. (24)

In that [context], "where" means in whichever rope of delusion; "therein" means among those knots; and "among the body and its primary [adjuncts]" refers to the body, the senses, and so forth. Since the conviction of selfhood regarding the body and such things is rooted in ignorance of one's true nature, it has that [ignorance] as its substratum. Just as a very firm knot cannot be severed without first cutting the rope upon which it rests...

Thus, without the severing of the rope of ignorance regarding one's true nature, the identification of the body and so forth as the self is difficult to abandon; this should be understood as the "knot. || 24 ||

By virtue of which this cycle of existence has expanded and is difficult to remedy, so too does the realization of selflessness arise in the world with respect to that which is based on mere appearance. (25)

"By virtue of which" means by virtue of the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth. "This" refers to what is well-known: *saṃsāra*, the continuous flow of the experience of pleasure and pain. He states the second knot with the word "likewise":
"in the locus of manifestation, like the reflection in a mirror."
In this world, which consists of mere manifestation, the notion of a non-self is the "second" [bond]. This is the meaning.

Since the manifestation of the non-self as an object of perception is preceded by the manifestation of the self as a perceiver in the form of the body and so forth, it should be understood as the second knot. || 25 ||

Thus, the knots consisting of the determination of the difference between the individual soul and the Lord are considered to have arisen from this [ignorance] long ago, and indeed, they have been repeatedly dissolved. (26)

By the phrase "and so forth," [is meant] the ascertainment of the mutual difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and [the Supreme], and so on. This is ignorance regarding one's own essential nature (*svarūpājñāna*). "For a long time" means from beginningless time.

The connection is that it has become repeatedly coiled, having attained the form of a knot. Just as a rope itself, through repeated coiling, is called a "knot," so too is this ignorance of one's own essential nature.

The intended meaning is that it is called a "knot" (granthi) because it is bound together by appearing as a limitation through the contraction of the region of the conscious self (cidātman) which has the body and so forth as its locus. || 26 ||
Consequently, the person (puruṣa) becomes bound by having entered into the form of that knot;
liberation from that bondage is said to result from the loosening of that knot. || 27 ||
Therefore, the sense is that just as animals bound by a rope are released through the loosening of a knot in the rope, so too are human beings [released] from the rope of ignorance. || 27 ||
That you, closing your own eyes, attain that state sufficiently—that state is your own nature, the unsurpassed, pure consciousness. (28)

Now, one might wonder: "What is this knot of my ignorance that is to be untied? Anticipating this doubt, he says "That which you [are]" (*yattvam*) in order to state that, when the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are restrained, there is no resting in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), and that this very [lack of rest] is of the nature of delusion.
The word "alam" means sufficient, adequate, or complete—that is, the full state (*pada*). That very state is your own innate form (*nijarūpa*); it is the unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
It is that which serves as the ultimate limit of all negations.
Tell me that: when, where, and in what form does that great mirror-surface of the entire variegated world not exist? (29)
The surface of the mirror is variegated; it is great and unlimited. By asking "when, where, and by whom," there is the rejection of limitations regarding time, place, and form. (29)

If you were to say that [an object] comes into being in a certain place with a certain form through your own self-awareness, then at that very time and place, that [object] would indeed be nothing other than the son of a barren woman. (30)
If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says: "When... [referring to] self-awareness as universal consciousness (*sāmānyaciti*).

If one were to say that at present there is no consciousness in this form, then that time and so forth would be nothing other than the son of a barren woman. For whatever time, place, or whatever form in which consciousness does not exist—that time and so forth [would be non-existent].

Does it manifest or not? In the first case, since time and other such factors are insentient (*jaḍa*) and thus non-self-luminous (*asvaprakāśa*), their manifestation would be impossible without identity with consciousness (*saṃvitti*); therefore, consciousness is established.
In the second case, for those things that do not manifest, their state of being a mere void (*tucchatva*) is difficult to avoid—this is the intended meaning. || 30 ||
Just as there is no reflection without a mirror, O Lord, so it is with that;
therefore, by abandoning that state, nothing exists anywhere at all.
He states that for time and other such factors, which are devoid of identity with consciousness, there is indeed non-existence, like a reflection without a mirror:
"the reflection. That term refers to universal consciousness. || 31 ||
What would be gained by opening your eyes?
As long as you think, "I know it thus," the knot will remain firm. (32)
Therefore, "from that" means because the self, which is consciousness, is unlimited. Thus, the knot consists of the conceit in the form: "I know the self through action. || 32 ||

That state has not been attained so long as it might be attained and yet not become [realized]; for whether you close or open your eyes, that state which you think you have attained—[is it truly so]? (33)
It does not become attained. If it is asked, "How can that which is being experienced be denied?", he says:

"That which is attained" [does] "not exist. The intended meaning is that because it is not perceived anywhere, it lacks the state of being a complete term consisting of universal consciousness (*sāmānyacaitanya*), due to its being delimited (*paricchinna*).
He clarifies this very point with the words "having closed" (nimīlya). || 33 ||
Therefore, that is not the state of plenitude because of its limitation by action and so forth.
O Lord, where does the great consciousness, which possesses the radiance of the fire of time, not exist? (34)

Action consists of cessation. By the word "beginning" (ādi), time is indicated. The sense is that there is a delimitation by means of the action of cessation, because [the object] appears externally at that specific time. || 34 ||
She who assimilates the vast accumulation of the fuel of conceptual constructions—
having realized the supreme state, she has no further duty remaining.

He explains the very nature of the fire of time (*kālānala*) [with the words]: "one's own self" (*svātman*). Just as the fire of time assimilates everything that falls into it into its own essence, so too does one assimilate everything appearing within one's own self through identity (*tādātmya*) into one's own essence; this is the intended meaning. He states that the delusion which holds that "the mind must be restrained" is to be abandoned: [The verse: Just as the fire of time consumes all things that fall into it, so too, by means of the practice of non-duality, one should cause the entire universe to enter into one's own self. (1.23) [The commentary: The sense is that just as the fire of time assimilates everything fallen into it into its own essence, so too does one assimilate everything appearing within one's own self through identity into one's own essence. Regarding the statement "the mind is to be restrained," he says that this delusion must be discarded: [The verse: The mind is not to be restrained, nor is it to be made to abide anywhere; rather, one should remain established in the state of the Self alone, free from all mental constructs. (1.24) [The commentary: The mind is not to be restrained—that is, it is not to be suppressed—nor is it to be fixed upon any external object. Rather, one should remain established solely in the state of the Self, which is devoid of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). This is because the mind is essentially of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*); therefore, it is not possible to restrain it elsewhere. For example, just as it is impossible to restrain the heat of fire, so too is it impossible to restrain the mind, which is of the nature of consciousness. Furthermore, since the mind is of the nature of consciousness, it cannot be fixed upon any other object, for it is impossible for consciousness to be established in something other than itself. Therefore, one should
"It is not those" means that the remainder would be the remainder. || 35 ||
Restraining [the mind], abandon the knot residing in the heart that thinks, "I shall see";
uproot this supreme and firm knot that thinks, "This is not I. (36)
"Having completely restrained [the mind], I see only its own true nature and nothing else"—abandon this knot which is of the nature of delusion.
He says "this" to indicate that one must abandon another, more fundamental knot that is the root of this one:
namely, the notion that the nature of the Self, which appears at the time of restraint as undifferentiated from the objects of perception, is likewise so at the time when there is no restraint.

Even though it appears as a form mixed with objects, its nature is that of the Self alone; moreover, that [nature] is indeed pure, because the object of perception is like a reflection—this is the intended meaning. || 36 ||
Behold the Self everywhere, augmented by indivisible bliss;
behold the entire world within the Self, like reflections in a mirror. (37)

He establishes this very point with the word "paśya" (behold). The sense is that in the entire web of appearing objects (*dṛśyāvabhāsajāla*), that which does not appear is unestablished, because everything that appears is pervaded by manifestation (*bhāna*), and manifestation itself is the very self (*ātman*). [Objection: But surely, it is manifestation-as-self that appears everywhere?

Nevertheless, if it is argued that this [state] in cessation (*nirodha*)—though appearing as if it were so—is not of the singular nature of bliss (*ānanda*), he says: "augmented by indivisible bliss. The meaning is that it is augmented, that is, filled, by unlimited bliss. The underlying intention here is that the very nature of one's own self as consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatā*) is itself the nature of bliss.

It is not something additional, because that would lead to the consequence of duality. Just as the term "consciousness" (saṃvit) is employed in reference to the Self—which is an indivisible, unitary reality devoid of attributes—in order to exclude its being insentient, so too is the term "bliss" (ānanda) employed to exclude its being of the nature of suffering. And as for [the bliss] at the time of cessation...
That experience of bliss is not produced by any specific quality of its own nature, because the nature [of Brahman] is devoid of distinctions;

rather, it is according to the maxim, "Desires themselves are great suffering— for one free from desire, how could that [suffering] exist?"— that the self-nature of the individual is assailed by an endless succession of latent desires for objects, like a forest engulfed by a wildfire.

People are destined for suffering. However, at the time of cessation (*nirodha*), because the appearance of duality no longer exists and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire rooted therein do not arise, one becomes exceptionally happy—like one who has cast off a burden placed upon the head. Thus, it is precisely the abandonment of the latent impressions of desire that is the root [of this state].

Since there is an experience of the nature of bliss even in cessation, it follows that even in the absence of cessation, the experience of being of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpatā*) is inevitable, according to the principle stated by the Blessed One: "When one abandons desires by destroying the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire" (*Bhagavadgītā* 2.55).
Now, [one might object]: since the appearance of duality, which is rooted in the latent impressions of desire, cannot be dispelled in the absence of cessation...

Anticipating the objection—"Since the manifestation of latent desires (kāma-vāsanā) is inevitable, how could suffering caused by them not arise?"—the author says: "Behold" (*paśya*). The meaning is that all duality appearing when [consciousness] is unceasing does not exist apart from one's own self, just like a reflection in a mirror. For, insofar as it is a reflection...

The meaning is that just as there is no arising of desire for an object already seen, so too, when it is ascertained that the entirety of the visible world is a reflection in the mirror of one's own self, there is neither desire nor suffering.
No longer contemplating the Self as being entirely present everywhere, accept the remainder [of existence] within yourself and remain established in well-being through your own true nature. 38.

Now, if everything consists of reflections within the Self, then for one who thinks, "I see nothing but the Self everywhere," he replies with the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*). This means both internally and externally. Regarding "everything" (*akhilam*):
it means all that appears, such as pleasure and so forth, as well as jars and so forth.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "I perceive the entire Self everywhere. Thus, having first ascertained, "I perceive the entire Self appearing everywhere," one no longer contemplates the initial portion—"the entire Self everywhere"—but rather contemplates the remaining form, devoid of the portion to be contemplated.

Having internally accepted the universal consciousness— which is the nature of being— as "I am," the sense is that you remain as one whose residual impression is "I am the nature of pure consciousness alone, distinct from the objects of thought. With such a self, your own unconditioned true nature, remain established in yourself.
The meaning is: "Be one who does not fall away from such firm support of your own true nature. As Vasiṣṭha said:
"Having known [this], one does not grieve" (Yogavāsiṣṭha 3.7.9). || 38 ||
Having heard these words spoken by his beloved, Hemacūḍa, whose disposition was pure, realized himself to be fulfilled and became free from delusion regarding all things. (39)

One whose latent disposition is white, whose internal organ is purified by the removal of all delusion, perceives the Self as full, appearing in a single form during both the states of meditative restraint (*nirodha*) and its absence. Since it is only in the state of restraint that the pure Self shines forth, such a person is free from delusion. (39)
Gradually, through the attainment of complete immersion (*samāveśa*), one whose contemplation has become firm may always sport with groups of young women such as Hemalekhā and others. (40)

Through the sequence of cultivating the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) in its previously described form, there arises an immersion (*samāveśa*) into that full, previously described state—a firm and unshakable self-identification—just like the immersion in the body that existed previously. As they say:
"The knowledge of the Self, which sublates the knowledge of the body as the Self, belongs only to him [who possesses it]."

"Even if he does not desire [liberation], he is liberated. Regarding the phrase "one of stable contemplation" (*sthirabhāvana*): the meaning is that after the attainment of immersion (*samāveśa*), his latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that state has become firm. The connection with the distant [subject] is "wandering, situated upon the earth. (40)
Having conquered the hosts of his enemies in battle, he ruled his own prosperous kingdom,
causing the scriptures to be heard and being heard himself, while accumulating stores of wealth.
Performing the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, and other principal sacrifices for twenty thousand years, he remains on earth as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 42 ||
Beholding his son established in the state of one liberated while living, King Muktācūḍa and his brother Maṇicūḍa also reflected thus: || 43 ||
The father of Hemacūḍa was King Muktācūḍa. || 43 ||
Why indeed is he not perceived here at all as he was before? For he does not rejoice excessively in happiness, nor does he tremble likewise in the face of suffering. (44)
He states the manner of that reflection: "What is this?"—this refers to Hemacūḍa. || 44 ||
Through equanimity, he indeed views gain and loss, as well as enemy and friend;
he performs the duties of a king like an actor on the stage. (45)
Like an actor, his inner intention is concealed. || 45 ||
He appears as if perpetually intoxicated, like one who drinks the wine of Kāpiśāya;
he performs his duties with great effort, as if his mind were always elsewhere. (46)
Kāpiśāyana is wine. || 46 ||
Then, having approached Hemacūḍa in some secluded place, they asked him for what reason he was thus, saying, "From where [have you come], sir? (47)
They both questioned that Hemacūḍa and Muktācūḍa regarding Maṇicūḍa.
Then Hemacūḍa explained his own situation to them both in turn;
those two, the brother and the father, were enlightened by Hemadūḍha.
Of those two, the father and the brother. || 48 ||
Having attained the supreme reality (*paratattva*), the two became liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
Then, the assembly of ministers also heard this account of the king’s departure from the world.
The course of the world, which exists as a state inseparable from the nature of the world itself. || 49 ||
Having reflected upon the nature of his own self, he then became one who has known what is to be known;
thus, in Viśālānagara, they gradually [realized] one another.
Having reflected upon and determined such a state of their own selves, they came to know [it] through mutual instruction;
this is the connection [of the words]. || 50 ||
Through this instruction, everyone—men and women, children and the elderly, even the groups of male and female servants—knows the truth, down to the cowherds and children. (51)
Reality is the true nature of things. || 51 ||
Having known all that is to be known and having abandoned the sense of "I" regarding the body, they indeed became [liberated];
there, no one possessed desire, anger, or even greed.
The connection is as follows: by those for whom greed alone is known as the primary object of knowledge intended in the scriptures, there is no such thing as "unseized" (anāhṛta). 52.
Nowhere is there anyone—whether a child or even an elder—who is not seized by anger, desire, and the like; all are devoted to worldly affairs through these very passions they have acquired. (53)

Regarding the phrase "of the child": although anger and the like generally arise constantly in both children and the elderly, whose natures are characterized by a lack of discernment, nevertheless—by virtue of the majesty of knowing the true reality (*samyaktattva*)—the root sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) regarding the body and so forth has been uprooted; thus, desire and the like, which are rooted therein, do not arise.
The intended meaning is as follows: If one asks for what purpose desire and the rest are brought forth, he says "brought forth" (*āhṛta*)—meaning for the sake of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).

For just as actors engage in incidental dramatic activity by means of desire and so forth that they have brought forth [for the performance], so it is with everyone in that [state]; this is the sense. || 53 ||
The mother plays with her child, speaking of matters that are not the truth;
indeed, male and female servants always attend upon their own master. (54)
Now, one might object: "Will not the investigation into reality (*tattvānusaṃdhāna*) become slack for certain individuals who are always intent on worldly activity and whose minds are immature?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "bālam" etc., to show that it is not so, because such worldly activity is conducive to the investigation into reality: "By the report of the supreme reality: 'Do not cry; you are Maheśvara; you do not [exist] in reality...'"
In the form beginning with "suffering" (duḥkha) and so forth; thus it should be understood in what follows as well. || 54 ||
Uttering words concerning the supreme reality to one another, they perform a dramatic dance with actors born from the context of that reality. (55)
With vessels born from the pursuit of reality, and wearing the garb of discernment, delusion, and so forth. || 55 ||
Singers sing words devoted solely to the discourse of discernment, while jesters constantly mock worldly conduct. (56)
The learned teachers caused the students to recite the scriptures, using circles of examples suitable for investigating the supreme reality. (57)
In this way, the men and women there, the male and female slaves, the actors and jesters, the servants, soldiers, ministers, artisans, and courtesans— [all were likewise transformed]. (58)

All of them, at the end of their experience of what is to be known, came to reside in the great city of Viśālā; by the power of their prior latent impressions alone, they remained devoted to worldly activity. (59)

Now, one might object: "If everyone there has already known all that is to be known, how can the king and others carry out all their worldly affairs, such as governing the kingdom? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Previously," and so forth. The sense is: just as a hero intoxicated by wine fights in the paths of weapons without stumbling, solely due to his prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), so it is here. (59)
He does not recollect what has passed, whether it be auspicious or likewise inauspicious;
nor does he pursue the future, which is the cause of joy, sorrow, and the like.
If it is asked, "How can the people there engage in worldly activity based on mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and of what nature is that [activity]? he says:

"He does not remember. Having seen that which has passed away—the means for suffering and so forth—and having perceived what has been attained, he does not connect it with future sorrow and the like. (60)
In the present, people are intent on worldly affairs, smiling, rejoicing, grieving, or as if angry every day, like those excessively intoxicated by honey.
In the present [moment], such as joy, pleasure, and so forth. || 61 ||
The sages, Sanaka and others, having arrived, called that city by the name "The City of Renowned Knowledge" (Prasiddhavidyānagara). || 62 ||
"Sanaka and the others" refers to Sanaka, Vāmadeva, and so forth; the connection is that they "arrived at the city. || 62 ||
Where even the parrots in their cages utter these words:
"Worship your own Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and free from the object of thought. (63)
The four verses beginning with "yatra" (where... are located at the end of the fourth chapter and have been explained previously. || 63 ||
There is no object of consciousness other than consciousness itself, like a reflection in a mirror;
consciousness is the object, consciousness is I, and consciousness is all that is moving and unmoving. (64)

Since everything shines by following consciousness, and that [consciousness] exists through its own sovereignty, therefore people [should know] consciousness as the illuminator of all and the support of all. (65)
Abandoning delusion, those of clear vision should resort to pure consciousness alone—that which even animals speak of so intensely. (66)
Even today, they call that place Prasiddhavidyānagara; thus was he indeed enlightened there in former times by Hemalekhā. (67)

Hemacūḍa became a learned man and likewise attained liberation while living (jīvanmukta), as did all the others, including the women and children; they all came to know the higher and the lower (the supreme and the mundane). || 68 ||
Therefore, association with the virtuous should first be the primary cause for attaining the highest good;
thus, one who desires the highest good should be intent on taking refuge in the virtuous. || 69 ||
Since all have become liberated through association with Hemalekhā, one should therefore be devoted to seeking refuge with the virtuous.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Narrative of Hemacūḍa," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Then the eleventh chapter:
Having heard this most wonderful account of Hemacūḍa,
Bhārgava, with a mind full of doubt, proceeded to ask a question.
In this chapter, Modapadya spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu, saying:
"By means of both perception and logical proof, it is established that the object of cognition is nothing other than consciousness."

Those [qualities] were [attained] by you. Knowledge is of the nature of the pure non-dual self; it is difficult, being contrary to all worldly experience, and unattainable through any means whatsoever. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, O Śrī Guru, this most wonderful knowledge that has been declared to me appears indeed difficult for me to grasp and impossible to accomplish in every respect.
How can this visible world have consciousness alone as its true nature?
For this is indeed unseen and absolute; it is to be accepted through faith and not otherwise.

He states the very point of its inequality: "How so? Since the duality of the seer and the seen is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), their being pure consciousness alone is unobserved. And this must be accepted merely on the basis of faith, not through perception or logical proof; such is the intended meaning. || 3 ||
Consciousness, when inseparable from its object, can never be experienced [by itself];
this is in every way untenable—how then could the mind ascend [to such a state]? (4)
He states precisely the absence of apprehension with the words "consciousness" (*citih*). "In any way whatsoever" (*kathañcana*) means by any operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is not to be experienced, nor is it to be made an object of experience. That such a consciousness exists is in no way tenable or logically consistent. Why? The sense is: how is it to be ascertained that such a consciousness exists?
"Indeed, I must be instructed here with all my heart out of compassion.
Thus addressed, Dattaguru spoke to Bhārgava.
Thinking that the Guru might suspect such audacity on his part due to this objection, he says: "Out of compassion.
Here, the object is pure consciousness. || 5 ||
Listen, O Rāma, I shall explain the reality of the visible world as it truly exists:
this entire visible universe is nothing but pure consciousness (dṛśimātra), and nothing else.

Since the object of cognition (*cetya*)—that is, the *caitya*—is like a "man's horn" apart from consciousness (*cit*), it follows that consciousness alone is established as being free from objects of cognition.
To state this, he defines the reality of the visible (*dṛśya-tattva*):
"Listen," etc. The reality (*tattva*) of the visible object of cognition is its essential nature (*svarūpa*); the meaning is that it is exactly as it is, not otherwise.
He states that very point: "This," etc. (6).
I shall state the proof for this; listen attentively and with a concentrated mind.
This visible world is an effect, because it is perceived as having arisen [from causes]. (7)

In this context, regarding the fact that the visible world is nothing but consciousness (*citimātratva*), one should understand that while the logical justification (*upapatti*)— that is, the reasoning—

is already correctly stated through the illustrative narrative (*upākhyāna*) of Hemacūḍa concerning the manner of perception, it is now specifically the logical justification itself that is being set forth. Therein, he first establishes that the visible world is an effect of the Seer (*dṛkkāryatā*).
"Etat" (this) refers to the effect, which is the object of the agent's operation. || 7 ||
This world is a new manifestation at every moment;
it appears as something ever-new, for this world arises at each very instant.
If it is asked, "What indeed is this 'origination' (utpatti)? he says: "It is a new manifestation" (*nūtanābhāsa*). The meaning is: appearing as something new.

For in common worldly experience, that which appears precisely as something new is said to be "originated. The sense is: because this world shines forth anew at every moment, therefore [it is so]. This will be explained further on. (8)
Some say that this world arises from a single, indivisible moment;
others say it consists of a collection of entities, comprising both the moving and the stationary.

Now, one might object: "The world is conventionally designated as a collection of perceptible things such as jars and the like; there is no single entity called 'the world' that exists apart from that collection.

Anticipating this objection, [the author] demonstrates his own position—that the world possesses a momentary and uniform nature—as accepted by the Vijñānavādin, beginning with the words "Some say... (*kecit*). Here:
This is the position of the Vijñānavādins: the cognizers consist of a stream of momentary consciousnesses;

in each successive cognition produced by preceding impressions (*saṃskāra*), there appear objective forms (*dṛśyākāra*). This is established by such experience as "the cognition having the form of a jar" or "the cognition having the form of a cloth."

Since the presence of an aspect (*ākāra*) within cognitions must necessarily be admitted, and since conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is established by that alone, an external object need not be admitted. For whatever spatial, temporal, or substantial aspect appears in a cognition, to that extent it is, at that very moment, a single undivided essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*). Thus, there is the moment of the bowl, the moment of the jujube fruit, and the moment of both the bowl and the jujube fruit.

Gradually, [the realization arises that] the world is momentary; it is nothing but consciousness (*vijñāna*), which consists of various times, places, and forms, and is an undivided single essence. For others, such as the followers of Kaṇāda, the world is merely a collection of categories (*padārtha*);
and that [collection], being of the nature of space and so forth, is stable and eternal, while being of the nature of jars and so forth, is perishable and non-eternal.

They say that the world is simply the collection of both stationary and moving entities. In this regard, proponents such as the followers of Kaṇāda are unable to state any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for external objects, because all worldly transactional activity necessarily culminates in nothing other than the forms of cognition themselves. Even so—
In some way, the external world untouched by linguistic convention is imagined as being like the teats of a goat;

however, the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins— which maintains that the world is a reflection within the conscious self— is partially favorable to our own position, as it holds [the mind] to undergo transformation at every moment.
"For all entities indeed undergo transformation at every moment, with the exception of the power of consciousness"—this is the reading found in the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī*. (See *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 5).
Indeed, [the statement] "entities [are so], with the exception of the power of consciousness," and so forth, is not contradicted by other systems; such is its [meaning].
It should be understood that this is the first proof. || 9 ||
In every respect, however, it is certain that [the world] possesses an origin;
therein, the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavāda) is not tenable, because it leads to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). || 10 ||

He states (*sarvathā*) that even though the world has been described by others according to their own whims, it is established—through the inference based on the reason of "being perceptible" (*dṛśyatva*), which is concordant with many scriptures—as being indeed characterized by origination. The meaning is: "in both ways," whether it be permanent (*sthira*) or momentary (*kṣaṇika*). This refers to that which is perceptible.

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the position of permanence. For one who has set out to establish that the world is equivalent to a human horn, the proof of its momentariness or non-momentariness is like adorning a corpse; this disregard for such arguments is indicated by the term "sarvathā" (in every way). Now, there is no material cause (*upādāna*) for the world established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The phrase "it is established" (*sidhyati*) is used to state that [the world] is equivalent to an illusion created by a magician without any material cause (*nirupādāna*); thus, he begins by sequentially refuting the views of those who assert the reality and the possession of a material cause (*sopādānatva*) of the world.
The word "therein" (*tatra*) means: when the fact that the world is an effect (*kāryatva*) has been established.

Regarding the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*): an effect arises without depending on a cause at all. Since the effect arises from its own intrinsic nature, and because the effect is non-existent prior to its arising, what could depend upon what? Furthermore, once it has arisen, being self-established, why would it depend on anything else? Therefore, just as a cause is independent of an effect—

The Cārvāka asserts the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*), stating that "the effect is likewise said to be inherent. He refutes this, saying "it is not appropriate," meaning it is not logical. The reason given is "due to over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgata*); the sense is that a jar produced without depending on a cause would also become a cloth. But for me...

Due to the diversity of the causes of a jar and a cloth, a jar cannot become a cloth. If it is asked, "Why could the very cause of a jar not be the cause of a cloth?"—understand that this is because of the diversity of their respective causes. (10)
Since the determination of cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance, and since our activities are based on corroboration, how could [the world] be accidental? (11)
If it is asked, "Why should it not be the case that the potsherd is the effect and the jar is the cause? he replies: "By positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," and so forth.

For positive concomitance is the pervasion of the complete set of causes by the effect; negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), however, is the pervasion of the absence of the effect by the absence of the cause. This is because, through the knowledge of these two, one ascertains the necessary nature of cause and effect.

If it is objected that since the cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) may be erroneous, how can the aforementioned certainty be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he replies: "Because of correspondence" (*saṃvādāt*). The point is this: if that cognition were erroneous, one who acted for the sake of an effect by relying upon its cause would encounter a discrepancy (*visaṃvāda*). Therefore...
How could an effect be accidental, that is, without a cause? || 11 ||
In some cases, however, even when the cause is not perceived, that unseen factor must indeed be postulated;
for it has been declared by all that it is logical to conform to the majority. (12)
If it is argued that no cause is observed for the occurrence of sudden suffering and so forth, he replies:

"In some cases," meaning that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is the cause. Now, is the unseen cause to be postulated as a cause by analogy with observed causes, or rather, because of the absence of observed causes, should it be considered causeless?

If it is argued that "the effect must be conceived as being nothing other than the cause," [the author] says: "Of many... That is, an effect is generally observed to be preceded by [its cause]; for even when [the cause] is not seen in some instances, [the effect] is [still understood].
The object of conceptual construction would have to be like that which is seen; otherwise, it would contradict universal worldly experience.

If it is asked, "Of what is there multiplicity?", he says: "frequently" (*bhūyas*). This means "many times. The sense is that, for the most part, the entire world has only visible causes. He states the fault in the contrary case with the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*); this means "if one were to accept [the existence of] causelessness. The syntactical connection is: "the universal activity of the world [would be impossible]. (13)
Otherwise, the process of manifestation would be contradicted; therefore, everything possesses a cause.
For this very reason, one who seeks a specific cause relies upon the effect as a logical reason (*kāryahetu*). (14)

If one were to employ a cause for the sake of an effect, the purposeful activity directed toward it would be rendered inconsistent and would fail to culminate in its result; that is to say, it would not invariably lead to the attainment of the result. However, the failure of an activity to culminate in its result in certain instances is...

The intended meaning is that [activity does not occur] due to the deficiency of the complete set of causes. Because activity culminates in its fruit, it demonstrates that activity toward a cause is for the sake of the effect; thus, he says "for this very reason. The connection is: "she is seen to be intent upon that" (*tatparā*). || 14 ||
The world is seen everywhere; therefore, this [world] is not anything at all. Some say that the effect is produced by atoms which are like non-existent things.

The meaning is that this position accepted by the Cārvākas cannot withstand any critical examination. Now, he introduces and refutes the doctrine of the Kaṇādas (Vaiśeṣikas), beginning with the words "some" (*kecit*). [It is] "unreal," meaning unperceived;
"arisen," meaning produced. || 15 ||
And that which is absolutely distinct from them would also be absolutely non-existent.

For the identity of the existent and the non-existent is indeed contradictory; (the connection is: "how could it not be contradictory?"—the intended meaning is: "it must certainly be contradictory") how could it not be so? || 16 ||

From those atoms [arises] a distinct effect. For atoms are inferred as the cause of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), which is the producer of the *trasareṇu* perceived in the rays of sunlight; this is established by the reason that the effect, the dyad, possesses parts. In this regard, the sequence of creation is as follows:

By the will of the Lord, conjoined with the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of sentient beings whose karma is matured, motion arises in the stable atoms (*paramāṇu*), which are otherwise subject to disintegration.
From that, two atoms subsequently join together. From that conjunction, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is produced. Again, by the will of the Lord alone, motion arises in the dyads; from that, in due order—
According to their system, a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) is produced by the conjunction of three *dvyaṇukas* (binary atoms), and in this manner, effects such as jars and the like arise.

Furthermore, they maintain that an effect, such as a *dvyaṇuka*, is absolutely distinct from its causes, such as the atoms (*paramāṇus*), and that after its destruction, it becomes utterly non-existent, comparable to a man’s horn. He refutes this [view] with the word "non-existent" (*asad*).

For it is not logical that a single pot should be non-existent prior to its production, existent thereafter, and then non-existent again after its destruction; this is because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory. || 16 ||
For that which is drunk and not drunk, and that which is manifest and unmanifest, cannot be one, because of their mutual contradiction and the resulting consequence of confusion and so forth. (17)

Anticipating the objection that there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence—even though they are respectively presence and absence—just as there is no contradiction between conjunction and its absence, he says: "Not so" (*na hi*). Because conjunction is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it does not contradict its own absence. Existence (*sattva*), however, in the case of a jar or other objects, consists in possessing *sattā* (the universal of being) through inherence (*samavāya*). And that [existence] is pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*).

It is precisely the contradiction of its own nature (*svabhāva*) [to be both yellow and not yellow]. Therefore, the point is that yellow and non-yellow cannot be one and the same. Now, one might object: "The nature of a thing must indeed be postulated in accordance with experience;
thus, even though the constituent parts (*samavāyin*) and the composite whole (*avayavin*) exist as spatially pervasive entities (*daiśikavyāpyavṛtti*), the jar exists [in its entirety]."

If it is argued that, in accordance with the experience "it does not exist," one must accept that [non-existence] is temporally non-pervasive, he replies: "Light. What is the suffix *ka* in the word *aprakāśaka*? A thing cannot be both light and non-light; otherwise, by following mere experience alone, a single [entity] would be [both].

If one accepts that darkness possesses two contradictory forms, then— in accordance with the experience that "darkness moves"— since darkness would be a substance, it could be argued that within that very same substance, luminosity arises through the production of a bright-white form,
while its state as darkness arises through the production of a black form.

The intended meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of identity between darkness and light. The connection [of the argument] is as follows: an object that is both yellow and not yellow, or both manifest and unmanifest, cannot be one, because they are contradictory.
Therefore, it is established that existence and non-existence are contradictory even when distinguished by time and place. Now, regarding darkness...
If it is argued that this would result in the violation of the rule that "for a substance to be visually perceived, it must be assisted by light," we say no;

for it is more appropriate to modify the rule itself in accordance with experience. Furthermore, regarding the doctrine of the composite whole (*avayavin*), he states other refutations as well: "because of the consequence of confusion (*sāṅkarya*) and so forth."

The meaning is that there would arise the contingency of confusion (*sāṅkarya*), consisting in the superimposition of contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should understand other defects, such as the proof of parts for the atom and the subversion of the fact that its conjunction is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). Regarding the aforementioned defects of confusion and the rest, they are common to all philosophical systems.
If it is argued that "I alone am not to be questioned regarding such defects," this is indeed true. Therefore,

these refutations were stated by the venerable teacher under the pretext of refuting the atomic theory (*aṇuvāda*), solely in order to censure all those who maintain the reality of duality (*dvaitasatyatvavādinaḥ*).
Furthermore, these criticisms directed at the Advaitins— who are intent on searching for the impossibility of duality—

are like the Vaiṣṇava weapon discharged by Bhagadatta against Vāsudeva (according to the Mahābhārata, Droṇaparva, the Vaiṣṇava weapon released by Bhagadatta was transformed into the Vaijayantī garland upon the chest of Vāsudeva).
(To be seen in chapter 29: It should be understood that these are indeed ornaments (the variants *dadūṣaṇā* and *dhyeyam* are to be known). || 17 ||
Alternatively, how could the initial activity arise from the will of a Lord?
Furthermore, the claim that the world originates from primordial nature (prakṛti) in a state of equilibrium among the qualities (guṇas) is also impossible.

Having thus accepted the world as established by others and having refuted it through [the fallacies of] confusion (*sāṅkarya*) and so forth, he now states a refutation that cuts off the very root, namely that the production of the world itself is impossible, beginning with the words "By the will of God" (*īśvara*).
For how could motion first arise in atoms by the will of God? [It cannot,] because the will of anyone toward anything occurs only at some specific time and place.

Because no activity is observed to arise in anything insentient; for if insentient things were to conform to the will of the Lord, then even weapons would fight against enemies on their own, conforming to the king's will without soldiers. Therefore, the meaning is that this theory of "initiation" (ārambhavāda) is not tenable.

Having thus rejected the doctrine of creation (*ārambhavāda*), he restates the position of the other school in order to refute the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*): "In the state of equilibrium of the qualities" (*guṇasāmye*). The non-theistic Sāṅkhyas, however, hold that *prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, [existing] by itself.
They say that [Prakṛti] transforms into the form of the world by way of an imbalance of its qualities (guṇa); this view, too, is untenable.

Because it would have to be sought as the cause of inequality, because it would be inferior as the cause of equality, because there is no conscious directing agent, and because no illustrative example is found. || 19 ||

If one asks why, he says: "Because of inequality" (*vaiṣamya*). For primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is, at the time of dissolution, characterized by the equilibrium of its qualities (*guṇa-sāmya*). At the end of dissolution, it is illogical for that inequality of qualities to arise without a cause. Nor does anything other than primordial nature exist during dissolution that could serve as the cause for the inequality of the qualities.

Furthermore, at the end of creation from this primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which possesses unequal qualities, there can be no cause for the equilibrium that serves as the occasion for dissolution. Now, is there not a cause for both the equilibrium and the disequilibrium of the qualities?
For others who maintain the existence of a Lord (*īśvara*), [this cause] is indeed the Lord himself, intended to avoid the charge of partiality and cruelty.

If it is argued that karma itself, through the inequality of its qualities (*guṇavaiṣamya*), is the cause [of the world's manifestation], he says: "Because of the lack of superintendence by a conscious being" (*cetanānadhiṣṭhānāt*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is not possible.
