This is because activity among insentient things is never observed without the operation of a conscious agent; therefore, [the world] cannot arise from primordial matter by itself in the form of the universe.
Transformation for the sake of bondage toward the person, as well as activity for liberation and cessation [from it], are not tenable.

Since activity or cessation in insentient things through the mere presence of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) is never observed without the impulsion of a conscious being, there is an absence of an illustrative example; thus, he states that this cannot be established even by inference: "dṛṣṭānta... [etc.].
Therefore, no cause for the world's effects is perceived;
since it is unperceived, scripture is its source, and there is no application of any other means of knowledge. || 20 ||

Since the determination of a cause for the world in this manner is not tenable, it follows that no material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is perceived. [Objection: But surely the effect in the form of the world is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and cannot be denied; if one were to accept that it has no cause, [it would follow that it is uncaused].

If it is argued that "the entry into the ultimate truth and the establishment of its causes must necessarily occur only by way of our stated path," he says: "But regarding the unseen... This means: regarding an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). "Scripture" (*śruti*) means traditional authority (*āgama*). "Root" (*mūla*) means the decisive means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why is this so?

If it is asked: "Not otherwise" (*nānyeti*)—[this means] there is no connection with another [means of knowledge] such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor is there any application [of it]; this is the meaning. || 20 ||
Because cognizers are incomplete, because the means of knowledge lacks finality, and because of the cause consisting in the repeated observation of the dissociation between action and agent. || 21 ||

If it is asked why this is so, he says: "of the knowers" (*pramātṝṇām*). For perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only when there is contact with the sense organs; and since knowers are limited and thus incomplete, there can be no operation of perception regarding heaven, Indra, and so forth, because contact with the sense organs is impossible in those cases. As for inference...

Precisely because it is rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no engagement with that which is eternally beyond the senses (*nityaparokṣa*). Alternatively, even if engagement were somehow established, since the operation of the means of knowledge known as inference (*anumāna*) would depend upon the ingenuity of the intellect, inference could proceed in other ways as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Something will be established regarding the subject at hand by means of inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, it is observed that among the non-Buddhists (*tairthika*), there are distinct tenets established by mere reasoning (*tarka*) alone; with this in mind, he says:
"of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasya*). This means "of inference. [Objection: But scripture (*āgama*) is indeed verbal testimony (*śabda*). That too—
Raising the objection as to how [scripture] can be a means of valid cognition regarding invisible matters such as heaven when it is employed by a limited knower, [the author],

intending to state that the authority of the Word does not belong to mere sound regarding an unseen object but rather to the Word of the Lord (Īśvara) such as the Śruti, proceeds to declare the preeminence of that scripture among the means of valid cognition.
In this context, he establishes the existence of God through the argument from effect (*kārya*).
The meaning is that, because it is observed repeatedly that an effect is invariably concomitant with a creator, the world must have a creator. (21)
This world has an agent because it comes into being, and he is indeed conscious;
for how could an ordinary person be the creator of an effect whose nature is inconceivable? (22)

"Accompanied by an agent. Now, an objection is raised: "The proof of God by means of inference is untenable, for it was stated immediately prior that inference does not establish what is eternally beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). To this it is replied:

There is no rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhūtatva*) between an effect and its material cause (*upādāna*), because such a rule is contradicted by effects produced by yogis. Now [the opponent objects]: [The text continues: "But..."

If it is argued that even in that case, by the power of the yogi’s will, the atoms themselves, suddenly assembled, may serve as the material cause, we say no; for this would not avoid the fallacy of deviation, since it would involve the transgression of the fixed sequence consisting of the *śivaka*, *stūpaka*, *kāpālikā*, and *kapāla* stages. This transgression of the fixed sequence beginning with the *śivaka*— [The text continues: ...is [the point]. Furthermore, if it were held that the yogi’s will alone is the cause, then there would be no distinction between the production of a jar and the production of a cloth, because the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would be identical. Moreover, if it were held that the atoms are produced from the atoms of the jar itself, then one would have to accept that the jar is eternal, because its constituent parts would never be destroyed. Therefore, the theory of the atomist is untenable. Thus, the Vaibhāṣika position is refuted. Now, the Sautrāntika position is considered. They hold that external objects are merely mental representations (*vijñaptimātra*). However, this too is incorrect, because it contradicts direct perception. For the existence of external objects is established by direct perception, inference, and scriptural authority. Since the external object is perceived as having color and shape, it cannot be denied. Furthermore, if the external object were non-existent, then the diversity of cognitions regarding the same object would be inexplicable. Therefore, the Sautrāntika view is also rejected. Consequently, the Yogācāra position remains. They maintain that all this is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and that the appearance of external objects is an illusion (*bhrānti*). This is correct, because the existence of external objects is logically untenable. For if an external object were to exist, it would have to be either an atom (*paramāṇu*) or an aggregate (*saṃcita*). It cannot be an atom, because an atom lacks the characteristics of an object of cognition, being partless and devoid of form. Nor can it be an aggregate, because an aggregate is nothing other than a collection of atoms, and thus shares the same defects. Therefore, the appearance of external objects is a mere construction of the mind. Thus, everything is consciousness-only. This concludes the refutation of the external world. Now, the nature of consciousness is considered. Consciousness is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), because it is luminous by nature. Just as fire illuminates itself, so too does consciousness know itself. Without self-cognition, the recollection of past cognitions would be impossible. Therefore, consciousness is self-luminous. Furthermore, consciousness is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because it arises and perishes in every instant. If it were permanent, there would be no difference between the states of bondage and liberation. Therefore, consciousness is momentary, self-cognizing, and devoid of external objects. This is the ultimate truth. Thus ends the exposition of the Yogācāra system. May there be peace.
That which is produced by the power of yoga is undeniable. For, since the effect is accomplished by that very power, the postulation of an assembly of atoms is irrational.
Furthermore, a yogi who constructs a jar solely through the well-known sequence of causes and so forth would be nothing other than a potter.

This is to be understood: for there is no rule of invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) that an effect must necessarily be inseparable from an agent; therefore, the inference that an effect possesses an agent is not subject to an infinite regress. Furthermore, even though the agent has been thus established, he is not insentient (*jaḍa*), because the nature of agency consists in possessing immediate, direct knowledge regarding the material cause (*upādāna*).
He says "because it is impossible in the insentient" (jaḍe 'sambhavāt), [and then] "because it is possible" (sambhavāt). || 22 ||
Therefore, that scripture possesses inconceivable power, as does its contemplation; for the Perfect One, it is an unimpeded means of valid cognition, superior in every respect. (23)

Since an ordinary agent is impossible for a work whose nature and effect are inconceivable, therefore the creator of the world possesses inconceivable power. The word "tat" (that) has its genitive case-ending elided; it refers to that [creator] who is full and possesses inconceivable power. His "reflective awareness" (*vimarśana*) consists of speech that brings about the realization of reality.
The operation is the scripture. It should be understood that because its power is inconceivable, its operation consists of verbal expression even though it is bodiless.

Since this scripture is of such a nature, it is therefore an unimpeded means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is in no way contradicted by others; for this very reason, it is [authoritative] in every respect.
This is the means of proof (prabala), which is superior and more excellent than the [other] means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 23 ||
In that regard, one Maheśāna was proclaimed at the beginning of creation;
for he is independent and without material cause, by virtue of the majesty of the fullness of his sovereignty.
Having made the promise, "I shall state the proof here that the object of sight is nothing but seeing" (11.7),
and having established through an extensive treatise that scripture (*āgama*) is the preeminent among the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
he restates the matter taught in scripture in order to fulfill his promise with ten verses, beginning with "Therein... (*tatra*).

This is the meaning according to scripture (*āgama*). He is described as being "devoid of material cause" (*upādānarahita*). Thus says the scripture: "In the beginning, this [universe] was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1); "Then there was neither non-existence nor existence" (*Ṛgveda* 10.129.1). For, indeed, without any collection of material causes, [the Lord manifests] upon the wall of His own self.

"Having sketched the variegated picture of the world with ease, this Maheśvara sports. Such is the beginning [of the verse]. The construction is as follows: "He manifests [the world] by virtue of the majesty—that is, the excellence or abundance—of His sovereignty. (24)
It manifests the painting of the world upon the wall of its own self for the sake of its own play, just as that which is imagined solely by oneself in a dream or a kingdom of the mind. (25)

"For the sake of luxury" means for the sake of play; just as in a dream or in a mental construction (*manorājya*), one imagines a body by oneself alone, without depending on material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth. || 25 ||
In that same way, one perceives this world as "I" and as "mine";
yet its true nature is not like the body, because the body serves as the cause for the cessation of dreams. (26)

Just as at that time one grasps [objects] through the sense of "I," so too this Lord grasps the world, which He Himself has imagined, precisely through the sense of "I. As it has been said: "The subject is called the Lord (pati) with respect to those entities that have become His own limbs" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 3.14). "Not those... [and so forth].
For just as a body imagined in a daydream is not your true nature, because it ceases to exist in dreams and other such states. (26)
Likewise, this world-body of yours does not exist at the time of dissolution because it has ceased;
for you are distinct from the body and such, consisting solely of pure consciousness. || 27 ||

He applies this to the subject of the illustration with the word "so" (*tathā*): [it refers to] this Lord. Although the world is grasped as the "I," it is not the body, because the world ceases to exist at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). Just as the conscious self (*cidātman*), which persists through states such as waking and so forth, is distinct from the body and other things that do not persist through those states.
In the same way, he says that Īśvara as well is pure consciousness alone, distinct from the world which does not persist through dissolution, [in the verse beginning] "dehādi" (verse 27).
Thus the Lord, the imperishable, whose singular body is consciousness and emptiness, has indeed manifested this variegated world within his own self. 28.
"Imperishable" (avyaya) is an epithet that establishes His distinction from the impermanent world; [it refers] to the Lord whose sole body is consciousness. || 28 ||
How could it ever unfold the painting of the world, since it is impossible for anything else to exist apart from consciousness?
For what could possibly come into being, or where, without consciousness? (29)
It has been stated that "the fullness of the Full is unimpeded" (11.23); [the author] now establishes that fullness by asking, "Where? The meaning is:

since no object of perception other than itself can exist anywhere else—outside of itself—where could the painting of the world manifest? If one asks why there is no possibility of anything other than itself existing anywhere, he says: "Because of Truth" (*ṛta*).
"When did he create it? Where? What was it like?"—this is the negation of time, place, and form. || 29 ||
That place where one might speak of the non-existence of consciousness cannot be established at all;
and by what could the non-existence of consciousness itself be established? Therefore, consciousness is supreme.

"In which [place]" (*yatra*): the sense is that where there is an absence of consciousness (*cit*), the manifestation of that place would be impossible, because establishment depends upon manifestation. "And [the] absence" (*abhāvaśca*): the sense is that since consciousness is the illuminator of all things, by what could its absence be established? Therefore, because the absence of consciousness is unestablished, it is supreme (*parā*) and cannot be negated.
Because it serves as the limit for negation. || 30 ||
The Great Beings, whose nature is to devour the world, appear full; like waves within the ocean, they shine without the Lord of Day. (31)

Therefore, she is Mahāsattā; she whose being (*sattā*) is great and undivided. For this very reason, because the world is pervaded by her, she is she whose nature is to swallow the world. For this very reason, she is full (*pūrṇā*). For this very reason, the world is inseparable from her;
thus he says "the ocean" as an illustration. (31)
Just as they do not exist, so indeed does the world not exist apart from the nature of consciousness;
therefore, this Mahādeva has pure consciousness as his very form. || 32 ||

For just as waves and the like are inseparable from the ocean and so forth, so too is the world inseparable from the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*). Since the world is inseparable from consciousness, the connection [of the verse] is that he existed as the embodiment of pure consciousness, devoid of even a trace of the visible. || 32 ||
It existed before creation; from it this world was produced and in it it remained; and at the end, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings dissolves into it.

Therefore, just as waves and the like—which possess origination and so forth—have as their very nature nothing but the ocean and its constituent elements, so too the world has as its nature nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra); this is the intended meaning. || 33 ||
Thus, the meaning well-established by scripture is not to be disputed;
for scripture is indeed a valid means of knowledge because it accords with reality regarding matters that are beyond perception. (34)

Regarding the word "iti": that which was stated in the ten verses beginning with "Therein, however, one... (11.24) is what is taught in the *Āgama*. It does not undergo contradiction; that is, it does not fall into the state of being an object of doubt. If one asks why this is so, he says: "Because it is unperceived [otherwise]. For when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is found to be non-discrepant in some instance, the object cognized by it is not contradicted. As for that which is a means of valid cognition...

The rule is that what is known through that [means of knowledge] is non-contradictory in all respects, and the object so cognized does not turn out to be otherwise. Scripture (*āgama*), however, is a means of valid cognition even when its objects are unperceived;

it is never contradicted. Therefore, an object established by it does not turn out to be otherwise. The sense is that, for this reason, scripture must in every respect be a means of valid cognition. || 34 ||
Since the accomplishments of gems, mantras, and so forth are seen everywhere, one of little wisdom would not understand the great fruit of gems and mantras. (35)
If it is objected that the Veda and other scriptures are not spoken by God because there is a lack of evidence, he says: "They are seen.

Since the accomplishments—the production of results—of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs as taught in the scriptures are seen everywhere among practitioners, therefore the scripture was uttered by the Omniscient One.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: since no one other than the Lord—being of limited wisdom—is capable of knowing (or: bestowing) the fruit resulting from gems and the like, he says: "No" (na). || 35 ||
Therefore, the scripture proclaimed by the Omniscient One indeed reveals all perspectives;
therein it is stated that at the very beginning of the world's creation, the Lord Himself was established.

"Omniscient" (*sarvadarśana*): "Seeing" (*darśana*) is that by which one sees; it is the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He whose seeing extends to everything—meaning, he whose object is both the seen and the unseen—is [the subject].

The "Lord" (*deva*) is the Sovereign whose form is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); by the word "only" (*eva*), there is an exclusion of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and other such principles. || 36 ||
From the very beginning, Maheśvara— who is endowed with perfect, pure, and absolute freedom— created the entire universe while remaining entirely without any substrate of appropriation.
If it is argued that even though He was initially alone, at the time of creation the Lord procures some material cause (*upādāna*) from somewhere, [the author] says "no":
"If the Lord manifests effects such as a jar without a material cause, how and where could He manifest them?
To this he says: "Because... [He is] full (*pūrṇa*), undivided (*aparicchinna*), pure (*svaccha*), uncreated (*akṛtrima*), and innate (*sahaja*).
He is endowed with that sovereignty. || 37 ||
The entire world-picture unfolds upon the wall of the conscious self;
that world does not exist externally, established anywhere outside. || 38 ||

"Consisting of consciousness" (*cidātman*): because, due to His fullness, there is no possibility of anything other than Himself, and He is endowed with perfect sovereignty, therefore the meaning is that He should manifest the entire universe as a painting upon the wall of His own nature as the conscious Self. If it is asked, "From what [source] is it known that He manifests [the world] upon the wall of the Self?", he says: (##-)
Because the Lord is all-pervading, no other location for him exists here;
and that which is situated in another place can by no means be established [as his true abode]. (39)

If it is asked why [it] is not possible, he says: "Because of fullness. Just as there is no room for anything else in a jar filled with rice, the meaning is that because space (*dig*) and so forth are filled by the Self (*ātman*), there is no room for anything else.
Even if one were to admit that the Self is not full, [the Self] would not exist elsewhere.
The world is established [only] through consciousness, because that which has gone outside the light of consciousness is not manifest; thus he says: "In another place," etc. (39).
And thus, just like a reflection upon the expanse of a mirror, the universe has unfolded within the Divine; in this way, everything is perfectly coherent.

Now, one might object: "This is inconsistent, because no instance is observed where one thing appears as having the nature of another; thus, it is impossible for the world to appear within the nature of the conscious Self. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And so it is," and "Like a mirror.
This means that just as reflections appear within the nature of a mirror, so too [does the world appear] within the divine nature of the conscious Self.
The meaning is that everything is consistent because of the acceptance [of the view] that the world appears as something manifested. || 40 ||
For the Lord of the world, as for a yogi, the activities of the universe are like those of a city of one's own imagination; such is the creation of the Lord, according to his own conviction. (41)

If it is objected that the performance of an action by an agent who lacks material causes (*nirupādāna*) is never observed anywhere, he replies with the words "of the world and so forth" (*jagadādeḥ*). This means "of the creator of the world. If it is then asked: "In that case, like a creation produced by a yogi, would the world not also be distinct from its own creator? And if so, how can it be said that there is no world apart from consciousness? he replies:
He intends as follows: the meaning is that the creation is not distinct from the Creator, just as a city of one's imagination is not distinct from the deity who is the creator of the world. || 41 ||
O Rāma, this mental creation of yours is purely composed of mind alone;
yet it appears as if abundant with manifold subjects, objects of cognition, and so forth.
If it is objected that even a city of imagination is indeed distinct from its creator, he says "no," beginning with the words "O Rāma" and so forth.
The connection is as follows: that mental creation which appears, abounding in imagined cities, is composed of mind (manomayī). || 42 ||
Though divided into many different forms, there is nothing anywhere else than the mind;
whatever arises from the mind remains therein and dissolves back into that very same place.

He establishes this very point with the words "aneketi" (not manifold). Although the mental creation is differentiated by various distinctions—that is, by excluded properties (*vyāvṛttadharma*)—it is connected as follows: since it has arisen in the mind, remains there, and is dissolved right there, it does not differ from the mind. || 43 ||
Just as that [creation] consists solely of the form of the mind, so too does the world [proceed] from Śiva.

Regarding the word "that": it refers to mental creation (*mānasī sṛṣṭiḥ*). Just as mental creation is composed of mind (*manomaya*) due to its arising from the mind and so forth, the meaning is that the world, which possesses arising and so forth from Śiva—the conscious self (*cidātman*)—is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*). Now, one might object:

If it is argued that for the universe produced from Śiva, there is only the nature of Śiva and not the nature of consciousness (cit), he says: "He" (sa). Now, suspecting that consciousness might have a physical form like a potter, he says "no": "without form" (avigrahā). This means she has no body or form distinct from consciousness. 44.
She is Tripura, whose singular form is the infinite power [of consciousness], the witness of all; that Consciousness is full in every respect, being devoid of all limitation. (45)
He states that this very *citi* (consciousness), which is the subject to be established in the present context, is *Tripura*: "Tripura.

Regarding her powers, there is this verse: "Power and the possessor of power are said to be the two categories of reality; all this world is his power, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power."
In the *Yogarājavyākhyā* on the *Paramārthasāra* composed by Abhinavagupta (p.

10), [the following] is cited as a verse from the *Śrīsarvamaṅgalāśāstra*: "By the principle stated as 'the entire world,' those infinite powers which consist of the manifestations of jars and so forth—their unity is their fusion; she whose nature is that [unity]."

The sense is that just as, for reflections appearing in a mirror, the mirror itself is the form consisting of their convergence, so it is here. Now, if it is argued that in that case, consciousness (*cit*) would also possess a non-conscious (*jaḍa*) nature like the mirror, he says: the sense is that the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) cannot belong to what is non-conscious. Furthermore, the fullness (*pūrṇatva*) previously mentioned—
He begins to accomplish it correctly: "That is consciousness" (45).
In this world, time and space are traditionally held to be the means of delimitation;
therein, space consists of form, while time consists of action.

If it is asked, "How then is it devoid of delimitation? he says: "Time. The point is that in the world, it is well known that only space and time possess the quality of being delimiters; [in this case], there is no such delimitation.
If it is further asked, "What is the nature of space and time, which are considered to be delimiters? he says:

Regarding the word *tatra*: it means "between those two. In the expression "here now there is a jar," the word "here" manifests as a location consisting of a house or the like, and "now" manifests as time consisting of morning and so forth. Among these, the location consisting of a house or the like is merely the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) of the earth and other elements; whereas time consists of the movement (*parispanda*) of the sun and other celestial bodies.

It is action alone. As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*: "By means of the diversity of forms, this Lord manifests spatial succession; and by means of the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He manifests temporal succession as well."

(2|5) Thus it is said. Likewise, time is merely the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, as well as the birth of various flowers and so forth. Indeed, it is not possible for space or time—which are indivisible—to be conditioned by any external adjunct (*upādhi*) such as the form of the Sunrise Mountain or the like, nor by the activity of the sun and so forth, in a manner that would make them something other than what they are. For...
Since all worldly transaction is carried out only by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is an absence of both proof and purpose for postulating [an intrinsic form];
for how could that consciousness, depending upon which either a form or an action arises, possess the capacity to delimit these two? Tell me. (46–47)

Having thus analyzed the essential nature of space and time, he establishes the absence of limitation by them for the conscious self (cidātman) with the words "yām" and so forth. For in the world, even for a man who is a householder with a lifespan of a hundred years,
there is [only] a single portion of that great time consisting of the Kali Yuga and of that space consisting of Jambūdvīpa— namely, the period of one hundred years.
Furthermore, by means of the house as a form and location, a delimitation is well known in the sense that "it has existed for this much time" and "it has existed in this place.

In the present context, the meaning is that although space and time exist as dependent on a single portion of the conscious self (cidātman), they somehow function as delimiters of the self in the form of shape and activity. || 47 ||
In what place and at what time is consciousness not present here? Tell that;
for how indeed could even that [place or time] exist where consciousness is absent? (48)

Now, it might be argued that space and time do not depend upon the conscious self (*cidātman*), because the conscious self resides in a single location within those two—which are vastly greater—just like a jar or similar objects.
To this, he says: "In what? That is to say, "where," meaning in space and time.
The meaning is "he knows. "So too" means that both place and time [are known]. For just as a jar, a bowl, and so forth are inseparable from clay, dependent upon clay, and do not exist without clay;
and just as an object reflected in a mirror is inseparable from the mirror, dependent upon the mirror, and [does not exist] without the mirror—
The meaning is that space and time do not exist independently of consciousness, nor does consciousness exist without them; therefore, they are indeed dependent upon it. || 48 ||

For the existence of objects is indeed nothing other than their manifestation; manifestation is said to be consciousness, for that which is not consciousness cannot possess the nature of manifestation. (49)

[Objection: "Is it not the case that consciousness, like sunlight, is the illuminator of objects? And so, just as a jar or other object exists in darkness even when devoid of sunlight, let the existence of space and so forth also exist even without consciousness? To this, he says: "Existence" (astitā). This means "being. For the being of objects is indeed nothing other than their manifestation.
For the light whose essence is sentient beings is consciousness alone. That which lacks consciousness is "non-conscious" (*acit*); the intended meaning is that it is not an object of consciousness.
Since non-consciousness has no luminosity, the meaning is that consciousness alone is light. And so, in the absence of solar light, in darkness—

Since the jar and other objects appear through light, the existence of the jar and so forth is distinct from that light; however, because there is no possibility of any kind of practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) with the jar and other objects apart from the illumination of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), the point is that the very existence of the jar and so forth is nothing but the illumination of consciousness. || 49 ||
But the Light (prakāśa) would be the supreme principle, which shines independently;
for insentient things are not self-luminous, as they shine only through connection with consciousness. (50)

[Objection: Let it be granted that the existence of entities consists in manifestation (*prakāśa*) alone; nevertheless, since there is a similarity in linguistic usage such as "the jar manifests" (*ghaṭaḥ prakāśate*) and "consciousness manifests" (*citiḥ prakāśate*), how can consciousness be the substratum of perceptible objects like jars? To this, he says: "Manifestation. That which manifests independently, without dependence on anything else—that is manifestation.
Thus, they are "sumukhya" (excellent-faced); [the variant reading] "mukhyaḥ" (principal) is also acceptable. Regarding "insentient" (*jaḍā*):
the meaning is that insentient things are distinct from the conscious self (*cidātman*), and are not self-luminous—that is, they do not possess a manifestation independent of anything else.

For [it is] by means of conjunction with consciousness—that is, by attaining the status of being an object of consciousness—that they are manifested. This is because those things which have not attained identity with consciousness are not manifested.
The meaning is that for insentient things, manifestation is independent. || 50 ||
Consciousness shines by itself, independent of anything else;
insentient things shine only by depending upon consciousness, and not otherwise. (51)

But consciousness is not like that; thus he says: "another" (*anyā*). It manifests in its own nature—which has not attained identity with anything else—during states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Therefore, because of the disparity in manifestation between consciousness and the insentient, it is only by depending on consciousness that insentient things manifest, and not independently; this is the meaning.
If things possess existence even when unmanifest, then listen:
the worldly distinction between "it exists" and "it does not exist" would not be established in this world. (52)

Suppose it is argued that, just as entities depend upon space (*ākāśa*), they likewise depend upon consciousness (*cit*); nevertheless, because of such conventional usages as "it exists" and "it is manifested," existence (*astitā*) is indeed distinct from manifestation (*prakāśa*), like [the distinction between] space and its contents. To this, he says: "In the first case, it does not exist. Or [is it the second]? In the first [case]:

Thinking that non-difference is already established between "pot-ness" and "jar-ness," which are co-extensive—just like the case of "pot-ness" and "kalaśatva"—he states the refutation regarding the second [alternative] with the words "It exists" (*asti*). The point is this: if a pot or the like possesses existence even while unmanifested, then the conventional distinction such as "this does not exist because it is unmanifested" would fail to be established. Now, if that is so...

If it is asked how such conventional usage as "it exists because it manifests" or "because it manifests, therefore it exists" is possible, it is replied that this is to be understood in the same way as [the inference] "the object of sight exists because it is perceptible," and so forth. || 52 ||
Therefore, the existence of objects in the world is nothing other than the light of consciousness;
for just as the reality of reflections exists only in the mirror. (53)

"Therefore" means that manifestation and existence are co-extensive (*samaniyata*). Here is the illustration: "Now," etc. This is stated with the intention of expressing the identity (*tādātmya*) between the attribute and the substrate: "In the mirror itself.
The meaning is that the very existence of the mirror is the existence of the reflections. || 53 ||
Likewise, consciousness is the existence of the world; therefore, everything becomes consciousness.
That which appears as something additional does so because of the greatness of its purity.

Thus, because consciousness (*cit*) and light (*prakāśa*) are identical in nature, consciousness is the existence of the world; therefore, the entire world is consciousness. Now, if everything is indeed consciousness alone, then why does it appear as "pot" or "cloth"—an appearance of additional parts—rather than appearing merely as "consciousness"? To this, he says: "The additional [parts]," meaning "due to the magnitude of the purity of that consciousness. Because of the greatness of that consciousness’s purity...
"By greatness" means by majesty. || 54 ||
The manifestation of a reflection occurs due to both hardness and purity;
however, depending on the degree of these two qualities, the reflection appears either clear or indistinct. (55)

Now, one might object: "While an excessive manifestation may occur in a mirror by way of reflection, how can there be an excessive manifestation in the case of the conscious Self (cidātman), which is the subject at hand? To answer this, he analyzes the cause of reflection, stating that it occurs precisely by way of reflection: "Hardness... (kāṭhinya). Hardness is the state of being devoid of the nature of consciousness. (k, kh:)

The remainder [of the sentence] is that the manifestation of a reflection would occur due to the nature of being filled with solidity; [this refers to] those two, namely solidity and purity, according to their relative degree—that is, by way of deficiency or excess. || 55 ||
This is indeed clearly perceived both in a mirror and in water;
for, due to their insentience, mirrors and the like are devoid of autonomy. (56)

Due to the predominance of hardness and clarity, a reflection is distinct in a mirror; due to their deficiency, a reflection is indistinct in water. This is clearly perceived by everyone. The point is that there is no appearance of a reflection on a wall because of the absence of clarity, nor in space because of the absence of hardness.

If it is objected that, in the manifestation of a reflection within itself, consciousness must require an external object (bimba), just as a mirror does, he replies: "Because of insentience. The connection is that the requirement for an object arises from [the nature of] insentient things. || 56 ||
The dependence of consciousness upon an object arises from its own pure sovereignty;
yet its independence [from objects] is established by itself through consciousness’s freedom from impurity, which is its inherent stainlessness. (57)
That sovereignty which is transparent, free from the impurity of limitation, and universal—because of that, consciousness has no dependence upon external images. As it has been said:
"The entire universe shines here within the Self."
"Just as a variegated arrangement [appears] within a mirror, consciousness is [recognized as] supreme and innate"—this is the reading found in the *Tantrasāra* (p.
19) and in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* (Vol. 2, p. 203).

In the *Paramārthasārayogarājavivṛti* (p. 39), however, the reading found in the root text itself is observed; furthermore, according to the reasoning (or method) of one's own reflection (*nijavimarśanasārayuktyā*), there is the reading found in the *Tantrasāra*: "by means of [the method]... (*vṛttyā*).
"The mirror does not grasp the universe in that same way.
(Tattvasaṅgraha, p. 19). Now, if it is asked how purity can belong to consciousness when it is possible for water and the like to become pure through substances such as *katakā*, he says:
"Purity," because, like space, it is free from impurity due to its non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*). || 57 ||
Multiplicity of flavors would indeed be impurity for the consciousness;
however, this is not so, because the power of consciousness is of the nature of oneness and is entirely indivisible.
Anticipating the objection—"What is this impurity residing in water and other elements that is said not to exist in the nature of consciousness?"—he says:

"aneka... (various). "Possessing manifold flavors" (*anekarasa*) means being mixed with other entities. For example, impurity in water consists in its being mixed with earthly dust; likewise, in a mirror, it consists in its being mixed with portions of glass and other materials. But is such [impurity]...

If it is asked, "Whence does the impurity of consciousness (*citi*) not arise?", he says: "Because of its uniformity (*aikātmyarūpyāt*). The possibility of impurity exists for composite things (*avayavin*) because of the joining of parts distinct from themselves within the intervals between their own constituent parts. The sense is that, because the conscious self (*cidātman*) is partless and thus uniform, there is no impurity. Having thus stated the cause for its purity, [he proceeds].

He states the reason for solidity as well: "Because it is indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*). The connection is: "because of its indivisibility, which is the cause of its non-empty nature. Non-empty nature (*riktātmatva*) means having the nature of space (*avakāśātmatva*); that is to say, possessing space. For in the world, a gradation of solidity is observed according to the degree of the compactness of parts. As for those parts...
An excess of cohesion corresponds to an excess of hardness; a deficiency of cohesion corresponds to a deficiency of hardness.

This is observed in the case of stone and water. Furthermore, an excess of cohesion is caused by an excess of connection between the constituent parts. For instance, because of whose constituent parts...

To the extent that [parts] are conjoined, there is a corresponding increase in cohesion and a corresponding increase in hardness; likewise, to the extent that a certain number of constituent parts are unconjoined,
there is a corresponding presence of internal space due to the partitioning by those parts and because of their hollow nature.
The meaning is that it possesses no excessive hardness; however, because consciousness (cit) is partless and indivisible, its nature is one of non-emptiness. || 58 ||
Because its own nature is never empty, its purity is supreme in every respect;
for that which appears as non-self appears only through association with another. (59)

Because its nature as a self is non-empty, the purity of consciousness (*citi*) is superior in every respect. The phrase "purity by nature" is also an elliptical expression for "hardness. Thus, the meaning is that the purity and hardness of consciousness are superior in every way to those of objects such as a mirror.

Because a gradation of space is possible within the constituent parts of composite objects, and because a gradation of the entry of other entities into those spaces is likewise possible, there exists a gradation of hardness and clarity; however,
because consciousness (*citi*) is partless and thus entirely devoid of internal space, it possesses neither hardness nor clarity.

The sense is that [the reflection] is superior to everything. Now, if it is argued that there is no reflection-hood because there is a lack of evidence for the world being a reflection, we reply: its reflection-hood is asserted because it possesses the defining characteristics of a reflection.
To state those characteristics of a reflection, he says: "asvataḥ" (not by itself), meaning appearing while not being connected with anything else.
The nature of being a reflection (*pratibimbatva*) consists in appearing through a connection with something else (*anya*).

Just as a reflected jar, which does not appear without a mirror, appears only through its connection with the mirror, so too the world—which does not appear without Consciousness (*cit*)—appears only through its connection with Consciousness; thus, the world is essentially of the nature of a reflection.
Those who know the true nature of a reflection describe the world as such—a reflection perceived by everyone. (60)
"Reflection" (pratibimba) means the state of being a reflection (pratibimbatva). Such is that which possesses the characteristics of a reflection. || 60 ||
It does not shine by itself anywhere, yet it shines by taking consciousness as its support;
therefore, the world is perfectly comparable to a reflection in a mirror.
He applies the characteristic [of the meter] to the world by means of "itself" (svataḥ); it is well-measured and even. 61.
The city of consciousness (cit), though colored by various other states, shines forth without deviating even in the slightest degree from its own essential nature, just like a mirror. (52)

Having thus established the reflectivity of consciousness (*citi*) by showing that the world possesses the characteristic of being a reflection, [the author] applies the definition of a reflector to consciousness in order to state its similarity to a mirror: "Consciousness...
[He states: "In the state of appearing as colored by the nature of another... (*anyasvarūpoparaktatvena bhāsamānatve*).
The state of having a nature that has not fallen away from reality is the capacity for receiving a reflection. Regarding the word "bhāsinī" (shining): it means having the nature of mere shining.
Therefore, the syntactical connection is: "precisely because [it] has not fallen away even in the slightest degree. || 62 ||
Just as reflections in a mirror are non-different from the mirror, so too the reflections of the conscious self are non-different from the conscious self. (63)
Having thus established the world's nature as a reflection through great effort, he states the conclusion: "Like a mirror," and so forth.
For the reflection in a mirror is determined to have the original object as its cause; likewise, the reflection of the world must have consciousness as its cause through its own inherent freedom. 64.

Regarding the statement, "Independence [arises] from the purity of one's own freedom" (11.57), it was said that there is no dependence on an original object (*bimba*) for the reflection in consciousness; he now begins to demonstrate this with the words "the mirror. That which has an original object as its cause is "caused by the original object" (*bimbahetu*). That which has freedom as its cause is the world (*jāgata*).
A reflection. || 64 ||
O Rāma, behold by your own volition those states reflected within yourself—states that are inseparable from their source yet appear without an external cause. 65.

Regarding the observation that a reflection is seen even without an original object (bimba), he says: "In one's own conceptualization" (*svasaṅkalpe*). This means within one's own self, which is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The sense is that for these [reflections], the manifestation is "without a cause" (*nirnimitta*), meaning that, like a reflection in a mirror, there is no dependence even on causes such as light.

The entities appearing in the kingdom of the mind (manorājya) through volition are reflections by virtue of possessing the characteristics of a reflection; it is well known that their manifestation occurs entirely without dependence on an original object (bimba) or the like. Thus, the meaning is that the world is a reflection within supreme consciousness. || 65 ||
Volition alone is proclaimed as the swelling sovereignty of consciousness;
in the state of non-volition, that consciousness is of a purely transparent nature.
He explains the object of volition (*saṅkalpa-padārtha*) as follows: "Volition" refers to that power called the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*).
Precisely because it is a power, it is non-different from the conscious self and possesses a subtle form.
When that [power] becomes swollen or nourished—that is to say, when it attains grossness by taking on the form of the visible world—[it is called volition].
Then, that very sovereignty of His is called "volition" (*saṅkalpa*).
For just as Your sovereignty itself takes the form of volition,
so too does it manifest various entities within You by way of reflection.

In the same way, the sense is that the sovereignty of Īśvara also manifests the universe. And at the time when there is no volitional thought, just as for you, consciousness—which is your very self—is devoid of reflections and consists solely of pure, transparent consciousness. (66)
Thus, prior to the emanation of consciousness, which is of a single pure form,
there existed a vast sovereignty consisting solely of volition.

Thus, that very sovereignty— which is vast and unlimited— belonging to the supreme consciousness (*parā citi*), which prior to creation existed in the state of dissolution as a single pure form, became at the beginning of creation of the nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*).
For in the state of pure consciousness, sovereignty remains as a single, undifferentiated essence, yet at the beginning of creation...
The meaning is that the very attainment of the form of the world constitutes the nature of volition (saṅkalpa). || 67 ||
Therefore, this world, consisting of reflected images, has appeared;
through the great stability of one's resolve, it shines forth for a long time. (68)

Then, by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), this world, consisting of reflected images, appears. Now, one might ask: "Just as the objects manifested by our own volition are unstable, why is it that the world manifested by the volition of the Lord (*īśvara*) is not likewise unstable? To this he says: "Vast" (*bṛhat*).

The meaning is that this world appears for a long time due to the stability of the vast creative resolve (saṅkalpa), because there is a rule that the manifestation born of resolve cannot exist for a duration shorter than that of the resolve itself. || 68 ||
The world appears as common [to all] because of the cause of its full autonomy;
for others, however, it appears as having a non-common nature due to their own incompleteness.
[Objection: Even so, that which arises from one's own volition appears only to oneself and not to another.
How then can the world born from the volition of the Lord appear as common to all? [Response:
He says: "It is common," because of the Lord’s perfect sovereignty.
The meaning is: "because of the cause of absolute sovereignty. The meaning of "due to its incompleteness" is:

due to the incompleteness of sovereignty, that is, due to the absence of absolute sovereignty. The Lord conceives this world as such—that it is perceivable by other subjects—and consequently it appears in that manner. By the individual soul (*jīva*), however, it is not so.
The point is that even though the universe is imagined [by the Lord], because it is perceived by other subjects, that aspect does not manifest due to a lack of autonomy. || 69 ||
To the extent that one abandons the contraction residing within oneself through practice by means of gems, mantras, and so forth, to that same extent does manifestation occur therein.

It has been stated that the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of living beings is incomplete, and therefore the [powers] conceived by them are non-common (*asādhāraṇya*). He says "through practice" (*abhyāsāt*) to show that to the extent that the contraction of that very sovereignty is removed by means, to that extent there is fullness.
Practice is the uninterrupted contemplation of the reality of the pure conscious self as "I. [The powers of] the jewel and the mantra...
In the case of what is well-known; [for example], the medicinal herb *ādinī*. By these [means] accomplished therein, which is conceived as being independent of that [external reality]. 70.
Behold, O Rāma, the magician who, through the application of no material cause, manifests the variegated world from mere volition alone in every respect. (71)
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Behold!

The sense is that a magician, by means of perfected gems, mantras, and so forth, manifests the diverse world in the form of elephants, horses, and the like from all sides through mere volition, without depending on any material cause for the universe. Or alternatively:
The mental creation possesses a unique instability and a lack of causal efficiency;
because it differs from external creation, he states another example:
"But [external creation] is indeed common, stable, and capable of performing its own causal function."
And thus he should withdraw the world into his own self; in this way, it shines forth.

That which is capable of its own causal efficiency—such as a jar's capacity for fetching water and so forth—a magician creates such a world and then withdraws everything he created back into himself. In this same way, the world created by the Lord also appears. || 72 ||
Behold that creation of the yogi, which is enveloped in complete stability;
for the external creation of the yogi is manifested through its limited nature. (73)

Now, even so, considering that the creation of a magician lasts for an extremely short time and thus possesses a lack of similarity (*vaisādṛśya*), he says: "of the yogin. [This refers to] the creation of stars and so forth by a yogin such as Viśvāmitra, which is encompassed by complete stability in the form of lasting until the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*).
The meaning is "behold. Now, if it is asked: "Even so, why is the creation of the yogi not [manifested] within his own essential nature (svasvarūpa), just like the creation of the Lord (Īśvara)?

he says: "But as for the yogi... Because an ordinary yogi, in comparison to the Lord, possesses a limited essential nature due to being circumscribed, and because he occupies an external location and possesses limited power, [his creation is] external.

The meaning is that creation is manifested. It should be understood that a yogin who has attained full perfection is capable, without depending on external factors, of manifesting the entire variety of the universe within his own essential nature alone, just like Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others. || 73 ||
Because it is immeasurable, this creation exists indeed only within the Lord of Consciousness;
for this very reason, due to its non-difference from the nature of consciousness, it lacks reality.

He says that God is not like this because he is "immeasurable" (*amitatvāt*). For this very reason, precisely because [the world] is created within him, the manifestation of one thing within another is exactly like a reflection; for a reflection—[as the text in manuscript *k* notes, the phrase "is exactly like a reflection" does not appear in *g*]—is indeed comparable to a reflection.

Just as there is unreality apart from the nature of a mirror, he states that the world is also unreal because it is inseparable from the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*)—thus [he says] "the nature of consciousness" (*cidātmatva*). || 74 ||
Just as the world, which is a reflection, cannot exist without the nature of a mirror, so too it attains unreality through investigation, and not otherwise. (75)
The logical connection is that the world is unreal. "For this very reason" means: precisely because it has the nature of a reflection. "Not otherwise" means:
when an investigation is made showing that this world consists of reflections, it does not attain reality. || 75 ||
One should not abandon the truth that is one's own nature, but one should relinquish what is untrue;
O Bhārgava, behold this world, which is exceedingly fickle by its very nature. (76)

Having thus established the unreality [of the world] by way of its being a reflection, he states—in passing—the definition of the real and the unreal in order to declare that the world is unreal because it possesses the characteristics of the unreal. He says: "The real.

Its meaning is this: that which has an unchanging intrinsic nature (*avyabhicarita-svabhāva*) is real; anything else is unreal. This refers to the world perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is exceedingly fickle and momentary. || 76 ||
Everything appears everywhere as a distinction between the real and the unreal;
investigate that [reality], which is like the appearance of a reflection in a mirror. (77)
If it is asked, "How does this certainty arise? he says: "By means of investigation" (*satya*). "Everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*) means in all respects.
"Investigate that entire world. If it is asked, "How? he says: "Like the appearance of a reflection in a mirror.
This is because the reflection and the mirror appear as having respectively an indeterminate and a determinate form.
The intended meaning is: "Examine how the manifestation of the world and the conscious self (cidātman) may come to be. || 77 ||
For the mirror is indeed immovable, while the reflection therein is moving;
likewise, the world is moving, while consciousness—pervading all things—is immovable. (78)
He applies this very point to the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*) following an investigation of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), stating: "In the mirror.
As long as the mirror remains unaltered—that is, without abandoning its own nature—there is reality in the reflections;
however, at the time when the reflection of a jar is replaced by the reflection of a cloth and so forth, it is altered, having abandoned its own nature.

The meaning is that [consciousness] is real. As for the word "thus": because the world, such as pots and so forth, is mutually excluded from one another, whereas consciousness is not excluded anywhere, it should be understood that the world is unreal and consciousness is real.
He states the word "all" to show that the mobility of the world and the immobility of consciousness are known by everyone. || 78 ||
For this very reason, entities possess a nature that cannot withstand analysis;
for instance, the light of the sun is indeed the illuminator of objects. (79)
"For this very reason" means precisely because of their unreality. For that which is unreal—such as a mirage, a hair-tuft, or a water-bubble—is indeed incapable of withstanding analysis.
The point is that when subjected to analysis, it would not be determined to be "this is such-and-such.
He establishes this very incapacity for analysis [with the verse]: "For in the case of entities... (79).
For those blind during the day, such as owls and others, the opposite is true: darkness acts like light.
Although these two—lightness and darkness—are distinct, their distinction is not clearly perceived [in this case]. (The sandhi in "vivikte'nayoḥ" is an archaic usage. 80.

The opposite is non-illuminating. It does not [exist] in that which is secluded when it has not attained seclusion. Of these two—the solar light and darkness—being an illuminator of objects is luminosity; being a non-illuminator is either the state of being opposed to light or the state of being darkness. And thus, because the solar light is an illuminator for humans and others, [it is luminous].

Just as [light] does not illuminate owls and the like, so too darkness does not illuminate humans and the like but does illuminate owls and the like; since it is impossible to distinguish which possesses the nature of illumination and which possesses the nature of obscurity, it is incapable of withstanding rational analysis.
The state of being. || 80 ||
In this way, poison may be lethal for one person while being non-toxic for another;
indeed, fear is observed to act as a deterrent even for humans and other beings. (81)

Thus, he states that for other things as well, there is no fixed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the word "thus": poison, such as *vatsanābha* and the like, may be fatal to humans and so forth, yet it is not poisonous and not fatal to the worms produced from it.
"Obstruction" (*pratighāta*) means the prevention of movement. (81)
For yogins, guhyakas, and others, it is characterized by non-obstruction;
as for time and space, they are vast as manifested by humans and other beings. (82)

Non-obstruction is its characteristic; the intended meaning is that it does not cause obstruction. He says "time" (kāla) [in verse 82] to show that the very same time and space which are perceived as long by humans and others are not long for gods and others.
That very same [object] appears in a reversed manner even to the gods and to yogis, just as distance is attributed to things like distant mountains when they appear in a mirror. (83)
If it is asked how there can be both distance and proximity for one and the same thing, he provides an illustration with the words "in a mirror."
In the same way, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) would not remain stable under investigation;
for indeed, nothing exists without the form of a substratum (*āśraya*). (84)

"Likewise" means: just as even a very long space seen in a mirror does not possess length because it is not distinct from the mirror, so too here, when the lack of luminosity and other such qualities of light and so forth appearing in consciousness are investigated, they do not remain stable; this is the meaning. Therefore—
The meaning is that because the world consists of reflections, it does not exist without the conscious self (cidātman) as its substratum. || 84 ||
That which appears as "it exists" is indeed the Great Goddess, Consciousness itself;
thus, you have correctly described the universe as having the single nature of Consciousness. (85)

Regarding the word "yad" (that which): just as the very nature of reflections appearing in a mirror is the mirror itself, so too, whatever appears as existing within the conscious self (*cidātman*) is nothing but consciousness, the Great Goddess (*maheśvarī*). Thus, in the manifestation of the variety consisting of reflections within herself, her own sovereignty alone is the cause, and not anything external as it is in the case of a mirror.

The term *bimba* (in manuscripts *k* and *kh*: *pratibimba*) is indicated [here]. Having established by means of this much of the text the point asked at the beginning of the chapter—namely, that there is no object of cognition (*caitya*; *k*, *kh*: *caitya*) other than consciousness—he concludes with "Thus" (*evam*). || 85 ||
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya, titled "The Exposition of the Reality of the World."]
[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the twelfth chapter:
Having thus heard the reality of the universe from the mouth of Dattātreya,
Bhārgava, his inner self still turbid with doubt, questioned him once more.

In this chapter, it is clearly stated through the narrative of Śaila that the appearance of the world as real occurs due to firm mental conditioning (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*) and the influence of the presiding deities (*adhipatis*).
"Thus, [the mind] is indeed consciousness alone"—[this refers to one] whose internal mind is turbid and defiled by doubt. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, indeed that which pertains to the world has been proclaimed by you as it was heard;
O Blessed One, just as you speak, so it is exactly thus and not otherwise.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "the nature of the world"; likewise, it is precisely of the nature of pure consciousness alone. || 2 ||
Nevertheless, from where does this [world] appear as always having truth as its essence?
Or from where have other intelligent people determined it to be true? (3)

Nevertheless, even though it is unreal, for what reason does it always appear as having the nature of reality? For while it is observed that unreal things such as a snake in a rope sometimes appear as unreal, how is it that this world always appears as having the nature of reality? This is the sense. [Objection: But surely this is like the blueness of the sky, perceived only by the deluded.
If it is argued that [the world] is known to be real, he says: "Or from what?"—that is, by others, namely other dualists who are intelligent and skilled in reasoning. (3)
Furthermore, what I have heard from you appears even more true to me; why is this?
O Lord, please tell me out of compassion how this delusion may be dispelled. (4)

Moreover, even though I have heard from you, my most trustworthy teacher, that this world is unreal along with its supporting arguments, why does it still appear to me as real? Explain this to me. || 4 ||
Thus questioned by the descendant of Bhṛgu, the noble-minded Dattātreya began to explain the root cause of the world's delusion regarding reality.

"Of great disposition" (*mahāśaya*) means one whose *āśaya*—that is, the mind (*citta*)—is "great," meaning its form as the conscious self (*cidātman*) is unlimited. The phrase "the root of that" refers to the delusion that the world is real; it is the cause of that [delusion]. || 5 ||
Listen, O Rāma, this is the eternal root of the world’s delusion:
that very firm conviction which is preceded by ignorance regarding reality. (6)

This is what will be explained hereafter. It is eternal (*sanātana*), meaning beginningless. He states this very point: "the object" (*vastu*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding an object is its apprehension as it is not; preceded by this, it is the firm mental cultivation (*dṛḍhabhāvana*) of an object in a form other than its true nature.
Firmness in such cultivation consists in being possessed of conviction (*śraddhāvat*). That [is ignorance].
The cause of the aforementioned delusion. || 6 ||
Behold how, through lack of discernment, one conceives the notion of "self" in the body;
where are the flesh, blood, and bones, and where is the exceedingly pure Self? (7)
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "In that regard," etc.

Without knowing the Self as having the nature of undivided consciousness, but knowing it incorrectly as being limited—[the phrase] "due to the firm conviction that the body is the Self" is to be supplied. [The term] "the notion of one's own Self" refers to [the notion] that "the body is the Self."
[He asks: "Why is the body not the self? [The author] says: "Where? It is exceedingly pure and has consciousness as its sole essence. (7)
Through the firmness of his meditation alone, the conscious self became embodied;
even though the Self in its nature as consciousness was known, delusion regarding the body persisted once more.
The firm conviction that the body is the self arises from the intense habitual cultivation of the notion of "self" with respect to the body.

Thus, even when it has been known through both reasoning and direct experience that the self is of the nature of consciousness and not the body, delusion occurs once again solely because of such habitual cultivation. (8)
In this very way, through meditative cultivation, the world indeed appears as true;
yet by cultivating it as contrary [to its nature], one may turn back firm delusion.

"Even so" means: just like the notion of a self [arises] through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the body, which is not the self. Through the cultivation of its firm reality, the world appears as real even though it has been correctly known to be unreal.
If it is objected that, this being the case, the notion of reality in the world would be unavoidable, he says "the opposite" to refute this.
One should constantly and firmly contemplate that this world is unreal; by doing so, one may turn back the delusion of its reality.
In whatever way one contemplates this world, for him it becomes exactly so. Behold how, through the concentrations and meditations of yogis, there occurs a correspondence with that very form. (10)

If it is asked, "How is it so?", he says, "In this very way, through the power of cultivation" (*bhāvanāsāmarthya*). If it is asked, "Where is this seen?", he says, "Of yogins. Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) are specific stages in the ripening of cultivation. The plural number is intended to refer to the internal subdivisions of concentration and the others.
The conformity of the world to that form, which is the attainment of accordance with one's cultivation. || 10 ||
In this regard, I shall relate to you a most wonderful ancient account (which is not subject to rebirth).
There is a supremely holy city named Sundara in Vaṅga. || 11 ||

In this regard, concerning the attainment of the world's conformity to its mental cultivation, I shall proceed—that is, I shall begin—to describe that which is supremely purifying and serves as a sacred ford. 11.
There dwelt a wise king renowned as Suṣeṇa;
his younger brother was Mahāsena, who was always devoted to his welfare.
The younger one is the youngest; he is a doer of what is pleasing to his brother. || 12 ||
The king, honored by all, ruled his kingdom according to dharma;
once, he worshipped the god Maheśvara with horse sacrifices.
There, all the princes, possessed of great strength and prowess, followed the sacrificial horse with a vast army. || 14 ||
At that sacrifice, they followed the horse during its ritual roaming.
Having conquered by force all the powerful obstructors of the horse, the king’s sons followed the steed and went to the bank of the Airāvatī river. || 15 ||
The obstructing enemies; the river Airāvatī; behind every horse, on the back of each horse. || 15 ||
There they saw the royal sage named Taṅgaṇa, a treasure-house of asceticism;
disregarding him due to their arrogance, they passed by him and went on.
There, on the bank of the Airāvatī; "in a manner of contempt" means without approaching [him] preceded by salutations and so forth. Those princes. || 16 ||
Seeing that, the son of the Taṅgaṇa, filled with rage at the contempt shown toward his father, seized that sacrificial horse while reviling the prince. (17)
Then those princes besieged him from all sides;
at that moment, the son of Taṅgaṇa also [seized] a boulder standing before him.
That son of the sage. || 18 ||
He entered, taking the horse while the princes were looking on;
seeing him with the horse hidden within the rock, the young princes [were amazed]. (19)
That son of the sage. || 19 ||
He shattered that mountain crag with various weapons individually;
from that pulverized crag, he emerged surrounded by a vast army.
By means of various [means], both superior and inferior; from that which is pulverized, from the pulverized portion. || 20 ||
Having emerged, the son of Taṅgaṇa conquered them in battle in an instant;
having slaughtered the army of Suṣeṇa, he captured the princes.
Those princes. || 21 ||
The one born of the Taṅgaṇas entered once more into the Gaṇḍaśaila cave;
then the remaining soldiers of the army went and reported this to the king.
Having gone to Sundarapura. || 22 ||
Upon the seizing of the princes along with their horses at Gaṇḍaśailaka,
Suṣeṇa was greatly amazed and spoke to his younger brother.
Having heard that, he was struck with wonder.
"O child, go quickly to that region where the sage Taṅgaṇa dwells;
those ascetics possess inconceivable power and are invincible by gods or men."
Since they are invincible, therefore, having propitiated them, it is the time for the horse sacrifice. || 24 ||
Having propitiated him and obtained the horse of the son, return quickly;
let not this season of spring, esteemed for sacrifices, pass away.
One should never harbor pride toward ascetics;
for when enraged, ascetics can indeed reduce the worlds to ashes in an instant. (26)
"Therefore, becoming intent on propitiating [him], accomplish your own purpose.
Having been thus instructed, Mahāsena quickly went to that place. (27)
The liberation of his own horse and others; he reached that region by means of the Taṅgaṇa river. || 27 ||
There he saw him, firm in his concentrated mind,
having attained the state of being like wood or a wall, with his senses, mind, and intellect stilled.
One by whom the mind has been firmly and correctly established—that is, fixed—within one's own self with unwavering stability;

for this very reason, it should be understood that the absence of physical restlessness is indicated by the words "like a piece of wood" and so forth, while the absence of restlessness in both the external and internal organs is indicated by the words "tranquil" and so forth. || 28 ||
Having prostrated like a staff before him who is absorbed in the contemplation of his own self within the ocean of the non-conceptual state, he then joined his palms in reverence.

The state of non-conceptualization is that from which the state of conceptualization—which consists of discernment through the forms of objects—has departed. Because that consciousness is undivided, it has the nature of the ocean; [the subject] is one in whom the manifestation of the self as "I," which is its own internal contemplation, remains deeply dissolved and abides in a subtle state therein.

It should be understood that even for one whose nature is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), there is an acceptance of subtle self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśana*) in accordance with the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Having thus bowed to that host [of deities], || 29 ||
Mahāsena praised the lord of sages with various hymns;
indeed, as he was thus offering praise, three days passed away.
Then his son, satisfied by the praise of his father, arrived;
he spoke to Mahāsena: "O King, I am pleased with your praise."
Then, on the fourth day. || 31 ||
"Tell me what you desire; I shall accomplish it without delay.
O great sage, I am the son of this lord, the great ascetic Taṅgaṇa."
"O lord of the earth, listen: this is not the time for speaking with my father;
he will be composed in mind only after twelve years have passed. (33)
The syntactical connection is that one should rise immediately thereafter. || 33 ||
He should arise from that meditative absorption; five years have passed there, and seven remain—such indeed is his ancient vow.
*Samaya* means a convention, that is to say, a resolve; [this refers to] "of this father of mine. || 34 ||
Tell me that which you desire; I shall do it for you.
Do not consider me a mere child, but know me as an ascetic equal to a father.
Therefore, for that reason, I shall do whatever you desire; O child, do not consider me to be incapable in this matter. || 35 ||
"Indeed, nothing in this world is impossible for ascetic yogins.
Having heard these words spoken by the young sage, the exceedingly intelligent Mahāsena [replied]. (36)
"Extremely intelligent" means that he knows the instability of children; this is the intended sense. || 36 ||
Having bowed to that son of the Taṅgaṇa with palms joined in reverence, he said to him:
"O son of a sage, if you truly do what is pleasing to me today... (37)
Today, I truly desire a brief conversation with your father, who has emerged from his meditative absorption; this is my most earnest wish. (38)
The word beginning with "pitur" ending in the genitive case is to be transformed into the instrumental case, because of its connection with the word "saha" (meaning:
because of its connection with the word "saha" situated in the second half of the verse). || 38 ||
"If I am worthy of your compassion, accomplish this quickly.
Having heard these words of the king, the son of the ascetic spoke again:
"O King, this desire of yours is indeed impossible to accomplish in every respect;
nevertheless, how could I fail to act otherwise after having given you my promise? (40)
The connection is: "How shall I speak? || 40 ||
I shall say something more; wait for it as you are entreated.
Behold for just a moment my power born of yoga.
Today this teacher of mine is established in the supremely pure state of peace;
who indeed could awaken him even by external efforts? (42)
In the state of peace, which is of a non-conceptual nature. || 42 ||
"Let me see; I shall awaken him by means of subtle yogic technique.
Having said this, she then entered [his body] and fully withdrew her senses.
If it is argued, "If this is entirely impossible, how will you enlighten him?", he says: "By means of subtle [yoga].

The sense is that for one like me, who knows the methods of subtle yoga, nothing is impossible. "Having entered" means having sat down. "Adequately" (alam) means having completely withdrawn and restrained the senses. || 43 ||
Having properly joined the apāna with the prāṇa and departed by means of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa),
he quickly entered his father's body, whose mind had already dissolved [into the Supreme].

Having thoroughly joined— that is, unified— the *prāṇa*, which is the internal air exiting outward, with the *apāna*, which is the external air entering inward; having restrained the *apāna* and, immediately after the complete formation of the *prāṇa* wind, having performed the external *kumbhaka* (retention).
The state [is as follows]: the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) whose nature is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). It has departed from the body in that form.
At the death of that father, the internal organ—which consists of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—dissolves and departs along with the vital breath; at that time, [it is] of the internal organ...

Precisely because of its state of dissolution (*līnatva*), it knows nothing at all. However, in the case of entering another's body (*parakāyapraveśa*), there is no dissolution of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); rather, through the perfection of the practice of external *kumbhaka*, one restrains the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by one's own will, and while remaining fully aware of the departure of the internal organ along with that [breath] and so forth, [one enters].
It should be understood that it goes out. || 44 ||
Having drawn him out, he awakened him and quickly departed;
just as the sage was about to enter his own body, he awoke.

Having withdrawn the mind—which had dissolved and been restrained within the father—he awakened him. For the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), dissolution (*laya*) is the attainment of the state of being composed of *tamas*; awakening (*prabodha*) is the attainment of the state of being composed of *rajas*;
and restraint (*nirodha*) is the attainment of the state of being composed of *sattva*—thus [it is] in the states of deep sleep, waking, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

The three states (daśās) are to be known. Although it is impossible to attract the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) because it is beyond the senses, nevertheless, it should be understood that for yogis, there is knowledge of what is beyond the senses through the power of yoga.
He has emerged from the body of his father; he is that Gaṇa. 45.
He then beheld the king standing before him, bowing and offering praise;
reflecting, "What is this?", he understood everything through his yogic vision.
All the activities of sons and others. || 46 ||
With a serene mind and a perfectly tranquil intellect, he addressed his son and said:
"My child, you must not act in this way; for anger is the enemy of asceticism. (47)

"Of serene mind" means that because his intellect is tranquil, he harbors no anger toward the king or his son; such was the state of mind regarding the seizure of the horse and so forth due to his lack of wrath. || 47 ||
For when the world is protected by the king, asceticism flourishes without obstacle;
the performance of acts that obstruct sacrifice is the very nature of the Daityas, never that of a sage. (48)

"The king is our benefactor; by harming him, we would be ungrateful," he says with the words "by the king. He further states with the word "sacrifice" that it is improper to create an obstacle to a sacrifice, even one performed by someone who has not been a benefactor. || 48 ||
"O Sumanas, quickly give the horse and even the princes to him;
let him depart at once so that there may be no lapse in the time for the sacrifice. (49)
"Sumanā" means having abandoned anger; this is the king's brother. 49.
Thus addressed, he entered Gaṇḍaśaila and, in a mere moment,
freed from his anger, affectionately gave the princes along with their horses to him.
He is the son of the sage; to that Mahāsena. 50.
Then, having sent his brothers' sons along with their horses toward the city,
Mahāsena, filled with great wonder, bowed down to that Taṅgaṇa.
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence and having propitiated the bull among sages, he asked:
"O Blessed One, I desire to know [the fate] of my brothers, the delighters of their kin. (52)
"Explain how they are situated within the interior of the Gaṇḍaśaila mountain.
Thus questioned by the king, the Taṅgaṇa then spoke to the monarch.
How so? The meaning is: because of the solidity of the boulder. || 53 ||
Listen, O King, I shall tell you: in former times I was a lord of the earth, and indeed for a long duration I ruled the world encircled by the ocean. (54)
Then, by the grace of Mahādeva, having understood Citīmadhīśvarī and reflecting upon Tripura as a world-abode devoid of essence, he [proceeded]. (55)

The consciousness whose nature is the Self; the configuration, that is, the state of existence, of the world which is the object of perception. "Tasteless" (nīrasam) means that, by virtue of being a reflection within consciousness, it has become devoid of substantial reality (nistattvabhūta). || 55 ||
Then, weary of the journey through this world, I renounced the kingdom among my sons and entered this forest; my virtuous wife followed me.
