He became disillusioned and conceived the thought that he had had enough of worldly affairs and social conduct.
As I was performing these austerities, billions of years passed by today;
even my wife has attained supreme perfection through her service to me.
Supreme perfection, which is liberation. || 57 ||

Then, at one time, because of the weight of my destined future, my beloved wife, though virtuous, became afflicted in her mind by desire while she was in a state of meditative concentration. Thus she was. (58)
Because of the weight of the object to be realized, and because that which is destined to come to pass cannot be averted;
the sense is that the mind, though restrained within meditative absorption (*samādhi*), has been aroused by its own inherent power (*kāmakāra*). || 58 ||
Seeing me established in meditative absorption with a steady inner self, she who desired pleasure, unable to endure the impulse of passion, cultivated her love for me.
That which has a long interval between its occurrences cannot be awakened instantaneously; [the yogin] cultivated the passion (rati) produced by me.
Having attained union with me through intense meditation,
she conceived a child and gave birth to this son who now stands before you.
Having placed her son on my lap and awakened me from my meditative absorption,
she dissolved her body into the elements and attained the state of the supreme ether.
Thus, having been struck by desire and having become weary even of her own body, she abandoned it; so he says: "Her son," etc.
Having made [him] her own (sātkṛtya), that is, having united him with herself. "The supreme void" (paravyoma) refers to the Supreme Brahman. || 61 ||
Then, seeing him on my lap and perceiving his supreme state, my mind was overcome with compassion; thus, he was raised by me.
This is the son of that wife. || 62 ||
Having once heard from me the account of how he formerly ruled the kingdom,
he became desirous of governing the realm and subsequently petitioned me.
"This is my son; [the image] was made by me. || 63 ||
Then, having attained supreme yogic power through my instruction,
he fashioned this world within the great stone by means of the yoga of meditative cultivation.
Yogic power (yogarddhi) is the sovereignty of yoga (yogaiśvarya). While this [power] stands before one... || 64 ||
This son of yours constantly rules the earth encircled by the ocean;
for those horses belonging to that king's world which were seized as his daughters have indeed been released. (65)
"Thus has this confinement at Gaṇḍaśaila been fully explained to you.
Having heard these words of the sage, the king questioned him further.
I have indeed heard this which you have spoken, which is most wonderful and supreme;
I desire to see that world—out of compassion, please show it to me. (67)
Thus entreated by the king, the sage commanded his son:
"My child, show him your entire world exactly as he desires."
Having spoken thus, Taṅgaṇa again entered into meditative absorption;
then the son of Taṅgaṇa approached that king and departed. (69)
Concentration is meditative absorption. || 69 ||
Then the young sage entered toward Gaṇḍaśaila;
however, O King, he was unable to enter while calling out to the son of the sage.
He entered Gaṇḍaśaila; the meaning is that he was calling out to the king, who was the one who had called the son of the sage. || 70 ||
Remaining within the boulder, he also challenged the king;
then, emerging once more, the son of the sage spoke to the monarch.
He too—meaning even that son of the sage—[did so]. || 71 ||
"O King, this world of yours is impossible for one who is not a yogi to enter;
due to a lack of yoga, this Gaṇḍaśaila has become a solid, impenetrable mass. (72)

Because it is impossible [otherwise], that is, without the accomplishment of the yoga of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāyoga*); "solid" means dense; "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*) means an obstacle to entry. || 72 ||
Out of respect for your father’s word, you must by all means be led away;
therefore, having deposited your body here in this hollow covered with grass, [depart]. (73)
Because it must necessarily be led [there], therefore: "in a hollow" means in a hole in the ground;
"covered with grass" is for the sake of protecting it from crows and other creatures that might harm the body. || 73 ||
"Having a body consisting of mind alone, enter the mountain with me.
Thus addressed, the king replied that he was unable to exit his body.
Upon exiting from the body. || 74 ||
"O Sage, instruct me on how I may cast off this body;
if I cast it off by force, I shall certainly meet my destruction in every way. (75)
By force, through the obstruction of breath, the tearing out of the tongue, and so forth; [he is] the obstructer. || 75 ||
To the king who was speaking thus, the son of the sage said with a laugh:
"Aha! You are ignorant of yoga; now, close your eyes. (76)
Having spoken thus, he entered while [the king] stood with eyes closed, and within half a moment,
having drawn out his body from that linga and cast that body into a pit, [he departed].
That royal body; that form of the king, his stout body. || 77 ||
Through the power of yoga, having settled upon the mountain together with the king,
he entered a state of deep sleep within a body produced by his own volition due to the physical frailty of his [former] body.
Due to the impairment of the gross body; [this occurs] when there is another body produced by one's own volition within the gross [state]. (78)
Having joined them together, he awakened him; then the king, having awakened, saw that his own [body] had been taken by the sage into the great sky. (79)

Having joined the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), one should proceed. Now, if it is asked how the princes and others were previously led while still possessed of their gross bodies (*sthūladeha*), the answer is as follows:

they were indeed led to the world of Śaila while in a state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*). For it is impossible for a non-yogi who is awake and possesses a natural gross body to behold that world. Thus it is said.
The intended meaning, established by the sense of the preceding and following passages, should be understood as "the efficacy of that yoga. || 79 ||
Beholding the vast, terrifying, and infinite sky above and all around him, he became afraid and said to the son of the sage: "O Sage, do not abandon me!"
On all sides, everywhere. || 80 ||
"Abandoned, I shall perish; I will fall down, left without refuge.
Seeing the king thus terrified, the son of the sage laughed and said: || 81 ||
"Abandon your fear, O King; do not let go. Behold this world situated within the mountain with complete fortitude. (82)
Listen; behold the world, the multitude of living beings. || 82 ||
Then, summoning his courage, the king looked down;
far below was a cloud accompanied by stars, shrouded in blinding darkness.

Then, immediately after hearing the words of the sage: "the cloudless sky" refers to the atmosphere; "shrouded in blinding darkness" means that because there exists a layer of outermost darkness above the world of the stars—this is the intended meaning. || 83 ||
Having entered that region, he then looked even further below (the absence of the suffix *aṭ* and the transposition of words are Vedic archaisms);
having arrived there, he was rendered motionless by the vast orb of the moon.
That region was the region of the stars. Having arrived there, near the lunar orb, the king became numbed by the cold. || 84 ||
Protected by the son of the Sage, who was as cool as the orb of the moon, he then reached the world of the sun and was scorched by its rays. (85)
With his body cooled by the yoga of the Sage’s son,
he beheld the entire world as if it were a reflection of the heavenly realm.
It exists like a reflection. || 86 ||
Then, staying together with the sage on the peak of the Golden Mountain, the lord of the earth beheld everything shown by the sage. (87)
With auspicious eyes bestowed by the Sage for beholding distant regions,
he saw himself upon the mountain named Lokāloka, which illuminates the worlds.

For the purpose of beholding two regions separated by a great distance (or, according to manuscript *kh*, two very distant regions), he possesses auspicious vision, his eyes being unimpeded (or, according to manuscript *k*, his eyes having been taken away). || 88 ||
Beyond that, he saw a mass of darkness, within which was the golden earth, along with the seven oceans and the seven continents, filled with rivers and mountains. (89)
"Outside of that" means outside of Lokāloka; "inside" means inside of Lokāloka. || 89 ||
All the worlds as well, including Indra and the other foremost gods, the Daityas, humans, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Kimpuruṣas, and so forth. || 90 ||
There, in Satyaloka, upon the shining mountain in Vaikuṇṭha, he beheld his own self as the son of a sage, in the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva (or Vidhi).
Having divided himself and established himself for the sake of the creation and other processes of all the worlds,
he then assumed another form and beheld [the world] after dividing the earth.
In the division of the earth, that is, in the world of men (bhūrloka). || 92 ||
Intent on the governance of the earth, he established himself as a sovereign ruler;
thus, having witnessed the supreme yogic power of the sage’s son.
Yogarddhi is the sovereign power of yoga. || 93 ||
Mahāsena was struck with wonder, and then the son of the sage said:
"O King, while you were observing this world, time has passed by."
Then, after the manifestation of the heavenly world (svarloka). || 94 ||
Even here, a period of twelve arbudas constitutes a single day;
let us go to that external world where my father resides.
What is measured as twelve arbuda years in the external world is but a single day in this world. || 95 ||
Having spoken thus, he again soared into the sky along with that king;
as before, emerging from that boulder-like rock, he came outside.
By the king, the supporter of the earth. || 96 ||
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Observation of the World of Gaṇḍaśaila," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Then the thirteenth chapter:
When Mahāsena had departed from the mountain, the son of the sage again [addressed him].
Having rendered the subtle body (liṅgadeha), which consists of mere latent impressions (saṃskāra), unconscious; || 1 ||
In this chapter, it is established through verses that the state of existence is the same in both sleep and waking, and that the visible world is accomplished solely by mental conception.
Due to the absence of the gross senses and so forth, as in deep sleep, there is only the residual impression (saṃskāra).
Having taken it up and gone outside, he threw it into that body;
then he raised up that [being] who was perfectly joined with the aged body.
Having emerged from the mountain, [he saw] that king who had previously been placed within a hollow of grass in that small body. || 2 ||
Then Mahāsena, having risen and observed the external world—
its earth, people, trees, and even its newly formed streams and pools— [beheld it all].
The new ones that have undergone a change of state. || 3 ||
He became exceedingly astonished and questioned the son of the sage:
"O highly fortunate one, what world indeed has been shown to me? (4)

Thinking that this was another world, as if it were within a mountain (*śailāntara*—meaning "in the midst of a mountain"), he asks: "Which one? He possesses great fortune (*bhāga*), that is, the excellence of yoga. 4.
"Never before seen in this city, explain this wonder!
Thus questioned, the son of the sage spoke to Mahāsena.
Listen, O King: this world which was formerly inhabited by us has, over the course of a long time, undergone a transformation.
The single day that passed for us while we were in the world of Śaila became,
in this place, a period of twelve arbudas of years.
If it is asked, "From what [cause] did it undergo this transformation?", he says: "The mountain... (verse 7).
The world has passed beyond this and has gone to another state of form;
behold everywhere the different modes of conduct and even the various languages. (8)
Therefore, because a great deal of time has elapsed. || 8 ||
In this very way, the stability of people is broken by time;
thus have I seen the condition of the world divided in many ways.
Behold, this is my Lord, my father, whose mind is composed in meditation;
this is that very place where you previously praised my father to me.
Behold this great mountain, where my world was beheld;
thousands of the descendants of your brother’s lineage have passed beyond it.
That city of yours which formerly stood in the land of Vaṅga, known by the name Sundara,
has now become a forest pervaded by herds of wild beasts.
In that case, in that region. || 12 ||
Born in your brother’s lineage, he is known as Vīrabāhu;
indeed, the lord of Mālava resides in the city named Viśālā on the bank of the Kṣiprā river. (13)
A king named Suśarman, a descendant of yours, also appeared among the Drāvidas in the city called Vardhana,
on the bank of the river Tāmraparṇī.
In this manner, the stability of the world always revolves;
thus, in a short time, this world becomes new again. (15)
It revolves; that is, it attains another state of transformation. || 15 ||
Even from this, after a long time, mountains, rivers, lakes, and the earth undergo transformation; such indeed is the course of the world.
Even from this time, which consists of twelve arbudas, the mountains and peaks [will remain]. || 16 ||
Mountains will sink into lowlands, and lowlands will rise to great heights;
desert lands will become marshy, and mountains will consist of sand. (17)
He says this very thing: "mountains," etc. Mountains are exceedingly high peaks; marshlands are those abounding in water. || 17 ||
The earth may be hard, consisting mostly of stone, yet it may become exceedingly soft;
even soft ground may, in some places, become like rock. (18)
The saline earth is *ūṣarā*, while the excellent earth is *urvarā*; the saline earth has the form of *ūṣara*. The pebbles are *śarkarāḥ*, yet the pebbles are essentially composed of jewels.
Fertile land is that which abounds in crops. || 19 ||
The alkaline water, once sweet and delicious, has now turned bitter;
at times there is an abundance of men, and at times a multitude of beasts.
At times, the world is seen to abound with worms, insects, and the like;
thus, this world has transformed diversely due to the differences in time. (21)
"It becomes transformed," so says Śaunaka. || 21 ||
"Therefore, in former times, this world of ours existed in just such a state.
Having heard these words of the sage’s son, that lord of the earth—
Therefore, because it results in a different transformation, such [an action] is like the unseen force (*apūrva*). 22.
Mahāsena, overcome with extreme grief, fell into a swoon;
then, consoled by the son of the sage, the king regained his consciousness.
Overwhelmed by extreme grief, he lamented most piteously for his brother,
his brother’s sons, his wife, and even himself.
The connection is that [he regards] even his own sons and so forth as himself. || 24 ||
Remembering his sons and others individually, he lamented, overcome with extreme grief;
then, seeing him clearly grieving for his brothers and others out of delusion, [he spoke].
That king. || 25 ||
The son of the sage spoke these words, desiring to awaken the king:
"O King, you are surely wise; why indeed do you grieve?"
With the desire to awaken, that is, with the wish to cause [him] to understand. || 26 ||
For the wise never perform an action that is fruitless;
he who performs an action without having reflected upon its result is a fool. (27)

If it is asked, "Why do you ask what the fruit of grieving is?", he says: "The wise [do not grieve]. If it is argued that there might still be some fruit [to grieving], he says: "Without reflection. (27)
"You grieve for something real; tell me, for what purpose indeed is this grieving?
Being thus addressed, King Mahāsena, being exceedingly distressed, spoke to him [that]. (28)
Do you not see, O Great Sage, the cause of my grief? Why do you ask for the reason from one whose everything has been taken away?
Even when only one person is slain, there would be grief for the world in every way; how much more so now that total destruction is at hand? Why do you ask [this] again? (30)
Why do you ask me the cause of my grief when I have met with total destruction? 30.
Thus addressed, the son of the sage spoke again as if smiling:
"O King, tell me, is this your eternal family tradition? (31)
"This is what should be grieved over when one's own kin have perished"—this is the eternal, traditionally handed-down teaching. (31)
If one does not perform mourning, a great transgression will occur;
however, if it is mourned, that which was lost is indeed obtained once again.
"Since there would be sin (*pratyavāya*) from not performing one's family duties (*kuladharma*), why do you grieve for that which is lost?
O King, reflect with fortitude; what fruit could there be in grieving?
If one should grieve for kinsmen who have perished, then listen. (32–33)
If it is argued that what is lost cannot be recovered, yet lamentation is fruitful because it conforms to the conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭācāra*), he says:

"Reflect" (*vimṛśa*). The meaning is: reflect upon what fruit has been obtained by those who lament in the world, such that it might belong to me. If it is argued that there is no fruit [otherworldly], but rather it is merely a family custom (*kuladharma*), he says: "Listen" (*śṛṇu*).
Relatives of the past, beginning with our grandfathers, have indeed perished;
why was all of that not grieved over before, such that it must now be grieved for forever? (34)
The meaning of "at all times" (sarvadā) is that your lifespan would not even be equal to the grief caused by the death of your infinite kinsmen. || 34 ||
Now, as for those relatives—whose kinship is it, or from where does it come to you?
For even those who are the worms in the excrement of one's own parents are [your kin]. (35)

Those are the brothers and so forth. From what cause does that state of being a relative of yours arise? If you say, "The state of being a brother and so forth belongs to me because of dwelling in the same womb and other such reasons," he says: "The mother... (verse 35).
Innumerable are those born from one's own body and even those connected to the body;
why would they not be one's kinsmen, or for what reason have they not been mourned? (36)
O King, reflect: who indeed are you, and for whom do you grieve over those who have perished?
Are you the body, or are you distinct from the body, while the body is merely a composite form? (37)
If it is argued that "I am indeed the body," he says: "The body is of the nature of a composite. (37)
Destruction is said to occur through the destruction of the aggregate or of a part thereof; however, the destruction of a part of the body at every moment is well-established. (38)

If it is argued, "I grieve only for those kinsmen who consist of bodies that have perished, [and not for myself], since I am merely this body composed of an aggregate of matter," he says [in response]:
having raised the alternative, "Or is it said by you that [grief occurs] when only a portion of that [body] is destroyed? he states the refutation regarding the second case:
"at every moment" (pratikṣaṇam). || 38 ||
There is a constant depletion of urine, feces, phlegm, nails, hair, and so forth; yet, the destruction of the entire aggregate is not perceived by any means whatsoever. (39)

If it is asked, "Why is there destruction at every moment? he says: "In the excrement," etc. Excrement is feces. Since a continuous decay is observed, therefore destruction at every moment is established. He refutes the first position [the view that the body is eternal] with:
"Your brother and so forth would clearly be a part of your body in the earth and other elements."
In the end, there remains only the indestructible space of the body.

If one asks "Why?", he says: "Of the brother and so forth. It is clearly established by universal experience that there must indeed be a portion of the earth and other elements constituting the body. If it is argued that the portion of the earth and so forth belonging to the body would simply perish, he says:
"In the end. Even if one accepts the destruction of the earth and other elements that constitute the body, in the final analysis...
The meaning is that, in the end, the destruction of the indestructible, solitary, and pure ether is difficult to establish.
"You are not the body, but rather the embodied one; yet you say, 'This is my body. Just as one says, 'My garment,' so too is that body [distinct from you]; tell me, how can you be it? (41)

And yet, this great delusion of yours is as follows; thus he says: "But you [are not]. The meaning is that [the self] related to the body is indeed other than the body. If one asks why, he says: "My body. Because you speak of "my body. If one asks what follows from speaking of "my body," he says: "Just as," namely, "my garment," and so forth.

Just as you do not exist as the cloth and other objects that are the referents of my cognition, so too you do not exist as the earth which is the referent of my cognition. This being the case, how could that body be you? Such is the meaning. 41.
If you are distinct from the body, what connection do you have with other bodies? Just as there is not even a trace of connection with brothers or clothes, so it is here. (42)
Having heard this, he says "If" in response to one who declares, "Truly, I am distinct from the body.

If it is asked, "Even though I am distinct from the body, why is there no connection with the bodies of my brothers and others? he replies, "Just as..."—meaning that just as you have no connection with the clothes of your brothers and others [so too with their bodies]. || 42 ||
Since there is no distinction [between them], when those bodies of theirs have perished, how can they grieve?
For [they think]: "This is my body, these are my senses, this is my life-breath, and this is my mind. (43)

"Because there is no distinction" means that since the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) regarding the body and clothing is equal, and since there is an absence of grief when the clothing of a brother or others is destroyed, how can there be sorrow at the destruction of the body, which is equivalent to clothing? Furthermore, he asks: for one who says "my body" and so forth, what is your nature, being distinct from the body and such?
"Maccharīram" means the senses (akṣāṇi). || 43 ||
"O King, tell me who you are as I ask you; what is your true nature?
Thus addressed, Mahāsena reflected for a moment.
Thus [ends the section beginning with] "Who are you? and so forth. || 44 ||
Then, unable to reach the end of the Sage’s question, he spoke most dejectedly:
"O Blessed One, I do not know who I am, even with my whole being. (45)

"Antam" means a final certainty. "Dīnataraḥ" (more wretched) means that, being distressed by the loss of his kinsmen and not recognizing his own self, he was as if he had reached the destruction of his very soul; thus he became more wretched. The syntactical connection is: "Then he said. "Even though I am intent on inquiry with my whole being, I do not know [the answer]. (45)
But by my very nature I am sorrowful, and I do not know the cause thereof; I have come to you for refuge in my wretchedness—O Blessed One, tell me what this is!

Not knowing even the cause for his grieving, he says: "By nature. The sense is that just as hunger, thirst, and so forth have no visible cause, so too is my grief. Having lost my kinsman, I am for the most part ruined in spirit; wretched, I have sought refuge in you. Therefore, what is this grief and the rest?
Tell me: is it with a cause, or is it without a cause? || 46 ||
Everyone grieves when any kinsman has died;
yet they do not recognize their own self, nor indeed do they grieve for another. 47.
He explains what was asked in general terms by the question "What is this?"—namely, that when even a single kinsman dies, everyone grieves; the remainder of the sense is: "Why is that so? || 47 ||
"Tell this clearly to me, your disciple, O Blessed One.
Thus questioned, the son of the Sage then spoke to Mahāsena: (48)
This refers to the cause of grieving for deceased relatives and so forth. "To you, my disciple. Now, after the question. || 48 ||
O King, listen: deluded by the illusion of the Great Goddess, people, failing to recognize their own true self, grieve in vain at all times. (49)

He says, "O King," indicating that they grieve because they do not know themselves, being deluded by the *māyā* of Tripura. Thus, it is stated that ignorance of the self (*ātmājñāna*) is the cause of grief, and that the cause of this ignorance of the self is precisely the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the Lord, the conscious Self, known as *māyā*. Even in the system of the Upaniṣads, there is fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

It should be understood that Māyā is the power of the Blessed One; because it is a portion of that [power], the ignorance (ajñāna) which veils the individual soul (jīva)—like cotton—is caused by it. || 49 ||
As long as the true reality of one's own self is not known, people indeed grieve; but having realized it, they never grieve again.

Having thus stated that ignorance is the cause of all misfortune, he says that the means of its removal is precisely the knowledge of the Self (ātmavijñāna), beginning with the words "yāvat" [verse 50]. "Sattattva" means one's own true nature (svarūpa). "Bhūyaḥ" means again.
The sense is that after such knowledge, they do not grieve as they did before. || 50 ||
Just as one whose mind is deluded by sleep grieves without recognizing it as a dream, so does a man deluded by the illusion arising from the spells of a magician. (51)

Regarding this, he states an illustration: "Just as... One who, not perceiving his own self as sleeping on a couch, laments in a dream after having had all his possessions stolen by thieves and the like encountered on some path within that dream; in the same way, one who is deluded by the illusion of a magician does not recognize his own self as being deluded.
The syntactical connection is that he grieves out of fear of the snake and so forth created by him. || 51 ||
Just as one grieves out of fear of a snake or similar creature imagined by the mind, so too does the deluded person, not knowing his own true nature, grieve because of illusion (māyā). 52.
"Mugdha" means deluded; "svam" means one's own self. || 52 ||

Just as one who has awakened from a dream, or one who understands the arrival of a magician's trick, does not grieve at anything nor for others who are joined with grief, but even laughs at them. (53)

He provides an illustration for the statement that "the knower has no sorrow" with the word "just as": Just as one who has awakened from a dream, perceiving himself seated upon his bed and considering the theft of all his possessions by thieves and others to be unreal, shakes off his grief and does not grieve again on account of it, even while seeing others grieve; so too [does the knower].
Even while laughing, he [thought]: "I have discovered that mantra of the magician which causes my delusion. (53)
Thus, those who know their own self and are liberated from māyā never grieve;
rather, they laugh at those like you who grieve, being deluded by māyā.
He applies this to the case under discussion with the words "in the same way" (evam). || 54 ||
Therefore, having realized that reality of the Self and having crossed over the difficult-to-traverse illusion,
O mighty-armed one, abandon the grief born of delusion through right discernment.

Therefore, for that reason; the meaning is: because sorrow has its root in ignorance. Having realized the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), having transcended—that is, crossed over—the insurmountable *māyā* which has transformed into the form of ignorance and is impossible for others to cross, and having emerged from the veil of *māyā* through the contemplation (*vimarśana*) and repeated inquiry (*anusandhāna*) into the existent reality of the Self.
Go there! || 55 ||
Thus addressed, Mahāsena spoke again to the Lord of Sages:
"O Blessed One, that illustration which was mentioned by you is indeed inconsistent."
The illustration consists of forms such as dreams, magical illusions, and so forth. || 56 ||
Whether dream-like or illusory, the world appears as essentially empty;
yet this waking world is real and the accomplisher of all purposes. (57)

He establishes this very inconsistency [with the words]: "In a dream," etc. A "magical" [object] is one produced by a magician, such as a thief, a snake, or the like. "Consisting of emptiness" means having the nature of non-existence. "Only" (*param*) means merely; the point is that its manifestation is a manifestation devoid of any real object. "This," etc.
The meaning is that it is established by the experience of all. Because it establishes all objects and is thus established by the experience of all, the meaning is that it is true. || 57 ||
"How can that which is uncontradicted and stable be equal to a dream?
Thus addressed, the highly intelligent son of the sage spoke again: (58)

Regarding the term "uncontradicted" (*abādhita*): the meaning is that the waking world-phenomenon (*jāgrat-prapañca*) is real because it is established by the experience of all people as being uncontradicted and stable due to its capacity to accomplish all purposes; whereas the dream-world-phenomenon (*svapna-prapañca*) and others are unreal because they are the opposite of this. || 58 ||
Listen, O King, to what you have said—that the illustration is inconsistent;
this is your second delusion, which is like that of one dreaming about a dream. (59)

"This" means the conclusion that the illustration is dissimilar. "The second" refers to the first delusion or error, which is the notion that the object of sight exists as something distinct from the seer and possesses a real nature;
therein, among those objects of sight, the idea that dream-objects and the like are unreal constitutes the second error. This occurs in the state of dreaming.
The meaning is that it is like the delusion of a snake in a rope for a person in a dream. || 59 ||
Even a dream-tree, at that time, does it not accomplish what is beneficial? Does it not remove the heat of travelers by providing shade? (60)

He provides an illustration, stating that the three reasons you have mentioned—such as the capacity to accomplish all purposes and so forth—apply to the dream state just as they do to the waking world: "In the dream... At that time, meaning during the dream; just as a tree in the waking state accomplishes a purpose, is uncontradicted, and is stable, so too is a tree in a dream.
The meaning is that at the time of sleep (or, according to k and kh, at dawn), it accomplishes all aims, being uncontradicted and stable. || 60 ||
Tell me, does one not satisfy the mortals and others seen in a dream with fruits and such?
Where in a dream is the dream-object sublated, and where is it perceived as stable (or rather, how could it be stable)?
If you say that everything is sublated during the waking state, listen:
is not the entire waking world also sublated during deep sleep? (62)

Regarding the phrase "the whole": if it is argued that the entire dream-tree and so forth are sublated because they do not appear during the waking state, [the author] says: the waking world is likewise indeed sublated because it does not appear during deep sleep.
If it is argued that it is not sublated because it persists even on the following day, [the author replies: so it is.
Tell me, where indeed does even a dream persist until the following day? (63)
Now, is it not the case that sublation (*bādha*) does not mean non-appearance, but rather the absence of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) in the form of a connection with a subsequent time? And thus: (Note:
In the place of the reading *...hetunā*, the reading *...anusandhānahetutā* appears. And so:

One might raise the objection (*āśaṅkate*)—expressed as "it is not sublated" (*na bādhitaḥ*)—on the grounds that there is continuity (*anuvṛtti*) of the waking world due to the cause of recognition such as "this is that very same [thing]" on the following day; thus, it is not sublated. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "If it is argued that, like a dream, it is not sublated."
He states that this is the same even for what occurs in a dream: "of what occurs in a dream," etc. (63).
If it is argued that continuity does not appear in a dream, O King, listen:
even in the waking state, where is there any appearance of continuity when there is no new manifestation?

If it is argued that the persistence of the dream-object is not experienced, he says (*jāgrati*) that this is the same even in the waking state. If one asks why this is so, he says (*navyāvabhāsakaḥ*) with the intention that it is because of impossibility; for in the waking state, a new object indeed manifests at every moment, and such being the case, how could persistence be possible?
The state of being. || 64 ||
If it is argued that although there is no appearance of continuity in the new [moment], it does appear elsewhere, listen:
likewise, even in a dream, continuity appears when there is a stable manifestation.

If it is argued that even though there is no persistence of new momentary entities such as actions and the like, the persistence of others such as the earth, mountains, and oceans is nonetheless unavoidable, [the author] replies that this is the same even in a dream, stating "likewise" (*tathā*). Regarding the phrase "in which there is a stable appearance" (*sthirabhāsane*): it refers to that in which the appearance (*bhāsana*) is stable, meaning it persists for a long duration such as years and so forth.
Regarding the dream: the point is that the persistence of sons, wife, and so forth within a long dream is established by the experience of everyone. || 65 ||
If it is argued that there is a persistence of falsehood therein [in the dream], then that is likewise the case even in the waking state.
Examine with a subtle intellect that object which exists established in the waking state. (66)

If it is argued that the appearance of persistence regarding things such as a son or a wife in a dream is of the nature of an error because they are unreal, [the author] says "jāgrati" (in the waking state), meaning that this is the same for you as well. The sense is that even in the waking state, the appearance of persistence is indeed of the nature of an error. How is this to be understood?
If it is asked: "What is meant by 'subtle'?"—the meaning is: by means of an intellect that is free from the conceit of stability inherited through a succession of the blind. || 66 ||
Since the body, trees, rivers, lamps, and so forth are distinguished by momentary change, how could their persistence possibly be of an unerring nature? (67)

"Deha" and so forth refers to the circle of clouds and the like. The meaning is: since the body and other such things are clearly known by everyone to be momentary, how could their persistence be anything but false? || 67 ||
Even for immovable things, there is no form that persists into a second moment,
as their very nature is constantly being broken apart by torrents of change.

If it is argued that even in the absence of persistence for the body and so forth, persistence might still be possible for mountains and the like, he says: "By waterfalls" (*nirjharaiḥ*). The meaning is that there is no form belonging to the second moment for mountains that are being split apart by incessant waterfalls. || 68 ||
Indeed, mountains are always being torn apart on all sides by mice, earthworms, boars, waterfalls, and other such creatures.
If it is objected that waterfalls do not possess the power to split mountains during the summer and other seasons, he says:
"By mice," and so forth. *Upadīkas* are those whose saliva causes wood and other materials to attain the state of earth (*mṛttikatvam*).
Specific types of worms (well-known in the vernacular by the name *dīmaka*), and so forth, including wild elephants and others. || 69 ||
Even mountains, oceans, and the earth itself are likewise subject to momentary change;
now I shall explain this to you, O King—behold it with a subtle intellect! (70)

"Bhūḥ" means the earth (*bhūmi*). Of those [worlds] such as the realm of the gods (*devaloka*) and others— which are considered primary among the mountains, oceans, and lands due to their stability— the ocean is so called because it is a confluence of river waters, and the land is so called because it is divided by rivers and the like.
Momentariness. To state in another way the similarity in continuity between the states of waking and dreaming, he says "Now" (atha); behold—that is, reflect upon it. || 70 ||
For the persistence of that which is limited is indeed the same in both the dream and waking states;
however, the persistence of that which is unlimited is extremely difficult to find in effects.
Regarding "delimited": Does the persistence of the waking state have a temporal limitation or not? In the first case, the delimited persistence of the dream-waking states is exactly the same.
In the second case, [the waking state] exists as an effect by virtue of its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*).
The meaning is that the uninterrupted persistence of the state of one who has attained perfection is indeed difficult to achieve. || 71 ||
If it is argued that persistence exists always by way of its causal form, then that causal form is indeed composed of earth and the other elements. (72)

Now, it might be argued that the proponent of the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*) accepts an absolute difference between the effect and its cause, and only in that case would there be room for the aforementioned defects. However, when relying upon the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), no defect whatsoever arises,
even though the waking state recedes in the form of an effect.
Anticipating the objection that [the world] persists by way of its causal form, he says "if it is argued thus" (*iti cet*) in order to provide a resolution.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of earth and so forth": the causal form consists of earth and so forth, because derived material things (*bhautika*) are effects of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Alternatively, it consists of earth and so forth.
The meaning is that the principle of Pradhāna is abundant with all effects, such as the earth and so forth; the sense is that every effect exists in its cause in a subtle form. || 72 ||
And that [nature] persists even in dreams, because earth and other elements indeed appear [then];
yet, the sublation of what belongs to a dream is experienced during the waking state. (73)

He says that even so, there is a similarity between dream-objects and [waking objects]: "And that" (tacceti). The meaning is: "in the form of a cause. He says "it is continuous" (anuvṛttam) because even in a dream, there is continuity since the form of the causes—earth and so forth—is manifest every day. Or else, [the word] "earth" (pṛthivī) [is used].

It is that which characterizes the effect. And thus, because the Pradhāna—the primordial cause of effects such as earth and so forth, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas) characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion—is manifest in a dream (variant k, gh:
"being manifest"), [the opponent objects]. He raises a further doubt in another manner with the word "atha" (now/if).
The meaning is that the sublation of dream-objects is experienced by everyone in the waking state. || 73 ||
If you argue that for no one anywhere does the sublation of the waking state ever appear, then listen; I shall explain: for sublation is indeed non-appearance. (74)
"‘It is not [the case] for one who is awake’ means that the sublation of the state of being awake does not manifest for any cognizer in any state whatsoever. He provides the resolution: "Listen.
Regarding "non-manifestation," the meaning is the absence of manifestation. Although in cases such as "this is silver," [the phrase] "this is not... [is used].

It should be understood that although the sublation (*bādha*) is said to be merely a contrary apprehension, such as "this is silver," nevertheless, because of the rule that only what is manifest is existent and the rule that non-manifestation entails non-existence, it is non-manifestation itself that is the cause of non-existence; thus it is called "sublation. || 74 ||
For even in deep sleep, the non-appearance of the entire world is experienced;
now, if you say that this is a sublation because it is a perception lacking valid means of knowledge, then listen.

Regarding the phrase "in deep sleep": the meaning is that the non-manifestation of the entire world without exception—which is experienced by everyone—is indeed a sublation (*bādha*). [Objection: But surely non-manifestation is not sublation, because there is the non-manifestation of a jar prior to the manifestation of that very jar.

Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of invalidity (*bādhatva*). However, he says "but it is something else" (*atheti*), meaning that the perception of non-validity (*apramāṇadarśana*) is what constitutes sublation (*bādha*).
The term *apramāṇa* is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary sense; thus, the meaning is the perception of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyadarśana*).
It is a matter of common experience for everyone that when one has awakened from a dream, there arises the cognition: "This was not valid. This very point...
The meaning is that no such sublation exists in the waking state. || 75 ||
There is indeed no measureless vision for those who are deluded like you;
however, for those who have realized the true nature of what is to be known, the measureless vision is manifest. (76)

For just as there is no perception of invalidity regarding dream-objects for the dreamer, so too there is no perception of invalidity regarding objects in the waking state for those who have not yet realized the true nature of the knowable; thus he says: "Invalidity... [referring to the verse beginning with] "In the waking state, there is the perception of invalidity. However, the supreme reality of the knowable is consciousness alone.

According to the principle that "the other [is the result]," for those who have realized the true nature of the knowable through knowledge, there is a clear perception of invalidity in the waking state. (76)
Therefore, this web of visible objects has a status identical to that of things seen in a dream;
even a long duration of time appears in a dream without any distinction [from a short one]. (77)

"Therefore" means that there is no disparity [between the two] because dream-objects possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth. If it is argued that waking objects appear for a long duration whereas dream objects do not, he says: "for a long duration.
"Without distinction" means that they appear without distinction, just as in the time of waking. || 77 ||
Therefore, an object that is uncontradicted, performs a causal function, and is stable is indeed [real]; for this reason, the state of waking is in every respect equal to the state of dreaming. (78)

"Therefore" means that, according to the direction already stated, there is an absence of inequality; the sense is that because [the dream state] possesses such qualities as being uncontradicted at its own time, the states of dreaming and waking are equal in every respect. || 78 ||
Just as the state of waking is clearly apprehended during the waking state, so too is the state of waking apprehended even in a dream. (79)

Anticipating the objection that even so there is a disparity—namely, that while for one who is awake the state of being awake appears [as such], the state of being awake does not appear for a dream—he offers a rebuttal with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). Now, in the waking state, there is a recollection of the dream and a recognition of the dream as being a dream; this is not the case in the dream state.

If it is argued that there is indeed a disparity because of the continuity of waking-state recollection (*anusandhāna*) and so forth in the dream state, that is true; for those who perceive only superficially, such a disparity certainly exists. However, for those of right vision (*samyagdarśin*), not even a trace of it remains. To explain: is there no recollection at all of the entire waking state during a dream, or is there some recollection of the waking state?

It is said that [the dream] does not exist; however, there is no fault in either case. For even while awake, the absence of any recollection of the entirety of the dream—or even the recollection of any part of it—is established by universal experience.
Nor should it be argued that there is some slight recollection of the dream while awake, whereas such is not the case for the dream itself; for [the nature of] recollection...

For memory is indeed such that there is the empirical occurrence of memories regarding waking activities, such as "On the previous day, I did not speak in this manner," and so forth. Likewise, in a dream, the entire process— including the apprehension of the waking state as being "waking"— such as "This was the waking state," remains entirely unimpeded.
It is to be known by those who investigate with subtlety. || 79 ||
This being so, O King, what distinction is there between dreaming and waking? Why, then, do you not grieve for your own kinsmen who appeared in your dream? (80)
Thus, when complete equality is established, therefore, because there is no distinction between dreaming and waking, reality in the world exists merely through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Even by the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one becomes empty and unimpeded. || 81 ||

If it is asked, "In that case, since there is such an equality between the dream and the waking states, why is it that for everyone there is the appearance of reality (*satyatā*) regarding the world?", he says: "Merely," and so forth. It is merely from the continuous mental cultivation (*anusandhāna*) of the thought "the world is real"; the meaning is that reality is based solely on that [cultivation]. He says "merely" to emphasize this.

The meaning is that it is "unreal" because it is preceded by a contrary mental impression (*viparītabhāvanā*). The words "is seen to remain" are to be supplied. For this very reason, if one were to cultivate the notion of emptiness, this very world would become empty, an object of the cognition of non-existence;
and like space, it would be unimpeded and non-obstructive. (81)
For when cultivation is stabilized by being free from the lack of immeasurability, it becomes identical with that very nature; this is the truth, O Lord of the Earth. (82)

Now, having raised the objection— "Why does the world, even though it is being meditated upon by me as emptiness, not attain the nature of emptiness?"— he states the manner in which meditation is perfected, in order to say that since that meditation is unperfected, the attainment of the nature of emptiness does not occur.
[The opponent claims: "There is no accomplishment [of the goal] through cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Cultivation is a continuous stream of cognitions in the form "this is such-and-such.
Its accomplishment consists precisely in its stability. Stability, moreover, is the absence of uprooting by means of the ascertainment that [the object] is not a valid cognition.
For example, there is the cultivation [arising from the error] "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl, [which is countered] by [the cognition] "this is not silver."

When [the object] is determined by knowledge to be invalid, it becomes uprooted—that is, its continuity is severed. This very cultivation (*bhāvanā*) remains unestablished. However, that which has been made stable through the absence of the determination of invalidity would be "unuprooted";
at that time, because it has been cultivated in the form of the object as its own nature, it would indeed become that very cultivation. It is cultivated...
The meaning is that one should fear what is common to all. Because it has been experienced by himself, he says: "This is true. 82.
As for the illustration here, this very world was seen by you;
having circumambulated this mountain, come, let us look at it now. 83.
An illustration (*nidarśana*) is an example (*udāharaṇa*). "By you" means by thee. [The Lord said: "You might have the apprehension that such a vast expanse could exist within this mountain;
therefore, let us go around this mountain and see," thus he says: "this" (*imam*). || 83 ||
Having spoken thus, he took the king by the hand and walked around;
having circumambulated the boulder-like rock, he met with the king once more.
He circumambulated the mountain; having circumambulated it together with the king, he then met him and returned to his own place. || 84 ||
Again the wise son of the sage spoke to Mahāsena:
"O King, this mountain has been seen; it is only a distance of one *gavyūti* on foot. (85)
A *medhāvin* is one who is highly skilled in awakening his disciples; a *gavyūti* is two *krośas*. 85.
Even while in the womb, this world was seen by you as vast and manifest;
is it waking, or is it a dream—whether real or of a false nature? (86)
"Manifest" means resembling the waking state. This appearance of my world—[whether it be] mountains and so forth—is either real or of a false nature; "one should discern" is the ellipsis. || 86 ||
That which is a single day in the world of Śaila is twelve arbudas of years here;
these have been experienced by you—discern between the true and the false. (87)
Because an infinite region is incompatible with a mountain measuring only one *pādagavyūti*, it is impossible to distinguish [the two] in this way;

likewise, because time is also incompatible [with such a small space], he says: "The world of mountains" (*śailaloka*). Outside, the region is only one *pādagavyūti* in extent, and the time is measured at twelve *arbudas*; internally, however, it is infinite.
Between these two, whose natures are mutually contradictory—the country consisting of a single day and time—discriminate between the real and the unreal. (87)
There can be no analytical distinction between this [world] and two different dreams;
therefore, know that this world has nothing more than mere imagination as its essence. (88)

If it is argued that what is internal is unreal because it contradicts the external, one could equally say that the external is also unreal because it contradicts the internal, since both appear equally; thus, no definitive conclusion can be reached. To illustrate this with an example, he says: "Discrimination," which has as its essence mere mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The meaning is that it has the nature of mere mental construction, like a dream, and nothing more than that. || 88 ||
Moreover, if this were not being cultivated [through meditation], it would dissolve in a mere moment;
therefore, O King, abandon grief by realizing that the world is like a dream. (89)
If this world of stone were not sustained by my creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), it would dissolve in a mere moment;
likewise, the external world would also dissolve if it were not sustained by Brahmā. This is the intended meaning.
Therefore, the world has nothing other than creative contemplation as its essence. || 89 ||
Having realized your own self to be composed of consciousness, like a dream, like a painted wall,
and like a reflection in a mirror, remain exactly as you are.

If one asks, "How may I abandon sorrow? he says: "Like those in a dream. For those things that appear in a dream are like a painting. It is undisputed that for a painting as it appears, there is no essential nature (*svarūpa*) existing apart from the wall, nor anything other than the unreal. And so, that which serves as the wall for the dream-painting—

Considering your own self to be of the nature of consciousness, like a reflection in a mirror, you remain as you are; just as you neither grieve nor rejoice when a kinsman seen in a dream perishes or when a kingdom is gained. || 90 ||
Understand the Self to be of the nature of consciousness, like a mirror for the variegated world of waking experience;
O Lord of the Earth, quickly become one whose heart is supremely gladdened. 91.

The syntactical connection is "understand it thus. Because there is absolute similarity between the dream state and the waking state, one should ascertain that waking states, like dream states, are merely reflections in the mirror of the conscious self (*cidātman*).

Having so ascertained, one remains untouched by the sorrows and other afflictions of the waking state, just as one is untouched by the sorrows and other afflictions of the dream state. For this very reason:

The meaning is that by the mere abandonment of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the bliss of the Self—which is manifested within the mind emptied of impressions—becomes [fully realized], just as the space manifested within a jar is revealed when the water has been removed. || 91 ||
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Vision of the World of the Mountain," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrītripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the fourteenth chapter:
Having heard the words of the sage and reflected upon them with a virtuous mind, and having realized that the stability of the world is like a dream, he quickly abandoned his grief. (1)
In this chapter, by means of excellent verses, he declares that the world consists of mere mental cultivation (bhāvanā),
as well as the attainment of that cultivation and the fundamental principles (tattvas) themselves, in due order.
Having heard that the world has as its essence nothing but mental conception, with a mind endowed with auspiciousness and right reasoning, [one should reflect]. || 1 ||
Taking heart and free from grief, he questioned the son of the sage once more:
"O son of the sage, O one of great intelligence, you are a seer of both the higher and the lower. (2)
Even when one knows the world's similarity to a dream, grief arises again due to the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); therefore, he says:
[The Lord] is the seer of the high and the low, the knower of that which is with senses and that which is beyond the senses. (2)
I consider that there is nothing even in the slightest degree unknown to you; therefore, please deign to explain to me that which I am about to ask. (3)
Therefore he says: "not from that. The construction is: "not known even in the slightest degree. || 3 ||
For you say that all this arises from mental cultivation; how then is it that when cultivated by me, nothing at all exists externally? (4)

The entire world—that world which, though repeatedly meditated upon by me as being composed of myself, remains external—could not possibly be common to all in every respect; how so? Such is the construction of the verse. || 4 ||
By you, through the perfection of meditative cultivation, the world of mountains was fashioned;
yet how could space and time be diverse simultaneously? (5)

The meaning is as follows: this is a detailed inquiry regarding the cause of establishment (*siddhihetu*), which was previously stated in brief in the preceding chapter—namely, that [the world] is imagined by you through the non-establishment of existence (*bhāvasiddhi*). What kind of thing is that "non-establishment of existence"?
Another question: "Even so" (*athāpi*)... "simultaneously" (*yugapat*) means at one and the same time, in one and the same place and time.
"How is it manifold?"—this is the meaning. || 5 ||
"Among those, which one of them is not afflicted?
Tell me that. Thus questioned, the son of the Sage began to speak.

In this regard, between the two things appearing as long and short, although it was stated in the previous chapter (*pūrvādhyāya*) that both are equal to a dream, nevertheless, being possessed by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of reality regarding the waking world, he asks again: "One or the other must be real. (6)
Volition is said to be creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), and it is twofold: accomplished (*siddhā*) and unaccomplished (*asiddhā*).

Accomplishment is the non-differentiation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); conceptual construction [arises] from being fixed upon a single object. (The reading *avikalpasut* is also explained in the commentary. || 7 ||

He states the subsequent [point] in sequence: "Conceptualization" (*saṅkalpa*). For conceptualization is indeed *bhāvanā* (cultivation). Conceptualization is a mental delineation such as "this is such-and-such. That is *bhāvanā*. If one asks, "What is this 'accomplishment' (*siddhi*) of it?
he says: "Accomplishment. This means that within the continuous stream of conceptualization "this is such-and-such," there is no [intermediate thought] "this is not such-and-such."

Non-mixture (*asambheda*) due to contradictory conceptualization is non-connection (*ayoga*). Thus, in order to bring about the non-mixture of conceptual constructions, he states the cause of conceptual construction: "But conceptual construction... The ellipsis is "would arise from being fixed upon one. The meaning is: because of grasping [something] as real through its being fixed upon one thing. This is the underlying point: in the external creation...

Because of the grasping at reality, there arises the conceptual construction of unreality regarding one's own mental creation; as long as there is such an intermingling of conceptual constructions, there is no accomplishment through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Alternatively, he says "but non-conceptual" (*avikalpas tu*) in order to state the means for the absence of conceptual construction. The meaning is that it is a mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) in which no conceptual construction exists.
"From one-pointedness": because the mind remains firmly fixed on a single object of volition alone;
the sense is that when the mind does not waver from the object of its volition, that volition becomes free of conceptual construction (*avikalpa*). || 7 ||
Behold, indeed, this world born through the contemplation of Brahman;
for it has been contemplated by all as having the nature of reality due to its extreme firmness.
And likewise, just as that which is cultivated through the meditative realization (*bhāvanā*) of a perfected being— whose nature consists of non-conceptual intentionality (*avikalpa-saṅkalpa*)—

appears as something common to all; so too, for anyone who, regarding that [appearance], becomes intent on non-conceptual intentionality by thinking "this is not real," that visible object appears to them in exactly that same way.

It would be so. For this very reason, he says "Brahman. This world was produced through the perfected contemplation (*siddhabhāvanā*) of Brahmā, the four-faced one. Because it has been contemplated as having the nature of reality (*satyarūpa*) by all subjects (*pramātṛ*) due to its extreme firmness resulting from practice over many births, it consequently appears as reality common to all; this is the implied meaning. || 8 ||

Likewise, in that which arises from one’s own conceptual construction, there is no cultivation of anything at all; this is merely a confusion of mental constructs, and therefore the cultivation [of such an object] is unestablished. (9)

Likewise, as in the creation of Brahmā, no one possesses the notion of reality regarding this world born of your own volition. There exists only this conceptual construction of yours—that "this is not real"—and the dissolution thereof. Therefore, your [notion of] mental cultivation is unestablished; for the establishment of mental cultivation would have to be manifoldly situated here.
Likewise, [he is so called] because of birth, a jewel, and medicinal herbs through their application. || 10 ||

If it is asked how the accomplishment of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) occurs for Brahmā and the others, he says: "Of meditative cultivation" [etc.]. In this world, O King, it may arise through austerity, the accomplishment of mantras, or a boon; that [accomplishment] of Brahmā is indeed by birth, while that of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas is by means of a jewel.

Regarding the question of whose realization through cultivation (*bhāvanāsiddhi*) is of what kind, he says: "By birth," etc. That realization through cultivation [is as follows]: "But for the gods, it arises from medicine; for yogins, from yoga; for ascetics, from austerity; and for those who employ mantras, from mantra. (12)
By means of medicine, that is, the nectar of immortality. || 12 ||
Indeed, through the attainment of a boon from the mouths of Viśvakarman, she became such that whatever was intended would manifest even when previous [intentions] were forgotten. (13)
[The deities] headed by Viśvakarman, beginning with Mayaprabhṛti (the *maya* is not present in *k*).
He explains the method for accomplishing through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) [with the words]: "that which is conceived" (*saṅkalpita*). This means "conception" (*saṅkalpana*).
It should be cultivated in such a way, it should be performed in such a way; the remainder is that it should become stable even when there is forgetting of what was previously [cultivated].

The initial undertaking of a resolve is such that, even when one forgets, "I have made this resolve in this way," the resolve becomes firm; such is the sense that one should form a resolve in this manner. || 13 ||
It remains stable as long as one does not recall the former [state];
in this very way, if the meditation on the non-conceptual is well-stabilized. (14)
Thus, he states that it is precisely the forgetting of what preceded that accomplishes the perfection of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), by saying "firmly" (*sthiram*).

Not remembering what came before, one should follow only the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*). The point is that through such long-term practice, as long as one does not remember what preceded [it]—[variant *gh*: "all"]—the meditative cultivation becomes firm. It is exactly thus.

The connection with the distant [conclusion] is as follows: if the cultivation of non-conceptuality—the cultivation undisturbed by contrary conceptualizations—is made firm solely through uninterrupted practice, then it will accomplish the great fruit. || 14 ||
As long as there is no piercing of conceptual construction through non-willing, that meditation is not perfected; only when it is perfected will it indeed bring about the great fruit.

Anticipating the objection, "For how long must cultivation be maintained with stability for it to be perfected? he says: "By means of non-desire. The meaning is that if there is no intermingling of conflicting conceptual constructions due to non-desire—that is, if [the mind] is well-stabilized—then at that time cultivation is perfected. As long as there is no intermingling of conceptual constructions by means of non-desire, [cultivation is not perfected].
To that extent, meditation is perfected and shall accomplish the great fruit—the universal cosmic egg and so forth;
however, because of your fragmentation by conceptual thought, your meditation has not been perfected.
Accomplish your meditation quickly if you desire to create.
But for you, because of the confusion of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not established; thus he says: "because of confusion" (verse 16).
Listen, O King, as I explain the twofold nature of place and time;
you are unacquainted with the worldly conventions of people, and therefore [this is so] for you. (17)
Having thus stated the answer to the first question, he states the answer to the second question: "Listen," etc. The connection is: "This appears wonderful to you. (17)
This wondrous thing indeed shines forth; listen, for I shall explain it to you correctly:
this nature of the world's existence is its manifestation in manifold forms. (18)
This is the simultaneous length and shortness of space and time. Here I state the cause:
it is the very nature of an entity to manifest through its own opposition. 18.
For the light of the sun alone, though single, exists in two ways:
as darkness for those blind by day, but as illumination for others. (19)

If it is asked, "How is this known to be so?", he cites certain such instances to state that it is "from repeated observation" (bhūyo-darśanāt): "only one," etc.; and he states the twofold nature [of the distinction] as "of those blind by day," etc. (verse 19).
Water obstructs the breath of humans, animals, and the like;
however, for fish and other such creatures, there is no obstruction of external breath while in water.
Of humans, cattle, and so forth, who are submerged within oneself; externally, in a place devoid of water. || 20 ||
Fire burns mortals and others, yet the partridge devours it;
fire is extinguished by water, yet it sometimes blazes within the water itself.
A partridge eats it, yet it does not burn him; [this occurs] in certain places such as the pits of the subterranean mare-fire (*vaḍavānala*). || 21 ||
Thus all things in the world exist in two forms;
likewise, whether they involve the functioning of sense organs or are otherwise devoid of sense organs. (22)

All things exist in a state of dual, contradictory forms. Among these, some are well-known, while others—such as the earth and so forth—are not well-known; yet they should be understood by the wise as being obstructive to mortals but non-obstructive to beings such as *piśācas*. Those possessing sense-faculties are directly perceptible.
Those things which are devoid of sense faculties and beyond perception possess mutually contradictory natures. || 22 ||
Indeed, by their very nature, they are contradictory by the hundreds and thousands; I shall state the proof for this—listen with a concentrated mind. (23)

He states that there are other entities as well—both those devoid of sense-faculties and those possessing them—which possess two contradictory natures (the word *dvi* is not present in the manuscript). He says: "By way of intrinsic nature. If it is asked how a single entity can have two contradictory forms, he begins to explain this with supporting arguments, starting with the words: "In this case" (verse 23).
For these visual objects are merely transformations of the eye;
apart from the visual [faculty], there is nothing visible anywhere in the external world.
He says that because entities do not exist externally, there is no contradiction—thus [he says] "these. (24)
Just as one whose eyes are afflicted by bile sees yellow externally, or as another person suffering from cataracts sees a single object as being double. (25)
Here is an illustration: "Just as," etc. A person with cataracts is one whose eyes are impaired by the defect of *timira*. || 25 ||
Thus, those with various defective eyes perceive the world in diverse ways.
There exists in the midst of the eastern ocean an island called Kāraṇḍaka. (26)

Thus, he states with examples how others also perceive the world in various ways due to the diversity of their defects of vision: "In that [Pūrvavideha] continent, people always perceive objects as red;
likewise, in the continent of Ramaṇaka, people always perceive them as such. (27)
They see all phenomena as red. || 27 ||
The entire mandala of phenomena is inverted, with above and below reversed;
likewise, in other continents, the mandala of phenomena is of various kinds.
"Upside down" means with the head downward and the feet upward, and so forth. || 28 ||
People indeed always see with the inherent nature of their eyes; however, if in some instance they perceive it otherwise, [it is an error]. (29)
He establishes that this is not a defect of their eyes, but rather their very nature, by saying "therein" (*tatra*). In those islands,

if the people see [the moon] as unred or non-inverted, then they must first restore their own eyes— by means of medicines, collyriums, and so forth— so that they are no longer defective, and then [the moon] will appear red and inverted just as before.
The meaning is "they see. || 29 ||
Indeed, they see with their eyes, aided by easily prepared medicine, exactly as before;
therefore, whatever is visible upon the surface of the earth is seen by the eye. (30)
To that extent, there would be a visual portion, as in the case of a yellow bile-colored eye;
likewise, for the olfactory and other sense organs, there are indeed portions consisting of odor and so forth. (31)

Just as the yellow color perceived by one with a bile-afflicted eye is itself a visual part, so too everything that is seen by a person's eye is nothing but a visual part. Having thus established that the object of the eye is a part of it, he extends this principle to the objects of the other sense organs as well: [The verse: "In the same way, the objects of the other senses are also parts of those [senses] themselves. (1.10ab) [The commentary: Just as the visual part is of the nature of the eye, so too the objects of the other senses are of the nature of those respective senses. Therefore, the objects of the senses are indeed parts of the senses themselves. Thus, the existence of the Self is established through the fact that the senses are instruments of perception. This is because an instrument cannot exist without an agent who employs it. Furthermore, since the senses are not self-aware, they must have another perceiver; therefore, the existence of the Self is proven. (1.10cd–11ab) [The commentary: It is understood that the senses are instruments because they are not self-luminous. "Thus" means: the sense that whatever is manifested by a particular sense organ possesses the nature of being a portion of that sense organ. || 31 ||
And those things belonging to the mind consist of mind alone; likewise, all that belongs to the world is [mind].
Even the sequence arises from the nature of the senses; therefore, there is nothing at all external.
(32) Thus, he states that even objects of the mind are portions of the mind: "And those things belonging to the mind... and so forth. And thus:

He states that because spatial sequence (*deśakrama*), temporal sequence (*kālakrama*), and sequential order of action (*kriyākrama*) are perceptible by the eye, they are aspects of space—saying, "sequence as well.
Sequence is the state of being situated in a prior-posterior relationship (*paurvāparyeṇāvasthitatvam*). Thus, spatial sequence is indeed direction (*dik*);
for instance, the conventional usage "Kāśī is east of Prayāga" refers precisely to such a sequence of the eastern [direction].

Thus, time is the sequence pertaining to action. It should be understood that for certain actions, it is precisely the sequence consisting of their state of being arranged in a temporal order (paurvāparya) that constitutes the object of the conventional usage of time, such as *ghaṭikā* and so forth. And thus, in whatever time, and in whatever manner, a place or a time [exists]...
Whether it appears as large or small, every such visual portion at that particular time is distinct;
thus, the point is that there is no fault of a single thing possessing two contradictory forms. || 32 ||
Listen, O King: that which appears in the world as "external" is the primordial ground of all worlds, like the wall upon which the picture of the universe is painted. (33)

Having thus established that the object of perception does not exist externally by means of the analogy of the yellow color and so forth appearing to those whose eyes are afflicted by bile (*pitta*) and other humors,
he now begins to prove that it does not exist even because of the impossibility of any portion of an external thing.

(-) "Listen," he says. Just as a wall is the support for a painting, the external object of the world is the first [requirement] because it serves as the substratum and the cause of the world-painting; this is the meaning. || 33 ||
Surely, the fixed point of departure (apādāna) for that external [action] must be stated; the body would be the point of departure, and nothing else is capable of being so. (34)

Regarding that aforementioned external external object, its fixed limit (*avadhi*), which serves as the ablative (*apādāna*), must be stated. Why? Because the ablative is required by the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*). Since it is impossible for a pot or other such things—even though they are external—to function as the ablative [in this context], the body itself must be the ablative.
He honors the body. || 34 ||
Furthermore, how could that [mountain] be the source (apādāna) for its appearance as being outside?
When it is said, "outside the mountain," the mountain itself would not be "outside. (35)
He states that even the body does not function as an *apādāna* (ablative point of departure), because it appears as being external; [this is expressed in the phrase] "of that too.
Here, the illustration is "from the mountain" (*parvatāt*). The meaning is that the mountain would not be external. || 35 ||
Just as a jar indeed appears outside, so too is the body;
yet it would not even be possible to say that it is "outside" the illuminator.

He states an illustration regarding the body being external [to the light]: "Just as" (*yathā*). Then, he raises the objection that the self (*ātman*) itself, which illuminates the interior of the body such as a jar, is the source (*apādāna*): "From the illuminator" (*bhāsakāt*).
The construction is to be understood as: "or rather, it should be stated in this way. (36)
There is no illumination for those things that have gone outside the light of a lamp or the sun; therefore, it is logical that the illuminator possesses an internal object of illumination. || 37 ||

Now, if the illuminator (*bhāsaka*) is the source (*apādāna*), then—just as there is no illumination for those situated in darkness outside the light of the sun—there would be no illumination at all for objects situated outside the illuminator; therefore, it must be admitted that the object of illumination (*bhāsya*) exists within the illuminator itself. And thus:
He states that the self, which illuminates those things situated outside, is not the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure), beginning with the words "dīpa" and so forth. 37.

But the body and so forth are not the illuminator, because they are themselves objects of illumination, like mountains and the like; for that which is an object of illumination in every respect is logically consistent [as being illuminated]. (38)

To this extent, it is established that since an external object cannot be identified as the source (*apādāna*), the appearance of external objects occurs within another illuminator— just like the appearance of the vast sky in a mirror. Now, because the object of illumination is of the same nature as the illuminator alone, one cannot say that the external object, which is the thing illuminated, has the illuminator as its source.

He analyzes the nature of the illuminator (*bhāsaka*) with the words "But the illuminator... [etc.]. Now, one might object: "Let it be that the body is both the illuminated (*bhāsya*) and the illuminator, on the basis of the experience 'I, who am gross, see'. To this he replies: "Not in every respect" (verse 38).
If that which illuminates were itself the object illuminated, there would be no finality for the illuminator;
moreover, it is not logical for something to be both the illuminator and the illuminated of itself. (39)
If it is asked, "What is the harm in the self being both the object of illumination and the illuminator?", [the response is:

if one and the same body were both the self-known (or self-awakened) object and its own knower, there would be a contradiction between the status of being an agent and that of being an object; whereas for another body, it would be the object of illumination.

If it is argued that [the self] is the illuminator, [we reply: since it is not established that what is itself being illuminated can be an illuminator, and because the bodies of illuminators would require another successive illuminator, there would be an infinite regress of illuminators which destroys the very root [of the argument]; thus he says: "Of the illuminator."
"It is not logical" means that it is because of the contradiction between being the agent and being the object; this is the remainder of the sense. || 39 ||
Therefore, it is the illuminator, pure, and having the singular nature of being the illuminator;
and that, in this world, is indeed of the nature of light, full, and consisting of a single essence.
Therefore, due to faults such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it is pure and non-manifest (*abhāsya*)—this is the meaning.
This very point is stated clearly as "having the single nature of being the illuminator" (*bhāsakaikasvarūpaka*). Now, one might object:
the illuminator possesses the activity of illumination, and activity is an impermanent property; thus, the state of being an illuminator...
If it is asked how [the Self] can have the single nature of being the illuminator given that it is delimited by time, he says:

"And that" (*tacceti*). The meaning is "the illuminator. Regarding the phrase "only of the nature of light" (*bhārūpameva hi*): unlike in the world, there is no distinction here between the agent and the action;
rather, the meaning is that the agent is of the very essence of the action. [This is] like the reflection in a mirror. Regarding the effect...

The intended meaning is that, because it is not distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), no action external to that nature is of any use. For this very reason, it is both full and of a single essence (*ekarasa*); "of a single essence" means that its self (*ātman*) is not mixed with any other entity. || 40 ||
By that [consciousness], space and time are pervaded; its fullness arises from its manifestation.
Since that which is non-existent has no manifestation, it is indeed of a single essence consisting of light.
By that which illuminates both the object (*bhāva*) and its form (*rūpa*). If one asks "Why?", he says: "Because of illumination.

The meaning is that because it illuminates everywhere, space and time are pervaded by it; for this very reason, it possesses fullness (*pūrṇatā*). For the illumination of the illuminator and the illuminated is not like that of a jar and a cloth, but rather like that of a mirror and its reflection. And thus, of the mirror...
The sense is that, just as the illuminator pervades its reflection, so too does it pervade the object of illumination.

Now, if it is asked why the non-difference of the object of illumination from the illuminator—based on the analogy of a reflection in a mirror—is postulated as something extraordinary and unworldly, he replies: "Because it is not of the nature of an object."
The meaning is: "of that which has not attained identity with the nature of light. Regarding the phrase "because of non-manifestation":

the meaning is that if the manifested object were not declared to be non-different from its illuminator, which is of the nature of light, then that object would not manifest at all.
