Therefore, the manifested object is indeed of the single essence of the nature of light. This is the intended sense here: if the manifested object...

If it has thus gone outside of the nature of light (*bhā-rūpa*), how is its manifestation possible? For manifestation is not a property of the object to be manifested (*bhāsya-dharma*) like blue and so forth; otherwise, it would follow that manifestation would occur at all times, and the conventional expression "it manifests to me" (*mama bhāsate*) would be untenable. Otherwise, there would even be the conventional expression "my blue. [Objection: But in the case of a jar and so forth...

Just as with sunlight, the manifestation of the object of illumination occurs through the incidence of another [light]; thus, the manifestation of the object of illumination is established by its connection with the manifestation of that other [light]. This might be so if there were a third relation between the object of illumination and the illuminator, similar to the conjunction between a jar and sunlight.

That very [connection] is not possible. For instance: is that connection of the nature of the object (*bhāsya*), or of the nature of the illuminator (*bhāsaka*), or of the nature of both, or of neither?
If it were of the nature of the object, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of another connection for its illumination.

If the illuminator were of the nature of illumination, then since it would consist of mere illumination, a distinction within the very nature of illumination (or *bhāsana*) is untenable, as has been demonstrated repeatedly; therefore, it is impossible for something to be related to itself. Nor can it be of both natures.

This is because there is a contradiction in a single entity possessing both forms—of being the manifestor (*bhāsana*) and the manifested (*bhāsya*)—due to their respective natures as consciousness (*cit*) and insentience (*jaḍa*).

Nor can it be of neither nature, for that would entail an abandonment of established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*); for that which is of neither nature is precisely the "ineffable" (*anirvacanīya*), and proponents of the theory of ineffability do not admit anything other than Brahman, whose nature is manifestation.

For they, accepting that the Brahman is full and that the appearance of the visible world is inexpressible, have indeed accepted that the visible world is like a reflection in a mirror; as they say: [##]

Thus, because it appears as if within [the Light] like a reflection in a mirror, it is established that this world also—like a reflection whose essence is of one flavor with the mirror—is of the nature of light alone, being of a single essence. || 41 ||

Whatever exists, whether internal or external, that is situated within the belly of the form of light—from that [light], it cannot be the apādāna (the point of departure), just as a mountain is not the point of departure for its own horn. || 42 ||

Regarding the term "end" (*anta*): whether it be an internal object or an external object, whatever it may be, because it is entirely contained within manifestation, its illuminator is the nature of the Self (*ātman*). This is just as a mountain is not the source (*apādāna*) for a particular peak situated within that mountain. || 42 ||
For such a nature of light, in which all conceptual proliferation has been swallowed up, shines by its own autonomy within itself, everywhere, and at all times. (43)

Thus, because the external objects that serve as the material cause for the variegated painting of the entire world are unestablished, [the world] is unestablished; just as there can be no painting when the wall is unestablished, so too, when the forms perceived in space and time are unestablished, it is like the forms of a snake, a stream of water, or holes in the ground appearing to one who has not recognized the rope.

Having established that the nature of light itself, which illuminates apertures and the like, consists of forms such as large and small spaces and durations of time, one now addresses the following doubt:
why should another manifestation—which appears within the sky as distinct entities—also not be a distinct object of illumination? Having raised this doubt:

He begins to pacify [the objection] with the words "of such a kind" (*evaṃvidham*). The meaning is that [the universe] remains having placed everything within its own belly. He states this very point with the words "devoured" (*grasta*) and "shines" (*bhāti*). It shines in this manner—being independent and not requiring anything else—at all places and at all times. || 43 ||
"This is declared to be the supreme consciousness, Tripurā, the Supreme Goddess;
those who know the Vedas call her Brahmā, and the best of Vaiṣṇavas call her Viṣṇu.
He states that this very [consciousness] is propounded as the primary principle in all the scriptures with the words "This... (etad).
This very form of light, the supreme consciousness, the unlimited power of consciousness, is called Tripurā Parameśvarī in the Tripure Śāstra. || 44 ||
Those supreme devotees of Śiva call him Śiva, and those devoted to Śakti call her Śakti;
if they were to speak of anything other than these forms, that would be insignificant. (45)

The Śāktas are those who are devoted to Śakti. If it is objected that the Vaiṣṇavas and others declare a form such as dark-blue like a cloud to be primary, he says: "This [is not so]. Apart from the nature of supreme consciousness (*paraciti*), if they were to declare anything else as primary, then that would be merely limited, being circumscribed by time and space.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that even by the name Tripurā and others, this very one must be declared as the primary [form]. || 45 ||
Pervaded by that power of consciousness (cicchakti), like a reflection in a mirror, its state of being an illuminator is produced by the object to be illuminated and does not exist inherently.

If it is objected that by the statement "having swallowed all phenomenal expansion," the pervasion of the world [by consciousness] would be like that of space itself, he says "no" by means of the word *tayā* (by that). Now, even if the entire world is non-different from its own essential nature, one might argue that the luminosity of consciousness (*cit*) must be a distinct attribute, just as blueness and so forth are distinct attributes of a jar and the like. And thus—
If it is argued that since the nature of light (bhārūpa) does not appear, it follows that its capacity to illuminate (bhāsakatva) also does not appear, he replies with the word "tasya" (of that).

This means "of the appearance. The point is that because that [appearance] is produced by the object of illumination (bhāsya), it is adventitious (aupādhika), like the redness of a hibiscus flower reflected in a crystal; therefore, even that [capacity to illuminate] is essentially nothing but a reflection. || 46 ||
But the commentary is submerged within the primary text, like a city in a mirror;
just as a city in a mirror does not exist apart from the mirror. (47)

Therefore, he says "but the object of manifestation" (*bhāsyaṃ tu*) to show that, like a city and so forth in a mirror, everything that is manifested is indeed submerged within the manifestation itself. He says "in the mirror" (*darpaṇe*) to show that, just as the city and other things appearing in a mirror are non-different from the mirror, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) appearing in consciousness is non-distinct from consciousness. || 47 ||
In the same way, the world shines within consciousness; it does not exist apart from it, just as [images] do not exist apart from a dense, uniform, and complete mirror-surface. (48)
Likewise, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the world appears in consciousness (*citi*) by way of being a reflection. Now, one might ask:

"Why this insistence that the appearance of the world in consciousness is exactly like a reflection in a mirror? Why is it not accepted as being like the appearance of the world in the sky? To this he says: "In the mirror... [and so on]. In its entirety...

[The mirror] is without holes, dense, with non-lax parts, uniform in form, and unmixed with other objects. For if it were perforated, an object situated behind it would appear; if its parts were lax, another object situated within the joints of the parts would appear;
and in a collection of objects, a variegated whole would appear. Such is the nature of the mirror.
The sense is that, because you are of such a nature, it is not possible for one who has been pierced by pride and the like to have an appearance there [of the truth]. || 48 ||
For just as a divided city is in no way possible, so too is it impossible in the case of the conscious self, which is full, perfectly dense, and of a single form. 49.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that just as [the reflection] is not logically tenable, so too one does not attain its production. Now, if it is argued that there is no specific distinction such that "there is no reflection in a mirror," but rather that the object itself is perceived by visual rays that are turned back after being obstructed by the mirror—[we reply: no, for this would also apply to objects obstructed by a wall.
Because that would entail the consequence of [the light] being grasped by the mouth. Nor should it be said that transparency is the determining factor for obstruction;

for, since obstruction is observed in the case of sunlight and the like by walls and other such objects, it is established that solidity alone is the regulating factor for obstruction, as seen even with a transparent mirror that is not permeated by taste.
Furthermore, because no obstruction is perceived, and because it is impossible for the hand placed at the side of a mirror to be grasped simultaneously with its reflection,
and because it is impossible for the face and other features of the reflection to have the mirror as their substrate or to appear facing [the observer]. (gh)
Nor is it possible for the appearance of an illusion— such as the reflection's dependence on the mirror in the face due to the defect of contact with the mirror by the visual rays,
or the appearance of duality in a hand placed at the side— to occur in a reflection [merely] through such a defect; rather,
it is only through a property of the mirror and so forth that serves as the cause that such a property [is perceived].
It must be stated that everything is consistent, including the fact that the mirror acts as the regulator for the obstruction of the visual rays; for,

rather than postulating that the visual rays in contact with the mirror manifest duality and the substratum-ness of the hand, face, and so forth [within the mirror] through the power of the mirror, it is more appropriate to postulate the reflection itself within the mirror.
Because this is logical; and in this way, it should be understood that even non-erroneous cognitions such as "this mirror is a likeness of the face" would be accounted for. || 49 ||
The world does not attain manifestation at all by its own nature, whereas space, being of the nature of vacuity, exists because it has the form of emptiness. (50)

The phrase "the world is distinct from this conscious self" and so forth [is raised]. He says "But space... because space is not like the conscious self; the word "but" (tu) serves to exclude similarity. [He asks] "Why? and answers: "That which has empty space as its essence. If one asks why, he says: [the following].
"Of the nature of emptiness" means because it is of the nature of non-existence. The intended meaning is that space is simply the absence of the four [elements], earth and so forth. || 50 ||
For how could consciousness—which is ever-present, non-empty in nature, and of a single flavor—ever tolerate duality in the world at any time or in any place? (51)

For this very reason, the dualistic world—which is distinct from oneself—is tolerated at all times and in all places within one's own body. But how could the conscious self (cidātman), being not of such a nature, tolerate duality within itself? To this he says: "Being" (satī).
Precisely because it is of the nature of existence (sadrūpa), it is of the nature of a non-empty self; its state of being of a single flavor (ekarasa) is its state of dense essential nature. || 51 ||
One should easily withstand even a second [reflection], like the nature of a mirror;
therefore, consciousness is like a mirror due to the majesty of the fullness of its sovereignty.

Just as a mirror is non-empty by virtue of its existence, is of a single essence due to its firm parts, and does not tolerate a second [reflection] within itself, so too is consciousness (*cit*). Thus he says: "Like a mirror. Therefore, this means that because a second thing is impossible within the conscious self, consciousness is like a mirror.
The connection [of the words] is: "By the power of the majesty of its own sovereignty, it should cause [the world] to appear within itself, which is non-dual. || 52 ||
In its own non-dual form, it illuminates all that is moving and unmoving— a second [reality] devoid of causes and material substrata, yet most wonderfully variegated.

It has been stated that, unlike a mirror, there is no dependence on an external object (*bimba*); rather, it manifests [the world] through the majesty of the abundance of its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*).

Sovereignty is the state of being independent of anything else. Its "abundance" (*bhara*) is its preponderance; this refers to its unlimited sovereignty. Through the "majesty" (*vaibhava*), that is, the greatness, of that [sovereignty], [it manifests] within its own nature, which is non-dual, undivided, and of the single essence of consciousness.

In its own nature, which is non-dual, it causes all that is moving and unmoving—devoid of and devoid from both efficient and material causes—to appear as a highly variegated display of mutually distinct forms. || 53 ||
Just as in a mirror, although many forms appear, their oneness shines forth clearly, undifferentiated and unimpaired. (54)

Thus, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as), stating that the unity of the conscious self (*cidātman*), even though it appears in various and manifold forms, remains entirely uncontradicted. [The phrase] "in its various forms as respective reflections" refers to the manifold nature [of the appearances].
"Without distinction" means from the perspective of the common nature of the mirror. "Unvitiated" means uncontradicted. || 54 ||
Thus, even though the world appears in many diverse ways, that which is established through thorough investigation is one and free from defects. (55)

Even while the diverse world, which resides within one's own self, is manifesting, that single, uncontradicted, and perfectly established [Self] is realized through hundreds of such recognitions as: "I who previously experienced dreams am the very same I who now experience the waking state."
The essential nature. || 55 ||
O King, behold within yourself the state of the kingdom of the mind;
though it possesses a body of manifold variety, it is nothing but pure consciousness.

Thus, although it has been established by the analogy of the mirror that the world is of the single nature of the conscious Self (cidātman), he explains it further with another illustration for the sake of perfect comprehension, beginning with "O King": even the state of a kingdom of the mind, though consisting of manifold diversities, is essentially nothing but consciousness. This is what is called a "kingdom of the mind."
Or rather, it is mental, consisting of volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*). For at the time of such construction, everything appears within one's own interior;
and it must be stated that this occurs solely by way of reflection (*pratibimba*). No dependence upon an external object (*bimba*) or the like is observed there.
Thus, it should be understood that this is a complete illustration. Furthermore, in the case of a kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*), there is no [dependence on] latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

It must be stated that there is a dependence on the subtle form of the entity, because it is not established that an entity consisting of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) can impart a reflection; otherwise, just as with the impression of a jar, a reflection of a jar would result in the mirror even when the lump of clay is facing it. || 56 ||
Whether in creation or even in dissolution, that consciousness remains entirely free of conceptual construction;
it is like a mirror, whether a reflection is present or absent.
Since the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) of the visible world is equal to a reflection in a mirror or a kingdom of the mind, he says:

"In creation. Just as the mirror maintains its nature as merely a mirror both during the state of the existence and the non-existence of the reflection, so too, during creation—at the time of the manifestation of the phenomenal world—and during dissolution, [it remains as such].
And at the time of that manifestation, that supreme consciousness is indeed free from conceptual construction; the sense is that it consists solely of the nature of pure consciousness. || 57 ||
Although consciousness is of such a single form, by virtue of its sovereignty, it may manifest the external within itself, just as the sky is reflected in a mirror. (58)
For this is the first creation, called ignorance (avidyā) and darkness (tamas);
the manifestation of the Full as a mere portion is called the external appearance. (59)
By this much of the text, the question has been addressed as to how there can be simultaneously both smallness and [largeness] or multiplicity of a single time and space;
[the answer is that] since external creation is like a kingdom of the mind, its essence being mere conceptualization, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

The resolution has been stated. Regarding the doubt as to how this creation, consisting of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*), could proceed from a consciousness that is eternally of a non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpaka-rūpa*)— given that the essence of creation consists merely of imagination— the [text] explains the process of creation according to the sequence of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) accepted in the scriptures.

In order to explain, at the outset, the emergence of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of all creation, he begins with the words "Thus" (*evam*). The meaning is: although its nature consists solely of non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-cidekarasa*), just as the sky appears in a mirror, so too that Consciousness (*cit*) manifests the objects of experience—both internal and external—as being "outside," which is the literal meaning of the word *bahiḥ*. Now, [one might ask], in a mirror...

If it is asked what the cause is for the appearance of space within the conscious self (*cidātman*), which is itself the external space that has become the reflected image (*bimba*), he says: "By reason of autonomy" (*svātantryahetutaḥ*). The meaning is: by reason of a cause whose nature is autonomy, which is the state of being independent of anything else. Because a mirror is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is dependent and thus requires an external object to serve as its reflected image.
Because it is non-inert by virtue of its sovereignty, it has no need for an external reflection (*bimba*). As they say:
"Just as the entire universe shines within itself here in all its diverse arrangements, like [images] within a mirror..."
"Furthermore, consciousness perceives the universe through the method whose essence is its own self-reflection (see the two footnotes on page 168); a mirror, however, does not do so. (TaSā p. 19)

"This" refers to that which has the nature of the manifestation of external objects; it is called "the first" because all creation is preceded by this manifestation. This very manifestation of externality is termed "ignorance" (avidyā) and "darkness" (tamas). If it is asked how there can be a manifestation of externality for the perfect conscious self (cidātman), he says: "of the perfect."

In reality, because there is no division, [the phrase] "as if by a part" means that the very manifestation of the Self as if by its own single part is precisely what constitutes the manifestation of the external. For the Supreme Lord, whose body consists solely of non-conceptual consciousness and whose nature is distinguished from the insentient, is called "autonomous. Insentience is called "dependent" because it requires something else for the manifestation of itself and others.

The independence (*svātantrya*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*) is said to consist in its not depending on anything else for the manifestation of itself and others. This very independence is expressed in the *Āgamas* by such terms as "power" (*śakti*), "action" (*kriyā*), and "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*). Furthermore, this independence pertains to the manifestation of the universe during the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), as well as at the beginning of dissolution (*pralaya*).

This [freedom] has as its object the manifestation of the essential nature alone, because even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) and so forth, the radiance of the essential nature remains unimpaired.

(Thus—[the reading within the brackets is not present in manuscript *gha*; it appears somewhat irrelevant]—this freedom is said to be the eternal, non-different attribute of Śiva at the end of dissolution.)
And that very sovereignty, when conjoined with the auxiliary factor of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings whose [karmic] impressions have matured, manifests its own nature as if by parts;
that is to say, it manifests it as something limited. This alone is the manifestation of the external, for the manifestation of the self as something limited is indeed [the external].
It is quite clear that [the appearance] is invariably concomitant with the manifestation of a location distinct from itself. || 59 ||
Due to the interruption of the full state of "I-ness," there arises the nature of "non-I-ness";
this very state is called the Unmanifest (avyakta) and is also described as the power of inertia (jaḍaśakti). || 60 ||

He further analyzes the very nature of the external with the word "pūrṇā" (complete). Just as when one's own body is pervaded by the complete sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), the state of non-"I-ness" does not exist even if a hand is severed— because it remains of the nature of "I-ness"— so too, through the manifestation of limitation within the Self, there is a state of non-"I-ness" regarding that portion which is other than the limited.

The state of "I-ness" (*ahantva*) consists in being distinct from that [limited] form; the intended meaning is that it is the absence of the attribute whose nature is the limited sense of "I. This very manifestation within the Self is what constitutes external manifestation.
Such a nature is called the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and the insentient power (*jaḍaśakti*). And thus, of the full conscious Self...

It has been stated that the Lord’s primary creation consists of the manifestation of external appearance— known as ignorance— which is characterized by the manifestation of the delimitation of His own Self through the power of autonomy (*svātantrya-śakti*). This very manifestation of the external is what [is understood] in the view of the followers of the Upaniṣads.

It is called "root-ignorance" (mūlāvidyā). Furthermore, the sovereignty of the Lord is precisely His power of consciousness (cicchakti). This [power] has three states: in the state of non-conceptuality such as dissolution (pralaya), it consists of the power of consciousness; at its conclusion, in the state of being oriented toward conceptualization, it consists of the power of illusion (māyāśakti).

In the state of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it takes the form of the insentient power (*jaḍa-śakti*) consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*). This very same [power] is described in some places as the "conscious nature" (*cit-prakṛti*) and in others, through the identity of *māyā* and *avidyā*, as the "insentient nature" (*jaḍa-prakṛti*), thus being presented in a twofold manner. As the Blessed One said:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect..."
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.
"O mighty-armed one, know that there is another, higher nature of Mine, distinct from this, which is the life-force by which this world is sustained" (Bhagavad Gītā 7.4–5).
The eightfold nature beginning with earth is the lower, insentient nature, which is the effect; however, the higher nature is—

The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), being like a mirror for reflections, constitutes the living soul of the universe; for this very reason, it has been stated that by means of this [power], the world consisting of the eightfold nature (*aṣṭaprakṛti*) is sustained. Now, prior to the manifestation of the insentient power, it is precisely this [consciousness] that impels the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings by acting as an auxiliary to the sovereignty of the Cause.

It must necessarily be admitted that there is the ripening of that [unmanifested world], the agent of ripening, and the time [of ripening]; otherwise, defects such as inequality would result. Furthermore, if this is admitted, the previously accepted position that prior to creation there remains only the non-dual conscious Self (cidātman) alone is abandoned. And yet—
For time is that which ripens the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings;

and whether it be identical with God (*īśvara*) or distinct from Him, in either case, because there is no other differentiating adjunct (*upādhi*) during the dissolution (*pralaya*), it remains uniform and of a single nature from the beginning of the dissolution until its conclusion. Consequently, in the second and subsequent moments of the dissolution...
If it is argued that creation occurs through the ripening of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), they say in response: In the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*),

since every effect exists in a subtle form within *māyā* even prior to creation, it is precisely that subtle time which has dissolved therein that acts as the ripener of the *adṛṣṭa* of living beings who have likewise dissolved in *māyā*.

Thus, because such māyā is non-different from the conscious self precisely by virtue of being its power (śakti), the acceptance of non-duality is maintained. Others, however, maintain that since creation is equal to a dream, a mental fantasy, or a magician’s illusion, there is not even a trace of logical necessity or purpose in it.

For just as the nature of the water in a mirage in the desert is logically untenable, so too is that of creation. It is for this very reason that the various methods of describing the process of creation found in the scriptures are consistent. The sequential description of creation—which is to be negated as distinct from the Self—is intended in some way to facilitate its conceptual apprehension by the mind prior to its negation. Therefore...

"Thus, there is neither creation nor dissolution, neither maintenance nor succession; in this way, the reality of the Self shines forth as a mass of consciousness and bliss. Thus they say, in accordance with the statements of the *Pārameśvara* and other scriptures. (60)
The consciousness here that appears as fragmented with respect to the external self is called the *śivatattva*; its manifestation is *śakti*. (51)

Having thus described the manifestation of primordial ignorance (*ādyavidyā*) at the beginning of creation, and intending to delineate the process of emanation according to the sequence of the *tattvas*, he first divides the *śivatattva*: "That which is consciousness" (*yā citiḥ*). Here, *tattva* means "the state of being that" (*tasya bhāvas tattvam*); it is said to be [the reality] that persists even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

The general form of earth and so forth. For instance, the general form of earth and so forth persists until the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), whereas the generality of a jar and so forth does not; for the dissolution of the elements is the great dissolution, since derivative objects such as jars are destroyed even before that. Here, at the time of creation, [there arises] the ignorance called *avidyā* of the external self.
That consciousness which manifests as fragmented is called the *śivatattva*. This is the intended meaning:
[the manifestation through the aspect of the *tattvas*] (*The text within parentheses is not present in manuscript G;
it appears irrelevant*). For instance:
Just as waves, which are mutually distinct, suddenly arise from the ocean which is of a single form and devoid of waves,
so too do infinite limited portions of one's own nature arise within the Supreme Consciousness-Self. And thus,
from the perspective of each of those limited portions of consciousness, there is the appearance of "self" and "other" or "internal" and "external" with respect to the Full Self.

However, the established position is that for Paraśiva there is no external manifestation. In that regard, the universal (sāmānya) which follows along with the infinite, pure, and limited aspects of consciousness is called the Śiva-tattva.
Yet, it should not be said that this very Śiva-tattva is identical in form to Paraśiva.

Because the universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) contains all particularities within it, whereas the nature of Paraśiva is devoid of both universals and particulars; thus, it is concluded that the Śiva-tattva is the universal of limited, non-conceptual consciousness (*paricchinnanirvikalpacitisāmānya*). Regarding "Power" (*śakti*): it is the "I-ness" (*aham*) of that limited, non-conceptual consciousness.
That which is manifestation is the second principle, the *śakti-tattva*, which is the universal nature of manifestation (*bhāsana-sāmānya*).

Although it has been stated that "the repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the 'I-consciousness' (*ahaṃbhāva*)" (*Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi* 22), and thus the manifestation of the "I" is the very nature of consciousness, and consequently there is no difference between the principles of Śiva and Śakti; [nevertheless, the former is the essential nature while the latter is its power].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that by virtue of being non-conceptual consciousness, it has the nature of the Śiva-tattva, and by virtue of being the manifestation of the "I" (aham), it has the nature of the Śakti-tattva. || 61 ||
That very external form, which is the great void and is imagined, is indeed remembered as being composed of Sadāśiva through the veiling of the sense of "I. (62)

And that which appears as external objects through the limited vision of consciousness—known as ignorance—is called the "Great Void" (*mahāśūnya*), because it serves as the substratum for the painting of the world and is thus equal to the great ether; it is "imagined" (*kalpita*) because it arises merely as a reflection of the limitation of one's own Self. Such is the nature of this external form.

When it conceals [the object] through the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*), by means of the state of "I-ness" (*ahantva*)— thinking "this is indeed I"— then that is known as the third principle, consisting of Sadāśiva. That very consciousness, though limited, manifests the external form— which is distinct from itself— as the object of the notion of "I" through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), in the form "I am this."
Thus, the third principle, Sadāśiva-tattva, is the universal consciousness characterized by manifestation and limitedness; this is the intended meaning.
That same [consciousness], when characterized primarily by insentience, is designated as Īśvara.
The awareness of these two, however, consists in the reflective discernment of both difference and non-difference. (63)
That very [state] is the Sadāśiva-tattva itself. When inertia (jāḍya) predominates, it is the fourth principle called Īśvara-tattva.

The Sadāśiva-tattva consists of an appearance in which consciousness is primary, arising from the infusion of the external "this" aspect (idam-aṃśa) by the "I" aspect (aham-aṃśa) which is of the nature of consciousness, in the form "I am this."

The *Īśvara-tattva*, however, consists of the appearance dominated by insentience (*jaḍya*), arising from the infusion of the conscious aspect of "I" (*aham*) into the insentient aspect of "this" (*idam*)— expressed as "this am I.
(The reading "*Īśvara-tattvam*" is not strictly necessary, yet it appears in all manuscripts.)
The sense is that it is "seen.

That consciousness and manifestation— which consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of both difference and non-difference between these two, Sadāśiva and Īśvara, in the form of "I am this" and "this is I"— is the fifth principle, *śuddhavidyā*.

The syntactical connection is "is declared. Although the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form of "I am this" and "this is I"— which consists of the reflective awareness of both difference and non-difference— is respectively the *sadāśiva-tattva* and the *īśvara-tattva*,
nevertheless, the fifth [tattva] is distinct from those two by virtue of its nature as a universal (*sāmānya-rūpa*) that underlies both modes of manifestation.
The principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyātattva) is to be known. || 63 ||

This is declared to be "pure knowledge" (śuddhavidyā); it is called pure because the power of differentiation has not yet taken root, and because there is the manifestation of the nature of non-duality.
"Thus much" means the pentad of principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā. "Pure" refers to the threefold nature of reality as pure, mixed, and impure;
among these, this pentad is declared to be "pure" in the scriptures. The reason for this is: "because it manifests as having the nature of non-duality."
Because it manifests as the non-dual nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Here too, he states the reason:

"because the power of differentiation has not yet emerged" (*bhedaśakteraprarūḍhyā*). The "power of differentiation" is the aforementioned insentient power (*jaḍaśakti*); its "non-emergence" means the absence of its manifestation in the form of fully developed effects. [This refers to that which is] of the nature of external manifestation.

The power of insentience (*jaḍaśakti*) possesses three states, like a seed, a sprout, and a tree. For just as there is a non-manifestation of the differentiation consisting of the sprout and so forth within the seed, so too there is a non-manifestation of the differentiation in the form of effects characterized by their own predominance within the power of insentience; at that time, it remains non-distinct from the conscious self (*cidātman*).

Purity arises from manifestation and the predominance of consciousness (*cit*). For when the differentiation of the subtle form of the effect emerges from the insentient power (*jaḍa-śakti*)—like a sprout [from a seed]—then, due to the predominance of both consciousness and the insentient, there is a state of mixture in the seven principles beginning with *māyā* and ending with *puruṣa*. When...

The meaning is that, like a tree, there is the growth of distinctions in the form of gross effects; at that time, due to the predominance of the non-conscious (acit), there is impurity belonging to the twenty-four principles (tattvas) beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with earth. || 64 ||
Then, when the conception of duality has taken root through the weight of consciousness’s own freedom,
the power of inertia assumes the state of the substratum (dharmin), while consciousness attains the nature of its attribute (dharma).

Now, immediately after the emanation of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*): when the intensity— the preponderance— of the freedom (*svātantrya*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*) has reached full maturity in the manifestation of duality, for within the pentad of pure principles, duality arises in the form of "I" and "this," which is the power of insentience (*jaḍaśakti*).

Because [the object] is submerged within consciousness (*cit*), there is currently no manifestation [of duality]. When the conceptualization of difference becomes manifest through the emergence of consciousness, "conceptualization of difference" refers to the mental construction of duality. In the pure principles (*tattvas*), the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) possesses the status of the substratum (*dharmin*), while the insentient aspect (*jaḍāṃśa*)—being submerged within that [consciousness]—possesses the status of a non-different attribute (*abhinnadharma*). For in the ordinary state, the reverse is the case; thus he says: [The verse: "The nature of the attributes of the insentient is the opposite of that which belongs to the pure principles. (1.20) In the pure principles, the insentient aspect is submerged within the aspect of consciousness and is therefore not perceived as distinct from it. Consequently, the insentient aspect is considered an attribute of the conscious substratum. In the ordinary state, however, the insentient aspect is predominant and the conscious aspect is submerged within it; thus, the relationship between substratum and attribute is reversed. Therefore, the nature of the attributes of the insentient is said to be the opposite of that found in the pure principles. This is because the insentient aspect is submerged within the aspect of consciousness in the pure principles, whereas in the ordinary state, the conscious aspect is submerged within the insentient. Thus, the relationship between substratum and attribute is inverted. This is what is meant by the statement: "The nature of the attributes of the insentient is the opposite of that which belongs to the pure principles. (1.20) *Note: The term *prarūḍhi* here denotes the full manifestation or firm establishment of a conceptual state.*
Then that power of inertia is called the principle of Māyā;
for Māyā is the intellect of differentiation, arising from the pervasive tendency toward duality.

Thus, when there is this reversal of the relationship between the property and the substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*), that insentient power (*jaḍaśakti*) attains the status of the substratum; it is the *māyātattva*. He states its essential nature as "māyā. Because of the abundance of differentiation—that is, the insentient power—it functions as the substratum.
Māyā, which consists of the common form of the cognition of the distinction between the two types of manifestation, is the principle (tattva) called Māyā. || 66 ||

Consciousness, when enveloped by an abundance of differentiation and characterized by contraction, attains the state of the individual soul (puruṣa) when permeated by the five coverings (kañcukas). || 67 ||

The abundance of differentiation (*bheda*) is its profusion; consciousness (*citi*) is enveloped or pervaded by that. When differentiation predominates, consciousness—having its aspect of pure awareness obscured—becomes contracted in nature. Pervaded by the five coverings (*kañcuka*) to be described hereafter, it becomes "sheathed" (*kañcukita*) and attains the state of the individual soul (*puruṣatva*). This is the general nature of consciousness when sheathed by the five coverings.

The intended meaning is that the *puruṣatattva* (the principle of the Person) should come [next]. Although the traditional sequence of the scriptures (*āgamika*) is that the pentad beginning with *kalā* follows immediately after *māyā*, and the *puruṣatattva* follows right after that, nevertheless, because *kalā* and the others are attributes of the *puruṣa*, the *puruṣa* is described first due to its primacy. || 67 ||
Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, and niyati constitute the pentad of coverings (kañcuka).
Kalā is the state of limited agency; vidyā is the state of limited knowledge. (68)
He speaks of the coverings themselves: "Kalā," etc. He states their essential nature: "Kalā is a little," etc.
Limited agency is *kalā*; limited knowledge is *vidyā*. (68)
Attachment, thirst, and the limitation of lifespan are said to be "time" (kāla); necessity and dependence—endowed with these, the person (puruṣa) [is bound]. (69)

*Trṣṇā* (thirst) is the general desire for sense objects in the form of "May this be mine"; *rāga* (attachment) is the same. *Pariccheda* (delimitation) is time (*kāla*), which is defined by a lifespan delimited to a duration such as one hundred years. *Niyati* (necessity) is a state of dependence consisting of the requirement for specific means in order to accomplish something. Endowed with these five aforementioned coverings (*kañcuka*s), beginning with *kalā* and ending with *niyati*, [the soul] is joined or enveloped.
The individual soul (puruṣa) is rendered limited. Supreme Śiva possesses five powers: omnificence, omniscience, eternal contentment, eternity, and absolute freedom.
When these are contracted, they are called the five coverings (kañcukas) of the individual soul. Thus, [the soul possesses] limited agency and so forth.
The meaning is that this category of principles, beginning with *kalā*, is distinct for each individual soul (*puruṣa*). || 69 ||
Presiding over the power of consciousness, the mass of latent impressions (vāsanā) of people, which consists of diverse beginningless karmas, exists and is called Prakṛti.

Regarding the phrase "the power of consciousness" (*citiśaktim*): it refers to the power of consciousness belonging to the conscious self (*cidātman*). It is the aggregate or collection of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—also termed the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—which are the residual traces of the various actions of people, such as white, black, and many other kinds, which have proceeded through a lineage from beginningless time.

The meaning is that she is called *prakṛti* because she remains abiding by presiding over the aspect of light (*prakāśāṃśa*), which is the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). The essential point is that *prakṛti* is the very aggregate of impressions (*saṃskāra*) from prior actions belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Furthermore, she possesses a threefold form because the fruit of actions is of three kinds.
For it is the differentiation of its states that is designated as "mind. || 71 ||

Since the fruits of actions are threefold—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those actions that produce such fruits are also threefold. Thus, it is said that *prakṛti*, composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, possesses these three forms:
"But the fruit... [referring to] this *prakṛti*. (71)
In deep sleep, Prakṛti is to be known; at its conclusion, it is called the mind (citta). Consciousness (cit) together with the mass of latent impressions (vāsanā) is declared to be the mind.
He says this very thing: "In deep sleep," etc. At the time of deep sleep, that mass of latent impressions (*vāsanā-piṇḍa*) is called *prakṛti*.

At the end of that—that is, at the end of deep sleep and at the beginning of waking and dreaming—that same mass of latent impressions is called the mind (*citta*). For that power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) which, accompanied by the mass of latent impressions, was called *prakṛti* during deep sleep, is that very same [power] at another time.
He says that it is called "mind" because of "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā). || 72 ||
This very [mind] is called "unmanifest" due to its state as a mass of latent impressions (vāsanā);
through the diversity of individuals, the mind becomes manifold. || 73 ||

In order to strengthen the identity of the two, having stated that "the *prakṛti* itself is the mind," he further states that "the mind itself is the *prakṛti*"—namely, "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Regarding the phrase "due to the state of being a mass of latent impressions" (*vāsanāpiṇḍabhāvataḥ*):
the intended meaning is that there is no difference between *prakṛti* and the mind because they share the same nature, consisting of a mass of latent impressions. Now...

In order to state the difference in the essential nature between the mind (*citta*) and the primordial spirit (*puruṣa*), he says: "of the spirits" (*puruṣāṇām*). The meaning is that because the spirits are distinct, the mind is also distinct; therefore, it is manifold. || 73 ||
For, through the non-differentiation of living beings, that [consciousness] indeed becomes one in deep sleep;
it attains the state of primordial nature (prakṛti), and at its conclusion, it returns to the state of the mind (citta).

Thus, although the mind is divided according to the distinction between individual persons, it becomes one in deep sleep due to the cause of the non-differentiation of the living beings (*jīva*). That very mind, having become unified in this way, is *prakṛti*; and that same [mind], becoming differentiated at the end of deep sleep, is called "the mind. He says "of the living beings" (*jīvānām*) because that is the mind; "at its end" means at the end of deep sleep. For the living being (*jīva*)...
The nature of consciousness is limited, and this limitation is produced by the body and so forth;

since the body and its like differ between the states of waking and dreaming, it is logical that there is a distinction among individual souls (*jīvas*). However, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because the body and so forth do not manifest, the appearance of limitation by them also does not exist within the Self.

Just as there is no distinction between waves in a waveless ocean, so too there is no distinction among individual souls (*jīvas*). And when there is no distinction among souls, the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of karma residing within them also form a single mass. This is *prakṛti*. What is called deep sleep (*suṣupti*) occurs when the karma that has reached full maturity has been exhausted through experience, while the other [karmas] have not yet matured.

Just like a fire whose fuel has been consumed, when the cognitive power of the conscious self lacks the ripened karma that connects it to objects, it does not turn outward; this state, occurring in the interim, is a specific condition devoid of experience.

This being the case, while the karmas of some remain unripened during that period of deep sleep, when the ripening of certain [other] karmas occurs, the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) is joined with the manifestation of objects by means of those ripened karmas. Thus, it is the power of cognition itself, characterized by the mass of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karmas that join one to objects, [that functions].
The meaning is "the mind. || 74 ||
For this very reason, a person is called "puruṣa" (spirit) on account of the predominance of consciousness;
however, due to the predominance of the unmanifest, he attains the nature of the mind.
This very thing is the mind itself. When there is a desire to emphasize the primacy of consciousness (*cit*), this same mind is called the "Person" (*puruṣa*);
when there is a desire to emphasize the primacy of nature (*prakṛti*), it is called "mind" (*citta*). Thus he says, "the Person is declared," and so forth.
[The phrase] *cittaprakṛtitām* means the state of being the nature of the mind, or its form as mind; alternatively, it means both the state of being mind and the state of being nature. And thus:
The intention of the specific treatise is that the mind is not a separate reality, but is rather included within either the Puruṣa or Prakṛti. || 75 ||
O best of kings, that internal organ is said to be threefold due to the difference in its functions, in the form of ego, intellect, and mind.
Such a primordial principle (*prakṛti-tattva*), consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is called the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

And that [internal organ] is of three kinds, because it possesses three types of functions consisting of self-identification (*abhimāna*), determination (*niścaya*), and volition (*saṅkalpa*); thus he says:
"due to the difference in function. Due to the difference in function, that primordial principle exists in the form of ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*).
The meaning is that it is threefold. || 76 ||
The group of five consisting of the organs of knowledge and action is distinct from that;
then there are the elements, beginning with ether and sound, categorized as gross and subtle. (77)
Thus that supreme consciousness, the witness of all, performs its play through the sequence of emanation and so forth, preceded by the manifestation of external appearances. (78)
Regarding "knowledge" (jñāna): the five organs of knowledge are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.

The five organs of action are speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. The five subtle elements are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. The five gross elements are ether, air, fire, water, and earth.

"From that" means from the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) which consists of the three *guṇas*. From the portions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* within the *ahaṅkāra*, there arose separately the pentad of the organs of cognition (*jñānendriyas*), the organs of action (*karmendriyas*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*). The sense is that from the subtle elements, the gross elements (*sthūlabhūtas*) came into being. This...

The detailed exposition on the determination of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) is to be found in the *Svacchanda-tantra* and other scriptures. Having thus determined the sequence of principles as it arose in the context of the discussion, he now returns to the subject at hand—the fact that the world has meditation alone as its essence—and explains this with the word "thus" (*evam*). Thus...
That supreme, undivided consciousness, well-known through the sequence of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*),
performs play (*krīḍā*) by sequentially effecting emanation, maintenance, and so forth, preceded by the manifestation of external appearances.
By the statement "she performs play," it is indicated that for the Supreme Consciousness, which is the Self, there is no other purpose in emanation and the rest.

"Regarding the phrase 'the witness of all': just as a witness is untainted by the virtues and defects residing in the subject of testimony, so too the Self of Consciousness (saṃvidātman) should be understood as untainted by the virtues and defects residing in creation and the rest. (78)
Therein, by the first [power], the illustrious Śrī Tripurā-śakti, Hiraṇyagarbha—who is Brahmā—is empowered for creation; this [universe] has arisen from his creative contemplation (bhāvanā).

Now, one might object: "Just as the world within the mountain arises from your own mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and thus has nothing but that cultivation as its essence, if this external world is likewise of the nature of mere mental cultivation, then by whose cultivation did it arise? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). This means: once it is established that the world has mental cultivation as its essence. By the first [verse].

By her who has become the cause of all; "in creation" means regarding the act of creation, that is, for the purpose of creation; "manifested" means made manifest through the power of contemplation (*bhāvanā*). The connection is as follows: this world has arisen through the contemplation of that Brahmā who is known as Hiraṇyagarbha. || 79 ||
But that consciousness which exists therein, manifesting in the form of "you" and "I," is indeed the supreme power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); no difference from it exists. (80)
Now, one might object: "If the world has been brought forth by Brahmā and others, how can Tripurā possess the status of being the creator of all?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therein. This means: in the general process of creation. Whether the world has been brought forth by Brahmā, by me, or by another—in whatever form it appears as "you," "I," and so forth—all of that [is her].

Tripurā, who is consciousness delimited [by objects], is indeed the Supreme; for just as there is no difference between the space delimited by a jar or the like and the Great Space (mahākāśa), so too here no difference exists. 80.
Duality appears as adventitious, for the adventitious condition is itself permeated by Brahman; when that contemplation is withdrawn, there is no manifestation of duality.

If it is asked, "In the absence of actual difference, how can there be the appearance of difference? he says: "But difference... This difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*), like that of the sky [caused] by jars and so forth; it is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, the vital breath, and so on. If it is asked, "From where does the limiting adjunct arise? he says: "Meditated upon as Brahman. The meaning is that it arises from the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of being the creator of this or that world.

Precisely because difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*), he says: "by the dissolution of that creative contemplation" (*tadbhāvanā*). When there is the withdrawal or cessation of the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of those [deities] who are the creators of the world, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) has dissolved, there is no appearance of difference—just as in the case of limited spaces such as jars—since the consciousnesses delimited by those adjuncts have perished, like limited spaces themselves.
(Herein ends the Gha-mātṛkā. || 81 ||
O Cit, that power of cultivation which has been obscured by you through māyā will attain perfection for you once that obscuration is removed. (82)

If it is asked, "Is it not the case that the consciousness-self possesses an innate sovereignty over creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), and why then is it not perceived by me?", he replies: "Of the consciousness" (*citaḥ*). The remainder of the sense is that its power of creative contemplation is veiled by *māyā*, which is the sovereign power of the Lord. When the veil of that creative contemplation is removed through the previously mentioned method, [it is perceived] by you.
That cultivation will attain accomplishment, which is the power of universal creation common to all. || 82 ||
Whether it be a place, a time, or some other thing, however and by whatever means it is visualized, so shall it appear there, according to the distinctions of being long or subtle. (83)

Some object, such as an elephant or a horse, by means of which [the yogi] has practiced meditation while unobstructed—that [object], such as its location or time, would appear there in the meditated place and so forth, according to the nature of the meditation, through the distinctions of being long or subtle. || 83 ||
That which was cultivated by me as a single day has been cultivated here by Brahmā for twelve hundred million (arbuda) such days.
This very point establishes the case for both the world of Śaila and the external world with the words "by me" (mayā). For the time being, it lasts for only one day.
Here, in the world created by Brahmā, the connection is that [the world] is manifested in form (rūpataḥ). || 84 ||
By him, this manifestation of long duration and swiftness was thus cultivated;
on a mountain fashioned by Brahmā, measuring two *gavyūti*s in extent, [here indeed the Ghamātṛkā came to rest]. || 85 ||

Precisely through that distinction in cultivation, there is the appearance of slowness or swiftness at one and the same time. He says "by Brahmā" [in verse 85] to show that it is exactly the same regarding space as well.
Because the infinite number of constituent parts has been meditated upon by me, there is infinity;
and thus both of these here are both true and indeed untrue. (86)
Thus, this too [is true] both for the space and time of the external world and for the space and time of the world of Śaila;

it is "true" because it possesses existence characterized as conventional reality—such as the capacity for causal efficiency—and yet it is "untrue" from the perspective of ultimate reality because it possesses existence that is subject to sublation in the form of non-manifestation. || 86 ||
You too, having first contemplated a space of one krośa and time consisting of a few *kalās*,
should further meditate upon that very same [space] as extending for infinite *yojanas*.

He says, "This is not surprising," [introducing the verse] with "You too": first, having visualized on the plane of internal conceptualization a region such as a mountain measuring one *krośa* and a subtle time consisting of *kalās*, then again visualize within that very same region of one *krośa* and that same duration of *kalās* a space of countless *yojanas* and an infinite duration of time.
The connection. || 87 ||
And it may shine even for an incalculable time, as long as there is cultivation;
therefore, this external world has its nature consisting solely of cultivation.

Just as a vast region such as mountains and cities appears in a mirror only a span wide, or as a long duration such as a year appears in a dream lasting but a moment, so too will whatever exists as one's mental cultivation (bhāvanā) appear accordingly.
The point is that once the veil of mental cultivation is removed, this very reality will appear as something common to all.

Therefore, the connection is as follows: this world, which is of the nature of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), appears externally within the unmanifest Self that is consciousness (*cidātman*). || 88 ||
O lord of men, it is indeed within the unmanifest nature of the conscious self that [the world] shines;
therefore, upon the wall of the external unmanifest, this world appears as a painting.

Therefore, because it consists merely of mental construction and is thus unreal, just as a painting has the wall alone as its essence, so too the world—which is like a painting on the wall of the unmanifest—has the unmanifest wall alone as its essence; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 89 ||
It would be merely the substrate of the unmanifest; it consists of consciousness as its own substrate.
For this very reason, even a distant place becomes accessible to the yogi after a long time.
Although this insentient power (jaḍa-śakti) has the unmanifest as its essence, it is indeed of the nature of consciousness (cidātmika), like a painting upon the wall of the conscious self.
This is because the world is unreal apart from the conscious self; thus, the grammatical connection is that "the yogis see [it as such]. || 90 ||
Having gone there in an instant, they certainly see it as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand;
therefore, whether far or near, or even after a long time or quickly—91.

Regarding the phrase "in an instant": the sense is that if distance were real, traveling [that distance] in an instant would be impossible. Therefore, because distance and so forth are unreal, the grammatical connection is as follows: having ascertained that "far," "near," and so on, have as their essence mere mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). [It is said:
"Established by mere mental cultivation, it rests upon the mirror of consciousness."
Having thus ascertained this, abandon delusion through the process of meditating on pure consciousness.
The meaning is as follows: having ascertained that this world is unreal apart from that [Self], being like a reflection resting in the mirror of the conscious Self (cidātman),

one should abandon the delusion of the reality of the world through the practice of the continuous and uninterrupted cultivation over a long period of time of the realization "I am that pure Consciousness alone which is distinct from the body and so forth."
"Therefore, you too shall become an independent son just like me.
Having heard these words of the sage's son, that best of sages—
Then, immediately after the cessation of the conceit of reality; || 93 ||
Having abandoned all delusion and known that which is to be known, one of virtuous intent should,
through the practice of meditative absorption, fully accomplish one's own true nature.
He has abandoned all delusion—namely, the delusion that the world is real, that the body is the self, and so forth.

He is one by whom the reality of the Self has been known as the mirror in which the world is reflected; for this very reason, his disposition (*āśaya*) is auspicious, being free from desire, anger, and other such passions. (94)
Then, having attained sovereignty and having dwelt for a long time,
he uproots the semblance of the body and takes refuge in the great ether.

Having attained sovereignty at the beginning of creation, and then, after dwelling for a long time, there occurs the uprooting of the appearance of the body—the abandonment even of that appearance of the body which has been sublated. This is the great void, the supreme consciousness free from conceptual construction. 95.
O Bhārgava, even Mahāsena attained supreme nirvāṇa;
thus, the world [is established] solely through the cause of the contemplation of the reality of existence. 96.
"Nirvāṇa" means that, having abandoned even the appearance of a body which persists as a residual impression once sublated,
he— possessing a form consisting solely of non-conceptual pure consciousness— attained the supreme nirvāṇa, which is disembodied liberation (videhamukti).
Thus, according to the manner described, the syntactical connection is that the world appears solely due to the cause of the cultivation of the notion of its reality.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, contemplate this: it shines by way of its true nature as the Self.
Through inquiry, the delusion residing in the mind shall come to rest. 97.
The world shines as the very form of Truth; reflect upon this which I have spoken, and investigate it. Through further investigation in the form of deep reflection, delusion shall come to rest. (97)
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the World of the Mountain," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the fifteenth chapter:
Having then heard this most wonderful narrative concerning the world of the mountain, Rāma, the scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage, was once again utterly amazed. (1)
Here, by means of verses equal in brilliance to gold, Aṣṭāvakra relates in brief the nature of the Self, both that which is knowable and that which is unknowable.

In the previous chapter, he was told by the Guru, "Reflect. Having gone to his own place, having ascertained [the matter] thoroughly with a pure intellect free from fallacious reasoning, and having returned, he asked about his doubt; thus [the author] says: "Having reflected" (vimṛśya). || 1 ||
Having reflected and reached a firm conclusion through pure intellect upon what was spoken by his guru,
he went again to Dattātreya, bowed down, and questioned him respectfully.
O Blessed One, regarding that which was spoken by you through various narratives, I have understood this essence from it through thorough reflection. (3)
"O Blessed One!"—the construction is: "Of that which was spoken by you, this much has been understood by me through reflection. (3)
Consciousness alone is real; that which is perceived therein is imagined.
It is falsely manifested, resembling a city in a mirror. (4)
He states that very point: "In perception" (*saṃvedana*). Regarding that perception, there is an illustration: "in a mirror.
For this very reason, it is falsely manifested; it is known to be unreal, false, and non-existent. || 4 ||
That consciousness is the supreme power, the Great Goddess whose nature is pure awareness;
she projects the variegated picture of the universe, differentiated by the unmanifest and other stages, upon the wall of her own self.
Thus, he states that in the manifestation of falsehood, the very cause is the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of consciousness itself—referring to it as "She" (*sā*).

In that context, where the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is imagined within a single act of consciousness, the qualifying attributes such as "consciousness" (*citi*) and so forth are employed to define its distinction from the object. Consciousness consists of the illumination of both self and other (*sva-paraprakāśamayī*), and is supreme (*paramā*). (Note: *para* does not exist [as an external entity]).

Her power is unlimited and difficult to perceive; her very form is consciousness itself. She is the sovereign and controller even of the great ones, such as Brahmā and others. The unmanifest is the external object [of perception]. || 5 ||
One should illuminate [reality], which is without material cause or external reason, solely through one's own freedom;
this much alone have I understood after investigating with a subtle intellect. (6)
The world is without material cause or efficient cause, arising solely from absolute freedom and having absolute freedom as its sole motive.

However, such a consciousness, devoid of an object of knowledge, has been described as impossible to perceive, because that which possesses an object of knowledge always exists [in association with one]. (7)
But without an object of knowledge, how could there be the apprehension of consciousness? Without that apprehension, the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) does not exist. (8)

Having stated the determined portion among those thus taught, he speaks of the remainder with the words "But" (*kiṃtu*). [The state] "devoid of an object of cognition" (*vedyavandhyā*) means pure (*śuddhā*) and free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpā*). The meaning is that she who has been described there cannot be apprehended. The reason for this is given as "of that which possesses an object of cognition" (*savedyāyāḥ*); the sense is that it is because she is always apprehended precisely as possessing an object of cognition. How so?

For that [consciousness] is necessarily perceived only in the form of the object of cognition, as in "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth. If it is argued that there is no perception of it, he says: "perception.
Even if it were of such a nature in reality, it is perception alone that accomplishes the goals of human life; otherwise, there would be nothing but bondage.
The meaning is that it would not be possible. || 8 ||
Liberation may also be the goal of human endeavor; what kind of liberation is it said to be?
If liberation occurs when there is consciousness, how can there be worldly activity in one who is liberated?
Another doubt: [the question] "What is the goal of man? refers to liberation (*mokṣa*). Of what kind is it? What is its nature?
Furthermore, there is another question: once higher knowledge has arisen, how does one conduct oneself immediately after being liberated while still alive? || 9 ||
Moreover, even the wise are seen to be intent upon worldly activity;
how then can it be said that their consciousness, which is the object of experience, remains liberated? (10)

If it is argued that "there is no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) for those who possess knowledge (*jñānin*)," he says "no," [introducing the verse] beginning with "jñāninaḥ. If it is asked, "But what is this contradiction regarding the worldly transaction of one who possesses knowledge? he says "how" (*katham*). Because worldly transaction consists of conceptual cognition (*savikalpajñāna*), it is stated that at that time, the object of experience is [conceptualized].
How can non-conceptual awareness remain established? || 10 ||
When pure consciousness is established, how could there be worldly activity?
Indeed, consciousness is of a single nature; thus, liberation too must be the one and only fruit.

Regarding the phrase "when [she] is established": the sense is that if one is established in non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpa-saṃvitti*), how can there be worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), given their mutual contradiction? Furthermore, since there is no difference between the knowledge that is the means to liberation and the liberation that is the fruit of knowledge, another question arises: how is it that the various states of the wise (*jñānin*) are seen to be distinct in the world?
(-) "Consciousness," thus [it is said]. || 11 ||
How then is it that a distinction among the wise is seen in the world regarding their state?
For some perform action at the proper time as enjoined by the true scriptures. (12)
He states the very same [point] regarding the different positions in the passage beginning with "some," etc.; "at the time" means at that particular time. 12.
Some propitiate the deity through various paths;
others, supreme in meditative concentration, have withdrawn the entire circle of their senses.
By those who have deviated from the paths, such as the Vedic and other ways. || 13 ||
Some perform austerities that wither the body and the senses; others clearly instruct their disciples through various distinct discourses.
By "pravacanaiḥ" is meant by words of instruction. || 14 ||
Some govern kingdoms according to the path prescribed by the science of polity (daṇḍanīti),
while others engage in debate with opponents in assemblies.
Some indeed compose various treatises incessantly,
while others always display nothing but sheer foolishness.
Mugdhatva means the state of being deluded. || 16 ||
But some here remain constantly engaged in a livelihood that is censured by the world;
they are proclaimed as "men of knowledge" (jñānins) through their abundant lamentations. (17)
"Vigarhyām" means censurable or blameworthy; "prathitāḥ" means renowned or famous. || 17 ||
How then, even when there is no difference between the means and the fruit, can there be a distinction in their stability?
Are these [beings] equal in consciousness, or do they depend upon degrees of excellence? (18)

"How is that? means: how is the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*) of these [beings]? Is it of a single form or manifold? To the question, "If it were of one kind, how could there be a differentiated state?", he says: "By the means" (*sādhanena*). This refers to knowledge and liberation, which are the fruit of the means. The explanation of the phrase "How is that? is: "What are these?"—namely, the gradations of knowledge (*jñānatāratamya*). 18
It behoves you to explain all of this in its entirety;
for your mind is naturally compassionate toward a disciple who has no other refuge but you. (19)
The connection is as follows: since the mind is by nature compassionate, you ought [to grant my request] regarding this entire collection of questions. || 19 ||
Thus questioned by the descendant of Bhṛgu, Atri’s son, with a serene mind,
considering the series of questions to be worthy, began to speak.
O Rāma, best among the wise, you will surely attain that state;
for you, being devoted to reflection, are capable of knowing it. (21)

"You touch that state. This means you are capable of knowing the nature of supreme consciousness as the Self. If one asks why this is so, he says: "Because you are devoted to the contemplation of the Real" (*sad-vimarśa*). Since you are devoted to the Real—that is, devoted to sound reasoning (*sattarka*)—you are empowered, meaning you are capable. || 21 ||
For this very thing is the descent of power (śaktipāta): namely, the true reflective awareness (sadvimarśana).
Without the descent of the Lord’s power, who could attain the highest good? || 22 ||

The descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of that Lord is the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*). It is called "descent of power" because it is the effect of the descent of power. Know that the task of the Self-deity is precisely this: [the attainment of] *śreyaḥ*, which is right reasoning (*sattarka*), the primary means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*). 22. Indeed, know that this alone is the duty.
That which is constant reflection on reality, when well-composed, should cause it to increase. 23.
He states that the sole function of Prasanneśvara is the production of correct reasoning (sutaraka), saying: "the function" (kṛtyam). || 23 ||
That which has been known by you is indeed such truth and nothing else;
yet, even though it is of that nature, what has been spoken by you possesses a form that is not perceived.

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): the connection is as follows—what you have stated as being known through the passage beginning with "tatra sāram iyaj jñātam" (15.3) is indeed exactly so; it is true that the other [knowledge] is not otherwise, yet what you have said—that such a body of supreme consciousness (*paracid-vapuḥ*) is not well-known—is [the point]. || 24 ||
This is not well understood by you, O Rāma, since you dwell in this manner;
for one who observes from a state of detachment knows only as much as he actually perceives.

That supreme consciousness manifests the world upon the wall of the self like a reflection in a mirror—this has not been well-known or directly realized by you; therefore, you state it as something external. If you argue that it is somehow already known, he replies: "as something external."
It does not feel; the meaning is that it does not feel because of the absence of the primary fruit of feeling. || 25 ||
For when that [consciousness] is correctly known, it pacifies the state of being a bystander;
yet the perception of being a bystander is like the perception in a dream. (26)

If it is argued that, although I have correctly understood [it], I have nevertheless described it from a detached standpoint (*tāṭasthyena*), he says: "Because... That is the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*).

The correct knowledge of the supreme consciousness, which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is the realization "I am. The intended meaning is: once this has been known, how could there be a description—on the grounds of detachment—of how that [consciousness] might subsequently manifest the world?

Cognition of something as a mere bystander is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). He states that the cognition of an object that is directly present (*aparokṣavastu*) as being indirect is indeed of the nature of an error, [beginning with the verse] "In a dream... (26).
Just as the acquisition of a treasure in a dream is of no benefit to men, so too would knowledge that remains merely peripheral fail to yield the primary fruit. (27)
He states that indirect knowledge is useless with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). It does not yield the primary fruit.

The meaning is that just as, although joy and the like may arise from the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl due to the attainment of silver, such joy is not the primary fruit, so it is here as well. || 27 ||
In this regard, I shall relate to you a most beautiful account of former times:
long ago, among the Videhas, there was a certain king who was exceedingly righteous. (28)
In this regard, [this refers to] the case where intermediate knowledge (taṭasthavijñāna) is not the primary fruit. || 28 ||
For Janaka was possessed of mature wisdom and was well-acquainted with both the higher and the lower;
once, he worshipped his own goddess with supreme sacrifices.
There arrived Brahmins and others who were learned,
ascetic, skilled in the arts, versed in the Vedas, performers of sacrifices, and even those who had conducted long sacrificial sessions (sattrins).
At that very moment, Varuṇa began to prepare for the sacrifice;
though he invited the Brahmins and others, they did not go there in great numbers.
In that Varuṇa sacrifice, "bhūriśaḥ" means many. || 31 ||
For they were highly pleased with Janaka, honored by him, and satisfied;
then Varuṇa’s heir arrived, endowed with the wealth of the Buddha.
The qualifying attribute "the progenitor" (*janaka*) serves as the reason for his arrival. In that regard, the reason is "honored" (*pūjita*), and so forth.

Now, immediately after the certainty that the Brāhmaṇas and others had not arrived, [there was] Varuṇa’s heir, his son; the meaning is that he was accompanied by *baudha*—that is, by prosperity related to the Buddha (*bauddha*).
The intended meaning is that he is skilled in reasoning. || 32 ||
Wearing the guise of a Brahmin, he approached the sacrificial hall by a deceitful path in order to lead away the Brahmins; having reached it, he joined the king with a blessing.
He arrived to lead [him] away by a crooked path, that is, by a deceptive route. || 33 ||
Glancing there at the members of the assembly while the courtiers were listening, he said:
"O King, your sacrificial ground does not shine at all. (34)
*Ākṣepa* means contempt. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "standing in the midst of the members of the assembly who were listening to the reproach."
Like a lotus pond due to the gathering of flocks of crows and herons, the assembly, graced by the multitudes of learned men, shone most brilliantly. (35)
Regarding the phrase "it does not shine," there is the following illustration: "the lotus. If one asks why, he says: "with [other] bees.
"Shining" means that while it is already beautiful by its own nature, it shines even more intensely [when surrounded]. || 35 ||
Just as an autumnal lake with its lotuses is graced by flocks of swans, so too, in this assembly,
I do not see even a single person who is truly distinguished by learning.
The example is "autumnal" (śārada). The connection is: because I do not see it, therefore it does not shine. || 36 ||
"May it be well with you; I shall depart, for my stay here would not be possible.
How can I enter this assembly hall which is so full of fools? (37)
Thus addressed by Vāruṇi, the members of the assembly immediately became enraged:
"O wretch of a twice-born! Why do you revile us from every side? (38)
The speech of those who are angry is "O wretch! [addressed] to everyone from all sides. || 38 ||
"What kind of such knowledge is this of yours, by which we have all been defeated? You boast in vain, O evil-minded one; having conquered us, you shall depart. (39)
The ellipsis "we have been conquered" is to be supplied. || 39 ||
"Generally, the learned who dwell on the earth are indeed united;
why then do you, O evil-minded one, wish to conquer the earth itself today? (40)
"Residing on the earth" means staying on the earth; the ellipsis is that they are "assembled here," meaning they have gathered together. || 40 ||
"Tell me, what knowledge do you possess by which you wish to defeat us?
When the members of the assembly had spoken thus, the son of Varuṇa replied to them once more.
"By an agreement, I shall conquer all of you in a mere moment;
but if I am defeated by you, I shall remain submerged in the ocean. (42)
By means of the convention and the formal pledge; he states the very convention: "I. || 42 ||
"I immerse you in this: whether it be victory or defeat.
Having thus entered into this agreement, let them debate with me. (43)
"Having approached" means having accepted. || 43 ||
Thus addressed, the members of the assembly gave their consent for the debate;
however, O twice-born ones, they engaged in an intense dispute with that son of Varuṇa.
Consensus, a formal proposition, and acceptance. || 44 ||
Jīva, the son of Varuṇa, defeated the Brahmins by means of sophistry and idle chatter;
thus, hundreds and thousands of Brahmins were submerged in the ocean.
"By way of cavil and wrangling. Discourse (*kathā*) is threefold, distinguished as *vāda* (debate), *jalpa* (wrangling), and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
