*Vāda* is discourse employed solely for the purpose of establishing one's own tenet.
*Jalpa* is that which is employed for both establishing one's own tenet and refuting the tenets of another.

Vitaṇḍā is that which is useful solely for refuting the established doctrines of others. He conquered some by way of *vitaṇḍā* and others by way of *jalpa*. Thereafter, the defeated Brahmins were submerged in the ocean. (45)
Those Brahmins who were submerged and carried away by those messengers of Varuṇa reached the sacrifice of Varuṇa and rejoiced greatly, being highly honored.
They were honored by Varuṇa. || 46 ||
Then, having heard that his father Kahola had been drowned,
his son Aṣṭāvakra arrived, a debater skilled in the sophistry of knowledge.
Having heard that his father had been defeated in debate, Aṣṭāvakra [confronted Bandin]; "vaitaṇḍya" refers to the practice of cavil (vitaṇḍā). || 47 ||
Having conquered Vāruṇi, he commanded him to immerse himself in the ocean;
then Vāruṇi, having become manifest, addressed the foremost of the twice-born.
He gave the command; that is, he ordered. Then, immediately after the command, he made himself manifest;
that is to say, he cast off his brahmin disguise. || 48 ||
Having been defeated by Aṣṭāvakra, he was brought back to his own place;
then, when the brahmins had arrived, the son of Kahola [Aṣṭāvakra] spoke most vehemently.
Out of pride, he overstepped all the brahmins whom he had previously released;
the brahmins, being insulted by Aṣṭāvakra, fell into great distress.
*Atyavartata* means he overcame or surpassed them; that is to say, by means of *avamāna* (disrespect). *Vimatāḥ* means those who were insulted or treated with contempt. || 50 ||
At that time, they sought refuge with a certain female ascetic who had arrived;
she, clad in saffron-colored garments, comforted those brahmins.
They went for refuge to him in order to shatter the pride of Aṣṭāvakra.
Wearing matted locks, eternally youthful, and possessing a captivating form,
she approached the assembly and spoke, having been most highly honored by the king.
By means of yoga, she is eternally youthful and free from old age.
O Vatsa, son of Kahola, you are exceedingly wise;
by you the Brahmins were liberated after defeating Varuṇi in debate.
I ask you something; speak it, setting aside all deceit—that state which, when known, brings about the attainment of complete immortality. (54)
Deceit is the path of cavil and idle chatter; that is to say, one should abandon the desire for victory.
"All immortality" means unconditioned immortality. || 54 ||
When that state is known, all doubt goes to its dissolution;
when it is not understood, there would be nothing left to be desired or sought after.
That which is to be wished for is the desired [object]. || 55 ||
"If that which is unknowable has been known by you, tell me quickly; approach me.
Thus questioned regarding his asceticism, the son of Kahola spoke.
If you have known that state, which is thus uncomprehendable, then speak to me; come near to me.
O female ascetic, listen as I speak further of that state which is known to me;
for there is nothing in this world, however small, that remains unknown to me. (57)

That state which was asked about by you—that very state—has been explained by me again and again. This which has been asked by you is, however, quite insignificant; that is to say, it is extremely trivial. || 57 ||
I have indeed thoroughly scrutinized all the scriptures;
I shall tell you that which you ask, O ascetic woman—listen to it according to the truth. (58)
"Thoroughly churned, thoroughly stirred," that is to say, "completely investigated. || 58 ||
For that is the cause of the entire world, devoid of beginning, middle, and end;
it is unconditioned by space and time, and consists of pure, indivisible consciousness. (59)
That is the very state you have asked about.

Because it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, he says "deśa" and so forth. By the words "pure" and "indivisible," the non-mixture with other entities—whether of a different or the same class—is expressed. || 59 ||
That supreme state, resembling a city in a mirror, is that upon which this entire world shines forth. (60)
Having relied upon the nature of consciousness as it has been explained—wherein "relying" does not mean [an external support] like the blue color of a jar—he says: "Like a mirror... (verse 60).
Having known that very [reality], one attains the state of immovable nectar;
just as when a mirror is known, no doubt whatsoever can arise.

Having realized that supreme state (*parama-pada*), he explains— by means of an illustration— that through its realization all doubts are removed and so forth, beginning with the verse "As in a mirror" (*ādarśa*). Just as when a mirror is known,
no doubt whatsoever arises regarding the reflections contained within it.
Because reflections consist solely of the nature of the mirror. || 61 ||
Just as it would not be unknown among infinite reflections, so too,
when the Supreme is fully realized, there would be nothing whatsoever left to be desired.

In this way, even that which is unknown would not exist as anything at all; or rather, nothing would remain to be desired, because once it is known to be a reflection, desire does not arise. Likewise, when the supreme, pure Self is known, since everything else is its reflection and thus non-different from it, there can be neither doubt regarding it nor anything remaining unknown.
The sense is that there would be nothing left to be desired. || 62 ||
And that too is unknowable by another, due to the absence of any knower and so forth;
thus, O ascetic, has that reality been elucidated through the perspective of the scriptures. (63)
Such a reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is indeed unknowable by another knower, because of the absence of any other knower.

The point is that if a second knower were insentient (jaḍa), its status as a knower would be lost; if it were sentient (ajaḍa), there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) due to the requirement of yet another knower for that one as well.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the instrument (karaṇa) should also be understood in this same way. This is discerned through the perspective of the scriptures (śāstradṛṣṭyā), and not through direct perception (pratyakṣeṇa).
It is known. || 63 ||
Having heard these words of Aṣṭāvakra, she spoke again:
"O son of a sage, what you have said is well-spoken, exactly as it should be, and is approved by all. (64)
What you have spoken accordingly is well-spoken and approved by all.
As for what was stated by you—that it is "unknowable" because of the absence of a knower—it follows that one must know it precisely in order to attain the immortal, imperishable state. (65)
Regarding this, he states that this much portion is contradictory: "As has been said" (verse 65).
How do you consider these preceding and following statements to be consistent? If you say it is unknowable, then explain why it does not exist. (66)

How do you consider the consistency of the preceding and following statements: "Having known that state which is unknowable, one attains the immortal state"? If you ask why, he says: "If it were unknowable... If it were unknowable, its very existence would be impossible, because that which is not known is not manifested, and thus its existence cannot even be established.
Existence (bhāvaḥ) [is that which is other than reality and yet possesses its existence] || 66 ||
If it exists, you must know it; do not say that it is unknowable.
Or perhaps, O Brahmin, this has been discerned by you through the perspective of the scriptures. (67)

He states another objection with the word "atha" (now): this reality of the Supreme Self is manifested—that is, ascertained—through the vision of the scriptures, which is to say, by means of knowledge derived from the [Vedic] texts. || 67 ||
You do not know that by yourself; therefore, it is not directly perceived [by you].
[Only] after seeing everything as it truly is, like a reflection, through direct perception. (68)

It is yourself, manifest; that reality which is the Supreme Self. You do not know it; it is not something beyond perception, nor is it an object of direct sensory experience. And yet, having seen the entire world existing there like a reflection—just as a reflection appears in a mirror—you [should look] at the mirror.
The sense is: how could this statement—"you do not perceive [it] through direct perception (pratyakṣa)"—be consistent? || 68 ||
"How is it that you do not recognize the mirror through direct perception?"—speaking thus in the midst of the assembly before this very Janaka. (69)
Thus, such speech—utterly inconsistent—was delivered in the midst of an assembly of scholars, and even there, before Janaka, the crest-jewel of the wise. (69)
"Why do you not consider yourself insulted? Tell me.
When she had spoken thus, he did not say anything at all. (70)

How do you not consider yourself as one who has been humiliated and insulted? The mere fact that your speech was poorly composed in the assembly is itself an indicator of your folly; the further conceit you have regarding the excellence of that very same speech is, moreover, a manifest sign of your stupidity—this is the intended meaning. || 70 ||
He became as if dejected and was immediately filled with shame;
standing for a moment with his face cast down, he reflected upon what had been prompted within him by her.
As if dejected, as if with a distracted mind; within, in the heart. || 71 ||
Not receiving an answer to that question, the best of the twice-born said to her:
"O ascetic, I do not know the words that would serve as an answer to your question."
The answer to the question of that female ascetic; [he spoke] to that female ascetic. || 72 ||
"I am your disciple; tell me this: how was this determined?
I do not speak that which is false, which destroys penance, and which is purposeless. (73)
This is what you have asked: "How is it consistent with the teaching that 'by knowing the unknowable, one attains immortality'? Speak!
To say "I know even that which is unknown" is a falsehood. (73)
Thus questioned by him out of sincerity, that ascetic woman, being pleased,
replied to Aṣṭāvakra in the hearing of the members of the assembly.
Of that Aṣṭāvakra. || 74 ||
O child, many have fallen into delusion precisely because they do not understand this;
it is unknowable through dry logic and is well-guarded in every respect.
This is the resolution of the aforementioned contradiction; it is not to be understood [otherwise] in any of the scriptures. 75.
Among all these members of the assembly, no one understands;
neither does this king know, nor do I, nor indeed anyone else. (76)
"No one perceives" — he states this very point again for the sake of clarity: "But not another. (76)
For in all disputes, this question-and-answer [method] is never found;
indeed, most scholars rely merely upon logic (tarka). // 77 //
This is not easily understood through reasoning, even by one of subtle intellect, anywhere, without service to a true guru and without the grace of the deity. (78)

The purport is that even for one of subtle intellect, this meaning is difficult to comprehend without serving a true guru preceded by the grace of the deity, and without the direct realization of the pure, non-dual reality of the Self. Therefore, O son of a sage, listen to this with a subtle mind; I shall explain it.
Even having heard this, it should not be understood by an intellect whose life-force is detachment.

"With a subtle and one-pointed intellect. If one asks why, it is because this is difficult to discern for one whose mind is not composed; thus he says, "not this. Its primary characteristic is like that of a life-force existing in a state of detachment. The intended meaning is that it is directed outwardly, being uncomposed within the Self. 79.
As long as this consciousness has not been declared within the Self, so long even that which is proclaimed and heard a thousand times is useless. 80.

"Consciousness is the web of births produced by the means of consciousness. Regarding the phrase "not mentioned as being in the Self": the meaning is that, having heard the teacher's words that "the Self is self-luminous like the sun," one should concentrate the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in order to reach a definitive conclusion as to whether "I am of such a nature" or "I am not," until one becomes oriented toward one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).
That which was spoken by the Guru and heard by himself. || 80 ||
Just as someone, out of negligence, might fail to recognize a pearl necklace around his own neck and, due to his deluded state, believe it has been stolen by thieves; (81)
Here is the illustration: "Just as" (yathā). "Through negligence" means through forgetfulness; "without knowing" means without seeing. 81–82.
Even though he has been awakened by someone saying, "He is indeed in your throat," as long as he does not point to himself and see him in his own throat...
"It is on your neck" means: without mentioning one's own self—that is, one's body—meaning, without bringing it before oneself;
that is to say, without directing the activity of the senses toward it. || 82 ||
Just as one does not perceive a necklace around one's own neck even upon subtle reflection,
so too did the daughter of the sage fail to recognize her own true nature, even though she had heard it.
Having perceived and heard their own intrinsic nature and their own essential form. || 83 ||
Even one who is exceedingly skillful would not express his inner self;
as long as that is so, how and where could it be known from the outside? (84)
The connection is with the phrase "having heard further. One whose mind is concentrated (*samāhitacitta*) should not utter [doubts] regarding the inner self;

that is, one should not be intent on determining whether the nature of the self is of such a kind or not, while remaining within its own essential form (*svarūpāntaḥ*). That is the nature of the self. || 84 ||
For just as a lamp illuminates objects on all sides, yet it never reaches a state of being illuminated by anything else anywhere; (85)

Having thus stated that the attainment of the fruit belongs only to one who is concentrated and inward-turned, he begins to explain—by means of an illustration—the manner of perceiving the primary reality of the Self, which is itself unperceivable, saying "Just as" (*yathā*). "Everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*) means in all places. Of some other lamp, by itself...
It does not become manifest. || 85 ||
It manifests by itself indeed, without depending on any other illuminator;
in this same way, all [phenomena] such as the sun exist as illuminators. (86)
In the same way, the sun and other luminaries, which illuminate others, shine by themselves through their own self-luminosity, independent of anything else. || 86 ||
And thus, on what grounds could it be appropriate to say that lamps do not exist or do not shine, simply because they lack luminosity? (87)
"And so it is. Is it reasonable to say that lamps and the like do not exist and do not shine because they lack the quality of being illuminated? The meaning is that it is not reasonable. || 87 ||
In this way, while lamps and the like exist as manifesting agents, tell me: how could that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is absolutely non-manifest, ever be revealed? (88)

"Thus" means as follows: when objects such as lamps, which are illuminated by consciousness, exist, how can you have any doubt regarding that nature of consciousness (*cittattva*) which, though being absolutely unilluminable and imperceptible, yet shines forth? "In that same way"—this is the connection [of the verse]. || 88 ||
It has been doubted whether that which is imperceptible can yet be manifest;
therefore, you should investigate this thoroughly with an inward-turned vision. (89)

"Vicikitsita" means doubt. The point is this: since it is observed that even insentient things like lamps—which are themselves not illuminated—possess illumination and existence, what doubt can there be regarding the nature of the conscious self (*cidātman*)? Therefore, because illumination and the like are possible for that which is not itself illuminated, one might ask whether the manifestation of the unilluminated conscious self exists by itself or not.
Investigate correctly. || 89 ||
This supreme power of consciousness is Tripurā, the refuge of all;
illuminating everything, when and where does she not shine? (90)

He states that while a delimited object such as a lamp, which is of the nature of light, may at some time or place fail to illuminate, consciousness (*citi*), being undelimited, can never be unmanifest; thus he says: "The power of consciousness" (*cic-chakti*).
It is supreme (*paramā*) because it is the cause of all and is the most excellent. It is Tripurā, the Fourth State (*turyā*). It is the refuge (*saṃśrayā*) of all.

Like a mirror for reflections, she is the locus of the universe. For this very reason, she is "illuminating all," because she manifests everything within herself. In what place, at what time, or in what form does she not shine?
The meaning is that she shines indeed everywhere, at all times, and in every form. (90)
When she does not manifest, what indeed would manifest then?
Even in her non-manifestation, it is that very power of consciousness (citiśakti) which shines forth.
That is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*). [Question: What would be manifested then? [Answer:
Nothing at all would be manifested; this is the meaning. [Objection: But in states such as deep sleep or cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), nothing is manifested;
therefore, the manifestation of consciousness is limited by time. [Reply: No, he says "by non-manifestation" (*aprakāśena*). It is not that it does not manifest.
The meaning is that even in this form, consciousness alone shines forth; otherwise, how could it be established that "it does not shine"? This is the intended sense. || 91 ||
Tell me, how could that which is unmanifest appear?
If it does appear, consider this most subtly: in what manner does it appear? (92)

If it is argued that in deep sleep (*suṣupti*) only the absence of manifestation appears, and not consciousness (*citi*), he replies with the words "aprakāśa" (non-manifestation). For non-manifestation is not self-manifesting, because that would be a contradiction. Therefore, it is established that consciousness alone is its manifester. Thus, the meaning is: how could consciousness, which is the manifester of the non-manifest, not itself shine? And so it is.
If consciousness were not manifest, even the non-manifest would not appear; therefore, one must simply say that consciousness is always manifest.
Thus, if consciousness shines at all times, does that consciousness shine by itself or does it shine through another?
You yourself should investigate this with a subtle vision—this is what he says with the word "bhāsate" (it shines). 92.
In this regard, even all those who are skillful and wise do not see;
because their vision is not internal, they are deluded and continue to wander in saṃsāra. 93.

[Objection: "But how can this be reflected upon? For it is a jar that, having been perceived, is reflected upon. Pure consciousness (*cit*), however, is unperceived; how then could it be an object of reflection? In response to this doubt, he says: "In this regard" (*atre*). This means:

with respect to its own nature, which is the object of pure consciousness. [He asks: "Why [is it so]? and answers: *Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence after the question "Why?". The translation reflects the available portion.*

"Those whose vision is unobstructed" means that because their vision is unobstructed, they do not see [in that manner]. Therefore, "by reason of having unobstructed vision" is the intended sense. || 93 ||
As long as the view does not abandon its active engagement,
so long will the state of "inner vision" (antardṛṣṭitā) certainly not arise in any way whatsoever.
If it is asked how there can be "internal vision," he says: "as long as... Vision is the mind;
its activity is volition (*saṅkalpa*). "It remains" means that it does not enter into states such as dreaming.
Having abandoned volition, it remains in the waking state alone and does not reach other states such as dreaming.
The state of being. || 94 ||
As long as the inward vision does not arise, one does not perceive that [reality].
When the inward vision is free from effort, how could it be accompanied by exertion? (95)

Thus, he says "as long as" (yāvat) to indicate that one does not perceive one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) without internal vision (*antardṛṣṭi*). He extracts the meaning of the term "internal vision" and states: "internal vision" (*antardṛṣṭi*). Internal vision is that vision of the mind (*manas*) from which all striving (*īhā*)—that is, volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*)—has departed. 95.
Having properly set aside that [conceptualization], take refuge in one's own true nature; then, having resorted to one's own momentary state, remain thereafter free from deliberation. 96.
Having completely and entirely abandoned that effort, take refuge in one's own nature, which is one's true form.
For the mind is, by its very nature, full—like a jar filled with space—by means of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), whose nature is pure consciousness;
yet it is also further filled with volitions (*saṅkalpa*), like a jar filled with rice. And so it is said:

Just as a jar filled with space remains unchanged even when a mere grain of rice is removed from it, so too the mind, which is already full of the Self, remains full even when mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) is removed; thus, one should understand that after the abandonment of volition, no further effort is required for resting in one's own nature (*svabhāva*). In this way, having resorted to one's own nature for a moment, or for some time—
He remains without reflective awareness; beyond that [is the state]. 96.
By reflecting through the gateway of memory, you then know it in its entirety;
that which is both unknowable and perfectly knowable is thus called Reality (tattva).
Recalling through the gateway of memory the state of resting in one's own nature, reflect upon that pure consciousness—

whether it manifests by itself or through another— in the state where there is an absence of volitional thought. From such reflection, that very essence of pure consciousness is said to be both unperceivable and perfectly perceivable.
Thus, you know all this by yourself; the meaning is that you will come to know it. || 97 ||
Having thus understood that which is beyond comprehension, one shall attain the state of immortality.
All this has been told to you; O son of a sage, salutations be unto you.

A person, having thus understood by themselves that which is otherwise unknowable and perceiving it as manifesting, attains the immortal state—the condition of liberation. He concludes with the word "this" (etad). || 98 ||
"I am departing with you, yet this was not understood by you from hearing it but once;
this king, the best among the wise, will enlighten you. (99)
"From hearing once" means from hearing [the teaching] briefly, just one time. || 99 ||
"Ask further; the king will surely sever all your doubts.
Having said this, she was honored by the king and saluted by the members of the assembly. (100)
Whatever doubt you may have in this matter, ask it; [let it be asked] by the members of the assembly, one by one. || 100 ||
Like a streak of cloud driven by the wind, it vanished in an instant.
This, O Rāma, has been explained to you regarding the nature of the process of perception.
Like a streak of cloud driven and impelled by the wind, it reaches disappearance—that is, concealment.

It should be understood that the teacher has thus concluded by stating the manner of perception, which was asked at the beginning of the chapter: "The process of perceiving the self—the pure conscious Self—is impossible to apprehend. || 101 ||
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Aṣṭāvakrīya in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Having heard this, Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, was filled with wonder within;
yet, unsatiated by hearing the narrative, he questioned the son of Atri once more.
In this chapter, that consciousness— both the knowable and the unknowable—
is thoroughly investigated through reasoned arguments, along with the distinctions between its states of suppression and sleep.
From the hearing of the discourse; that is, from listening to the discourse. || 1 ||
"O Blessed One, this ancient account which has been heard is indeed wonderful.
Thus spoke the great sage Aṣṭāvakra to the king once more.
The syntactical connection is that he asked what [was asked]. || 2 ||
Tell me in its entirety what the king replied to him;
oh, this wondrous narrative has never been heard by me anywhere! (3)
"O Guru, out of compassion, tell me the entire essence of the functioning of consciousness. Thus questioned, the great sage Dattātreya then [spoke].
The "functioning of consciousness" (*vijñānavṛtta*) refers to the process of consciousness (*vijñānaprakriyā*), which constitutes its very essence and primary meaning therein.
It is a narrative in the form of a dialogue between Janaka and Aṣṭāvakra. "Inquired" (*anuyukta*) means asked. || 4 ||
He related it to Bhārgava as being supremely purifying;
listen, O Bhārgava, to what was spoken by the high-souled Janaka.
When the female ascetic had departed, Aṣṭāvakra, the son of the sage,
approached the preeminent king accompanied by many brahmins.
To his father, the preeminent among kings. || 6 ||
"Listen attentively as I relate that which was briefly stated by the female ascetic, yet which is of great significance. (7)
Because from this [practice] arises the great benefit known as liberation; such is what was stated by Tāpasī. (7)
O King, Lord of Videha, because it was spoken in brief, I did not fully understand that which was said by that female ascetic.
Aṣṭāvakra asks with the words beginning "O King," and so forth; because it was stated in brief, I did not understand the reason.
"O treasury of compassion, explain how that which is both knowledge and the unknowable can be so;
thus questioned by Janaka, he spoke to him as if in wonder."

"How can I know that state of pure consciousness which is unknowable? How can that which is unknowable become known to me?"—this is the sense. He speaks as if in wonder, as if struck by amazement, because one who asks about such reality is so difficult to find.
"O son of a sage, listen to the words now being spoken by me."
For that is not un-knowable in every respect, nor indeed is it knowable in every respect.
That is the reality of the pure conscious self. || 10 ||
If it were entirely unknowable, tell me, what could the Guru say?
Since the Guru would impart the reality (tattva), one should therefore take refuge in the Guru from the very beginning. || 11 ||

Regarding the phrase "unknowable" (*avedya*): the implication is that if it were entirely unknowable, there could be no instruction from a teacher nor any fruit thereof. Since the teacher can indeed make it known, one should take refuge in the teacher; therefore, it is not absolutely unknowable. || 11 ||
This knowledge is indeed extremely easy to attain and yet difficult to practice;
for one whose vision has been turned away [from worldly objects], it becomes easily attained.

This experience is the knowledge of the pure conscious self. If one asks why this is so, it is said: "This" (referring to the one for whom) the vision of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has turned away [from external objects] and is directed inward.
For one who remains with a vision directed only outward, that [knowledge] is exceedingly difficult to attain.
It is entirely indefinable and, moreover, unknowable in every respect.
"Outward-looking vision" is vision directed externally; it is that which cannot be defined as "this" in any way and is unperceivable. || 13 ||
Even that which is to be known may somehow be defined by another form;
whatever is seen here, by that very thing it is called "the knowable. (14)
Even so, this [cognition] is to be defined and known by means of another form—that is, by way of the exclusion of what it is not (*atad-vyāvṛtti*).
If it is asked, "But surely others maintain that cognition is known by another cognition; how is that? he says:
"Whatever... Whatever visible object, such as a jar, you perceive, cognition is likewise perceived by others in that very same form.

It is said to be "the object of cognition. And thus, in such cases as "I am the knower of the jar," the point is that cognition is cognized only in a form other than the jar and so forth, and not by itself. For [as for] cognition... [Note:
In the manuscript *kh*, the reading "tān paśyasi iha" appears in place of "jñānasya hi"].

Its innate form is the mere generality of consciousness (*jñānasāmānyamātra*), permeated by infinite cognitions delimited by their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*). For this very reason, it is undelimited by space, time, and form. Furthermore, it must be understood that this [consciousness] is indeed unobjectifiable (*avedya*), because its cognition cannot be established by means of anything other than itself. || 14 ||
Whatever appears to you, contemplate that with a focused mind:
the power of manifestation, devoid of any manifested object, is the support for all manifestations. (15)
If it is asked, "In that case, how can I know this reality of the Self, which consists of such undivided knowledge? he says: "That which...
That whatever knowledge of yours appears in the form of a jar or other objects, [know it] through a sound intellect—free from fallacious reasoning—and clarified by true faith.
"Discern it through wisdom. If one asks, "How is it to be discerned? he says: "By illuminating.

For in that cognition of a jar, there are two components: the jar and the cognition. Therein, the jar is the object to be illuminated, and the cognition is the illumination itself. That very cognition, whose nature is pure illumination—

It is called the power of manifestation (*bhāna-śakti*). And that [power] is devoid of anything manifested (*bhāsya-hīnā*). For the object manifested by that power of manifestation—whether it be the clay of a jar or its blue color—is not included within its own nature; therefore, the meaning is that it is "devoid of anything manifested. Regarding the phrase "all manifestations" (*sarva-bhāna*): these are the manifestations that occur through the distinction of objects or the distinction of persons.
Although appearing as if distinct, they all share a common substratum; for,

setting aside the objective aspect of manifestations, their non-difference is established because their essential nature cannot otherwise be described as divided, since they consist of the totality of all manifestations.
The meaning is that it is the substratum of all manifestations. || 15 ||
"O son of the sage, know that very thing to be the Reality (tattva);
it is only the object of knowledge, not the act of knowing itself, since that which does not shine forth by itself cannot be known. (16)
That very [power] is the aforementioned power of manifestation (*bhāna-śakti*). That reality (*tattva*) is the reality of the pure conscious self (*śuddha-cid-ātma-tattva*).

Thus, it has been stated that the reality of the self is precisely the power of manifestation, which pervades all cognitions limited by adjuncts (*upādhi*). Now, the difference appearing within cognition is indeed not...
He begins to prove that [the object] is indeed natural, but rather adventitious (*aupādhika*), stating: "It is only the cognizable.

That which appears in the cognition of a jar or the like—the aspect of the cognizable consisting of the jar and so forth—is precisely that [object], not the *vitti* (consciousness), nor the cognition itself.
The sense is that for the aspect of cognition, the jar or the like, which has become the cognizable, is not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). As for that...
Because the object of knowledge does not manifest by itself; the object of knowledge is not of the nature of consciousness. The sense is that this is because it lacks self-luminosity. || 16 ||
Cognition is distinct [from the object], for the object of knowledge is never known by itself;
indeed, the object of knowledge, which possesses a different form, is known only through cognition. (17)

Therefore, consciousness (*vitti*) is distinct from the object of consciousness (*vedya*). It is by means of this consciousness that the object of consciousness is known—that is, it is manifested. For the object of consciousness never manifests by itself, as consciousness does. Since the object of consciousness is known only through consciousness, the object of consciousness possesses a nature distinct from consciousness. || 17 ||
Cognition is never divided by the various distinctions of its objects;
for distinction is a property of the object of cognition and can never touch the cognition itself.

Therefore, consciousness (*vitti*) is not divided anywhere by the diversity of its various objects of knowledge (*vedya*). If it is objected that there is indeed a division in consciousness, as in the cognition "this is the cognition of a jar, not the cognition of a cloth"—just as one says "this is a jar, not a cloth"—the author replies "no," stating "division" (*bheda*). [This division is merely figurative], just as one says "this is the space of the jar" or "this is the space of the hut."
Thus, that distinction belongs only to the perceived attributes of the jar and so forth; there is not even a touch of distinction in consciousness itself.
Since the differentiation of forms appears only on the side of the object of cognition, see for yourself that, having separated the object by means of the intellect, it is devoid of form.

If it is asked why the perceived difference does not belong solely to the cognition itself, he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*). For a difference must be stated as being due to a mutual difference in form (*ākāra*);

and since such a difference in form—consisting of shapes such as white, blue, or circular—is manifested only on the side of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), it cannot belong to a cognition that is devoid of form (*nirākārā*).
This is a distinction. He says "Behold! to show that this is not a statement based on indirect inference, but rather something perceived directly:
having separated the object of cognition from consciousness by means of a subtle intellect and reasoning free from conceptual construction, behold consciousness itself as devoid of form. 19.
Just as a mirror is a replica of the reflected object, so too this consciousness,
by assuming the form of the visible, attains a state of manifoldness.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Like a reflection" (*bimba*). For just as a mirror, though uniform in nature, assumes the likeness of various reflected objects, so too this Consciousness (*cit*), by virtue of sustaining (*dhṛti*) the forms of perceivable things such as jars—namely their shapes like blue or circular—attains a manifold appearance, yet it does not [itself become manifold].
The meaning is "from itself. || 20 ||
Thus, this consciousness is to be known as having a form distinct from the objects of knowledge;
however, that consciousness, which is the refuge of the universe, is not knowable by its own nature.
"Thus" means in the manner described; this [consciousness] has been introduced as that which is excluded from the object of knowledge (*vedya*).

This very consciousness (*vitti*), by virtue of its form being excluded from the object of knowledge—once the exclusion of objects of knowledge has been effected through negation, such that "this is it" and "this is not it"—remains as a residual form.
It would be unknowable, yet this consciousness is not unknowable by its very nature in such a way [as to be unmanifest].
Regarding the phrase "the refuge of the universe": limited consciousness, such as that which perceives a jar or other objects, might somehow be considered knowable;
however, pure consciousness, being the refuge of the universe and unlimited, is not something that can be known in this manner—this is the intended meaning. || 21 ||
Since this form belongs to the knower, it is therefore not an object of knowledge;
O Aṣṭāvakra, contemplate clearly that one's own innate nature is of such a kind.

He states the reason for this with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). Since pure consciousness (*śuddhā vittiḥ*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the knower (*veditṛ*), it is not an object of knowledge (*vedya*). This is the intended meaning here: because pure consciousness is the form of the knower, the operation of an instrument does not apply to the agent; therefore, it is not an object of knowledge in that sense, but rather [is known] as the Self (*ātman*).

When the negation has been made that "this is not the Self" regarding everything— including the manifest body and all objects of cognition— then, because the nature of one's own Self cannot be negated, it remains as the limit of negation;
subsequently to the negation of everything else, when nothing other is perceived, it shines forth by itself for one who has emerged from that [state of negation].
Through the reflective awareness of that state, it becomes as if an object of knowledge; such is the nature of the knower-self. || 22 ||
You are neither the body, nor the vital breath, nor even the mind, because of their instability.
The body is a collection of constituent elements; how then could that be your true nature? (23)

He explains the very manner of this investigation: "But you are not [the body]," and so forth. Because of instability—that is, because the body, vital breath, and mind lack a stable, unitary form—once the self's stable, unitary nature is established through continuous recognition (anusandhāna), how could the body and other such things, which consist of unstable elements like a collection of tissues, be your true nature? || 23 ||
And that [notion], when appearing as an object other than itself, would transcend the "I"-cognition;
in this way, both the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas) would likewise transcend the "I"-intellect.

He states another reason as well: "And that" (*tac ca*). This means the body and so forth. Because the self (*ātman*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it possesses a nature that always flashes forth as "I. The body and so forth, however, are not like that. For at the time when other objects such as a jar are being perceived, the body and so forth—
"One should transcend the manifestation of 'I', the notion of 'I-ness' (ahaṃdhī)"— meaning one should go beyond it so that the thought "I" no longer manifests.
Nor should it be argued that even at the time of cognizing a jar or similar objects, the body and so forth manifest as "I," for at the time of cognizing a jar,
the body and other such things are perceived as possessing qualities such as being fair-skinned or tall.

Because vibration (*sphuraṇa*) is not established by experience, and because there would be the consequence of the body being described as "tall" or "fair" in cognitions of jars and the like; or else, the phrase "appearing as another object" means that this [body] appears as a non-self, such as "this is my body," by way of having another as its object. Not so.
Nor should it be said that at the time of the manifestation of a jar or the like, there is no manifestation of the pure Self as "I" (aham);

for if that were the case, it would follow that the jar and so forth would not be manifest. For a lamp or similar object, which is considered to be a source of illumination, is never seen to illuminate a jar or the like while itself remaining unmanifest. And at that time...

It must be stated that even while manifesting, it does not flash forth as "I," because manifestation is necessarily associated with some specific form; it cannot be mere nothingness, for that would result in insentience (*jaḍatva*). Thus, by virtue of its inherent fitness, it manifests precisely as "I. For this very reason, those who maintain the self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of cognitions [assert that] "I [know] the jar..."

The form "I know" is thus accepted. Furthermore, if the manifestation of one's own nature as "I" were not admitted in cognitions such as that of a jar, then the impossibility of doubt or error—such as "Am I or am I not?"—would be logically untenable. Nor [is it the case] that at the time of the cognition of a jar, there is [the thought] "I."

It must be stated that throbbing (sphuraṇa) has only the body and so forth as its object; for although such a state might be possible at the time of cognizing a jar or the like, it is impossible at the time of cognizing the body and so forth, such as in the cognition "this is my body.
Nor [is it possible] at the time of the cognition "this is Caitra."

It must be stated that even for Caitra’s conscious self, there is a transcendence of the "I-notion" (ahaṃbuddhi) by virtue of being an object of the "this"-cognition (idam-pratyaya); for at that time, Caitra’s "I"-cognition remains intact. Nor can it be said that the "I"-cognition is absent during deep sleep or meditative absorption (samādhi), because [the "I"-notion exists] even at those times in accordance with the subsequent recollection (smṛti).

Because the fulfillment of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) is accepted as such and is desired by all. Now, if it is argued that since the Self is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) during deep sleep and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the conceptual cognition "I" (*aham iti*) cannot then be possible—here the knowers of the truth of the scriptures say: indeed, the cognition of "I" is of two kinds: the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)...

"And it is with conceptualization (savikalpa). Conceptualization (vikalpa) means difference; that which is accompanied by this is "with conceptualization" (savikalpa). That which is other than this is "without conceptualization" (nirvikalpa).
Thus, the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), which has as its object the body and so forth delimited [by limiting adjuncts], is "with conceptualization" because it has difference as its object.

However, in the states of meditative absorption (samādhi) and deep sleep, the notion of "I" is [without conceptualization] because it does not touch upon difference, having as its object only the essential nature (svarūpa).

Regarding the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*): one should not suspect that the admission of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) during meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and similar states entails the presence of the "threefold circle" (*tripuṭī*). For at that time, since only the notion of "I" remains, there is no manifestation of the distinction between the cognition, the cognizer, and the object of cognition. This has been stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: [The text continues with the citation from the Pratyabhijñā.]

"That reflective awareness which, though its nature is light, has speech as its body, is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for that is defined as a determinative cognition (*viniścaya*) dependent upon a duality. (1.53) This very "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is designated in the scriptures by such terms as "full I-ness" (*pūrṇāhantā*) and "full manifestation" (*pūrṇakhyāti*). Of this...
The conventional expression “the body of speech” and so forth is used because full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) is perceived as the cause of the future signs of speech;

however, it should be understood that in reality, at that time, there is no state of being composed of gross sound. Furthermore, such a nature of full subjectivity cannot be denied of the non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpacit*).

Because [otherwise] insentience (*jaḍatva*) would result. As it was stated by the blessed Hari: "If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, illumination would not shine forth, for that [speech] is what performs reflective awareness" (*Vākyapadīya* 1.124).
And likewise in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*: [text follows].

"Otherwise, they know that the nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); for even when light is colored by an object, it is like a crystal, which is comparable to something insentient. (1.42).
Thus, the state of being the "I" (*ahaṃrūpatā*) of the non-conceptual conscious self has also been stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:
"In childhood and so forth, as well as in the waking state and so forth—thus, even through all changing states—that which persists, shining inwardly as 'I' at all times" (*Daśaślokī*, verse 7).
"In this way" means: distinct from Your nature. He states that very reason [for its being distinct] with the words "the notion of 'I'" (verse 24).
This supreme consciousness does not exist apart from the notion of "I";
therefore, O Aṣṭāvakra, in reality you are that consciousness which knows all.
Since the consciousness of "I" does not exist apart from pure awareness (cit), you are therefore that very awareness which knows all. || 25 ||
Behold: with the eyes turned inward, those of supreme intellect perceive their own self as pure consciousness alone, seeing it at the very moment of instruction.

He says that such a reality of the Self is not something beyond perception: "Behold" (paśya). If it is objected, "But surely we shall behold it at a later time through the sequence beginning with hearing and followed by reflection and so forth," he replies: "The instruction" (ādeśa). The meaning is: at the very time of the teaching, that is, at the time of hearing. [One beholds] one's own Self. 26.
This eyeball of yours is not the eye; that which is called the mind is declared to be the eye, for by it you see in dreams—that is said to be the primary eye.
If it is asked, "How can there be a turning back of the eye, whose very nature is to radiate outward? he says:

"The eye. What is intended here by the term "eye" in the phrase "the turned-back eye" is not this physical eyeball visible to all externally, but rather the mind itself that is expressed by the word "eye. But how [can the mind...]?
If it is argued that "the state of being the eye" (*cakṣuṣṭvatva*) [is the defining characteristic], he states that this very thing is the primary eye with the words "by which" (*yena*).

The sense is that because the operation of the physical eye in the waking state is dependent upon the mind, and because in dreams the mind itself takes the form of the eye, the mind alone is the primary eye. || 27 ||
O Brahmin, listen: even its turning back is proclaimed;
for one whose eye does not turn back indeed sees nothing at all. (28)
The meaning is that for one whose primary eye is the mind in the form of mental resolve, nothing at all is seen without the turning back of the mind. || 28 ||
If, desiring to see something with the eye, one should turn back completely from all other objects and firmly fix [the gaze] upon that very thing alone; || 29 ||

He explains this very point [with the verse beginning] "didṛkṣuḥ": if a person desiring to see something withdraws the mind from all other things besides that which he wishes to see, and joins the mind to that very object of desire with steadiness and firmness, then that [object] shines forth; such is the syntactical connection. || 29 ||
Then it appears clearly, but never at any other time;
for at other times, that which stands before one does not appear clearly anywhere.

That [object] was desired to be seen; however, at other times—during periods when the mind does not turn back toward it—it does not appear clearly in its specific form even though it is manifesting. Thus he says: "at other times. (30)
It would be as if it were unmanifested for one whose eye does not turn back;
know, O Brahmin, that the state of the ear, the skin, and the other senses is likewise established. (31)
Thus, he says "it appeared as if not appearing" (abhāta), meaning it appeared indistinctly, as if non-existent. This is just like the case of the eyes.
The sense is that only for one whose mind has turned inward is there the perception of sound and other objects through the ears and other senses. || 31 ||
In the same way, the manifestation of pleasure and pain occurs through the mind alone;
nothing can be experienced by one whose mind has not turned back [toward the object]. 32.
He states that the manifestation of mental pleasure and so forth is likewise [dependent on this]: "By the mind" (manasā). Therefore, the person ought to know [this];
hence, there must be single-minded devotion to that and the turning away of the eye.
When the mind is turned inward, it becomes pure and manifests its own true nature. (33)

Therefore, because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is observed in the manner described, the mind’s exclusive orientation toward that which is desired to be seen and its exclusion from everything else is required for the manifestation of that which is desired to be seen; this is the implied meaning.
It is the mind itself, turned inward, that manifests the innate nature of the Self. Not [the senses].
(The meaning of this will become clear immediately hereafter. The sense is that his exclusive devotion to that [goal] is required. || 33 ||
In this regard, I shall explain it to you; listen with focused attention.
This Self is beyond the range of the senses, yet it is also within the range of the mind.
In this regard, concerning the manifestation of the Self, listen to that specific distinction which I shall declare: it is both beyond the range of the mind and within its range. (34)
In this matter, many who fail to distinguish between scripture and tradition become bewildered;
for the state of being an object of the mind exists externally in two ways. (35)

In this context, [the author] begins to explain the fact that the self is an object of the mind and the absence thereof—starting with the word "mind" (manaḥ)—referring to external objects which are not the self. (35)
The turning away from all other things constitutes the supreme state of being intent upon that [the Self];
for even when there is merely a turning away of the mind from other things, [that is the goal]. (36)

He explains this very twofold nature [with the words] "the first" (*ādyā*). Turning away from things other than those desired to be seen is the first; the second is "devotion to that" (*tatparatā*), which is exclusive concentration upon that. Thus, the mental activity (*manovyāpāra*) is of two kinds: the turning away from others and devotion to that. If it is argued, "Let there be merely the turning away from others, but let there be no devotion to that," he says: "from others" (*anyebhyaḥ*). || 36 ||
That which does not manifest any object at all among the peripheral sounds, for that reason, even here, the supreme mental activity is directed toward that [object]. (37)

In the state of indifference during neutral occasions, since no object whatsoever would be manifested, it follows that for the manifestation of an object here, another mental operation—namely, being intent upon that [object]—must be admitted as the second [factor]; this is the remainder [of the argument]. Even though there is no fault in the mere fact of being intent upon that being a mental operation, [the point remains].
Nevertheless, it should be understood that in the phrase "merely intent upon that," the meaning of the word "mere" (mātra) itself is the exclusion of anything else. || 37 ||
Thus, while for entities that are differentiated there is the appearance of two functions,
since consciousness is non-differentiated, it cannot be so in this case.

In the manner thus described, there is the manifestation of excluded entities—that is, limited objective things—by means of two mental operations; however, this is not the case with respect to the conscious self (cidātman), for its manifestation does not depend on two such operations. || 38 ||
But it may manifest [an object] merely by turning away from others, just as [one looks] into a mirror placed in front for the purpose of seeing something. (39)

If it is asked, "In that case, how does its manifestation occur?", he says: "From others. The mind, consisting of consciousness, would manifest itself. Here is an illustration: "Just as," for the purpose of seeing a certain reflection. (39)
However, for one who desires to see a reflection in a mirror, the turning away from other objects and the facing toward that [mirror] are indeed required. (40)

For one who desires to see the original object (bimba), it is necessary that [the mirror] be turned away from reflections other than that [specific] reflection and be oriented toward that reflection. (40)
When one desires to see the sky reflected in a mirror, one’s purpose is indeed fulfilled merely by turning away from other things. (41)

Having stated that the manifestation of any reflection within a mirror requires two operations, he says "the sky" to indicate that in the perception of the sky—the reflection not contained within it—there is no requirement for two operations. [This is] in comparison to other reflections; [it is] the fulfillment of the purpose.
The establishment of the manifestation of reflections and the sky. || 41 ||
The sky pervades everywhere and is always present within the mirror; yet, being unturned away from it, it does not appear when covered by other things. (42)

He establishes this very point with the words "the sky" (*gaganam*). The sky reflected in the mirror is all-pervasive, eternally present, and not excluded from any of the reflections contained within it.
This being the case, if one asks why it does not appear at the time when the reflections appear, he says: "But by others... (*kiṃtu cānyaiḥ*).
The meaning is: "by other reflections. || 42 ||
Since it is the substratum of all and is omnipresent, yet covered by those [afflictions], it shines forth only through their mere reversal. (43)

It is also the substratum of all reflections; though it is present everywhere within the mirror, it is not covered by those reflections. Therefore, by the mere turning away from the reflections, the sky shines forth. Even so, for one who stands as a bystander, there is still a requirement for that which transcends the manifestation of that sky.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that for one who desires to see a reflection and is intent upon a mirror, the appearance of space occurs through the mere disappearance of another reflection by virtue of that very intentness toward the mirror; no other intentness is required.
(kh, g: this is to be meditated upon). || 43 ||
Thus, O twice-born one, consciousness is all-pervading, abiding as the support of all; at all times it is completely full within the mind, like space.

He applies this to the subject of the analogy with the word "thus" (*evam*). "At all times" means that even at the time when objects such as jars appear, it does not abandon its omnipresence and other qualities, just like a mirror or the sky.
As in the mirror, so in the mind, [consciousness] is full, like the sky. (44)
Therefore, it is maintained that the mind consists merely of the exclusion of other objects;
see, O Brahmin, where and when is consciousness not manifesting? (45)

Because the mind is always full, it is maintained that the "turning back" (pratyāvṛttatva) of the mind consists merely in its turning away from non-self-objects toward the manifestation of the nature of the self as consciousness. The intended meaning here is this: [of the pure conscious self...]

Since it is established that the mind is all-pervasive by virtue of its being situated within the mind, and since the mind—which is distinct from other things and self-luminous—is turned inward toward itself, its natural orientation toward itself is already established; thus, there is no need for a newly acquired state of being directed toward that [Self]. This establishes that consciousness is all-pervasive with the words: "Behold" (paśya). || 45 ||
When and where that [object] does not exist, neither then nor there;
therefore, in the manifestation of the conscious self, the mind undergoes a transformation into something else.

That is the locus (*citi*). "Not when" (*na yadā*)—the meaning is that if [it were said] "when" (*yadā*), which refers to time, or "where" (*yatra*), which refers to space, then it would not be established.
Therefore, the connection is that because [consciousness] is all-pervasive (*sarvagatatvāt*), only the exclusion of anything else (*anyaparāvṛtti*) is required. || 46 ||
Mere dependence alone never constitutes being present before one;
it is precisely because of the absence of such presence that [the object] is held to be unknowable. (47)
Since facing [toward the object] is established by its very nature, it is not required as something new; thus he says, "not at all.
He states that the fact that the conscious self (cidātman) is not an object of knowledge is said precisely because of the non-reliance on such facing; thus he says, "facing," etc.
For this very reason, that reality is said to be cognizable by the pure mind alone; for purity with respect to other [objects] is indeed mental exclusion. (48)

"From this very fact" means: precisely because the state of being unobjectifiable (avedyatva) is caused by the lack of dependence on [the presence of] an object. If it is asked, "What is this purity?", he says:
"From others... (verse 48).
This alone is said to be the supreme means for the knowledge of reality:
for as long as the mind is not pure, how can there be knowledge? (49)

This very thing is the exclusion of others; it is the supreme, primary means (*sādhana*). He states its status as the primary means by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "as long as" (*yāvat*). || 49 ||
When the mind is indeed pure, how could knowledge not certainly arise?
Every means for its purification is exhausted right here.

He states its primary importance even through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the words "pure" (*śuddha*). He says that all means taught in the scriptures, such as ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsanā*), are employed solely for the purification of the mind, with the words "exhausted" (*upakṣīṇa*). Here, in this context, it refers to the purification of that mind. || 50 ||
Whether it be ritual action, spiritual practice, or even detachment and the like, these are employed solely for the purification of the mind and not otherwise. (51)

He states this very point clearly with the words "or action," etc.; by "etc.," devotion, faith, and so forth are included. And it is not otherwise; there is no direct application [of these] toward knowledge. || 51 ||
"Therefore, that supreme form shines forth with a pure mind.
Having heard what was spoken by the king, Tvaṣṭāvakra spoke again:
Therefore, since all means of accomplishment are exhausted in the purification of the mind, the supreme body is the Self whose nature is pure consciousness; [this was taught] by King Janaka. 52.
O King, you have stated that mental withdrawal from other objects is indeed [the means];
yet if that [withdrawal] is merely the supreme consciousness, it shines forth by means of the mind. (53)

You have stated that if the mind’s turning away from other things— disregarding its devotion to them— is accomplished as a solitary state directed toward nothing else, then the nature of the pure Self shines forth. (53)
In that state of deep sleep, the mind would then be completely withdrawn;
therefore, what need is there for other means? Through mere sleep alone, one's purpose is accomplished.

If this were so, then because the mind is turned away toward something else during deep sleep, that nature of the Self would manifest; consequently, spiritual practices would be rendered useless. Thus he says: "What is the use of practices? (54)
Thus questioned by the Brahmin, the king then spoke:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall tell you the resolution. (55)
"Paryanuyuktaḥ" means being questioned or challenged. || 55 ||
It is true that in deep sleep there is a complete turning away of the mind; yet how could its state of being dissolved manifest that [turning away]? (56)
He states the resolution: "It is true," and so forth. It is true that there is a complete transformation (*parāvṛtti*).
This [transformation] consists in the mind's nature as mind (*manastva*), its capacity to manifest objects, and its state of purity, which is to say, its *sāttvika* nature.
[The mind] was dissolved, meaning it was shrouded by *tamas*. Therefore, how could it manifest that pure consciousness?
How is it that [it is] not non-existent? || 56 ||
The sky does not appear on a mirror smeared with collyrium; however, in some cases it appears merely through its reflection from other objects. (57)
Here is an illustration: "by means of soot" (verse 57).
Thus, when the mind is smeared by sleep or distracted by other things, it cannot manifest consciousness anywhere, precisely because of its unfitness [for that task]. (58)

He applies this to the case at hand with the word "thus" (evam). By means of sleep, which is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*) and a dull power (*jaḍa-śakti*), the mind would not manifest consciousness anywhere, precisely because it has undergone a transformation into something else. If one asks why, he says:
"because of its unfitness" (ayogyatvāt). || 58 ||
Otherwise, why would that [consciousness] not arise even from clods of earth, walls, and the like?
Therefore, it indeed shines forth through a mind that is both capable and pure. (59)
It should appear to a fit mind. If even an unfit object were to appear,
then even when clods of earth and the like are grasped in the hand, moved away from others, turned around, and placed facing a jar or similar object, the jar and so forth [would still appear].

He asks: "Why does that consciousness not manifest through mere transformations alone? He replies: "Otherwise. [This means] by walls and so forth, through walls and so forth. Therefore, he says: "From that," meaning that for one whose mind is pure and fit [for yoga], the pure consciousness shines;
hence, nothing at all manifests to a newborn infant.
Moreover, listen as I speak: for when a mirror is smeared with soot, [the reflection does not appear]. (60)
Therefore, because the mind of a newborn infant is incapable [of such reflection], he states another solution accompanied by an illustration:
"Even though the reflection of ink exists there unperceived, it is not distinguished due to its contact [with the surface], for its own nature has not been removed. (61)

When a mirror is smeared with ink, the reflection of that ink is unperceived by anyone. If it is asked, "If it exists, why is it not perceived?", he replies: "Because of its adhesion. If it is further asked, "On what basis is this postulated?", he replies: "Because of its nature.
That is, because its nature is to grasp a reflection situated directly in front of it; [it is so] because of non-exclusion, meaning non-departure from that nature.
The sense is that in a mirror, whose nature is to receive a reflection of what is placed directly before it, the reflection of soot is necessarily required. || 61 ||
Likewise, the mind situated in deep sleep is indeed closely merged with sleep itself;
therefore, because there is no turning away from anything else, it would not illuminate that [sleep]. (52)
He applies this to the case at hand with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). Like a mirror smeared with soot, the mind is smeared by sleep;

therefore, due to this connection with sleep, because it grasps the form of sleep and because there is no turning toward anything else in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the mind would not manifest that pure consciousness (*cit*). || 62 ||
Therefore, even sleep and forgetfulness may occur for one who has emerged [from samādhi], as well as that state of delusion which is experienced during that condition. (63)

Therefore, because sleep is perceived during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the recollection of sleep—expressed by one who has emerged from deep sleep as "I was not aware of anything"—is possible; for the point is that recollection is invariably preceded by perception. This is precisely because it is admitted that there is a conjunction with sleep during that state of deep sleep.
It should be understood that even that which was postulated on the basis of the recollection, "a state of delusion consisting of sleep is experienced," is possible. || 63 ||
I shall explain that to you correctly; listen attentively with a concentrated mind.
The state of the mind is twofold, distinguished by the categories of illumination (prakāśa) and reflection (amarśa).

Having thus refuted the possibility of the manifestation of the Self during deep sleep— on the grounds that in deep sleep the mind, having dissolved its nature as "mind," is intent on sleep and lacks any other mental activity— he now begins to refute that defect further by analyzing the distinctions between the essential natures of deep sleep and the other states, starting with the word "tataḥ" (therefore). That...

The distinction between deep sleep (suṣupti) and samādhi is as follows: the state of illumination (prakāśa) is the state of objective awareness (āmarśa), while [the state of] reflective awareness (vimarśa) is the state of [subjective] contemplation. || 64 ||
That which is the resting upon external objects is called *prakāśa* (manifestation);
that which is the reflection upon it within itself is indeed declared to be *vimarśa* (self-awareness). || 65 ||

He clarifies the essential nature of these two with the words "externally" (*bahih*). The resting of the mind upon external objects—that is, its connection with them—is *prakāśa*; it is called the state of manifestation. This [state] consists of the fusion with words, such as "this object is of such-and-such a nature," regarding that very same object which has been grasped as a reflection within the mind itself.

Discernment (*vicāra*) is that very reflection (*vimarśa*), the state of reflection. This is the intended meaning here: first, the mind becomes connected with objects such as a jar through the doorways of the senses and so forth. At that time, the object, such as a jar, manifests in an undifferentiated form, devoid of any verbal designation such as "this is a jar. This alone—

Those who maintain that the validity of cognitions is extrinsic (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) assert that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), which is the cause of conceptual cognition (*savikalpajñāna*), is always inferable. This very [non-conceptual cognition] is described in the scriptures as the "illumination of the object" (*vastuprakāśa*) or the "perception of the object" (*vastudarśana*). Thus, in the moment immediately following the illumination of the object...

The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—which consists of the investigation of the essential nature [of an object] as excluded from others through the association with words such as "this is such-and-such" regarding that mental form which is a reflection of external objects like jars—is called conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*). This is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "In this way, 'this is such-and-such'..."
That by virtue of which an object is established as a means of valid cognition is itself a new arising of its own manifestation.

Thus, that [consciousness], whose nature is internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is the uncontradicted cognition regarding an object that is designated by a single name and is undivided by space, time, and so forth. (2.16) Without differentiation among objects, manifestation would be free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
Reflective awareness (vimarśa) is conceptual (savikalpaka) due to its association with words and its differentiation [of objects]. || 66 ||

He states this clearly: "In 'manifestation' (prakāśa), [it is] due to non-differentiation"—that is, manifestation of things in an undifferentiated form would be non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka); this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Due to differentiation," that is, through the differentiation of forms by means of association with words, the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of things would be conceptual (savikalpaka). || 66 ||
"This is of such a kind"—free from the intermingling of words, this non-conceptual light consists in the direct perception of the thing-in-itself. (67)
Furthermore, this very point is explained by means of two verses, beginning with "This" (ayam). || 67 ||
"This is of such a kind"—this [cognition] is rooted in the perception of the object; its form is permeated by words, and it manifests as the nature of deliberation (vicāra). (68)

That which has vast perception as its non-conceptual root cause—of which it is said, "this is of such a kind"—is that whose manifestation consists of investigation; the remainder is that it is conceptual (savikalpaka). || 68 ||
Whether internal, novel, or otherwise, it is celebrated as "reflective awareness" (vimarśa).
Among these, that which is a novel manifestation is declared to be of the nature of direct experience (anubhava). (69)

Such an internal reflection (*vimarśa*), which has the mental image as its object, is declared to be of two kinds: the novel (*abhinava*) and the other (*anya*). Among those two, that which is the novel manifestation consists of direct experience (*anubhava*). (69)
Another [aspect] consists of the continuity of memory and arises from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, the mind always exists endowed with these two kinds of powers. (70)

That which is other than this—the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of recollection and synthesis (*anusandhāna*), arising from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and produced by impressions born of prior experience—is thus the conceptual construction. In this manner, the mind (*manas*) becomes endowed with a twofold power of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*amarśa*), characterized respectively as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). || 70 ||

This state of deep sleep, whose nature consists of both sleep and light, persists for a long time; yet when it abounds in the awareness of waking, it is called the "unconfused state" (*amūḍhadaśā*). (The word *amūḍha* is to be read as two separate words: *ca* and *amūḍha*). || 71 ||

Having thus established the twofold nature of the mind, he begins to demonstrate that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is a state of delusion: "Sleep" (*nidrā*). Deep sleep is of the nature of that light which has sleep as its object—that is, non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). It is long-established.

The meaning is that [the waking state] is not momentary, unlike the non-conceptual cognition of a jar or similar objects. The word *ca* has the sense of "but. As for the waking state (*jāgaradaśā*), it is "abounding in reflective awareness" (*āmarśabahulā*); that is, it is that in which reflective awarenesses—which are conceptual cognitions—are numerous. Because many conceptual cognitions arise following each single non-conceptual cognition, it is "abounding in reflective awareness," and for this reason, it is called "waking" (*jāgrat*). Thus, because of that reason, it is [so designated].
One who is not deluded is called "awake. The intended meaning is that delusion occurs due to the absence of self-awareness (*āmarśa*) in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). || 71 ||
Since deep sleep consists of a density of light and is characterized by insentience,
for this very reason, it is like the density of light from a lamp and such.

The meaning is that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is dense with light and consists solely of light, yet it is devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Therefore, deep sleep is of the nature of stupor; that is to say, it is a state of stupor. Herein lies the point:
for although the conscious self (*cidātmā*) has the singular form of light, it is not [merely that].

[The Self] is not like a fragment of stone, as would follow from the consequence of insentience for those who maintain that the Self is merely quiescent; rather, it is of the nature of a vibrating light. Indeed, since this nature of vibrating light does not exist in lamps and the like, there is a distinction from the insentient. This very state of being a vibrating form is consciousness (*caitanya*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the power of cognition (*citiśakti*), action (*kriyā*), and vibration (*spanda*).

In the Āgamas, this is expressed by such terms as "supreme egoity" (*parāhaṃtā*). Precisely because it possesses such a nature, the Supreme Self has the power to bring forth the activity of the universe. As the Teachers have said: "If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is capable of bringing forth [creation];
if it were not so, the Lord would indeed not be able even to stir."

(Sau0 La0 1.1). For here, the intended meaning is not that Śiva is joined with the power of *māyā*, which is indefinable and illusory in nature; rather, [it is said]: "At that very moment, you bestow upon him the state of union (*sāyujya*) with yourself" (Sau0 La0 1.22), and "Blessed are those few who worship you, the wave of consciousness-bliss" (Sau0 La0 1.3).

"Thus, O Great Illusion (mahāmāyā—this being the reading of the printed text), you are some ineffable Fourth State (turyā), whose boundless majesty is difficult to comprehend; you cause the universe to wander, O Queen of the Supreme Brahman" (Saubhāgyalaghupañcāśikā 2.58). And so it is said.
For this would result in the untenability of defining the nature of the power currently under discussion.

Nor should it be argued that because the world is like the horn of a hare, and its activity shares that same character, the acceptance of the Supreme Self as having the aforementioned nature is purposeless; for such an argument would entail the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). [This applies] to the world...

For if one were to admit that [the Self] is like the horn of a hare, then there would follow the consequence that such scriptural, traditional, and authoritative texts as "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), "The origin etc. of this [world] from which" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2), and "That from which this has arisen," are merely the ravings of a madman. Nor is this the case.

It should not be argued that there is no consequence of falling into the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) because the supreme conscious self (*paracidātman*) is accepted [as existing]; for the referent of the term "acceptance" is unestablished, as it is included within the world and is therefore as unreal as a hare's horn.

Now, one might object: "If the nature of the world is accepted, the consequence of duality (*dvaita*) follows; for it is said: 'There is not even the slightest diversity here' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19)."

If you argue that this contradicts such scriptural passages as (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.19), you are ignorant of this non-dualistic (Advaita) scripture. For nowhere does the non-dualistic scripture teach the voidness of the world; rather, it says, "Being alone was this in the beginning" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1) and "All this has that as its self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).

"Non-difference from That [the cause] results from such terms as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa-śabda) and others" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14). Since the reality of the world is established by such scriptural passages as "This very Supreme Self alone shines forth in the form of the world," there is no loss of non-duality (advaita-hāni) either; for, just as a city reflected within a mirror is not distinct [from the mirror], [so too is the world not distinct from Brahman].

Even though an object appears, its nature remains that of the mirror alone; thus, there is no loss of the mirror’s non-dual character. Likewise, when the world appears within the Supreme Consciousness-Self, it is nothing but the Supreme Consciousness-Self;

therefore, there is no loss of the nature of non-duality. As for the negation found in such passages as "There is no diversity here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19), [it serves to negate the reality of perceived difference].
What is intended is that [the state] culminates in mere duality. For this very reason: "The knowledge that 'everything is illusion' is proclaimed as ignorance;
the knowledge that 'everything is Śiva'—that the knowers of knowledge recognize as true knowledge."

The net of appearances such as jars, cloths, and carts, when known to be unreal, is ignorance; indeed, that same net of appearances such as jars, cloths, and carts, when well-known to be real, is wisdom. (Yogavāsiṣṭha 6, pūrvārdha 10.45)

Thus, there is a consistency with the arguments set forth in the *Sūtasamhitā*, the *Vāsiṣṭha*, and other such works. Accordingly, the Supreme Consciousness-Self, by its own absolute freedom— known as *māyā*— manifests its very own Self in the form of a manifold cosmic diversity, from the perspective of the individual souls (*jīvas*) who are limited conscious selves manifested by that [Self].

When the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) has been thus manifested, the perception of duality (*dvaitadṛṣṭi*) is the bondage of living beings, and the perception of non-duality (*advaitadṛṣṭi*) is liberation. Sovereignty is the manifestation of the universal form; the manifestation of individual souls, as well as the manifestations of their bondage and liberation—all this is like reflections in a mirror, [displayed] by the Blessed One.
Manifested through its own autonomy, it has as its sole essence mere manifestation, like a dream or a city of one’s imagination.
(In the manuscripts *k* and *kh*, it reads: "But the manifestation is of the nature of the singular consciousness of the Other"; thus everything is faultless.
And so, within the Self that is the supreme consciousness, there exists the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which constitutes its very life. This is the case even in deep sleep.

The connection is as follows: "stupidity" is determined by all the learned to be due to the obscuration of the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) by the reflection of the dull power (*jaḍa-śakti*) consisting of sleep.
Although objects such as jars are of the single essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*), they possess dullness precisely because the aspect of reflective awareness does not manifest therein.

Thus it is also with the light of a lamp, however intense it may be. Therefore, the essential point is that the non-emergence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is the cause of insentience (*jāḍya*). || 72 ||
This state of utter delusion is determined in every way by all the wise;
the first-born sleep, which is unmanifest, is here called the Great Void (mahāśūnya). || 73 ||
It has been stated that in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), due to being covered by *nidrā*, there is no manifestation of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). If one asks, "What is this *nidrā*?", he says:

"*Nidrā* is the first-born unmanifest (*avyakta*). This refers to that external manifestation which is inseparable from the contraction of one's own nature (*svarūpa-saṅkoca*) that appears at the very beginning of creation.
