Because it is the very nature of the wall-painting of the universe—as previously illustrated—and because it is the first to arise, it is called "the first-born" (*prathamaja*). Since it is not manifested by any form anywhere, it is "unmanifested" (*avyakta*).

Precisely for this reason, due to the absence of form and so forth, it is the "great void" (*mahāśūnya*). In this context, it is referred to as "sleep" (*nidrā*) within deep slumber (*suṣupti*). || 73 ||
Deep sleep has no common state [of objectivity], yet its manifestation occurs;
even at the time of perceiving an object, the mind in the waking state is of this same nature.
"There is no path for the universal" means that the object (padavī) of the cognition "it does not exist"—

that is to say, the absence of the universal of the perceptible— is precisely the aforementioned unmanifest (avyakta), which is absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva). This is because, in accordance with the memory "I did not know anything while in deep sleep," the phrase "nothing" refers to the absence of the universal of the perceptible.

The sense is that it "shines forth. For deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is indeed the state of the manifestation of such sleep; the perception of objects is the non-conceptual [cognition] of jars and so forth. Even at that time—just as in the waking state—the mind remains entirely deluded, as it is in the state of deep sleep. (74)
However, it is obscured by the flood of conceptual constructions arising in subsequent moments;
in deep sleep, this is due to its being densely packed with the manifestation of unmanifest power.
If it is objected that, unlike in deep sleep, no state of delusion is ever experienced while one is awake, the author replies with the words "But... (*kiṃ tu*).

In the waking state, because the non-conceptual [awareness] is momentary, the state of delusion is concealed by the aggregate of conceptual cognitions that arise immediately thereafter. Now, it is well known elsewhere that the mind (*manas*) dissolves in deep sleep.

If it is asked how the mind can be said to be the illuminator of sleep— given that in passages such as the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* it is stated, "At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved" (1.13)— the author replies with the words "In deep sleep.
The intended meaning is that because the mind consists solely of the manifestation of unmanifest power (*avyakta-śakti*), the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) does not emerge.
The connection is with the word "discerning" (viviñcantī). || 75 ||
Those who possess discernment investigate thus: "The mind has dissolved.
Even at the time of perceiving an object, the mind remains dissolved in this very way. (76)

Regarding the term "mind" (*mana*): because at that time the mind is stable due to its uniform nature of being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), those skilled in discernment discern and determine that the mind has dissolved simply by the absence of moment-to-moment changing modifications. [This occurs when the mind] has attained a state directed toward the object of cognition (*cetya*).

Based on such statements as "the essence of consciousness (cittattva) is called the mind (citta)," it is said that the very reality of the conscious self (cidātmatattva), appearing as if it were expanding toward objects, is termed the "mind" (manas). He states [in verse 76] that because in deep sleep there is no state of expansion due to its stability, the mind is equivalent to the time of indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) of objects such as jars, which consists in the seeing of things—thus he says: "the object" (vastu).
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall tell you a secret from my own experience, wherein even the learned who discern the most subtle truths may be bewildered. (77)

Having thus established the insentience (*jaḍatā*) of deep sleep, he begins to establish the distinction between meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and deep sleep with the words "Listen" (*śṛṇu*). He states the reason for its secrecy with the words "Wherein" (*yatra*): even those who are skilled in discerning the true nature of subtle objects [fail] regarding this matter about to be described.
They become deluded. || 77 ||
Non-conceptual meditative absorption, deep sleep, and the perception of reality—
these three are of one kind, due to the density of their luminosity.

He states that very point: "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*). Non-conceptual *samādhi* is the abiding of the conscious self (*cidātman*) as the nature of pure self-luminosity. Deep sleep and the perception of objects are the manifestations of unmanifest states such as jars and the like. These three are of one kind and equal. Among them:

The reason is "due to the density of manifestation. This means because its nature as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has not yet emerged. For in all three aforementioned states, there is an absence of the gross conceptualizing power (*vikalpa-śakti*) consisting of reflective awareness—which takes the form of words such as "this is such-and-such"—because they consist solely of pure manifestation (*prakāśa*).
The intended meaning is the density of light. || 78 ||
For ordinary people, a distinction is indeed perceived based on a difference in reflective awareness;
in that case, the firm conclusion is simply that the cause is a difference in the objects of cognition.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is there a distinction in conventional usage such as 'this is deep sleep' or 'this is meditative absorption' (samādhi)? he replies:

"Due to the difference in reflective awareness" (*vimarśabheda*). The meaning is: although there is equality in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is a distinction due to the difference in reflective awareness consisting of the subsequent recollection (*anusandhāna*) and so forth that arises after each state.

One should understand that there is a difference in the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) following these [states]: after *samādhi*, "I remained silent for such a long time"; after deep sleep (*suṣupti*), "I was not aware of anything at all"; and after perceiving an object, "this is a jar. If it is objected that since the cause is the same, the effect must necessarily be the same, so how can there be a difference in reflective awareness? To this he says: [The text continues: ...the difference in the nature of reflective awareness is due to the difference in the objects of cognition. Just as a single seed produces different sprouts according to the differences in soil, water, and fertilizer, so too, although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is one, its modifications (*vṛtti*) differ according to the differences in the objects of cognition. Therefore, even though the cause is the same, the difference in the effect is established by the difference in the objects. Thus, the diversity of reflective awareness is explained.

It should not be argued that there is also a difference in the essential nature of samādhi and the other [yogic states], because they lack the conceptualization (vikalpa) consisting of the commingling of words, and thus they possess no difference in their essential nature. || 79 ||
In meditative absorption (samādhi), there is pure consciousness alone; in sleep, it is indeed unmanifest;
and in perception, there is the appearance of differentiation—thus the object of manifestation exists in three ways. (80)

He speaks of the distinct objects themselves [in the verse beginning] "In meditative absorption" (*samādhau*). Pure consciousness (*kevalaciti*) is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), unmingled with the forms of visible bodies and so forth. The "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) is said to be that which constitutes the external referent (*bahiḥpadasyārthabhūta*). "Distinct appearances" (*bhinnabhāsa*) are things such as jars, appearing as differentiated (*vyāvṛttatvena*).

Although consciousness possesses no objectivity (*vedyatva*) in the sense of being illumined by another, nevertheless, since its dependence upon the activity of the pure mind has been established, it should be understood that it possesses a form of objectivity in some sense.
Even when there is a difference between the objects of illumination, the light itself remains purely non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Therefore, they declare him simply as "dense with light. || 81 ||
If it is argued that when the objects of illumination differ, a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of samādhi and the other states is necessary, he replies with the words "bhāsyeti.

However, the appearance (*bhāsa*) of samādhi and the rest is not different, because they are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). For conceptual construction, which is the mingling with words (*śabdānusambheda*), is what differentiates the essential nature [of a cognition]; since that is absent in the present case, there is no difference in essential nature—this is the intended meaning.
Because it is devoid of reflection due to the non-distinction from sound, they declare that the various states such as *samādhi* are dense with light. || 81 ||
Because both meditative absorption (samādhi) and deep sleep last for a long time, they are subsequently and clearly reflected upon by everyone. (82)

If it is objected: "Since the triad beginning with *samādhi* is equal [to deep sleep], why is the perception of reality (*vastudarśana*) not clearly reflected upon by everyone at a later time, just as in the case of *samādhi* and deep sleep? he says: "And *samādhi*... [and] "...because it occurs over a long period. The meaning is: because it is not momentary (*akṣaṇikatvāt*). || 82 ||
Because of its momentariness, perception is indeed not clearly deliberated;
likewise, meditative absorption and sleep, being momentary, are not deliberated. (83)

Just as the perception of an object is not clearly reflected upon at a later time because of its momentariness, so too the momentary meditative absorption (*kṣaṇika-samādhi*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*) are not reflected upon; thus he says "in this way" (*evam*). (83)
Just as deep sleep is momentary, so too does meditative absorption (samādhi) exist;
indeed, deep sleep is perceived by those with subtle vision through their familiarity [with it]. (84)

Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) exist at the beginning of the waking state and so forth. Among these, momentary deep sleep is perceived by those of subtle vision through familiarity with the experience of prolonged deep sleep;
thus he says "it" (referring to deep sleep), meaning "momentary. || 84 ||
O Brahman, due to a lack of familiarity, this subtle samādhi is not perceived by any living beings, even during their states of worldly activity. (85)

Because it has not been experienced and is therefore unfamiliar, concentration (*samādhi*) is not reflected upon; thus he says: "Concentration" (in versions *k* and *kh*, this phrase is followed by "... [omitted] ... for all," which is absent in others). It is subtle and momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
If one asks, "To whom does this momentary concentration belong? he replies: "For all. That is, even in all ten states.
The meaning is "even in the states of waking and so forth"; the grammatical construction is "there are concentrations" (samādhayaḥ santi). || 85 ||
Subtle meditative absorptions (samādhis) exist, yet they do not shine forth due to a lack of realization;
that which occurs while awake without reflection is declared to be samādhi. (86)
If it is asked, "In that case, why do those meditative absorptions (samādhis) not manifest? he says: "Due to lack of proficiency" (*avyutpattyā*).
This means because of a lack of familiarity with their own nature. If it is asked, "What kind of absorption occurs during the waking state? he says: "In the waking state...
That which is non-reflective—that state of absence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—is absorption. || 86 ||
Samādhi is defined as the mere absence of reflective awareness (vimarśa);
therefore, its status as samādhi is established both in deep sleep and in [pure] perception. || 87 ||
He states the definition of samādhi: "vimarśa... (verse 87). For this very reason, it is established that both deep sleep and the perception of reality possess the nature of samādhi.
However, these two do not possess the status of primary samādhi;
because they are permeated by the latent impressions of the awareness of duality, they lack primacy. (88)
If it is argued that, in that case, the fruit of samādhi would be achieved through deep sleep (*suṣupti*) alone, he says "no"—"but rather" (*kiṃ tu*).

Regarding these two, namely deep sleep and the perception of reality: "by the non-reflection on difference" (*bhedāmarśanena*). "Difference" (*bheda*) is the objective world which is not the Self; the "reflection" (*āmarśana*) upon that is conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), and its "residual impression" (*saṃskāra*) [is what is meant].

Because it is pregnant with— that is, joined to— a subtle form consisting of power (*śaktimaya*), there arises after deep sleep a conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) that reflects upon the distinction between the forms of sleep and the jar, such as "I was not aware of anything" and, following the perception of an object, "This is a jar. Of these two...

That subtle form consisting of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), which is composed of potentiality (*śakti*), exists within its own cause during deep sleep and during the perception of reality. The sense is that proponents of the theory of pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) accept that the effect persists within the cause in the form of a latent impression. This refers to the subsequent reflection following meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Difference should be understood as having the pure conscious self alone as its object. || 88 ||
In the waking state, perception occurs in the form of non-reflection;
nevertheless, I shall explain it to you—listen with respect, O son of a sage. (89)

He says "vision" (*darśana*) to show that just as deep sleep and samādhi are non-momentary and consist of non-reflection (*avimarśana*), so too do momentary deep sleep and samādhi exist within the waking state. That which is the vision consisting of momentary deep sleep and samādhi regarding the self and the intellect (*citta*) during the waking state— this too [is such].

The meaning is that it is of a nature consisting solely of non-investigation, just like the perception of a jar or similar objects. [Objection: "In that case, does it not follow that even *samādhi* would be a state of insentience (*jaḍa*), similar to deep sleep (*suṣupti*)? To this he says: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Although equality has indeed been reached, the meaning is that I shall nevertheless explain a subtle distinction. || 89 ||
That which is unmanifest and first-born has no commonality whatsoever;
for its appearance is simply "it does not exist," consisting of absolute non-existence. (90)

Thus, having promised a specific definition in order to exclude the charge of insentience against samādhi, he begins to examine the object of deep sleep (suṣupti) and samādhi for that very purpose: "the unmanifest" (avyakta). That which is the first-born at the beginning of creation, the external referent of the word "outside," namely the unmanifest—that does not exist; it is neither a universal (sāmānya) nor an individual (nāsti).

It is the object of the cognition of generality; that is to say, the absence of the general class of objects of perception. He points to experience as evidence for the claim that the absence of the general class of objects of perception appears during deep sleep, stating:
"it does not exist. For indeed, that which appears in deep sleep appears precisely as "it does not exist" in a general sense.

Therefore, the meaning is that in that state, only the absolute non-existence of the visible manifests. Since one who has emerged from deep sleep (suṣupti) possesses the memory, "I was not aware of anything," it must be stated that the experience in deep sleep is precisely "it does not exist. Thus, the intended sense is that the general absence of all objects of perception is established as what is manifesting at that time. || 90 ||
This is called deep sleep; it is the inert power (jaḍa-śakti) of consciousness, because that which appears in perception does not exist as a locus of manifestation.
And thus, he states that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is established as a state of insentience (*jaḍadaśātva*): "This" (*eṣā*).

That very unmanifest power of insentience (*avyaktātmakajaḍaśakti*), which consists of the absolute non-existence of the general class of objects (*dṛśyasāmānyātyantābhāvarūpā*) belonging to consciousness—the Supreme Consciousness-Self (*paracidātman*)—is what is called "deep sleep. For this reason, in deep sleep, regarding perception—that is, knowledge—...

Knowledge, while appearing, has no locus for its appearance; there is no appearance [of objects], as the absolute non-existence of the perceivable is the locus—that is, the object—of that which is inert power. This is because, in the perception occurring at the time of deep sleep, it is precisely the object of the appearance of memory—namely, "I knew nothing"—that appears as knowledge.

The meaning is that, since the nature of deep sleep as being of the form of an insentient power is established by the rule that it possesses a form identical to that of memory, deep sleep itself is of an insentient nature. || 91 ||

Therefore, that which appears in samādhi as consciousness (citi) is of the nature of Brahman; it would otherwise be merely deep sleep (suṣupti), associated with the perception of insentience. || 92 ||

"From this" means: because of the recollection upon emerging from deep sleep (*suṣupti*). The meaning is that deep sleep alone—being conjoined with the perception of the insentient, which is the knowledge of the absolute non-existence consisting of the power of the insentient—is [what is meant], and not *samādhi*.
Now, one might ask: why should the power of the insentient not also belong to that which appears in *samādhi*, just as it does in deep sleep?

As for what was said [in the verse], "in samādhi": *samādhi* is the state of the mind—which has turned away from objects that are not the Self—abiding in the form of the inwardly directed conscious Self (*pratyak-cid-ātman*). Consequently, there is an absence of the manifestation of inert power (*jaḍa-śakti*). Now, one might object: since the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the inwardly directed consciousness, possesses a limited form...

If it is argued that even the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which consists of the power of insentience (*jaḍa-śakti*), has manifestation during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he says: "That [consciousness] has the form of Brahman. The meaning is that consciousness, manifesting in meditative absorption, has the form of Brahman because it is "vast" (*bṛhat*) due to its being undivided (*anavacchinna*). || 92 ||
How could that Goddess Suṣupti—who consumes time and space, who does not destroy appearances, and who consists entirely of existence—be anything other than such? (93)
If it is asked, "Whence comes the unlimitedness of consciousness as it appears in samādhi?", he says: "Devouring" (*bhakṣiṇī*).
This means that it has the nature of devouring—that is, swallowing—time and space.
Precisely at the time of the appearance of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as a jar, which delimit space...

Just as there is no appearance of the space within a jar or similar objects at any time other than when they are present, so too in the present case, there is no appearance of the spatial, temporal, and formal limitations of consciousness— which are but sprouts of its insentient power— from the objects of perception [or from the locations] by means of the mind.
Because it does not appear as something transformed, because it is undivided, and because it is the nature of universal consciousness (*sāmānyaciti*),
that consciousness is of the nature of Brahman— devouring time, space, and so forth— as it is the form pervading all limited cognitions that manifest every object.

This is the state of being (*bhāva*). For one whose consciousness is limited, there arises the notion that "here now this form exists" and "here now this form does not exist"—it is through this that the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) is established. However, because [consciousness] is unlimited, it destroys the appearance of absolute non-existence by means of the realization that "this does not exist. Regarding this [realization] that "it does not exist":

The absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that constitutes the meaning of the negative particle *na*, although its very life depends on the light of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), abandons its emptiness by being infused with existence through its connection with the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). The intended meaning is that even the empty referent of the negative particle attains existence through its relation to consciousness; thus, [the cognition] destroys the mere appearance of non-existence.

Therefore, since a connection with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is impossible in any way—whether as a positive entity or as a negative absence—that Supreme Consciousness, the Goddess whose sole nature is luminosity, consists of existence and is a single mass of being; how could She ever be insentient by nature, like deep sleep?
This is the meaning. || 93 ||
Therefore, one cannot achieve the goal of life merely through deep sleep;
thus, Janaka awakened Aṣṭāvakra with teachings on liberation.
Therefore, because it is of the nature of insentience (*jaḍa*), it is distinct from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He concludes with the words "he caused [him] to awaken" (*bodhayāmāsa*);
thus, the grammatical connection is "he caused [him] to awaken. || 94 ||
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Aṣṭāvakrīya section of the Jñānakhaṇḍa within the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the seventeenth chapter:
Having heard what was thus spoken by Janaka, Aṣṭāvakra questioned the king again; O Bhārgava, listen with care to that which I shall relate. (g: listen with self-restraint).
Here, the momentary concentrations (kṣaṇasamādhi) have been described by means of illusory verses;
neither the human goal nor the sequence for attaining knowledge is achieved through them.
Thus, even while awake, there exist momentary concentrations. || 1 ||
O King, regarding what you have said—that even in the state of worldly activity there exist subtle states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—explain that clearly to me according to the *tantra*.
That is the locus of momentary meditative absorption. 2.
"In which states of life are those whose nature is non-conceptual consciousness found?
Thus questioned by him, the noble-minded king then spoke.

He clarifies this very point with the words "in the states" (*daśāsu*). This refers to which intermediate states between the waking and dreaming states, which consist of empirical activity (*vyavahāra*). Those meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) consist of the non-conceptualizing consciousness (*nirvikalpa-cit*). He whose "receptacle" (*āśaya*), that is, the mind (*citta*), is "great," meaning unlimited; he whose mental faculty has the form of unlimited consciousness—this is what is meant by "ever-absorbed" (*nitya-samāhita*). || 3 ||
Listen, O Brahman, I shall explain the meditative absorptions (samādhis) regarding worldly affairs:
when one is first embraced by a fresh beloved.

I shall now declare those meditative absorptions (samādhis) that occur in worldly experience. He says that very thing: "By the beloved" means by one who is dear to the mind; "by the new" means by one never before enjoyed; "at first" refers to the commencement of the onset of passion;
"when embraced" means when firmly held in an embrace. || 4 ||
At that time, for a moment, the person knows neither the external nor the internal;
he does not remain overcome by sleep—that is declared to be samādhi. || 5 ||

"At that time" means at the moment of embracing; "at first," for just a moment, one does not perceive the external—such as direction, place, or time—nor the internal, such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. Now, one might object: if there is an absence of perception of both the external and the internal, one would be in a state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).

He says [in response]: "Not overcome by sleep. He who remains even without having fallen into a state of delusion through the onset of sleep—this is "momentary samādhi" (kṣaṇasamādhi) during the state of worldly activity. || 5 ||
O Sage, when something that has been long desired and deemed unattainable suddenly comes to pass, that indeed is [the result of merit].
Whatever object has been desired for a long time, [obtained] suddenly at a time when its acquisition was not expected. (6)
At that time, for a moment, the person knows neither the external nor the internal;
he does not remain overcome by sleep—that is declared to be samādhi.
Then, the passage beginning with "he does not know" has fulfilled its purpose. || 7 ||
Walking somewhere unexpectedly, fearless and with a joyful mind, if he should suddenly behold a tiger or some other creature equal to death; || 8 ||
"Unexpected" here means that it is not an object of possibility, such as [the thought] that a tiger or similar creature might appear; "equal to death" means comparable to death. || 8 ||
At that time, for a moment, the person knows neither the external nor the internal;
he does not remain overcome by sleep—that is declared to be samādhi.
When one suddenly hears that his own very beloved son or others, as well as his master engaged in household duties, have indeed died while being free from illness; || 10 ||
Capable and competent in the work of the household. || 10 ||
At that time, for a moment, the person knows neither the external nor the internal;
he does not remain overcome by sleep—that is declared to be samādhi. || 11 ||
Now I shall speak of another way as well; listen to the arising of samādhi:
within the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there exist samādhis. (12)

Thus, when great bliss, joy, fear, or sorrow arise suddenly, at that initial moment, the mind remains in its own nature without conceptual reflection. Having stated that this is the state of momentary concentration (*kṣaṇika-samādhi*), he begins to describe other [forms] as well, starting with the word "now" (*atha*). This refers to the occurrence of concentration in another way, by means of a different method.
[He explains] that very state of stability: "The waking state," and so forth. The waking state (*jāgrad*) is the condition of the activity of the external senses.
The dreaming state (*svapna*) is the condition of the gross activity of the mind alone (*manas*). The deep sleep state (*suṣupti*) is the condition of the mind's activity during sleep.
Furthermore, in the interval between these, the mind remains for a moment without reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*). These are the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
O Sage, for one who perceives something at a distance with one-pointed intellect, the mind attains the nature of length, like a leech moving along a series of blades of grass. (13)

He states another method: "At a distance. Just as the mind of a person looking at the sun in the distant vault of the sky lengthens from its support on one blade of grass to its support on another blade of grass, so too the mind situated in the body extends its length as far as the solar orb.

Because a distracted mind, due to its flickering here and there, does not attain length in a straight form, it is said that one must use "one-pointed intelligence"; this means having a mind solely intent upon the solar orb.

Always observe the mind in the body as consisting of the appearance of the body, and likewise in objects as consisting of the nature of objects; in the interval between these two, observe that which is called the non-conceptual mind.
When the mind exists in this way, within the body it takes the form of the body, and in the state of the solar orb it takes the form of the [inner] object.
This is *samādhi*. Thus, at all times during the perception of external objects, the mind exists;
observe that. Nor should it be said that the mind is of the nature of space in the interval between the body and the sun, for [the mind is not] space.

Because the mind, being formless, cannot possess the form of the sky; nor can it be said that the sky is perceived by the mind through the gateway of the eyes, for perception through the eyes is possible only for that which possesses color-form (*rūpa*), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving even air. And as for how the mind could have the form of the body and so forth at that time—

It must be stated that this is "abiding in its own nature alone," because even though it assumes various forms through the limitations of the body and so forth, its abiding in its own nature remains intact due to its formlessness in the interval. He will explain the state of absorption (*samāhitatva*) of such a portion of the mind on the occasion of describing the highest type of knower (*uttama-jñānin*), who consists of great mental concentration (verse 19).

From verse 80 of this chapter up to its conclusion, the following is observed: Janaka and others, though liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), remained engaged in activities such as governing their kingdoms; because one part of their mind was occupied with worldly affairs while another part was concentrated in meditative absorption (*samāhita*), they were described as being "always absorbed" for that very reason.
It is consistent. || 14 ||

What is the use of saying more here? Listen, O Subtle Investigator (*sūkṣmavimarśana*): in worldly transaction, the cognition of even a single person does not appear as something unitary. (The reading *sūkṣmavimarśanam* is the universal one.)

What is the use of speaking at great length? Listen: subtle meditative absorptions (*sūkṣma-samādhi*) exist at all times; they are thus described. By the address "O Subtle Investigator" (*sūkṣma-vimarśana*), the subtlety of the meaning about to be stated should be understood.

In worldly experience, during both waking and dreaming states, the continuous stream of cognitions taking on the forms of jars and other objects is established by universal experience; for it is not otherwise.
All that is indeed one single cognition, because the difference in its forms is established by universal experience. || 15 ||
This extended worldly discourse consists of a collection of fragmentary cognitions;
for this very reason, indeed, all the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) describe it in such a manner. (16)

This pervasive worldly discourse consists merely of a collection of fragmented cognitions delimited by various forms; the intended meaning is that if cognition were a single unity, such discourse would be impossible.
It is precisely because cognition is not a unity that the teachers who propounded the systems of other schools—the Sugata, Kaṇabhuj, and so forth—[held their respective views].
All [the sages], beginning with Prabhṛti, describe them. || 16 ||

Whether regarding the self or even the intellect as differentiated by the distinctions of each moment, one remains in a state free from conceptual construction amidst the flood of intervening moments. (17)

Regarding what they describe, he says: "The self" (*ātmānam*). The Sugata stated that the self is precisely the stream of cognitions differentiated by momentary distinctions. Kaṇāda, however, said that cognition (*buddhi*) is the attribute (*dharma*) of such a self.
By this, the agreement of other teachers regarding the existence of momentary cognition is to be understood as having been stated. Thus, in the case of the distinction of cognitions...

Once this is established, he states the subject at hand: "In the interval between those" (*tadantare*). Between momentary cognitions, a state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*) persists. It is not the case that the cognition of a jar is identical to the subsequent cognition of a cloth, because their unity is not perceived and because it would entail the consequence of them being a single composite object (*samūhālambana*). And thus, this being established:
Since the intermediate state between different cognitions is indeed unavoidable, the non-conceptual nature of the mind remains intact at that time. || 17 ||
O son of Kahola, know this: for those who truly know, there is meditative absorption at every moment;
for anyone else, such absorption is like the horn of a hare.

The grammatical connection is: "Know it to be like the horn of a hare. For those who know—that is, for those who are familiar with the true nature of samādhi—it is different; [it is] other than that which has not realized the true nature of samādhi. || 18 ||
Having heard what was spoken by Janaka, that twice-born man asked again:
"O King, how can there be non-conceptual composure when one is thus engaged in worldly activity? (19)
Having heard that there is meditative absorption (samādhi) for people at every moment—thus, the connection is: "if there is meditative absorption at every moment" [then so on]. || 19 ||
If it were present in all [beings], then how could there be transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), given that in deep sleep and even in perception, it appears as inert and unmanifest? (20)

The meaning is: since samādhi alone accomplishes the goal of human life (puruṣārtha), how could there be further transmigratory existence? If it is objected that this [samādhi] does not accomplish the goal of human life in the same way as deep sleep (suṣupti) and so forth, he replies with the words "In deep sleep" (suṣuptau).

[This means: in non-conceptual knowledge, which is the perception of the reality consisting of consciousness, and in deep sleep, where unmanifest objects such as jars—which are insentient by nature—[are perceived].
And because it does not illuminate [the truth], the connection is that it does not accomplish the purpose of man. || 20 ||
Since it does not serve as a means to achieve human goals, and since samādhi is indeed non-conceptual, its nature being that of pure, manifest consciousness—how then can there be rebirth again? 21.

"Concentration is not like this," he says, [introducing the verse] "But concentration... [meaning] non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), which does not manifest any insentient object other than its own nature. If one asks why it is so, he says, "Pure...
Because it is non-conceptual, it consists in the manifestation of its own full nature; therefore...
Furthermore, immediately after attaining such a samādhi, how can there be further transmigration? || 21 ||
For this very consciousness, known as the non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi), which is the cause of the supreme good, is that which destroys the lineage of ignorance. 22.
"There is no other knowledge than this that destroys the multitude of ignorance," he says: "This very [knowledge]" (verse 22).

The word *vijñāna* refers to the knowledge that is one's own essential nature (*svarūpabhūta*) manifesting during meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "That which is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), that is this very [knowledge]."
"Tell me this, O Indra among kings, which destroys all doubts.
Thus questioned, the protector of the earth spoke to that bull among sages.
This dialogue of questions and answers is the destroyer of all doubts. || 23 ||
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim this supreme secret:
through ignorance, this cycle of worldly existence has proceeded from beginningless time. (24)

This is the supreme, ultimate secret. He begins to explain that through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), ignorance—the cause of saṃsāra—is ceased, starting with the words "from ignorance" (*ajñānāt*). This [fact] is established by the experience of everyone. 24.
Existing as a continuous flow consisting of the manifestations of pleasure and pain, it is indeed experienced by everyone at all times as something uninterrupted, like a dream. (25)

"What is the nature of saṃsāra? he asks, and says: "It is like pleasure," and so forth. Now, one might object that since saṃsāra is established by the experience of all beings, it must be real; and because it would not cease, there would follow the undesirable consequence of no liberation. To this he replies: "Like a dream. Although it persists as a continuous flow at all times and is uninterrupted, [it is nonetheless unreal] for everyone.
The meaning is that it is not real, because it is experienced like a dream. || 25 ||
But it has been clearly demonstrated that its cessation occurs through knowledge alone;
that knowledge, though accompanied by conceptual construction, is the dispeller of ignorance. (26)

Because it is experienced like a dream, it is rooted in ignorance; therefore, the learned have determined that the cessation of that ignorance, along with its effects (*sakārya*—variant: *sarvakārya*), occurs through knowledge alone.
Thus he says: "cessation. If one asks what kind of knowledge is that which removes that ignorance, he says:

"Regarding the phrase *tajjñānam* (that knowledge): since it is the primary means for the destruction of ignorance—that is, the complete eradication of ignorance—that knowledge, known as conceptual (*savikalpa*), consists of the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "I am He. This is the essential point here."

For one who possesses the means of knowledge such as dispassion (*vairāgya*), there arises through hearing (*śravaṇa*) an indirect (*parokṣa*) cognition of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). Then, once the Self has been indirectly known, doubt is removed through correct reflection (*manana*). Thereafter, through meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the force of contrary conceptions—which are dependent upon deep-seated impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of the notion of "I" and so forth directed toward the body and other such things—[is eliminated].

It is the immediate knowledge of the pure inner self (*pratyagātman*). From that arises the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—in the form "I am He"—which penetrates the indivisible oneness of the supreme self as understood through the scriptures and the inner self. This very recognition...

It is the destroyer of ignorance, which is the root of saṃsāra. Now, if this [knowledge] is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), then, according to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*—"For a determinate cognition (*viniścaya*) is said to depend on a pair"—it would be erroneous because its object is duality; therefore, it could not be the remover of ignorance.
If it is argued that this is what is called "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*), we reply: this is not a cognition whose object is duality.
For instance, when someone previously saw Caitra in Daśārṇa and another asks, "Who is this? he replies, "This is that very Caitra.
Thus, by the sentence "This is that Caitra," duality is not understood; rather, it is the answer to the question [that establishes identity].

For, if the latter [the answer] had as its object only the essential nature [of the Self], it would result in being inconsistent with that [question]. Nor can the identity of those two contradictory things denoted by the words "that" and "this" be established,
such that the answer could possibly share the same subject matter as the question.

Therefore, by means of both components—*tat* ("that") and *idam* ("this")—the mere physical body of Caitra is indicated as extracted [from its context]. Likewise, in the present case as well, by means of both components of the expression *so 'ham* ("I am he"), it is the undivided pure consciousness alone that is recognized; thus, there is no fault. But then, how is this...?

If it is argued that [this state] is conceptual (*savikalpa*), listen: it is conceptual because it is similar to well-known conceptual cognitions in its lack of identity with the components of verbal expression (*abhilāpāṃśa*). Alternatively, it is conceptual because it is distinct from well-known non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpa*) which are devoid of the components of verbal expression. Now, one might object that even knowledge consisting of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*)...

"It has precisely the same object as the present recognition. Now, if it is asked: "Since even the knowledge consisting of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) has precisely the same object as the present recognition, how can that [absorption] be the remover of ignorance?"—it is replied:
Even when the object is the same, there is a difference in the result due to the difference in the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) that produce them. For instance,
in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*),
the mind— which is turned away from non-self entities— is assisted by the presentation of the referents of the words "that" and "I."

The reason is that in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind alone functions without depending on the presence of verbal expression (*nirukta*). Indeed, mere recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "this is that very jar" has as its object only the undivided reality (*akhaṇḍavastu*).
Thus, even though the recognition "this is that jar" shares the same objective domain as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose object is merely the jar, [it differs in its nature].

It should be noted that since everyone must accept that the difference in results is caused solely by a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no need here to postulate anything such as an "unseen force" (*apūrva*). || 26 ||
Ignorance is not removed by non-conceptual cognition;
non-conceptual cognition is not contradicted by anything. || 27 ||

He begins to demonstrate that non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), which is distinct from recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and takes the form of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), does not destroy ignorance (*ajñāna*). He asks: "Why does it not cease [ignorance]?
and answers: "Because it is not contradictory," stating: "Non-conceptual... (verse 27).
Non-conceptual consciousness is the support for conceptual [consciousness];
it is well-established like a wall for various and manifold appearances. (28)

Here is the illustration: "variegated" (vicitrā). The meaning is that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is the substratum for conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), just as a wall is the substratum for variegated appearances. || 28 ||
Non-conceptual knowledge is called "pure" knowledge; for it is precisely therein that conceptual constructions arise, and thus it is "with conceptualization. (29)

If it is asked how this is so, he says: "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*). "Pure knowledge" (*kevala-jñāna*) means pure knowledge devoid of the reflection of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-pratibimba*). "In that very [state]" means in pure knowledge itself. For just as in a perfectly clean mirror, at the moment when a reflected image faces it...

The sense is that while it is indeed of the nature of a reflection, it is called "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) because, within pure cognition itself during the state of mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), there is the manifestation of various forms. || 29 ||
Ignorance is precisely that knowledge called "conceptual" (savikalpa) and nothing else;
it exists in many forms, abiding as both cause and effect. (30)
If it is asked, "Even though non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has conceptual knowledge (*savikalpa*) as its basis, why does it not contradict ignorance (*ajñāna*)?", he says:
"Ignorance... [and] "...not the other. This means that it is neither the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), nor is it the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
Herein lies the acceptance of scripture regarding the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness (*śuddhacid-vapuṣ*): [text continues].
That very state of radiant manifestation which is distinguished from the insentient is itself autonomy (*svātantrya*), designated as the power of *māyā*.

In that same way, the world is manifested preceded by the manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*). Alternatively, the phrase "not other than" has the purpose of negating the mere absence of knowledge; that is ignorance, which is of the nature of a cause.
That which consists of action is of many kinds. || 30 ||
The cause has been declared to consist in the non-manifestation of one's own fullness;
the conscious self (cidātman) is indeed complete because it is devoid of all limitation. (31)

He analyzes this very twofold nature [as follows]: "The cause" means that ignorance is the form of the cause, which is precisely the non-manifestation of one's own fullness (*svātmapūrṇatvākhyāti*). Now, one might raise the objection: "But 'non-manifestation of fullness' refers to the absence of manifestation, which is indeed the absence of knowledge. In response to this doubt, he explains the very meaning of the term *pūrṇatvākhyāti*.
In order to analyze [the nature of the self], he first defines fullness: "The conscious Self" (cidātman). || 31 ||
For the practitioner of the means of limitation, such as *kalā* and the rest, there exists that manifestation of the self as being incomplete. (32)
If it is asked, "From what does the avoidance of limitation arise? he says: "By means of limitation.

For the cause, the motive, or the basis of limitation—whether time, space, or form, such that one might say "this exists now," "here," or "in this way"—only these three are well-known. Yet even these three cannot serve as delimiters of the conscious Self (cidātman), just as a mirror [cannot delimit] reflections.

Because it is the very means of establishing the true nature of the conscious self (*cidātman*). For the reflection in a mirror, which serves to establish the mirror's own nature, cannot be its delimiting factor; such is the sense here as well.
Thus, that manifestation of such a self—which is undivided by time and so forth—as being incomplete is what persists.
The connection is that what is called the non-manifestation of fullness (pūrṇatvākhyāti) is the root ignorance (mūlājñāna). || 32 ||
In this context, the notion "I am here now" is indeed the root ignorance;
the manifestation of the body as the self and so forth is merely its foliage. (33)

He delineates the nature of incomplete manifestation (*apūrṇakhyāti*) with the words "here," etc. Of that very same root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), the appearance consisting of effects—predominantly like sprouts—such as the appearance of identifying the body as the self, i.e., appearances such as "I am fat," "I am blind," and so forth, is called "ignorance of the body" (*kāyājñāna*); this is the sense. This is according to the position of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*).

However, in this context, [the notion] "I am now" is to be understood as the ignorance of the primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), because it is the first effect of ignorance, arising from the mental modification (*vṛtti*) [of "I am"]. || 33 ||
Transmigration does not cease until ignorance has been removed;
however, without the perfect realization of the Self, ignorance does not cease.
He states that ignorance is the root of saṃsāra and its cessation occurs through knowledge alone: "Of ignorance... (verse 34).
And that perfect realization of the Self is well-established as being of two kinds:
indirect and direct; the indirect [knowledge] arises from the teacher and the scriptures. (verse 35)

"And that" means that which removes ignorance. "From the teacher and the scripture" means from hearing the scripture taught by the teacher; the word "arisen" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The phrase "from the teacher and the scripture" is intended to indicate that knowledge does not arise for one who has not taken refuge in a teacher. || 35 ||
Thus it is established that this is not the direct cause of the goal of human existence;
rather, whatever knowledge you may possess arising from the hearing of the scriptures [is what matters]. (36)

That is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). It is not the direct cause for the cessation of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, which is the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Janaka said to Aṣṭāvakra: "Of what kind yours... [referring to] that which arises from hearing the scriptures—that is, from listening to the sacred texts; in other words, it is indirect. || 36 ||
They do not declare that [knowledge] accepted merely through faith yields the fruit;
for direct cognition is born from the ripening of meditative concentration. (37)

The sense is that what is accepted merely through faith is not certain to yield the fruit, because indirect knowledge lacks the capacity to directly remove the delusion of saṃsāra. If indirect knowledge does not directly accomplish the goal of human life, by what means does it accomplish it?

If it is asked, "By means of what kind of direct knowledge? he says: "direct" (*aparokṣam*). He further explains that even such [knowledge], if it is merely superficial and obstructed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body and so forth, does not accomplish the goal of man; thus he says: "in meditative absorption" (*samādhau*).
The ripening of meditative absorption is its excellence; [the knowledge] produced by that is "unshakable," which is the intended meaning. This is the underlying point:

Because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of the sense of "I" with respect to the body and so forth have been associated for a long time, even when a direct perception occurs once in those of impure intellect, that superficial knowledge (*āpātajñāna*) is ineffective as it does not instill firm residual traces (*saṃskāra*); therefore, [liberation results] from that knowledge established through the excellence of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Because of the instilling of firm impressions, and because of the dissolution of the latent tendencies for the ego-identification with the body and so forth, there is no further connection with misfortune. || 37 ||
Indeed, meditative absorption (samādhi) preceded by knowledge, which is capable of destroying ignorance along with its conceptual proliferation and brings about auspicious results,
shall certainly give rise to higher cognition (vijñāna).

Regarding the term *saprapañca*: the meaning is that only immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge—firm like the [erroneous] cognition of the body as the self, unassailed by doubt or misconception, and having pure consciousness as its object—is capable of destroying ignorance along with its manifold manifestations (*saprapañca-ajñāna*) and brings about the fruit of liberation. Now, one might object:

It is the excellence of *samādhi* alone that produces such direct (*aparokṣa*) knowledge; and since this succession of *samādhis* as described exists for all [beings] during the waking state and so forth, why is there no [such] knowledge? To this he says:
"Samādhi. "Preceded by knowledge" means preceded by indirect (*parokṣa*) knowledge. [This is] *vijñāna*.
Direct knowledge. || 38 ||
Therefore, for the ignorant, no benefit arises even if samādhi occurs, just as one who does not recognize a ruby may see a gem in a treasury room [and yet remain unaware of its value]. (39)

Therefore, because there is an absence of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), the connection is that for those who lack knowledge, even when *samādhi* exists, the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is not possible. Now, one might object: even so, since those who know the meaning of the scriptures possess indirect knowledge, why would the goal of human life not be attained by them through the aforementioned natural *samādhis*?
Anticipating this objection, he begins to provide a resolution by means of an illustration with the words "Just as" (yathā). The construction is as follows:
that person who has not recognized the ruby from afar, having arrived at the treasury, even while seeing the ruby, does not know, "This is that very ruby. || 39 ||
Just as one who has never before seen a jewel does not know it, yet upon seeing it, becomes intent on it and immediately recognizes that very jewel; so too [does the yogin recognize the Self]. (40)

Just as a person who has heard of and understood a gem through hearing its description—that is, known it indirectly—might see that very gem somewhere in a treasury or similar place and become intent upon it, [that person is distinct from the former one]. (k, kh: ...having seen the gem...)
He recognizes the gem, thinking, "This is that very gem. || 40 ||
O Brahmin, even one who is highly skilled, if not intent upon it, does not recognize a jewel even when seeing it repeatedly here on earth, despite having heard of it. (41)
When another person, though having heard about the jewel, is not intent upon it, and upon seeing the jewel asks, "What is this?", then—
even though he sees the jewel again and is very clever— he does not recognize it here in this world as "this is that very jewel," for the reason that he was not intent upon it. || 41 ||
Likewise, the deluded do not find the fruit that rests upon discernment; because of their ignorance, even the learned, though possessed of learning and knowledge, do not find it.

Having thus established the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he applies it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). The ignorant, because they lack direct knowledge due to being unacquainted [with the truth], do not find through their natural meditative absorptions (*svābhāvikasamādhi*) the fruit residing in consciousness that destroys ignorance. But the wise, who know the scriptures—
The logical connection is that even those possessed of indirect knowledge produced by hearing do not understand [this]. || 42 ||
But because they lack devotion to that [goal], they do not understand it at all;
for just as one who looks at a star may see it yet not recognize it anywhere. (43)

Regarding the phrase "because of the lack of intent for that": the meaning is that it is due to the failure to attain the firm resolve that one's own body, as taught in the scriptures, is in every respect the supreme spiritual form (cinmaya) distinct from the body and so forth, and must therefore be made directly perceptible through the complete accomplishment of its means of realization.

Furthermore, because this matter is extremely subtle, he begins its elucidation by means of another illustration, starting with "Just as" (yathā). The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the deluded person does not know. || 43 ||
The deluded person, devoid of the knowledge derived from sacred learning, does not truly know even when endowed with such knowledge;
for even while seeing, he does not perceive because he lacks devotion to that [Reality].
"Devoid of scriptural knowledge" means one who lacks the knowledge produced by hearing the characteristics of the planet Venus.

Such a fool, even when seeing the star Venus in the sky at some time, does not recognize it, thinking, "This is the star Venus. Another person, though possessed of scriptural knowledge, [fails to recognize it] because he has abandoned devotion to that [subject], by me—
Because he has abandoned the dogmatic attachment that "the pupil of the eye must be known in every way," even while looking at that pupil, he does not perceive it.

But that wise man who, having heard [the teachings] concerning Śukra and Tārā and the characteristics of the directions, forms, and so forth, becomes intent on the thought, "I must know this in every way," [attains success]. || 45 ||

But that intelligent man, skilled in reasoning and deliberation, who— having heard the descriptive statements regarding the characteristics of direction, appearance, and so forth, such as "the star Śukra is located in the western direction, visible immediately after sunset, radiant in form, and white in color"— becomes intent on the thought, "I must know the true nature of the star Śukra in every respect."
The logical connection is that "he will recognize. || 45 ||
One who observes with a one-pointed mind will clearly recognize it;
others, however, are deluded by ignorance because they lack such focused intent.

With a one-pointed mind, his consciousness turned away from everything else, he applies the established meaning of the illustration to the subject of the illustration, saying "in this way. The ignorant are so called because they lack knowledge of things beyond the senses (*parokṣajñāna*); others possess the knowledge of things beyond the senses produced by the scriptures, [and thus understand] the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
The construction is as follows: "They do not understand because they avoid being intent upon [the thought], 'This reality of the Self must be known by me in every way. 46.
O Brahmin, they do not recognize their own selves during those states of meditative absorption;
due to ill fortune, they wander for alms like one who has forgotten his own treasure-trove. 47.
Even though momentary concentrations (*kṣaṇika-samādhi*) exist, those who know the scriptures do not realize their own true self due to a lack of focused intent.

Herein lies the essential truth: first, through the scriptures and other means, one comes to know indirectly that the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātmatattva*), distinguished from the body and so forth, and the reality of the supreme self (*parātmatattva*), distinguished from the world, are of the single essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*) and are unlimited.
Then, once [the object] has been known through indirect means,
one dispels all doubts by means of correct reasoning (sattarka) that accords with scripture and consists of reflection (manana), which is characterized by the contemplation of logical arguments.
Thereafter...

One performs nididhyāsana, known as meditation (dhyāna), which consists of maintaining a continuous flow of mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) in the form "I am the undivided nature of consciousness, distinct from the visible body and so forth.
By this, the contrary conception (*viparītabhāvanā*) consisting of the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth becomes loosened. Thereafter—
From the ripening of the aforementioned *nididhyāsana*,
there arises *savikalpa-samādhi*, which consists of the effortless persistence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the aforementioned form.
In this *savikalpa-samādhi*, there is the clear manifestation of distinctions such as the object of meditation and the meditator.

When this very [practice] reaches maturity through the excellence of its cultivation, such that the subtle portion of internal ego-inflation dissolves in the form of the thought "I am meditating," there remains only the state consisting of the pure consciousness that is the object of meditation;
this is *nirvikalpa-samādhi*. For this is the direct perception (*aparokṣa*) of the reality of the pure Self. Thereafter—

Having emerged from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one reflects upon the pure form of one's own self that has manifested therein and the supreme form of the Self known from the scriptures, and thus recognizes: "I am indeed That. For otherwise, due to the absence of both the deluded person and the knower of the scriptures possessing the state of being intent on indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*), there would be no arising of such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
"Because recognition does not arise, the goal of human life is not accomplished. (Regarding the phrase "due to ill fortune":
he states this very point by way of an illustration with the words "alms," etc.; the ellipsis is "and these [people] likewise. || 47 ||
Therefore, all these ten stages are devoid of the objects of meditative absorptions;
for this very reason, the non-conceptual state always belongs to children. (48)

"Therefore" means: because they are of no use for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). These are the states of the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) consisting of the intervals between the aforementioned waking, dreaming, and so forth. Precisely because they are purposeless, these are the states consisting of the intervals between the immediately preceding waking, dreaming, and so forth. Precisely because they are purposeless.

The remainder [of the meaning] is that there exists, at all times, an uninterrupted and non-momentary indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka) regarding pure consciousness (śuddhacid) even in newborn infants. || 48 ||
O Brahmin, it would not accomplish the fruit because ignorance has not been removed;
for that knowledge which consists of recognition is conceptual (savikalpaka). (49)

Therefore, that [cognition] would have to accomplish its own effect, which consists in the cessation of ignorance. If it is asked, "How is this known?", he says: "Because of the persistence of ignorance," meaning because ignorance has not ceased.
Consequently, [the cognition] consisting of recognition is of a conceptual nature, according to the reasoning already stated.
He states that knowledge alone is the destroyer of ignorance: "consisting of recognition" (pratyabhijñātmakam). || 49 ||
That very ignorance, which is the root of saṃsāra, it shall turn back;
for one's own self as deity is satisfied by [devotions] performed over many lifetimes. (50)
He states that such recognition is extremely rare due to the difficulty of attaining its means, saying "aneka...
(verse 50). The words "by performed meritorious deeds" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

At that time, and not at any other time even after millions of eons, does one attain the state of being mute; likewise, the state of sentience among those born into existence is supremely difficult to obtain.

The phrase "when it occurs" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The meaning is that at other times—in the absence of merit (sukṛta)—the state of desiring liberation (mumukṣutva) is not attained even in periods extending for millions of aeons, as one is led away by desirable and prohibited actions.
He states that the means for attaining the desire for liberation is also extremely difficult to find: "consciousness" (cetana-tva). || 51 ||
Even among those [beings], a human birth is in every way extremely difficult to obtain;
even therein, a subtle intellect is indeed exceedingly difficult to find. (52)
Even among those sentient beings, and even there, when human status has been attained. || 52 ||

Behold, O Brahmin, that which is mobile is not seen to be equal even to a hundredth part of the stationary beings; nor indeed is anything seen to be equal even to a hundredth part of those [mobile beings]. (53)
He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration: "Behold!"—even of those mobile beings. || 53 ||
There is no equality even in the state of being human; contemplate this well, for millions of humans are seen to be equal to beasts. (54)
Humanity is the human species. Even among humans, there are those who, by birth, are equal to beasts in their conduct. || 54 ||
There are also millions of other mortals who do not know what is existent or non-existent, nor merit or even sin; they are engaged in worldly activity, intent upon their desires. (55)

He explains this very point clearly with the words "ya" (those who): "sat" means good conduct; "asat" means bad conduct. Others also—though intelligent and skilled in reasoning and refutation—who, being intent on desire, have set out, that is, have resorted to the path of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*). || 55 ||
Those who take pride in a mere semblance of scholarship delight in the coming and going [of conceptual proliferation];
yet among such people, there are some others who are truly wise.

"Coming and going" refers to impermanent fruits such as rebirth in heaven and so forth. If it is asked why even those who know the scriptures do not desire the fruit of the ultimate truth, he says: "By a semblance of scholarship. This means they have become arrogant, having attained conceit through a semblance of knowledge—a mere appearance of wisdom. The point is that for those possessed of such conceit, the absence of discrimination between the real and the unreal is perfectly evident.
Among such people who have studied the scriptures, there are some of an intelligent nature who are somewhat skilled in discernment.
Even those whose minds are entirely defiled are nihilists regarding the state of non-duality;
for them, the supreme state of non-duality is obscured by the Māyā of the Blessed One. (57)

Those whose minds are defiled by the impurities of sinful impressions and who are intent on denying the state of non-duality through their adherence to duality—how can it be so? To this he says: "The knowledge of non-duality is extremely difficult to attain," [beginning with] the word "Bhagavat. (57)
How can that state be attained by all those who are blinded by illusion and possessed of little fortune?
For that state does not even enter the intellect of those blinded by illusion. (58)
"By those of little fortune" (the meaning is as in k, kh):
the sense is that non-dual knowledge arises only from the ripening of extreme merit. || 58 ||
Others are unfortunate; for even when [the truth] has ascended to their intellect here, they vainly adhere to it and repeatedly deny it through evil imaginings. (59)

Having stated that thus, for those blinded by illusion and ill-fated, the state of the non-dual Self does not become established in the intellect even when heard, he says the following to show that others, moreover, abandon it even when it has been established in the intellect:
"Those of such a kind who persist in their obstinacy deny [the truth] through false imaginings and fallacious arguments."

The sense is that they, out of a stubborn insistence that our dualistic doctrine must not be abandoned, deny [the existence of] objectless knowledge through fallacious arguments such as, "If it exists, it would be perceived just like a jar. || 59 ||

Oh, how wondrous is the illusory power of the Blessed One! Even while beholding the Great State, people indeed cast it away with their evil imaginings, like a wish-fulfilling gem held in their own hands.

He says that even this is merely the play of illusion: "Aho! [The ignorant] abandon the great state—the state of the undivided non-dual Self—as if it were a mere fragment of glass, having lost the wish-fulfilling gem already in their hands, through nothing but false conceptualizations. 60.
Those by whose propitiation her own personal deity is satisfied are liberated from illusion; they possess sound reasoning and are endowed with faith. (61)

If it is asked why this is so, he says "of those [who lack it]" because of the absence of the grace of the deity. The sense is that the attainment of the highest good occurs only through the grace of the deity, accompanied by sound reasoning and faith. || 61 ||
Those who find rest in the supreme non-duality attain the highest state;
O Brahmin, listen with self-restraint as I shall describe that sequence to you.
That sequence is the sequence for attaining the supreme good. || 62 ||
Devotion to the deity is attained through the merits accumulated over infinite lifetimes;
having propitiated [the deity] for a very long time by means of that devotion, one subsequently attains the Supreme through His grace.
Regarding the word "infinite" (*ananta*): through the merits accumulated over infinite births, devotion is attained by means of association with the virtuous and hearing of the majesty of the Deity.
By that devotion, one subsequently attains detachment; such is the grammatical connection. || 63 ||
One should attain detachment toward the multitude of enjoyments and devotion to that [detachment]; and being endowed with both detachment and devotion, as well as with faith, || 64 ||
From devotion to the deity arises discernment; from that, through the perception of defects in the multitude of enjoyments and sense objects, there comes a distaste.
"Rasa" means attachment; its departure is "vairasya"—that is to say, dispassion (*vairāgya*). From that, by turning away from sense objects, [there follows] the [means to attain] the supreme good.
He says that one becomes intent upon faith, service to the guru, and so forth: "A distaste for [worldly things]," and so on. (64)
Having obtained a true guru, one comes to know the supreme state of non-duality through his instruction;
this knowledge is indeed indirect (parokṣa), which is the realization that "non-duality exists here. (55)
"By his proclamation" means by his word. This knowledge is the knowledge produced from hearing the words of the guru.
If one asks what kind of knowledge it is, he says: "It exists. (65)
Then one should properly investigate non-duality, which is one's own self as the deity; having established it through sound reasoning, one should destroy all doubts by means of that.
Then, immediately after the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by hearing [the scriptures],

one should establish and bring about the logical justification— by means of sound reasoning consistent with the scriptures— as to whether or not this indirect knowledge of the non-dual Self as the Divine is indeed possible.
One should reflect—that is, one should bring it within the scope of certainty. By such reflection, which consists of mental deliberation (*manana*), one should destroy doubts.
By the use of the plural "doubts," it is made known that all doubts concerning the means of knowledge, non-duality, liberation, and so forth, must be destroyed. 66
Then, one should diligently and with reverence contemplate the non-dual reality known as the Self until it becomes directly perceived, even by means of forceful mental application.

Then, immediately after such reflection—that is, after the non-dual reality of the Self has been ascertained through reflection—one should meditate upon it and maintain the mind in that very form. And this should be done with reverence. Reverence means not neglecting; it is the conviction: "I must certainly know this by meditating upon it. Even if the mind is extremely fickle, one should [maintain] that very form.

Even if it cannot be held [in place], one should nevertheless hold it with effort, even by forceful means, and must not desist from that. Effort, moreover, must be most intense: pressing hand against hand, grinding teeth against teeth, and crushing limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind. (Yogavāsiṣṭha Sāra 4)

17) Thus it is stated by Vasiṣṭha (in the *Vāsiṣṭha-ukta*). The forceful method (*haṭhavṛtti*), however, consists of breath control (*prāṇasaṃyama*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth. If one asks, "For how long should one meditate in this manner? he says: "Until direct perception" (*āparokṣam*). The meaning is: until the limit of direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*). || 67 ||
Then, having made that supreme state the object of conceptual thought and meditated upon it, one destroys ignorance, the root of saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt. (68)
Then, immediately after the direct realization of the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātmatattva*) through such *nididhyāsana*,
one meditates upon the reality of the inner self and the supreme state— the reality of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatattva*)—
making them the objects of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), that is to say, recognizing them with the thought "I am He. Of this...

It should be understood that although recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is equal to non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) insofar as its object is an undivided reality, it is still conceptual (*vikalpaka*) because of the difference between its causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) and its result.
Thus, the reality of the non-dual Self, when made the object of such conceptualization, destroys ignorance. || 68 ||
Having attained the supreme state in the mature, non-conceptual meditation known as samādhi,
one subsequently recollects it and becomes possessed of recognition.

He clarifies this very point further with the word "matured" (*pakva*). When there is meditation upon the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātmatattva*), which has been ascertained through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), and that meditation has reached maturity, such matured meditation alone is non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). This is the distinction here: meditation itself, according to its varying degrees of ripeness...

There is both conceptual concentration (*savikalpa-samādhi*) and non-conceptual concentration (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). For instance, having formed the intention, "May the mind remain for a long time in the very form of the pure Self," and not forgetting that intention, one continues it in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); this is [conceptual concentration] as long as one follows the support of the object of meditation within the mind.
When the state of the mind being in the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is interrupted in the interim due to the forgetting of the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), that is *dhyāna*.

Through the excellence of the practice of such *dhyāna*, when the state of the mind being in the form of the object of meditation continues for as long as desired without the interruption of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the resolve, that is *savikalpa-samādhi*.

Through the excellence of the practice of this samādhi, when the mind continues to take on the form of the object of meditation for as long as desired, without depending on volitional mental impressions (*saṅkalpa-saṃskāra*), it is called "non-conceptual samādhi" (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). As it has been said in the *Paramānanda*:
O Maheśvarī, even when there is recollection, meditation is said to exist because of the continuity [of that recollection].
"But when there is recollection without interruption, samādhi consists of the qualities;
when there is no recollection due to the absence of interruption, that samādhi is called the fruit.
Thus, in such non-conceptual samādhi consisting of matured meditation, the supreme state is pure.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having attained and made the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātmatattva*) an object of experience, and subsequently, at the moment following emergence from meditation (*vyutthāna*), having recollected the reality of the inner self experienced during *samādhi* and the reality of the supreme self (*parātmatattva*) as determined by the scriptures, one becomes possessed of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "I am that non-dual Self. Now, [an objection]: [Note: The provided text ends with "nanu" (now/if it be objected), indicating the beginning of a potential objection or further commentary.]

Since samādhi is a non-conceptual illumination, how can there be recollection of it for one who has emerged from it, given that only conceptual mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produce recollection? For indeed, non-conceptual [cognition] is merely the illumination of objects such as a jar; it is not a mental impression that produces recollection. Otherwise, on the path...

For one who is walking, there would follow the consequence of remembering all objects seen through non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-dṛṣṭa*). Indeed, not everything seen non-conceptually on the road is remembered; for what is remembered is only that which was known through conceptual cognition (*savikalpa-jñāta*), such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth.
Therefore, regarding what was seen non-conceptually, only that portion for which conceptualization subsequently arises is [remembered] as "something."

If it is argued that the distinction in memory— such as [the thoughts] "it is high," "it is a human," "it is a man," or "it is Devadatta"— is thus established, on this point some say that in the moment following meditative absorption (*samādhi*), memory occurs only through the gateway of conceptualization (*savikalpa*). Others, however, [hold that this is not so] because the pure inner self (*pratyagātman*) cannot be an object of conceptualization.

Memory arises precisely from the experience of *samādhi*. Nor should it be argued that the pure [Self] cannot be the object in *savikalpa-samādhi*; for since *savikalpa-samādhi* consists of the aforementioned conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*), it does not have the pure nature as its object. Now, one might ask: how can there be a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the *nirvikalpa* [state]?
If it is argued that memory arises only from conceptualization (*savikalpa*), we reply: there is no such rule that memory proceeds solely from conceptualization.

For conceptualization is the appearance of difference; however, even for those who have perceived [an object] non-conceptually (*nirvikalpa*) on the path, memory is possible in a general form such as "something" (*kiñcit*). For this very reason, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), for one who perceives non-conceptually—
The recollection of the unmanifest as previously described is established [only] when its form has been produced;

for otherwise, it would follow that there would be no recollection in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). Thus, in whatever cognition a certain portion of an object clearly manifests, a recollection of that object occurs at a later time to that same extent. For indeed, [recollection] does not occur for that which was never perceived.

Although every aspect shines forth within omniscient knowledge, according to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*—namely, "but [only] some aspect shines forth according to one's inclination and according to one's need" (2.18)—only a certain portion manifests. For this very reason, the consensus of those who know the scriptures is that every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a form of memory (*smṛti*). And thus, in the non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*),...
They say that through the manifestation of the pure nature, the recollection of the pure nature becomes possible;
the detailed exposition of this, however, should be seen in the *Pratyabhijñātātparyavivṛti*. || 69 ||
Through the direct conceptualization, "I am that non-dual Self," he swiftly destroys ignorance— the root of transmigratory existence— along with all its constituent parts.

From such a direct conceptual cognition in the form of recognition—as meaning that which is complete with its limbs, entire, and together with its effects—one who has recognized the reality of the Self destroys [the cycle of existence]. || 70 ||
The maturation of meditative absorption is indeed the complete abandonment of conceptual construction.
Conceptual construction is the manifestation of diversity; non-conceptual [wisdom] is its singular opposite. (71)
He analyzes what was stated—that mature meditation (*pakvadhyāna*) itself is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)—with the words "of meditation" (*dhyānasya*).
He states the very meaning of the term "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) with the word "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*): conceptualization is manifold or various kinds of manifestation (*khyāti*);
