non-conceptual [manifestation] is a single or uniform kind of manifestation. In the cognition "the pot is blue," the knowledge is that the pot is blue.
Due to the threefold nature of its forms, there is conceptualization (*savikalpatva*);
because meditative absorption lacks forms such as a jar and consists solely of the nature of knowledge, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpatva*). || 71 ||
By the mere non-apprehension of anything else, conceptual construction is abandoned;
once conceptual construction is abandoned, the non-conceptual state remains spontaneously of its own accord. (72)
If it is asked how the non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*) of knowledge is accomplished, he says: "By other [means].

The meaning is that by the mere avoidance of mental activity (*manovyāpāra*) consisting of the representation of a self (*anātmollekha*), the state of possessing various forms (*vividhākāratā*) ceases in knowledge. By the word "mere" (*mātra*), its ease of accomplishment is indicated because the means required are minimal.
He says that the attainment of non-conceptuality occurs merely by abandoning conceptual construction: "Conceptual construction... (verse 72).
Just as when a painting is wiped away, only the pure wall remains; for the preparation of the pure wall is indeed the very act of wiping away the painting.
Here is an illustration: "citra" [means] "saṃmārṣṭi," which is "saṃmārjanaṃ" (the act of sweeping). || 73 ||
Thus, when conceptual construction is eliminated, the mind becomes non-conceptual by its own nature;
for the attainment of the non-conceptual self consists precisely in the relinquishing of conceptual construction.
He applies this to the case under discussion with the word "thus" (evam): [it means] in the case of exclusion (apoha), by way of non-representation, that is, by way of its removal. || 74 ||
Indeed, there is no other purifying state to be attained beyond this;
even the wise are deluded herein because of the greatness of Māyā. 75.

Just as the true nature of a pure mirror is established merely by the removal of an object from before it, so too the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*) is established merely through non-apprehension (*anullekha*).
Having stated this, he says "not beyond this" (*nātaḥ*), meaning that the very nature of non-conceptuality is the supreme fruit, and there is nothing superior to it.

"Pure" (pāvana) means pure because it is free from the defects of the suffering of saṃsāra. Here, even the wise—the learned—[strive] for the attainment of such an eternally attained nature on account of its majesty, that is, its greatness. || 75 ||
Indeed, this state was perceived in an instant by those of superior intellect;
for, O Brahmin, there are three types of qualified practitioners: the highest, the lowest, and the middling. (76)
The phrase "it would be characterized" is the ellipsis to be supplied for the "highly intelligent and most qualified" [practitioners].
He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "in three ways" (tridhā), etc. (verse 76).
The best [practitioners] realize that state at the very time of the single instruction;
for them, both investigation and meditation become equal to the time of hearing [the teaching]. || 77 ||

The "single instruction" (sakṛdādeśa) is the primary teaching. If it is asked how deliberation, meditation, and so forth can occur in a single moment, he says: "deliberation" (vicāra). It should occur at the very time of hearing [the teaching]. || 77 ||
For the supreme ones, there is indeed no affliction upon attaining that state.
Formerly, at night, when the moonlight beautifully adorned the sky, I [was with] Nidāgha... 78.
Here he gives an illustration of his own self with the word "I. "Nidāgha" means the hot season. The connection is with the phrase "in the adorned courtyard of the garden. || 78 ||
Embraced by his beloved in the courtyard of a blossoming garden,
he sat upon a costly couch, reeling from the intoxication of wine.
The most excellent, the supreme. || 79 ||
I heard the words of the hosts of Siddhas in the sky, sweet as honey; indeed,
at that time, I realized the state that rests upon the reality of non-duality.
"Sweet as honey" means delicate and beautiful. If one asks what kind of speech it was, he says: "Non-dual," etc.; I understood it at that very time, at the moment of hearing. (80)
That was indeed realized through investigation and likewise through meditation;
thus, within half a muhūrta, he knew that purifying state.

Thus, at that very time, during the period of hearing, it was understood through reflection (*vicāra*), contemplation (*manana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*)— even through *nididhyāsana* culminating in non-conceptual samādhi— and recognized in this manner. Having thus, within the duration of half a muhūrta, known that purifying state, the state of the non-dual Self.
Once again, for a moment, my mind became fully concentrated,
as I was completely submerged in an ocean of supreme bliss.

With my mind properly fixed upon that very state of the non-dual Self, I became for a moment possessed of nirvikalpa-samādhi. Regarding the word "paramānanda": the sense is that I was completely submerged in the ocean of supreme bliss, consisting solely of the bliss of Brahman. || 82 ||
Then, having regained my mindfulness, I became intent on inquiry:
"Aha! This is indeed a wondrous state, overflowing with the nectar of bliss. (83)
Then, immediately after meditative absorption, he was devoted to investigation, intent solely upon investigation. || 83 ||
I am once again entering that unprecedented state which I have attained;
even the bliss of Indra and the other gods is not worth even a fraction of it.
"I enter that state of the Self"—the meaning is that there I become one whose mind is concentrated.
"Of this bliss of samādhi," even its fullness is enough. 84.
Even a mere fraction of this bliss is not equal to the happiness of Brahmā;
until today, this time of mine has indeed been spent in vain. (85)
All happiness, from that of Brahmā down to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha—every such happiness has been spent by me;
the time has been passed in vain because I have not attained the bliss under discussion. 85.
Just as one who, unaware of his own treasure-store filled with wish-fulfilling gems, wanders about begging for alms merely desiring a handful of flour; (86)

He describes, with an illustration, the people's longing for the pleasure of sense objects due to their lack of recognition of the bliss of their own Self, [beginning with] the words "without knowing" (*aviditvā*). "Sva" means one's own. || 86 ||
Alas! People, thus deluded by ignorance regarding the bliss of their own self, obtain only a mere fragment of external pleasure through great exertions. (87)
They are utterly deluded by ignorance regarding the bliss of their own self. || 87 ||
Therefore, enough for me of this futile exertion for a mere fragment of external pleasure;
let me rather be forever intent upon the mass of infinite bliss.
What need have I for this external conventional discourse, which is like grinding what has already been ground, consisting as it does merely of words of reproach? (89)

"Enough with this pleasure derived from sense objects; therefore, what purpose do I have for external worldly activity that leads to them?"—this is the implied meaning. By the word "upālambha," it is meant as a ground for reproach. || 89 ||
Those same foods, those very garlands, those beds, those various ornaments, and those enjoyments with women [are now yours]. (90)
He states that this is equivalent to grinding what has already been ground: "Those [objects]," meaning those which have been enjoyed more than once. || 90 ||
Even though they are mostly long-settled leftovers, I consume them again;
because of my tendency to follow the crowd, no sense of disgust arises in me. (91)

"Following those who have gone before" means following the path of one's ancestors, such as fathers and grandfathers, and engaging in the same conduct; that is to say, being intent on non-investigation. "Disgust" refers to [disgust] toward the enjoyment of objects that are mostly stale. || 91 ||
Having thus resolved, just as I was again intent upon turning inward,
another most auspicious reflection presented itself to me.
One who is intent upon inwardness; "vimarśa" means deliberation. || 92 ||
"Alas! What is this delusion of my mind that has come upon me in this way?
Though I am standing right here, I am that very Self, completely filled with bliss. (93)

He says that very thing: "Aho! The sense is that because the bliss experienced in samādhi shines forth at all times as its very nature, this renewed engagement [with worldly objects] is due to delusion (*moha*). That very [bliss] is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*) itself. || 93 ||
What more do I wish to do, or what is yet to be attained by me?
What have I not yet obtained, where, when, or how shall it be attained? (94)
How? By what means? || 94 ||
How indeed could the attainment of that which has not yet been attained be possible? Oh, how could there be any action within my own nature, which is infinite consciousness and bliss? (95)

He says "of that which has not been attained" because, according to the principle stated in the *Bhagavad Gītā* (2.27), "If there were the attainment of pleasure for one who has not [previously] attained it, then death is certain for one who has been born," such pleasure would necessarily be impermanent.
He says "aho" (oh! because no action whatsoever is possible for him who is actionless (*niṣkriya*). || 95 ||
Even the body, the senses, and the internal organ are indeed like those in a dream;
all of these belong to me alone, who am the indivisible, singular Self of Consciousness. 96.

If it is argued that although there is no direct activity for the Self whose nature is full consciousness (*pūrṇacidātman*), it might occur through the medium of the body and so forth, [the author] says: "The body... The sense is that since those [body, etc. are unreal, there can be no activity even through them. If it is further argued: "Even when the object does not exist, transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) does not cease for a person who meditates on sense-objects... [as stated in the verse beginning with *dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ*].

If it is argued that the fruit [of liberation] would arise through the restraint of the mind, according to the frequently cited reading: "Just as there is the attainment of misfortune in a dream" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.27.4), he says: "Of Me alone. All those things belonging to each individual soul, from the separate body up to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), belong to Me alone.
Why is this so? Because of the qualifying phrase "of the indivisible, unitary Self that is Consciousness" (akhaṇḍaikacidātmanaḥ). || 96 ||
In that case, even if one internal organ were restrained, what would it matter?
For indeed, my other mental faculties remain unrestrained. (97)

And if it is asked why this is so, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). Among those internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), what fruit would there be from the suppression of only one internal organ contained within this body? The sense is: none at all.
If it is argued that through the suppression of the internal organ, the cessation of distraction (*vikṣepa*) would occur, he says: "The others," etc. Of one...
The meaning is that even when others are ceased, because [the mind] itself is not ceased, there is no cessation of distraction by means of that [cessation]. || 97 ||
And so, what would happen to me if one mind were ceased?
For minds both ceased and unceased shine forth abundantly within me. (98)

If it is argued that by the cessation of this [particular] mind, there would be the cessation of distraction within the limitation of this body, he says: "And so it is. The sense is that if distractions exist across the limitations of many bodies, the cessation of distraction in a single body is not sufficient for [the goal]. If it is objected that your mind is one and no other, he says: "The [minds] are restrained," just as...

Just as a single mind shines forth in the world, so too do the minds of yogis who have restrained them, as well as the unrestrained minds of others, shine within me alone; since there is no distinction [between them], the sense is that all these belong to me alone. || 98 ||
Even when all minds have ceased, there is no cessation for me; since I am like the vast expanse of great space, how could there be any cessation for me? (99)
He says that even upon the cessation of the mind, there can be no distinction whatsoever for me, who am of one uniform nature devoid of difference:
"The pervasive nature [of the Self] beyond the Great Space should be understood, since even the Great Space is illuminated by the light of the conscious Self. (99)
Thus, how could there be a state of meditative absorption (samādhi) in me, whose nature is full bliss, who am full of the bliss of consciousness, and who am more full than even the sky? (100)
Thus, he says "in this way" (*evam*), explaining that even when the mind is ceased, because there is no distinction in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), even *samādhi* is not possible.

*Samādhi* is defined as the manifestation of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*) when the visible world (*dṛśya*) does not appear. And this is not possible [for me], because even while the visible world appears, there is no cessation of bliss in me, whose form is undivided bliss.
(Ānanda: [He] says that for me there is no possibility of action that brings about good or evil:

"O Consciousness and Bliss," etc. By the phrase "of Him who is completely filled with infinite consciousness," it is indicated that there is nothing to be attained through any action whatsoever, whether it be the manifestation of one's own nature or the appearance of bliss. || 100 ||
How could my action be such that both the auspicious and the inauspicious exist, given my greatness, even though [the action] is non-dual,
amidst the infinite appearances of bodies and selves? (101)

The word "what" (*keti*) implies a question regarding the nature of action (*kriyāsvarūpa*). He says [in the verse] "ananteṣu" etc., meaning that for me, who am distinct from the body, there is nothing [to be gained] by an action appearing even within the body.
He says [in the verse] "manmahitvataḥ," meaning that the appearance of action and so forth occurs solely through my own majesty. || 101 ||
What is there to be done, or what is there not to be done, by means of the appearance of an action or even its absence? For me, there is not even a trace of such a thing. (102)
Therefore, he says that for me there is neither "what is to be done" nor "what is not to be done," [expressed as]: "or what is to be done. (102)
Therefore, what would it matter if there were cessation? Whether in meditative absorption or not, I am filled with bliss, possessing a nature that is ever-true and complete. (103)

Since I am, whether in a state of meditative absorption or non-absorption, of the nature of reality and replete with bliss, there is no fruit whatsoever to be gained through cessation; thus he says: "Therefore," etc. (103).
"Let this body remain in whatever activity it is currently engaged; as for me, I am in every way established in my own self, dwelling in the temple of supreme bliss. (104)

Since neither ritual action nor its fruit is possible in Me, He says: "In whom... Being established in oneself (*svasthaḥ*) means being situated in one's true nature due to the abandonment of the identification with the body as the self (*dehāhaṃbhāva*). 104.
I am of the nature of light that never sets, perfectly full, and stainless;
such is my state as proclaimed for one who is most highly qualified. (105)
"Before the sun has set" means that his nature is the undifferentiated consciousness (*aparicchinna-cid-rūpa*). "Unguiled" (*nirañjana*) means free from the defilement of action (*kriyā-mālinya*).
Thus, "abiding" refers to the manner of attaining knowledge according to the method described. || 105 ||
For those of inferior capacity, the fruit born of knowledge arises through many births; for those of middling capacity, however, it comes through gradual hearing and reflection. (106)

For those of inferior capacity, the fruit of knowledge does not arise in a single lifetime; for those of middling capacity, knowledge comes through the gradual passage of time; but it is not as it is for the superior ones, who attain it instantaneously at that very moment.
And from that constant reflection, knowledge is born;
then, concentration joined with the fruit of higher wisdom becomes difficult to attain. (107)
Then, immediately after that contemplation, knowledge arises; this knowledge is recognition. || 107 ||
What is the use of a hundred concentrations if they are devoid of the fruit of wisdom?
Therefore, for those who lack wisdom, there is no fruit from those concentrations. (108)
Therefore, because samādhi devoid of the fruit consisting of consciousness is useless, [it is surpassed] by those moments of samādhi established during the waking state and so forth. || 108 ||
Even in the world, as one travels along paths, if one does not discern the objects revealed by non-conceptual cognition, one's ignorance regarding them does not cease. (109)
If it is asked, "Why is this so? [the author] states, with an illustration, that it is because non-conceptual [awareness] does not remove ignorance: "In the world... [Verse 109].
For one who remains without cognizing—that is, without forming a conceptual distinction regarding the object—his ignorance is not removed.
The consciousness known as non-conceptual is one's own innate nature, which is pure awareness alone;
though it is manifest at all times, it is indeed as if unmanifest.

If it is asked, "How can there be the cessation of ignorance through non-conceptual [knowledge]? [the author] says "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), meaning that knowledge is the remover of ignorance precisely by virtue of having the same object.
The sense is that mere knowledge is without an [external] object; and that is the pure essential nature. That is the non-conceptual, which exists at all times.
Even at the time of conceptualization. || 110 ||
Precisely by the covering over of conceptual constructions, there occurs the removal of conceptual constructions;
that which was already manifest appears once more as if newly arisen from the beginning.

If it is asked why it is said to be "appearing as non-appearing," he replies: "By conceptual constructions" (*vikalpa*). Knowledge in the form of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is like a mirror, serving as the locus for the reflections of all conceptual constructions. Therefore, because it is covered by conceptual constructions, the meaning is that although it appears, it is of the nature of non-appearance, like a mirror filled with reflections. For this very reason, upon the abandonment of conceptual constructions—
He says that even though it is always appearing, it becomes as if newly born (*bhātakalpa*) from a state of being unprecedented;
thus he states: "of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpānām*). || 111 ||
Through the non-differentiation of knowledge and the object of knowledge, that which was unknown is said to be known;
in this way, this becomes the supreme sequence for the realization of the Self. || 112 ||

Previously, because it was mixed with the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), that very [state] was called "unknown" due to the non-differentiation and non-separateness of knowledge and the object of knowledge; upon the removal of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is said to be "known.
He concludes with the word "thus" (*evam*). It is "supreme" (*uttama*) because it bestows the highest fruit. (112)
O Brahmin, having heard this further, you ought to understand it through reflection;
then, by realizing the true nature of the Self, you will have accomplished your purpose.

Furthermore, again; that is, after the reflection and meditative absorption consisting of deliberation and profound contemplation (*vicāra-dhyāna-ātmaka-manana-nididhyāsānantaram*); having realized, that is, having recognized [the Self] through the realization "I am He" (*vijñāya so'ham iti pratyabhijñāya*). || 113 ||
Thus instructed by Janaka, the great sage Tvaṣṭrāvakra,
having been honored and granted leave, respectfully departed for his own abode.
The construction is as follows: "Instructed" means taught by Janaka; "honored" means with respect, preceded by reflection and meditation.

Having understood the supreme state through prior reflection and meditation, and having shaken off all doubts, he quickly became liberated while living. (The reading "sarvasandehān" follows the commentary; however, according to the *ṭīkā*, the reading is "sarvasandeham").

The supreme state is the non-dual reality of the Self. "All doubt" refers to such doubts as: "How can that which is unknowable become knowable? By the word "swiftly," Aṣṭāvakra’s status as a person of the highest qualification is illuminated. (115)
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the Aṣṭāvakrīya in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
O Bhārgava, thus has that consciousness been described as being devoid of any object of knowledge;
indeed, its state of perception has been heard of in many ways.
In this context, the nature of liberation, the mind, space, bondage, and the reality that exists is described in sequence by those who have attained the bridge.
Thus, according to the manner stated by Janaka; she is of the nature of the Self. Of that consciousness which is devoid of an object of knowledge (vedya). || 1 ||
Deluded by illusion, people do not understand this due to a lack of discernment;
that state is perceived only by one with subtle vision, and never otherwise. (2)

"Due to a lack of proficiency," that is, through a failure to recognize its true nature, they do not know that consciousness. "That state" refers to the state of consciousness devoid of any object of knowledge. This is perceived by those with "subtle vision," meaning those whose minds are not directed toward external objects. (2)
What is the use of much speaking, O Rāma? Listen; I shall tell you the essence:
that which is to be known is known by the mind; therefore, the mind is not an object of knowledge.
At the beginning of the fifteenth chapter,
it was stated by Bhārgava that "such a consciousness, devoid of an object of knowledge, is impossible to perceive" (15.7).
Although this has already been established through the dialogue between Janaka and Aṣṭāvakra, he describes it once more for the sake of its ascent into the mind.
"What is the use of saying more? [It is said: "By the mind. It is well known that everything that is knowable is known by the mind.
Therefore, since there is no instrument for the knowledge of the mind's own nature, the mind is not an object of knowledge. || 3 ||
And thus, it may be possible that even the mind exists when liberated from the object of cognition;
that mind is designated as "awareness" (vitti) when it is liberated from the object of cognition. || 4 ||

"And likewise" means: when the unperceivability of the mind is established. It might be possible that even a mind devoid of objects exists during the intervals between perceptions of objects, because the nature of a cause is to be inactive during the intervals between its effects; such is the sense.

He says "That mind" (tanmanaḥ) to show that it is indeed easy to realize that such a mind, when freed from the object of knowledge, is consciousness itself. The sense is that the mind, when liberated from the knowable, is the pure reality of the Self. || 4 ||
For that [consciousness], being of the very nature of apprehension, is indeed always known;
otherwise, if it depended upon another apprehension, there would be blindness due to infinite regress.

Now, one might object that if the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is such as to be non-objective (*avedya*), then its cognition for the sake of accomplishing the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*) would be impossible;

anticipating this doubt, he says: "By perception" (*upalabdhi*). The meaning is that [the Self] is known precisely by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), shining forth as such; the point is that in its manifestation there is no dependence on anything else. Of that...

He states the defect [arising] from the non-acceptance of self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva): "anyā" and so forth. "Anyā" means another perception distinct from itself; "tadapekṣāyām" means in dependence upon that. The sense is that if cognition (*vitti*) were known by another cognition, and that [second] cognition by yet another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and consequently nothing at all would be manifest. || 5 ||
O Bhārgava, do you not speak because you perceive some entity?
If you do not speak, then you do not exist; how then can there be a question for you?
The phrase "someone" (*kañcit*) demonstrates that the conscious self (*cidātman*) is always self-luminous.

The meaning is: "Why do you not appear at the time of perceiving a jar and so forth? If you do not appear at the time of the appearance of other things, then you do not exist at that time, because existence depends upon being manifested. [If you say,] "This is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*),"...
He states the impossibility of the question with the words "tataḥ" (therefore). || 6 ||
Aha! Being yourself of the nature of a sky-flower, how can you desire my welfare? Consider this: how could I possibly establish you as a self? (7)

He mocks one who says "the self does not exist" with the word "Aho! Consider this: how can I establish your self for you, who yourself deny your own self? It is like trying to prevent another from killing someone who has already set out to die himself.
The sense is that for a fool who has set out to restrain his own self when its protection seems impossible, it is impossible for anyone else to effect the means of self-realization. || 7 ||
"If you say, 'I do not know you specifically, though you shine forth in a general way,' then, O Rāma, that very general form of yours is indeed imperishable."

[The opponent] objects: "Surely I do not deny the self; rather, I desire to know the self, which appears in a general way, in its specific form. [The author replies: "In a general way. Even in the world, a question arises from a general knowledge only when there is a desire to know the specific details; therefore, the sense is that I am not ignorant.

He concludes: "It is indeed the universal alone. In the world, such a question is possible regarding jars and other objects which consist of both universals and particulars; however, it is not possible regarding that which is of an indivisible, unitary nature, like the sky, which lacks the nature of both universal and particular.
Therefore, that which you have perceived as the universal nature of the self is, in reality, devoid of universality for you.
Form is imperishable and eternal; the meaning is that whatever else appears as the self, such as the body and so forth, being impermanent, is not your form. || 8 ||
Your body consists of nothing more than this, devoid even of a trace of distinction;
alas, though you know this, you continue to delude yourself in vain!

"That which shines forth as the universal consciousness (saṃvitsāmānya), devoid of all particularities such as the state of being the seen and the seer—that alone is your own true nature. Having known this, you nevertheless continue to be utterly deluded in vain"—thus he says with the word "Aho! (verse 9).
Furthermore, everything that illuminates must have a specific object as its domain;
therefore, you indeed shine by yourself in the form of the universal.

[Objection: "In that case, would not my body be the general cognition (*jñānasāmānya*) which illuminates each respective object such as a jar or a cloth? [Reply: He says "the illuminator" (*bhāsakam*) to show that this is not so. The meaning is that since the cognition which illuminates each specific object is itself constituted by the form of that specific object to be illuminated, it does not possess your nature merely by virtue of being an illuminator. Therefore...

You shine by yourself alone, independent of anything else, in the form of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). Whether it be the universal (*sāmānya*) or the particular (*viśeṣa*), they appear only in mutual conjunction and not in independence; however, the conscious self (*cidātman*) shines with a form that is devoid of both universal and particular—this is the intended meaning. || 10 ||
If you appear as the self through the body and so forth, listen, for I shall explain it to you:
you appear as the self of the body solely through mental construction (saṅkalpa), and not otherwise.

One might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that I have no manifestation in the form of the universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*) described by you, but rather only in the form of the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth? To dispel this doubt, he says: "The body... and so on.

The body and so forth possess the nature of the self because they are the objects of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃbuddhi*); and that [nature] exists only at the time of the volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*) of each respective body and so on.

Thus he says: "the body is the self. The meaning is that it appears as the selfhood of the body only through a volitional construction that delineates the form of the body and so forth, and not by its own nature. || 11 ||

Examine with a subtle vision whether, apart from the body of another, there is anything that appears as "your" body within the conceptual construction; for if it were so, then that [other's] body would indeed become yours.

He clarifies this very point with the words "vibhāvaya" (realize): "Does the nature of the body appear to you at the time of conceptualization when objects such as a jar, which are other than the body, are manifest? Does it not appear? This is the meaning. Now, even if the state of being a body appears, in reality, for me who am the conscious self (*cidātman*)—

If it is argued that the body and so forth are "mine" because of a relationship [to the self], then since the relationship is no different in the case of the objects of perception such as a jar, those too would become your body; thus he says: "The body... (verse 12).
Thus it is conceived: whatever body there is, that indeed is [the Self].
Therefore, you would be composed of everything; how then could you be merely the body-self? (13)

Now, if it is argued that even so, because the body is merely an limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the conscious self who possesses the notion of "I," the body is also its true nature— then [we reply]: at the time of cognizing a jar or the like,
since the cognition consisting of the volition toward the jar and so forth is itself the possessor of the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyayin), it would follow that the jar and other objects [are the self].

Since even a jar or other object would be your form because it serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for its own cognition, you would therefore consist of all manifesting phenomena in their sequential succession, and not merely have the body as your self; thus he says:
"In this way" (*evam*). || 13 ||
Therefore, your body cannot be an object of sight because of the possibility of deviation;
therefore, you are of the nature of pure vision alone, for the seer can never be the seen.

"Therefore" means because [the Self] has attained the state of consisting of everything. If it is argued that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "Because of deviation" (*vyabhicārataḥ*).

This means that at the time when this or that object appears, there is an absence of connection with the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) and so forth regarding other things. Therefore, since it is logically impossible for the visible object (*dṛśya*) to have your nature, for this very reason, the vision (*dṛk*) which is your own self cannot be of the nature of the visible object.
To this he says: "It is not vision" (na dṛk). || 14 ||
That self-radiance is devoid of even a trace of any specific visible form,
yet it is variegated by the diverse and manifold distinctions of bodies, places, and times.

Having extracted the very nature of the Self, he says: "She" (*sā*). This means that vision (*dṛk*) is the essential nature of the Self. It is self-luminous (*svaprabhā*), meaning its form is self-manifesting; the sense is that it is devoid of dependence on anything else for the manifestation of its own nature. "In the form of the visible" (*dṛśyarūpā*)—the sense is that its form is pure vision alone (*śuddhadṛṅmātra*). [Objection: But [what of] the entire range of particulars, such as the body, location, and so forth?
If it is asked, "Since she is solely intent upon that [one reality], how can she be devoid of even a trace of differentiation? he says: "She is *deha*.
The sense is that she possesses the painting of the world, variegated by the diversity of the manifold differentiated forms, like a mirror variegated by reflections. || 15 ||
Therefore, by abandoning mere conceptualization,
perceive your own self as the remaining form of pure consciousness that stands beyond.

"Therefore" means that, just as the variety of reflections in a mirror is rooted in the original object (*bimba*), so too the variety of the world in consciousness (*citi*) is rooted in volition (*saṅkalpa*). "Situated beyond" means that which, after the abandonment of volition, is manifested from itself. "The remainder" refers to that which constitutes the limit for the relinquishing of volition. || 16 ||
Thus, when it has been observed once, that which remains because of its lack of defining characteristics—that ignorance which is the cause of all saṃsāra—is dissolved. (17)
Thus, when one’s own Self has been once characterized and recognized through the abandonment of conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*),

then, because that which resides within it— the body and so forth— is no longer characterized, ignorance— which is the cause of the sense of "I" regarding that body and so on— dissolves simply by the absence of such conceiving, such as "I am fat" or "I am a Brahmin."

The sense is that the cessation of ignorance occurs only through the recognition of the Self (*ātmapratyabhijñāna*), which is capable of uprooting the identification with the body and so forth; it does not occur through a momentary meditative absorption (*kṣaṇikasamādhi*) or through a superficial, non-conceptual recognition (*āpātapratyabhijñāna*). || 17 ||
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth;
rather, for one whose true nature is purified through the abandonment of conceptual construction, liberation is simply that manifestation itself.

Now, raising the objection—“In that case, after the cessation of ignorance, when, where, and of what nature is liberation attained?”—he says: “There is no [separate] liberation. The sense is that at the very moment of abandoning volitional constructs (*saṅkalpa*), liberation—which consists in the manifestation of one's own true nature within the Self itself—occurs. || 18 ||
But because it is of the nature of one's own true self, it can never be unattained;
rather, fulfillment is achieved solely through the removal of delusion. (19)
He says "sa" (that), meaning that such liberation is not something new that is attained, because its nature consists in the manifestation of one's own true essence.

If it is objected that, in that case, this much effort in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth would be useless, he says "kevalam" (merely), meaning that [liberation is merely] the removal of delusion, which is ignorance. || 19 ||
No other liberation is possible, because it would be produced and thus subject to destruction;
for if it were distinct from one's own nature, it would indeed be like a hare's horn.
If it is asked: "Why is liberation not accepted as something entirely distinct from the aforementioned knowledge, just like heaven and other such rewards?

[the author] replies: "Because that [liberation], being something produced, would necessarily be subject to destruction. Thus he says: "It is not another. Therefore, the connection is: "Therefore, liberation is not another [thing]. (20)
One's own nature is complete in every respect; how could liberation exist elsewhere? If liberation were to exist within one's own nature, it would be like a reflection in a mirror.
If it is asked, "Why is it comparable to the horn of a hare? he says: "The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
The sense is that since nothing external to the intrinsic nature is established—because [all such things] have been correctly analyzed—liberation will never be achieved anywhere.
Now, if it is argued, "Let liberation be the intrinsic nature itself, just like the world," then [it must be] non-different from the intrinsic nature, like a reflection.
Thus he says: "In its own nature" (svarūpe). || 21 ||
Even in the world, liberation is not conceived of apart from the cessation of bondage;
cessation would be non-existence itself, so how could that which is real have the nature of non-existence? (22)

He states that even in the world, liberation (*mokṣa*) is not a separate entity by saying "even in the world" (*loke’pi*). For liberation is the departure [from bondage], and departure is the destruction of bondage.

Destruction, moreover, is non-existence through annihilation (*dhvaṃsābhāva*). Thus, since non-existence is real and yet would have to be a positive entity (*bhāvatva*), it would follow that a single thing would possess both contradictory forms—existence and non-existence. This is the intended meaning. || 22 ||
An entity consisting of both existence and non-existence is not possible anywhere;
likewise, the entities in a dream possess the nature of both existence and non-existence. (23)

"Consisting of both existence and non-existence" means that a thing possessing two contradictory forms is not possible anywhere; it does not attain reality. This is the point: existence (*bhāvatva*) is being (*sattva*), and non-existence (*abhāvatva*) is non-being (*asattva*);
a single entity possessing both these forms is impossible due to contradiction. Thus, the absence of bondage is not something distinct, but rather—

"It has the very nature of the Self which is its substratum. Now, one might object: "If the absence of bondage were the nature of the Self, then the Self itself would possess the contradictory nature of both existence and non-existence. Anticipating this doubt, it is said that because all such properties as existence and non-existence are unestablished apart from the Self, there is no contradiction in its nature; thus, [the author] speaks of the one.

He states that if one were to admit a dual nature consisting of two contradictory forms, it would follow that dream-objects of that kind would be real; thus he says, "And so" (*tathā ca*). Because they are the objects of both the cognitions "it exists" and "it does not exist," they possess a dual nature. The connection [of the sentence] is: "they would be real. (23)
If it is argued that those [cognitions] are real while these are unreal because they are subject to sublation, listen:
sublation is a cognition of non-existence occurring at a time when the original cognition has ceased. (24)

Now, one might object: "The objects of a dream do not possess reality in either sense, because their existence as entities within that state is sublated. Anticipating this, [the author] says "Because of the cause of sublation," etc., to show that since everything other than the Self is subject to sublation, even liberation will not be established as something distinct [from the Self]. [He explains: "The unreality of that which has been sublated..."
He states the definition of sublation (*bādha*) in order to explain it: "Sublation" means that the very cognition of non-existence, such as "the jar does not exist," is sublation.

Now, one might object that since the cognition "the self does not exist" could possibly arise for someone even regarding the self, it would follow that the self is unreal due to being sublated; to this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "occurring at a time when there is an absence of cognition": since the self is eternally luminous, the absence of cognition is impossible;
therefore, the intended meaning is that [the self] is not unreal. || 24 ||
He for whom there is such a connection with sublation is unreal, and not the other;
for there exists a sublation of everything that is perceived at the time when [the perception] is no longer present. (25)

Of whatever [object], such as a jar, there might be a connection with sublation—consisting of a cognition of its absence at a time when the cognition of it has ceased—in that case, it would be unreal. For it is not otherwise;
that is, one devoid of such a connection with sublation is not unreal. Regarding the phrase "at a time when there is no cognition": this refers to all that is perceived.
The meaning is that it is unreal because of the existence of sublation in the form of the cognition of non-existence at a time when the causal conditions [for its production] are absent. || 25 ||
Therefore, that which exists in the nature of both being and non-being must be unreal,
for it never, anywhere, possesses even a slight touch of non-existence.

Therefore, because it is subject to the aforementioned sublation, it exists as both being and non-being; that is, the mere object of perception which becomes the objective domain of both the cognitions "it exists" and "it does not exist. For such an entity, there is at some time or in some place even a slight touch of non-existence.
There is no connection with the condition of non-existence at a time when the conditions are absent. || 26 ||
Such is the nature of consciousness, which exists as the truth in its entirety;
therefore, liberation separate from it could not possibly be real in any way. (27)

Such a reality, the very essence of consciousness (cidātmatattva), which is free from affliction, alone is real. If it is objected that at the time of the cognition of a jar or other objects there is no cognition of the conscious self, he replies with the words "by its entire nature" (sarvātmanā). The meaning is that because it exists as manifesting itself in its entirety through the analogy of a reflection in a mirror, there is never a time when it is not cognized.
"Therefore" means: because everything that is perceived as distinct from the Self is non-existent. || 27 ||
Liberation is said to be the simultaneous manifestation of one's true nature;
consciousness is proclaimed to be complete by the mere cessation of the object of thought. (28)

Since everything other than one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is unreal, that which is "full" is the essential nature which is unlimited; its "simultaneous manifestation" is an unlimited manifestation. Because ignorance (*avidyā*) has been destroyed, it means it is unobscured by ignorance. [Objection: But how can there be [an obscuration] of consciousness (*cit*), whose very nature is eternally full?

If it is argued that fullness occurs only in the state of liberation, he says: "cetya... (the object of thought). The meaning is that although [consciousness] is full by its very nature, it becomes as if incomplete due to contact with objects of thought (*cetya*). || 28 ||
The very appearance of an object of consciousness constitutes the contraction of this consciousness;
when there is no appearance of an object, consciousness is full, being devoid of limitation. (29)

He says this very thing: "cetyeti" (with respect to the object of consciousness). This refers to this consciousness (*cit*). The sense is: just as the nature of a mirror appears as if contracted by reflections, so it is here.
For just as the mirror remains undivided even when reflections appear within it, so too consciousness remains full even when objects of consciousness (*cetya*) appear; thus he says: [the following].
If its delimitation by time and so forth is being examined, tell me: would that delimitation be unperceived or perceived? (30)

Thus, he begins to explain that the appearance of limitation for consciousness (*citi*) occurs solely through the objects of thought (*cetya*) inherent within itself, and not through time and so forth in reality—by means of the words "by time and so forth" (*kālādibhiḥ*).

For that consciousness, "limitation" refers to time and so forth as the limiters; the meaning is whether they are perceived (*cetita*) or unperceived (*acetita*), or whether they are illuminated by the light of consciousness or not. (30)

For [the argument] would be unestablished in the case of the insentient; in the case of the sentient, that very [consciousness] is the pervader. Whatever existence in the world is conceived as delimited by time, [is so delimited] through that [consciousness]. (31)

"In the insentient" means in that which is not perceived by consciousness; that is to say, in that which is not illuminated by consciousness. "It would be unestablished" means that because that which is not an object of consciousness is equivalent to a hare's horn, it would be unestablished—this is the sense. "In the sentient" means in that which is perceived by consciousness. "That very consciousness" means that very consciousness itself. "Pervasive" means like a mirror [is pervaded] by reflections pervading the mirror. (k, kh)
The meaning is that there is no limitation of consciousness by time and so forth, because they are pervaded by that very consciousness.
He establishes this very point with an illustration: "In the world," [it is] conceived and seen. || 31 ||
When the time of existence and the time of manifestation have attained the state of the delimited and the delimiting,
and are both pervaded by consciousness, then they indeed become of such a nature.

Regarding that, he says that such is the state of affairs: "The object and time. For the object and time, which are pervaded by and manifested through consciousness, their nature as the delimited and the delimiting consists precisely in being of such a kind. || 32 ||
But if there were no pervasion [of consciousness], how could there be any determination by consciousness?
When the object of cognition exists outside of consciousness, that would constitute a limitation. || 33 ||
In that regard, he states "in the case of non-pervasion" (*avyāptau*), meaning that if neither of the two— the object to be delimited (*paricchedya*) nor the delimiting agent (*paricchedaka*)—
is pervaded by consciousness (*cit*), the delimitation is not established. Thus, in the present context,

since it must necessarily be admitted that time (*kāla*) and so forth— which are considered to be the delimiting agents— are pervaded by consciousness, [the argument proceeds] by means of that which is pervaded (*vyāpyena*).

The meaning is that it is impossible for there to be a delimitation of the all-pervasive [consciousness] by time and so forth. He says "of consciousness" (citeḥ) to address the objection: if it were possible for that which is intended as the delimiter—time and so forth—to exist outside of consciousness, being unpermeated by consciousness, then there could be a delimitation of consciousness by it. That [would be the case] then. || 33 ||
The establishment of "citing" and "the external" is not possible in any way;
for how could that which is external be established if it is devoid of connection with consciousness? (34)

He states that the establishment of the essential nature belongs only to that which is manifest through the pervasion of consciousness (cit), and not to anything else: "Of consciousness" (citer), etc. (34).
The relation, too, cannot be a single part; likewise, the other [the whole] would remain unestablished.
Since only that portion of the relation is perceived, nothing else is established. (35)

[Objection: Surely the nature of an entity is established through its connection with consciousness (*cit*). Thus, just as the nature of a staff is established in relation to a jar, the nature of time and so forth is established, and the non-pervasion of consciousness is also established, by virtue of consciousness's connection with a single part (*ekadeśa*) of time and so forth. To this, he says: "Connection. It is improper to say that the connection with consciousness is merely a single part of time and so forth.

That being the case, the other part [of the object] would remain unestablished due to its connection with consciousness. If one asks why, he says: "Because of the absence of that other part" (tatsambandha-), [verse 35].

Therefore, let it be accepted that even external objects are submerged within consciousness; and thus, let it be accepted that the object of cognition is also submerged by way of its very self-nature. (36)
Since one does not achieve perfection as long as one is submerged in consciousness, therefore—

for the sake of establishing the true nature of that upon which the entire picture of the visible world appears against the background of the unmanifest— one must also accept that even external objects are submerged in consciousness. And thus:

Just as the objects of paintings situated on a wall are submerged by the light of a lamp, so too should the object of cognition (cetya) be understood as submerged within consciousness (cit). Thus he says: "Therefore... (36).
How could that which is submerged within itself be its own perceiver?
O Rāma, reflect upon such an object of cognition with sound reasoning. (37)
Thus, he says "How so? because it is impossible for time and the like—which are themselves submerged within [the Self]—to delimit the Self.

Having stated that time and the other factors which delimit cannot themselves be delimiters because they are pervaded [by the Self], he now states that just as the sky is not delimited by jars and the like which pervade the sky, there is likewise no delimitation of the conscious Self (cidātman).

To indicate that there is no visible object separate from the conscious self (cidātman), just as a jar or similar object [is not separate] from the sky, he begins to establish this by saying "the object of thought" (cetyam). Such [an object] is submerged in consciousness. 37.
An object appearing within [another] would have to consist of a reflection;
for no object existing within the interior of another object is ever clearly seen in the world. (38)

He states the very manner of this reflection (*vicāra*): "Of consciousness" (*citeḥ*). An object of cognition (*cetya*) that appears internally by being submerged in consciousness must consist solely of a reflection (*pratibimba*), because otherwise it would be impossible to define it, and because it possesses the defining characteristics of a reflection. This has already been elaborated upon previously (in the twelfth chapter).
And in the fourteenth chapter, he demonstrates the very impossibility [of the contrary] by stating: "Not by means of a positive entity," etc. (38).
If that were so, O Rāma, there would indeed be a confusion of all things;
therefore, the external object you have described is entirely rooted in delusion.

Having demonstrated the non-perception of a distinct entity within the body of an entity, he states the fault of confusion (*sāṅkarya*) that would result from such an admission: "of entities," etc. The meaning is that if the mutual natures of a jar, a cloth, and so forth were to be included within one another, then a jar would become a cloth, and a cloth would become a jar. Likewise...

And because it is like a reflection in a mirror, the object of perception is not distinct from the conscious self; this is the intended meaning. He establishes its non-distinctness by another method with the words "external objects" (*bahiḥpadārtha*), which means "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). It was stated previously (in the twelfth chapter) that [this perception] is rooted in delusion, meaning it is rooted in ignorance of one's own true nature (*svarūpājñāna*).
Tell me, how could there be any reality for those entities that depend upon it?
For one's own self, whose nature is consciousness, is always [present] in the form of each and every entity. (40)

The sense is that those things which have that [consciousness] as their substratum—namely, external objects whose nature is unmanifest—possess no reality apart from their locus, just like paintings situated on a wall superimposed through delusion.
Therefore, the syntactical connection is as follows: one's own Self alone, whose nature is consciousness (*cit*), always manifests in the form of various perceived objects.
"It shines forth by the power of its own freedom; nothing more exists anywhere.
Having heard these words, Bhārgava questioned him again.

If it is asked, "Why does it appear in this way? he says: "By its own freedom" (*svācchandyena*). It appears by means of the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) designated as *māyā*, like the creation of an illusory net (*indrajāla*) imagined by a magician.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever exists anywhere apart from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). 41.
O Blessed One, what has been stated by you appears difficult for me to comprehend, because it is impossible that pure consciousness alone could manifest as a manifold variety. (42)
It appears difficult to accomplish because it is impossible for consciousness—which is pure, partless, and one—to manifest as manifold. || 42 ||
The reality is perceived by all as twofold: consciousness and the object of consciousness.
Among these, the object of consciousness is to be illumined by consciousness; may your consciousness be self-luminous. (43)

He clarifies the very impossibility [of the opponent's position] with the words "consciousness" (citiḥ). The intended meaning is that it is manifested by all, established by the experience of everyone, and thus undeniable. In that case, between those two [the self and consciousness], let that consciousness be self-luminous; the intended meaning is that the self-luminosity of consciousness should remain exactly as you have stated it. || 43 ||

Just as an object, even though it appears through light, exists as distinct from that light, so too may the object of cognition (cetya), though illumined by consciousness (cit), be of a different nature.
He establishes with an illustration that the object of consciousness (*cetya*) is distinct from consciousness (*cit*): "Just as...
The meaning is: just as light is distinct from the appearance of light, so too let the object of consciousness be distinct from consciousness. || 44 ||
One should not ascend to the experience that "the object of consciousness (cetya) is of the nature of consciousness (cid-ātman)";
nevertheless, this was previously stated by the high-souled Janaka. (45)

One should not ascend to [the level of] direct experience, because that would contradict all empirical experience; the meaning is that the identity of consciousness (*cit*) and the object of consciousness (*cetya*) is not an object of experience. [This concludes] another objection. Now, the connection with the distant [phrase] is as follows: "How is it that what was stated by you—that which was spoken by Janaka—is so? || 45 ||
By the mere abandonment of volitional constructs, the mind becomes free from conceptualization;
that very state of non-conceptuality is the knowledge that destroys saṃsāra. (46)
He repeats the very words of Janaka: "The conceptualization... and so forth. That very [state] is the non-conceptual mind itself;
the meaning is that it brings about the cessation of saṃsāra by means of recognition (pratyabhijñā), thereby destroying saṃsāra. || 46 ||
For it has been stated that "that indeed is the form of the self"; how could that be so?
For the mind is declared to be the instrument of the self in the acts of cognition and action. (47)

He states the impossibility of the grounds for the objection—namely, "How could it be?"—with the words "For of the self" (ātmano hi), etc., regarding knowledge-action, that is, the activity of cognition. (47)
If the mind were not [distinct] from the Self, how could it be distinguished from the insentient?
O Blessed One, surely the distinction of the mind from the insentient must arise from the Self. (48)
The mind (*manas*) is that which performs the act of consciousness for the conscious self; he says "the mind" [in verse 48] because, in its absence, the self would necessarily be insentient.
For bondage or liberation of the self clearly occurs through the mind alone.

The mind with conceptualization (savikalpa) is bondage; (the sense is that, by figuratively treating cause and effect as non-different, it is said that "the mind is bondage" and "the mind is liberation"). Liberation would be the state without conceptualization (nirvikalpaka). || 49 ||
He states that even the bondage and liberation of the self are caused by the mind, saying "by the mind alone.

The sense is that because the mind is the primary cause of bondage and liberation, it is figuratively called "bondage" and "liberation" through the metaphorical identification of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*). Thus: "Bondage... liberation. (49)
How then can the mind itself be the Self, for the mind is known to be an instrument?
Even when the non-conceptual state is fully realized, duality nevertheless remains.
It was stated previously that the non-conceptual mind alone is the Self; to the question "How is that so?", he replies: "That [is] because of that. The meaning is:

because the identity of the agent and the instrument is untenable. Therefore, by the analogy of a reflection in a mirror, even though there is an apparent unity with the object of perception, duality remains for the mind (or "by the mind"). This is the meaning.
Moreover, it is observed in the world that he who possesses illusion is indeed deluded; for an illusion cannot be unreal—how, then, could non-duality (advaita) exist? || 51 ||
He raises an objection [with the words] "Now" (atha), [arguing that] even though the object of error is unreal, because the nature of the error itself is real, duality remains as a residue. || 51 ||
Causal efficiency is never observed in an unreal entity;
for every worldly object is stable and performs causal efficiency. (52)
Causal efficacy and stability are not observed in unreal things such as a rope-snake;
how then can that which performs causal efficacy—which is stable and merely perceived—be unreal? To this he says:
"Causal efficacy... (verse 52).
Tell me, how can that be untrue, since non-duality is thereby established? Furthermore, if all cognition is illusory, how can there be a distinction between illusion and non-illusion? (53)

Since the world is unreal, non-duality (advaita) is established pre-eminently. If all cognition of the perceptible is of the nature of error, then, in the absence of any other non-erroneous cognition, how can there be the conventional distinction between "error" and "non-error"? To this he says: "All... (verse 53).
"Or how could delusion be entirely uniform? Tell me, O Guru;
this doubt has long been revolving within my heart. (54)
He asks how there could be an error of the same form for all [beings], and says: "Error" (verse 54).
Having heard this question, Dattātreya, the knower of all things,
his soul delighted by the excellent inquiry, began to speak.
He who possesses all knowledge is the omniscient one. || 55 ||
O Rāma, you have asked well; this has been explained by me once more.
One should further refine it until there is complete satisfaction of the mind.

Furthermore, since you have asked this, it has already been explained for the most part; the intended meaning is that none of this constitutes an entirely unprecedented question. If one asks, "In that case, how is this [question] valid?", he says:
"As far as... Satisfaction arises from the removal of doubt. One should "purify," that is, investigate. || 56 ||
How could even a guru speak of what is in the mind of another without being asked?
For, due to the diversity of the intellects of living beings, reasoning remains distinct for each.

That which was in the mind of the disciple was what he desired to know. He says "of living beings" (*prāṇinām*) because a further question is also appropriate; for due to differences in intellect, there are differences in reasoning. The point is that since it is impossible for the teacher to know the reasoning residing in the heart of the disciple, doubt cannot be dispelled by a single instruction. || 57 ||
Who can be freed from doubt without asking about their own desired object? For knowledge is firmly established only for one who asks; indeed, inquiry is the seed for investigation. (58)
Since doubt does not cease for one who does not ask, knowledge belongs only to the questioner and not to anyone else;
thus he says, "without having asked. He further states that determination arises from questioning itself;
thus he says, "questioning. || 58 ||
Knowledge cannot belong to one who does not inquire; therefore, one should learn from the teacher by means of questioning.
It is possible that consciousness is indeed one, yet it appears as manifold due to its diversity.
Then, because the questioner lacks knowledge, [the author] begins to provide the answer in sequence: "Consciousness" (citih). || 59 ||
Just as a single mirror [reflects] many images, see that in dreams, conceptual constructions, and the like, the mind alone is indeed one. 60.
If it is asked how [this] could be possible, he states an example: "of a single form.
Since there is a disparity because a mirror depends upon a reflected object, he provides another example: "Behold the dream... (60).
For it shines forth through the manifold variety of the seer, the seeing, and the seen;
in this way, that very consciousness, though pure, appears in diverse forms. (61)

In the conceptual construction of dreams and mental kingdoms, the mind alone shines forth with a variety of forms such as the observer and so on, without depending on an external object like a physical image;
in this very same way, pure consciousness appears in its various manifestations.
For even in a dream, consciousness manifests in two ways: as the subject and as the object. Indeed, does a blind person not perceive an object without the aid of light? (62)
Having thus established the manifold nature of consciousness (*citi*), he refutes the second objection with the words "consciousness" (*citi*).

The meaning is that just as the duality between consciousness and the object of consciousness (*cetya*) does not exist in reality even though it appears to everyone in a dream, so too the duality appearing to everyone in the waking state does not exist. Now, by means of light...

Just as a manifest pot and the like are not other than consciousness, so too the manifest object of sight is not other than consciousness; thus, to resolve the third objection, he says: "Light. This is because there is no deviation from the pervasion that "whatever does not appear without X is of the nature of X," as seen in the case of a blind person who perceives through the skin even without light.
Because jars and other such things appear [in consciousness]. || 62 ||
It is said that for one who is blind, a form appears as a mere semblance in memory;
but since consciousness does not manifest [externally] in this way, what could ever appear, when, or where? (63)
If it is argued that even so, since a form appears without light, it follows that light and form are non-different, he says:
"of the blind. Even though a form appears to one born blind, because for all others besides him the form also appears in memory without depending on light, it does not have the nature of light.

The meaning is "of form. However, since there is no deviation whatsoever in the present case, he says: "not so. He demonstrates this very point with the words: "of consciousness" (*citeḥ*). At what time (*kadā*)—that is, in the world (*loke*)—and in what place (*kutra deśe*), does anything shine forth independently of consciousness? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 63 ||
Just as no reflection appears at all without a mirror, so too a reflection cannot exist apart from the mirror. (64)

He states an example for the pervasion under discussion with the word "just as" (yathā). Just as a reflection does not appear without a mirror, for this very reason, the reflection is not something distinct from the mirror. || 64 ||
Thus, apart from consciousness (cit), nothing whatsoever exists as something additional; for this very reason, there is indeed no other mind whatsoever apart from consciousness.
He applies this to the case under discussion with the word "thus" (*evam*). "For this very reason" means: because the mind, too, is equal to that which is seen [as an object].
Just as the mind exists in a dream, so too does the mind exist even in the waking state;
the mind alone is the instrument imagined for the accomplishment of its functions.

Here is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): "Just as" (*yathā*). For in a dream, because the knower, the act of knowing, the instrument of knowledge, and the object of knowledge are of one and the same nature, there is no separate mind; likewise, even the waking mind does not exist separately—this is the meaning. Just as in a dream, by means of the imagined mind alone...
He says that even while [the Lord] is thus awake, there is the accomplishment of all tasks: "It is imagined" (verse 66).
O Rāma, just as a dream-ax might be the instrument for the cutting down of a tree, how can an action that is unreal in nature have a real instrument? (67)
Since the act of cutting down a tree in a dream is unreal, its instrument—the axe—is likewise unreal;
similarly, because the object of perception is unreal, the cognition of it is also unreal, and thus its cause is also unreal.
He says this with the word "just as" (*yathā*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "Just as the axe [is the cause] in the cutting of a tree, so too is the mind."
He states that the unreality of the mind is unavoidable: "The act... (verse 67).
By whom has anyone ever been well-pierced by a non-existent human horn?
Therefore, O Rāma, the mind does not exist; moreover, that which is non-existent cannot be the cause of an effect. (68)
Since both cause and effect are unreal, action (*kriyā*) is all the more unreal;
he states this with an illustration: "unreal," etc. The *kāraka* is the instrument (*karaṇa*). || 68 ||
The mind is said to be that which performs the action of seeing in a dream;
likewise, O Rāma, the mind never performs any action at all.
Having already been explained, [the term] "dream" is stated once more with an illustration to further strengthen the point.
The conscious self, being purely and transparently free, conceives of the mind and so forth, and engages in worldly transaction through the distinctions of the seen, the seer, and so on. (70)
If it is asked, "In that case, how does this manifold appearance of bondage, liberation, and so forth occur? he replies: "The conscious Self" (*cidātma*).

"Transparent," "unobstructed," "self-willed" means autonomy (*svātantrya*). The meaning is that, like a magician, one should conduct all worldly affairs by means of one's own power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) alone. || 70 ||
In some places, however, it remains solely in the form of the non-conceptual;
hear, O Bhārgava, how the reality of consciousness (cittattva), though itself completely full, exists thus.

In some places and at other times, during the intermediate states, he begins to demonstrate that the very self of consciousness (*cidātman*) alone shines everywhere in both conceptualized (*savikalpa*) and non-conceptualized (*nirvikalpa*) forms, saying: "Listen" (verse 71).
Because it is consciousness, it is not equal to space; therefore, it is established as self-luminous.
Space and the conscious self have not attained any state of difference. (72)

He says that although it is as full as space, the reality of the Self is not equal to space because its nature is consciousness—namely, "not equal to space. Since its form is consciousness, the essence of the Self is self-luminous;
it is not insentient like space. Even though there is complete similarity between space and the Self [in terms of all-pervasiveness], [the Self differs in being conscious].
He states that consciousness alone is the additional attribute of the self: "And space," etc. (72).
He is full, subtle, stainless, unborn, infinite, and formless;
though the support of all, his self is unattached, existing both within and outside of everything. || 73 ||

He states the common attributes of these two: "Full," and so forth. "Full" means all-pervasive. "Subtle" means having a non-obstructive form. "Stainless" means having a single essence. "Unborn and infinite" means untouched by prior non-existence or destruction. "Formless" means devoid of parts or structural configuration.
Though the support of all, its nature is unattached; though the substratum of all, it is untouched. It exists both within and without all, and is woven through everything.
In that regard, the distinction is that consciousness exists [in the Self], whereas it does not exist in space;
yet in reality, it is the Self alone, which is full of consciousness, that is called "space."

Thus, even though everything is identical, he states that consciousness alone is the distinguishing feature within the self—this is what is meant by "the distinction. That [distinction] is consciousness. For the difference between space and the self is not real; thus he says, "but in reality. || 74 ||
For not even the slightest difference exists between the Self and space;
that which is space is indeed the Self, and that which is the Self is indeed space. (75)
The ignorant, through delusion, perceive the nature of the Self as being like space,
just as an owl perceives the light of the sun as mere darkness.
The ignorant perceive the Self as space. Here is an illustration: "Of the sun," etc.

Just as an owl, due to a defect in its own eyes, perceives even the sunlight of the sun as being of the nature of darkness, so too do people, due to the defect of ignorance, perceive the Self itself as space. 76.
Those who possess discernment perceive space itself as consisting of the consciousness of the Self;
for the supreme Consciousness, the Sovereign Mistress, [manifests] through the glory of her own pure autonomy. 77.

The wise and learned, however, perceive space itself as the nature of the self-consciousness (*ātmacidrūpa*). He establishes this very point by saying "the supreme consciousness" (*parā citiḥ*). The connection is as follows: the Supreme Lord, whose nature is supreme consciousness, would cause [all things] to manifest through the majesty—that is, the greatness—of His own pure sovereignty. || 77 ||
One should illuminate the self as divided into many parts,
just as, O Rāma, one perceives one's own self as manifold and distinct within a dream.
Here is the illustration: "Just as" (yathā). The grammatical connection is "you illuminate separately" (pṛthag bhāsayasi). || 78 ||
For in this very way You manifest [Yourself] through the distinctions of humans and so forth;
indeed, even this manifold appearance is perceived only by those whose vision is limited.

In this very way, the manifestation of the conscious self (cidātman) is indeed manifold; yet, even though there is a manifold manifestation of one's own self, it is not so from its own perspective. Thus he says: "as manifold" (anekadhā). || 79 ||
The supreme consciousness itself, by its own vision, is indeed of the nature of the full Self;
just as a single magician manifests himself in many forms. (80)
Here is an illustration: "the magician. (80)
Illuminating [all things] there, it shines by itself through its own vision to those who behold it;
thus, that supreme consciousness is indeed one and changeless. (81)

Just as a magician, though concealed by his own magic and appearing in many forms to those whose vision is veiled by that illusion, appears as only one to those whose own vision is not obstructed by the magic; so too does the supreme consciousness (parā citiḥ),
though appearing in many ways to those whose vision is veiled by ignorance manifested through its own māyā.
He says that, according to his own view, she is of one unchanging form: "Thus she" (verse 81).
For even though it shines as a single pure form, it appears divided in many ways; veiled by māyā, it causes those whose own natures are thus delimited to perceive [it] accordingly.
She is that whose light is pure, of a single flavor, one, and indivisible. || 82 ||
This very veil of illusion would appear as a limitation to one whose vision is restricted, just as a magician, though enveloped by illusion, appears differently to the eyes of others. || 83 ||

Just as multiplicity exists only from another's perspective, so too does being veiled by illusion exist only from another's perspective; he states this with an illustration: "Illusion" (māyā). The sense is that, from one's own perspective, there is no veil and no multiplicity. || 83 ||
Māyā is the absolute sovereignty of the Supreme Consciousness, which is exceedingly difficult to accomplish;
even in this world, other yogis, mantra-experts, and magicians [possess a limited form of it]. (84)
Now, one might object: "It is not possible for the Supreme Consciousness-Self, whose nature is exclusively pure consciousness, to manifest in such a manifold form.
Anticipating this doubt, he states the nature of *māyā*—in order to show that everything is possible through the power of *māyā*—with the words: "*Māyā*.
That which accomplishes what is difficult to achieve for the Supreme Consciousness-Self is *māyā*.
The meaning is that such absolute and supreme sovereignty is *māyā*. Here is an illustration: "even in the world," etc. (84).
Having attained their respective autonomy, which was previously concealed, they indeed accomplish even the impossible through some clever reasoning; therefore, this is not at all surprising.

Regarding the phrase "it is covered": for although those headed by the yogis are in reality nothing other than the supreme conscious Self and are thus endowed with full sovereignty, nevertheless, that sovereignty is obscured by the *māyā* of the supreme consciousness;
having attained a manifestation of some portion of sovereignty through the excellent application of yoga and other means—whereby that sovereignty was previously obscured—one [perceives it].

By virtue of the absence of any fixed cause, they bring about even such difficult-to-accomplish things as elephants, horses, and so forth. Thus, in the present case, it is not surprising that this world appears from the power of the undivided *māyā* of the Supreme Consciousness-Self; this is the meaning. || 85 ||
In this way, O descendant of Bhṛgu, the body of one's own self is manifested as manifoldly divided through the clear sovereignty of the supreme consciousness. 86.
Thus, according to the reasoning already stated. || 86 ||
But the delimitation of the ego is well-rested in a single part;
that very state, renowned as incompleteness, is celebrated as ignorance (avidyā). (87)
If it is asked, "What kind of limitation can there be for the full conscious Self (cidātman)? he says:
"Limitation" refers to the conceit of egoity (ahaṃbhāva). For the conscious Self is distinct from the inert light of lamps and the like;
its nature is a throbbing radiance. It is the resting upon the non-self of such a radiance whose essence is this throbbing manifestation.
This very state is the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*). The sense of "I" is repose within one's own self. As it has been stated in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*:

"That which is the sense of 'I' is called the full sense of 'I' (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), because it is the repose of the supreme conscious Self in its entire nature, and because it is unlimited (*aparicchinna*). (In some manuscripts: *aparicchinnapūrṇa*).
Even for one whose nature is such— complete and undivided— that which appears as a mere portion due to the power of *māyā* called "autonomy" (*svātantrya*),

and the resting within one's own self therein, is called "limitation" (*pariccheda*). This occurs when the Supreme Self, from its state of fullness (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), [appears limited] through its own power of *māyā*.

The intended meaning is that the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) regarding only a portion of one's own self is what constitutes limitation. The word *api* has the sense of *eva* (only). That which is celebrated in the scriptures as the manifestation of incompleteness (*apūrṇatvakhyāti*) and as ignorance (*avidyā*), that alone is the incomplete sense of "I" (*apūrṇāhaṃbhāva*). || 87 ||
In this matter, many logicians, though even learned, are deluded;
for, by not examining their own self and remaining fixed in an outward gaze, they fail to understand. (88)

And thus, because the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) comes to rest in one part [of the Self], all other regions of the conscious Self appear as space; therefore, it is established that space is not distinct from the Self. Regarding this non-difference of space from the Self, people are deluded. If one asks why they are deluded, he says: "one's own Self," and so forth.

"Without having proclaimed" means that even though the meaning has been heard and understood, one has not performed *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) regarding its immediate nature. The reason for this is stated as "because of abiding in an outward gaze. || 88 ||
Until one has examined oneself by not citing whatever has been taught by the guru—whether it be true, false, or otherwise—one should indeed not look [at the truth]. (89)

Therefore, he says "taught by the Guru" [in verse 89], because without immediate intuition preceded by contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), there is no attainment of the fruit consisting in the cessation of ignorance. Whether it be the real, whose nature is luminosity and so forth, or the other, the unreal, whose nature is non-luminosity and so forth.
So long as one does not attain the fruit through the direct realization of the Self as heard from scripture, therefore I have said, O Rāma: "Observe it within yourself with a steady gaze."

The fruit, which culminates in direct realization (*aparokṣa*), consists of the destruction of ignorance and so forth; it does not arise merely from the indirect nature [of knowledge] derived from hearing the scripture itself, nor from the mere indirectness produced by listening. This is seen from the perspective of one who has abandoned outward-directedness through the vision of Reality (*saddṛśā*). (90)
That consciousness which is the supreme goddess, whose form is universal, is composed of light because her nature is excluded from that of the insentient. || 91 ||

Furthermore, having first described the nature of the means of delimitation (*pariccheda-kāraṇa*), he begins to very clearly describe the nature of space (*ākāśa*): "Consciousness" (*cit*). It is the universal form of all things, devoid of the delimitation of the forms of the visible (*dṛśya-ākāra*). Because its nature is excluded from the insentient (*jaḍa*), it consists of luminosity (*prakāśa-mayī*).
