The meaning is that she consists of light, which is distinct from insentient objects such as lamps and the like. || 91 ||
Therefore, rest within one's own self is the ego-sense (*ahantā*) which takes on the form of the "other.
Insentient things, when resting within the conscious self, shine forth within the conscious self. (92)

Therefore, the remainder of the sentence is that there arises for him a supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*), which is unlimited and whose nature is other than [the limited ego], consisting of repose within one's own self. He states that insentient things lack such repose in their own selves by saying "insentient things" (*jaḍāḥ*). || 92 ||
They do not shine by themselves in their own nature; therefore, there is no resting within their own self.
Consciousness alone, however, always rests within itself without dependence on anything else.

He explains this very point clearly with the words: "not in its own nature" (*na svarūpe*). Because insentient things (*jaḍa*) manifest only by depending on the conscious self (*cidātman*), they lack manifestation within themselves independently; therefore, they do not rest in their own selves.
Consciousness (*cit*), however, always rests in itself through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), independently and without depending on anything else, such as the insentient.
The connection is that because it is manifest, its resting within itself is logically established. || 93 ||
Because it is manifest within itself, rest therein is logically established;
this is that supreme, full I-consciousness which does not exist in insentient things. (94)

"It arises" means that the dependence on another for the manifestation of its own nature—which does not exist in the case of the insentient—is precisely what constitutes "resting in one's own self"; this is the intended meaning. This very resting in one's own self is full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). || 94 ||
This [consciousness] is devoid of the touch of exclusion because it is free from conceptual determination;
for everything is contained within it, just as a city is reflected in a mirror. (95)
If it is asked, "From where does the fullness of this non-duality arise?", he says: "By the exclusion...
The sense is that it is devoid of contact with exclusion—that is, difference—in every respect, being entirely free from any connection to duality. If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says:
"Like a city in a reflection, everything exists in identity with this very consciousness whose nature is the fullness of non-duality."

The visible object. Therefore, because there is no other distinct entity apart from itself that could serve as a delimiter, and due to the absence of such delimitation, there is no contact with exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). || 95 ||
For how and by what could there be exclusion or delimitation?
Thus, for that which is of a perfect nature, there exists a perfect manifestation.

Therefore, he states that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and so forth are not possible—[saying] "exclusion. Again, having extracted the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness), he says "thus" (*evam*). The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: it is precisely that full, undivided manifestation of the essential nature of consciousness, which belongs to the consciousness whose own nature is full, that is being described. || 96 ||
That very state is called repose in one's own self and the fullness of I-consciousness (pūrṇāhantā);
for this, O Rāma, is indeed the undivided, single essence, and it is just this much.

Now, one might object: "Even so, since there is a duality of entities—consciousness (*citi*) and the full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*)—there would still be a limitation. Anticipating this, he says: "undivided" (*akhaṇḍa*). Both of these—consciousness and the full I-consciousness—are a single undivided essence. They are undivided, one, a single essence, pure consciousness alone. || 97 ||
In its manifestation, that [reality] appears as if manifold;
such indeed is its sovereignty, for power is essentially composed of it.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is there a twofold teaching?", he says: "It is *nirūpaṇa*. That is the *cittattva* (the reality of consciousness).
This alone is indeed the undivided single essence, which is also sovereignty (*svātantrya*). Full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*) and sovereignty are nothing but power (*śakti*);
therefore, the meaning is that [consciousness] consists of that and has that as its sole essence. || 98 ||
Just as light and heat abide inseparably within fire, so too [this power] consists of a single essence accompanied by repose in absolute freedom. (99)
He provides an illustration for the non-separateness of the power that is the object of the conventional usage of difference: "illumination," [meaning] consciousness accompanied [by it]. 99.
For this very power called Māyā is supremely difficult to accomplish;
like a mirror, it exists within its own nature as that which has the single essence of consciousness.

This very [consciousness] is the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness). It accomplishes even that which is difficult to accomplish (*durghaṭa*). It explains this very state of being difficult to accomplish with the words "like a mirror" (verse 100).
Even while appearing through the manifestation of manifold variety, it shines forth;
likewise, even at the time of such manifestation, there is no departure from its own essential nature.

Even though it is variegated by reflections, just as a mirror of a single form [remains itself], consciousness—though its own nature is of a single form—shines forth through the appearance of the world's diversity; yet, even at the time of the appearance of that diversity, it does not deviate from its own nature which is the single essence of consciousness.
That this very thing occurs is what constitutes its "extreme difficulty" (atidurghaṭatva), so it is understood. || 101 ||
That appearance which consists of delimitation is called the appearance of the non-Self;
it is ignorance, the inert power, and it is indeed the Void and primordial nature (prakṛti). || 102 ||

Thus, that manifestation of the delimitation of one's own self through the māyā called "independence" is itself the manifestation of the non-self. Because of the identity between the manifesting appearance and the manifested object, it is said: "That is ignorance (avidyā). 102.
Absolute non-existence, the darkness of space, and the first creation—all that is declared to be the primordial limitation. (103)
Everything from the appearance of the non-self (*anātma*) up to the end of the first creation has been described as that very initial act of delimitation (*paricchedana*).
Through *māyā*,
the manifestation of the non-self, which is inseparable from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the primordial delimitation, is expressed by such terms as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth.
This is the meaning. || 103 ||
O Rāma, for that one who is the perfectly full Self and has indeed established himself in rest, the appearance of space is produced by the delusion of partiality. 104.

Having thus stated the very nature of space (*ākāśa*), he expresses it again in two verses by means of a different approach, beginning with "O Rāma, that which... [referring to] that [state] of resting in the full Self; [it is] produced by the delusion of partiality. (104)
Therefore, that portion of the self which is devoid of the conceit of "self" is indeed declared to be space; for it is the cause of saṃsāra. || 105 ||

Therefore, due to the delusion that the sense of "I" occupies only a single part [of the self], the notion of a self is the state of egoism (*ahaṃbhāva*). That portion of the self which is devoid of the notion of a self is indeed space (*ākāśa*). That very space is the cause of saṃsāra. || 105 ||
This alone would be the distinction, which is the sole domain of the limited vision of the bound soul (paśu).
O Rāma, behold with a subtle vision that very space which is perceived by you. (106)
If it is asked, "How can space (*ākāśa*) be the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)?", he replies with the word "this" (*eṣa*). The meaning is that it is space itself.

The point is this: since the appearance of duality is inseparable from the manifestation of space—which is illumined by the knowledge of the limited self (*paricchinnātman*) that is the cause of transmigratory existence—it is precisely this duality that constitutes space as the cause of transmigratory existence.
It brings about the experience of the non-difference between space and the Self: "Rāma. (106)
The self of the multitudes of living beings there is indeed consciousness itself;
it is that which always shines as space within other bodies, even as it does for you.

Regarding the word "tatra" (therein): it means "of such a region of space. Regarding "jīvarāśīnām" (of the multitudes of living beings): it refers to embodied souls. The construction is: "That space, which is that very Self. || 107 ||
That very Self of theirs would consist of a mass of consciousness and bliss;
thus, the body of consciousness remains swallowed by the space imagined by itself. (108)

That very space which always shines as yours within other bodies would be their own Self, consisting of the mass of consciousness and bliss; for it is impossible for two distinct entities to occupy the same location. Thus, the implication is that your Self is likewise [the Self] of all.
And so, the sense is this: wherever and whatever space appears, that very space is the Self of the embodied beings residing therein.
Having thus established the identity of space and the Self, he defines the nature of the mind with the word "evam" (thus):
[the mind] is swallowed by space, that is, delimited by space. 108.
That very [consciousness] is called the mind (manas), for it is indeed the Self and nothing else;
however, because of its primary role as a veil, the mind is designated as the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa). || 109 ||
That very [consciousness] delimited by space is indeed the body of consciousness (*cid-vapu*). Therefore, the Self alone is the mind; the other is not.

Now, to dispel the doubt as to how there can be a distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) if the mind is nothing but the Self, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). This means: given that the mind is established as being the Self itself. "Because of the predominance of concealment" (*āvaraṇa-mukhyatvāt*).

The principle of consciousness (cittattva) veiled by the power of inertia (jaḍaśakti) is indeed the individual soul (jīva). In that state, because of the predominance of the power of inertia which consists of obscuration, the "means of knowledge" (pramāṇa)—meaning the instrument of cognition—is the mind (manas). || 109 ||
But primarily due to being veiled, the cognizer is called the *jīva*;
likewise, although the conscious self is veiled by space, it is [still] essentially [conscious]. (110)
He states that, because the state of having a covered mind is predominant, the *jīva* alone is the subject (*pramātṛ*), saying "covered" (*āvṛta*).

Thus, although [the self] is already covered by the insentient power whose nature is space, which is imagined through its own sovereignty, he says "thus" (*evam*) to indicate that it is further covered even by the body composed of the five elements. || 110 ||
In the sky—which is soft, exceedingly relaxed, void, and pure—one imagines hardness, clinging, density, and impurity. (111)
In this regard, he first explains how space itself takes on the form of air and so forth through the manifestation of other qualities, stating: "In space.

[This means] in space—which is soft (*komala*), devoid of touch (*sparśābhāvavat*), lax (*śithila*), with unjoined parts (*asaṃśliṣṭāvayava*), dense (*nirghana*), not compact (*anibiḍa*), and stainless (*amala*)—there arises hardness (*kaṭhinatva*), which is touch (*sparśa*), cohesion (*śliṣṭatā*), the state of having joined parts (*saṃśliṣṭāvayavatā*), and density (*ghanatā*).
The connection is as follows: "having manifested the elements through the conceptualizations of density, impurity, and filth.
Having manifested the elements, the self-identifying body (dehātman) is likewise enveloped by the body;
like a lamp placed within the interior of a jar, it shines, pervading the belly. || 112 ||

Regarding the term "elements" (*bhūtāni*): by imagining touch in space (*ākāśa*), which is itself devoid of touch, it becomes air (*vāyu*). By imagining that very air, whose parts are unjoined, to have joined parts, it becomes fire (*tejas*). For fire indeed possesses joined parts in comparison to air, since [the latter] has unjoined parts.

When that very light, which has become solidified, comes within the range of the eye, it appears as earth. Through the conceptualization of density (*ghanatā*) for that same light which is essentially non-dense (*nirghana*), it acquires the nature of water; for water indeed possesses density, by virtue of which impact (*abhighāta*) is possible. And through the conceptualization of impurity (*mālinya*) for that same pure water, it acquires the nature of earth.

And there is impurity in the earth, because, like a jar or similar object submerged in water, that which is submerged in the earth is not perceived. Being thus enveloped by a body composed of such a mass of elements, he became identified with the body through the sense of identity with the body; this is the implied meaning. Thus, [he attained] the state of being the body-self.

He states, with an illustration, that even when it has attained the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatā), it does not abandon [its own nature]: "Like a jar," etc. It should be construed as: "just as it appears. || 112 ||
In this way, he remains as the essence of a hidden lamp, appearing only within another body, illuminating only that which is inside it.

This conscious self is merely a manifestation; its nature consists solely of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). Its essential form is like a lamp hidden inside a jar—just as a lamp illuminates only the interior of a jar, so too does this self illuminate only the interior of the body. 113.
Just as the light of a lamp issues forth externally through a hole in a jar,
even so does consciousness issue forth repeatedly through the gateway of the senses.

He states, with an illustration, that even the cognition of a jar and so forth, though arising through the channels of the senses such as the eyes, is indeed of the nature of the Self: "The light of a lamp," etc. Regarding the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*): the meaning is that consciousness, which is eternally luminous, shines forth again in the form of various objects as if it were something newly arisen. || 114 ||
But there is no departure for consciousness, because it is full and inactive;
the covering of its own self is space, which is the power of manifestation of the conscious self. (115)
If it is asked, "How is liberation possible for consciousness, which is like space?", he says: "Liberation.
In reality, there is no liberation of consciousness; rather, he says "one's own self" to indicate that it is merely an appearance thereof. || 115 ||

As long as one restrains [the mind], so long does the emergence [of reality] appear; this is the activity of the mind, which constitutes the removal of the obscuration through its manifestation. (116)

"As far as" means this: as long as ignorance—which consists of space, is of the nature of an insentient power (*jaḍaśakti*), and serves as a veil for one's own self—prevents the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) which is the manifestation of the conscious self (*cidātman*), so long does the departure of consciousness appear.
Herein lies the essential truth: [it belongs] to the supreme conscious self.

The limited subject, the individual soul (*jīva*), is that which manifests as a delimited sense of "I" through the projection of its own freedom. It consists of the light of consciousness situated within the body, like a lamp placed inside a jar.
Just as the motionless darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp emerging from a hole in the jar, so too is [the darkness] removed from the conscious Self.

Wherever there is the manifestation of the power of manifestation (*sphūrti-śakti*) caused by the contact of the senses and so forth with their respective objects, there Consciousness (*citi*), through the cessation of the ignorance designated as "space" and so on which veils it, appears as if it has expanded.
Thus, he states that the very cessation of this veil is also the operation of the mind (*manas*): "The mind... (verse 116).
Therefore, O Rāma, the mind is not something other than the Self; the Self alone is called the mind.
Consciousness, though by nature immovable, is termed "mind" when it is in a state of motion. (117)

"Therefore" means that because the mind is essentially the self of consciousness (cidātman) characterized by veiling (āvaraṇa). He states this very point again by extracting it: "and it moves. || 117 ||
O Rāma, the striking against [objects] through the manifestation of consciousness is indeed the movement of the intellect;
this very thing constitutes conceptual construction, which ceases when one is entirely free from conceptual construction.

He states the meaning of the term "movement" (*calana*): "āvṛtti" and so forth. This very thing is movement itself. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "when the exclusion of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is movement, has been accomplished. (118)
O Rāma, abandon all doubt regarding this: non-conceptual, perfect consciousness is what is called liberation; it occurs through the total relinquishing of conceptual construction.
The form of plenitude (*pūrṇarūpa*). Since limitation is produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is the state of plenitude.
The meaning is that such a state of plenitude is itself liberation. In this context, non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpavijñāna*) is the very nature of liberation.
One might think that some residue of obscuration remains, but there is no obscuration at all;
for obscuration does not truly exist, since it is imagined by the [mind] itself.

He states the nature of doubt: "Even when free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there may remain a residue of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*). Because this takes the form of a possibility, it is a doubt. Now, one might object: "How can the cessation of obscuration occur merely by abiding in the non-conceptual state? Anticipating this, he says: "It does not exist at all," because obscuration is [fictitious], like a snake in a rope, and is [removed] by that very [realization].
The meaning is: "because it is imagined. || 120 ||
Just as one who has himself become bound by an enemy within a mental projection remains there being struck and threatened until he abandons that conceptual construction. (121)

Regarding this, he states an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). The connection is: "one should act in the absence of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) during the occasion of the 'kingdom of the mind' (*manorājya*). || 121 ||
One may perform beating or even threatening, yet it dissolves;
consider how the bondage remains there, and likewise here as well.

The phrase "yāvattāvat" (as long as) has the meaning of "yadā tadā" (at that time). Thus, when striking and so forth have ceased through the abandonment of volitional intention (*saṅkalpa*), at that very moment, is bondage left over? The meaning is: it is not left over. "Likewise here too" means that when volitional intention is abandoned, bondage is not left over. || 122 ||
From beginningless time, there has never been bondage for anyone other than mere delusion; cast aside this dull-souled error and investigate: what is this so-called bondage? (123)

He states that there is no bondage for anyone, anywhere, at any time, that transcends conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), by saying "beginningless" (*anādi*). [The word] "here" refers to this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). If it is objected, "In that case, is not this sequence of instruction and so forth useless?", he says "no," by saying "insentient" (*jaḍa*).
The sense is that bondage is produced solely by the delusion of duality consisting of insentient matter. || 123 ||
This very great bondage, which is the conviction in the reality of bondage, exists like a seizure by a yakṣa for the foolish person who is terrified by what is false. (124)
He states that bondage itself is to be discarded, specifically the conviction in the reality of bondage—this is what "this" refers to.

The point is that even when there is knowledge of one's true nature (*svarūpa*), if the delusion regarding the reality of bondage persists, the fruit of knowledge will not arise; therefore, this [delusion] alone is the primary bondage. Regarding its capacity to produce misfortune:
The example is: "it is false. (124)
As long as even a wise person does not abandon this delusion of bondage, he will not be liberated from cyclic existence anywhere, despite his great efforts. (125)
The delusion regarding the reality of bondage [occurs] at some time or in some place. || 125 ||
What is this bondage, and how could it belong to the stainless self whose nature is consciousness, when [the world] is manifested within the mirror of its own self in the form of reflections? (126)
He says that bondage cannot be established unless it is superimposed: "What is this?

This is an objection regarding the very nature of bondage—what kind of bondage can there be for the stainless Self of Consciousness, which is like space and unattached? And how could such a connection [between the Self and bondage] even occur? Now, as for bondage...

If it is argued that [the world] might exist as reflections of the objects of perception appearing within [consciousness], even though they lack existence apart from the conscious self (cidātman), he says "no," [stating]: "by those consisting of reflections" (pratibimbātmakaiḥ). || 126 ||
If bondage were like a reflection in a mirror or a fire in a mirage, then the notion of the reality of bondage would be merely the mind’s conviction of its own existence. (127)

He states the absolute impossibility of bondage through objects that have become the nature of reflections within one’s own self, [in the verse beginning] "That mirror... He states that there is no bondage other than the two kinds of delusion—the notion that "there is a self" and the notion that "bondage is real"—[in the verse beginning] "of bondage... (127).
Apart from these two, there is no bondage for anyone anywhere;
as long as these two remain sufficient, they are cleansed by the great waters of right inquiry.
The "dual impurity" refers to the impurity consisting of the two aforementioned types of delusion.
In this matter of destroying saṃsāra, he has not yet been cleansed;
neither I, nor Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor even Śaṅkara [is capable of it].
He says that for one whose aforementioned two-fold delusion has not been destroyed through inquiry, worldly existence is difficult to overcome:
"Or rather, Tripurā, who is of the nature of knowledge, is in no way capable [of liberating].
Therefore, O Rāma, having abandoned this duality, become happy. (130)
The pair refers to the two aforementioned delusions. || 130 ||
Therefore, O Rāma, when the mind is established in its non-conceptual form, because it consists of nothing but the Self, duality does not remain. 131.

Having thus established what arose from the context, he concludes the refutation of the objection that "duality would result because the mind exists even in the state of non-conceptualization" with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
The meaning is: "because [the world] is not other than the mind. Of that mind. || 131 ||
This mind does not shine as something other than in the form of "this" and so forth;
when "this" and the rest are abandoned, that which consists of mere shining remains.

Having extracted the form of the mind, he says: "This [is it]. It is distinct from mere appearance. The intended meaning is that the Self itself, when conjoined with the form of the object of perception, is the mind. || 132 ||
The delusion of a snake in a rope occurs with respect to an object regarded as real;
for it is certain that the appearance of the snake manifests within the form of the rope. (133)

He also refutes duality by means of the very nature of error, [saying] "in the case of the rope": "In the case of the rope—the object regarded as real—the error of the rope-snake is that which makes the snake appear. (133)

In that case, even though the snake is sublated, because it is supported by the rope, the cognition of the rope—which is distinct from the Self whose nature is consciousness—remains established. (134)

Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): even when the superimposed snake and so forth in an error such as that of a rope-snake are sublated, the erroneous cognition remains uncontradicted as a cognition of that rope for the cognizer, by virtue of having the rope as its object. This is the meaning. || 134 ||

When that very rope, imagined through the example of a dream, is [realized as] a mere cognition of a snake, then once the rope is sublated, how could that cognition remain, and what would its basis be? (135)

He says "that" (*sā*) to show that this is not the case in the present context. The meaning is: when, by means of the analogy of the dream, there is the certainty that "this rope was imagined in consciousness," then, upon the sublation (*bādha*) of even the rope, what basis would that cognition have apart from the cognizer, or what form would it retain? It is like the space within a jar when the jar is destroyed.
The intended meaning is that [the disciple] is taught separately. || 135 ||
Therefore, when the object of perception is sublated, that cognition is indeed pure vision;
since it is not distinct from the nature of consciousness, how could duality exist by means of it? (136)

Therefore, because there is no remainder of erroneous cognition—that cognition being the cognition of the visible—it does not differ from the conscious self (cidātman); how, then, could duality arise through that delusive cognition? || 136 ||
For causal efficiency is clearly observed to be quite stable even in the case of dream-objects;
indeed, it is recognized by everyone that dream-objects are stable within the dream state. (137)
He rejects the position that "the visible is real because it performs causal efficiency" with the words "causal efficiency.

[Causal efficiency] is "stable," meaning uncontradicted at that time. He states that the stability of dream-objects is established by the experience of dreaming itself with the words "dream... (verse 137).
There would be only this much difference between the manifestations of dream and waking:
in the waking state, there is certainly a firm conviction regarding the falsity of the dream. (138)
If it is asked, "What then is the difference between dreaming and waking?", he says: "It is just this much"—namely, the certainty of the falsity of what was experienced in a dream. || 138 ||
The determination of falsity does not arise in the waking state merely because it occurs in a dream; by this much alone, the reality of waking experience would not be established. (139)
In a dream, there is no determination of the falsity of what was experienced during the waking state; it is by this very distinction [that they differ]. 139.
Just as the stability and causal efficacy of objects are perceived during the waking state, tell me: is that same [stability and efficacy] perceived in a dream, or is it not? (140)
He states that causal efficiency and stability are equal in both waking and dreaming, saying "just as" (yathā). The construction is: "Why is it not seen in the same way in a dream? || 140 ||

In a dream, waking-state entities do not exist; nor do dream-entities exist in the waking state. Furthermore, they appear neither as performers of causal efficacy nor as stable, and the same applies to their counterparts in the waking state.
Therefore, for that reason, the pair consisting of waking and dreaming is equal. || 141 ||
Analyze with a subtle vision: what difference is there between the past and a dream?
Behold, even in that which is produced by a magician, there is stability as well as causal efficiency.

What is the difference between the past and a dream? The meaning is that there is none at all. To facilitate the mind's ascent [to higher states], he provides another example experienced while awake, saying "Behold" (paśya): [this refers to] the elephants, horses, and so forth created by a magician. 142.
Is it then truly real, or is it a creation of a magician?
Indeed, the distinction between the real and the unreal is not understood by common people. 143.

"By that much alone"—that is, by means of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and stability alone. If it is asked, "Even though those two are equal, why is there the conventional distinction that one is real and the other is unreal?", he says "real" (*satya*), explaining: "Because of the absence of a discernment between the real and the unreal. (143)
Therefore, being thus deluded, they declared that the world is indeed real;
for they say, O Rāma, that the truth is that which is never touched by non-existence. (144)
If it is asked, "What then is the definition of those two? he states the definition of reality (*satya*): "never" (*kadāpi*).
This means not touched by non-existence (*abhāva*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); that is to say, it is not the counter-correlate of non-existence. || 144 ||
Non-existence would indeed result from non-manifestation; however, there is never a non-manifestation of consciousness anywhere.
For non-manifestation belongs to non-conscious things, owing to the appearance of multiplicity.

If it is argued that there is non-contact with the conscious self (*cidātman*) because of the absence [of objects] in some respect, [the author] says "non-existence" (*abhāva*), because since non-existence is known through the means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), such [non-apprehension] is impossible for the conscious self; thus, its non-existence is not established. [The phrase] "due to non-appearance" (*abhanāt*) refers to the non-apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Non-existence would be established as something cognized (*pramita*); [this applies] to non-conscious things (*acitām*).
He states that there is a non-manifestation of all visible things in every respect: "non-manifestation. The reason for this is:
"due to multiplicity" (anekatva). || 145 ||
For non-sentient existence consists entirely in the manifestation of mutual absence;
O Rāma, investigate this: when and where could there ever be the non-manifestation of consciousness? (146)
If it is asked, "Even though there is the appearance of multiplicity among visible objects, how is it that [the underlying unity] does not appear? he says: "Mutually...
Inert objects such as jars and the like, which constitute the visible world, appear as mutually non-existent because they are manifold.
Jars and other such things, being mutually distinct, appear precisely as differentiated from what is other than themselves. And thus:

The point is this: because only those visible objects that possess mutual absence from one another appear, they are non-conscious entities due to the manifestation of their mutual absence. He states that the conscious self (*cidātman*) is not like this, saying "the non-manifestation of consciousness. This is because jars and other such things appear only as being submerged within the conscious self by way of being its reflections.
The sense is that its manifestation might perhaps be established at some time. || 146 ||
Tell me, how could consciousness shine when it does not shine? Or, if it does not shine, how could it shine? For if it were non-shining, both [consciousness and its object] would be non-existent.

An objection is raised: "In states such as deep sleep, where there is no perception of any visible object, consciousness (cit) is not perceived; therefore, consciousness itself must be non-existent. Anticipating this, he says: "When... (yadā). At that time when consciousness does not appear, how could that very time denoted by the word "when" (yadā) appear? Furthermore, why would it not appear?

Or how could the non-perception of consciousness (cid-anupalabdhi), as previously stated, appear? The intended meaning is that even the non-perceptions of those two times [past and future] are themselves illumined by consciousness. If it is argued that even if the non-perceptions of those two times do not appear, the absence of consciousness will nonetheless be established, he says: "In the case of non-appearance" (*abhāne*). "Of those two" (*tad-dvayoḥ*) refers to that time and its non-perception. || 147 ||
O Rāma, because consciousness arises from fear alone, that consciousness is indeed real.
O Rāma, listen to the distinction between the real and the unreal; I shall explain it to you in brief. (148)
The meaning is as follows: because the non-existence [of the object] at that time and its non-perception at that time are unestablished due to their absence, its perception alone is established.

Therefore, since its non-existence is not proven, having thus established the reality of the conscious self (cidātman) and the unreality of the visible world apart from it, [the author] provides the definition of the real and the unreal once more for the sake of further strengthening this very point.
He says "rāma" in order to state it by way of another method. || 148 ||
That which appears independently would be real, while the other is unreal;
otherwise, even things such as a rope-snake would surely be real. (149)
"Independent of anything else" means that what is self-luminous is real, while the other is unreal; this is the essential meaning. "Otherwise" means:

if it is argued that what is sublated by the cognition of non-existence, such as "it does not exist," is unreal, whereas what is unsublated is real. "In the case of the rope" refers to a situation where, following the cognition of a snake in a rope and so forth, the sublating cognition—such as "this is not a snake"—has not yet arisen.
The meaning is that even [the killing of] snakes and so forth would become true [i.e., meritorious]. || 149 ||
For negation is indeed the cognition of non-existence; yet that [cognition] could occur even when [the object] exists.
Furthermore, the cognition of existence would clearly occur even in the case of non-existence. (150)
He establishes this very point with the words "sublation" (bādha): Sublation, as accepted by you, is the cognition of non-existence;

and that [cognition] would be possible even when an entity is intended to exist. Furthermore, since there is a cognition of existence regarding a non-entity that is not intended to exist, it is clear that an uncontradicted cognition of reality is also possible.

This is established by universal experience. The point is that, according to their view, that which is considered true would be sublated, while that which is considered untrue would remain unsublated. || 150 ||
Therefore, the position that "the uncontradicted is true and the contradicted is false" would not be tenable, because it is subject to deviation in every respect. (151)

Therefore, because of the aforementioned over-extension: your position—that what is not sublated is true and what is sublated is false—is not tenable, since, according to the manner explained, it is subject to contradiction in every respect. || 151 ||
If consciousness were not manifest, nothing at all would exist, nor would even that [consciousness] exist in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, whoever says that consciousness does not manifest is a harsh fellow among logicians. (152)
In my view, there is no fault because consciousness (*cit*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), whereas that which is distinct from consciousness is not self-luminous;

this is the sense in which it is said that "self-luminosity must be admitted. Mocking and censuring the logician (*tārkika*) who does not accept the eternal luminosity of consciousness on the grounds that it is illuminated by another, [the author] says:
"Therefore" means: because of the aforementioned logical inconsistency. || 152 ||
He would say, "I am not"; in that case, by what could anything be said? For one who always has doubt regarding the self due to its appearance and disappearance. (153)
By what is it said that something is "settled"? The intended meaning is that, due to extreme stupidity, one is unfit for a settled reply.
He should dispel the delusion of others through skillful compositions of reasoning;
then even this Gaṇḍaśilā shall destroy the delusion of others.
One should connect the sentence as follows: "If he were to destroy the delusion of people by composing treatises characterized by the weaving of logical arguments (tarka). || 154 ||
Therefore, reality does not consist merely in the appearance of causal efficiency;
for indeed, every cognition is nothing but an error, without a doubt. (155)

Therefore, since the distinction between the real and the unreal has been explained in the manner stated above, he begins [the following] to dispel the doubt that if all cognition were erroneous, there would be no distinction between error and non-error: "All indeed... (verse 155).
This other great delusion is the determination of non-delusion regarding those [objects];
for just as there may be delusion prior to a subverting cognition, so it is here. (156)
Regarding those cognitions which are delusive errors: if it is asked, "If all cognition is of the nature of error, how does it appear as non-delusive?", he says: "Just as... (verse 156).
For the consciousness of the entire world remains as if it were non-erroneous, yet just as the cognition of silver is of the nature of an error due to the cognition of mother-of-pearl. (157)
If it is asked, "In that case, when is their erroneous nature apprehended?", he says: "Just as... (verse 157).
Thus, from the realization of the conscious self (cidātman), all knowledge is seen to be of the nature of error;
it appears as a universal delusion of the sky being blue, common to all. || 158 ||
From the direct realization of the non-dual, full conscious Self through the knowledge of the conscious Self, all worldly cognition [arises].
[The text] dispels the doubt as to how an error can be common to everyone with the words "as in the sky"; it should be construed as "just as [in the case of the sky], so [is this]. 158.
This delusion of all beings arises from the cause of defects;
non-delusion is pure consciousness, which exists as the nature of the self of consciousness. (159)
Regarding the phrase "due to the cause of a defect": the meaning is that it is because the defect of ignorance is similar [in its obstructive nature] to the defect of distance.
He establishes that it is non-erroneous with the words "pure consciousness" (śuddhavijñāna): it is of the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra) permeating all cognitions. || 159 ||
Thus has that which you asked been explained by me in accordance with reason;
O Rāma, casting aside all doubt here, resolve what has been spoken.
He summarizes with the word "thus": "That which is connected with reasoning" means that which is logically consistent; this has been proclaimed by me. 160.
As for that which was previously asked—how there can be worldly discourse regarding one who is liberated—I shall explain that to you, O Rāma; listen properly with a concentrated mind.
Previously, at the beginning of the fifteenth chapter, it was asked: "How does worldly conduct proceed for one who is liberated? || 161 ||
For in this world, even liberated men of knowledge— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
are distressed moment by moment by the enjoyments brought about by their *prārabdha* karma.

Regarding the lowest [type], he says: "By what has begun" (*prārabdha*). This refers to the enjoyments that have arrived—that is, the pleasures and pains produced by sense objects—which have been encountered or obtained. || 162 ||
O Rāma, those who know only their own individual form are considered to be of dull intellect;
for they do not realize [the Self], even while experiencing the fruits of their prārabdha karma.
Even those who know the nature of the full Self, because they perceive defects in sensual pleasure, are distressed by pleasure and pain at their respective times;
this means they are of dull intellect or inferior intellect. [They are thus] regarding the objects already attained. 163.
Those who remain amidst millions of diverse fruits of their past actions (prārabdha) are remembered as the wise, like bees dwelling within honey. || 164 ||

If it is asked, "How do they not know?", he says: "Like honey and milk. This refers to those whose internal minds are constantly and perfectly concentrated; [their experience is] like the experience of pleasure and pain arising from a gentle breeze or the bite of a mosquito during deep sleep.
The meaning is that the experience of pleasure and pain at the initial moment belongs to those of middling knowledge (*madhyajñānin*).
(In manuscript *kh*, it reads *madhyamānā*. || 164 ||
They do not fall away from their established state, nor are they agitated by multitudes of calamities;
they are not struck with wonder by marvels, nor do they rejoice in great pleasures. (165)
Of abiding in one's own state, which is absorption in one's true nature. || 165 ||
Those who are peaceful within and outwardly like the world are the best among the wise;
thus, through the differentiation of the intellect and the differentiation in the ripening of knowledge.
They are inwardly tranquil, being free from the agitation produced by desire, anger, and other such passions;

they are outwardly equal to the ignorant world because they engage in worldly affairs in the same manner as others. These are not the lowest class of knowers (*adhamajñānin*), for whom there is no constant absorption in their own true nature (*svarūpasamādhi*), but rather whose meditation is interrupted at intervals by the force of past karma (*prārabdha*) and the remnants of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

This is a conjunction with afflictions (*kleśayoga*). This person is not liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), but rather possesses isolated knowledge (*kevalajñānī*); the other two are liberated while living.

Among them, the second has fully matured cessation-concentration (*nirodhasamādhi*), while the third has fully matured external concentration (*bāhyasamādhi*). Thus, he states "in this way" (*evam*) to show that even among the third type, there is a diversity of conventional usage based on distinctions such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. (166)
Due to the power of the remnants of *prārabdha* karma, worldly activities become diverse;
even their conduct may occur like that of one intoxicated by honey and the like. (167)
Of those wise ones. || 167 ||
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Tātparyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Jñānakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrītripurārahasya*.]
[Now begins the nineteenth chapter:
Having heard this from the mouth of Dattātreya, the delighter of the Bhṛgus again asked about the sequence of conduct for those who are liberated, in due order. (1)

He introduces Rāma’s question in order to describe the state of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), which was briefly mentioned at the end of the previous chapter, as well as the cause for its various classifications: "Thus," etc. (1).
O Blessed One, explain this to me further in detail:
how it is that through the differentiation of the intellect, there arises the manifold variety in the ripening of knowledge.
He clarifies what was just stated with the words "yathā" (just as): "The ripening of knowledge" (*jñānapāka*) is the unshakeability of the attainment of knowledge;

however, knowledge is indeed of one kind, consisting solely in the manifestation of one's own self. And that alone should be the goal (*upeya*), which consists in the realization of liberation (*mokṣa*). (3)

It implies the variety in the ripening of knowledge—[this is] "knowledge. Because of which: that which consists of its manifestation means that which consists of the manifestation of the nature of knowledge. || 3 ||
Therefore, explain how it is that, based on the difference in cognition, there is a difference in the cooking;
or else, whether the means of accomplishment also differ or not.

Therefore, because the means to liberation and liberation itself are of one and the same nature, the sense is this: even though there is a distinction in the intensity or dullness of the intellect, since the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*) are of a single kind, how could there not be a variety in the ripening of knowledge? Knowledge has its support in knowledge.
The means of accomplishment. || 4 ||
Thus questioned by him once more, Dattātreya, the treasure-house of compassion,
began to explain that very matter in detail.
By that Rāma; that very same object, which is the differentiation of the maturation of knowledge. || 5 ||
Listen, O Rāma, for I shall proclaim this most excellent secret:
there is no distinction in the practice of means, nor is knowledge a diverse means.
There is no distinction in the means for attaining gnosis. He states this very point clearly: "gnosis," [verse 6].
Due to the gradation of the means, the attainment of the fruit is differentiated;
however, when the practice is complete, knowledge is accomplished without effort. (7)

The attainment of the fruit, which is the perfection of knowledge, results from the gradations of the means—that is, from the cause of their being small or not small. Regarding the phrase "but when full": it refers to the completion of the perfection of the means accumulated through many previous births. || 7 ||
Due to the gradation of merit (apūrta), there may be a dependence on you [the Lord] through effort;
however, in reality, no means whatsoever is of any use for the attainment of knowledge.

He says [in verse 8]: "In reality..."—meaning that when the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are complete, knowledge is achieved without effort, like the falling of a fruit from the sky (though the reading *phalapāta* is not found in manuscript k); whereas in the case of incomplete means, there is a dependence on varying degrees of effort according to the degree of that incompleteness.
Knowledge is never something to be produced, for it is established by its very nature;
consciousness itself is cognition, and that is always self-luminous.

If it is argued that because [the self] is by nature its own form, even though the means of proof (*sādhana*) are of no use for its production, they may nonetheless be useful for its cognition, he replies: "Consciousness" (*caitanya*). || 9 ||
In that regard, what need is there for a means of realization in that which is of the nature of eternal manifestation? Consciousness is deposited within the exceedingly pure casket of the mind. (10)
He describes the utility of the means for removing that very obscuration by way of the analogy of a gem—
namely, "consciousness" (*caitanya*) and "extremely pure.
Just as a ruby within a crystal casket remains unobscured, so too consciousness, even when situated within the mind (*citta*), is indeed unobscured.
(The meaning is that it is indeed a verse. || 10 ||
One who is submerged in the mire of infinite latent impressions (vāsanā) is not perceived at all;
[this occurs] when the mire of latent impressions is thoroughly cleansed by the waters of cessation (nirodha).

"Ananta" (infinite): the meaning is that because consciousness is contained within the mind—which is like a crystal vessel filled with a flood of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) comparable to mud—even though it is like a ruby, it is not perceived in its true nature. He states the method for perceiving it: "nirodha" (cessation); when cleansing has been performed. || 11 ||
O Rāma, when the casket of the mind has been joined together over a long time with effort by means of the sharp instrument of investigation, it is then opened by means of sound reasoning.
He reflects; then, the sequence is that once the cleansing of the mud has been performed.
This is because the cessation in the form of *nididhyāsana* (meditative absorption) becomes possible immediately after the reflection (*vicāra*) consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.
[This occurs] in the mental casket (*cittakaraṇḍa*) which has been joined together for a long time—since beginningless time—and has attained identification with the body and other such things.

The meaning is that when [the Self] has been opened up by the instrument of the scrutiny of investigation (*vicāra-tīkṣya-yantra*)—that is, through hearing accompanied by reflection (*manana*) and reasoning—and has been discriminated from the body and so forth, there occurs the abandonment of identification with the visible body and other such things. || 12 ||
But consciousness is perceived as manifesting like a gem;
therefore, O Rāma, the means for the removal of latent impressions is prescribed.

Consciousness (*caitanya*) itself, having attained identity with the body and so forth, is called the mind (*citta*). Its very identity with the body and so forth is its "clashing" (*saṅghaṭṭana*). The discernment of that [mind] from the body and so forth is its "unveiling" (*udghāṭana*). Upon the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through restraint (*nirodha*), there is no further attainment of identity with the body and so forth. Thus...

He says that the reality of the Self, which is consciousness, once discriminated from the body and so forth through *vicāra*, is perceived by means of *nirodha* as self-luminous like a gem: "shining" (*bhāsamānam*). Therefore, since no means of realization (*sādhana*) is required for its own nature, a means is prescribed [only] for the sake of recollection (*smṛti*). || 13 ||
Due to the presence of greater or lesser latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the intellect (*buddhi*) becomes manifold;
for whichever person a stream of latent impressions remains, having veiled the intellect to such an extent, [that is his state]. (14)

He says that for one whose mental impressions (*vāsanā*)—whether few or many—are diminished through means such as merit accumulated in previous births, the requirement for spiritual practice (*sādhana*) is correspondingly small or large: "For whom... (verse 14).
O descendant of Bhṛgu, the means for its attainment depend upon that very [knowledge] alone;
various latent impressions (vāsanās) have been described therein, and among them, I shall tell you the principal ones. (15)

In that regard, he enumerates certain powerful latent impressions (*vāsanās*) which must be diligently eliminated: "latent impression" (*vāsanā*) means formative predispositions (*saṃskāras*). || 15 ||
For that [obstacle] is indeed threefold, according to the distinction between offense (*aparādha*), action (*karman*), and desire (*kāma*).
Lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) alone is the primary offense, which brings about one's own destruction. (16)

Distinguishing these [defects] in sequence, he states the first fault: "lack of faith" (*aśraddhā*). Faith (*śraddhā*) is the firm conviction that whatever is taught by the Guru and the scriptures is exactly so; the absence of that is lack of faith. (16)
Moreover, erroneous perception is indeed a human failing;
for those who are generally skilled in the arts are surely subject to error.

He states that even the erroneous apprehension (*viparītagraha*), which is like a sprout from the seed of ignorance, is a human error (*puruṣāparādha*): "erroneous," etc. It is "human" (*pauruṣa*) because it is accepted as being of the nature of the person. He says "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) to indicate that even for the great ones who possess knowledge of the scriptures, the non-arising of knowledge occurs precisely due to this [error]. || 17 ||
Indeed, through the company of the virtuous, the study of scriptures, and yoga, they know the supreme reality;
yet that supreme reality is without distinction—it neither exists nor can it possibly exist.
Even when the means such as association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) are present, [the Lord] speaks of various contrary misconceptions:
"That [Reality] does not exist; it cannot be known by anyone anywhere.
Even having known the supreme reality, this is not the supreme reality."
It would be so. || 19 ||
The second [objection] is that it cannot be known. The third is that even after knowing it through the means culminating in *nididhyāsana*, one might think, "This is not the supreme reality. || 19 ||
"How can liberation arise from this knowledge? and so forth—such [questions] have been established in many ways; or else, there may be a misconception regarding this, or even a doubt about it. (20)
[This occurs] from the knowledge of that [Self] which has been made directly manifest through meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*). By the word "etc.
(*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such [views] as "there is no liberation consisting of isolation" (*kaivalya-mokṣa*).
He states that even doubt regarding this—like a misconception contrary to what was taught—is a human error: "doubt concerning this" (*etatsaṃśaya*).
Human transgression, however, is proclaimed to consist of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the like;
for there are hundreds and thousands who are skilled in the sciences of the scriptures. (21)
"This very fault is what is called 'imprint' (vāsanā) today," he says: "The fault," [verse 21].

O Rāma, those who have entered into the cycle of worldly existence are struck down by this [ignorance], due to the force of the impressions of past misdeeds; yet, that which remains established in the intellect— || 22 ||
By this [verse], the latent impression (vāsanā) consisting of offense is [explained]. He states the second latent impression with the word "formerly" (pure). || 22 ||
The impurity of the instruction is an obstacle to its reception, by which it is indeed not grasped even when correctly taught by the teachers. (23)
Stain is dullness; by which [stain], while it remains in the intellect... || 23 ||
That is called the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*), which is difficult to overcome even through cessation;
desire remains as a residue of action, infinite and branching in many ways. (24)

This is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of karma. "Difficult to conquer" means that while most latent impressions are to be conquered through the cessation of all [desires], this one is particularly difficult to conquer. He states the third [type] as "desire" (*kāma*): it is a collection of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) consisting of residual duties in the form of "this must be done, that must be done"; it is infinite, extensive, and possessed of many branches.
It has innumerable divisions. || 24 ||
Someone might indeed count the number of waves in the ocean of Rāma, or the atoms of the earth, or likewise the multitude of stars. (25)
He defines the state of being incalculable itself: "Rāma," [it is said]. (25)
For it is impossible to even enumerate a single one of the desires;
O Rāma, this third latent impression of desire has been fully described to you. (26)
Even for a single person. || 26 ||
O Rāma, this demoness of desire known as hope is indeed vaster than space and more unshakable than even the mountain that supports the earth. (27)
He states its very infinity with the words "from space" (*ākāśāt*). It is "vast" because it pervades the entire world, or because it is difficult to fill.
He says it is "immovable" (*acala*) because it is impossible to dispel. It is called "the Piśācī"; for by this very desire-impulse (*kāmavāsanā*), this entire world remains like one who is insane.
By which this world, being constantly tormented by punishment, cries out in lamentation. || 28 ||

It brings about the state of being a *piśācī* (by the phrase) "by this. The word "seized" (*grasta*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. By which [means]: through the devouring of the *piśācī* of hope, certain people in the world become most fortunate; by resorting to the great mantra, those men shine forth, liberated from her, with all their limbs cooled. (29)
"Ke'pi" means "the supreme among people. "Mahāmantra" refers to supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*). || 29 ||
O Rāma, because the mind is completely overwhelmed by these three latent impressions (vāsanās), that reality (tattva) certainly does not manifest.
By these [powers], which can assume any form at will for the sake of committing offenses, that very reality—the reality of the Self—is made eternally manifest, even though it is already so.
Therefore, the fruit of every means of accomplishment is the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Among these, the first ceases through the certain realization of its own fault. (31)

Therefore, since no means of practice are applicable to the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is eternally immediate, he states the specific means for the destruction of each of the three kinds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) with the word "therein" (*tatra*). This means "among those [impressions]. The first [set] consists of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) and so forth, which take the form of offenses (*aparādha*). [The reason they are offenses is] because of the certainty that they are indeed offenses on my part.
This is because of the certainty that the non-arising of knowledge is rooted solely in this very fault. || 31 ||
The second [type of impurity] may be removed by a single birth, or even by many births, through the grace of the Lord; it cannot be removed otherwise, even by ten million arguments.

The second is the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) consisting of delusion. By the grace of the Lord (*īśvaraprasāda*), that which is small is removed in a single birth, while that which is not small is removed over many births; it cannot be otherwise without the grace of the Lord.
The third [type of doubt] may be dispelled by excellent means such as detachment;
indeed, detachment arises only through the perception of faults, and never otherwise. (33)

The third is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of desire. Regarding the cause for dispassion (*vairāgya*), he says: "solely by the perception of defects. This means by constantly contemplating the defects in sense-objects.
By this [it is implied] the certainty of their faulty nature, as well as divine grace and the investigation of the teacher’s instruction.
The worship of the Lord should be understood as the cause [of liberation] in due order. || 33 ||
O Bhārgava, depending on whether those aforementioned latent impressions (vāsanās) are small or large in their differentiation, there arises a corresponding small or large state of that [result].
Regarding the aforementioned latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and the perception of their defects: there is a dependence on whether these are slight or not slight.
That is to say, when the latent impressions are slight, it depends on the degree of the perception of defects, the strength of one's resolve, and so forth. || 34 ||
Among these, the first is the root of all; it is the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva) and nothing else.
For without the desire for liberation, hearing, reflection, and so forth [are ineffective]. (35)

Among those means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this is the root of all and the cause for the perfection of all means; for this very reason, it is the first. If it is objected that even without the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), there exist means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) for those proficient in the scriptures, [the author] replies "desire for liberation" (*mumukṣā*), because [those other means] do not culminate in the fruit. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is included. (35)
It should not be merely like a craft, devoid of connection with the primary fruit;
the supreme state is not attained by the mere knowledge of a craft. (36)

He states that because there is an absence of the fruit-bearing direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), the mere attainment of knowledge regarding the system of the scriptures—like a craft (*śilpa*)—does not, by itself, result in the great fruit consisting of the cessation of saṃsāra: "Not a craft," etc. (36).
But for those by whom [the teachings] have been heard and properly investigated without a desire for liberation, all of it will indeed be as useless as ornaments upon a corpse. (37)
He states that the perfection of means is useless for one who does not desire liberation: "mumukṣām" (desire for liberation), etc. (37).
O Rāma, that dull desire for liberation would likewise be entirely in vain,
just as a general desire for the mere hearing of the description of fruits does not bring about those fruits.

He states that even a desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) that is not intense is futile; thus he says "futile. That *mumukṣā*—which, by virtue of the scriptural declarations of rewards (*phala-śruti*), exists as a common, non-intense longing in all—is just like [other desires] that do not bring about their respective fruits; he explains this with the word "just as" (*yathā*). || 38 ||
The desire arising subsequent to the scriptural declaration of rewards does not bring about the fruit of action;
for whom indeed would that [desire] not exist, since it is a property of the individual soul? (39)
He explains this very point clearly with the word "phala" (the fruit): desire is not intense; that is the desire.
The sense is that if it were productive of results for everyone, then everyone would possess every possible result. || 39 ||
Therefore, there is no fruit from a desire for liberation that is merely superficial;
rather, the fruit of that [desire] comes quickly, provided the desire for liberation is intense. (The word *tasyā* is to be split as *tasyā aciram*; the *sandhi* is archaic. || 40 ||

Therefore, because there is no fruit for weak desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), he says "as" (verse 40) to show that even when it is not weak, the fruit of that desire— whether intense, more intense, or otherwise— will arise without delay in proportion to its intensity.
That desire for liberation which is most preeminent is indeed sufficient to generate engagement in the collection of means; for that is what is called "devotion to that" (tatparatā). (41)
"Enough" means "excessively. This refers to excessive engagement in the means of accomplishment. || 41 ||
Just as one whose entire body has been thoroughly burned does not require anything else that is cool,
so too, when one is liberated, one indeed requires nothing else in any way whatsoever.
An illustration regarding intense desire for liberation (tīvramumukṣā) is given by the word "just as" (yathā): it requires nothing other than cold water and so forth. || 42 ||
That desire for liberation must be intense and capable of accomplishing its fruit;
it arises solely through the perception of defects in everything other than liberation. (43)
He states the cause for intense desire for liberation (tīvramumukṣā): "This" (eṣā); that is to say, intense desire for liberation. || 43 ||
Through the gateway of intense dispassion, one gradually attains intensity;
for it is through the perception of defects that dispassion destroys attachment to sense objects. (44)

He describes the sequence of the arising of the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) through the perception of defects (*doṣadṛṣṭi*), beginning with the words "intense" (*tīvra*). "By way of dispassion" (*vairāgyamukhataḥ*) means by means of the gateway of dispassion. Ordinary desire for liberation itself gradually attains intensity; he states that sequence with the words "through the perception of defects. Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the turning away from sense objects. (44)
Through dispassion arises the desire for liberation; from that comes intense single-minded devotion. Single-minded devotion toward the means of practice arises from extreme intensity. (45)
Because from that [state] arises—that is, the birth—of devotion to that [goal]. || 45 ||
"One shall swiftly obtain the fruit by one's exceedingly intense nature alone.
Having heard these words of Dattātreya, Bhārgava spoke again.
He states that intense desire for liberation (*tīvramumukṣutva*) achieves the fruit only by means of intense application (*tīvrapravṛtti*), in the verse beginning with "atitīvra" (46).
With a mind full of doubt, he asked about a very great uncertainty:
"O Blessed One, it has been stated by you that association with the virtuous is the primary cause. (47)
The root cause is the primary cause. || 47 ||
Is it the grace of the Lord, or is it the perception of defects? What is the primary original cause, and how might that attainment come about? (48)

It has been stated that association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*), the grace of the Lord (*īśvarānugraha*), and the perception of defects (*doṣadṛṣṭi*) are the root causes. Among these, one asks: what is the primary and original cause? And what is the cause of even that? [The text asks: "What is the beginning?
For it is certain that nothing can exist without a cause.
How could that be so without a cause? Tell me this in detail.
If it is objected that "it has no cause at all," [the author] says "no" with the intention of showing that this would entail the consequence of its being accidental (ākasmikatva). || 49 ||
Thus questioned, Dattātreya, the ocean of compassion, said to Rāma:
"O Bhārgava, listen; I shall tell you of the supreme source of ultimate welfare."
"Paramodbhavam" means the supreme, most excellent, primordial origin; that is to say, the primary cause of the highest good (śreyaḥ). || 50 ||
That divine consciousness is supreme, which, through the majesty of its own sovereignty, manifests the variegated picture of the universe within itself alone, like a reflection in a mirror. (51)

Association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) alone is the root cause; and that [occurs] by virtue of the ripening of various natural merits (*prākṛtavicitrasukṛta*). Having first examined the engagement in karma, he says "para-" etc., in order to explain this. That [association] is well-known as the subject to be expounded in this treatise. Of one's own independence...
One should connect [the phrase] "manifesting the wondrous universe" with "by the power, the majesty, and the greatness of Māyā. || 51 ||
That very same supreme [power], having assumed the body known as Hiraṇyagarbha,
acted out of a desire for the welfare of living beings who were shrouded by beginningless ignorance.
That alone is the supreme consciousness. || 52 ||
It causes the ocean of scriptures to unfold, fulfilling all desires;
therein, living beings possess by their very nature various latent impressions of desire. (53)

"For them, sensual desires alone are beneficial," thus [the author] opens the ocean of scripture to fulfill all desires. If one asks, "How is it that sensual desires are beneficial for living beings? he says: "Therein," meaning in creation, by their very nature; through the beginningless latent impression (*vāsanā*) of desire, there is the experience of desire.
The meaning is that from the experience of that [object], the latent impression (vāsanā) arises. || 53 ||
"Thinking thus, 'How may there be prosperity for them? he became intent on such reflection and created in every way rites of desire that yield various fruits. (54)

For those who have fallen into the stream of birth and death solely due to the latent impressions of desire (*kāmavāsanā*), Hiraṇyagarbha, intent on their welfare, created and expounded within the ocean of the scriptures precisely the rituals for the fulfillment of desires (*kāmyakarman*) in every respect and everywhere. || 54 ||
For indeed, a person acts either toward what is existent or what is non-existent by their very nature;
and likewise, it occurs through the power of the ripening of some particular karma. (55)
In that regard, he first explains the manner of obtaining human birth: "Whether existent or non-existent, by way of its own nature through the latent impressions of karma. (55)
Wandering through various wombs, having attained human birth, one becomes inclined toward desirable actions under the influence of desire. (56)
"Upasaṅgataḥ" means arrived; "karmaṇyabhimukhaḥ pravṛttaḥ" means directed toward and engaged in the ritual action. || 56 ||
If, through a particular desire, one becomes devoted to the Lord, then one should, as an incidental consequence, study the scriptures concerning the Lord. || 57 ||
Due to a specific desire— that is, by a particular longing such as "May the fruit of this optional rite accrue to me without obstacle"—
one engages in an optional rite prompted by the scriptural injunction regarding its fruit;
yet, that [engagement] is frustrated because the fruit is not obtained due to a deficiency arising from subtle karma.

Having analyzed this very point, he says: "By desire" (*kāmyā*). Seeking the means to attain what is desired through the latent impression of desire, one engages in that [action] based on the scriptural revelation of desirable fruits. In that regard, because of even a slight deficiency or omission of even a minute portion of the ritual action (*sūkṣmakarman*), its failure is necessarily to be expected.

Frustrated and suffering because he has not attained that fruit, he goes to some virtuous person whose intentions are fulfilled and whose desires are attained, in order to take refuge [with him], out of a desire to know what must be done so that he might obtain the fruit of his actions; such is the grammatical connection. || 58 ||
Driven solely by the desire to know what ought to be done, one should approach some virtuous person; through the course of that association, one might here and there hear of greatness.
"By virtue of that occasion" means: although virtuous persons remain entirely averse to sensual desires, nevertheless,

on whatever occasion there may be among virtuous persons in any place or at any time— a specific discourse consisting of mutual questions and answers— it is therein that the majesty of Maheśvara [is revealed].
One should listen. This has been stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "The virtuous should always be approached even if they do not instruct us;
for whatever casual conversation they may have becomes their instruction" (*Yogavāsiṣṭhasāra* 1.7).
Furthermore, O Bhārgava, due to the ripening of his former merits, Maheśvara’s grace will subsequently lead him toward the practice of propitiating that deity.
"By whose remembrance and by whose utterance of the name, whatever is deficient in asceticism, sacrifice, ritual acts, and so forth, immediately attains completeness—I bow to that Acyuta.
This complete verse is frequently seen in works on devotion (*bhakti*). [The phrase from the source is: "by remembrance and by the utterance of the name."

Having heard such greatness as this, one should thereafter examine the scriptures of the Lord. Then, through the power of the ripening of merit, there shall arise an inclination toward propitiating Him (or, according to the variant *tatpratipādane*, toward understanding His teachings). || 60 ||
Therefore, through the ripening of prior merit, having approached the company of the virtuous,
one attains the series of steps to the highest good, which is exceedingly difficult to find.
Thus, he concludes that the attainment of the highest good occurs gradually, preceded by association with the virtuous, solely through the ripening of prior merit: "Therefore," [he says]. || 61 ||
It is generally declared that the attainment of the highest good has its root in the company of the virtuous;
though in some cases it may occur through extraordinary merit or even through supreme austerity.
By means of supreme merit and supreme austerity performed for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord. || 62 ||
For one attains the higher good suddenly, like a fruit falling from the sky;
therefore, due to the diversity of causes, there is a diversity in the attainment of the higher good.

[This occurs] through merit and other factors performed in previous births; "suddenly" means unexpectedly, without [the aid of] association with the virtuous and so forth. Therefore, due to this diversity of causes—namely, the diversity arising from the smallness or largeness of the means that destroy the latent impressions (vāsanās) which veil one's true nature—the variety in the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*) results from the gradations in the cessation of those latent impressions that veil knowledge.
The meaning is that there is a diversity of cognitions. || 63 ||
And thus, due to differences in intellect, the varying degrees of latent impressions (vāsanā),
and the varying degrees of spiritual practices, the state of the knowers of reality is manifold.

"And likewise" means: once the gradation of knowledge has been established. [This is so] because of the difference in intellects due to the gradation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for there is no equality of latent impressions in every intellect.
For this very reason, he says "of the means" to show that there is no equality of the means of attainment. || 64 ||
For one whose latent impressions regarding the intrinsic nature of cognition have indeed become sparse, the accomplishment of knowledge will be sufficient through very slight means alone. (65)

Having analyzed this very point, he says: "From one's own nature" (*svabhāvāt*). This refers to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of meritorious actions and so forth performed in the past. "Rare" (*viralāḥ*) means few.
"Adequate" (*alam*) means that the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*) is entirely unobstructed. || 65 ||
For one whose nature is completely pure and free from even a trace of latent impressions, great knowledge arises through even a slight cause. (66)
By its very nature—that is, due to the refinement resulting from the excellence of meritorious actions and so forth—the mind is completely purified; this is the implied sense.

By a mere slight cause, as in the case of Janaka, it becomes, upon merely hearing [the truth] once, exceedingly great, unshakable, and similar to knowledge matured through long-term practice. || 66 ||
For one whose mind is extremely dense with habitual tendencies by its very nature,
even though knowledge has arisen, it remains obscured for a kalpa.
By its very nature, due to the conditioning of extremely evil karma, it is a concealer that is incapable of destroying ignorance. || 67 ||
That very [state], once accomplished, after a long time again attains fullness;
for this very reason, various conditions are observed among the wise. (68)

By that very [means], by one who possesses knowledge that has been veiled; it is accomplished through the excellence of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), after a long time—whether by one or many births—to fullness, which is the capacity for the destruction of ignorance. Precisely for this reason, because of the difference in the state of the intellect (*buddhisthiti*) due to the difference in the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of past actions. || 68 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, there is a difference in the state [of the self] due to the differentiation in the ripening of the mind;
therefore, it arises from the varying degrees of the veiling of the intellect by latent impressions (vāsanās). (69)
He states this very point clearly: "In the mind," etc. This refers to the distinction in the state of the Knower. He analyzes this further:
"For knowledge is seen to be diverse, and likewise there would be a difference in its state.
O Rāma, behold the mutual difference in the state of the Knowers. (70)
The distinction regarding the state of the Knower. He illustrates this very point with the example: "Rāma," etc. (70).
They are indeed knowers of the true nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
behold the difference in their respective states, which arises from the qualities born of their own natures.
They are knowers of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma and so forth do not exist in their minds, their knowledge is unobstructed.
[They perceive] the differentiation of states, the intentness upon creation and so forth, and the qualities of *sattva* and the other primary constituents (*prākṛtaguṇa*). (71)
It is in no way possible to speak of any impurity in their knowledge;
nevertheless, the greatness of its inherent quality remains indeed distinct.

It cannot be said that there is an obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) consisting in the impurity of knowledge, because sovereignty such as omniscience is well-established; nevertheless, even though [the soul] possesses pure knowledge... || 72 ||
Just as the body of a wise person, being fair, does not turn dark, so too the intrinsic nature of the mind does not undergo any other state. || 73 ||
He states that knowledge does not suppress its own nature with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 73 ||
O Rāma, look upon us thus— Atri’s sons who abide as men of knowledge—
and upon Durvāsas, Candramas, and myself, who have fallen into a state of difference.
And he illustrates his own case with the words: "us. (74)

Behold Vasiṣṭha, who is prone to anger and desire, who has abandoned all external marks and possessions, yet remains most intent on ritual action; and behold Sanaka and the others, who have renounced all worldly ties.
He describes precisely their distinct states with the words "the angry one" and so forth. *Liṅga* refers to the marks of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
*Parigraha* refers to possessions such as a wife, wealth, and the like. *Nyāsinaḥ* means renunciants (*saṃnyāsinaḥ*). || 75 ||
[Nārada], who was immersed in devotion; [Bhārgava], who was composing poetry;
[Vasiṣṭha], who took refuge with the faction of the Daityas; and [Atri], the preceptor who took refuge with the gods. || 76 ||
The descendant of Bhṛgu, Śukra; composing poetry, creating the work of a seer (kavi). || 76 ||
Behold Janaka, the eloquent King Vyāsa himself, who was devoted to the composition of the scriptures; and likewise behold Bharata, the renunciant. (77)
Vāgmin means eloquent; Bharata refers to Jaḍabharata. || 77 ||
Behold other wise men whose states of being are diverse by nature;
I shall declare a secret to you, so listen, O delighter of Bhṛgu’s lineage. (78)
[He mentions] others such as Cyavana, Yājñavalkya, Viśvāmitra, and so forth. Thus, in order to state the cause for the difference in their status, he says:
"The secret" (rahasyam). || 78 ||
Regarding the three kinds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have been described, that which is the second—born of karma and consisting of delusion—is the greatest of all. (79)
The threefold [desire] for wrongful action consists of desire for form; it is [superior] to all desires for wrongful tendencies. || 79 ||
But those wise ones in whose minds not even a trace of that exists are free from faults; for them, the latent impressions of desire and the like [no longer remain]. (80)

The residue of that karmic impression does not exist because the means previously acquired have been destroyed; this is understood to mean that they are called "intelligent" (*medhāvin*). Furthermore, there is no fault because of the absence of specific karma caused by oneself.
