The connection is that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and so forth have not dissolved (*avilīnā*). || 80 ||
Furthermore, those [impurities] that have been dissolved through practice do not act as obstacles to knowledge;
therefore, detachment and the like are of no use to them. (81)
"By practice" means that they have not dissolved due to the absence of practice; this is the sense. "Not obstructive to knowledge":

the intended meaning here is that for those whose minds are utterly deluded by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma, even in the absence of latent impressions of offenses and the like, [knowledge does not arise] simply because of their delusion.

The arising of knowledge: for those whose minds are slightly deluded due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of very slight karma, the latent impressions of offenses and desire act as obstacles to knowledge. However, for those in whom the latent impressions of offensive karma do not exist even in the slightest degree, the latent impressions of desire do not act as obstacles to knowledge. "Therefore" means because the latent impressions of desire do not act as an obstacle.
By the word "etcetera," the perception of faults [is indicated]. || 81 ||
Indeed, neither further reflection nor meditative absorption is required;
for by the mere act of hearing once, both reflection and meditation are accomplished. (82)
He states that reflection (*manana*) and the other means are no more useful than dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, by saying "or not" (*na vā*). "Repeatedly" (*bhūyaḥ*) means many times.
He describes the sequence for the arising of knowledge in them by saying "at once" (*sakṛt*). || 82 ||

At that time, having attained even slightly the state where the reality of those [spiritual] stages is known and free from doubt, they become liberated while living (jīvanmukta), like Janaka and others. (83)
"At that time" means at the time of hearing; "that state" refers to the state of the perfect Self. || 83 ||
Indeed, due to the power of practicing what is contrary [to reality], even those of pure intellect have not properly eliminated the subtle latent impressions of desire and the like. (84)
Precisely because knowledge is not an obstacle [to them], the latent impressions of desire, anger, and so forth have not been destroyed. || 84 ||
Therefore, even when that state has been realized by them, those previously existing latent impressions of desire and so forth continue to function incessantly as before. (85)
Therefore, because it has not been destroyed by repeated practice. || 85 ||
Not even slightly would there be any stain upon their intellect by those [faults];
for they are declared by the wise to be liberated and possessed of great dignity. (86)

"Smearing" (*lepa*) is the impurity that causes the loss of one's true nature. And thus, for those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire, anger, and so forth— arisen from specific *prārabdha* karma—
are not destroyed because they have not practiced detachment and the like, and which do not obstruct knowledge, even after the arising of knowledge, [the smearing remains].
The meaning is that [the characteristics] such as desirousness and anger [are absent].

Having thus established the distinction in their state, he also speaks of the distinction in their excellence and so forth among the knowers: "For they are fully described as being full of great reverence; they are the highest," is the ellipsis. || 86 ||
But for that mind which is deluded by attachment to the latent impressions of karma, knowledge shall not arise even if it is proclaimed by Śiva at any time. (87)
He says that knowledge will certainly not arise when there is firmness in both offenses and the latent impressions of karma: "O Rāma, karma... and so forth.

For those who possess even firm offenses, there can be no [liberation] by any means whatsoever, provided that they still possess a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of either offense or karma. (88)
The logical connection is that knowledge would not exist because the latent impression (vāsanā) is too slight. || 88 ||
O Bhārgava, although those whose nature is desire are few, they become numerous for him through extensive hearing, reflection, and meditative absorptions.
The latent impressions (vāsanās) consist of desire. "Abundant" means those produced by repeated hearing [of the scriptures] and so forth. || 89 ||
Consciousness arises after a long time and with great effort;
its practical application is minimal there, due to the excellence of practice. (90)
For him, due to the excellence of his practice of meditative concentration there, his worldly activity is minimal,
serving only for the maintenance of the body.
If the mind has become almost destroyed due to the absence of latent impressions (*nirvāsana*),
such persons are declared by the wise to be those of middling capacity who have destroyed the mind. (91)

Thus, for those who are intent on very limited worldly activity, if the mind— having its latent tendencies for desire and so forth destroyed by the excellence of yoga-attainment— becomes as if lost and is constantly restrained, then such knowers are the middling ones whose minds are "lost. (91)
However, for some among them, because their practice has not reached its highest degree, the mental state remains undestroyed, though the latent impressions have become sparse. (92)

Among those very ones who have reached the culmination of yoga, if some among them are indolent, their mind may remain undestroyed due to the lack of excellence in practice, resulting in the persistence of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 92 ||
But they are said to possess mental activity (samanaska) and are indeed endowed with dull knowledge;
these others, however, possess absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna) and are likewise liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He states that these people of dull intellect are not liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) with the words "only" (*kevala*); others, however, are the middling and superior knowers. (93)
For those possessing absolute knowledge (kevalajñānin) indeed experience suffering that has been perceived;
they are said to be subject to their *prārabdha* karma, and upon the end of the body, they become partakers of liberation. || 94 ||

He says that in the absence of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), there would be the experience of perceived suffering, [expressing this with the word] "kevala": "dependent on prārabdha" means governed by the force of past actions already set in motion. || 94 ||
Those who are said to have lost their minds have failed to overcome *prārabdha*;
for on the ground of the mind, the seed of *prārabdha* becomes the sprout of experience (*bhoga*). (95)
But others say that [the fruits of action] are not dependent on what has already begun (*prārabdha*). He says "He who... [meaning] that which is overcome is conquered.
If one asks, "Well then, what would that *prārabdha* be?", he says "The mind" [meaning] that it perishes by itself. || 95 ||
Due to the absence of the mental ground (manobhūmi), that which was initiated [as karma] will, over time,
perish like a seed remaining in a granary, its power having been destroyed.
He explains the manner of its destruction with an illustration: "From the ground of the mind" (manobhūmeḥ).

The sense is that, like a seed situated in a granary, [the mind], having its power destroyed over time due to the absence of connection with the mind, perishes at the time of disembodied liberation (videhamukti) because of the destruction of its support, the subtle body (liṅgadeha). || 96 ||
Just as one who is exceedingly wise may perform fifteen tasks simultaneously somewhere and remain unerring, so too [is this]. (97)
Now he begins the description of the great abundance of beings among the ignorant, starting with the word "yathā" (just as):
simultaneously, at one and the same time. || 97 ||
Furthermore, such actions based on manual skill are observed, such that a person is perceived as simultaneously walking, speaking, and acting. (98)
Such wise persons have been frequently seen many times in the world. He illustrates this very point with the word "just as":
"In that case, how could there be a threefold activity with a single mind? [For] the teacher would have to observe many students simultaneously. (99)
Thus, he explains how multiple actions can occur simultaneously with a single mind by saying "therein" (tatreti).
This means "among the persons mentioned. Another example is given: "of those who study" (adhyetṝṇām) || 99 ||
"O Rāma, that enemy of yours who was slain—the Arjuna who was the lord of the Haihayas—was one whose pronunciation of Apabhraṃśa was established through the distinction of phonemes. (100)

Regarding the term *apabhraṃśa*: it refers to a corrupted word (*apaśabda*) established through a deviation from the phonemes (*ayathāvarṇa*), due to the difference between the phonemes uttered immediately after one's own [intended] utterance. Another example is: *rāma yasta iti*.
*Sahasrabāhu*, simultaneously with many weapons, [pierced him] individually.
The wise one fought without faltering wherever he was seen by you.
"With weapons" means with missiles and arms; "without faltering" means without deviating from the path of the discharge of those various weapons;
"by you" refers to you. || 101 ||
Their mind, having become manifold and following those respective sequences, accomplishes various tasks exactly as they are to be accomplished. 102.
Thus, since two distinct actions cannot occur simultaneously with a single mind, he says "of them" (*teṣām*). This means:
of those who are intelligent, such as Arjuna and others. "Following their respective sequences" (*tattatkramānugam*) means:
endowed with a sequence of operations conducive to the accomplishment of their respective tasks. || 102 ||
Even the view of a self directed toward external objects is never contradictory for those who possess supreme knowledge; such persons are truly full of great respect [for the truth]. (103)

The view of self is a mind having the aspect of a self; and even when directed toward external objects, it has the aspect of those objects as well. Because the mind is manifold, this is not contradictory. || 103 ||
That which has been commenced on the plane of the mind becomes separately sprouted;
yet each and every such [sprout], as it arises again and again, is consumed by the fire of knowledge.
Having thus established that those possessing supreme knowledge are characterized by great self-respect, he describes the absence of the experience of *prārabdha* karma:
"That *prārabdha*," etc. It is "sprouted," meaning it possesses sprouts in the form of pleasure and pain.
Nevertheless, he states that it does not culminate in fruit: "It may be," etc. That which has become [manifest] in the form of a sprout—become.
The meaning is that each respective *prārabdha* karma, being repeatedly burnt by the fire of knowledge, does not persist for even two moments. || 104 ||
The encounter with pleasure and pain arises from the sprout of the seed of *prārabdha*; its reflection is said to be the fruit. But how can there be a fruit when the sprout has been burnt? (105)

The sprout of the seed consisting of *prārabdha* (commenced karma) is the connection with pleasure and pain. The fruit of pleasure and so forth is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), while the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that pleasure and so forth is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). The intended meaning is that pleasure and so forth appear only at the initial moment; their subsequent practical engagement occurs through recollections brought about by those [experiences].
For it is observed that even a mature man is seen playing with a child. || 106 ||

If it is asked, "In that case, since there is an absence of synthesis due to the cognition of mere appearance (*apātapratyaya*) everywhere, how is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) possible?", he says:
"Brought forth" (*āhṛta*). Synthesis does not arise for them spontaneously;
rather, having forcibly brought forth by their own will the synthesis required for worldly transaction, they engage in such transaction. This is so even in worldly transaction.
He states, with an illustration, that joy and the like caused by that [object] do not arise from within: "Just as... (verse 106).
They are elated when a stone, an elephant, or the like is destroyed, and dejected when it is not;
thus those with great pride rejoice and despair over their undertakings. (107)

Regarding the phrase "of stone elephants and so forth": just as a child feels despondent when his own elephant or horse is destroyed, or rejoices when the elephant or horse of the opponent in a battle-game made of stone and other materials is destroyed, so too an adult, though outwardly rejoicing or feeling despondent, does not undergo any internal transformation. This is the meaning. Thus, for ordinary people... [the text continues].
Due to the conviction that the visible world is real, and because of the strength of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), there occurs a forceful mental pursuit even against one’s will;

from this, joy and sorrow arise. However, for the highest knower (*uttamajñānin*), because of the conviction in unreality, the latent impressions become weakened, and [the mind] remains naturally [detached].

The sense is that even though there is an absence of continuous connection (*anusandhi*) and so forth everywhere, external worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by such connection due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) acquired through effort; this is for the sake of establishing conventional usage.
Just as, for example, joy and agitation do not exist internally for one who is occupied with another task.
Thus, their conduct and their established state are equal in all respects.

He states another illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). Regarding the phrase "na cāntarā" (nor in the interval): even when there is no joy or other emotion in the interval between gain and loss during the worldly dealings of another person, [the yogi] rejoices and grieves for the sake of pleasing the heart of that other person; this is the meaning. "Of them" refers to those of supreme knowledge (*uttamajñānin*). "Equal" means that their attitude toward their own task is like that toward the task of another. || 108 ||

But for the wise and the knowers, it is for the sake of destroying latent impressions (vāsanā), since there is an absence of the practice of contradictory impressions, their suppression, and so forth. (109)
He extracts and establishes the cause for the difference in the conduct of the wise: "of the intelligent," etc.
Persistence [in worldly activity] occurs due to the non-destruction of prior latent impressions (vāsanā);
therefore, some are devoted to ritual action (karmaniṣṭha), while others are full of desire or anger.

Regarding the term *anuvṛtti*: the meaning is that even after [the attainment of] knowledge (*jñāna*), there will certainly be a persistence of those respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which correspond to previously performed actions and are neither obstructive to knowledge nor destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Therefore...
Because of the persistence of those respective latent impressions (vāsanās). || 110 ||
Those of supreme knowledge shine while being intent upon various modes of conduct;
among them, he who possesses a mind is indeed described as one of dull knowledge.
He states that even one of dull intellect is equal to one of supreme intellect during the state of meditative absorption: "possessing the mind" (samanaska), [verse 111].
By him as well, everything that is to be known has been determined to be unreal;
for in the states of meditative absorption (samādhi), nothing whatsoever appears when there is awareness of one's own true nature.

Even by that one of dull intellect, during the states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), at whatever time there occurs the realization— that is, the continuous contemplation— of one's own nature as the non-dual conscious self, at that very time nothing whatsoever appears as an object of knowledge (*vedya*). And thus, for him, that [state] is not non-existent, just as it is for other knowers.
The meaning is that [it is free] from joy, sorrow, and so forth. || 112 ||
Concentration (samādhi) is indeed said to be nothing other than the reflective awareness of one's own essential nature;
for the non-conceptual nature [of consciousness] is always the support of all things.
Having thus described the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for those of dull intellect, [the text describes] that of the superior one:

"O Blessed One, the realization of the self as reality (*tattvātmabodha*) alone is the fire that consumes the grass of all desires; it is what is denoted by the word 'samādhi,' and not merely remaining in silence."
In accordance with the manner stated by Vasiṣṭha in *Yogavāsiṣṭha* (5.62.8), he defines the form of innate absorption (*sahajasamādhi*) as follows:

[the state of] "stupefied absorption" (*mūḍhasamādhi*). Now, one might object: even for practitioners of Haṭhayoga, when they attain absorption, it is the very reality of the self as free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) that appears, just as it does for the knowers of truth; so why is that not considered absorption? To this, he says:
"Non-conceptual" means it is always manifest; this is the connection [of the words]. || 113 ||
For indeed, that [reality] vibrates within everyone; if it did not vibrate, nothing at all would exist.
Likewise, it shines forth free from conceptual construction during the aforementioned states.
The ellipsis implies that if that [consciousness] does not manifest, nothing at all would manifest. "Free from conceptual construction" means having the nature of non-conceptual selfhood.
"In the aforementioned states" refers to those states occurring within the intervals of limited cognition. 114.
O Bhārgava, by that alone, samādhi does not indeed belong to all; it is traditionally taught as belonging only to those who are endowed with that reflective awareness (vimarśa). 115.

He says "tāvatā" (by that much alone) because samādhi is not accomplished merely by the manifestation of the non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpasvarūpa*) without the knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpajñāna*). If for the practitioners of Haṭhayoga the mere manifestation of their own nature during the time of suppression were to constitute samādhi, then [it would follow] for all those aforementioned states...
The intended meaning is that there would be the state of *samādhi*.

For those who possess the realization of the reality of the Self as free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), their cessation preceded by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of continuous recollection is precisely what is remembered by the wise as their *samādhi*.

In this regard, here is the secret of consciousness: the practitioner of Haṭhayoga who has not yet become acquainted with the reality of the non-conceptual self of consciousness through hearing and other means is of two kinds— the one who has fully mastered the eight limbs as taught by Patañjali.

Having resolved upon the abandonment of the manifestation of the conceptualization of non-self through the excellence and maturation of *prāṇāyāma* preceded by the practice of the six rites (*ṣaṭkarma*) and so forth as taught in the Tantras,
and having gradually cast off all conceptualizations, one finally manifests the absence of all conceptualization; thereafter, even that manifestation [is abandoned].
Having abandoned that [state], one remains as a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). And thus says the Pātañjala Sūtra:

"The other [samādhi] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation and consists of the residue of latent impressions" (1.18). As for the second [type], it occurs when the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) enters deeply into the *suṣumṇā*, at the beginning of which there is exhaustion born from the restraint of the breath.

By the mere entry into the *suṣumṇā*, one becomes happy as if from the removal of a burden because [the mind] has been destroyed; thereafter, the mind becomes almost unconscious, as if seized by intoxication and fainting. At that time, both states possess the nature of bliss, like deep sleep (*suṣupti*). This is for one who has realized the reality of the non-conceptual self of consciousness through the *praṇava* and other means.

For the practitioner of knowledge (*jñānayogin*), however, even prior to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*)— which is free from the veil of ignorance (*avidyāvaraṇa*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)— is indeed constantly manifesting, variegated by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as seen in a mirror decorated by the sequence of reflections. Therefore, at the beginning of meditative absorption and so forth, having discarded the conceptual portion, one is the witness (*sākṣī*) to the departure of the conceptual portion.

"The throbbing, non-conceptual form of consciousness remains as the residue. Nor should it be said that even the practitioner of *haṭha-yoga* remains in that very form at that time; for such a form exists in the *samādhi* of the practitioner of *jñāna-yoga*, wherein both parts—ignorance as an obstruction and distraction—are abandoned. But for the practitioner of *haṭha-yoga* at that time, however...

Even the essential nature (svarūpa), though its portions of ignorance and distraction have been removed, would still remain veiled by the portion of the veil of ignorance (jñānāvaraṇa). For the knower (jñānin), however, because the portion of the veil has been destroyed through direct knowledge (aparokṣajñāna), the essential nature is unobscured; such is the distinction. Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the difference between deep sleep (suṣupti) and samādhi for the practitioners of Haṭha Yoga?"

It is said that in deep sleep, due to a transformation of the mind into tamas, it is possessed of intense delusion— like the darkness seen when the sky is covered by thick, dense clouds; whereas in samādhi,
it is due to a transformation of the mind into sattva.

Although the reality of the Self is luminous, it does not shine clearly when veiled by ignorance, like the sun obscured by clouds; however, for the knower, through the transformation of the mind into purity (*sattva*) and the absence of the veil of ignorance,
it shines intensely, like the sun situated in the midst of a cloudless, clear sky.

It should be understood that the passage beginning with "That is the reality of the Self" (tadātmatattvam) and so forth has merely entered the path of experience for those who have already realized the reality of the Self; thus, nothing new is presented here. || 115 ||
Even consciousness, though intent upon empirical activity, is devoid of any object to be known;
it is like the blueness of the sky, which is not perceived when one looks again and again.

Having thus established that for the wise alone the state of *samādhi* constitutes true *samādhi*, he states that for the highest class of knowers, *samādhi* remains unimpeded even during the time of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), beginning with the words "In worldly activity" (*vyavahāra*). *Samādhi* is defined as the state of consciousness devoid of connection with any object of knowledge; [this] holds true for the highest knowers even while they are engaged in worldly activity.
The meaning is that cognition is indeed devoid of any connection with an object of knowledge. He establishes this very point with the words "viditam" (known). 116.
When [an object] is known as unreal, consciousness is not joined with it;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between the manifestation of reality and unreality. (117)

The meaning is this: even though blueness is perceived while being known as unreal, once it has been understood as unreal, upon subsequent observation, the cognition of that blueness is no longer conjoined with it as before.
If it is argued that the connection with the object is necessarily required for the cognition of blueness, he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

The meaning is the acceptance of a connection with an object. Regarding the phrase "of the manifestations of reality and unreality": for one who possesses the subverting cognition that "there is no blueness in space," there is a manifestation of space that is real—that is, true; and for one devoid of the aforementioned subverting cognition, there is a manifestation regarding space that is unreal—that is, untrue.

If one were to admit a relation of "blueness" to both of them, there would be no distinction between them. Nor can this undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) be accepted, because the difference in causal efficiency (arthakriyābheda) is established by the experience of everyone. For one who knows the reality of a mirage-water does not act toward fetching that water and so forth in the same way as one who does not know its reality. Therefore, for the knower of reality...

The point is that there is no connection between the cognition [of the object] and the water. Nor should it be argued that activity is obstructed by the cognition of a sublation (*bādhajñāna*), because the non-occurrence of activity is established simply by the absence of the [already] postulated causes;
therefore, the postulation of [the cognition of sublation as] an obstructer is improper. || 117 ||
Likewise, for an object of knowledge that has not been grasped as real, there can be no connection whatsoever with its cognition; for this very reason, it is so for the wise. (118)

He applies [the principle] from the illustrative example to the subject of the illustration with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). There would be no connection whatsoever for a knower with an object of knowledge (*vedya*) that is apprehended as unreal; therefore, the connection is that the cognition (*vitti*) of knowers must be devoid of an object of knowledge. || 118 ||
Cognition devoid of an object of knowledge occurs because that which has been sublated continues to appear;
this state is even more so for one who is mindless, and therefore it is the state of Unmanī.
"Devoid of the object of knowledge" (*vedyarahita*) means being devoid of any connection with an object of knowledge. The reason for this is:

"because that which is sublated appears [to the knower]. The intended meaning is as follows: just as water and so forth, when not sublated, appear to an ignorant person as being connected with mirages and the like, it is not so for the knower.

"It appears as being connected with the subject through its connection with the mental modification (*vitti*). For one who is without mind—the middling knower—there is an even greater absence of connection with the object in the mental modification. The reason for this is stated by the word "since" (*yataḥ*).
That state of his is called the "transmental" (*unmanī*) condition. || 119 ||
Where the mind is indeed motionless, that is said to be the state of Unmanī;
the movement of the mind would be its contact with the object of perception known as the Real. || 120 ||

He clarifies this very point with the words "the mind" (*manaḥ*). "In which"—that is, in whatever state—the connection with an object of knowledge (*vedyasambandha*) would occur when the mind is occupied with its objects. The sense is that for one of intermediate knowledge (*madhyajñānin*), there is no connection with an object of knowledge due to the absence of mental activity (*manovyāpāra*). Now, [if that is so,] then...

The meaning is that for one of supreme knowledge, there is movement of the mind, which constitutes a connection with an object of cognition (*vedya*). If it is objected that, in that case, there would indeed be a connection with an object of cognition due to the movement of the mind of one possessing supreme knowledge, he says: "of the mind.
The intended meaning here is that what is meant by "movement of the mind" is simply the engagement with an object of cognition known as being real.
O Bhārgava, these ten states of the possessor of supreme knowledge exist simultaneously; he is always both emerged from meditation and established in samādhi.

These ten states—the extreme immobility of the mind and the flickering appearance of contact with unreal objects of cognition—occur simultaneously, at one and the same time. The sense is that because the minds of the highest knowers are highly expansive, a manifold state of the mind may arise all at once. For this very reason, he says: "At all times" (sarvadā). || 121 ||
Therefore, even for that [consciousness], cognition is established as being devoid of an object of knowledge.
Thus indeed has been fully explained whatever was previously asked by you.

Therefore, because the mind is of two kinds, even for that [mind] of the one possessing supreme knowledge, he concludes with "thus" (evam). [Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Distinctions in the State of the Knower," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Tripurārahasya.]
[Now the twentieth chapter.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient account; listen to that.
Formerly, in the midst of the assembly of Brahmā, in the exceedingly pure Satyaloka— || 1 ||
Having bowed to the pair of feet of my venerable guru and having remembered the supreme consciousness, Tripurā,
who is the inner self of all, I shall clearly expound this Vidyā-gītā.

Through his grace, may this effort be successful for the complete purification of one's own intellect, for the perfect realization of one's state as his servant, and for the satisfaction of other people devoted to him.

In this work, for the sake of easily achieving awakening, the entire subject matter is summarized by means of verses arranged like a lattice and is expressed in the form of songs of knowledge (vidyāgīta).

Desiring to state the entire meaning of the treatise in summary form for the sake of establishing excellence of conviction and for the easy understanding of qualified disciples, Dattaguru begins by teaching the *Vidyāgītā*— which is directly propounded by the power of Vidyā— under the guise of describing the state of the Knower (*jñānin*) along with its means.
Regarding the word *atra*: it means "in that [context]" where the state of the knowers (*jñānin*) was previously asked about. *Purā* means in former times. *Vṛttam* means past;
a discourse on knowledge (*jñāna-prasaṅga*), consisting of the investigation of the subtle within the subtle, took place.
Sanaka and the others, as well as Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu—[2].
"Subtle" means having the nature of extremely subtle inquiry. The grammatical construction is: "Sanaka and the others assembled. || 2 ||
Bhṛgu, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pracetas, and likewise Nārada; Cyavana, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and Gautama. (3)
Śukra (or Śuka), Parāśara, Vyāsa, Kaṇva, and Kāśyapa; Dakṣa, Sumantu, Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Devala as well. || 4 ||
In this way, other hosts of sages and even the most eminent royal sages,
all gathered together there at that most great Brahma-sacrifice.
At the Brahma-sacrifice, in the context of the sacrifice of knowledge.
They engaged in intense deliberation through analyses of the most subtle among the subtle;
then all those sages questioned Brahmā regarding that matter.
O Blessed One, among the wise in this world we are those who have known the higher and the lower; for us, various states of being appear according to the diversity of our natures. (7)
Due to the difference in their innate natures, and due to the difference in their natural predispositions. || 7 ||
Some are always established in meditative absorption, some delight in investigation;
others are immersed in devotion, while still others rely upon ritual action.
He says that very thing: "Some," etc. (8).
But some are intent on worldly affairs, like men who look outward;
among these, which one is truly superior? You should tell us this.
Among those [states], such as the station of meditative concentration (samādhi), he is superior; that is, most excellent. || 9 ||
"O Creator, we each indeed know our own side to be the superior one.
Thus questioned, Brahmā spoke, perceiving that their minds were not yet at peace.
If it is argued that "surely all of you have mastered the sciences (*vidyā*) and are therefore naturally capable of understanding this [matter]," he replies:

"one's own respective position" (*svasvapakṣam*). That is, each person considers their own respective position alone to be superior because it is constructed with scriptural authority and logical reasoning.

The construction is: "Because [I] know [this], you ought to speak. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Even I do not know this. If it is asked, "Why did the omniscient Creator (Vidhi) speak thus? he replies: "Those whose minds are unconfident," meaning those whose hearts are struck by lack of faith (*aśraddhā*). Even though a resolution has been stated here by me, one should not think that his own position has been asserted by him as well.
The sense is: "thinking that they will seize [it]. || 10 ||
"O Lords of Sages, even I do not know this with my whole being; therefore, only the omniscient Supreme Lord would know this matter. (11)

"With his whole self" means with all his parts, that is to say, without any doubt. "Therefore" (tataḥ) means for that reason. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "we go there. To make it known that there is no ignorance whatsoever in that Supreme Lord, he is called "the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*). || 11 ||
Having said, "I shall go there to inquire about the matter," he went there with them;
having approached the Lord of the Gods of gods, who was met by Viṣṇu.

There, on Kailāsa, in the presence of the Omniscient One; having spoken thus, immediately thereafter at that very moment, he went together with Sanaka and the others—meaning, having approached and reached Mahādeva, the Lord of the Gods of gods, who had arrived accompanied by Viṣṇu. || 12 ||
The Creator, the progenitor of the worlds, asked that question of the foremost sages;
and Śiva, having heard the question, understood what was in the mind of Brahmā.

The sages posed that question—"Who is the best among those who possess knowledge, yet abide in different states?"—because they were not yet fully confident, thinking, "They will not accept my words. (13)
Perceiving that the sages were not yet reassured in their minds, the Lord reflected:
"Whatever I have said here might indeed prove futile."
"Thinking thus" means: having perceived that the sages were not yet confident in their minds from the perspective of yoga.

He states the very manner of his reflection with the words "something," etc.; the grammatical connection is "by me also. Here, it refers to the subject of the question at hand. The particle "nanu" indicates a possibility or a tentative inquiry. || 14 ||
Thinking, "The sages, possessed of faithlessness, might regard this as their own side," Maheśvara, the God of gods, replied. (15)

If it is asked, "Why would what you have said be in vain? he replies: "Because it is their own position. They would understand that this is Mahādeva’s own position. If it is asked, "Why is this so? he says: "Because they are struck by lack of faith," meaning "they are possessed of lack of faith. [Thus,] what I have said is in vain.
Thinking that it "might be so," [he said]. || 15 ||
"Listen, O sages! Even I do not know this very clearly;
therefore, let us meditate upon the Blessed Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign. (16)

By this much of the text, the supreme excellence of the subject matter expounded in this treatise is established, since it was not even known by Sanaka and others; furthermore, by stating that even the speech of Brahmā and others would be futile,
it is shown that lack of faith is a powerful obstacle to knowledge.
Since ignorance is considered possible even among Brahmā and the other ṛṣis, it is indicated that ignorance is difficult to dispel and that the embodied forms possessing attributes are limited. Now,
for the purpose of realizing the supreme excellence of the Supreme Deity— the pure power of consciousness (*śuddhacicchakti*)— which is the subject to be established in this treatise:

He cites the words of Mahādeva in order to state that through meditation upon that [reality], all doubts of the sages are removed, preceded by the destruction of lack of faith: "Listen! This refers to what you have asked. For this reason, since there is an absence of the removal of doubt regarding the subject at hand, and because the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) is opposed to ignorance (*avidyā*), it does not [arise otherwise].

The intended meaning is that there would be a lack of faith in what has been said. By the term "Parameśvarī," the sense is that even though she lacks speech and other such faculties, she is indeed capable of cutting through our doubts because she is endowed with perfect sovereignty. || 16 ||
"By his grace, we understand even that which is of hidden meaning; beyond that [is nothing further].
Having been addressed thus by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, all the sages [responded]. 17.
"Of extracted meaning" means of secret meaning. "Thereafter" means after [the mind] has been purified through meditation.
Thus it was spoken by Śiva. || 17 ||
They should meditate upon the Great Goddess of Knowledge, Tripurā, whose body is consciousness;
thus is Tripurā, whose body is consciousness, meditated upon by all.

The intended meaning is that Maheśānī is independent in the granting of desired objects; she is Tripurā because she exists prior to the triad of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; and she is Turyā (the Fourth State), which is unlimited. Regarding the phrase "having consciousness as her body":
it means she is all-knowing because her nature is unobscured consciousness, being free from even a trace of ignorance and its effects.

The capacity to determine the meaning of the question is thus illuminated; for, in the manner described, [the deity] exists in a form capable of granting one's desired object, since otherwise the attainment of the fruit would be impossible. As it has been said: "In whatever way one meditates upon Him, in that very way [He appears]."
"O Lord, you approach as the wish-fulfilling gem. || 18 ||
The supreme [power], consisting of the ether of consciousness and composed of sound, became manifest;
a resonance as deep as a thundercloud arose in the courtyard of the sky. 19.

Consisting of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), it is of the singular nature of undivided consciousness; for this very reason, because it is devoid of even a trace of the defects of the visible world (*dṛśya*), it is supreme (*parā*) and most excellent.
If it is asked how the manifestation of such a reality is possible, he says: "consisting of sound" (*śabdamayī*).
The intended meaning is that, in the form of sound, it makes itself manifest to Brahmā and the other gods, bringing it within the range of their senses.

He states that very same thing in the following verse: "abhavad iti" (it became). A great, deep sound, like the roar of clouds, [arose] in the courtyard of the sky, that is, in the expanse of space. || 19 ||
"Let the hosts of sages say what you have meditated upon; let that desired object be quickly accomplished.
For indeed, the wish of some who are devoted to me shall never fail. (20)

He states the very nature of the sound (*niḥsvana-svarūpa*) [as "let them speak"]. The address "the hosts of sages" (*ṛṣigaṇāḥ*), excluding Brahmā and the others, is because the cause for the meditation in the form of the question resides in the hosts of sages.
"What" (*kiṃ*) means for what purpose. "By you" (*vaḥ*) refers to by yourselves. The connection is: "let them speak that which is desired (*tad-īhitam*) by you. "Swiftly" (*drutam*).

The intended meaning is that when I am pleased, there shall be no delay in the attainment of the fruit. He says this very thing: "of those"—meaning of those devotees of mine—"it shall not be lost," that is, it shall not be separated by the intervention of time. || 20 ||
Having heard these supreme words, the eminent sages prostrated;
thereafter, even Brahmā and the others praised him with various hymns.

Having heard [the sound] manifested in the form of speech through the door of the sense of hearing and having brought it to their hearts, Brahmā and the others prostrated themselves; even Brahmā and the rest prostrated like a staff. Following that—that is, immediately after the prostration—[they spoke]. || 21 ||
Then the hosts of sages spoke that Vidyā, the Mistress of Tripura:
"Salutations to you, O Great Goddess; O Śrīvidyā, O Mistress of Tripura! (22)

Now, the connection is that immediately after the praise by Brahmā and the others, they praised Vidyā. The venerable, radiant Vidyā is of the nature of uninterrupted light; she is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpā*), and for that very reason she is Tripurā, the Fourth (*turyā*), whose form is the non-dual pure consciousness. Although her essential nature is such, she is the Sovereign (*īśvarī*) because she possesses the power of infinite sovereignty. || 22 ||
O Supreme Goddess, you are the creator of all without exception, the sustainer within your own self, and the dissolver of everything; salutations to you!

The sovereignty over the creation and so forth of the entire universe belongs to you alone; therefore, he says that you alone are the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*) with the words "aśeṣa" (without remainder). The meaning is that you are the one who establishes [all things] within your own self—which is like a mirror—in your own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and thus the sustainer of the world which is like a reflection. [This is expressed by the term] "svātmani" (in your own self).
This should also be applied to such passages as "that which produces [the effect] through its capacity" (yogyatayotpādayitrī) and so forth. || 23 ||
You are eternally new, since there is no birth for you;
you are indeed always possessed of a fresh nature, since there is no decay for you.
He states that although you are the substratum of the entire world which possesses arising and destruction, you yourself have neither arising nor destruction, by saying "anūtana" (not new).

"Nūtana" means that which possesses arising. By the phrase "since there is no old age," the sense is that there is no state of transformation consisting in the attainment of another form through the cessation of the existing form.
And this should be understood as indicating the absence of all modifications without exception. || 24 ||
You are all, you are the essence of all; you are omniscient and the delighter of all.
You are not-all, you do not go everywhere, you are without essence, and you are not omniscient nor the delighter of all. || 25 ||

He describes that sovereignty [with the verse]: "Thou art all" (*sarvāsi*). Just as a mirror consists of reflections, because the world manifested within Thy own self is Thy very nature, Thou alone art everything. If it be asked, "How can she whose form is unchanging and non-dual possess the nature of all infinite modifications?", he says:

"Thou art the essence of all" (*sarvasārāsi*). "Essence" (*sāra*) means a firm, imperishable form. And thus, because it persists everywhere—in things such as jars—as the true nature that is the unchanging essence, just as clay persists in jars and the like, it possesses the nature of being the essence of all. Now, what is this primary essence?
If it is argued that [the Lord] is not pervasive because he exists in the form of the power of insentience (*jaḍaśakti*), he says "no":

"Omniscient" (*sarvajña*). This means that he is pervasive everywhere in the form of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) which consists of knowledge. But is it not the case that even the light of consciousness...

If it be argued that [the Lord], being devoid of autonomy, would be indifferent and merely a cause for action (*prakṛta*), and thus—due to his lack of autonomy—would share the same fate as inert matter like the Sāṃkhyas, [the author] says "no," stating: "[He is] the one who causes all joy. His very autonomy is bliss; bliss is the transformation of universal I-consciousness (Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā 1).

13) According to the principle stated in such passages, she is "possessing all joy" because of her absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*) in all respects; the meaning is that her nature is one of unlimited bliss (*aparicchinna-ānanda*). Even in the world, it is perfectly clear that to whatever extent one possesses sovereignty, to that same extent one possesses bliss. To whatever extent one possesses dependence (*pāratantrya*), [to that same extent one lacks bliss].

The intended meaning is that as long as there is a covering of bliss (*ānanda*), so long does dependence persist; and as long as dependence ceases, so long is bliss manifested. Since, among the aforementioned attributes, all things are essentially nothing more than manifestations and are thus non-different [from consciousness], they are in reality the self of all and so forth.

He says "it does not exist" (nāsti), [beginning with] "not all-pervading," and so forth. He states that if there were omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), there would be essence (*sāratā*); since there is no omnipresence, there is an absence of essence. Thus he says: "Not all-pervading, it is without essence. (25)
O Goddess, salutations to you again; salutations to you in front and behind, below and above, on the sides—in every direction, salutations, salutations to you.

Having thus offered praise, because it is necessary to perform prostration in the presence [of the deity] and because it is difficult for the supreme goddess to be present in person (*aśarīriṇī*), and because she pervades all directions and times—such as in front and behind—one's self—the sages prostrate themselves from all sides, saying "O Goddess! repeatedly, that is, an immeasurable number of times. (26)
Tell me what other form of yours there is— your sovereignty, your knowledge,
the fruit, its means, the primary practitioner, and the perfected one as well. (27)

Having thus paid homage to the deity with praise, they ask about the matter they wish to know, saying, "Speak. Although they have set out with the highest desire for knowledge among those who possess it, nevertheless, being satisfied by the attainment of the meeting with the supreme deity that was so difficult to obtain, [they inquire] even regarding a matter already known.
In order to achieve firm conviction, the sages posed ten questions.

Regarding the word "param" (the supreme), there are two questions—concerning the supreme form and the non-supreme form—depending on whether the vowel "a" is elided or not, as required by the subsequent answers. [The Lord said: "That is sovereignty; that is knowledge; that is the primary [aspect] of knowledge."
The fruit, the means, and the practitioner are established within knowledge (or: knowledge is established). || 27 ||
O Goddess, tell me further in due order about the supreme pinnacle of accomplishment and that which is the most excellent among all accomplishments; salutations again and again to you. (28)

The word "siddheḥ" is in the singular number used for the sake of the genus (*jāti*). The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*); the meaning is "among the accomplishments" (*siddhīnām madhye*).

"Supreme" (*paramām*) means the principal, the ultimate limit, the final stage; the intended sense is that after attaining this, there is no other accomplishment to be attained. [This refers to] among those who have attained the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñāna-siddhi*). || 28 ||
Thus questioned, the Great Vidyā began to speak, feeling compassion for the assembly of sages, with supreme words of clear meaning. (29)

She was questioned from all sides by all the sages; being further gratified by their prostrations and devotion, she proceeded to speak with pre-eminence through a logical application capable of severing all doubts.
If it is asked what the motive for her reply was, given that her own desires were already fulfilled, he says: "out of compassion" (*dayamānā*).
It is clear in meaning and free from doubt; it is supremely beautiful and a delight to the ears. || 29 ||
Listen, all you sages, for I shall explain it all to you in due order;
having indeed drawn forth this nectar from the ocean of the scriptures, I give it to you. (30)
He addresses the listeners, saying, "Listen! That which you have asked, I give to you—the essential portion, like nectar—from the ocean of scripture, the sea of treatises. (30)
In which this entire world—arising, abiding, and dissolving like a reflection in a mirror—is always manifest to all. (31)
Having thus brought the primary subject of inquiry before us, he establishes the supreme form (*paraṃ rūpam*) [with the words] "wherein.

The connection with the sixth verse is as follows: "My supreme intuition (*parā pratibhā*) is declared to be the supreme form. Here, intuition (*pratibhā*), which consists of the various forms of perceivable objects such as pots and cloths and is denoted by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), [is that which is meant].
It exists as self-luminous and undeniable. If it were denied, neither the question nor the answer would be possible, because questioning and answering depend upon that [self-luminosity].
For its nature is not established as merely momentary appearances in the form of various objects of perception.
Because the connection of memory and so forth would otherwise be impossible,

that form [of consciousness] is indeed the Great Intuition (*mahāpratibhā*), which is the thread running through the multitude of portions of mirrors delimited by various reflections. Thus, this supreme intuition (*parā pratibhā*), whose nature is universal knowledge, undelimited by space, time, and the like, is my supreme, fundamental all-encompassing [consciousness].
The intended meaning is "form" (rūpa). That very [form] is specified by the five verses beginning with "wherein" (yatra) for the sake of its ascent into the mind (*cittāroha*).

Wherein—in which supreme manifestation (*parapratibhā*)—this entire world, established through direct perception, is always present: as arisen, it has as its object a new appearance; as persisting, it has as its object a stream of appearances; and as dissolved, it has as its object the absence of appearance.
It appears sequentially to all subjects. Now, if it is argued that it appears as something separate, like a jar on the ground, he says "no," adding: "like a reflection in a mirror.
Just as there is the appearance of the arising, persistence, and dissolution of a reflection in a mirror, so too the world appears within the supreme consciousness without any distinction from it.
"The manifestation of arising and so forth. || 31 ||
That which appears in the form of the world to those who do not know the Self,
shines for yogis as the non-conceptual alone within the Self.

If it is asked, "In the case of a mirror, the appearance of a reflection is caused by an external object; how then can the manifestation of the world occur in the supreme consciousness (parapratibhā)? [the author] replies that it is caused by the power of Māyā called "one's own sovereignty" (svasvātantrya), stating:
"That very... That which is the very reality called the supreme consciousness (parapratibhā) [is the cause] for those who do not know their true self.

For those whose minds are veiled by ignorance— which consists of various states of the power of *māyā*— and whose eyes are obscured by the defect of jaundice, the very form of the world appears as yellow, just as a conch shell [appears] yellow. That which is the reality for yogins is precisely that.

For those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge, that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and devoid of the forms of dualistic appearances shines forth. If it is objected: "Even so, since 'that' shines for 'him,' there is still no disappearance of the duality between the object of illumination and the illuminator," he replies: "In the Self alone.

That is to say, within one's own Self, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and which is entirely devoid even of a trace of the appearance of objects such as the body, there shines only the pure "I" (*kevalamaham*).
The meaning is that it manifests in the form of the mere seer. || 32 ||
Like a deep and still ocean, it possesses an appearance of immobility because those with true devotion, through their excessive love and freedom from deceit, perceive it as such. (33)

Now, one might object: "Even so, that [consciousness] cannot be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), because at that time only a stream of momentary pure cognitions (*kevalajñāna*) appears, and since those momentary pure cognitions are mutually distinct. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Profound... (*gambhīra*).
For yogis, the reality of the Self becomes a steady manifestation, like a deep and still ocean.
It should be understood that "deep" refers to its lack of spatial limitation and "still" refers to its lack of temporal limitation.
The intended meaning is that its manifestation occurs precisely as an infinite and non-dual form. Thus...

He states that this very reality is also served by the best of devotees: "by those who are well-devoted" (*yat subhaktaiḥ*). The connection is with the word "served. "Well-devoted" (*subhakta*) refers to those who know the reality of the supreme Self, for they worship (*bhajanti*) excellently by abandoning the impurity of duality. "With excessive love" (*atiśayaprītyā*): love is attachment, a particular modification of the mind; of that—
Excellence consists in being without limit. This joy is not possible for dualists;

for, according to the statement, "Everything becomes dear for the sake of the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), their joy in the Supreme Self is for the sake of the [individual] self, and thus it is excluded from [true] self-joy and is inferior.

And because there is an absence of lack of limit [to its extent]. It should be understood that for the Advaitins, since the Supreme Self is non-different from one's own self, the pleasure derived from Him has no other purpose; thus, the aforementioned defect does not apply. Regarding the phrase "due to the avoidance of deceit" (*kaitavavarjanāt*):
*kaitava* means guile (*śāṭhya*; in manuscripts *kh* and *g*: *kāpaṭya*). For example, as a courtesan displays affection toward libertines...

They practice that deception, for their primary affection is directed toward wealth. Since they display even a secondary affection directed toward a paramour as if it were primary, that affection arises from deceit;
thus, the devotion of dualists is of this very nature—so should the wise reflect. || 33 ||
Even though one has known the non-dual state of intrinsic nature by its own inherent power,
it is cultivated by those who are intensely devoted after having removed the sense of duality.

If it is asked how the service of the Supreme Self, who is one's own self, can be possible for Advaitins—since there can be no such thing without the discernment of a distinction between the served and the server—the author replies: "having removed the state of duality.
The "state" (*bhāva*) is the existence (*sattā*) of duality (*vibheda*). Having removed that.

"Having known by force" means through the knowledge that discerns the distinction [between self and other]. He says this very thing: "even having known. That is, even having known the supreme reality of the Self (*parātmatattva*), which is the non-dual, peerless state to be attained. If it is asked, "How can there be the removal of the sense of duality for one who possesses such knowledge? he replies: "by the very nature of things, spontaneously."

This is because the mind’s own nature (*svabhāva*) arises from its own inherent tendency (*svarasa*). For just as certain wise ones perform actions such as ruling a kingdom due to the force of past impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), so too does this [state] arise from the diversity of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*); such is the meaning.
If it is objected that serving those of such a kind would be preceded by disrespect, he says: "by them" (*tair*).
The meaning is: "by those endowed with devotion directed toward that. || 34 ||
When that internal thread of life within the senses, mind, and other faculties is absent, nothing whatsoever would exist—that which is indicated by the scriptures. (35)

It is called *akṣa*. The sense organs (*indriyāṇi*) are the *akṣas*; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), namely the mind (*manas*), as well as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, and the body. That which is their inherent nature (*svabhāvabhūta*), like a mirror for reflections, is the internal [reality]. Alternatively, that which is internal to these is the thread of life (*prāṇasūtra*). For instance:

Just as a puppeteer makes various movements by means of the very thread located within [the puppets], which is equal to their life-force and the cause of all their motions, so too is there for the eyes and other organs an internal thread of vital breath (*prāṇa*) that serves as the cause of each respective movement.
Moreover, in the absence or non-manifestation of this [thread], nothing at all would exist or attain its being. Such being the case...

If it is asked, "What is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the supreme reality (*paratattva*)?", he says that it is the scripture itself by way of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*), namely: "that which is taught in the scripture. One should thus connect [the meaning as follows]: the Supreme Goddess, who is intent on the play of the universe, is of the aforementioned nature—the very unconditioned intuition (*pratibhā*); this alone is my supreme, real form. || 35 ||
That supreme creative intuition (pratibhā) of the Goddess is declared by me to be my own supreme form,
situated above the many cosmic eggs in the ocean of nectar.

Having thus established the supreme form (*para-rūpa*), he now proceeds to describe the other form (*apara-rūpa*) by first defining the manifest form with qualities (*saguṇa-mūrti*) relevant to the present context, beginning with the words "of the cosmic eggs" (*brahmāṇḍānām*).
This statement, starting with "of the cosmic eggs," serves to demonstrate her infinite sovereignty (*anavadhikaiśvarya*).
In order to praise [the Lord] as being superior to the embodied forms possessing attributes, [he is placed] in the ocean of nectar, the sea of ambrosial water.
In the Nīpa grove on Maṇidvīpa, within the beautiful temple of the Cintāmaṇi jewel,
upon a couch composed of the five Brahmans, is the form of Tripurasundarī.
On Maṇidvīpa— an island consisting of nine sections fashioned from jewels of the nine precious gems— in the forest of *nīpas*, which are a specific type of *kadamba* tree,
there is the *cintāmaṇi*, a particular gem that grants the fruits desired by devotees [at the time of the churning for nectar].

With great effort, the gods obtained a single [being]: the beautiful Tripura-sundara, who dwells within the three cities—the abodes of waking and the other states—upon a couch whose frame consists of the four forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, which is composed of the five Brahmans, and whose surface is Sadāśiva; he who resides in a lovely palace constructed from clusters of such jewels.

That supreme form, which is the reality of the supreme conscious self, is exceedingly beautiful because it is desirable to all; it is that which is followed [by all], and its related form—which is manifested solely by means of its own sovereignty for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees—is [the subject]. 37.
O lords of sages, that which is called Aparā is the primordial couple;
likewise are Sadāśiva and Īśāna, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Three-eyed One.

The primordial couple, devoid of origin and consisting of the forms of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, was previously established in the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa. Although it is stated therein that their manifestation occurs through the grace of Brahmā and others— which is a form of birth— nevertheless, there is no *ādi* (beginning) or cause [for them].
By the analysis of the compound *yasya* ("of which"), it should be understood that there is an avoidance of origination from any cause distinct from one's own sovereignty (*svasvātantrya*).
That which is of such a nature is indeed my other form. Having thus described the *pradhāna* as another form, [the Lord says]: "Whatever being possesses glory" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.41).
41) Thus, according to the principle stated by the Blessed One, he also mentions those whose forms are subordinate, beginning with "likewise" (*tathā*).

Sadāśiva and the other four are the presiding deities over the fivefold activities consisting of grace (*anugraha*), concealment (*tirodhāna*), emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*laya*). || 38 ||
Gaṇeśa, Skanda, the guardians of the quarters, the Śaktis, the Gaṇadevatās, the Yātudhānas, the Suras, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, the Kiṃpuruṣas, and others; || 39 ||

Gaṇeśa is Vināyaka; Skanda is Ṣaṇmukha; the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) are Indra and the others; the Śaktis are those previously mentioned, headed by Kumārī and Lakṣmī, as well as others; the Gaṇadevatās are the Vasus, Rudras, and others who exist in the form of hosts. The syntactical connection is that [these], beginning with the Yātudhānas and ending with the Kiṃpuruṣas, are to be worshipped. || 39 ||
All my other forms are proclaimed as worthy of worship;
yet those who are deluded by my māyā do not know me in every respect.
Whatever forms among the Yātudhānas, Asuras, and others are worthy of worship, all those are my other bodies (tanūs).
Thus, he says "my" (mama) to indicate that those deluded by Māyā do not recognize me as existing everywhere in those various forms;
the sense is that they do not realize that all those forms are indeed related to me. 40.
When I alone am worshipped by all of them, I bestow the desired fruit.
There is no one else besides me who is worthy of worship or who grants rewards. 41.

If it is asked, "Whence are those forms associated with you?", [the Lord] says, "I alone am the one to be worshipped and the bestower of fruits" (referring to the verse beginning with *pūjitā*). "Desired" (*īhitam*) means what is wished for. If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says, "Not from me" (*na mattaḥ*), because the capacity to grant fruits corresponding to the worship performed is difficult to establish in anything other than Consciousness (*saṃvit*). || 41 ||
Just as whoever meditates upon me shall obtain my fruit,
so too has my sovereignty been declared by the hosts of sages to be unlimited.
Just as that fruit is given by me from myself as the giver of that fruit—of such a nature [is she]. He answers the third question with the word "mine" (*mama*): it is unlimited and infinite. 42.
O best of sages, independent of anything whatsoever, I, who am non-dual and composed of consciousness, manifest in the form of the infinite world.

In this regard, he states the primary sovereignty: "without depending at all" (*anapekṣyaiva*). The meaning is: "I manifest in the form of the universe without depending on any cause whatsoever that is distinct from my own nature. Now, one might object:
"Even in the absence of a cause external to one's own nature, the state of being the universe could still occur by depending on the distinctions among one's own parts. To this, he says: "No."

To explain [the term] "consisting of non-dual consciousness": the intended meaning is that because it is undivided pure consciousness alone, there is no such thing as a "part" (aṃśa) belonging to me. || 43 ||
Even as these things constantly manifest, I do not waver from my non-dual conscious nature;
this is my primary sovereignty, which brings about the manifestation of even the most difficult-to-accomplish objects. (44)

If it is objected: "Surely, even though you were previously pure non-dual consciousness (*advaya-cinmātra*), after assuming the form of the world, there would arise a state of manifold and diverse forms," he replies: "In that way" (*tathā*). Even while constantly manifesting in the form of the variegated world, I do not transcend—that is, I do not abandon—my own essential nature (*vapuḥ*), which consists of the non-dual conscious self.

The sense is that because the manifold form of the world is like a reflection, there is no obstruction to my own essential nature. This refers to the manifestation in the form of the manifold world even of that which consists solely of non-dual consciousness (cinmātra) from which nothing has departed.
"Vibhāvana" means the bringing about or the accomplishment of an impossible thing. || 44 ||
O sages, behold my sovereignty with a subtle vision;
I am the sole abode of all, omnipresent, and established as the absolute consciousness (citi).
I alone exist as the substratum of all that is visible, pervading and permeating everything through my nature as pure consciousness and non-dual reality; behold such is my sovereignty.
Having long wandered through saṃsāra by not recognizing myself through my own māyā, I have now, having again known my own Self, become a disciple at the feet of the Guru. (46)
He describes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) as the power to effect the impossible, saying: "by my own *māyā*.

By that power of *māyā* which is related to myself and consists of supreme freedom (*paramasvātantrya*), I, having not known myself—having made my own self covered by ignorance—have been wandering for a long time, from beginningless time.

Having fallen into the stream of birth and death, she attained the state—the true nature—of the disciple; then, having once again learned her own self, the reality of the Self, from the presence of the Guru, she became liberated—this is the connection [of the verses]. || 46 ||
Though eternally liberated, I am released again and again;
devoid of any material cause or accumulation, I create such a world as this.

Since this ignorance and so forth are illusory in nature, there is an absence of real bondage; thus, although eternally liberated, I am liberated again and again. And yet, such an infinite and diverse world—devoid of any accumulation of material cause—arises in such a way that it exists entirely without the assembly of causes such as a material substratum.
I create. || 47 ||
Thus, there are many successions of my sovereign powers;
they could not be counted even by one with a thousand mouths. (48)
That sovereignty cannot be calculated even by Ādiśeṣa, who possesses a thousand mouths; the sense is that it is infinite. || 48 ||
Listen; I shall speak briefly of my own sovereignty from its summary.
This manifold course of the world has been spread forth everywhere by the Creator. (49)

He expresses the very infinity of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) by means of another figurative turn: "Let them hear," etc. That which has the form of the world (*jagadrūpī*) is its worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), that is to say, its manifestation (*avabhāsa*). This [manifestation] is beginningless and endless, and is entirely manifest (*sarvāparokṣabhūtā*). It is "fully extended" (*samprasāritā*), meaning it is manifested as being spread forth in the form of stable causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is perfectly uncontradicted.
My knowledge is manifold,
distinguished by categories such as duality and non-duality; and its fruit is likewise diverse, due to the distinction between the higher and the lower.

Having thus established the supreme, the intermediate, and the lower sovereignty of the Self and the Other, he states the answer to the fourth question for the sake of achieving liberation from the bondage of ignorance manifested therein: "Mama" (mine).
He explains its manifold nature with the word "dvaite" (in duality); that is, the knowledge of duality is [the means of] worship.

Non-duality is of the nature of direct experience; it is supreme and non-indirect (*paramaparokṣa*), while the other is indirect (*parokṣa*). Thus, because knowledge is of many kinds, he says "in many ways" (*bahudhā*) to indicate that the fruit is also manifold. || 50 ||
But dualistic knowledge is manifold because it has a second object as its support;
that is said to be mere meditation, comparable to a kingdom seen in a dream and so forth. (51)
He states the reason for the manifold nature of dualistic ignorance (*dvaitājñāna*) with the words: "because it has a second object of support" (*dvitīyālambanaṃ yataḥ*).

The meaning is that dualistic knowledge is precisely the meditation by a practitioner upon various objects such as forms, mantras, and so forth, which are distinct from his own essential nature (*svarūpa*). In order to illuminate the inferiority of this knowledge compared to non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*), [the author says...].
The qualification (is that it) is comparable to a kingdom in a dream and so forth; by "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of a kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*) and other such things is intended.

It should be understood that because meditation consists of the continuous connection of recollections, it lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*) and is therefore similar to the delusion of a kingdom in a dream. || 51 ||
And that too should be known as fruitful, since it is determined by necessity;
furthermore, although there are various [other types], that alone is indeed the primary one therein.

If it is objected that, since knowledge of duality consisting of meditation is equivalent to an error, it would follow that it is fruitless, he says: "And that too... The meaning is: "even though it has the form of memory. It should be understood as being indeed fruitful. If one asks how this is so, he says:
"Because it is determined by necessity. Even though [it is] memory...
Although there is no direct or indirect attainment of the primary fruit of this context— which consists generally in the cessation of ignorance—

nevertheless, it should be understood that these specific prescribed recollections possess the aforementioned fruit by means of purifying the mind, as they are regulated by the power of the Lord's destiny.

Now, it was stated that dualistic cognition is of various kinds due to the diversity of its objective supports (*ālambana*). In this regard, if one asks whether all of these are equal or whether some are primary, he says: "and the other" (*aparam ca*). The meaning is "and duality" (*dvaitam ca*). || 52 ||
The supreme meditation, which is superior to the previously mentioned primary [meditations],
follows the sequence of the primary fruits; non-dual gnosis alone is declared to be the supreme gnosis.

If one asks, "What is that? he says: "proktam" (it has been taught). That meditation which has as its sole object the primary and secondary form taught in the passage beginning with "of the many cosmic eggs" (20.36), that alone is the primary [meditation]. If one asks why, he says: "the sequence of the primary fruit."

The meaning is: "the primary sequence" refers to that sequence of the collection of means for knowledge—such as the purification of the mind—which is directly attainable (*sākṣāt-prāpya*) by means of the fruit. Through meditation on the supreme form (*mukhyāpara-rūpa*), there is the direct attainment of the means for knowledge; however, through meditation on Sadāśiva and others, this occurs by way of attaining that [supreme] meditation.
This is to be understood: since the knowledge of duality consisting of meditation lacks the capacity to directly destroy ignorance, he states "Advaita...
[to show] that the non-dual knowledge which directly destroys ignorance is indeed superior.
"Supreme knowledge" (paravijñāna) means the most excellent knowledge. || 53 ||
Without propitiating me, how can the supreme, glorious, and ultimate knowledge known as non-duality (advaita) be attained? (54)

If it is argued that enough with this inferior knowledge of duality, and that everyone should instead resort to the supreme non-dual knowledge alone, he says: "Me" (*mām*). [This refers to] the glorious Vidyā known as Śrīvidyā, the supreme [form], which—according to the stated principle that "among bodies, the head is foremost"—is the qualified form within the [divine] embodiments.
Without having worshipped Sadāśiva and other supreme deities for a long time—that is, for a great duration—how could the non-dual knowledge (advaita-vidyā) be attained?
The sense is that it certainly could not be attained. "Vidyā" means knowledge. || 54 ||
That very non-dual consciousness is the absolute, supreme Cit;
its awareness of its own pure state is that which overcomes the awareness of duality. (55)

Having thus defined the knowledge of duality, he speaks of the supreme non-dual knowledge, which consists of direct perception (*aparokṣa*), saying: "That very [consciousness]" (*tadeva*). That very consciousness (*cit*)—which is absolute (*kevalā*), devoid of even a trace of the duality of the visible (*dṛśya*), supreme (*parā*), and unlimited (*anavacchinna*), and which has been described as the supreme nature—is itself the realization of non-duality (*advaitavijñāna*). Now, one might object:

If it is asked: "How can that which consists of the absolute consciousness (kevalaciti) whose nature is the aforementioned 'supreme form'—being the locus of the world together with ignorance like a wall for a painting—be the remover of ignorance? [The author] says: "Of that" (tasyāḥ).

This refers to the pure state of the supreme consciousness, whose nature is devoid of any admixture with the appearance of objects of knowledge, and whose form is a general awareness devoid of specific knowable things.
The direct knowledge [attained] through that [non-conceptual] awareness by means of a flawless means of valid cognition is what overcomes the awareness of duality;
it is that which overcomes— that is, produces the rejection of— the appearance of duality by generating the apprehension of its invalidity.

That is to say, it is that which effects the incapacity for producing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). For just as when a mirror is known, the capacity to produce purposeful action such as fear regarding the reflections therein—such as snakes, tigers, and so forth—is rendered incapable, such is the intended meaning. || 55 ||
O best of sages, when the mind merges entirely into its own self alone, then that very [mind] becomes manifest as pure consciousness (vijñāna). || 56 ||

He further clarifies this very point in detail: "The mind" (*cittam*). When—at which time—one knows for oneself, through direct intuition, one's own self (*ātmānam*) which is essentially the nature of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyayin*), which is free from the stain of the forms of the objects of perception (*dṛśyākārakalaṅka*), and which is the universal form of consciousness (*sāmānyacidrūpa*) persisting through all states; [the word] "only" (*kevalam*) means...

It also follows into the mind (*citta*). That is to say, it is even devoid of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the state of conceptual meditation (*savikalpa-samādhi*), such as "I am turned away from the visible world" or "I am turned toward the Self. Such a mind is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) which is the expanding form of consciousness (*cit*). It "should fully attain" (*abhisampatet*), meaning [it should attain] on all sides.

The essential meaning is this: when non-conceptual samādhi occurs through the abandonment of all distinctions, by attaining a complete and perfect unification with everything, and by the immersion of the mind into the pure conscious self (śuddhacidātman), thereby achieving identity with that; then, for one who has emerged from that samādhi, that very same [reality] which was experienced during samādhi—

That very pure nature of consciousness, which has become manifest, would be recognized as "I" through an undivided form; that very recognition described above is called the supreme knowledge (vijñāna)— this is the implied meaning— whether by means of scripture or by reasoning, it is the shining forth of the absolute Self alone.
The destruction of the appearance of the body and so forth as the self is called knowledge. || 57 ||
Having thus defined supreme knowledge (*para-jñāna*), he defines the nature of inferior knowledge (*apara-jñāna*) [with the words] "from scripture" (*śrutitaḥ*).

"From scripture" means by hearing the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-śravaṇa*). "Or from reasoning" (*yuktitaḥ*) means either by means of pure logic (*kevala-tarka*). It is the "manifestation" (*vibhāsana*)—specifically in the form of a definitive certainty—of the "pure self" (*kevalātman*), which is the conscious self (*cidātman*) devoid of limitations such as the body and so forth.

Regarding that which appears as something indirect (*parokṣa*), he explains what kind of thing it is with the words "the body and so forth" (*dehādi*). It is the destruction— that is, the apprehension of its lack of validity— of that appearance of selfhood (*ātmatvāvabhāsa*), which is the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), occurring with respect to the limited objects of perception such as the body and vital breath.

Such a manifestation of the absolute Self is called *aparajñāna* (lower knowledge). Now, if it is argued that establishing knowledge through logic alone—that is, by means of mere reasoning—is contrary to the non-dualistic scriptures (*advaita-śāstra*), it is replied:
for those of the highest qualification, there exists a form of knowledge called "without means" (*anupāya*) even without [the standard stages of] hearing and so forth.

Because that which is produced by mere reasoning alone is accepted in the scriptures; as it has been said: "The knowledge of the most excellent, however, does not depend upon a teacher or the scriptures. Furthermore, Vāmadeva, Karkaṭika, and others are well known as possessors of knowledge even without having undergone formal study.
That alone is true knowledge by which nothing whatsoever, even while appearing, manifests in any way at all.

Having thus examined the higher and lower knowledge in succession, he now speaks of the supreme knowledge in five verses for the sake of discerning it from dualistic knowledge by way of its result (*phaloddeśena*):
"That very [knowledge]... Whatever is visible, even though it appears, [is that which is known] by some knowledge somewhere.

The meaning is that in no way whatsoever—that is, by no means at all—should it appear as something separate; rather, for one who has realized the true nature of the mirror, it should not appear as having a distinct existence, like a reflection [which does not exist apart from the mirror]. Because it is uncontradicted by any particularity, that very thing becomes supreme knowledge. || 58 ||
That alone is non-dual knowledge (advaita-vijñāna) by which nothing whatsoever remains unknown, even in the slightest degree, at any time.
