For just as, through knowledge of the true nature of a mirror, a reflection is never unknown even in the slightest degree— whether at the time of its appearance or at any other time— so too, that knowledge by which nothing whatsoever among the objects of perception remains unknown is indeed non-dual knowledge (advaita-vijñāna). || 59 ||
O best of ascetics, that consciousness which indeed consists of the nature of the self of all cognitions is itself the supreme non-dual consciousness. 60.

That cognition which constitutes the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpa*)— like a great mirror— to which there correspond the portions of the mirror delimited by reflections, namely all those determinate cognitions of specific objects that exclude [other things] such as a jar; the word "indeed" (*khalu*) has the sense of emphasis (*eva*), meaning that it is the very nature of the Self and not otherwise in any way.

The intended meaning is as follows: that very [consciousness] is the supreme realization of non-duality (*paramadvaitavijñāna*). Now, one might ask: how can a cognition consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) have the nature of the essence of all-knowingness?
If it is asked how the pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*), which is the object of recognition, could possess such a nature, it is replied:
Because, due to the cognition of absolute non-difference between the reflection within a mirror and a portion of the mirror itself, such conventional usage is possible. || 60 ||
When such a realization has arisen, long-accumulated doubts dissolve like masses of clouds by the wind; for that is the supreme state.

Just as when the true nature of a mirror is known, all doubts regarding the essential character of its reflections dissolve through the certainty that they are nothing but the mirror itself; so too, when such realization arises, the doubts concerning the visible world— whether creation has primordial nature (*pradhāna*) as its source or atoms (*paramāṇu*) as its source— dissolve within the body.

Doubts concerning the seer, such as "Am I the breath? and so forth—which have been accumulated for a long time from beginningless past and stored within the heart—dissolve, just as masses of clouds are dispersed by the wind; this is intended to indicate that there is no delay in their dissolution. That is knowledge. 61.
That in which all latent impressions of desire and the like do not exist at all,
like a snake whose fangs have been broken— that is remembered as the supreme realization.

Just as for one who has realized the true nature of a mirror, all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as desire and aversion residing in its reflection dissolve; likewise, the intended meaning is that when [the Self] is known, all latent impressions of desire and so forth residing in the object of perception (*dṛśya*) become "nothing," that is, they lose their form and are extinguished. However, certain latent impressions may persist due to the force of *prārabdha* karma and other factors.

Even though they are not lost, they would be like a snake with broken fangs; for just as a serpent whose venomous fangs are broken does not bring about calamities such as death, so too those latent impressions (*vāsanās*) do not bestow the calamity of future births, according to the principle:
"Upon the attainment [of Brahman], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins" (*Brahma-sūtra* 4.1.13).
Because, through the latent impressions of desire and so forth, there is no clinging to the fruits of actions performed. || 62 ||
The fruit of consciousness is the dissolution of all sufferings;
the attainment of ultimate fearlessness is called the fruit, which is liberation.

Having thus defined knowledge, he defines its fruit: "of consciousness. [This refers to] the dissolution of all sufferings, such as those of the body and so forth. Although the dissolution of all suffering exists in states such as deep sleep, nevertheless, because there is fear due to the possibility of future suffering, he says: "absolute" (*atyanta*). This alone is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus it is said. || 63 ||
Fear arises from the conceptualization of duality; once non-duality is firmly known, how could the conceptualization of duality remain? It would vanish like darkness at the rising of the sun. (64)

If it is asked, "From what does his attainment of absolute fearlessness arise?", he says: "Fear. In the world, fear is well known to arise precisely from the conception of a second entity, such as "this is a tiger" or "this is a scorpion," because in deep sleep, fear is absent due to the absence of the conception of duality. When non-duality is firmly realized, [fear ceases].

When non-dual knowledge free from doubt has arisen, because ignorance is destroyed by that knowledge, there is no further conceptualization of duality due to the absence of its cause; thus he asks, "Why? The sense is that just as when the true nature of the mirror is known, there is no longer any certainty regarding the duality of its reflections, so it is in this case as well. || 64 ||
O sages, there is no fear anywhere when one is free from the conceptualization of duality;
therefore, whatever else might result from that would necessarily be fear in every respect. (65)
He says that even the possibility of fear does not exist when one is free from the dualistic conceptualization that is the cause of fear— referring to the verse beginning with "The seers" (*ṛṣayaḥ*).

Having stated that in any place or at any time, one's own nature, devoid of dualistic conceptualization, is itself the fruit consisting of liberation, he says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that nothing other than this nature possesses the quality of being a fruit characterized by fearlessness.
Because the very nature described [in the preceding verses] is itself the fruit; however, that which is other than this nature is indeed fear, because it produces fear—this is the meaning. || 65 ||
But the second [position] would have an end, because it is observed repeatedly in the world.
Where there is an end, there is fear in every respect; therefore, how could fearlessness arise from that? (66)
In order to establish that very thing which causes fear, he says: "It is finite" (*antavat*). This means "subject to destruction.

"The second is other" (*dvitīyam anyat*). If it is asked, "How is this known?", he replies: "Because [of its being seen] repeatedly" (*bhūyaḥ*). The meaning is that in the world, the finitude of sons, wives, houses, wealth, and so forth, is observed in many ways.
Therefore, there must be fear in every respect regarding that which is peaceful yet perishable; how, then, could fearlessness arise from that which is peaceful? || 66 ||
Union is invariably determined to end in separation;
therefore, it is certain that even the attainment of results will perish. (67)

Thus, having established that another [entity] is a source of fear by virtue of its own nature being finite, it is shown that its relation is likewise a source of fear; hence the term "mahā-saṃyoga" (great conjunction). "Sambandha" means relation.
"Viprayogānta": *viprayoga* is separation, which is the destruction of one's own nature (*svarūpa-nāśa*); that relation whose end is such is perishable.
To such an extent that this kind of relationship has been manifested and observed by everyone; therefore, even the connection or union with the fruit would surely perish. || 67 ||
As long as another fruit is proclaimed, so long is it declared to be fear;
but that very same fruit, when it takes the form of fearlessness, is what everyone describes as the true result.

Therefore, he says "as long as" (*yāvat*), explaining that any other fruit is indeed fraught with fear because it is impermanent both in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and in its relationship [to the self] (*sambandhataḥ*).
Consequently, the fruit called liberation (*mokṣa*), which is taught in the non-dual scriptures (*advaita-śāstra*), is nothing other than the very nature of the Self itself.
"All the wise declare that very [state] to be the fruit in the form of fearlessness because of its excellence," thus he says:
"That very... The connection is with the words "that which is that very... (referring to *etad* in the variant reading *etade*). || 68 ||
When liberation is proclaimed as the fruit that is indeed non-different from the Self, then the knower, the knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the fruit itself become one. (69)

"That which is non-different from the Self is itself the fruit whose nature is fearlessness; all declare this. Such a fruit alone is proclaimed as liberation"—this is the construction of the sentence.
To demonstrate analytically that the fruit called liberation is indeed the very nature of the non-dual Self, he says:

By the words "jñātṛ" and so forth: the syntactical connection is that when there is oneness due to the non-appearance of the distinction between the knower, the act of knowing, the object known, and the fruit [of knowledge], then [that state arises]. || 69 ||
For then there is supreme liberation, devoid of all fear;
it is knowledge free from conceptualization and mental construction, and devoid of delusion.

The supreme liberation would be superior to that which is well-known from the dualistic scriptures (*dvaita-śāstra*). Here, the qualifying phrase "devoid of all fear" contains the reason [for its superiority]. The intended meaning is that no other liberation than this one is devoid of all fear. [This applies] to the knower and so forth...
He establishes its oneness by first indicating its essential nature: "Knowledge" (jñānam).

Where there is the abandonment—that is, the relinquishing—of those specific mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that have non-duality as their object; and if it is objected that this [state] also exists in deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth, he says: "free from delusion" (*mauḍhyavivarjitam*).
The meaning is that knowledge is the manifestation of one's own pure nature. || 70 ||
At the outset, the nature of the Knower as the pure Self is unperceived;
therefore, it is only the teacher and the scripture that can make it perceived, and nothing else. 71.

He states that this very [state] is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the knower, saying: "of the knower. Now, if knowledge is indeed of such a nature, one might object that it must have existed even at the beginning; to this he says: "having the nature of a pure self.
The sense is that the true nature, devoid of volition (*saṅkalpa*) and delusion (*mauḍhya*), did not exist previously. But surely...

If it is argued that [the self] remains present during states such as the intervals between cognitions (*jñānāntarāla*) which are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), he says: "unperceived at first.

The intended meaning is that although it remains present, it is not perceived—that is, it is not recognized—because it has not been experienced due to its being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatva*).
Therefore, since cognition is not distinct from its own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*), the nature of that which is unperceived due to delusion (*moha*)...
The teacher and the scripture are merely indicators by means of the method for dispelling delusion; nothing else. This means that they have no other function. || 71 ||
For this very thing is designated as the nature of that which is to be known:
as long as any differentiation pertaining to the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge appears. (72)

This very [consciousness] is free from the dullness of conceptual construction (saṅkalpa) and is of the nature of pure awareness (saṃvid-rūpa). Having thus established the single form of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, he states that this alone is the real nature of the knower and the rest: "The knower... etc. As long as duality appears through the non-avoidance of conceptual construction... (72)

As long as the distinction between the knower and the rest remains, neither the knower nor knowledge nor the object of knowledge can ever exist anywhere; this is when their mutual difference has dissolved. (73)
He states that, for that long, the appearing nature of the knower and so forth cannot be real—this is indicated by the word "tāvat" (for that long).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when, through the complete abandonment of all conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), the mutual distinction appearing between the knower and so forth has dissolved, then there is the attainment of the true nature (*satyasvarūpa*) of the knower and so forth. || 73 ||
Then, the perfection of the knower and so forth is remembered as having this very [realization] as its fruit;
from the knower up to the fruit of knowledge, there is no difference in reality. (74)
"Etadeva" means "of this very nature," that is to say, having the form of such a knower and so forth. The fruit is traditionally known as supreme liberation (*paramokṣa*).

Now, one might ask: even if the knower, the object of knowledge, and the fruit are one, how can there be that unity for the knowledge consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which is of the nature of a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*)? To this it is replied:

For the mind (*citta*) is indeed consciousness that is limited and veiled by the power of insentience (*jaḍa-śakti*). A particular modification (*vṛtti-viśeṣa*) of that [mind], namely recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), takes on the form of undivided consciousness. Therefore, when ignorance is removed, the power of insentience that causes limitation dissolves; and when the mind has dissolved into the true nature of consciousness (*cit-tattva*), [recognition manifests].
Since that very recognition has attained the state of full consciousness, its identity [with the Self] is indeed unavoidable.
Therefore, he says "jñātrādi" (beginning with the knower), meaning that in reality there is no difference between the knower and the others, up to the fruit. || 74 ||
A distinction is conceptually constructed therein for the sake of establishing conventional usage;
therefore, there is absolutely no fruit to be obtained here that was not already attained previously.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is the conventional usage of distinctions such as the knower and so forth explained in the scriptures? [the author] says: "It is devised for the sake of instruction," using the word *vyavahāra*. In that context, within the scriptures; therefore, because there is no distinction among the knower and the rest.
(Verse 75) "The Self alone, through Māyā, appears in the form of the knower, the knowledge, the object known, and the fruit."
As long as it appears, so long indeed does saṃsāra persist, immovable as a mountain.

As long as there is the conceptualization of difference through ignorance, so long does this saṃsāra—consisting of birth, death, and so forth, manifested by ignorance—remain firmly established; thus he says: "The Self alone... When, by means of *māyā* or ignorance, this [reality] which is devoid of difference appears in some way or another...
May saṃsāra go to dissolution, like a scattered cloud by the wind. || 77 ||

When—at whatever time—by some means, through that which is exceedingly difficult to accomplish and rooted solely in the grace of the deity, such as the instruction of a true guru and so forth, all this [universe] appearing as the differentiation of the knower and the rest should shine forth as entirely devoid of differentiation; then it shall go to dissolution. This is for the purpose of illuminating the state of dissolution as being without remainder and without delay.
The example is "a severed cloud"; the meaning is a fragment of a cloud separated from a great mass. || 77 ||
Devotion to such great liberation is indeed the means;
when that devotion is complete, no other means is required.
Having thus established the fruit, he states the means: "In this way. In the Great Liberation (mahāmokṣa), that is, in full liberation.
He says "devotion to that" (*tatparatva*) in order to state that devotion alone is the primary means; it is "desired," meaning it is employed for the sake of achieving the fruit. || 78 ||
But if that single-minded devotion is incomplete, what is the use of thousands of excellent means?
Therefore, devotion alone is the primary means for liberation. (79)
He also states its primacy through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "incomplete" (*apūrṇa*). The sense is: what is the use of a thousand excellent means?
Even with a multitude of perfectly correct means, there is no arising of the fruit. Therefore, it is thus established by both positive and negative concomitance.
The state of being established in the intent is "I shall accomplish this in every way";
he who is joined with such intent is liberated in every respect. (80)
*Tātarya* is the state of being intent upon that [goal]. He states its essential nature as "in every way" (*sarvathā*). This, however, refers precisely to this very subject at hand:

the fruit known as liberation. It is a specific state of mental activity characterized by an inability to tolerate delay in the accomplishment of the means for attaining it, with the thought, "I shall certainly achieve this. Such a person is indeed liberated.
The meaning is that because the means to that [liberation] necessarily culminates in the fruit, he is essentially one who has already attained liberation. || 80 ||
One may be liberated in days, months, or years, or perhaps in another birth;
the distinction between long and swift [liberation] depends on the degree of purity of the intellect. (81)

He states that the result is indeed inevitable with the words "in days. Now, one might ask: if the completion of the means is uniform in its nature, how can there be a disparity in the delay of time? To this he replies:
"by the purity of the intellect. The sense is that the degree of delay in time corresponds to the degree of impurity in the intellect.
But in the intellect there are many defects that destroy all goals,
by which people are constantly cooked in this terrible cycle of existence.
He defines the very turbidity of the intellect (*buddhimālinya*) with the words "But in the intellect" (*buddhau tu*).

[It refers to] those defects by which all human goals, such as dharma and the rest, are destroyed. "Thus they are cooked" means that through the attainment of birth, death, and so forth, they experience suffering; this is the intended meaning. || 82 ||
Among those, the first is lack of confidence, the second is the latent impression of desire, and the third is said to be dullness; thus is the summary of the threefold defects.
He enumerates those very [obstacles] with the word "therein" (*tatra*). This means: among the defects. "Lack of confidence" (*anāśvāsa*) is a lack of trust;

it is the absence of a firm conviction that "this is exactly so" regarding the meanings of the scriptures. Its primacy [is established] by virtue of its being the chief among the obstacles to the means of accomplishment. "Latent desire for pleasure" (*kāmavāsanā*) refers to longing for sense objects and the like. "Stolidity" (*jāḍyatā*)...
Inertness (*jaḍatva*) is the dullness of the mind, consisting of the quality of darkness (*tamaḥ*), which has as its cause the failure to grasp the meaning of the scriptures.
Regarding the term "compendium" (*saṃgraha*): the intention is that their expansion consists of infinite branches and sub-branches. || 83 ||
Lack of confidence is of two kinds: doubt and error.
"Does liberation exist or not?"—this and the like is cited as the first [doubt]. (84)
He states the internal subdivisions of the first [type] with the words "of two kinds. He explains its very nature with the words "liberation.
This is also an illustration [for further discussion], such as whether there is a return for the liberated one or not. 84.
The first misconception in this regard would be that "liberation does not exist at all";
these two, however, are the primary obstacles to the intended meaning. (85)

The misconception that "liberation does not exist at all" is one [type of error]. By the word "etcetera," [the text refers to] such [errors] as "rebirth certainly exists. Regarding the obstruction to such lack of confidence, he says: "But these two...
The meaning is "these two alone. Because even that which has been commenced possesses a common obstructive quality, it is called "primary."
(The state of being primary. || 85 ||
Through erroneous conviction, these two will perish in succession;
in this matter, the primary means is the cutting off of the root, and there is no other.

He states the means for refuting this [doubt] as "the contrary" (*viparīta*). A firm conviction that "liberation will indeed occur"—which is the opposite of the aforementioned doubt and so forth—is "certainty" (*niścaya*). These two—the aforementioned doubt and the misconception (*viparyaya*)—are [the objects to be refuted]. The phrase "in sequence" refers to [the removal of] certainty.

The meaning is that, through the gradual progression of the strengthening of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of [right] knowledge in accordance with its own nature, there occurs the gradual destruction of the persistence of impressions such as doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the like. If it is asked, "How can certainty arise while doubt and error (*viparyaya*) still exist?", he states the means for this: "here" (in verse 86). The sense is: "in the case of certainty. || 86 ||
The root of lack of confidence, however, is the contemplation of fallacious reasoning;
having abandoned that, one should strive for the establishment of the practice of sound reasoning. (87)
If it is asked, "What is this 'cutting off the root'?", he says: "of lack of confidence" (*anāśvāsasya*). This refers to the contemplation of reasoning that is contrary to confidence.

Having abandoned that contemplation of contrary reasoning, there is the "turning toward" (*āvartanasya*) right reasoning—that is, reasoning conducive to the confidence consisting of the aforementioned possibility.
"Preparation" (*prasādhana*) is the mental activity conducive to the practice and its subsequent pursuit; when that has been performed.
A perverted certainty arises, preceded by the cutting away of the root;
thereafter, through the emergence of faith, lack of confidence perishes. (88)

The "contrary conviction" (*viparītaniścaya*) is of the nature of the aforementioned cultivation (*bhāvanā*). It is preceded by the severing of the root—that is, preceded by the severing of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) caused by contrary reasoning (*tarka*). Then, immediately thereafter, due to the arising of faith (*śraddhā*), which is the aforementioned cultivation, this very cultivation in the form of contrary conviction becomes firm.
It is called "faith" (śraddhā). It perishes; it ceases. || 88 ||
The latent impressions of desire and the like act as obstacles to the hearing of the teachings;
a mind permeated by the latent impressions of desire and the like does not engage at all [in such study]. (89)
He states the second defect that is being obstructed: "kāmādi" (due to desire, etc.). It is an impediment to the intellect (*buddhi*).
It is the cause for the meaning of what has been heard not entering into the intellect. That intellect does not engage at all with the meaning spoken by the teacher;
it does not grasp that meaning whatsoever. || 89 ||

Even in the world, a man of desire who is constantly and solely intent on meditating upon the object of his longing does not see what stands before him, nor does he hear what is spoken by those nearby.

In this regard, he establishes what is well-known in the world with the words "even in the world" (*loke 'pi*). Regarding that which is desired, such as a woman, wealth, and so forth; even a sound uttered into the ear, though spoken directly into the ear, one would not hear it. || 90 ||
For one whose mind is thus permeated by desire and the like, even that which has been heard is equal to what has not been heard;
therefore, one should conquer the latent tendencies of desire and the like through the perfection of dispassion. 91.

Therefore, for one who is perfumed by desire and the like— that is, whose mind is permeated by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of desire and so forth— it may happen that even what has been heard is equal to what has not been heard because it does not ascend into the heart, owing to such devotion to meditation as previously described. Consequently, because it acts as an obstacle to hearing, [one must rely on] the perfection of dispassion (*vairāgya*), which is freedom from craving (*vaitṛṣṇya*).
One should conquer through prosperity. || 91 ||
There are thousands of latent impressions (vāsanās), headed by desire and anger;
among them, desire is the root, and when that is destroyed, nothing remains.

Regarding the phrase "the latent impressions of desire and so forth" (*kāmādivāsanā*), he explains the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) and the primacy of the latent impression of desire as follows: "They exist," etc.

The latent impression of desire (*kāmavāsanā*) and the latent impression of anger (*krodhavāsanā*) are mentioned; by the word "and so forth," which has the sense of "beginning with" (*ādyartha*), there are the latent impressions of greed, pride, envy, and so on. Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for sense objects. Anger (*krodha*) is the thought: "This person has harmed me in every way."

The mental fluctuations such as "he should be killed" and so forth—those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) residing in the mind that serve as the cause for the sudden arising of desire and the like merely by seeing their respective objects—are to be known as *vāsanā*. Since anger and the rest are rooted in desire, he states that desire is primary; the meaning is "among those *vāsanās*. For indeed...
The ellipsis implies that "something such as anger and so forth might arise. || 92 ||
Then, through the application of dispassion, one should destroy the latent impression of desire;
for desire is said to be hope, which persists in the form "may this be mine. (93)
Then, because desire is primary, he states the nature of desire: "Hope," etc. Thus hope remains established. 93.
Among those things that can be accomplished, it is gross; among those that cannot be accomplished, it remains subtle.
Through the yoga of firm dispassion, one should utterly destroy it all.

He states its infinity [with the words] "in regard to attainable things": regarding attainable things such as women, wealth, and so forth, it is gross (*sthūla*), consisting of the form of desire in the thought, "May this be mine. Regarding unattainable things such as splitting the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and so forth, it is subtle (*sūkṣma*), consisting of the aforementioned latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Through the application of firm dispassion (*vairāgya*), [it is abandoned] for all time.

By means of yoga, through the attainment of intense detachment—which is distinct from the detachment born of [contemplating] charnel grounds and so forth—one [abandons] all that latent impression (vāsanā), both gross and subtle. || 94 ||
In that regard, the root is the non-consideration of the defects of desire at every moment;
through aversion toward sense objects, one should destroy the latent impressions (vāsanā). || 95 ||
In that regard, concerning firm detachment (*dṛḍhavairāgya*): the "defect" (*doṣa*) of desirable objects of enjoyment, such as women, wealth, and so forth, [is explained as follows].

The commentary’s construction of the text is that the defect consists in their perishability; the defect consists in their causing suffering through destruction; and the defect consists in their being causes of fear through the contemplation of their anticipated destruction.

In manuscript K, the reading found within the brackets is observed as follows: "(naśvaratva-nāśena duḥkhapradatva-sambhāvita-##-) (naśvaratvena nāśena duḥkhapradatvena sambhāvitanāśānusandhānena bhayahetutvādirūpaḥ)."
It is probable that [this] exists in the form of a marginal note (*ṭippaṇī*) within the *Mūlamātṛkā*.

Its "reflection" (*parāmarśa*) is its contemplation (*anusandhāna*). Aversion toward sense objects, the absence of contemplation regarding the nature of sense objects, and the indulgence in excessive [pleasures] unsuitable for the maintenance of the body [constitute this]. || 95 ||
O best of sages, that third defect of the intellect which is established in the form of dullness is entirely incurable by means of practice.
Consisting of dullness, it is an abundance of the tamasic portion caused by past evil karma;
it is impossible to remove through practices such as repeated cultivation. || 96 ||
That dullness by which one does not ascend to the intellect even when the intended meaning has been heard is indeed a great defect, for it destroys the goals of human endeavor. (97)
If it is argued, "Let it be; what is the use of that one [cause]? The result will come from the abundance of other means," he says:

"By which... The meaning is: "by the persistence of dullness. By the word "and" (ca), all other remaining means are included. It is the destroyer—that is, the obstacle—to the human goal, whether it be the cessation of ignorance or liberation. || 97 ||
In this matter, there is indeed no cause other than the service of one's own deity;
by the gradations of such service, I remove his dullness. (98)
In that regard, concerning the destruction of dullness: without the service—consisting of recitation, worship, meditation, and so forth—of me, who am the form of the deity of the Self. || 98 ||
For one whose mind is joined with dullness, the attainment of the fruit may occur either immediately or in a future birth, depending on whether that dullness is slight or not. || 99 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to the smallness of dullness" (*jāḍyālpa*): the distinction is as follows—if there is a smallness of dullness and a non-smallness (greatness) of service, it occurs immediately; if there is a smallness of dullness and a smallness of service, or a non-smallness (greatness) of both dullness and service, it occurs after a long time; and if there is a non-smallness (greatness) of dullness and a smallness of service, it occurs in a future birth. || 99 ||
The perfection of all means of accomplishment comes to me alone through my own vow, and it approaches whoever always approaches me with devotion, free from deceit. (100)

Having thus stated that service to Me is the cause for the destruction of dullness (*jāḍya*), he says "all" (*sarva*) to show that this is necessary even for those who are free from dullness. "All" refers to the perfection of the means such as association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*), which consist of the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of being intent upon other things and so forth. "From devotion" (*praṇidhānataḥ*) means through service in the form of meditation and the like. The word "should be" (*bhavet*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

He explains this very point clearly with the words "he approaches" (upayāti). The meaning is "he serves. "With devotion" means with uninterrupted affection. "Without guile" means without deceit; the sense is that it is done without desire for reward (niṣkāmanayā). || 100 ||
He who [worships] me, the Sovereign Goddess who causes the expansion of all intelligence, shall quickly become a perfected one by shaking off that which is contrary to spiritual accomplishment. (101)
Such is that disciple. An adversary is an obstacle. "Kṛtī" means one who has accomplished his purpose. He is the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
[She is] of a nature to effect the expansion and activity of the intellect of all. 101.
If, out of delusion, one disregards [the teacher] and becomes intent solely on the means of practice, one will be frustrated at every step, and the fruit may or may not be attained. 102.

"Disregarding" means not accepting [the teaching]. For this very reason, one who possesses a state of delusion—that is, one whose mind is deluded—would be "frustrated," meaning struck down by obstacles. He states that even regarding the attainment of the fruit, there is only doubt: "The fruit... (verse 102).
Therefore, for the sages, the primary intent (tātparya) should be the means;
indeed, one who possesses such intent alone is considered the supreme practitioner. || 103 ||

He concludes the exposition of the means (*sādhana*) with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The sense is that the absence of the fruit for one who possesses the [correct] purport is caused by defects of the intellect. Dispassion, tranquility (*śama*), and so forth, are what remove obstacles;
the worship of the deity (*devatopāsana*) is the common cause for accomplishing the task. Therefore, devotion to that alone is primary here.
The meaning is "the cause. He states the proof: "In this way" (evam). The sense is that only one who possesses the aforementioned primary intention is the primary practitioner (sādhaka). || 103 ||
In that regard, the practitioner endowed with devotion to me is honored by all;
his perfection consists in self-determination and the realization that the body is not the self.
In that regard, those who possess devotion to That [are meant]. "Endowed with devotion to Me" means being attached to Me; that is to say, being intent on My service.

This implies he is the best of practitioners (*sādhaka*), honored by all, because the practice of that [devotion] necessarily culminates in its fruit. Having thus described the practitioner, He defines perfection (*siddhi*) as follows: "Perfection is the resolve of the self. Resolve (*vyavasāya*) is the determination of the self.
Certainty. If it is asked what that resolve (*vyavasiti*) is like, he says: "In the body" (*deha*).

Because of the ascertainment of the nature of the pure Self, there arises the realization of the non-selfhood of the body, the vital breath, and so forth; that is, through the determination of the true nature of the pure Self, the conceit of selfhood regarding the body, the vital breath, and the rest ceases.
The intended meaning. || 104 ||
The cultivation of the notion of self is certainly established in relation to the body and so forth;
however, the mere absence of that cultivation is accomplishment free from delusion. (105)

He clarifies this very point further with the words "as the nature of the Self" (*ātmatvena*). The cultivation of the nature of the Self is the conceit (*abhimāna*) consisting of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of continuous experience. It is ever-present for all.
Regarding the phrase "the non-cultivation of that": it is the non-cultivation of the nature of the Self with respect to the body and so forth, due to a contrary conviction.

The cessation of the persistence of those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—this alone is *siddhi*. If it is objected that such an absence of the persistence of latent impressions exists even in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says:
"devoid of delusion" (*mauḍhyavivarjitam*). Although a latent impression does indeed exist even in deep sleep, nevertheless...

It should be understood that "dissolved" means being almost entirely severed; or alternatively, it should be understood as intended to exclude the liberation of the Sāṃkhya school and others, which consists in merging into primordial nature (prakṛti). || 105 ||
The self is determined by all [factors] together, not by the self alone;
for this very reason, a succession of great calamities has been encountered. (106)

He establishes the specific result of the contemplation of the body as the self (*dehānātmabhāvanā*) [with the words]: "As the self" (*ātmeti*). It is determined by all [beings], not merely as a self distinct from the body and so forth, but rather as consisting of the body and so forth. Precisely for this reason—namely, due to the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) of the body and so forth—it is held by all ignorant ones as being identical with the body and so forth. For this very reason...
It has been attained by all ignorant people precisely because of their lack of discrimination regarding the body and so forth. 106.
Therefore, that which is pure consciousness alone, which illumines the body and so forth—the firm conviction that the Self is that alone destroys all doubt. (107)

Therefore, because non-discrimination is the cause of misfortune, the firm conviction of the Self (*ātmavyavasiti*)— the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*) directed toward that which is pure consciousness alone, by whose light the body, vital breath, and so forth are manifested—
is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), for it destroys all doubts concerning the nature of one's own self and its objects.

This is the logical connection (*anvaya*). And thus, because the conscious self (*cidātman*), being of the nature of self-luminosity, is always manifest as "I," its manifestation is not something new; rather, its "attainment" (*siddhi*) consists solely in the non-manifestation of that [self] through the discrimination of it from the body and so forth, which had previously been appearing [as identical] due to non-discrimination (*aviveka*). || 107 ||
The wise declare that this is true perfection; there is no perfection higher than this.
Other perfections, such as the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) and likewise the powers of atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth, [are inferior]. (108)

Therefore, since the accomplishment consisting of the firm conviction of the Self [is attained], there is nothing else to be obtained as a fruit immediately following this. If it is objected that there are other accomplishments such as *khecaritva* (the power of moving through the air), he replies with the word "accomplishments" (*siddhayaḥ*).
These include *khecaritva*, entering another's body, and so forth, as well as the powers of *aṇiman*, *laghiman*, and the rest. || 108 ||
But they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the accomplishment of self-knowledge;
for all those accomplishments are limited by space and time. (109)

He says "ātma" (the Self) to show that they [the Siddhis] are not equal to this even by a single part. A "kalā" is a sixteenth part; the meaning is that they do not deserve even equality with that. If one asks why this is so, he says "tāḥ" (they). [The Siddhis such as] *khecarī* and the rest have an existence only within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and up until the end of the Brahma-cycle; thus, they are limited by space and time. || 109 ||
This may be the undivided knowledge of one's own self, whose nature is Śiva;
all those [other sciences] are well-established within the means for attaining the knowledge of one's own self. || 110 ||

This is the accomplishment (*siddhi*) consisting of self-knowledge. Regarding the term "one's own self" (*svātman*): the meaning is that because it consists of the knowledge of one’s own self—which is Śiva, whose nature is full consciousness and bliss—there is no separation by time or space. He now demonstrates that these [other accomplishments] are included within this one: [The verse: "The accomplishment of the eight powers, the accomplishment of the [five] elements, the accomplishment of the mantras, and the accomplishment of the supreme state. (10.23) The accomplishment of the eight powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) consists of the power of atomization (*aṇimā*), the power of levitation (*laghimā*), the power of extension (*mahimā*), the power of attainment (*prāpti*), the power of sovereignty (*īśitva*), the power of subjugation (*vaśitva*), the power of irresistible will (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*), and the power of the ability to assume any form at will (*kāmarūpitva*). Among these, the power of atomization is the state of becoming as subtle as an atom; the power of levitation is the state of becoming light like cotton-wool; the power of extension is the state of becoming large like Mount Meru; the power of attainment is the state of reaching anything desired, such as touching the moon with one's hand; the power of sovereignty is the state of being the master over all things, like a king; the power of subjugation is the state of bringing all beings under one's control; the power of irresistible will is the state of having one's intentions unimpeded, such that whatever one desires occurs exactly so; and the power of assuming any form at will is the state of taking on various forms according to one's desire. These are called the "eight accomplishments" (*aṣṭasiddhi*). The accomplishment of the elements (*bhūtasiddhi*) is the mastery over the five gross elements: earth, water, fire, air, and ether. Among these, mastery over earth is the state of being able to move through solid ground as if it were water; mastery over water is the state of not sinking when entering water as if it were dry land; mastery over fire is the state of remaining unburnt even when entering fire; mastery over air is the state of moving through the air as if it were space; and mastery over ether is the state of passing through walls and other obstacles as if they were non-existent. These are called the "accomplishment of the elements. The accomplishment of the mantras (*mantrasiddhi*) is the state of attaining the power of the mantras, whereby one can accomplish all rites simply by reciting them. This is called the "accomplishment of the mantras. The accomplishment of the supreme state (*paramasiddhi*) is the state of attaining the supreme reality, which is the realization of the Self as Śiva. This is called the "accomplishment of the supreme state. He explains how these are included within the accomplishment of self-knowledge: "Because they are included within this very [accomplishment], there is no separate enumeration of them. (10.24ab) Since these accomplishments are contained within the accomplishment of self-knowledge, they are not enumerated separately from it. This is the meaning. Furthermore, he states: "And because they are included within the accomplishment of the supreme state, there is no separate enumeration of them. (10.24cd) Since these accomplishments are also included within the accomplishment of the supreme state, they are not enumerated separately from it. This is the meaning. Thus, the accomplishment of self-knowledge is the most excellent among all accomplishments. Therefore, one should strive for its attainment. This is the conclusion. Regarding the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*): it means the attainment of a particular state or the perfection of a specific quality. It is used here in the sense of the attainment of a particular state. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to indicate inclusion. The word "this" (*iyam*) refers to the accomplishment of self-knowledge. The word "because" (*yasmāt*) indicates the reason. The word "within this" (*etadantarbhūtatvāt*) means being included within this very accomplishment. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) indicates the consequence. The word "no separate enumeration" (*na pṛthaggaṇanā*) means there is no distinct counting. The word "of them" (*tāsām*) refers to those [other accomplishments]. The word "is explained" (*nirūpayati*) means it is demonstrated. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. The word "because" (*yasmāt*) indicates the reason. The word "within the accomplishment of the supreme state" (*paramasiddhyantarbhūtatvāt*) means being included within the accomplishment of the supreme state. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) indicates the consequence. The word "no separate enumeration" (*na pṛthaggaṇanā*) means there is no distinct counting. "Within one's own self" (*svātman*) refers to those perfections (*siddhis*). He demonstrates that they are included within this [state] by saying "within one's own self. The meaning is that those perfections are well-established as being achievable solely through a portion of the means for attaining knowledge (*jñāna-sādhana*). || 110 ||

These [doctrines] serve as obstacles to the practice of the knowledge of the Self; what is the purpose of those [other systems], which are equal to a magical illusion or the attainment of a phantom self? (111)

If it is asked, "In that case, why are these accomplishments (*siddhi*) not seen among those who possess knowledge? he says: "By the science of the Self" (*ātmavidyā*). Upon the application—that is, the attainment—of the science of the Self, these accomplishments serve as the instigators or causes of an obstacle (*antarāya*, *vighna*). Therefore, for those with an intense desire for liberation (*tīvramumukṣu*), they do not [arise] because they take the form of obstacles.
The meaning is "engagement. If it is asked, "Why is there no engagement in such things that yield great fruits? he says:

"What is gained by them? By those insignificant accomplishments, such as the power of moving through the air (*khecaratva*) and so forth—which are like magical illusions (*indrajāla*)—is the desired goal called liberation (*mokṣa*) attained? It is not attained.
This is the meaning. || 111 ||

For one for whom even the state of Brahmā itself would be regarded as equal to a blade of grass, how insignificant are these supernatural powers (*siddhis*), which are merely causes for the wasting away of time? (112)

If it is asked, "Whence is this [attainment] supramundane, and why even such things as the power of moving through the air (*khecaratva*) are not desired?", he says: "Of whom" (*yasya*). For one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), the state of Brahman (*brahmapada*)—that is, the world of truth (*satyaloka*)—is attained directly; this is the ellipsis. It is "equal" (*saṃmita*) to that [liberation]. For him, these supernatural powers (*siddhi*) are merely obstacles to other forms of knowledge and are causes for the wasting away of time. || 112 ||
Therefore, no other accomplishment can exist than the accomplishment of the knowledge of the Self,
by which there shall be the destruction of ultimate sorrow and the attainment of intense bliss.

Therefore, because it is trivial, there is no other [result] superior to the establishment of consciousness; this is the meaning. If one asks "Why?", he states the unique fruit of knowledge with the words "yayā" (by which). This means by the establishment of knowledge. "Ānandasāndratā" means the state of having bliss as its sole essence. || 113 ||
That alone is the true accomplishment, and no other, for it liberates one from the devouring jaws of death.
This accomplishment of self-knowledge arises through various distinctions in practice. (114)

She alone is the bestower of such fruits. "Swallowing" (grāsa) refers to the devouring by Death; the sense is that liberation from that is not [attained] through any other supernatural power (siddhi). Having thus defined *siddhi*, he begins to describe its ripening (*pāka*) in the form of fullness with the words "this" (*iyam*). [This occurs] due to the gradations resulting from the differences in practice (*abhyāsa*). || 114 ||
Due to the distinctions in the purity of the intellect and due to the distinctions in its maturation, the summary [of the lineage] is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior. (115)

Regarding the term "buddhi": due to the degrees of practice and the clarity of the intellect (*buddhinairmalya*), the ripening of the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*) is also manifold, distinguished as superior, middling, and so forth.
The accomplishment of knowledge consists in the direct intuitive awareness (*pratyakṣavimarśana*) of the self as the pure consciousness-form transcending the body and other such [limitations].
The meaning is that its practice is a specific stage of maturation corresponding to a continuous stream of reflective awareness in a single form. || 115 ||
In this world, the sages among the twice-born are those whose learning accords with the recited Vedas;
through their intelligence and great practice, they are engaged in hundreds of activities. (116)

To explain this very point, he states an illustration: "In the world," etc. "O Sages" is an address. "That which is recited by the twice-born"—meaning the Veda that has been properly retained through memorization and study—"is equal to it," meaning identical to it. He describes the threefold nature of the recited Veda with the word "medhayā": [it is] possessed of retention (*dhāraṇā*).
The meaning is "by means of the intellect. Practice consists of forms such as repetition and so forth. || 116 ||
Even that supreme Vedic revelation which has been recited with unerring phonemes—
whether by one who is concentrated in his practice or at another time by one who is not so concentrated.

"Api" means: that Vedic recitation (*śruti*) which, held by one of exceeding intelligence through intense practice, remains free from errors in syllables—even while performing many activities during the time of recitation despite being crowded with hundreds of other tasks—is the best. "Syllable" (*varṇa*) is an elliptical expression for "vowel" (*svara*) as well; that recitation which is performed without any inversion of syllables or vowels is the superior one. This refers to the time of [actual] recitation.

That which is unimpeded when one is not in a state of meditative concentration—meaning when the mind has not yet reached the sequence of stages attained through hearing—is the intermediate [level]. (117)
Just as before, the middle tone (madhyamā-śruti) should be recited without faltering;
for it should always arise precisely through the yoga of continuous mental application.
As before, that hearing which is unerring regarding phonemes and so forth—due to the application of mental synthesis and precisely because of being concentrated—is likewise unerring. 118.
The recitation of the Śruti that is entirely free from error is indeed the lowest (or, according to *k*: the middling);
in this very manner, O three sages, the accomplishment of the knowledge of the Self has been declared.
The inferior [view]. Having established the illustration, he applies it to the subject of the illustration with the words "in this very same way" (evameva). || 119 ||
That which, in great transactions, is either always connected when there is an absence of connection, or is always connected even when that [connection] is absent; || 120 ||

That which is the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*) is the state of abiding in knowledge (*jñānasthiti*). This occurs even while engaged in great worldly activities (*mahāvyavahāra*), such as the duties of governing a kingdom; even when there is an absence of meditative absorption (*samāhitatva*) due to the avoidance of mental synthesis (*pratisandhāna*); and at other times when there is an absence of activity and the avoidance of mental synthesis, or indeed when mental synthesis is present at all times—therein lies the state of being neither deficient nor excessive.
The logical connection is "it might be. || 120 ||
It may be without deficiency or excess, and thus it is classified as superior, middling, or inferior;
herein, the superior alone is described as the supreme pinnacle of perfection.

"Anyūnā" (not deficient) means that there is a single uniformity due to the absence of forgetfulness and so forth; this is the intended meaning. That attainment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*) is, for the three [types of practitioners], respectively superior, middling, and inferior. Among these three attainments of knowledge, the superior alone is the ultimate pinnacle of the attainment of knowledge. 121.
Even in states such as dreaming,
when there is the supreme state which is equal to the very moment of discernment, that is the most excellent accomplishment.

Having thus described the supreme pinnacle of the attainment of knowledge through illustrations, he further explains this very same point by way of different methods for the sake of knowing its attainment within oneself and in others, beginning with the words "In a dream," and so forth.
By the word "first" (*ādya*), the state of external conceptualization is meant; it is similar to the moment of investigation (*vicārakṣaṇa*).
By abandoning the sense of "I" with respect to the body and so forth, it takes the form of the sense of "I" as pure consciousness alone. 122.
When, through the conscious cultivation of effort in all worldly transactions,
one's activity proceeds toward perfection, that is declared to be the supreme limit.

If activity were to occur spontaneously, the latent impression (saṃskāra) would not be awakened; rather, activity occurs through the awakening of the latent impression by one's own effort, as in the case of acquired knowledge (āhāryajñāna). || 123 ||
When stability in the supreme self of pure consciousness is achieved effortlessly and remains unimpeded, then perfection has reached its ultimate limit.

"Effortlessly indeed": for just as worldly people have external activity effortlessly, so too there is an unimpeded and uninterrupted state within the supreme self of consciousness, which is undivided by the body and other such limitations. 124.
One who is intent on worldly activity does not see, even while seeing entities;
for when duality [disappears], that is indeed the perfection attained to fullness.

Having thus explained the manner [of practice] for the sake of the knowledge that constitutes the supreme limit of the accomplishment of knowledge regarding one's own state (*svagata*), he speaks regarding the knowledge regarding the state of others (*paragata*) as follows: "In conventional discourse... Even while perceiving entities, he does not perceive duality.
The occasional impairment of conventional discourse resulting from the non-perception of duality can indeed be known by others.
When one acts even during waking and other states as if asleep,
that indeed is the state of perfection, having attained fullness.
Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of waking" and so forth: because of the interruption of the connection between the preceding and succeeding moments, one remains as if asleep. || 126 ||
Having thus attained perfection, he is called the best among the perfected ones;
though constantly engaged in worldly affairs, he never abandons meditative absorption.
He answers the final question, which is the primary one, with the word "thus" (*evam*).

Having attained the perfection of knowledge whose nature is the aforementioned supreme limit (*parākāṣṭhā*), he further explains this in many ways because it is the subject matter of the primary question, [beginning with] the words "in worldly practice" (*vyavahāra*). Even for one intent on worldly practice, it is not...
The meaning is "the interruption of meditative absorption. || 127 ||
At all times, that wise one is considered the best among those who have attained perfection;
he always understands the state of various types of knowers.
The connection is that [the mind] never lets go. One who is intelligent (medhāvī) possesses such excellence of retention;
he knows the state of the various [objects], whether superior, middling, or otherwise, which exist at all times. || 128 ||
By virtue of his own direct experience within himself, he is considered the best among the perfected ones (siddhas),
for in him there is not even a trace of doubt or desire.
"By one's own experience" means by the experience of the existence of all things residing within oneself, according to the maxim: "Do not avoid the feet of a snake [thinking it is a rope].
"Doubt" refers to the fact that the ignorance which is its root has been destroyed; this is the intended meaning. || 129 ||
He who is fearless amidst worldly affairs is considered the best among those who have attained perfection; for all pleasure, all pain, and all worldly activity [are but his play]. 130.

"Fearless" means that there is an absence of concern regarding loss, gain, and so forth; this is the intended sense. "Worldly activity" refers to actions such as seeing, touching, and the like, which pertain to the world. || 130 ||
He recognizes [the Self] within his very own self; he is considered the best among the perfected ones (siddhas). He perceives the self, though extremely bound, as liberated. (131)
"Regarding 'in one's own self' (*svātmani*): because one's own self is known as the substratum for the reflections of worldly activity, like a mirror.

Regarding 'absolutely' (*atyanta*): because one's own self is known as the nature of universal consciousness (*sāmānyacidrūpa*), one perceives every bound and liberated individual soul (*jīva*) as having attained identity with one's own self; for that [Self], being the thread running through all things, is the Self of all."
He who is the Self of all within his own self is considered the highest among the perfected ones (siddhas), he who always clearly perceives the nets of bondage within his own self. (132)

Although he perceives within himself the bondage of all living beings—since he is the self of all and the substratum of all—he does not seek liberation, because he is certain of their unreality. || 132 ||
He does not seek liberation anywhere; he is considered the best among the Siddhas.
"I alone am the supreme Siddha here; there is never any difference between us. (133)
Somewhere, at some time, he praises the Supreme Siddha—namely, the "Supreme Siddha"—in this world. || 133 ||
This has indeed been declared very clearly by me in response to your inquiry;
having understood this which I have spoken, one is never deluded anywhere.
"He brings this together" means: it is the answer to the questions. "By one who is questioned" means by one who has been asked.
"People do not become deluded. || 134 ||
Having spoken thus, O descendant of Bhṛgu, that supreme knowledge became silent;
and having heard all this, the sages cast away their doubts. (135)
He concludes the Vidyāgītā with the words "ity uktvā" (having said this). "Apahāya" means having abandoned or left behind. || 135 ||
Having bowed to Śiva and the other lords of the world, they went each to his own abode.
This Vidyāgītā, which destroys the multitude of sins, has been told by me to you.
"Niveśana" means a place of abiding. He praises the *Gītā*: "The destroyer of the flood of sins. That which has been heard and understood in its meaning destroys the multitude of evils. || 136 ||
This most excellent Gītā of Knowledge, which bestows the empire of one's own self when heard and properly reflected upon, is the direct manifestation of Knowledge itself. (137)

Having been further investigated through reflection and made heart-felt, liberation—whose nature is the empire of one's own self consisting of perfect bliss—is superior to other Gītās. The reason for this is that it is "direct knowledge" (sākṣād-vidyā). This is because [in other Gītās], Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others who expound them appear as embodied beings.
It should be understood that this is because equality is impossible. || 137 ||
To those who recite it daily, she herself, being pleased, bestows knowledge;
for those sinking in the ocean of the darkness of saṃsāra, it shall become a boat. 138.
He says "for those who read" because even for those who are incapable of understanding, there will be a gradual fruit through the grace of the knowledge (*vidyā*) simply by reading it;
he calls it "the savior" (*tāraka*) because it delivers those submerged in the ocean of darkness consisting of ignorance, which is the cause of *saṃsāra*.
(-) Regarding "saṃsāra": it means a boat for crossing over, or the sun. || 138 ||
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Song of Wisdom," in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
Thus, according to my understanding, this Vidyā has been sung and explained by me in due order;
may it be perfectly offered at the lotus feet of Śrīvidyā.
Where am I, dull-witted and unlearned in song, and where is this profound intention?
This effort is for the sake of purifying my own self; how could it have arisen from association with others?
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the commentary on the Vidyāgītā, in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
Having heard these words spoken by the sage Dattātreya, Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, became as if already liberated from the delusion of the net of ignorance. || 1 ||
In this regard, for those who have entered the path, the primary means of attaining knowledge—
the definition and the true nature of the scripture— have been declared in the form of questions and answers.
He introduces the question of Bhārgava with the words "Having heard thus," etc. He says "as if liberated" because a remainder of doubt still exists. || 1 ||
Having bowed once more with great devotion, he asked the son of Atri something further:
"O Blessed One, please explain the well-determined means for attaining consciousness."
He asked something. || 2 ||
That which is essential, easily attainable, and directly bestows fruit, as well as the characteristics of the wise, by means of which I may quickly recognize them. (3)
If it is argued that the means of accomplishment has already been explained previously, he says: "The essence," and so forth; [referring to] those who possess knowledge.
How is it that the minds of the wise remain unattached even while they maintain their composure during the union with and separation from the body, and likewise while engaging in worldly activities?
"Dehasaṃyoga... and so forth.

For the wise who perform worldly activity through the medium of the body, there is an "unattached" state—meaning free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—regarding the conjunction and disjunction with the body, or the appearance and non-appearance of the body. || 4 ||
"You ought to explain all of this clearly to me out of great compassion.
Thus was the son of Atri questioned by the son of Jamadagni.
All this, beginning with the means of accomplishment (sādhana), [is thus established]. || 5 ||
Being satisfied, the ocean of compassion spoke, addressing Bhārgava:
"Listen, O Rāma, I shall proclaim the secret means for attaining knowledge."
He was satisfied by the correct question, which was imbued with devotion; [he then spoke] the secret, which is not well-known in the scriptures.
The primary means for attaining knowledge is the supreme grace of the deity, which belongs to one who has approached the deity that is one's own self with total devotion. (7)

The supreme favor (*anugraha*) is the acceptance [of the devotee] as one's own, thinking: "This person is my most devoted follower; this desire of his must certainly be fulfilled. He states the cause for such favor: "with all his being" (*sarvabhāvataḥ*), meaning through speech, mind, and action. "Approached" (*upasaṅgataḥ*) means having properly attained proximity.

The intended meaning is that he is one who constantly does not abandon the contemplation of the deity; being solely intent on the practices of recitation and meditation, he [worships] his own Self as the deity abiding within him as the inner controller.
It is certain that for such a person, knowledge becomes very easy to attain;
O Rāma, this has been declared as the supreme means for attaining knowledge.
For one who is devoted to the aforementioned deity, this constitutes devotion to the deity as proclaimed in the secret scriptures. (8)
This alone, independent of anything else, is capable of accomplishing the fruit;
setting this aside, nothing else here can properly grant the result.

He establishes its state as the most supreme with the words "anyat" (other). This refers to being intent upon that [the goal]. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis, meaning "this alone. "Kṣamaṃ" means capable. This refers to being intent upon that. "Anyat" means other [practices] such as hearing and so forth. These do not grant the complete fruit. Without the grace of the deity, mere hearing and so forth do not culminate in the fruit.
The meaning is that knowledge would not arise. || 9 ||
Listen here, O Rāma, to the reason for this; it shall be explained with its underlying cause.
That which is pure consciousness—the absolute awareness that illuminates everything—[is the cause]. (10)

In this context, it means that without grace (*anugraha*), there is no fruit; rather, this [grace] necessarily results in the fruit as its primary aim. "With cause" means accompanied by visible causes. He establishes this very point with the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*):
consciousness is the result. It is the universal, absolute consciousness (*citi*) which illumines everything. (10)
As for that imagined obscuration which belongs to its nature as light, its true nature is indicated by the removal of that [obscuration] through investigation. (11)
If it is asked how that [consciousness], which is of the nature of self-luminosity, can be the fruit, he says: "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*).
The *sandhi* (euphonic combination) is archaic (*ārṣa*). [It refers to] that which is called the obscuration of ignorance (*avidyā*), imagined by the sovereignty of consciousness itself.
Through investigation in the form of hearing and so forth, by the removal—that is, the destruction—of that obscuration, [there is the attainment] of that pure consciousness.
The recognition "That am I" would be the indicator of one's own true nature. || 11 ||

And that [attainment] is very difficult for others who are intent upon external things; it is easily obtained by devotees through the abandonment of intentness on other matters and by being intent on Him alone. || 12 ||
And that [is] both the essential nature and the indicator; by the word "and" (ca), [he implies] the fruit, such as abiding in the absolute Self alone.
If it is asked how this is easily accessible to those devoted to the deities, he says: "for the devotees. || 12 ||
It is indeed certain that [the goal] becomes easily attainable and quickly reached;
for one who is thus devoted to the deity, even with very few other means of accomplishment, [success follows]. (13)
Regarding the word *sulabham* (easily obtained): for those whose minds are turned outward, being intent on external things such as the wealth of women and so forth, it is difficult to obtain;
however, for those intent upon their own Self as the deity, because their minds lack outward orientation, it is easily obtained—this is the sense.
He explains the sequence of the arising of knowledge and its fruit through its very ease of attainment for one who is devoted to the deity, starting with the word *devatā*. Thus:
Having become intent upon the deity through the actions of speech, mind, and body, he possesses even the slightest and temporary means of practice such as detachment and the like. || 13 ||
Having somehow realized the Self, one should describe it to others;
O Rāma, by constantly describing it, one shall attain complete immersion (samāveśa).
In some way, whether indirectly or directly; others who desire to know; always, at all times; absorption—that is, the state of the mind taking on that [object's] form. || 14 ||
Thus, when absorption through investigation and the other means has become firm, that mind, having attained the state of Śiva, is devoid of both joy and agitation. (15)

Thus, for one whose mind is thus absorbed through investigations and the like—that is, through the contemplation of the essential nature of investigation—the firmness of absorption consists in the effortless attainment of the mind's conformity to that [divine] form. This results in the state of Śiva, which is the singular nature of the pure conscious self; for this very reason, it is devoid of joy and agitation. (15)
Wherever he goes, that which is there he makes over to Śiva;
thus does the possessor of supreme wisdom, established in the state of one liberated while living, act. || 16 ||

Wherever anything is perceived, that mind renders all that perception subject to Śiva, making it one with the form of Śiva alone. The sense is that even in connection with the perceived object, it does not abandon its nature as the conscious self. || 16 ||
Therefore, through the yoga of pure devotion, this further description for others is the most excellent means; there is nothing else equal to it.

Therefore, because such a great fruit is obtained in this manner, this is equal to the investigation into the reality of one's own self (svātmatattva) performed with devotion and total dedication to the deity. || 17 ||
O Rāma, there is no other means equal to devotion for defining [the truth];
indeed, the characteristics of the wise are difficult to discern.
To state the answer to the second question, he says: "Of the knowers" (jñāninām). || 18 ||
Since that is the innermost of all, it is beyond the reach of the eyes, speech, and other senses; it can never be defined or characterized by others in any way.

Because the Knower abides in the form of pure consciousness alone, His true nature is within everything, including the body and so forth. For this very reason, he says "not with the eyes," etc.; and for this very reason, he says "not to be defined," meaning not to be known as possessing defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). || 19 ||

Just as one's mastery of the scriptures is not recognized anywhere in the world by others, so too one's [inner state] is not perceived by others through the body, clothing, ornaments, and the like. (20)
Here is an illustration: "Just as," [it is said], "the state of being a knower is not perceived. (20)
For wisdom is indeed to be known only through self-awareness and not otherwise, just as the capacity to perceive the taste of a relished flavor is known, O Bhārgava. (21)

He says "learnedness" (*vidvattā*) to show that just as the knowledge of sweet and other tastes is to be known solely through one's own experience, so too is the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*). "Taste-related" refers to the state of being a knower of taste. || 21 ||
Nevertheless, it is indeed perceived by the clever and learned through their speech and other means,
just as one's own path is known by tiny ants.
"Even so" (tathāpi) means even though it is difficult to discern. [One discerns] the speech, the serenity of the face, and other such qualities of that knower (jñānin).

Here is the illustration: "Just as" (yathā). Just as the path of tiny ants is known only by them, the characteristic of a knower is to be known only by a knower; this is the intended meaning. || 22 ||
There are indeed many coarse signs, but they are not definitive;
there are others that are subtle signs, which are truly difficult for others to discern.
If it is objected that there are coarse characteristics such as tranquility (*śānti*) and so forth, [the author] says "they exist" to show that these are fallacious;
"by others" means by those who are ignorant. || 23 ||
Indeed, it is observed that defining, speaking, and likewise demonstrating the means of proof can be performed by others just as they are by those possessed of knowledge. (24)
He establishes the deviation of those characterized by gross signs with the words "examination," and so forth.

The "simulation" (*abhinaya*) of the means, such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the like, is the wearing of its outward marks for the purpose of showing them to others—by other ignorant, hypocritical people. (24)
That means of knowledge which, when practiced by those with impure internal organs,
becomes firmly established for them— that is proclaimed as its defining characteristic.

If it is asked, "Let them be; what are those coarse characteristics? he says: "stainless" (*anirmala*). The purport is that for those whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is stainless, the practice of the means to knowledge (*jñāna-sādhana*), such as dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, is not required. That means by which [the mind] becomes stable, that is, which remains steady without effort. || 25 ||
One who is unable to be distinguished by honor or dishonor, gain or loss, victory or defeat— one should know him to be the best among the wise.
He says that very thing: "of whom" (yasya). The intended meaning is that for whom there is no specific change such as a brightening of the face and so forth due to honors and the like. || 26 ||
When questioned regarding discourses on the experience of his own self, even concerning its hidden meaning, the best among the wise should respond instantly and without hesitation. (27)

The hidden meaning, such as the experience of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth, [is understood] instantly, without even reflecting. For it is well known that in the description of an experienced object, there is neither doubt nor delay of time. || 27 ||
Indeed, he who possesses an intense enthusiasm for the accounts of knowledge, and who shows no aversion toward its investigation—that is truly the characteristic of a knower. (28)
In the determination of the process of knowledge, non-aversion is the state of being oriented toward it. || 28 ||
One who is by nature free from worldly undertakings, contented, pure in mind, and tranquil even in the midst of great calamities—he shall be the most excellent among the wise. (29)

Non-undertaking is non-engagement; by nature, that is, without effort. The mind’s lack of outward orientation is purity of mind, being free from desire and the like. One whose self is peaceful is devoid of agitation. || 29 ||
O best of the Bhārgavas, these and other such marks are undoubtedly firm indicators for the wise when examining their own selves. (30)
By the word "etcetera," non-attachment to the visible world and so forth are meant. When examining one's own state of being a knower (*jñānitva*), these signs are firm and unerring;

however, it is impossible to distinguish whether these belong to another as superimposed or not superimposed. Therefore, the sense is that they do not constitute the characteristics of another's state of being a knower. || 30 ||
The practitioner, however, should always be intent upon the examination of his own self, just as one who is skilled in the examination of another applies himself to that task. (31)
If it is objected that self-examination is indeed useless, he says "no": "the practitioner" (*sādhaka*). This means one who is skillful, being adept at investigating subtle matters. || 31 ||
Thus examining oneself, how could one not attain perfection?
For when one is intent on not considering the virtues and faults of others, [one attains it]. (32)
"How could he not attain it? means that he will certainly attain it. He states the method of examination with the words "when" (*yadā*).
The sense is that for one who is intent on investigating the virtues and defects of others, there will be no reflection upon his own virtues and so forth. || 32 ||
One should be intent on investigating one's own virtues and faults;
then, through the attainment of all means of accomplishment, one will reach perfection.

"Devoted to reflection" means intent on reflection. When that reflection upon qualities and defects has been performed, he will attain perfection through the abandonment of defects, the acquisition of qualities, and the fulfillment of the means for knowledge. || 33 ||
Thus have the characteristics of the wise been described, O descendant of Bhṛgu;
they are in every way useful for the examination of one's own self.
He summarizes the meaning that has been explained with the word "thus" (evam). || 34 ||
But these others are inconclusive when examined by others;
for, O descendant of Bhṛgu, those who possess knowledge have minds that are utterly pure.
These characteristics are non-exclusive and deviant. Previously, the deviation regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among hypocrites was stated;
now he states the deviation regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). This means: for which reason.
Their accomplishment is established by means of proofs that are successful only at first sight;
therefore, they are intent on activities that merely conform to their prior latent impressions.

As for those who, by their very nature, are devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of transgressive actions, even though they achieve knowledge through means that fall upon them at that moment, their previously established latent impressions of desire and so forth do not cease; consequently, they remain intent on their own worldly activities and behave like the ignorant. Since the aforementioned characteristics are absent in them, how can they [be considered liberated]?
The sense is that they are to be examined. || 36 ||
How are those who engage in common worldly affairs to be examined?
However, the wise, through the power of their practice, should perform that examination. (37)

Those whose worldly dealings are common and shared by all. He says, "But the wise," because it is possible for the wise to perform the examination of the wise; due to the power—that is, the majesty—of the practice of knowledge, [they can discern] from a mere superficial glance, just as jewel-examiners do.
For those of dull intellect, its abiding in the body is indeed like that of a fool.
The connection [of the sentence] is that they should perform an examination even from a mere superficial glance. Here is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): "Just as" (*yathā*).

For indeed, jewel-examiners (*ratnaparīkṣaka*), by virtue of the greatness of their excellence in the practice of familiarity with the true nature of jewels, perform an examination of jewels—determining whether "this is artificial" or "this is natural"—even upon a superficial glance; in the same way...

The meaning is "even for the wise. Having thus defined the characteristics of the knower, he describes their state as the answer to the third question, beginning with the word "manda" (insignificant). "Dehasaṃsthā" means identification with the body, the activity resulting from that, and its fruit; they are "mūḍhasamā," equal to the ignorant. || 38 ||
For as long as they have not attained innate samādhi, they remain incomplete in form while intent upon analytical investigation. (39)

If it is asked, "Why is it so?", he says: "Because... [The term] *sahaja* means occurring at all times. If it is asked, "In what way are they equal to the deluded?", he says: "As long as... [The term] *vimarśana* refers to the contemplation of one's own nature (*svarūpānusaṃdhāna*) of that which consists of the full form of pure consciousness alone. (39)
When they are averse to inquiry, then, because they consist of the body, they experience pleasure and pain and remain in a state of extreme similarity to beasts. (40)
Averse to reflection, they have abandoned further inquiry. || 40 ||
Even though they find satisfaction from time to time through the attainment of the state of fullness,
that state of theirs which belongs to the fettered (paśu) remains situated within the interval of true reflective awareness.

If it is objected that there can be no liberation from that knowledge because it is sublated, he says "no," [introducing the verse with] "In the middle. By means of the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the state of plenitude (*pūrṇadaśā*), they are "tranquil" (*nirvṛtāḥ*), meaning their torments of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) have perished.

He states that for them, the state of being a bound soul (*paśusthiti*) occurring in the interval between those states of plenitude does not lead to bondage, [with the words] "for them" (*teṣām*). 41.
It does not lead to bondage, remaining like a burnt rope;
for when the two ends of a cloth are well-dyed with lacquer solutions, [they do not bind]. (42)
