In this regard, there is an illustration: "burnt," etc. He establishes the absence of binding power during that state of being an animal with the words: "lac," etc. (42).
By pervasion, even the middle of his garment would become red with lac; in the same way, his worldly activity remains within the awareness of consciousness (cid-āmarśana). 43.

Regarding the word "by pervasion" (*vyāptyā*): just as if both ends of a cloth were thoroughly dyed with lac juice, the entire middle of the garment would become red with lac through that pervasion; in the same way, for that person of dull intellect, the worldly activity of the state of bondage (*paśudaśā*) situated within his contemplation (*anusandhāna*) becomes nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
The meaning is "for the sake of binding. || 43 ||
Having attained oneness with the Self whose nature is consciousness, it does not lead to bondage;
for those of middling realization, there is no connection with the body whatsoever. (44)
He describes the state of those with middling knowledge: "Middling," etc. (44).
The wise declare that the grasping of the body as the self is the conjunction with the body;
that, O Rāma, never exists for one who possesses intermediate discernment.
If it is asked, "How can there be no connection for one who possesses a body?", he says: "The body... That refers to the grasping of the body as the self.
Due to the excellence of his practice, his mind is indeed always absorbed;
with his heart perpetually concentrated, he has no worldly activity at all.

If it is asked, "Why not? he says: "Because of the dissolution of the mind" (verse 46). "Dissolved" means restrained by the abandonment of volitional constructions (*saṅkalpa*). This refers to that person of middling knowledge.
Even his maintenance of the bodily journey is like deep sleep;
just as someone situated in deep sleep remains in some place by means of mere latent impressions (vāsanā). || 47 ||

If it is argued that she possesses activities such as eating and so forth, [the author] states her lack of efficacy with the words "yaḥ" (who). If it is asked why this is so, he states, with an illustration, that it is because she is a mere appearance, using the words "yathā" (just as). *Vāsanā* is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). || 47 ||
Having said something and having done something, one does not later know anything at all;
just as one who is intoxicated by liquor does not truly know even while speaking and acting.
Another example (—): "Just as" (yathā) || 48 ||
In this way, this great yogin has transcended the worldly course of life;
even while performing some action at some time, he does not perceive it again.
The "course" (yātrā) is worldly activity; "gone outside of that" means devoid of it. He does not perceive again—that is, he does not mentally engage with it. || 49 ||
However, that body shall always persist due to the impressions of past actions (*prārabdha-vāsanā*);
for even one who is supreme and possesses perfect realization has no such body at all.

If it is asked, "In the absence of continuous reflection (*anusandhāna*), how can bodily activity be sustained?", he says: "By the *prārabdha*... *Vāsanā* means latent impression (*saṃskāra*). The sense is that just as a child engages in suckling milk through a latent impression awakened by the *prārabdha* [karma], so it is here. He describes the state of the superior [yogi] with the words: "But he who... (50).
This [consciousness] carries out worldly activity while remaining like a charioteer;
just as one performing the operation of driving a chariot is not the physical body of the chariot itself. (51)

If it is asked, "What then is the distinction of this from the former? he says: "Conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*). If it is asked, "How does it effect this? he says: "Like a chariot" (*ratha*). He demonstrates this very point with the words: "Just as" (*yathā*) || 51 ||
In this very way, the charioteer is one who is intent upon the activities of the body;
neither the embodied soul nor the activity itself is [the true self], for the self consists of pure consciousness.
"Not 'one who possesses a body' (dehī)"—the intended meaning is that one has abandoned the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding both the body and its activities. || 52 ||
Internally he possesses a pure and tranquil mind, yet externally he engages in worldly affairs,
just as an actor in a drama assumes a dual form while disguised in female attire.

"Internally" (*antar*) means extremely transparent (*atyaccha*), devoid even of a trace of the form of the visible; for this very reason, his inner self (*svānta*) remains perfectly established in its own essential nature alone. "Internally" refers to the vision of one's own self alone; "externally" (*bahiḥ*) refers even to the worldly perspective.
Such a person is the supreme knower (*uttamajñānī*). Here is an illustration: "Just as," namely, a man disguised as a woman. (53)
Just as a mature man, free from the faults of a child, plays with a playing boy, so too does he, whose intention is stainless, remain intent on the play of the world. (54)

An illustration regarding the absence of the fruit of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is given by the word "as follows" (*yathā*). He is devoid of joy and other emotions caused by victory or defeat associated with play due to that defect. This is the one of superior knowledge (*uttama-jñānī*).
(54) The one of middling knowledge (*madhya-jñānī*) is one whose state is immovable through the excellence of cessation (*nirodha*).
The immovable state of this discernment arises from its excellence. || 55 ||

He states the cause for the distinction between the positions of the middling and the superior [practitioners] with the words "middling" (*madhya*) and so forth. The excellence of cessation (*nirodha*) is its highest limit. For this superior knower, the excellence of discernment (*vicāra*) consists in its culminating in the fruit that takes the form of unshakable certainty. || 55 ||
The distinction between the middling and the superior [practitioners] arises from the ripening of their intelligence;
in this regard, listen as I relate to you a dialogue between two wise men. (56)
If it is asked, "Why is it that the state [of certainty] is differentiated by such a difference in the means of accomplishment? he says: "Of cognition" (*buddheḥ*).

The meaning is this: when defects such as error are slight in cognition, a determination free from doubt arises through mere investigation alone by means of some degree of suppression; however, when they are not slight, there is a requirement for a greater amount of suppression.

It should be understood that the answer to the question— how the mind of the wise remains unattached even during worldly activity— is essentially what has already been stated. Thus, because the attachment of one with dull knowledge is characterized by weak roots due to being interrupted by frequent intervals of self-inquiry, it is not firm.

Thus, the mind is unattached due to the absence of reflection upon those two [objects] and due to their weakened state. This is the dialogue that destroys all doubts, occurring in the context of the process of higher knowledge (vijñāna). 56.
In ancient times, there was a king named Ratnāṅgada, the lord of the mountains;
he resided in a city called Amṛtā along the Vipāśā river.
Along the Vipāśā, on the bank of the river Vipāśā, stood a city. || 57 ||
His two sons,
Rukmāṅgada and Hemāṅgada, were exceedingly wise and remained as very dear to Janaka as his own self.
The two wise ones possessed stainless discernment; they were beloved and dear. || 58 ||
Among them, Rukmāṅgada was indeed one who had reached the further shore of the scriptures;
Hemāṅgada, possessed of great discernment, became the foremost among the wise.
Both of them, surrounded by their entire armies,
went out and proceeded into the dense forest during the spring months for the sake of hunting.
Regarding the phrase "in the springtimes" (*vasanteṣu*): the plural number indicates many days. "Gahana" means a forest, a great wilderness (*mahāraṇya*). || 60 ||
There, having killed many deer, tigers, rabbits, and even buffaloes, they became utterly exhausted and reached a lake where they stayed.
a golden lake. || 61 ||
On the opposite bank of that lake, under a banyan tree, there is a Brahmarākṣasa who knows the essence of all the śāstras and debates extensively with learned men.
"He is staying in the nyagrodha, that is, the vaṭa tree"—this is the ellipsis. "Alam" means "excessively. || 62 ||
O Bhārgava, Rukmāṅgada, having heard from the mouth of a spy that they had been conquered, remained for a long time devouring them, being curious about their dispute.
The learned ones were conquered; the spies were those who brought news; having heard the conduct of the Brahmarākṣasa.
Having gone there accompanied by his brother, he became intent on debate;
he was defeated in those debates and seized by the Brahmarākṣasa.
There, in that region of the banyan tree, by that *brahmarākṣasa*. 64.
Then Rukmāṅgada, having seen that, spoke to Hemāṅgada:
"O Brahmarākṣasa, you ought not to devour him."
Rukmāṅgada has been captured; him, that Brahmarākṣasa; this, my brother. || 65 ||
"Having conquered me, his younger brother, you may then devour us both together.
Hearing Hemāṅgada's words, the Brahmarākṣasa replied:
"Indeed, you have taken me as your younger brother; we two are brothers."
For food has been obtained after a long time; hunger oppresses me.
Having broken my fast with this, I shall debate with you.
By this [act], your brother [performed] the breaking of the fast, which marks the completion of the fast. || 67 ||
"O King, my resolve is this: after I have conquered even you and devoured you, may I be thoroughly satiated by you. (68)
After a long time, this boon was obtained from the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
however, once a disciple of Vasiṣṭha arrived and was devoured.
This [verse] describes the attainment of a boon consisting of the devouring of the conquered one: "At some time... [etc. (69). Here, he who arrived was devoured by me.
He was cursed by that high-souled one with the name Devarāta:
"Henceforth, O Brahmarākṣasa, after devouring a human being from here..."
The disciple was named Devarāta. On account of his eating [the food], he spoke the manner of the curse: "From this moment, your face shall be burnt," said the sage to me later.
Then, having been entreated by me once more, he granted me an excellent boon. (71)
The grammatical connection is "thus cursed. After the curse was incurred, "bhūyaḥ" means many times. || 71 ||
"Devour all mortals who are defeated in debates from every side!"—thus, I then devour those who have been defeated in debate by him. (72)

He stated the boon itself [with the words] "in debates," etc.; the syntactical connection is that he thus granted the boon. "That" means for that reason. "Then" means immediately after that; the syntactical connection is that [the boon] was obtained. || 72 ||
"O King, this food which I have obtained after a long time is superior to all else;
having eaten it, I shall then defeat you in debate. (73)
Therefore, for that reason. || 73 ||
Having spoken thus, Hemāṅgada addressed him again as he was intent on devouring [him]:
"O Brahmarākṣasa, listen for a moment to my words, as I entreat you most earnestly. (74)
Tell me this: having obtained even something from him, do you abandon him?
If so, I shall give that very thing to you and release my brother.
Whatever little [there may be], having obtained that, give it to this brother of mine. || 75 ||
Thus addressed, that Brahmarākṣasa spoke again to the king:
"Listen, O King, there is nothing indeed by which I might release him. (76)
He says that there is nothing dearer than this: "Listen" (verse 76).
Who would renounce food, which is as dear as life itself, when it has arrived at the proper time?
However, I have one condition: there are questions residing within my heart. (77)
In that regard, the reason is: "What is *prāṇa*? [The word] "time" (*kāle*) means at the time of hunger. "Attained" (*upasaṅgatam*) means arrived.
"Agreement" (*samayaḥ*) means a promise. He states that very thing: "the question," and so forth. || 77 ||
"If they answer me, then I shall release your brother.
Thereupon Hemāṅgada said, "Ask them; I will speak with you. (78)
Those questions; by means of obtaining the answers to those questions; those questions. || 78 ||
Having been addressed thus, the Brahmarākṣasa questioned that prince with a series of cryptic questions; I shall relate them to you in due order, so listen, O Bhārgava. (79)
"Hidden questions" refers to questions that possess concealed answers. || 79 ||
O prince, tell me this: what would that be which is spread out from space and yet more subtle than an atom; what is its form, and where does it abide? 80.
He states those very questions: "From space," and so forth. That [inquiry] is in the form of what was asked. 80.
Listen, O Brahmarākṣasa: it is spread out from the sky to the earth, subtle down to the level of the atom, its form throbbing, and established within one's own self. 81.
He states the subsequent [verse] in sequence, beginning with "vitata" and so forth. *Citi* is the nature of Brahman, the universal consciousness.
Its subtlety arises from its being the innermost of all and its being beyond the reach of the senses. It is "established in its own self," meaning it abides in its very own essential nature. (81)
How can that which is singular and exceedingly vast become more subtle?
O Prince, tell me this: what is its nature of vibration, and what is its essence? (82)
How could it be both spread out and subtle, and yet one? || 82 ||
"O Brahmarākṣasa, listen: because it is the cause, it is pervasive; and because it is subtle and ungraspable, it is consciousness, the self, and the state of radiance. (83)

It is spread out through all-pervasive extension by virtue of being the material cause; because it is ungraspable, its radiance and its self are nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra). The intended meaning is that there is nothing beyond this. || 83 ||
What is the basis for perceiving that, or how is it perceived?
And what would be the purpose of such perception? Tell me this, O son of a king. (84)

Regarding the perception of that *cit*: how so? "How" is a question concerning the means (*sādhana*); "what" is a question concerning the result (*phala*). Intellect (*dhī*) is the locus; however, through one's own one-pointedness (*svaikāgrya*), it is perceived.
There can be no birth [of the object] through perception—listen, O Brahmarākṣasa! (85)

In the *suṣṭhu* (well) state, there is one-pointedness free from delusion through indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), characterized by the non-appearance of the form of the object. Alternatively, it is one-pointedness directed toward itself; that is, the attainment of the mind’s own nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) by abandoning the form of the object. By this, the "samādhi of the deluded" (*mūḍhasamādhi*) is excluded. || 85 ||
"What is this 'intellect' (dhī) that you have described? What is its one-pointedness like?
Or what might its birth be? Tell me this, O prince. (86)

The intellect (dhī) is consciousness (citi) veiled by inertia; one-pointedness (aikāgrya) is resting in one's own self. Birth is the notion that the body is the self—listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa! (87)

Inertia is the previously mentioned power of insentience called the Unmanifest (avyakta); it is repose within one's own self, characterized by a lack of orientation toward the objective world. || 87 ||
Why is consciousness not perceived, or by what is it perceived?
Or how has birth been attained? Tell me this, O son of a king. (88)
From what cause? By what instrument? || 88 ||
Due to lack of discrimination, it is not perceived; it is perceived by the Self.
Birth arises from the conceit of agency; listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa! (89)
"By oneself" means by one's own self, that is to say, independently of any other instrument. || 89 ||
What is this lack of discernment spoken of by you, and what might the self be?
Or what is this conceit of agency? Tell me this, O prince. (90)
"Non-discrimination is the lack of knowledge of their distinctness; ask your own Self regarding this within your own self.
That which arises from its latent impressions is conceit; listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa! (91)

Non-distinct knowledge (*apṛthagjñāna*) is the superimposition of identity. Regarding the phrase "the Self": the sense is that because it is difficult to define [in its own nature], because the means for perceiving it have already been stated, because it cannot be negated, and because it is of the nature of the immediate (*pratyak*), it can be known by itself alone. The latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the cognition "I am the agent" with respect to that [Self].
Formative force (saṃskāra). || 91 ||
By what is this lack of discrimination destroyed, and what indeed is its cause?
What, moreover, would be the cause of that? O prince, tell me this. (92)
Of that which destroys non-discrimination; and of its cause as well. || 92 ||
Through inquiry (*vicāra*), that [attachment] is indeed destroyed; detachment (*vairāgya*) is its cause (*kāraṇa*).
The cause of that is the perception of defects (*doṣadṛṣṭi*); listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa! (93)
The vision of the defects in sense objects. || 93 ||
What would be the inquiry, or what do they declare to be dispassion?
And what is called the perception of defects? Tell me this, O prince. (94)
Through the examination of the seer and the seen, there is the avoidance of the seen;
for that perception of suffering regarding the seen occurs—listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa! (95)

Investigation (*parīkṣā*) is the discernment of the true nature of the seer and the seen, preceded by the desire to know; that is *vicāra*. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the complete renunciation of that passion for the seen. The perception of the seen as a means to suffering is the vision of defects (*doṣadṛṣṭi*). || 95 ||
By what would all this come to be, or from whom is it obtained? What might be its cause therein? Tell me this, O prince. (96)
All this refers to investigation and so forth. By what means? By the nidāna, which is the root cause. || 96 ||
Through the grace of the deity, everything is indeed accomplished by means of devotion;
the primary cause is association with the virtuous—listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa. 97.
That is grace. || 97 ||
Who is declared to be the deity, and what is that devotion said to be? And of what kind are the virtuous said to be? Tell me this, O prince! (98)
Devotion to the Sustainer of the world is said to be the state of being intent upon that deity.
O Brahmarākṣasa, listen: the virtuous are peaceful and compassionate. (99)
The Mother of the World, the Ruler of the World; devotion to Her means being inclined toward Her. || 99 ||
"Who in this world is always afraid? Who is always overcome by suffering?
Or who is always possessed by wretchedness? Tell me this, O prince. (100)
O Brahmarākṣasa, listen: one who possesses a large family is always afraid of poverty, is miserable, seized by hope, and is perpetually wretched. (101)
"Who in this world could be fearless? Who could also be free from suffering?
And who could always be undepressed (or: never lacking)? Tell me this, O prince. (102)
Fearless, free from attachment, devoid of suffering, with a conquered mind, having known that which is to be known and possessing a noble self—listen, O Brahmarākṣasa! (103)
The knower is one who has known that which is to be known. || 103 ||
For who in this world would be imperceptible, and who is seen without a body?
What activity could there be for one devoid of action? Speak on this, O prince. (104)
Videha means devoid of a body. || 104 ||
For one liberated while living is difficult to perceive, being bodiless even while possessing a body;
his actions are said to be actionless—listen to this, O Brahmarākṣasa! (105)

This one who is liberated while living cannot be characterized by others; because of the absence of egoistic identification with bodily activity, the liberated-while-living is both bodiless and free from outward action. 105.
"What exists and what does not exist in the world? What could be absolutely impossible?
Having said this much, O King, quickly release my elder brother. (106)
These are the final three questions. 106.
The seer exists, but the seen does not; indeed, worldly transaction is impossible.
This has been said: O Brahmarākṣasa, release my brother quickly! 107.

The commonality of vision is pure consciousness. Precisely because of the absence of any object of vision, the possibility of any linguistic or practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) concerning it is non-existent. || 107 ||
Having heard this, the Brahmarākṣasa was then satisfied and released Rukmāṅgada;
thereafter, he indeed became a Brāhmaṇa once more.
This is the answer to the question: he was that Brahmarākṣasa. 108.
Seeing him radiant, an embodiment of asceticism, appearing in the form of a Brahmin, the two princes asked him in doubt, "Who are you? (109)
Seeing the Brahmarākṣasas in the form of Brāhmaṇas, the two became apprehensive and fell into doubt. || 109 ||
Then the foremost of brahmins spoke of his own conduct exactly as it was:
"In former times, I was a brahmin well-known throughout Magadha."
It is just as it is, existing exactly according to its true nature;
he is renowned for his qualities such as scholarship and the like. || 110 ||
Known as Vasumān, he was an expert in all the scriptures;
however, in assemblies, he was repeatedly defeated by me, who was proud of my learning.
Then, having defeated the sage Aṣṭaka in the assembly of the Lord of Magadha, that extremely arrogant man, though surrounded by hundreds of learned brahmins, [confronted him]. (112)
Seeking debate, I approached him who knows both the high and the low and who is perfectly tranquil;
I was one solely skilled in dry logic regarding the investigation of self-knowledge. (113)
Precisely because he knows both the higher and the lower, he is perfectly tranquil; yet, through his discernment, he has engaged in debate for the sake of the argument.
Then I rebuked him using only logical arguments; his reply, however, was full of conciliatory words and greatly reinforced by numerous scriptural citations. (114)
He was Aṣṭaka. || 114 ||
Having corrupted him with webs of sophistry, I became intent on reviling him;
yet, even though I reviled him in many ways while in the royal assembly, [he remained unperturbed]. (115)
Having also refuted the statement regarding composure, [the author states: "Adhikṣepa" means contempt or insult. || 115 ||
Then the disciple of that great-souled one became silent;
meanwhile, Kāśyapa had cursed me out of the power of his anger in the assembly of kings. (116)
Aṣṭaka is peaceful. 116.
"O lowest of the twice-born, you revile me, your teacher, at an improper time;
therefore, for a long period of time, you shall become a Brahmarākṣasa. (117)
"In an improper place," even in the absence of a cause for censure. || 117 ||
Having been cursed by him in this manner, I was then extremely terrified; trembling, I quickly bowed down to the sage and sought refuge with Aṣṭaka. || 118 ||
Trembling with fear of the curse, he was shaken. || 118 ||
Then, though I was his adversary, he became peaceful in mind and showed compassion toward me;
he granted me an end to the curse—listen as I relate it to you. (119)
The end is the limit of the release from the curse; that is the conclusion of the curse. || 119 ||
For when you have asked me questions and I have answered them,
and those answers are established solely by means of reasoning, then anyone at all will be able to provide a rebuttal.
One wise person [alone] has rendered those [objections] which were established by you defective in their responses, and thus left them without a reply. 120.
"O wise one, you shall then be liberated from that curse;
today, O prince, you are finally released from that curse after a long time."
"From that curse"—that is, from the curse of the eight disciples of that kind—"from you"—meaning from you. || 121 ||
"I consider you to be a great-souled one, who has known what is to be known, the best among men.
When addressed thus by that brahmin, the prince was filled with wonder. (122)
Therefore, for that reason. || 122 ||
Then, having been questioned by him in every respect, the prince,
after fully instructing Vasuman, returned to his own city.
Being questioned by that brahmin, he explained the matters correctly after being asked. || 123 ||
Having prostrated before that Vasumān together with his brothers and soldiers, [he said:
"O Bhārgava, all this which was asked by you has been related to you."
He summarizes this with the words "etad" (this). || 124 ||
[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Rākṣasa-episode of the Jñānakhaṇḍa within the glorious Tripurārahasya.]
[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Tātparyadīpikā, a commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Tripurārahasya.]
[Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Having heard this account of the Rākṣasa, Rāma, the scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage,
once again questioned the Lord of the Avadhūta family with humble devotion.
Here, the conduct of the wise has been described through verses employing metaphorical imagery,
and the reality of the process of knowledge has been explained with extreme conciseness.
He introduces the question of Bhārgava with the words "Having heard" (śrutvā). *Praśraya* means humility (*vinaya*). || 1 ||
O Blessed One, what did Hemāṅgada ask that twice-born man who was freed from the curse, and what did he say? Please tell me this out of compassion.
"I have an extreme curiosity in this matter; it cannot be a small thing.
Thus questioned, the compassionate Dattātreya spoke again: ||| 3 ||

Regarding the hearing of that conversation here, the reason for it is stated as "not that" (na tat). The meaning is that nothing spoken by such a highly learned Brahmin when questioned by the prince could ever be insignificant. || 3 ||
"O Rāma, I shall declare to you that which was spoken of great significance.
Then Vasumān questioned Hemāṅgada, who stood before him.
The prince replied while standing nearby. || 4 ||
"O Prince, I ask you something; please respond.
I learned that from the Lord of the Aṣṭakas from the very beginning."
That is the supreme reality of the Self; I have known it, I have understood it from the very beginning—at the outset. || 5 ||
Furthermore, through your words, the supreme state has been correctly understood;
however, how can such a condition as this belong to one who has realized the truth?
These [actions] are yours; this [conduct] consists of activities such as hunting and so forth. (6)

How can that which is easily understood through knowledge and yet devoted to worldly convention be known, such that the existence of both darkness and light could possibly occur in one and the same place? (7)
If it is asked what the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) here is, he says: "How?"—the ellipsis being "how could one be intent upon worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).
If it is argued that this might be possible for those who know the supreme reality just as it is for those who know the [mere] scriptures, he says "no":
"Just as the coexistence of darkness and light in one place is indeed contradictory."
The meaning is that this too could indeed be so. || 7 ||
"O prince, tell me this correctly as it truly is.
Thus questioned, Hemāṅgada spoke to that best of brahmins.
This mode of conduct is contradictory for one who possesses knowledge. || 8 ||
O Brahmin, even today your delusion has not been completely destroyed.
How can knowledge arising from one's own self be sublated by worldly convention?
"Completely destroyed" means utterly annihilated. If one asks why, it is said: "by way of worldly convention" (*vyavahāreṇa*).

Is there a contradiction with knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the Self by way of worldly convention? Or is there a contradiction with a specific kind of knowledge consisting of the recognition "I am the destroyer of ignorance"? Thus, the objection is formulated.

The universal reading [of the word] is not necessary, because its meaning is already conveyed by the word *uta*. Having thus raised the alternative, he says "not the first" (*nādya*), [asking]: "What knowledge is sublated?
That which has its existence or persistence in the form of its own self—[the question] "what" (*kim*) is used here as an interrogative particle (*ākṣepe*).
(Objection: The meaning is that [the self] is not afflicted. || 9 ||
If knowledge were sublated by virtue of conventional usage, then how could there be the attainment of the human goal, since it would indeed be equivalent to dream-cognition? (10)

If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says: "By conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*). If, by means of conventional usage, there were a sublation of knowledge that constitutes one's own true nature, then—just like dream-knowledge—that [knowledge] would be unreal.
Consequently, for a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) endowed with such a nature, their very essence would be destroyed; thus, for whom and how could there be the human goal known as liberation?
The state of being. || 10 ||
All this worldly transaction occurs by depending upon cognition;
yet that very cognition is sublated by it—explain to me how that can be so. (11)

Furthermore, since linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is dependent upon knowledge that constitutes its very nature (*svarūpa*), how can it be a sublater of that knowledge? To this he says: "All," etc. By that—namely, by linguistic usage mixed with [the notion of] self—that is, by the sublation of knowledge through linguistic usage. || 11 ||
Indeed, that alone is knowledge in which this world shines;
for all worldly activity arises from volition, and everything is manifested within knowledge. 12.

He states that, like reflections in a mirror, it is consciousness itself— constituting its own essential nature— that serves as the basis for all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*), by saying "consciousness" (*jñāna*). Furthermore, does the specific cognition that destroys the second [ignorance] (*ajñāna*) also terminate its own essential nature through worldly transaction?

Having raised the alternative that [the cognition] might either be the grasper of invalidity or not, he says "from conceptual construction" (saṅkalpāt) in order to refute the second [alternative], because since its own nature (svarūpa) is momentary, it does not depend on a sublater. This refers to the cognition which constitutes its own nature. 12.
By means of a mind free from conceptual construction, having once perceived that form [of the Self], one becomes fulfilled and liberated from bondage; this is a firm certainty. (13)

Regarding the phrase "by means of non-conceptualization" (*asaṅkalpena*): one's own true nature (*svasvarūpa*), which has become as if obscured by the worldly activity consisting of the appearance of rejection, acceptance, and so forth—arising from conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*) in the form of the mental representation of various words—is [revealed]. (g)

Having known one's own nature (*svarūpa*) as something indirect through hearing and other means, and having experienced it directly through the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) consisting of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*),
one then perceives it once with the intellect and recognizes it once as "I am that," thereby becoming one who has accomplished his purpose. And thus:
The sense is that because there is recognition of the form of the subsequent characteristic (*anulakṣaṇa*) even once, ignorance is destroyed; consequently, one is completely liberated from bondage.
Thus, since uncontradicted conceptual constructions do not arise again, the apprehension of invalidity does not arise. || 13 ||
"Therefore, O Brahmin, this question of yours is not approved by those of great intelligence.
Then Vasuman spoke again to that noble-minded prince:
"Therefore, since the absence of sublation by means of worldly convention is clear," having heard this, he spoke again. (14)
"It is true, O Prince, that this has been well-determined by me as well:
for here, self-nature is said to be non-conceptual awareness. (15)

"Thus," meaning according to the manner stated by you; nevertheless, he demonstrates that even when worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is carried out, error would necessarily arise, [in the verse] beginning with "the essential nature" (*svarūpa*). || 15 ||
Furthermore, when [the mind] has fallen into the state of conceptualization, how could there not be delusion?
For conceptualization itself is indeed delusion, just as the snake [is imagined] in a rope. (16)

Furthermore, regarding the term "error" (*bhrānti*): the meaning is that since linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is impossible without the conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) that delineates various forms (*ākāra*), there must indeed be error when a form—which does not exist in its own nature and is contradictory [to it]—appears.
He states that "error" is precisely the nature of the contradictory conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of the self, which is of the nature of cognition; thus he says: "conceptualization. From that...
If one asks why, he says: "Just as. The sense is that just as a snake in a rope brings about misfortune, so too does the appearance of conceptual construction bring about misfortune. || 16 ||
Listen, O Brahmin; you do not understand the determination of delusion and non-delusion. Even for those who know it, the sky appears blue—though there is no blueness in the sky.

He states the answer: "Listen. He says, "Listen," [and] "it is not an error," meaning that for those who have realized the truth, their conventional usage is not a delusion. He clarifies this very point by means of an example: "The sky...
Even for those who know that the sky is not blue... [verse 17].
And sometimes people employ the conventional expression "the sky is blue";
yet, merely because of that, such cognition is not called an error. (18)
At a certain time, by that mere conventional usage, that cognition of those who know the reality of space (*gaganatattvavedinām*)—namely, the cognition "the sky is blue"—[is established]. || 18 ||
For that [cognition] is an error for one who does not know reality, whereas for one who knows reality, it is indeed valid knowledge;
that cognition, its life-force being its validity, is like a great snake whose venom has been destroyed. (19)
In one who does not know reality—that is, one who is unacquainted with the true nature of the sky—there arises the cognition that "the sky is blue.

Now, if it is asked how a single type of cognition can take both the form of error and valid knowledge depending on the difference between persons, [the author] says "hatā" (struck), indicating that there is indeed a distinction between those two; for of cognitions...

Validity is the very life-force [of cognition], by virtue of which purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) arises. For instance, the cognition of a snake produces purposeful action such as fear and trembling. When the invalidity of that snake-cognition is apprehended through a contradictory cognition in the form "this is not a snake," then, because its life-force of validity has been destroyed, it is like a dead snake and no longer functions.

[The definition of validity is] the capacity to perform a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) arising from fear and so forth. And thus, for those who know the true nature of the sky, the cognition "the sky is blue"—whose very life of validity has been destroyed—lacks the capacity to perform a purposeful action;
therefore, by virtue of its distinction from the cognition of one ignorant of the true nature of the sky, it does not constitute an error. || 19 ||
The conventional usage regarding a reflection in a mirror is the same for both the one who recognizes it as such and the one who does not; nevertheless, there is a distinction between the two.

Regarding the term "mirror": for one who has realized the true nature of the sky, the conventional usage of the expression "the sky is blue" would be equivalent to the conventional usage of "this is an elephant" in the case of an elephant reflected in a mirror.
Therefore, whether one is familiar with the sky or not, the expression "the sky is blue" [is used].
There is a distinction between the two cognitions. || 20 ||
For the knower, that cognition is indeed valid knowledge; for the ignorant, however, it is of the nature of error.
For those who possess knowledge, every worldly transaction is indeed [the result of] knowledge. || 21 ||

"Of the knower" means that for one who knows the true nature of the sky (*gaganatattva*), it is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*); the sense is that there is no occurrence of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) prompted by error.
That cognition is the cognition "the sky is blue. He applies this to the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words: "for the knowers, it is indeed knowledge.
As stated previously, because its status as valid knowledge is destroyed [by the realization of the truth], it does not bring about any undesirable consequence.
The sense is that not every conventional transaction (vyavahāra), even if it exists, brings about the intended object. || 21 ||
It is comparable to the conventional usage of reflections in a mirror;
therefore, because of this recognition, no further arising of delusion occurs.

He states that the activity of the knower (*jñānin*) is equivalent to the activity of a reflection in a mirror (with the words beginning with) "darpaṇa. Therefore, because that [ordinary] activity is sublated, [he says] "of error" (*bhrānteḥ*).
The sense is that since the activity of the knower consists of mere knowledge (*jñāna-mātra*), it does not possess the nature of error. || 22 ||
That which is produced solely by ignorance is removed by knowledge;
but why would that which is produced by a defect dissolve through mere knowledge? (23)

If it is asked: "Just as the snake born of the ignorance regarding a rope ceases through the knowledge of that [rope], why does the visible object appearing [as real] not cease through non-dual knowledge arising from the ignorance regarding the non-dual Self?"—he replies with the word "kevalam" (only). Why would it dissolve? The meaning is: "it would dissolve. [This refers to] the knowledge.
The intended meaning is that there is an absence of being the cause for its dissolution. || 23 ||
For this very reason, even though he knows both, one afflicted by cataracts sees [two moons];
this appearance of the world, however, arises from the defect of karma. (24)
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). If it is asked, "What fault or cause is there in the arising of the world?", he replies:
"Karma" (*karman*). || 24 ||
Therefore, until the dissolution of karma, worldly activity does not cease;
once that karma is exhausted, the non-dual consciousness remains as the residue.

Therefore, because it cannot be destroyed by mere knowledge (*jñānamātreṇa*), when karma has been exhausted through the bestowal of its fruit upon completion, the nature of the Self—which is non-dual consciousness devoid of the appearance of the world—remains. This is because the world is rooted in karma, which arises from the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth, and that [sense of "I"] is rooted in ignorance (*ajñāna*). As for ignorance...

The intended meaning is that even though [the world] has ceased through knowledge, the world does not appear in its true nature solely because of the dissolution of the karma already set in motion. || 25 ||
"Therefore, for those possessed of discernment, there can never be the occurrence of delusion.
Having heard this, the brahmin questioned the prince once again.

Therefore, since conventional practice consists of mere cognition, there is no possibility of error [regarding the cognition of the sacrificial act], having heard that it is a non-dual appearance arising from the remainder of karma. || 26 ||
"O Prince, how can action be possible for the wise?
Even when touched by the fire of knowledge, how does the cotton of action remain? (27)
He raises an objection as to how there can be a remainder of karma for the wise, saying: "Ah! (verse 27).
Then Hemāṅgada, the prince, spoke to that brāhmaṇa:
"O Brāhmaṇa, listen; I shall explain the threefold action of the wise."
Now, following the question of the Brahmins: the connection is that for all knowers of reality, the threefold action would be the same. || 28 ||
For all [of these], the unripened and the ripened, as well as the "struck" (hata) and the "arisen" (udita), would be equal; therein, that which is not middling perishes through knowledge. (29)

He states their names: "unripe" (*apakva*). Karma is threefold: accumulated (*sañcita*), commenced (*prārabdha*), and being performed (*kriyamāṇa*). Among those, by means of knowledge, two [types] other than the commenced karma—which has reached its fruition—perish. || 29 ||
Time is the ripener of karmas, established as fixed by destiny;
it is said that a karma is "ripe" when it has been mostly ripened by time.

He analyzes their essential nature with the words "of actions," and so forth. Time—which consists of a sequential mass of activities regulated by *niyati* (the principle of necessity) in the form of the Lord’s volition, such that "the ripening of this action shall occur after such a duration of time"—is the ripener of actions. Regarding the phrase "mostly ripened": for when there is ultimate ripening, everything occurs simultaneously.
The intended meaning is that it must indeed be oriented toward the yielding of fruit. || 30 ||
Know that what was uncooked becomes cooked immediately upon the arising of knowledge;
and know that what was done or committed is destroyed because of the destruction of its origin through knowledge. (31)
"Unripe" (apācita) means that it is not fit for ripening even within the span of a man's lifetime; this refers to karma performed immediately [after death].
He explains the etymological significance of the name by saying "destroyed" (hata): the meaning is that [the karma] arises because its power to yield fruit has been destroyed by knowledge. || 31 ||
In that regard, karma that has reached maturity is said to be "commenced";
like an arrow released from a bow, it remains until it yields its fruit. (32)
"It remains indeed" means that it is not destroyed by knowledge; this is the sense. || 32 ||

The manifestation of the world, which is rooted in that [nescience], remains—despite being equal to an illusion due to the gradations of knowledge—not an actual illusion, because of the difference in its results. (33)

"Rooted in that" means rooted in *prārabdha-karma*. He says "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*) to explain how that manifestation of the world remains for the wise—such as those who are superior and so forth—due to the uniformity of the ripening of their knowledge; [he asks] "from what cause is there no delusion? [The answer is: "from gradation," in the form of being dull, very dull, and so forth. Why is there no delusion?
If it is asked why, he says: "Because of the difference in results. This means because of the difference in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). || 33 ||
That produces a clear result at that very time for those of dull intellect;
for those of middling intellect it is not clear, yet for the wise it is the manifestation of the fruit.
He describes, in sequence, the very difference in the fruits of the manifestation of the world for those of dull, middling, and superior knowledge:
"it would produce. At its own time, the manifestation of the world would produce a fruit in the form of pleasure and so forth for those of dull knowledge.
For those of middling knowledge, that manifestation of the fruit exists at the time of the world’s manifestation just as it does for those of dull knowledge.
But that [state] is indistinct; its nature is like the pleasure and pain arising from the bite of a mosquito or a gentle breeze during light deep sleep—this is the sense. || 34 ||
But for the most excellent ones, O Brahmin, there is both the fruit at that very moment and its clear manifestation;
yet that which is like a hare's horn is not said to have such a fruit.

For the supreme knowers, however, at the time when the world is being incinerated, even though results such as pleasure appear clearly from the perspective of others, they are equal to the horns of a hare from their own perspective; therefore, it is said that those are not their results. || 35 ||
For the ignorant, the fruit of karma is nourished through prior mental continuity;
yet that fruit is further nurtured by them through the connection between what precedes and what follows.

Having thus stated in general the distinction in the results appearing as the world for those possessing knowledge, [the author] now speaks first of the manner of the result for the ignorant in order to further describe this very point in detail: "of the ignorant" (*ajñāninām*).
This is an elaboration of the term "nourished" (*puṣṭam*) from the previous context; [this is indicated by] "previous," etc., because of the arrival of happiness.

Because of long-term recollection— thinking "such happiness will be mine in the future" and "such happiness was experienced by me in the past"— it becomes nourished in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*),
and remains within as that which gives rise to passion and other afflictions. || 36 ||
For the wise, attachment to the fruit [of action] is severed through constant contemplation of the Self;
therefore, the fruit produced by prārabdha-karma does not nourish the dull-witted.

For those who are dull-witted, even though they possess knowledge, the contemplation of its fruit is interrupted from time to time due to their lack of self-contemplation; therefore, unlike that of the ignorant, it does not become fully nourished. || 37 ||
And for those of middling knowledge, that fruit [of action] exists in states of dull sleep;
it has become subtle, like the pain caused by a mosquito or similar insect. || 38 ||
For those of middling knowledge who always possess the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*), during the states when they are separated from that absorption,
the pleasure or pain resulting from the fruits of past actions (*prārabdhaphala*) becomes subtle, like the slight pain or pleasure caused by a mosquito or a gentle breeze during deep sleep. || 38 ||
For those of supreme wisdom, that fruit remains full even though it has already been [attained];
by the power of the knowledge of the abiding Self, it becomes like a burnt rope. 39.

To those of supreme wisdom who possess external meditative absorption (*bāhyasamādhi*), from the perspective of others, this [world] appears as the fruit of the manifestation of the visible (*dṛśyābhāsa-phala*). Although it remains fully present as being fit for conventional usage—such as "this person is happy" or "this person is suffering"—from the perspective of [the sage's own] vision of happiness and so forth, it becomes like a burnt rope. If one asks why this is so, he says:

Regarding the word "sthitā" (established): for one of middling knowledge, the contemplation of one's true nature (*svarūpānusandhāna*) is interrupted by a lapse from meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
however, for the superior one, it becomes like a burnt rope due to the greatness of the state of self-knowledge, which consists of constant contemplation—this is the intended meaning. || 39 ||
Just as a man in the course of a drama, having assumed another costume, may experience joy or sorrow without undergoing any internal transformation; || 40 ||

He shows the manner in which the possessor of supreme knowledge experiences that bliss and so forth with the words "as follows" (yathā). "Another guise" (veṣāntaram) means the guise of a woman. "Rejoicing and desponding" refers to acting out [the roles of] the birth of a son, separation from a husband, and so on. || 40 ||
Thus, this one who abides in knowledge, being endowed with the perfectly full fruit, is not touched by fruits; therefore, that fruit is like the horn of a hare.
Though rejoicing at the worldly attainment of a kingdom or grieving at the death of a son and so forth,

even when attached to fully ripened fruits, he is not touched by them because of his firm conviction that everything is nothing but his own Self; since there is no second entity apart from the fruit, he does not possess the conceit of a connection with results.
This is the intended meaning. || 41 ||
Indeed, the pure self is not perceived at all by the ignorant;
therefore, they regard the body as the self, lacking investigation into the reality of what is seen. (42)

If it is asked, "How can those who are ignorant have the conceit of a connection with the fruits [of action]? the answer is: because, due to the absence of self-knowledge, they are certain of the reality of the perceptible world. Thus he says: "By the ignorant" (verse 42). Those who have identified their bodies with the Self, considering their own selves to consist of the body and so forth, are those for whom there is no critical inquiry into the unreality of the perceptible world.
Although the self is known by those of dull intellect to consist of pure consciousness, and the world is seen as unreal, nevertheless, this is due to the slowness of their practice. (43)

If it is asked how those of dull intellect experience the fruit [of their practice], [the author] says "those of dull intellect," explaining that it occurs because they occasionally forget the contemplation of the true nature (svarūpa) and consequently fall into the identification of the body with the self.
He states the cause of this forgetfulness as "due to the slowness of practice" (abhyāsamāndyataḥ). || 43 ||
Those whose knowledge was drawn forth by prior latent impressions (vāsanā) experienced, from time to time, the manifestation of the body as the self and the appearance of the world as real. (44)

Those whose knowledge—consisting of a continuous synthesis—is carried away and interrupted by latent impressions (vāsanā) are persons of dull intellect. They experience the manifestation of the self within the body and the appearance of reality in the world from time to time, just as before, prior to the arising of [true] knowledge. || 44 ||
Furthermore, by means of the latent impression of knowledge (*jñāna-vāsanā*), they shake off the unreal view;
and in this way, the latent impressions of true and false knowledge mutually [cancel one another]. (45)

If it is objected that there would be a renewed attachment to saṃsāra for these [liberated ones], he says "bhūyaḥ" (again). By means of the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previously practiced [ignorance]; "asatīm" refers to those whose objects are the body, the self, and so forth; the connection is that the latent impressions have merged with one another. || 45 ||
Therefore, O Brahmin, when these two are added together, the result in the middle is clear;
yet even though their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are equal, they are not identical. (46)

"In the middle" means at the time of the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of false knowledge. Now, if it is argued that since the two latent impressions are thus equal, that knowledge would be obstructed and therefore incapable of achieving liberation (*mokṣa*), he says "even when equal" (*same 'pi*) to show this is not so. The meaning is: "even though they possess an identical mode of persistence. || 46 ||
The other impression is sublated by the impression of truth and knowledge;
however, the impression of truth is not sublated by a false impression.

If it is asked why they are not equal, he says "because the latent impression of ignorance has been sublated" (*satya-*) [verse 47]. The other is the latent impression of nescience (*avidyā-vāsanā*). He says "and not... because the latent impression of reality, being produced by a powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be sublated by a false latent impression.
Overcome by false latent impressions, one forgets the absolute Supreme (the *para*).
Therefore, having ascertained that false latent impression to be of the nature of delusion, [one should abandon it]. (48)

If it is asked: "Once false impressions (*mithyāvāsanā*) have been sublated, how can there be the persistence of those impressions at the time of the cessation of true impressions (*satyavāsanā*)?", he says: "It is false. Due to the lack of excellence in practice, the false impression—though sublated, having been cultivated through infinite births—continues to persist. Therefore...
Through the awakening of *prārabdha* karma, having forgotten the pure supreme latent impression (*vāsanā*), one becomes possessed by false latent impressions.

Then, O best of Brahmins, one who is established in true latent impressions determines that the attained false latent impressions are of the nature of delusion; having shaken them off, one attains the true latent impression.
Consequently, the latent impression of reality is never sublated anywhere. || 49 ||

The connection is as follows: having determined that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is false and of the nature of delusion, one then shakes it off; subsequently, one attains—that is, reaches—the true latent impression, because of the certainty that the false latent impression is an error. || 49 ||
For the intermediate [type of person], there is neither forgetfulness nor false cognition;
however, for one who does not forget, false cognition may occasionally arise through the very power of desire. (50)

Having thus described the state of one with dull knowledge, he states the state of the middling person: "Of the middling one. For one who has not forgotten the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of truth, while in the intermediate state—that is, during the condition of bodily activity—there arises, by his own will, a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) employed for practical conduct, even though he has not forgotten that latent impression of truth.
It would be so. || 50 ||
This state has been described for the perfected one (siddha); now listen as it is told for the practitioner (sādhaka):
to the extent that he remains intent upon that [practice], to that same extent his non-forgetfulness increases. (51)

Having thus described the state of the middling [practitioner] in general, he says [the following] to explain the state of the two types respectively, since that [middling practitioner] is twofold by way of being one who has already attained [perfection] and one who is striving for its attainment: "Of the one who has attained" (siddhasya). "Devoted to that" (tatparaḥ) means devoted to the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Elevated" (*ucchritā*) means firm non-forgetfulness. || 51 ||
For the *pūrṇa* there is no loss of memory, nor any false cognition,
even through effort;
for the *uttama*, O Brahmin, there is likewise no distinction between meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and worldly activity.

Regarding the one who is full, having reached the further shore through the practice of samādhi by means of effort and by his own will, he describes the state of the supreme knower with the words "of the supreme" (uttamasya). || 52 ||
There is not even the slightest difference [between them], because there is constant non-forgetfulness;
for that person who is devoted to samādhi, there exists a state of non-forgetfulness.

There is no difference in stability. The reason for this is stated as "since" (*yataḥ*). If it is asked, "In that case, what is the difference between the middling and the superior [stages]? he says: "That which... If it is asked, "In that case, what is the difference between the middling and the superior?
he says: "That which... It is non-forgetfulness. (53)
O Brahmin, this [state] becomes the ground of false knowledge for those who, though being superior, act out of their own will or under the influence of past karma. (54)

That is non-forgetfulness (*avismṛti*). The intended meaning is that in states of false knowledge, it might become slightly faded, and in states of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the latent impression of reality (*satyavāsanā*) might appear as if interrupted. He says "But he who... to show that for the supreme [yogi], there is never any fading due to non-forgetfulness. "By his own will" (*svācchandyāt*) means by his own desire.
Whether engaged in worldly activity due to prārabdha karma or intent upon samādhi, the meaning is that his non-forgetfulness remains unfading. || 54 ||
One should become intent upon that samādhi, and one's lack of mindfulness (asmr̥ti) shall indeed never fade;
listen now to the truth, O Brahmin, regarding those of middling and superior knowledge. (55)

Having thus established the result of the middling and superior [levels of practice] by accepting their commencement, he now states that for those two there is no commencement at all, saying "in reality" (vastutaḥ). || 55 ||
There is no action whatsoever that exists for them, since they have attained perfection;
for they do not perceive anything at all that is distinct from the nature of pure consciousness.
Even regarding whatever *prārabdha* karma exists: if it is asked why there is no *prārabdha* for those who have attained fullness (*pūrṇatva*), he says:

"Consciousness" (*saṃvit*). Because—since—those of middling and superior capacity do not perceive anything whatsoever apart from the Self that is consciousness. The intended meaning here is as follows:
The unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of karma is postulated in accordance with its fruit.

Since the fruit is observed in those who possess knowledge, it is accepted that *prārabdha* karma is not terminated by knowledge. Furthermore, since that fruit occurs only in one whose knowledge is weak, *prārabdha* karma should be postulated for him alone, and not for the other two [types of knowers]. This is the fruit.

And that alone becomes [the Self] which, having ascended to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as pleasure and so forth, appears as one's own; for it is not reasonable to say that what has ascended to the internal organ in the middling or superior [levels of] *samādhi* appears as one's own, because pleasure and so forth do not appear at all during *samādhi*, and [only] upon emergence (*vyutthāna*).

Just as reflections consist solely of the mirror, so too, because the non-self— which is merely the object of perception— is realized as being nothing but the vision of one's own self, pleasure and other states that appear as the self alone do not appear as belonging to oneself. Nor does it appear even as "one's own self."

It must be stated that pleasure and the like have *prārabdha* karma alone as their cause; for otherwise, since pleasure and so forth appear even when they belong to another, they would—by virtue of the commonality of being appearances—necessarily have one's own *prārabdha* as their root.
Indeed, it cannot be maintained that such [pleasure] has only another’s *prārabdha* as its root, because others perceive it as belonging to themselves.
This is because only pleasure and the like that are being experienced have their commencement caused by *prārabdha*;

for that which is known as one's own is a fruit with respect to oneself, whereas that which is known as belonging to another— lacking the experience of a connection to oneself such as "I am happy"— is equivalent to a jar or similar object and is therefore not a fruit with respect to that person.
(k, kh: having attained the fruit) | Therefore, since there is an absence of happiness that has become their fruit, there is no purpose in postulating *prārabdha* (commenced karma).

However, for those of dull intellect, because they forget the continuous contemplation of the true impression (*satyavāsanā*) that "everything is consciousness alone" (*saṃvinmātra*), [they remain bound].

When one is engaged in worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), there arises a purpose for postulating *prārabdha* (the momentum of past karma), because at that time pleasure and so forth appear as belonging to oneself. Now, it may be argued that for those of dull intellect,
when the contemplation of their true nature (*vāstava-svarūpa*) is interrupted, contrary cognitions (*viparīta-pratyaya*) can arise.
If it is argued that for one whose knowledge of that [Self] is obstructed by contrary cognitions, there is no direct accomplishment of the human goal, some say: "This is indeed true.
However, for those who know reality, because ignorance ceases at the very moment of right knowledge, the obscuration of one's own nature [is removed].
Because it has been destroyed, only the power of ignorance that causes distraction— which is conditioned by *prārabdha* karma— persists for a short time.
Once the *prārabdha* karma is naturally exhausted through the mere granting of its fruit, there is an absence of karma that would necessitate another body,
and an absence of the cause for the arising of further ignorance that veils one's true nature.

When the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that produces conceptual constructions is destroyed—like a fire without fuel—the impossibility of another body and the remaining of nothing but the Self as Brahman follow; thus, liberation is indeed inevitable. However, for one whose knowledge has been sublated by contrary notions, there is no correct knowledge, but only a semblance of knowledge (*jñānābhāsa*). Therefore...

Thus, the distinction between the possessor of perfect knowledge (*kevalajñānin*) and the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) as taught in the scriptures is logically consistent. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that for one of duller intellect, due to the absence of constant contemplation, there would be the contingency of another body at the time of death through the recollection of contrary things caused by *prārabdha* karma, according to the principle of Bhagavad Gītā 8.6: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body... This is not the case.

Because even for those possessing middling or superior knowledge, contrary mental impressions caused by *prārabdha* karma are difficult to ward off; and because the verse beginning with "whichever [object] one perceives" (*yaṃ yaṃ vāpi*) refers to those other than the knower, ignorance— which perishes simultaneously with knowledge— is [only removed] upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha*.

[This is] an additional reading. For, in order to prevent the contingency that pleasure and so forth—which have not yet become results [of past karma]—are accidental, one must somehow accept the existence of *prārabdha* (commenced karma). However, the statement that these two [the liberated soul and the Lord] do not possess *prārabdha* is because they are unlike the *prārabdha* of those of dull intellect—or, as in the *k* and *kh* manuscripts, because they are the opposite of what is similar to it.
This is to be applied [to the following]:
because the phrase "or whatever" (*yaṃ vā*) refers to something other than the Knower (*jñānin*), and since ignorance is destroyed simultaneously with knowledge,
at the time of death, even the mind of the Knower is destroyed upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma.

Because distorted memory (*viparītasmṛti*) is impossible [for them]. Thus, the distinction between one possessing absolute knowledge (*kevalajñānin*) and one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) should be understood through the presence or absence of experienced suffering. For this very reason it has been said: "Whether in a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or in the house of an outcaste (*śvapaca*), even if one loses consciousness while casting off the body..."

"Simultaneous with [the arising of] knowledge, one who is liberated goes to absolute isolation (*kaivalya*), his sorrow destroyed. (Pañcārthabhāṣya 83). Likewise: "Once [Śiva-nature] has been known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), from scripture, or from the words of a guru, as being Śiva-nature residing in all things, by means of a firm conviction through the instrument [of the intellect]... (K, Kh: ...).
"There is no purpose whatsoever to be achieved anywhere, even by means of meditative cultivation.
How could a remainder of karma persist, since everything has been reduced to ashes by the fire of consciousness? Therefore, for them, nothing whatsoever remains.

Since everything is seen to be non-different from the nature of consciousness, for those of middling or superior capacity—as opposed to those of dull intellect—no remaining karma in the form of *prārabdha* persists; thus he says: "Karma. All duality is nothing but karma. [57]
It is seen by others as if it were the work of a magician;
listen, O Brahmin, I shall explain the secret to you in brief. (58)
If it is objected that even for those of supreme knowledge, effects resulting from *prārabdha-karma*—such as joy and sorrow—are observed, he replies with the word "aindra" (of Indra).

Just as the work of a magician, such as the cutting off of his own head, is seen by others but not by himself, so too is the case with this [knower's] joy and so forth; this is the sense. For the knowers...
He says that it is not karma because of its equality with Śiva: "Listen," etc. (58).
That very vision which belongs to Śiva is said to be the vision of the wise;
there is not even the slightest difference between them—this is the truth, of this there is no doubt. (59)
Vision (dṛśiḥ)—which is the nature of one's own self consisting solely of pure consciousness—is thus not subject to the remainder of prārabdha karma; this is the intended meaning. || 59 ||
"Therefore, not even the slightest karma follows those who possess knowledge.
Having heard this as explained by Hemāṅgada, that Vasumān [was filled with wonder]. || 60 ||
A little [more]: among the middling and superior knowers. Thus ends everything spoken by the prince. 60.
Freed from all doubt and with a mind made clear through higher knowledge,
he was honored by the princes and others, and returned to his own abode.
After the two princes had reached their own city,
Rāma, having heard this, again questioned the sage, the son of Atri.
Indeed, this knowledge has been heard by me as it emerged from your mouth, O Guru;
my doubt is destroyed, and that great state has been understood. (63)
That great state has the nature of pure, non-dual consciousness.
The self, which is pure consciousness pervading everything, shines everywhere;
nevertheless, you have explained all of this from the very beginning.

He states his own experience: "All," etc. That consciousness which is the underlying thread (*anusyūtā*) in all cognitions delimited by the forms of objects of knowledge—a consciousness whose nature is pure *cit*—that alone is my Self; it shines forth for me everywhere, both externally and internally. Although I have accomplished all that was to be done, nevertheless, because the aforementioned meaning must not be forgotten:
He asks, "Even so," [meaning] "Please state in brief all the points that have been declared. || 64 ||
Speak again in brief, O Guru, of that consciousness which is most essential, so that it may be held by me with my whole being. (65)
Tell me that which must be maintained by me with my whole being, for as long as it shall endure.
Thus questioned by Rāma, the son of Atri spoke again:
"Listen, O Rāma, I shall speak once more that which is the most essential of all. (66)
The most essential of everything that has been taught.

That supreme consciousness, which is the sovereign mistress and consists of the fullness of "I-ness," is always, through the majesty of its power of Māyā known as absolute freedom (svātantrya), [the source of manifestation].
She who is experienced by you as your own self (*svātman*) is the Supreme Sovereign (*parameśānī*), whose nature is to exercise supreme lordship over all;
the sense is that she is endowed with ultimate autonomy (*paramasvātantrya*). If one asks what that autonomy is, he says:
"consisting of the fullness of I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhantāmayī*). For some attribute must necessarily be admitted for consciousness (*citi*) in order to distinguish it from the insentient.

And that [consciousness] is indeed the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpasphūrti*). Manifestation is of two kinds: that established in common worldly experience—namely, "I" (*aham*) and "this" (*idam*)—and [the other].

Among these, since the manifestation as "this" is dependent upon another and would lead to an infinite regress due to its reliance on something else, it must be said that the manifestation of consciousness is only as "I. That...

And I am "limited" (*kalā*) because my manifestation within the body and so forth is incomplete due to the delimitation of time and other factors. This [consciousness], however, is "complete" (*pūrṇā*) because it rests in the consciousness that is the means for realizing the true nature of all time and other such categories. Therefore, it is called the "complete I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). Since it is not distinct from one's own essential nature, it is said to be "consisting thereof" (*tanmayī*). It is precisely of this undivided nature...

This detailed exposition at the very occasion of the *citerupadeśa* (instruction on consciousness) is for the sake of providing a thorough acquaintance with its true nature (*svarūpa*). For this very reason, it is *parā* (supreme) and *anuttarā* (unexcelled). That state in which the supreme consciousness (*parāciti*) rests within an object of perception (*dṛśya*) external to itself is *ahantā* (I-consciousness). When that same [consciousness] rests within the body and so forth, it is called "limited" (*paricchinnā*). [In contrast, it is the pure consciousness] turned away from the body and so forth...

This state of rest is called the "full I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhantā*). Such consciousness, through the majesty of its power of *māyā*—which is termed "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*)—is itself the full I-consciousness that, at the beginning of creation, becomes the will-nature of the desiring creator; thus, at the time of emanation, it is called "sovereignty" when it is the agent's action, and "māyā."

In the present context, however, action (*kriyā*) is indeed not of the nature of physical vibration (*parispanda*) or transformation (*pariṇāma*), but rather of the nature of manifestation (*avabhāsa*), like the appearance of a reflection in a mirror.
And thus, full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) as freedom (*svātantrya*) is said to consist of the triad of powers: knowledge, will, and action.

The meaning of the connection is as follows: the *māyā-śakti* possesses majesty (*māhātmyam*), greatness (*mahitvam*), and expansion (*ucchūnatā*); from that [expansion], it causes the manifestation of the universe.

By the word "always" (*sadā*), the sense is that because [this power] constitutes the very nature of the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*), there is no limitation by time regarding the manifestation of the universe.
For this very reason, it has been said: "Always for the sake of the emission and withdrawal of creation" (*Śiva-stotra-uttara*, 20.9), and so forth.
One who accomplishes the seemingly impossible surely manifests the world like a reflection in a mirror; hear the manner of that process in due order. (68)

The connection is with the phrase "by virtue of the majesty of performing that which is difficult to accomplish. This means: by virtue of being the sole, unaided agent of that which is difficult to accomplish. Thus, even at the time of the manifestation of the world, one's own state as non-dual pure consciousness remains unimpeded; this he states by way of an illustration:
"Reflects" means that manner of manifesting the world. "Successively" refers to the sequence of cause and effect.
That supreme consciousness, which is full and expanded by the sense of "I am full," manifests its own essential nature in two ways by virtue of its sovereignty.
That which was described immediately prior: augmented by the full sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), it is an undivided manifestation of one's own nature;
that is to say, it is a plenitude, a single mass of manifestation.
It is the very form of one's own self, a density of the manifestation of consciousness. 69.
When, even within a single part, the sense of "I" appears as incomplete, then the second part emerges from that sense of "I. (70)

He explains this very duality [with the words] "therein" (*tatra*). This means: in its own nature (*svarūpe*). When, after manifesting two parts, an incomplete sense of "I" (*apūrṇāhaṃbhāva*) is also manifested in one part, then that which is the second portion is the portion other than itself (*svetara-bhāga*).

From that state of "I-ness" known as incomplete, he emerged from the incomplete sense of ego; by the word "api" (also/even), it is indicated that this [emergence] is distinct from the perfect "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) which constitutes his true nature. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no loss of his essential nature. Having manifested two parts within his own self, [he remains] in one of those parts...
The meaning is that by manifesting the delimited sense of "I," it manifests the other portion—the non-"I" aspect—which has not been pervaded by the sense of "I. || 70 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, through that very vision, the external became unmanifest;
endowed with an incomplete sense of "I," he is called Sadāśiva.
This portion which is not overcome by the sense of "I" becomes the unmanifest form of external objects; indeed,

every manifestation of conceptualization, from the two-fold division up to external objects, occurs solely through the vision of the conscious element (*cidaṃśa*) as it is overcome by a limited sense of "I," and not otherwise.

He says "by the vision of the full consciousness" (pūrṇacid-dṛṣṭyā), meaning "by that very vision. This very aspect of consciousness (cidaṃśa) endowed with the limited sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is called Sadāśiva; whom the followers of the Upaniṣads call Īśvara. || 71 ||

Seeing that unmanifest portion as if distinct from himself—though he is Sadāśiva himself—"from himself" means from his own self; even while seeing it as distinct, he remained constantly intent on the synthesis "I am this," being devoted to the sense of identity (*abhimāna*). (In manuscripts *k* and *kh*, the phrase "devoted to the sense of identity" does not appear.)
The remainder [is as follows]: The followers of the Upaniṣads, however, employ terms such as *avidyā* (ignorance) and *māyā* (illusion) to refer precisely to this unmanifest portion (*avyaktabhāga*).
Just as our ownership exists through the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) even though our bodies appear as distinct entities, so too should it be understood that this belongs to the Unmanifest. || 72 ||
Desiring again to create the manifold world through his own sovereignty, he, being this very [Self], has resorted to this unmanifest body of his, thinking, "I am this. (73)

He is indeed Sadāśiva himself. "By his own sovereignty," meaning by his nature as the self-subsistent I-consciousness (*svāhaṃbhāva*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "having seen his own body in its unmanifest form. The connection is: when he is intent on the contemplation that "I am established in this very unmanifest form. (73)
Thus, intent on such reflection, the Lord appeared;
yet it was the Lord himself who was possessed by the ego-sense within the unmanifest.

Then Sadāśiva alone appeared as Īśvara. The sense is that Sadāśiva is intent on the contemplation of consciousness as predominant, thinking "I am this," whereas Īśvara is intent on the contemplation of the unmanifest (the objective) as predominant, thinking "This is I.
The connection is that Īśvara himself, permeated by the conceit "I am the unmanifest," became threefold. || 74 ||
He manifested in three ways through the forms of Rudra, Hari, and Hiraṇyagarbha,
as the illuminators of the aggregate consisting of the seer, the seen, the eater, and the food.

Therein, the Lord, by His own sovereignty, having manifested the unmanifest in its manifold forms through the qualities of *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas*, [appears] in three ways as the triad of Rudra, Hari, and Indra— consisting of three groups— through the conceit of a limited sense of "I" (*ahantā*) within the innumerable portions of the unmanifest that are delimited by those respective qualities.

It came into being. Regarding the three activities of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he says: "The Seer. The "great mass" is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). With the intention of referring to its multiplicity, he says: "the aggregate. These are the manifestors of origination. (75)
There were various weapons, likewise assuming those forms;
there were also many monkeys, intent upon his destruction. (76)
"Established in that form" means they are established in the form of the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*); that is to say, they are the ones who maintain them.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "the Rudras were intent upon withdrawal. || 76 ||
In this manner, many Rudras have come into being; such is the process of the world. This reality of the universe is like a reflection in a mirror.
The meaning is that there have been many Rudras. Here, because the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) are infinite, it should be understood that Brahmā and the others are likewise infinite.

"The ordinance of the world" refers to its creation. Having spoken thus, he states that even such a reality of the world is non-different from supreme consciousness, using the words "like a mirror" (*darpaṇa*). || 77 ||
O Rāma, it shines forth alone; indeed, nothing has ever been born.
The supreme consciousness is always of the nature of the fullness of the "I-sense" (ahaṃbhāva). || 78 ||

Thus, the very manifestation [of consciousness] is the arising of the world and so forth; there is no beginning or transformation of it. To this he says: "It shines" (*bhāsate*). Because its essence consists solely in such manifestation, even in the appearance of the world, he states that the supreme consciousness (*parā citiḥ*) does not deviate from its own nature: "The supreme consciousness. (78)
Though manifold and complete,
it remains augmented by the sense of "I," just as you, O Rāma, are augmented by the sense of "I" throughout the entire body.

In reality, because [the universe] from Sadāśiva down to a mere worm consists of the subtle elements (tanmātra), she is full even of the limited sense of "I" that is infinite; thus he says, "she remains.
The connection is: "she remains as form itself. He establishes this very point with an illustration: "just as... (verse 79).
Just as one who is intent on various activities through distinct states of "I-ness" such as the eyes and so forth [remains the same person],
even so is the supreme consciousness, which rests upon the fullness of the I-consciousness (pūrṇāhaṃtā).
Just as you, although possessing the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) pervading your entire body,
possess a collection of individual "I-senses" located in each specific part such as the eyes which perceive form and so forth; in exactly the same way, that supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*),
although it is the locus of the incomplete "I-sense" (*apūrṇāhantā*) extending from Sadāśiva down to a blade of grass, is likewise [all-pervasive].
