In reality, it is that very supreme consciousness which shines forth in this manner. || 81 ||

"In reality" (vastutaḥ) means that, in truth, she is indeed the supreme consciousness itself, which does not manifest in the forms of the limited "I-ness" (paricchinnāhaṃtā) or the "ever-blessed Śiva" (sadāśiva) and so forth, which are [merely] the full "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃtā). || 81 ||
Although you, whose nature consists of the ego-identification with the body, are by yourself incapable of perceiving form, taste, and so forth,
yet by attaining identity with the sense organs, [you perceive them].

Now, he explains in sequence, with an illustration, that although omniscience and omnipotence belong to Sadāśiva—the pure, supreme consciousness—in reality there is no such thing as agency and so forth [on His part]. He says:
"The body," etc. Without first attaining identity with the eyes and other [senses], and having attained identity with the sense organs—that is, identity with the faculties—everything [is perceived].
The connection is: "you take. || 82 ||
In this way, Lord Sadāśiva constantly grasps everything;
by his own nature, he consists of the non-difference of all things within the entire range from Brahmā down to a clump of grass.
He applies this to the subject of the illustration with the word "thus": "In this way, by being the inner controller of all, he consists of the non-duality of all. (83)
Having attained internal identity [with it], he both knows and acts;
for that form of yours is indeed non-conceptual and the support of all.

It knows and acts as everything. "As how" means: your non-conceptual, pure consciousness-nature, which stands in the place of a mirror, and [the world] which stands in the place of a reflection—consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, which is the support of all things, even though it exists [within you]. || 84 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, it knows nothing at all, yet it acts;
even so is the supreme consciousness, the refuge of all the worlds. 85.

It knows nothing and yet acts; the sense is that, in reality, both the object of knowledge and the action are nothing but its own self. It applies this to the subject of the analogy with the words "In the same way" (evam). || 85 ||
He perceives not even a trace of difference anywhere, nor does he create one;
this entire world appears within that very [consciousness] alone. (86)
"At some time. If it is asked, "Why is this so? [the author] says, "Because the object of knowledge and its effect consist of that alone," thus:
"This much... (verse 86).

Due to its own sovereignty, everything that appears as the world is produced from it like a reflection in a mirror; the manifestation of the entire universe is nothing other than the manifestation of that [consciousness] itself.

He says that [the Lord] manifests and brings forth the universe through His own sovereignty, just as reflections appear in a mirror through its own power; this is expressed by the phrase "by His sovereignty. The connection is: "[He] manifests and is abundant. Manifestation means "intensively. All... [g:]
The sense is that existence (*sattva*) is dependent upon that [consciousness]. For this very reason, he says "of the world," meaning of that supreme consciousness.
Just as the appearance of reflections occurs solely within the reflection in a mirror, so too, in this case, you, I, and others—the perceivers—are indeed composed of pure vision. 88.
He states that the perceivers, like the perceived, are also nothing but that [consciousness]—in the verse beginning with "here" (atra). The meaning is: in this world. || 88 ||
In the absence of contact with the visible, there is only pure consciousness and nothing else, just as a mirror remains [unaffected] when it is not in contact with jars and other objects. (89)

The true nature of those things which appear as consisting of vision is pure supreme consciousness itself, provided there is no contact with or manifestation of the object of sight. He establishes this by means of an illustration: "A jar," etc.
This refers to that portion of the mirror which is delimited by the reflection of a jar or other object. || 89 ||
Just as a pure mirror appears divided due to reflections, so too, when the appearance of the visible world produced by conceptual construction is wiped away, [the Self remains as it is]. 90.
He states that even at the time of reflection, the distinction (*bheda*)—or rather, the perception of distinction—is conditioned by the form of the reflection:
"Supreme consciousness, whose nature is non-dual, remains as the residual [reality];
and this [consciousness] is a mass of great bliss, because it is devoid of even a trace of suffering. (91)

When the visible world appearing through mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) has been wiped away by its non-perception, that which remains—abiding as the witness of that non-perception—is none other than the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*), whose nature is non-dual self-awareness (*svātmasaṃvid*).
To establish that such a state constitutes the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), he describes it as being of the nature of bliss: "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*).

"Thick" means dense with great, boundless bliss; that is to say, she is of the nature of indivisible bliss (*akhaṇḍānanda*). If one asks why this is so, he says: "suffering," etc. Since suffering is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it is absent from her essential nature (*svarūpa*) in reality; therefore, she is of the nature of indivisible bliss. || 91 ||
Because it consists of a mass of all-bliss, it is desired by all;
for bliss is the very nature of the Self, and that is what is desired by everyone. (92)

"Of all" (sarva): she whose form—that is, her essential nature—is "dense" (ghana), meaning compact, with those joys belonging to all living beings which manifest through the revelation of sense objects;
that is to say, her essential nature consists solely of the bliss experienced by all. This is shown by the statement of the reason: "it is exactly thus."

He establishes [the point] with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). The syllogism is as follows: the Self (*ātman*) has bliss as its sole nature (*ānandaikarūpa*), because it is desired by all, like the pleasure derived from a woman. Now, one might object: "Bliss that is desired by all is an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*); how then could it be of the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)? Desiring to ward off this objection, he says:
Regarding "pleasure": the very nature of the self must be pleasure, because it is desired by all; for that which is not so [desired] is not so, just as with pain—this is the formal argument. || 92 ||

That for whose sake the state of having a body and so forth exists, which is not desired by anyone, and of which even a mere fragment is called "the bliss of sense objects"—[that is the ultimate reality]. (93)

Anticipating the objection that this reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to desired objects such as the body, women, and wealth—which are not [included in the definition]—he says: "for the sake of which. For the body and so forth lack the status of being the primary object of desire;
rather, the body and so forth are desired for the sake of the happiness of the non-self (*anātman*).

Thus, for those who seek the happiness of heaven and so forth, the abandonment of the body through fasting and other means is logically consistent. For this very reason, he states "that which" (*yad*), meaning that the nature of the self is never, under any circumstances, something undesired. Therefore, the self alone is the primary object of desire.

The sense is that [the self] is of the nature of bliss (*sukhātmaka*). Now, one might object: since the pleasure derived from women and the like is clearly experienced as something to be enjoyed (*bhogya*), and no pleasure distinct from that is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the self cannot be of the nature of bliss.
To this he says: "Of whomsoever... That is to say, even a mere fragment (*leśa*) of that very bliss of the self (*ātmānanda*) constitutes the bliss of sense-objects (*viṣayānanda*).
This is the meaning of what is stated in the scriptures (*āgama*). Just as in the case of the inactive sky,

activity is perceived in its portion delimited by objects such as jars due to adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), and just as the consciousness-self (*cidātman*), which is itself unknowable, possesses knowability through the delimitation of the visible world due to adventitious conditions, so too is it with pleasure (*sukha*).
The intention is that the state of being an object of enjoyment is adventitious, consisting of the mark of delimitation. || 93 ||
That very consciousness manifests in the abandonment of the burden and so forth, as well as in deep sleep;
it is called "bliss" because it alone is desirable. (94)

Now, to dispel the doubt that the self merely desires happiness and does not possess the nature of happiness itself due to a lack of evidence, he says: "That very [self]... This refers to the bliss that constitutes its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). "The removal of the burden" means its abandonment; by the word "etcetera," the state of the immediate cessation of unbearable headaches and so forth is included.
And it manifests in deep sleep. The purport here is this: the bliss experienced by everyone immediately after waking from sleep is undeniable and established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Since that [bliss] does not have contact with women and so forth as its cause—being, in fact, causeless—it is of the nature of one's own essential being (*svarūpa*).

Nor is it proper to say that [pleasure] is caused by the abandonment of the mental faculty (*bhāratī*), because the abandonment of the mental faculty is a non-entity (*abhāva*), and it is not accepted that a positive entity (*bhāva*) arises from a non-entity. For at that time, nothing else exists that could serve as the cause of pleasure;
therefore, pleasure is indeed of the very nature of that [state]. But [one might object]: at that time...
Anticipating the objection that the nature of pleasure appears through delusion as nothing other than the cessation of intense suffering, he says:
"In deep sleep. Even a person who is healthy experiences great, causeless happiness in deep sleep; for the memory of one who has awakened—"I slept happily"—is impossible to deny. And that...

It is indeed its very own nature (*svarūpa*). For if bliss were not admitted there [in deep sleep], the activity of all beings, from cattle and commoners upward, during the state of profound sleep would not be possible. Now, if it is asked: "If bliss constitutes the very nature [of consciousness], why is it not experienced at all times?"—it is replied: just as, for example, the foundational resonance (*ādhāra-dhvani*) exists for everyone...

Although it is constantly present, it is concealed by external sound; for this very reason, it is heard when the ears are firmly plugged and so forth. In the same way, the bliss of one's own Self is obscured by the suffering of one who is being scorched by the forest fire of the flood of all latent impressions, such as desire and the sense of duty.

Due to the dissolution of that flood of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) into its own cause during deep sleep, there is the manifestation of the bliss of the Self (*ātmasukha*), just as sound is manifested for one whose ears are covered. This occurs because, at the time of carrying a burden, the suffering produced by the flood of latent impressions is eclipsed by the great suffering caused by the burden itself.

The suffering of worldly existence (*bhāra-duḥkha*) alone has taken root. When that suffering ceases through the abandonment of worldly existence, the bliss of the Self (*ātma-sukha*) becomes manifest, up until the point where the suffering born of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arises.
The pleasure derived from objects such as women is also like this; for indeed, latent impressions are infinite, like thorns.

Constantly pecking at the heart, they remain concentrated there; when there arises the possibility of attaining one particular object, because the desire for that object is so intense, the resulting torment becomes so acute that all other latent impressions (*vāsanās*) become as if hidden. Then, upon the attainment of that object, through the pacification of great suffering—

The happiness of the Self becomes manifest up until the point where other desires arise; therefore, because it is the object of all longing, the conscious Self alone is called "bliss" (ānanda). Thus he says: "Consciousness itself... (verse 94).
The deluded do not recognize the great bliss that is their own self;
they perceive it as divided due to the diversity of its manifesting agents. || 95 ||

If it is asked, "In that case, since all happiness is one's own self, why do they not know this? [the author] says: "The deluded. The meaning is that they do not know precisely because of their delusion.
[Happiness appears] as distinct from its own true nature. Here he states the reason: "Of the manifestors. [This refers to] the manifestor.

The meaning is that, because of the differences among women and other objects, they perceive them as arising and perishing at each respective moment, and thus they do not know their true nature as a stable self. || 95 ||
For just as objects appearing in a mirror, by virtue of their causal conditions, appear as if distinct for as long as there is cognition of the mirror; so indeed it is.

He provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as), stating that just as ignorant people perceive happiness—which is their own self—as distinct, so too they perceive the world—which is non-different from their own self—as distinct.
[The phrase] "from the cause which is the nature of the reflection" refers to the mirror. The expression "as long as there is cognition of the mirror" means "this is the mirror."
The phrase "capable of receiving a reflection" means specifically "up to the point of cognition.

The meaning is that entities consisting of reflections appear as if they were distinct; however, the underlying intention is that they do not appear as such, for all this is merely the mirror itself. || 96 ||
Once the nature of the reflection has been understood, that which appears as before does not exist as something distinct from the mirror; for the mirror is indeed pure.

When those [reflections] are known to be reflections preceded by the cognition of the mirror, then—although they appear as before—they know that all of them do not exist as distinct from the mirror; rather, they know that "this entire [array] is simply the pure mirror. This is the implied conclusion. 97.
Thus, for one who has known reality, this entire world, though appearing in such a manner, is nothing other than his own self alone. 98.
He applies this to the case under discussion with the word "thus" (evam). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "and the other does not appear. || 98 ||
Just as a jar and the like exist in clay, just as ornaments exist in gold,
and just as statues exist in stone, so too does the world exist within the Self that is consciousness.

With the intention of refuting the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), he begins to demonstrate through examples that the world is not distinct from the conscious Self (*cidātman*): "The jar and so forth... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "...manifests within the conscious Self. (99)
O descendant of Bhṛgu, the view that "the world does not exist at all" is indeed incomplete;
for a contrary conviction such as "it does not exist" can never be established.
Regarding the word "world" (*jagat*): proponents of the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) maintain that error occurs without any underlying substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna*).
This [section] is undertaken for the purpose of refuting their view. For according to their doctrine, the cognition "this is silver" has a non-existent object;
likewise, the cognition of the world also has a non-existent object. This is preceded by the certainty that "the world does not exist."

The established position is that liberation consists in the attainment of the nature of emptiness when the cultivation of the world ceases through the long-term cultivation of emptiness itself. He refutes this, saying: "The world does not exist. This means it is incomplete and of the nature of an error. For just as a jar or the like is not non-existent in every respect, but is indeed existent in the form of clay and so forth, so too is the world.

For in every respect it is non-existent, yet it exists as the very form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Therefore, the conviction that the world is absolutely non-existent is merely an error; this is the intended meaning. If one asks why, he says: "It does not exist. For the contrary conviction that it does not exist in any way whatsoever cannot be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). || 100 ||
Since the perception of the world as the self of the practitioner arises clearly once again, how could the dissolution of the world occur merely by a curse? (101)

If it is asked why this is so, he says: "By the proving [agent]" (*sādhaka*). This is because, even after the negation of everything, the perception of the world as the very nature of the conscious self (*cidātman*)—which proves both the positions of "it exists" and "it does not exist"—is once again clearly possible. This remains true even when jars and other objects are negated as being non-existent in their state of transformation (*vikāra*).

Just as there is no negation of the clay in the form of the jar, so too, even when the visible world is negated in its aspect as "the seen," there is no negation of its manifestation in the form of the Seer; thus, there is no non-existence of that which is appearing.
Herein lies the truth: for the world appears as permeated by Consciousness (cit), just as jars and other objects appear as permeated by clay.
Here, the opponent objects in every way, because he accepts the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) regarding that which appears. To this it is replied:

since the negator is included within the category of the object to be negated, the negation itself cannot be established; therefore, there is no negation of the negator, who is of the nature of the underlying, persisting consciousness (*anugata-cidātman*). This is the view of the opponent.

The intention behind this universal negation (*sarvaniṣedha*)—namely, "nothing exists"—is as follows: for consciousness (*cit*), conceptualization (*savikalpa*) is its very nature, and that indeed is *saṃsāra*. Since non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpacit*) lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*), the establishment of liberation (*mokṣa*) occurs through the negation of everything. Because it is impossible for a negator to negate [himself], the world does not undergo total dissolution merely by the pronouncement of the word "it does not exist."

Thus he says: "It does not exist. For that which establishes everything—the pure conscious self, free from conceptual construction and self-luminous—is manifest during states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*) even when all [other] things are negated. || 101 ||
Just as an entire city in a mirror exists by virtue of the nature of the mirror, so too the world is declared to be true, having the singular form of the conscious self. 102.

Now, raising the doubt as to what kind of thing this "portion to be negated" (niṣedhyāṃśa) is in the context of non-duality (advaita), he says: "Like a reflection in a mirror," and so forth. On this point, the followers of the Upaniṣads say: "The world, which is indefinable (anirvacanīya) in terms of being existent, non-existent, and so on, is what is to be negated, like a reflection in a mirror. But the followers of Āgama, however—
The manifestation of the world is like the manifestation of a city in a mirror;

just as the reflection possesses the nature of the mirror, so too the world possesses reality by virtue of having consciousness (*cit*) as its nature. If it is asked, "In that case, what is to be negated? we reply: "Duality. If it is further asked, "Is duality included within the world, or not? [the answer is: it is included.
If it is argued that in the first case [of duality] its negation is impossible because it exists as real, and in the second case its indefinability (anirvacanīyatva) is unavoidable, it is replied:

even duality is included within the world itself. Now, if so, how can there be a negation of duality which is real? Listen: for in this system, the object of manifestation is not distinct from the act of manifestation.

Since duality does not exceed the appearance of delusion, the negation of duality does not result in the removal of the delusion of duality. For this very reason it has been said: [—this verse is also seen cited in Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha’s *Spandakārikāvivṛti*].
It should be observed (p. 163): "Oneness is not of a different characteristic from separateness;

reality is established as a single essence through the forms of both separateness and oneness. Even in the theory of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), is the negation itself indeterminable or is it real? In the first case, there would be no negation of the world. In the second case...

There is the consequence of duality. Nor should it be argued that because negation has the nature of its own substratum, it is of the nature of Brahman and thus there is no consequence of duality; for if one were to accept that negation—which is perceived as non-self—is of the nature of the Self, then one would necessarily have to accept that the entire universe is also of the nature of the Self.

Since what was stated by the opponent is also not defective— (note: after "svīkārasya," the reading "anirvacanīyatvasya" is an addition to be justified as stating that the negation results in this meaning because of existence)— nor should it be suspected that non-existence itself is identical with its locus.

Because it is possible to establish that the entire universe is of the nature of existence (or non-existence) through such means as the fact that the distinction from what is other than itself is its own essential nature; thus, whether by negation or otherwise,
there is only the one conscious Self once the delusion consisting of the appearance of duality has been dispelled.

The very fact that [the teachings] have the human goal as their purpose constitutes the nature of the non-dual (advaita) scripture. Therefore, it should be understood that those seeking liberation must not become attached to various philosophical systems rooted in mere reasoning.
Just as a city reflected in a mirror is not distinct from the mirror itself, so too is reality of the singular form of the conscious Self alone.

Regarding the word "jagat" (the world): it is not proper to object by asking, "Just because it has been stated that the world is real in the form of the conscious Self (*cidātman*), why does the world exist in the form of the conscious Self?"—for this would be equivalent to objecting to the statement "nescience (*avidyā*) is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*)" by asking, "Does nescience exist? Precisely because its indeterminability has been stated, it exists in that manner.

It should be understood that the objection, "Does it exist? is improper; likewise, when it is stated that "everything is not distinct from consciousness," the objection, "Does everything exist? is also untenable. || 102 ||
This would be full consciousness because of the abandonment of contraction;
by the excellence of its own majesty, the Seer itself has attained the state of the seen. (103)

Thus, he states that the very knowledge "all this is true" is complete knowledge (*pūrṇajñāna*), by saying "complete. If one asks why, he says: "contraction," etc. There is a duality of the "seen" (*dṛśya*) and the "seer" (*dṛk*). Even when it is said that the seen does not exist there, there remains the appearance of contraction caused by the absence of the seen. (k, kh)

(The manifestation of the absence of contraction): Since it has been stated that "all that is visible is nothing but vision, like a reflection in a mirror," the sense is that there is no appearance of contraction;
this alone is full consciousness (*pūrṇavijñāna*). Therefore, there is nothing apart from vision.
He concludes [the discussion on] the visible by stating "it is indeed the Seer. His own majesty is his own sovereignty. || 103 ||
Just as a city [appears] in a mirror, so too is this compendium of the meaning of the scriptures;
there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither the practitioner nor the means of practice. (104)

Here is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): "Just as" (*yathā*). Having summarized everything stated from the beginning, he concludes by saying "this" (*eṣa*). Again, having summarized the essence of the meaning already explained, he says:
"There is no bondage. This is because everything that appears as distinct from the Seer (*dṛk*) exists according to the analogy of a reflection.

Because it consists of pure perception alone and lacks any bondage apart from its own essential nature, there is no bondage; for that very reason, there is no liberation, nor is there a practitioner or a means of practice. (104)
The indivisible, non-dual power of Consciousness is Tripurā herself who manifests;
she alone is both ignorance and knowledge, as well as bondage and the means to liberation.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is this that appears as such variety?", he says: "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍā*). By "indivisible," internal differentiation is excluded; by "non-dual" (*advayā*), the exclusion of both heterogeneous and homogeneous differentiation is intended.

Such a power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—which is the third state (*triparā*) and the fourth (*turyā*)—is that very same [power] which, like a mirror, manifests in a state of variety. Therefore, it is she alone who...
"He said 'all'—that very [consciousness]," [it is said]. || 105 ||
O Bhārgava, only this much is to be known; nothing else exists.
This sequence of realization has been declared to you from the beginning, O Rāma. (106)

Therefore, bondage arises solely from ignorance. Thus, he says "But this... [to show] that one achieves the goal through knowledge alone; the meaning is that this refers to the attainment of the means from the very beginning. || 106 ||
Having thoroughly understood this, a person never again grieves anywhere;
O Nārada, this is the Section on Knowledge (Jñānakhaṇḍa), which is established through sound reasoning. 107.

Having thoroughly understood this section on knowledge with an intellect free from fallacious reasoning, and having experienced it according to its meaning through prior deliberation; by the word "person" (jana), it is indicated here that there is no restriction regarding specific qualifications such as caste or stage of life (varṇāśrama). [This applies] at some point, until the fall of the body.

Either previously or immediately [following]. Hāritāyana said to Nārada: "O Nārada! *Upapatti* means reasoning; *upalabdhi* means experience. That in which both are well-formed (*susthu-rūpa*) is so described. || 107 ||
Whose delusion arising from ignorance would not be destroyed by hearing this?
Yet, for one whose delusion does not reach peace even after hearing this, it will never cease. 108.
"Moha" means delusion. Whose delusion would it not destroy? The meaning is that it surely destroys the delusion of everyone. "Śāntim" means cessation [or destruction]. || 108 ||
By what means in this world might knowledge of that stone-man arise?
For once this has been heard (or performed), it will produce firm realization.

That person made of stone is utterly dull-witted; by what means, then, could knowledge arise for him? The meaning is: by no means whatsoever. He says "just once" (*sakṛdeva*) to show that knowledge arises for those of pure intellect upon hearing [the teaching] but once. || 109 ||
How could that which is known in two or three ways not produce [realization] for one who is dull-witted?
This is considered to be the pacifier of the flood of sins when heard, and the bestower of higher knowledge. 110.
"For one who is dull and of dull intellect"—the meaning is that how could the knowledge heard [from scripture] not produce [realization], even if it be twofold or threefold?
Rather, it certainly would produce it. He praises the section on knowledge with the words "this" (etad): "heard" means without understanding the meaning;
"matured" means understood according to its meaning. || 110 ||
When written down, it destroys the defects of vision; when worshipped, it purifies the mind;
and when constantly practiced, it eliminates delusion. (111)

The defect of vision (*dṛṣṭidoṣa*). The defect of the external sense organ (*dṛṣṭi*) is its inclination toward objects. The purification of the mind is through the pacification of defects such as passion (*rāga*). Ignorance (*mūḍhatā*) is the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*). Thorough cultivation (*pariśīlana*) is repeated investigation. || 111 ||
When that form which has become the self of all is clearly understood through investigation, there shall be liberation; otherwise, there is bondage. That [liberation] is indeed Tripurā, who is Hrīṃ.
At the end of the treatise, he composes a maṅgala consisting of a description of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is to be established:

"All," etc. The form (*rūpa*) which is the supreme consciousness (*paraciti*), which constitutes the self (*ātmabhūta*)—that is, the essential nature (*svabhāvabhūta*)—of all entities (*bhāva*) consisting of the stationary and the moving.

Having reflected that reflections reside [within] like a mirror; having ascertained through sound reasoning that all objects of cognition (*cetya*) are nothing but consciousness (*citimātra*), because they appear without following after [consciousness], just like reflections whose nature is the mirror alone; and having clearly realized them as being directly present—[that is,] if one has recognized [it] through self-recognition (*pratyabhijñāta*) that "I am consciousness which has become the self of all."

The remainder [of the verse] is as follows: "Liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra would occur; otherwise, if it were not realized, bondage alone would remain firm. When it is realized, liberation occurs in that very form; otherwise, there would be bondage. Since bondage and liberation do not exceed the essential nature [of consciousness], this is indeed logical. That which is such supreme consciousness (parā citiḥ) is...

Tripura alone is that which is to be expounded in this present context. She is *hrīṃ*, because she is the essence of the meaning of the Śakti-praṇava, and thus her very form is that [syllable]—for there is no difference between the signified and the signifier. Thus all is auspicious. 112.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the Tripurārahasya, the most excellent of histories, within the twelve-thousand-verse compendium.]
This excellent commentary on the Jñānakhaṇḍa of the secret [text] of Tripurā, titled Tātparyadīpikā, has been composed for the pleasure of Tripurā. || 1 ||
In the Draviḍa country, within the city of Anuhālāsya, there are five esteemed villages; among them is situated the village of Mahāpuṣkara. || 2 ||
He is the rising moon of auspicious digits from the milky ocean of the Dravidian lineage,
and he holds the status of a radiant pearl upon the noble bamboo-stalk of the Bṛhaccharaṇa family.
The son of that [father] was the illustrious scholar named Śrīnivāsa, the great sacrificer Vaidyanātha, whose mind was purified by true knowledge. (4)
One who knows the true principles of the Śruti and Āgama, whose intention is devoted to Tripurā,
[will appear] when 4,932 years of the Kali Yuga have passed.
He has composed this *Tātparyadīpikā*, an extremely clear and excellent commentary on the *Jñānakhaṇḍa* of the secret [text] of Tripurā.
It may be that some fault has occurred here on my part due to ignorance, for corruption through linguistic deviation can arise from every side;
nevertheless, the wise, whose minds are well-disposed, will surely purify it at my very request as a disciple. (7)
Where am I, of dull intellect, and where is this entire essence of the science of higher knowledge?
This eloquence of mine, though I am mute, has come forth solely through the supreme grace of the venerable Tripurā.
For this *Tātparyadīpikā* has been elucidated for the purification of one's own self;
may it always serve to bring about the blossoming of the bliss of Tripurā, the Supreme Consciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Tātparyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Jñānakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrītripurārahasya*, composed by the wise Śrīnivāsa (in manuscripts k and kh, simply "Budha").
